units.la: AD CHRISTIANISS. FRANCIÆ REGEM HENRICVM II.
units.tr: TO THE MOST CHRISTIAN HENRY II, KING OF FRANCE.

units.la: REGES Dij mortales, immortalitatem consequi possunt duabus potissimum rationibus, literarum honore, & armorum gloria. Qua duo aeternitati paranda officia, uni olim Palladi mystice attributa, post paucos, sed maximos Principes Alexandrum, Cæsarem, & Carolum Magnum simul sic præstitit, & ea exercuit felicissima memoria Rex Franciscus pater tuus (ô Rex Christianissime) ut consum-mandam armorum gloriam filio relinquens, literarum honorem ad summum extulerit. Tu vero utrumque sic es amplexus, ut togata militia decus patri aliquatenus concedens, rerum bellicarum victorias, & triumphos persequaris, pari nixu iuxtà, atque successu. Quamobrem cùm huius utriusque laudis memoranda exempla ad te, supra cæteros omnes Christianos Principes referri debeant: hoc ipsum volumen, quod illa continet, tibi dicandum iure statuimus. In quo illustrissimi quique ab orbe condito ad tuum usque Regnum homines, qui duplicem hanc, aut alterutram immortalitatis viam affectarunt: & imagine vivacissimè picta, & historia verissimè scripta, per succedentium temporum, & Imperiorum seriem spectantur, tanquam in triumphali pompa procedentes: capitibus tantum per lunarem veluti fenestellam prominentibus: ex quibus, quasi leonem ab unguibus reli-quam corporis faciem, sed & mentem ipsam licet estimare. Hoc igitur polycephalon opus curiosa conquisitione investigatum, & multis vigiliis elabo-ratum, tua inclytissima Maiestatis Imperio tueri dignabere: quod sanè jam non nostrum, sed tuum absoluto dedicationis voto esse incipit: cùm Rex ille sis, cui & labores nostros, & res nostras, & nosmetipsos debere profitemur.
units.tr: Kings are mortal gods, and they can attain immortality chiefly by two means: the honour of letters and the glory of arms. Your father, King Francis, of most felicitous memory (O most Christian King), exercised and practised these two duties, which were once mystically attributed to the goddess Pallas, and which only a few very great princes before him, Alexander, Caesar and Charlemagne, had performed together. He left the glory of arms to his son to complete, and raised the honour of letters to its highest point. You, however, have embraced both so fully that, while conceding to your father some share of the robes of peace, you pursue the victories and triumphs of war, with equal effort and equal success. Therefore, since the memorable examples of both kinds of praise ought to be referred to you above all other Christian princes, we have rightly resolved to dedicate to you this very volume, which contains them. In it, the most illustrious men from the foundation of the world down to your own reign, who aspired to this twofold way, or to one of the two, of immortality, are viewed, portrayed in a most lively image and recorded in a most truthful history, in the succession of the ages and empires, as though they were advancing in a triumphal procession, with only their heads projecting through a small lunar window. From these, as one may judge the lion from its claws, one may also estimate the rest of the body, and indeed the mind itself. Be pleased, then, to protect under the auspices of your most renowned Majesty this many-headed work, investigated with careful inquiry and elaborated with many vigils. Indeed it now begins to belong not to us but to you, the vow of dedication having been fulfilled, since you are that king to whom we confess we owe our labours, our possessions and ourselves.

units.la: QUEMADMODUM in Megalensibus sub versatilium scenarum umbraculis, præter cætera ludorum ornamenta, variæ diuersarum personarum formæ quondam visæ sunt spectabiles:sic in hoc orbe terrarum, amplissimo sub cœlorum velis theatro, nihil dignius conspici potest, quàm humana facies, in qua (etiam ex Dæmonum confessione) admirandum, & venerabile Dei spectrum inest: virtutumque omniū signa in spatio tam angusto, sed augusto, clarè relucent. De cuius etiam eximia, & excelsa dignitate, sic cecinit Ouidius:
units.tr: JUST AS in the Megalesian Games, beneath the awnings of the revolving stages, among the other ornaments of the shows, the varied forms of different persons were once seen to be striking, so in this world, the widest theatre under the canopy of the heavens, nothing more worthy of sight can be seen than the human face, in which (even by the confession of the demons) the wondrous and venerable image of God dwells, and the signs of all the virtues shine out clearly in a space so narrow yet so noble. Of its singular and lofty dignity Ovid sang thus:

units.la: Pronáque cùm spectent animalia cætera terram: Os homini sublime dedit, cœlúmque videre: Iussit & erectos ad sydera tollere vultus.
units.tr: While the other animals look down towards the earth, he gave man a face raised up, and bade him see the heavens, and lift his upright countenance to the stars.

units.la: Quamobrem veteres illi, de propaganda immortali Nobilium personarum, & sua ipsorum gloria solliciti: valdéque prudenter antiquitatis memoriam conseruantes, & doctrinæ posteritatis prouidentes: virorum, & fœminarum illustrium formas, non modò literis, ac hypographis, tanquam certis quibusdam lineamentis depinxerunt: quinetiam eas adseruari curarunt in posteritatem, idolis, tabulis, signis, statis, scalptis, exaratis, conflatis, & percussis. Ac præcipuè speciosissimam & nobilissimam hominis partem (quam Natura maximè conspicuam, & semper apertam esse voluit) nimirum faciem, in metallicis numismatum orbiculis, parmulísque æreis, argenteis, & aureis signarunt, & expresserunt. Idq; duabus potissimum rationibus. Primum quòd numismata sint literis magis durabilia: cùm propter suam ex solido metallo naturam, tùm propter diligentem eorum in reconditis thesauris asseruationem. Deinde quòd (iuxta Regis Candaulis apud Herodotum sententiam) certiores sint homini quàm aures, oculi. Nam (vt ait Horatius) Segnius irritant animos demissa per aurem, Quàm quæ sunt oculis subiecta fidelibus, & quæ Ipse sibi tradit spectator.
units.tr: For this reason those ancients, anxious to perpetuate the immortal memory of noble persons and their own glory, and very prudently preserving the memory of antiquity and providing for the learning of posterity, not only depicted the forms of illustrious men and women in writing and engravings, as by certain outlines, but also took care to preserve them for posterity in statues, tablets, images, busts, carvings, paintings, castings and stampings. And chiefly they marked and portrayed the most beautiful and noblest part of man, which Nature willed to be most conspicuous and always open, namely the face, on the metal discs of coins and on bronze, silver and gold shields. And this for two main reasons. First, because coins are more durable than writings, both on account of their nature, being made of solid metal, and on account of their careful keeping in hidden treasuries. Second, because (according to the opinion of King Candaules in Herodotus) they are more trustworthy to man than his ears and eyes. For (as Horace says) Things passed on through the ear stir the mind more feebly than those placed under faithful eyes, and those that the viewer himself takes in.

units.la: Porrò illæ Numismatum figuræ à materia fusilis vel percussi metalli, Metallæ, extenuatóque elemento Medallæ sunt appellatæ vt Dedalæ olim figuræ dicebantur. Nisi quis Medallas quasi Imperatorias à verbo ΜΕΔΑΩ quod est Impero, magis deduci velit: quoniam Imperatorum plærasque facies iis sint impressæ. Eæ autem ad æternum venerandæ antiquitatis honorem vindicandum his temporibus curiosis per viros studiosos partim fuerunt exquisitæ, partim ex Antiquorum sepulchris erutæ, & è terræ latebris effossæ, partim fortuito repertæ, pricorum vtriusque sexus hominum proprias formas, & naturales, sic ad viuum referentes: vt ex illis, qui & quales fuerint signati ex vultu tanquam ex mentis speculo ratione Physiognomica cöiectari liceat. Sunt etenim (vt à sapientibus dictū) vultus animorum indices: in quarum rerum consideratione nos Antiquariis, & studiosis omnibus gratificari cupientes nulli neque labori, neque sumptui pepercimus ad eiusmodi eiconas cephalicas vndique conquirendas, ex diuersis gentium oris, & à magnatibus viris auro, ære, argento, cöflatas percussàsve aut gemis exculptas, prout maximo cuiq; visum fuit fui, & suæ charissimæ antiquitatis memoriā cöseruare. Ad quos etiam magnates, & Principes viros peruenerūt, & alienæ, & exteræ prisćorum, qui excelluerūt, hominū imagines: quas ab repertoribus feré pauperibus, & terrā versantibus obtinuerunt, vel prece, vel precio, vel vi, vel munere oblata, nempè rei vt rarisimæ, ita preciosisimæ. Metallinas illas seu Medallinas effigies lineamētis ad Archetypum deduci, ac deinde imprimi curauimus: fuscripto ad singulas summario rerum memorabiliū argumento ex optimis quibusque Historiographis, & Chronicis breuiter collecto: seruatóque teporum, ætatum, Imperiorū, ac Regnorum sibi succedentium, aut concurrentiū ordine. Totúmq; opus ab rerum, & personarū inuestigatione prompta, Promptuariū dici placuit.
units.tr: Moreover, those figures of coins, formed from the fused or stamped metal, were called medals (from metal, and from the thinned element, medals), just as the figures of Daedalus were once called Daedal. Unless someone prefers that medals be derived, as it were, from the Imperial, from the verb ΜΕΔΑΩ, which means to rule, since most faces of emperors are impressed upon them. These, indeed, to vindicate the eternal honour of venerable antiquity, have in these curious times been sought out in part by studious men, in part dug up from the tombs of the ancients and unearthed from the hiding places of the earth, and in part found by chance, representing the proper and natural forms of men and women of both sexes so faithfully to life that from them, by physiognomic reasoning, one may conjecture who and what sort of people they were, from their countenance as from a mirror of the mind. For (as the wise have said) the countenances are indicators of the minds. Wishing to gratify antiquaries and all studious men in the consideration of such things, we have spared neither labour nor expense in gathering from every quarter such heads in likeness, drawn from the mouths of various peoples, and struck, cast or carved in gold, bronze or silver, supplied by great men, as each of us thought fit to preserve the memory of his own most dear antiquity. Images of famous men of old, foreign and alien to our own, have also come to great men and princes, which they obtained from the finders, who were for the most part poor men who dig in the earth, offered either by prayer, by price, by force or by gift, since they are as rare as they are precious. We have taken care to have these metal or medal effigies brought to their archetypes in outlines and then printed; to each one we have added a summary of the memorable events, briefly gathered from the best historians and chronicles, keeping the order of times, ages, empires and kingdoms succeeding or coexisting. The whole work, from its ready investigation of things and persons, was pleased to be called a Promptuary.

units.la: In quo eorum qui à mūdi primordiis exiterunt, homines memorabiles spectandos oculos oculis, atq; oribus ora, & præclara eorum facta legenda coram exhibemus. Quod sane opus vt infiniti prope fuit laboris: sic plurimi fructus id quoque fore speramus. Huius nanque theatri spectatores nō solum oculos delectabunt, nec pictura pascent inani: verumetiā animos suos dignissima rerū, & personarū cognitione exsatiabūt. Et qui iampridē in viuis esse desierūt: eos ab inferis in lucē reuocatos veluti per speculū coram intuebuntur loquentes intelligent: faciētes contemplabūtur, retroacta tempora ab omni hominū memoria ad suum seculū reuocabūt. Denique exempla vitae cuiuslibet vndecunque sumēt: & haec lecta narrādo illud obtinebūt: vt antequā fuerint ipsi, cum iis qui amplius non sunt, olim fuisse videatur.
units.tr: In it we present to be seen by the eyes, face to face, the men of memory who have existed from the beginning of the world, and their famous deeds to be read. This work, indeed, has cost nearly infinite labour, and we hope it will also bring the greatest fruit. For the spectators of this theatre will not only delight their eyes, nor feed them with empty painting; they will also satisfy their minds with the most worthy knowledge of things and persons. And those who long ago ceased to be among the living, recalled from the underworld into the light, they will look upon as if through a mirror, and will understand them speaking; they will contemplate them acting, and they will recall the times past, removed from all human memory, to their own age. Finally, they will take examples of any kind of life from wherever they may come, and by recounting what they have read they will bring it about that, before they themselves existed, they seem to have lived long ago with those who no longer exist.

units.la: Caeterum ne quis lege Cornelia nos falsi arguat, quòd cōmētitias, seu factitias quasdā figuras velut adulterina numismata in publicū sparserimus: cōcedatur cōfessioni venia ὡς τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνα-[?] τοῦ[?] ἀναρτῶσι[?]. Priscorum enim hominū qui ante diluuiū, & ante inuentas pingendi, & scalpendi artes vixisse memorantur, vt Adae, Abrahae, & Patriarcharum ἡνωνας[?] nō negamus à nobis fuisse per imaginationē effictas: & cum nullū haberemus Prototypū, ex descripta eorū Natura, moribus, aetate, regione, & rebus gestis φανταστικῶς[?] fuisse cōformatas. Quī minus enim nobis id liceat: quàm Phidię statuario nobilissimo, qui ex pauculis Homeri versibus formam [illegible, ~6 letters] diuinauit: & Olympium fabricauit? Quàm Zeusidi qui ex selectis quinq; Agrigentinarū virginum formis pulcherrimā Deā cogitatione apprehēdit, ac repraesentauit? Quī minus quàm Asinio Pollioni, qui Autorū suę bibliothecae imagines ex eorū scriptis confingere primus Romanorū est ausus? Deniq; quī minus quàm illi, qui Homeri superioris arte inuenta: faciem ex ipsius Poëmate & ingenio coniectatus est? Quare hoc nobis minus vitio datum iri confidimus. Nam vt in hanc sententiam scripsit Plin. Quae non sunt finguntur: pariuntque desyderia non tradita vultus. Et maius nullum est felicitatis specimen: quam semper omnes scire cupere, qualis fuerit aliquis. Haec ille. Nos igitur talia imitati exempla, sine exemplo rationem tantum historiae secuti, & phantasiam, adiuti etiam consilio, ac iudicio, doctorum qui nobis sunt amici primorum hominum, & nonnullorum mediis etiam temporibus τῶν ἀγεγράφων[?] imagines excogitauimus. Ad hoc scilicet vt Historia nostra quemadmodum scripta, sic etiam picta suum habeat principium. Exinde etiā non raro nobis cōtigit habuisse à primoribus viris duo, tria, quatuorve, aut plura unius & eiusdem Imperatoris, Regis, Principis, aut alterius hominis illustris numismata:antiqua quidem illa, & (ut apparebat) minimè suppositá: sed tamen omnino inter se dissimilia, aut propter ætatis incremetum, aut personarum formæ mutationem, aut regionum ubi signabantur differentiam, aut aliud quoduis accidens. Et nos certè ex iis tam multis, & tam variis eiconibus, optimas & verissimas quasque pro prudentum hominum iudicio selegimus. Quare si quis forte extiterit, qui quas habet Metallicas imagines: & ab illis, hasce nostras dissimiles deprahedat: ne statim nos falsi arguat. At is sciat neque suas, neque nostras in orbe solas haberi: & nos (si rixari liberet) eodem argumento, sed maiori meliorîque ratione suas illius falsas, & suppositas posse contendere. Quicunque enim visurus sit venturis seculis Argentea, aut Ærea Cephalica Caroli quinti Imperatoris Serenissimi, aut Christianissimi Francorum Regis Henrici secundi, aut Solymani magni Turcarum Despotæ (qui omnes hodie viuunt & regnant) ex ea tanta diuersitate, atque dissimilitudine: quòd aliorum quidem capita sint senilia, aliorum iuuenilia, barbata, imberbia, armata, inermia, nuda, operta, & pileata, inornata, & coronata lauro, auro vel diademate: si ea ideo protinus falsa iudicabit: nae is omni prorsus iudicio carere videbitur: perspecta ætatum, temporum, locorum, & habituum mutatione: præsertim cùm ipsa in ambitu εἰκονογραφὴ[?] ubique similis, ubique eadem, veritatem satis arguat. Proinde nemo ex illis formarum varietatibus calumniandi occasionem arripiat. Denique (ut finem faciamus) hîc habes (ò lectòr) thesaurum locupletissimum omnium exemplorum virtutis, gloriæ, honoris, & immortalitatis. Hîc enim tibi cernere licet coràm capita quasi viua, & ora pene spirantia maximorum & primorum, in nationibus & populis virorum, qui leges tulerunt, imperarunt, regna rexerunt, mores constituerunt, linguas excoluerunt, doctrinas & artes exercuerunt, & qui denique ingenio, virtute, præstantia, ac rebus gestis terra, & mari famam immortalem sibi pararunt. Tu ad eum te compara modum, ut per egregias tuarum virtutum laudes, tui quoq; imago in posterioribus huius libri reformationibus locū habere insigne digna censeatur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone accuse us of falsehood under the Cornelian law, because we have scattered among the public certain fictitious or made-up figures, like counterfeit coins: let pardon be granted to the confession, as (the Greek words are illegible here). For we do not deny that the images of men of old who are recorded to have lived before the Flood, and before the arts of painting and carving were invented, such as Adam, Abraham and the Patriarchs, were fashioned by us through imagination; and since we had no prototype, we formed them phantastically from a description of their nature, manners, age, region and deeds. Why should this be less permitted to us than to Phidias, the most noble sculptor, who from a few verses of Homer divined the form [illegible, about six letters] and fashioned the Olympian Zeus? Than to Zeuxis, who from the selected forms of five maidens of Agrigentum grasped and represented in thought the most beautiful goddess? Less than to Asinius Pollio, who was the first of the Romans to dare to fashion the images of the authors of his library from their writings? Finally, less than to those who, by the art of the earlier Homer, conjectured his face from his poem and genius? Wherefore we trust that this will be less blamed on us. For, as Pliny wrote to this effect: Things that do not exist are invented, and the desire for a face that has not been handed down gives birth to them. And there is no greater sign of happiness than for all to desire always to know what someone was like. So he. We, therefore, imitating such examples, following without example only the reasoning of history and imagination, and aided also by the counsel and judgement of learned friends, have devised images of the first men and of some even in the middle ages of the written ones. To this end, of course, that our history, as it is written, so also may have its beginning in painting. Thence it has not seldom happened to us to have from leading men two, three, four or more coins of one and the same emperor, king, prince or other famous man: ancient ones indeed, and (as it appeared) by no means spurious, but yet entirely unlike one another, either because of the increase of age, or the change of the person's face, or the difference of the regions where they were struck, or some other accident. And we, indeed, from so many and so varied effigies have chosen the best and truest ones, according to the judgement of prudent men. Wherefore, if anyone perhaps arises who, from the metal images he has, detects ours as dissimilar to them, let him not at once accuse us of falsehood. Let him know that neither his nor ours are the only ones in the world; and if he likes to dispute, we could on the same ground, but with greater and better reason, contend that his are the false and spurious ones. For whoever will see in coming ages the silver or bronze heads of the most Serene Emperor Charles V, or of the Most Christian King of the French Henry II, or of Suleiman the Great, Despot of the Turks (all of whom live and reign today), from that so great diversity and dissimilarity, in that some heads are of old men, others of young, some bearded, some beardless, some armed, some unarmed, some bare, some covered, some capped, some unadorned, and some crowned with laurel, gold or diadem: if he at once judges them false on that account, he will seem altogether to lack all judgement, since the change of ages, times, places and dress is well known; especially since the very iconography, everywhere similar and everywhere the same, sufficiently proves the truth. Therefore let no one seize the occasion of slander from these varieties of forms. Finally (to make an end), here you have, reader, the richest treasury of all examples of virtue, glory, honour and immortality. For here you may see before you, as if alive, heads and faces almost breathing, of the greatest and foremost men among nations and peoples, who gave laws, held command, ruled kingdoms, established customs, cultivated languages, practised teachings and arts, and who by their talent, virtue, excellence and deeds have won for themselves immortal fame by land and sea. Prepare yourself to that manner, so that through the distinguished praises of your virtues your own image too may be judged worthy to hold a notable place in the later editions of this book.

units.la: HISTORIAM scripturo ratio in primis temporum, hominum,& gestorum est habenda. In quibus cum diversos autores varie dissentientes animadverteremus, unum tandem sequendum nobis proposuimus Phrygionem, ut planissimum ita verissimū Chronographū. Eadem est in nostrorū quoque tēporum scriptoribus varietas: ut in Mediolanensi Historia deprahendere licet: quam sane ex autorum scriptione, (arrogantes contemptores ne videremur) data opera excripsimus. Verumtamen exquisitæ veritatis, acsedulæ nostræ diligentiæ exhibendæ gratia, certiorem aliquem temporum ordinem subscripsimus ad hunc modum.
units.tr: In histories, reason must first take account of times, persons and events. When I noticed that various authors disagree among themselves on these, I resolved to follow in the end Phrygio, as the clearest and at the same time the most truthful chronographer. The same variety is found among the writers of our own times, as may be seen in the History of Milan, which I have indeed copied out with care from the writings of authors, so that I might not seem a contemptuous scorner of them. Nevertheless, for the sake of exact truth and to show my diligent care, I have set down a more certain order of times in the following manner.

units.la: Primus Dux Mediolani fuit Io. Galeacius, cuius Res gestas scripserunt S. Antoninus, Florentiæ Archiepiscopus, Supplem. Chronic. & Pau. Iovius, qui tres de exitu vitæ conveniunt anno 1402. at de Principatus initio neutiquam. Iovius nanque nihil meminit. S. Antoninus ab anno 1385. principium statuit. Supplem. Chron. ab anno 1382. Sed nec iidem in Principatus duratione consentiunt. Iovius illi annos assignat 24. Supplemen. 37. Archiepiscopus non numerat. Ex quorum rationibus, tandem colligimus, (Iovium & gravissimum autorem, & in hoc verissimum secuti) principium Ducatus Mediolanensis fuisse ab anno D. 1378. Io. Maria Vicecomes Dux Mediolanensis secundus, illico patri successor, Ducatum obtinuit annos 10. proinde mortuus est anno 1412. Philippus Maria Dux tertius, vacante per interregni tempus aula, populari tumultu, postea anno 1413. in pristinum Maiorum statu est erectus: in quo sietit[?] annos 33. Itaque decessit anno 1446. Et hoc idem adstruit S. Antoninus Archiep. qui temporibus vixit iisdem. Sphortia Dux quartus popular factione vexatus est annos tres, priusquam ad Ducatum perveniret: quem tandem vi armata est adeptus, anno 1449. (ut scribit Archiepiscopus) & in eo resedit annos 16. Quare necesse est vita decessisse anno 1465. Supplemen. autem annum addit. Galeacius Maria Dux quintus est designatus eodem anno 1466. in quo vixit annos decem, mortuus est anno 1476. Ioā. Maria Sphortia Dux sextus, duodecimo post patris patris mortem die Principatū adiit, anno iam incipiente 1476. eumque tenuit sub Ludovico Sphortia, cognomento Moro, socero suo, usque ad annum 1494. fuit ergo tempus Ducatus, eius annorum 18. & aliquot mensium. Ludovicus Sphortia cognomento Morus, mox nepoti contra ius succedens, Ducatum invasit eodem anno 1494. Rexitque annos 5. & sex menses, donec captivus in Galliam ductus est anno 1500. Porrò non ignores (candide Lector) plerosque scriptores in chronologia neglexisse dies, & menses annis superaccedentes: quæ sane omissio, temporum progressu multiplicata, ordinem chronicum turbavit. Illud quoque te admonere voluimus, nos ad nonnullarum finè historiarum, unum tantum, aut certè duos allegasse autores, tametsi ex pluribus excepta forent. Quamobrem si non omnia apud illum unum, aut alterum autorem scripta comperies, ne protinus commentitia existimes. Idcirco enim reliquos praeteriimus, ne citatorum congerie graves, & ostentatione superstitiosi videremur. Quod si in iis quoque autoribus dissidentia nonnunquam loca inveneris: existima ex rei ipsius iudicio, nos quantum fieri potuit discordes cōciliasse, & ex dubiis vero simillima quæque & maximè consentanea desumpsisse. Postremò hoc etiam observabis, eodem scriptore chronico, seu historico diversis temporibus, ac regionibus saepius impresso, ac identidem retractato, & emendato, & amplificato, chartas, & capita nonnulla immutari potuisse. Unde si quis aliter citata, quàm in suo legat exemplari, is iustissimam nostram consideret rationem: quà examinata, aut paulò ante, aut paulò post comperiet quadrare Chronologiam.
units.tr: The first Duke of Milan was Gian Galeazzo, whose deeds were written by St Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, in the Supplementum Chronicorum, and by Paolo Giovio; these agree that he died in 1402, but by no means about the beginning of his rule, for Giovio says nothing about it, while St Antoninus fixes the beginning in 1385 and the Supplementum in 1382. Nor do they agree about the length of his rule: Giovio assigns him 24 years, the Supplementum 37, and the Archbishop does not count it. From their reasons we finally conclude (following Giovio, a most weighty author and in this the most accurate) that the beginning of the Duchy of Milan was in the year of our Lord 1378. Giovanni Maria Visconti, the second Duke of Milan, immediately succeeded his father and held the duchy for 10 years, and so he died in 1412. Filippo Maria, the third duke, while the court stood vacant during the interregnum, was raised up by a popular tumult; afterwards, in 1413, the state was restored to its former ancestral condition, and in it he remained 33 years. Thus he died in 1446, and St Antoninus the Archbishop, who lived in the same times, confirms this too. Sforza, the fourth duke, was harassed by a popular faction for three years before he came to the duchy, which at last he gained by armed force in 1449 (as the Archbishop writes), and he remained in it 16 years. Therefore he must have died in 1465, though the Supplementum adds a year. Galeazzo Maria, the fifth duke, was designated in the same year, 1466, in which he lived ten years; he died in 1476. Giovanni Maria Sforza, the sixth duke, entered upon the rule on the twelfth day after his father's death, the year now beginning 1476, and he held it under Ludovico Sforza, surnamed il Moro, his father-in-law, until the year 1494. The time of his duchy was therefore 18 years and some months. Ludovico Sforza, surnamed il Moro, succeeding his nephew against right soon afterwards, seized the duchy in the same year, 1494, and ruled for 5 years and six months, until he was led captive into France in 1500. Moreover, let not you, kind reader, be ignorant that most writers have neglected in chronology the days and months that exceed the years; this omission, multiplied as time went on, has disturbed the chronological order. We wished also to warn you that for some histories we have cited only one, or at most two, authors, although they could have been taken from several. Therefore, if you do not find everything in that one or other author, do not at once think it made up. For we have passed over the rest for this reason, lest we should seem burdensome by a heap of citations and ostentatious in a superstitious way. But if you find places of disagreement sometimes even among those authors, judge from the nature of the matter itself that we have reconciled the discordant as far as could be done, and from the doubtful have taken whatever is most likely and most consistent. Finally, you will also observe that in the same chronicle or history, printed many times in different places and times, and repeatedly revised, corrected and enlarged, some sheets and chapters may have been changed. Hence if anyone reads the citations differently from how they are in his own copy, let him consider our most just reasoning: by examining it, either a little before or a little after, he will find that the chronology agrees.

units.la: DOCET nos sacra scriptura quemadmodum in principio creauerit Deus cœlum & terram: atque vt sexto die formauit hominem (Adam inquam ac Euam) ad imaginem & similitudinem suam: deinde vt Adamo collocato in terrestri paradiso, prohibuerit,cum interminatione mortis, de ligno scientiæ boni & mali edere. At verò à serpente decepta prima mulier,mandatum transgressa,de fructu vetito edit: ac virum suum protoplastum ad edendum illexit:quare statim sub iugum peccati & mortis traditi sunt: atque è paradiso illo semper virente,& sponte omnia ferente eiecti,in terram execratam,in quâ laboribus & sudoribus infinitis vitam transigerent. Adam itaque terram exercuit:Euam vxorem cognouit,quæ peperit illi Cain, deinde Abel, qui à fratre Cain per inuidiam occisus est. Gen. 1. 2. 3. & 4. cap.
units.tr: Holy Scripture teaches us how God in the beginning created heaven and earth, and how on the sixth day he formed man (Adam, I mean, and Eve) in his own image and likeness; then how, when Adam had been placed in the earthly paradise, he forbade him, on pain of death, to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But the first woman, deceived by the serpent, transgressed the commandment and ate of the forbidden fruit, and enticed her husband, the first-formed man, to eat as well; therefore they were at once brought under the yoke of sin and death, and were cast out of that paradise, always green and bearing all things of its own accord, into a cursed earth, in which they were to spend their life in infinite labours and sweat. Adam therefore tilled the earth, and knew his wife Eve, who bore him Cain, and then Abel, who was slain out of envy by his brother Cain. Gen. chapters 1, 2, 3 and 4.

units.la: ADAM annos natus 130. genuit Seth,à quo patres pietate insignes originem traxere. Seth natus annos 105. genuit Enos: hic cœpit inuocare nomen Domini. Enos,annorum 90.genuit Cainam. Cainam annorum 70. genuit Malaleel. Malaleel annorum 65.genuit Iared. Iared annorum 162. genuit Henoch. Henoch annorum 65. genuit Mathusalam. Porrò Henoch annos natus 365, sublatus est à Deo, nec apparuit. Mathusala annorum 187.genuit Lamech. Lamech annorum 182. genuit Noe. Noe annorum 500. genuit Sem,Cham & Iaphet,100.annis ante diluuium. Erat itaque 600.annorum Noe tempore diluuij. Obiit Adam anno ætatis suæ 930. Vide Gene.cap.5.&7. NOE F.LA. SEM I F.NO.
units.tr: Adam, when he was 130 years old, begat Seth, from whom the fathers distinguished for piety derived their origin. Seth, at the age of 105, begat Enos; he began to call upon the name of the Lord. Enos, at the age of 90, begat Cainan. Cainan, at the age of 70, begat Mahalalel. Mahalalel, at the age of 65, begat Jared. Jared, at the age of 162, begat Enoch. Enoch, at the age of 65, begat Methuselah. Moreover, Enoch, when he was 365 years old, was taken up by God and did not appear. Methuselah, at the age of 187, begat Lamech. Lamech, at the age of 182, begat Noah. Noah, at the age of 500, begat Shem, Ham and Japheth, 100 years before the flood. Noah was therefore 600 years old at the time of the flood. Adam died in the 930th year of his age. See Gen. chapters 5 and 7. NOAH, son of Lamech. SHEM, son of Noah.

units.la: NOE filius Lamech, vir sanè fuit pius ac probus, ac proinde pietate ac iustitia Deo acceptis. huius tempore gigantes quidam omnes nationes infestabant: quare statuit Deus delere omnia animantia, seruato Noe cum familia eius. Iubet itaq;ipsi Noe vt arcam fabricet (hanc centum annis perfecit) & vt in eam ingrediatur, assumátque secum ex omni animantium genere masculum & fœmellam: quibus in arcam ingressis, longam cubitorum 300. altam 30. pluit super terram 40. diebus, & 40. noctibus, adeò vt quindecim cubitis eminentissimos montes aqua superaret. Tunc omne animal tam rationis cōpos, quàm expers, aquis obrutum est anno à condito mundo 1656. ante Christum natum 2306. At verò post 150. dies recordatus est Deus ipsius Noe, incepitque aqua decrescere: stetitque arca super montes Armeniæ. Tandem post aliquot etiam dies ex arca exiens Noe cum familia, ac Deo gratias agens, sacra peregit. Cæterùm ostendit illi Deus arcum in nubibus in signum fœderis perpetui, terram vniuersam in posterum aquarū inundatione nunquam submersum iri. Vide Gene.cap.7.8.&9.
units.tr: Noah, son of Lamech, was indeed a man pious and upright, and therefore acceptable to God for piety and righteousness. In his time certain giants were troubling all nations; therefore God resolved to destroy all living creatures, Noah with his family being preserved. He therefore commands Noah to build an ark (he completed it in a hundred years) and to enter it, taking with him a male and a female of every kind of living creature; when they had entered the ark, which was 300 cubits long and 30 high, it rained upon the earth for 40 days and 40 nights, so that the water covered the highest mountains by fifteen cubits. Then every animal, whether endowed with reason or without it, was overwhelmed by the waters, in the year from the creation of the world 1656, before the birth of Christ 2306. But after 150 days God remembered Noah, and the water began to decrease; the ark rested upon the mountains of Armenia. Finally, after some more days, Noah came out of the ark with his family, gave thanks to God and performed sacrifice. Moreover God showed him a rainbow in the clouds as a sign of an everlasting covenant, that the whole earth would never again be submerged by a flood of waters. See Gen. chapters 7, 8 and 9.

units.la: SEM, filius Noe, mares quinque genuit: primus horum fuit Ælam, à quo Ælamitæ orti sunt. Hi fuere præcipui inter Persas. Secundus, Assur: ab hoc Assyrij prognati. Tertius, Arphaxad: à quo Arphaxadæi dicti, qui postea Chaldæi sunt vocati. Quartus, Lud: vnde Lydi originem traxere. Quintus, Aram: hic nomen suum Aramenis dedit, quos Græci Syros vocant. Vide Gene.10.& 11.cap. & Paralip.cap.1.Iosephi lib.1. Antiqui. cap.14.
units.tr: Shem, son of Noah, begat five sons; the first of these was Elam, from whom the Elamites arose. These were foremost among the Persians. The second, Asshur: from him the Assyrians were descended. The third, Arphaxad: from whom the Arphaxadites, who were afterwards called Chaldeans, are named. The fourth, Lud: from whom the Lydians derived their origin. The fifth, Aram: he gave his name to the Arameans, whom the Greeks call Syrians. See Gen. chapters 10 and 11, and 1 Chron. chapter 1; Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapter 14.

units.la: CHAM filius Noe, cùm patrem primum vitisatorem, suóque inuento inebriatum ludibrio habuisset, ab eodem tulit maledictionem. Hic genuit filios quatuor, primum nomine Chus, à quo Æthiopes, qui inde Chusæi dicebantur, originem traxere: secundum nomine Mesraim: ab hoc Mesræi dicti, aliàs etiā Ægyptij: nam Mesrim Hebraicè Ægyptum significat: tertium nomine Phut: à quo Libes, quos Phutos de nomine suo vocauit: quartum verò nomine Chanaan, vnde Chananæi, atque Chananæa eorum regio dicta, quæ postea Iudæa vocata est. Vide Gen.cap.9.&10.item Ioseph.lib.Antiq.1.cap.12.
units.tr: Ham, son of Noah, when he had mocked his father, the first vine-planter, who had become drunk from his own invention, incurred a curse from him. He begat four sons: the first by name Cush, from whom the Ethiopians, who were called Cushites from him, derived their origin; the second by name Mizraim: from him they were called Mizraites, otherwise also Egyptians, for Mizraim in Hebrew signifies Egypt; the third by name Put, from whom the Libyans, whom he named Phutites after his own name; and the fourth indeed by name Canaan, whence the Canaanites, and their region was called Canaan, which was afterwards called Judea. See Gen. chapter 9 and 10; likewise Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapter 12.

units.la: IAPHET cum fratre suo Sem accepit benedictionem à patre, quòd ambo retecta patris verenda velassent. Porrò Iaphet genuit filios septem: primum nomine Gomer, à quo Gomeritæ, qui à Græcis postea Galatæ dicti sunt. Secundum Magog, à quo Magogæ, à Græcis Scythæ nuncupati. Tertium Madai, à quo Medi. Quartum Iauan, à quo Iones. Quintum Tubal, à quo Iberi, qui nunc Hispani. Sextum Mosoch, à quo Moschini, qui postea Capadoces dicti sunt. Septimum Thiras, qui eos apud quos primatum tenuit, Thirenses appellauit, qui postea à Græcis Thraces sunt vocitati. Tot, tantæque gentes, ac nationes à filiis Iaphet originem sumpsere. Cæterùm hi tres fratres, Iaphet, Sem, & Cham, nati sunt ipsi Noe 100. annis ante diluuium, vti iam supra diximus. Vide vt supra. ARPHAXAD FIL. SEM SALA FIL. AR[?]
units.tr: Iaphet, together with his brother Sem, received a blessing from their father, because the two of them covered their father's nakedness. Iaphet then begot seven sons. The first, named Gomer, was the father of the Gomerites, who were later called Galatians by the Greeks. The second was Magog, from whom the Magogites came, called Scythians by the Greeks. The third was Madai, from whom the Medes descended. The fourth was Javan, from whom the Ionians came. The fifth was Tubal, from whom the Iberians came, who are now the Spaniards. The sixth was Meshech, from whom the Moschians came, later called Cappadocians. The seventh was Tiras, who named the people among whom he held the primacy Thirenses; these were later called Thracians by the Greeks. So many and so great peoples and nations took their origin from the sons of Iaphet. Moreover, these three brothers, Iaphet, Sem and Ham, were born to Noah himself one hundred years before the flood, as we have already said above. See above. ARPHAXAD SON OF SEM, SALA SON OF AR[?]

units.la: ARPHAXAD filius Sem, genitus est biennio post diluuium, videlicet anno ab orbe condito 1658. ante Christum natum 2364. Hic cum esset annorum 35. genuit Salè: vixitque Arphaxad postquam genuit Salè 303. vet. editio 403. annis: genuitque filios & filias. Ab hoc Arphaxad, vt supra dixi, originem habet Chaldæorum gens, à quibus Chaldæa regio dicta, quæ in Asiæ maioris partibus sita est, Arabiæ contermina, longè latéque in planiciem porrecta, aquis deficiens, in qua olim Babylon magna condita est. Vide Gene.ca.10.& 11.[?]& Supplem. Chron.lib.2. Porrò Arphaxad quos instituit, Arphaxadæos nominauit, vt ait Iosep.lib.Antiq.1.ca.14. Cæterum D.Augu.lib.de Ciuit.Dei 16. scribit Arphaxad genuisse Cainam, septuaginta interpretum opinionem secutus.
units.tr: Arphaxad, son of Sem, was born two years after the flood, that is, in the year 1658 from the creation of the world, 2364 years before the birth of Christ. When he was thirty-five years old he begot Sala, and Arphaxad lived after he begot Sala 303 years (the old edition says 403 years), and he begot sons and daughters. From this Arphaxad, as I said above, the nation of the Chaldeans takes its origin, and from them the region was called Chaldea. It lies in the parts of Greater Asia, borders on Arabia, stretches far and wide over a plain, and lacks water; in it the great Babylon was once founded. See Genesis chapters 10 and 11, and the Supplement of Chronicles, book 2. Moreover, Arphaxad named the people he established Arphaxadites, as Josephus says in Antiquities, book 1, chapter 14. But St. Augustine, in The City of God, book 16, writes that Arphaxad begot Cainan, following the opinion of the Seventy interpreters.

units.la: SALE filius Arphaxad, cum esset annorum triginta, genuit Heber, ac postea vixit annos 403. quo temporis spacio filios complures ac filias genuit. Vide Genesin capite vndecimo. Ab hoc Sale, autore Iosephó, Sarmatæ orti sunt, à quibus regiones Sarmaticæ nomen obtinuerunt, quæ sunt duæ, altera in Europa, altera verò, quam Tartariam nuncupamus, in Asia maiore sita est. Porrò ea ipsa est Asiatica Sarmatia quæ ab hoc Sale denominationem accepit Sarmatiæ. Fertur hæc regio nunc esse deserta ac incognita, in qua tamen olim conditæ fuerunt tres celeberrimæ vrbes, nempe Hermonasa, Oenatia, & Tyramba. Cæterum sunt qui scribant Caucasos montes in hac esse provincia, cuius portæ à nonnullis (qui tamen falso, ac magno errore ducuntur) Caspiæ sunt dictæ. Vide Ptolemæum lib.3.& 5.
units.tr: Sale, son of Arphaxad, when he was thirty years old, begot Heber, and afterwards lived 403 years, during which span of time he begot many sons and daughters. See Genesis chapter 11. From this Sale, according to Josephus, the Sarmatians arose, from whom the regions called Sarmatian took their name. There are two of these: one in Europe, and the other, which we call Tartary, lies in Greater Asia. Moreover, that is the Asiatic Sarmatia which received the name Sarmatia from this Sale. This region is reported to be now deserted and unknown, yet three very famous cities were once founded there, namely Hermonassa, Oenatia and Tyramba. Some write that the Caucasus mountains lie in this province, whose gates were called Caspian by some (though they are misled by a false and great error). See Ptolemy, books 3 and 5.

units.la: HEBER, filius Sale, cùm esset annorum 34. genuit Phaleg, anno mundi 1758. ante Christum natum 2204. vixitque postea 430. annos, generans filios & filias. mortuus est autem anno ætatis 464. ab hoc Iudæi orti, qui inde Hebræi dicuntur. præterea in diuisione linguarū, mansit lingua Hebraica penes solam suam generationē. Tunc temporis hæc lingua Hebraica, vocabatur humana, quod omnes homines Hebræa lingua loquerentur. Habuit autē Heber alterum filium nomine Iectan, cuius meminit Moyses: hic multos genuit filios, quorum habitatio erat à Messa pergentibus vsque Sephar, montem orientalem: erant itaque ij ex progenie pij Noë, secundum populos & nationes suas. Hæc prouincia Messa, sita est in Iudæa, vt ait Hieronymus, Vide Gene. 10. & 11. cap. Iosephum lib. 1. Anti. cap.14.
units.tr: Heber, son of Sale, when he was thirty-four years old, begot Phaleg, in the year of the world 1758, 2204 years before the birth of Christ. He then lived 430 years, begetting sons and daughters. He died at the age of 464. From him the Jews arose, who are therefore called Hebrews. Moreover, at the division of tongues, the Hebrew language remained with his family alone. At that time this Hebrew language was called the human tongue, because all men spoke the Hebrew language. Heber also had another son, named Joktan, whom Moses mentions. He begot many sons, whose dwelling extended from Mesha, as one goes toward Sephar, the eastern mountain. These were therefore of the posterity of the pious Noah, according to their peoples and nations. This province of Mesha, as Jerome says, lies in Judaea. See Genesis chapters 10 and 11, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapter 14.

units.la: PHALEG, filius Heber, cùm esset annorum 30. genuit Reu, anno mundi 1788. ante Christum 2174. vixitque postea 239. annos, generans filios & filias, & mortuus est. Phaleg autem diuisionem Hebræi vocant: dictus igitur Phaleg, quoniam secundum diuisionē habitationum natus est, quādo in linguas terra diuisa est. Huius temporibus initium ac originem cœpit regnum Scytharum, sub rege nomine Tanaïs. Hoc regnum in plaga Septentrionali Asiæ, ad Imaum montem situm est. Videto Gen.cap.11. item Auguft.de ciuit.Dei,lib.16.cap.11. SATURNUS BABILON BEL. IUPITER.
units.tr: Phaleg, son of Heber, when he was thirty years old, begot Reu, in the year of the world 1788, 2174 years before Christ. He then lived 239 years, begetting sons and daughters, and he died. The Hebrews call Phaleg "division"; he was therefore named Phaleg because he was born at the division of dwelling-places, when the earth was divided into tongues. In his times the kingdom of the Scythians began and had its origin, under a king named Tanais. This kingdom lay on the northern side of Asia, near Mount Imaus. See Genesis chapter 11; also Augustine, The City of God, book 16, chapter 11. SATURN, BABYLON, BEL, JUPITER.

units.la: NEMROD Saturnus, filius Chus, filij Cham, filij Noë, cœpit esse potens in terra. Fuit autem principiū regni eius Babylon, Arach, Achad & Chalanne, in terra Sennaar, anno mūdi 1788. ante Christum 2174. nempe ipso eodem anno supradicto quo genitus est Reu. Hoc regnante facta est linguarum cōfusio in ædificatione turris Babel. Josephus lib. Anti.1.cap.9.citat hæc verba Sibyllæ: Cum omnes homines unius vocis existerent, quidam turrim ædificaverūt excelsam, tanquam ascensuri per eam in cœlum: Dij vero immittētes ventos, everterunt turrim, & voce propria unicuique partiti sunt: propterea Babyloniam vocari contigit civitatem, hoc est confusionem. Vide Gene. cap.10.& 11.& Berosum lib.4.& 5.
units.tr: Nimrod, Saturn, son of Cush, son of Ham, son of Noah, began to be powerful on the earth. The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, Erech, Akkad and Calneh, in the land of Shinar, in the year of the world 1788, 2174 years before Christ, that very same year mentioned above in which Reu was born. In his reign the confusion of tongues took place during the building of the tower of Babel. Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapter 9, cites these words of the Sibyl: "When all men were of one voice, some built a lofty tower, as if they would ascend into heaven by it; but the gods, sending winds, overturned the tower, and divided them, each one by his own tongue; therefore it happened that the city was called Babylon, that is, confusion." See Genesis chapters 10 and 11, and Berosus, books 4 and 5.

units.la: BELUS Juppiter, quum pater suus Nemrod imperitasset 56. annos, regnauit ipse filius, anno mundi 1844. ante Christum natū 2118. Hic designata fundamenta Babyloniæ, oppidi magis quàm urbis similitudine, erexit. pace fruebatur usque circa finem imperij sui. Berosum cōsule li.5. ut supra. Imperauit Belus hic annos 62.
units.tr: Belus Jupiter, when his father Nimrod had reigned 56 years, his own son reigned, in the year of the world 1844, 2118 years before the birth of Christ. He laid out the foundations of Babylon, and erected it with the look of a town rather than a city. He enjoyed peace until near the end of his rule. Consult Berosus, book 5, as above. This Belus reigned 62 years.

units.la: COMERUS Gallus more Scythico, unde venerat, docuit suos Italos urbem curribus componere. Vide Bero. lib. 5. Justi. lib. j. Diod. Si. lib. 3. & Anni. Viterben. REGV FIL.PEI SARVG FIL.REG
units.tr: Comerus the Gaul, according to the Scythian custom from which he had come, taught his Italians to lay out a city with chariots. See Berosus, book 5; Justin, book 1; Diodorus Siculus, book 3; and Annius of Viterbo. REGV SON OF PEI, SARUG SON OF REG

units.la: REV, siue Rhagau,filius Phaleg, anno ætatis 32.genuit Sarug:hic erat annus mundi 1820. ante Christum natum 2142.vixítque postea 207.annos,generans filios & filias:multa templa ædificauit.Huius tempore principes aliquot à subditis adorati sunt: quinetiam quatuor regna initiū sumpsere:videlicet Scytharum,quibus rex fuit Tanaïs,à quo dictus est Tanaïs fluuius: Amazonum, quæ ex Scythis ortæ,primùm ad Tanaïm habitarunt,deinde ad Thermodoonta , qui inde Amazonius fluuius dictus est:item regnum Aegypti,cui primus rex fuit Sores,siue (vt nonnulli aiunt)Vexores. Quartū fuit regnum Boëmorum, qui Ducè habebant nomine Boëmum.Vide Gene.11.cap.Iusti. lib.1.Eufe.& Chro.Boëmorum.
units.tr: Reu, or Ragau, son of Phaleg, when he was thirty-two years old, begot Serug; this was in the year of the world 1820, 2142 years before the birth of Christ. He then lived 207 years, begetting sons and daughters. He built many temples. In his time several princes were worshipped by their subjects. Indeed four kingdoms took their beginning: that of the Scythians, whose king was Tanais, from whom the river Tanais was named; that of the Amazons, who were sprung from the Scythians and first dwelt near the Tanais, then near the Thermodon, from which the river was called the Amazonian; likewise the kingdom of Egypt, whose first king was Sores, or (as some say) Vexores; and fourth, the kingdom of the Bohemians, who had as their leader a man named Boemus. See Genesis chapter 11; Justin, book 1; Eusebius, Chronicle; and the Bohemians.

units.la: SARVG,filius Reu,annos natus 30. genuit Nachor, anno mundi 1850. ante Christum natum 2113.vixítque 200.annos, generans filios & filias.Anno 25. ætatis huius,initium ac originem cœpit regnum Assyriorum,omnium maximum,durauítq; (vt Augustinus ait lib.de ciuit.Dei 18.cap.21.)annos 1305. Sarug annorum 230.obiit diem.Gene.11. NINVS ASSYR. R. EX [?] SOROASTES MAG. R. BACT. [?]
units.tr: Serug, son of Reu, when he was thirty years old, begot Nahor, in the year of the world 1850, 2113 years before the birth of Christ. He lived 200 years, begetting sons and daughters. In the twenty-fifth year of his life the kingdom of the Assyrians, the greatest of all, began and had its origin, and it lasted (as Augustine says, The City of God, book 18, chapter 21) 1305 years. Serug died at the age of 230. Genesis 11. NINUS, KING OF ASSYRIA; EX [?]; SOROASTES, MAGIAN KING OF BACTRIA [?]

units.la: NINVS, Beli filius, tertius Babyloniorum Rex fuit, anno mundi 1906. ante Christum natum 2056. Regnauit hic 52. annos, omnibus viribus suis sumptis, omnibus bellum inferens, nulli parcés, propter summam regnandi cupiditatem. Primus Babylonicum regnum propagauit, statuam in honore patris Beli erexit, ad quam qui confugerent, omni crimine absolverentur. Huius exemplo adducti multi, statuas in memoriam patrum erexere. Inde idololatria initium coepit: inde nomina haec, Bel, Baal, Bel-phegor, & Bel-zebub. Videto Hierony.to.6. super Hoseam cap.2. & Bero.lib.5.
units.tr: Ninus, son of Belus, was the third king of the Babylonians, in the year of the world 1906, 2056 years before the birth of Christ. He reigned 52 years, having taken up all his forces, making war on all, sparing no one, because of his immense desire to rule. He first extended the Babylonian kingdom, and erected a statue in honour of his father Belus, to which whoever fled would be absolved of every crime. Many, led by his example, erected statues in memory of their fathers. From this idolatry took its beginning; hence these names: Bel, Baal, Baal-peor, and Baal-zebub. See Jerome, vol. 6, on Hosea chapter 2, and Berosus, book 5.

units.la: ZOROASTES, vt multi autumāt, erat is ipse filius Noë nomine Cham. Fuit hic primus Bactrianorū Rex, primus item artis magicæ inuentor, atque septem artium liberalium, & cursus cœli ac stellarū. Sunt qui memoriæ prodiderint eum simul ac natus est risisse: quod nequaquam fertur bonum omen: cùm nascētes vulgò vagiant. Fuit itaque à Nino victus: fuit quoque ipse Ninus sagitta ictus, quo vulnere periit, hæredem filium relinquens, nomine Niniam. Ninus ciuitatem Niniuen ædificauit, trium dierum circuitum habentem, quam Cyrus Assyriorum Rex euertit. August.lib.de ciuita.Dei 21.cap.14.Euse.Plin. lib.30.cap.7.
units.tr: Zoroaster, as many think, was that same son of Noah named Ham. He was the first king of the Bactrians, and likewise the first inventor of the magic art, and of the seven liberal arts, and of the course of the heavens and the stars. Some have recorded that he laughed as soon as he was born, which is by no means regarded as a good omen, since newborns commonly cry. He was therefore conquered by Ninus; Ninus himself was also struck by an arrow, of which wound he died, leaving an heir, a son named Ninyas. Ninus built the city of Nineveh, having a circuit of three days, which Cyrus, king of the Assyrians, overthrew. See Augustine, The City of God, book 21, chapter 14; Eusebius; Pliny, book 30, chapter 7.

units.la: TVYSCON,qui à Moyse vocatur Ascenas,filius Gomeri,filij Iaphet primogeniti fuit. Sarmatis,qui iuxta Poloniâ habitant,& nunc inter Germanos annumeratur,originê praebuit, quos literas docuit,ac legibus formauit: regni Germanici initium dedit anno mundi 1909.ante Christum natum 2 0 5 3. Hic cum 150.annos regnasset,mortuus,atque inter deos relatus est. A Gomero originê habent Cimbri,qui ex Italia cedentes, Daciam, & illa versus Septentrionem loca incoluerunt, quae nos vulgò dicimus Danemarc. Videto Berosum lib.5[?].
units.tr: Tuyscon, whom Moses calls Ascenas, was a son of Gomer, the firstborn son of Japheth. He gave origin to the Sarmatians, who live near Poland and are now counted among the Germans; he taught them letters and formed them by laws. He gave the beginning of the German kingdom in the year of the world 1909, before the birth of Christ 2053. He reigned 150 years, died, and was counted among the gods. The Cimbri have their origin from Gomer; they left Italy, settled Dacia and the regions toward the north, which we commonly call Denmark. See Berosus, book 5[?].

units.la: SAMOTES,cognomentô Dis,hoc etiam tempore,& eodem anno,quo suprà,Celtas legibus formauit. Fuit hic primus Gallorum rex, iuxta Berosum lib.5[?].cui essentitur Caesar, sexto Commentariorum libro, in haec verba : Galli se omnes à Dite pa-tre prognatos praedicant.Non erat illa tempestate quisquâ hoc Samote doctior,aut sapientior,ac propterea Samotes dictus est. Ab hoc Samoteae Galliae dictae, nempe à quo in regnum redactae essent:testatur id Dioge.Laer.in vita Philosophorum. Vide Berosum vt supra. NACHOR FIL. SAR THARE FIL NAC
units.tr: Samotes, surnamed Dis, at this same time and in the same year as above, gave laws to the Celts. He was the first king of the Gauls, according to Berosus, book 5[?]. Caesar, in the sixth book of his Commentaries, is cited for these words: "The Gauls all claim to be descended from Father Dis." At that time there was no one more learned or wiser than this Samotes, and for that reason he was called Samotes. From him the regions of Gaul were called Samotea, namely because they had been brought under his kingdom: Diogenes Laertius attests this in the Life of the Philosophers. See Berosus as above. NACHOR SON OF SAR, THARE SON OF NACHOR

units.la: NACHOR, filius Sarug, cum esset annorum 29 genuit Thare, anno mundi 1879. ante Christum natum 2083. vixit postea 119.annos, generans filios ac filias. in summa vixit annos 148. & mortuus est. Gene.11. Circa haec tempora Sicyoniorum regnum incepit, quibus primus rex fuit Aegialeus, à quo Aegialea dicta, quae nunc Peloponnesus. Consule Plin.lib.4.cap.5.
units.tr: Nachor, son of Serug, when he was twenty-nine years old, begot Terah, in the year of the world 1879, before the birth of Christ 2083. He afterwards lived 119 years, begetting sons and daughters. In all he lived 148 years, and he died. Genesis 11. Around this time the kingdom of the Sicyonians began; its first king was Aegialeus, from whom Aegialea, now the Peloponnese, was named. Consult Pliny, book 4, chapter 5.

units.la: THARE, filius Nachor, septuaginta annos natus genuit Abram(qui postea vocatus est Abraham)anno à mundo condito 1949.ante Christum natum 2013. genuit praeterea alterum nomine Nachor,& Aran: vixitque in summa 205.annos. Porrò Abraham genuit Ismaël & Isaac, ut videbitur inferius. Nachor, frater Abraham, ex Melcha genuit Hus, patrē Iob, & Camuel, patrem Syrorum, ac Bathuel, patrē Rebeccae: atque alios praeterea, horum fratres, numero quinque. Thare autem, tum propter Chaldaeorum idololatriā, qui tunc ignem praecipuè colebant, tum propter obitum filij sui Aran, in Mesopotamiā perrexit, ac in vrbe nomine Charan, obiit. Vide Gene.11.&2 2.cap. & Isidor.
units.tr: Terah, son of Nachor, aged seventy years, begot Abram (who was afterwards called Abraham) in the year 1949 from the creation of the world, before the birth of Christ 2013. He also begot another named Nachor, and Haran; and he lived 205 years in all. Moreover, Abraham begot Ishmael and Isaac, as will be seen below. Nachor, Abraham's brother, begot from Milcah Uz, father of Job, and Kemuel, father of the Syrians, and Bethuel, father of Rebekah; and besides these, five others, their brothers, in number. But Terah, both on account of the idolatry of the Chaldeans, who then especially worshipped fire, and on account of the death of his son Haran, set out for Mesopotamia and died in a city named Haran. See Genesis 11 and 12 chapters, and Isidore.

units.la: IANVS, anno Nini supradicti decimo, ex Africa ad Celtiberos venit, vbi duas colonias diuisit, à se dictas Noëlas, & Noëglas. Anno autem 19. eiusdem Nini, in Italiam veniens, cum comperisset Camesenuum (qui est Cham) praeter opinionem corrumpentem iuuentutem, tribus illum annis aequo animo fert: deinde, aliquot illi coloniis assignatis, eum Italia excedere, omnes colonos Comeros corruptos montana trans Ianiculum amnem colere iubet: illisque filiam suam Cranā Helernam, id est suffragio ab his electam, & axaltatam reginam, cum sceptro albo dat. Hic Ianigenas suos cognominatos Razenuos, docuit Physicam, & Astronomiam: diuinationes & ritus scripsit, anno mundi 1948. ante Christum natum 2014. quamobrem fui ipsum eisdem nominibus & veneratione diuina sunt prosecuti, quibus in Armenia Saga, vsi erant. Berosus lib.5.
units.tr: Janus, in the tenth year of the aforementioned Ninus, came from Africa to the Celtiberians, where he divided two colonies, named after himself, Noëlas and Noëglas. In the nineteenth year of the same Ninus, coming to Italy, when he had discovered that Camesenuus (who is Ham) was corrupting the youth contrary to expectation, he bore it with equanimity for three years; then, after assigning some colonies to him, he ordered him to leave Italy, and ordered all the corrupted colonists to dwell in the mountains beyond the river Janiculum. To them he gave his daughter Crana, and Helerna, that is, the queen chosen and raised up by their vote, together with a white sceptre. He taught his Janigenae, who were surnamed Razenui, physics and astronomy; he wrote divinations and rites, in the year of the world 1948, before the birth of Christ 2014. For this reason they followed him with the same names and divine honour which they had used in Armenia for Saga. Berosus, book 5.

units.la: VESTA vxor fuit Iani, quae sempiternum ignem custodiedum virginibus puellis edoctis sacra, tradidit anno mundi 1963. ante Christum natum 1999. Hinc Vestalium superstitio successu temporis manauit: hae à sexto ad decimū annum huic collegio tradebantur, cum 30. annos manssent, fas erat nubere: si qua stupri comperta foret, viua sub terrā defodiebatur: viciffim ignem sacrum custodiebāt: quem siqua extingui sineret, flagro cedebatur. Titus Liuius lib.1. August.de ciui.Dei.libr.4. cap.10. DIONYSIVS PALLADON V.M.
units.tr: Vesta was the wife of Janus, who handed down, in the year of the world 1963, before the birth of Christ 1999, the rites of keeping the everlasting fire, having taught them to virgin girls. From this, the superstition of the Vestals gradually arose: these were handed over to this college from the sixth to the tenth year of age; when they had remained thirty years, they were permitted to marry. If any were discovered to have committed unchastity, she was buried alive under the ground; in turn, they guarded the sacred fire, and if one let it go out, she was beaten with a whip. Livy, book 1. Augustine, On the City of God, book 4, chapter 10. DIONYSIUS PALLADON, V.M.

units.la: DIONYSIVS, Hammonis filius,armis sumptis Rheam & Camesenuum regno paterno pellens,& secū Osirim horum filium retinens, in filiumque suum adoptans , eum de nomine patris sui Hammonem Jovem cognominauit, uti à magistro Olympo Olympicum ,eique totius Aegypti regnum tradidit, anno ab orbe condito 1948.ante Christum natum 2014. post nouem annos Barzanes Sabatij filius in Armenia à Nino superatur. Videto Berosum lib.5.
units.tr: Dionysius, son of Hammon, taking up arms and driving Rhea and Camesenuus from his father's kingdom, and keeping Osiris, their son, with him and adopting him as his own son, surnamed him Jupiter Hammon after his father's name, just as from his teacher Olympus he was called Olympicus; and he handed over to him the whole kingdom of Egypt, in the year 1948 from the founding of the world, before the birth of Christ 2014. Nine years later, Barzanes, son of Sabatius, was overcome in Armenia by Ninus. See Berosus, book 5.

units.la: PALLADON virgo, à Græcis dicta Minerva, anno 43. regni Nini(de quo supra mētionem feci)apud Tritonidem lacum infantula exposita est:atq; ab eodē Dionysio, Jove etiam Libyco cognominato,adoptata in filiam:hæc omnem militiam prima Libycos docuit. Hæc item(secundum alios qui eandem Palladem vocant)lanificium antea incognitum invenit,& docuit,& textrinū officium:hinc lanifices,fullones,tinctores,textricésque puellæ eam pro Dea coluere. dicitur præterea usum olei invenisse ac docuisse:& numeros deniq; ipsos,quadrigas, atque arma.Bero.lib.5.Supple.Chro.
units.tr: Palladon, a virgin called Minerva by the Greeks, was exposed as a little infant in the 43rd year of the reign of Ninus (of whom I have made mention above) at Lake Tritonis; and she was adopted as a daughter by the same Dionysius, also surnamed Libyan Jupiter. She first taught all military arts to the Libyans. She, too (according to others who call her the same Pallas), discovered and taught wool-working, previously unknown, and the craft of weaving; hence wool-workers, fullers, dyers and weaving girls worshipped her as a goddess. It is further said that she discovered and taught the use of oil; and finally numbers themselves, the four-horse chariot, and arms. Berosus, book 5; Supplementum Chronicorum.

units.la: OSIRIS, Camesenui & Rheae filius, imperauit Aegyptiis annis 35. Hic Rex magnus, & pro Deo habitus est: hic, anno mundi 2008. ante Christum natum 1954. qui erat annus nonus regni Zameis Niniae, Regis Babylonis, inuētis à se & sorore adolescentula frumēto, & frugibus, cœpit docere illa in Palæstina. inde reuersus in Aegyptum, & inuēto aratro, & his quae ad agriculturam pertinebant, sensim vniuersum peragrauit orbem, docens quæcunque inuenerat: & ita vniuerso imperauit orbi, exceptis gentibus quae iam in Babyloniorum venerāt potestatem. Vide Bero.lib.5.
units.tr: Osiris, son of Camesenuus and Rhea, ruled the Egyptians for 35 years. This great king was also regarded as a god. In the year of the world 2008, before the birth of Christ 1954, which was the ninth year of Zameis Ninias, king of Babylon, having found wheat and grains with his sister, a young woman, he began to teach these in Palestine. Returning from there to Egypt, and having invented the plough and the things pertaining to agriculture, he gradually travelled over the whole world, teaching whatever he had discovered; and thus he ruled over the whole world, except for the nations which had already come under the power of the Babylonians. See Berosus, book 5.

units.la: ISIS maxima, dicta etiā Iuno Aegyptia, soror & vxor Osi-ridis, magni apud Aegyptios nominis extitit: testatur eius epitaphium in columna, in hæc verba olim sculptum: Ego Isis sum Aegypti regina à ☿Mercurio erudita. Quæ ego legibus statui, nullus soluet. Ego sum vxor Osiridis. Ego sum prima frugum inuentrix. Ego sum Ori regis mater. Ego sum in astro Canis refulgens. Mihi Bubastya vrbs condita est. Gaude, gaude Aegypte, quae me nutristi.
units.tr: Isis, the greatest, also called Egyptian Juno, sister and wife of Osiris, was of great renown among the Egyptians. Her epitaph on a column, once carved in these words, attests this: "I, Isis, am the queen of Egypt, taught by Mercury. What I have established by laws, no one shall dissolve. I am the wife of Osiris. I am the first inventor of crops. I am the mother of King Orus. I shine in the star of the Dog. The city of Bubastis was founded for me. Rejoice, rejoice, Egypt, which nursed me."

units.la: Plura qui volet, legat primum & secundum librum Diodori Siculi, de fabulo.antiq.gestis. SEMIRAMIS BABYL. LON. NINAS ZAMEIS
units.tr: Whoever wishes more may read the first and second books of Diodorus Siculus, On the Ancient Fables and Deeds. SEMIRAMIS, BABYLON, LON., NINIAS ZAMEIS

units.la: SEMIRAMIS post obitum Nini coniugis fui,imperauit Assyriæ anno mundi 1958. ante Christum natum 2004. Hæc etiam bonam Asiæ partem tenuit, tantaque regnandi cupiditate tenebatur,ut sexum virilem mentita,simularit se defuncti Nini filium. Hæc Babylonem,ex oppido, vrbem maximam fecit,ut magis dici posset eam ædificasse quàm ampliasse.Hæc Aethiopiam ac Aegyptum regno suo adiecit.Sed & Indiæ bellum intulit,quò præter illam & Alexandrum,nemo penetrauit.Fertur duxisse in Indiam aduersus Staurobatē Indorum Regem, terdecies centena millia peditum, equitum quingenta millia, currus ad millia centum, naues bis mille : hominésque in elephantis, quatuor cubitorum gladios gestantes. Hæc cum pulcherrimis militibus coibat, quos postea occidebat. Ad postremum, concubitum filij cum petiissel, ab eodem merito intersecta est, 42. annos post Ninum, regno potita. Vide Berosum lib.5.Diod.lib.3.Iusti.lib.1.Herodo.1.
units.tr: Semiramis, after the death of Ninus, her husband, ruled Assyria in the year of the world 1958, before the birth of Christ 2004. She also held a good part of Asia, and was so possessed by desire to rule that, pretending to be a man, she feigned herself to be a son of the dead Ninus. She made Babylon, from a town, the greatest city, so that it could more truly be said she had built it rather than enlarged it. She added Ethiopia and Egypt to her kingdom. But she also waged war on India, to which, besides her and Alexander, no one penetrated. It is said that she led into India, against Staurobates, king of the Indians, 1,300,000 foot soldiers, 500,000 horsemen, 100,000 chariots, 2,000 ships, and men on elephants carrying swords four cubits long. She used to lie with the most handsome soldiers, whom she afterwards killed. At last, when she sought intercourse with her own son, she was rightly slain by him, having held the kingdom 42 years after Ninus. See Berosus, book 5; Diodorus, book 3; Justin, book 1; Herodotus, book 1.

units.la: ZAMEIS Ninias Babyloniorū seu Assyriorum rex quintus,post matrē Semiramidem, quam occiderat, imperauit annos 38. quorum primus erat annus mundi 2000. ante Christum natum 1962. Hic in sacris scripturis vocatur Amraphel. Belli studia deposuit: in fœminarum turba consenuit: ornauit tamen templa Deorum. Vide. Gene. 14. cap. & Berosum lib.5. Iust.lib.1.Diodo.Sicu.lib.3.
units.tr: Zameis Ninias, the fifth king of the Babylonians or Assyrians, after his mother Semiramis, whom he had killed, ruled for 38 years, the first of which was the year of the world 2000, before the birth of Christ 1962. In Holy Scripture he is called Amraphel. He laid aside the pursuits of war and grew old amid a crowd of women; he nevertheless adorned the temples of the gods. See Genesis 14, and Berosus, book 5; Justin, book 1; Diodorus Siculus, book 3.

units.la: ABRAHAM filius Thare, Deo fuit charissimus, cuius iussu paretem, patriam, omnésque reliquit cognatos: & assumpto Lot abiit in Chanaan peregrinatum, anno mundi 2024. ante Christum natum 1938. promisit illi Deus se in semine illius benedicturu omnes gentes: de semine siquidé huius nascituru erat Christus. huic promissioni adiecta est circuncisio: itaque se & suos circuncidit, annos natus 99. haec circuncisio indicabat vitam æternā habituros, piè in Deum per Christum credentes. Anno ætatis 86. ex ancilla Agar genuit Ismaël, quam illi permisit vxor Sara, cum hæc minimè pareret. At verò nihilominus annos ipse natus centum, & Sara nonaginta, genuerunt, fauore diuino, ipsum Isaac. Abraham obiit diem suum annos natus 175. sepelierunt eum filij sui in Hebron cum Sara, quæ illic sepulta erat, iam ante annos 38. Vide Gene. 11. cap. vsq; ad 25. item Iose. lib. Anti. 1. à cap. 16. vsque ad 26. Post mortem vxoris Sarę, Abraham aliam duxit vxorem, nomine Ceturam, ex qua filios sustulit sex.
units.tr: Abraham, son of Terah, was most dear to God. At God's command he left his father, his country and all his kinsfolk, and, taking Lot with him, went away to travel in Canaan, in the year of the world 2024, before the birth of Christ 1938. God promised him that he would bless all nations in his seed, for from the seed of this man Christ was to be born. To this promise circumcision was added; accordingly he circumcised himself and his people, at the age of 99. This circumcision signified that those who believed piously in God through Christ would have eternal life. In his eighty-sixth year he begot Ishmael from the maidservant Hagar, whom his wife Sarah allowed him to take, since she was not bearing children. But nevertheless, when he was a hundred years old and Sarah ninety, they, by divine favour, begot Isaac himself. Abraham died at the age of 175 and his sons buried him in Hebron with Sarah, who had already been buried there 38 years before. See Genesis 11 chapter through 25; likewise Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, from chapter 16 to 26. After the death of his wife Sarah, Abraham took another wife, named Keturah, by whom he had six sons.

units.la: SARA, filia Aran, vxor Abraham, proba atque insignis matrona extitit, pulchra quidem ac viro charissima, patientissima & prudentissima mulier. Hæc vti dictum est, annos nata 90. non sine miraculo, Isaac peperit, cùm antea sterilis esset. annos nata 127. moritur. Vide Gene. 23. cap. AGAR [?] ANC. SAR. [?] ISMA EL.
units.tr: SARA, daughter of Haran, wife of Abraham, was an upright and outstanding matron: beautiful indeed and most dear to her husband, a woman most patient and most prudent. This woman, as has been said, at the age of ninety, not without a miracle, bore Isaac, although she had been barren before. She died at the age of 127. See Gen. 23.

units.la: AGAR cùm grauida esset,spreuit dominam suam Saram: quamobrē eam Sara asperrimè coarguit & afflixit,cùm habuisset ius in illā à viro suo : quare Agar fugam arripuit:ab Angelo autem commonefacta,ad dominam rediit,& peperit Ismaël.
units.tr: When Hagar was pregnant, she despised her mistress Sarah; therefore Sarah rebuked her most harshly and afflicted her, since she had authority over her from her husband. Hagar thereupon fled; but, admonished by an angel, she returned to her mistress and bore Ishmael.

units.la: ISMAEL, filius Abraham ex Agar,natus est anno mundi 2036. ante Christum natum 1926. Hic in desertis locis habitauit, quádo iuuenis vnà cum matre ab Abraham dimissus est: factúsque est sagittarius : dedit illi mater vxoré de terra Aegypti,ex qua liberos duodecim sustulit,vnumquéque principem tribus suæ. Obiit Ismaël, anno ætatis 137. Vide Genes. 16. & 25.cap.item Joseph.lib.antiq.1.cap.18.& 21.
units.tr: ISHMAEL, son of Abraham by Hagar, was born in the year of the world 2036, before the birth of Christ 1926. He dwelt in the wilderness, when, as a youth, he was sent away by Abraham together with his mother; and he became an archer. His mother gave him a wife from the land of Egypt, by whom he begot twelve sons, each a prince of his tribe. Ishmael died at the age of 137. See Gen. 16 and 25, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapters 18 and 21.

units.la: Anno duodecimo à natiuitate Ismaël,Sodoma, Gomorrha, Adama,& Seboim,ciuitates, propter peccata incolētium,funditus euersæ sunt cum incolis , igne & sulphure diuinitus immisso. Solus Lot cum duabus filiabus euasit, diuina clementia vt discederet præmonitus:cuius vxor in statuam salis versa est, anno mundi 2048. ante Christum natum 1914. posthæc anno vno atque altero,natus est Isaac. Vide Gene.cap.19.Josephum, lib.1.cap.19.
units.tr: In the twelfth year after the birth of Ishmael, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, cities destroyed utterly with their inhabitants because of the sins of those who dwelt there, were overthrown by fire and brimstone sent from God. Only Lot escaped with his two daughters, warned by divine mercy to depart; his wife was turned into a pillar of salt. This was in the year of the world 2048, before the birth of Christ 1914. Within a year or two after this, Isaac was born. See Gen. chapter 19, and Josephus, book 1, chapter 19.

units.la: Circa hæc tempora Arius , sextus Assyriorum rex , colleċto exercitu post patris Niniæ obitum , Bactrianos ac omnes Caspios subiecit.Bero.lib.5. F. ABR. ISAAC REBECCA VX. ISAAC
units.tr: About this time Arius, sixth king of the Assyrians, after the death of his father Ninyas, gathered an army and subdued the Bactrians and all the Caspians. Berosus, book 5.

units.la: ISAAC, filius Abrahæ & Saræ, natus est 14. annos post Ismaelem: oblatus anno ætatis 13. vt alij volunt 25. qui erat annus mundi 2073. ante Christum natum 1889. anno ætatis 40. vxorem duxit Rebeccam filiam Bathuelis Syri, de Mesopotamia, sororem Laban, vt Abraham pater eius statuerat. anno 60. nati sunt illi ex Rebecca gemelli, prior Esau rufus, & totus hispidus: alter, Iacob, protinus egressus est, plantam fratris manu tenens. anno ætatis 180. mortuus est, & appositus populo suo. Vide Gene. 25. & 35. cap. item Iosep. lib. Anti. 1. cap. 26. & 28.
units.tr: ISAAC, son of Abraham and Sarah, was born fourteen years after Ishmael; he was offered up at the age of thirteen, or, as others hold, at twenty-five, which was the year of the world 2073, before the birth of Christ 1889. At the age of forty he married Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Syrian, from Mesopotamia, sister of Laban, as Abraham his father had arranged. In his sixtieth year twins were born to him by Rebekah: the first, Esau, ruddy and all hairy; the other, Jacob, came out immediately, holding his brother's heel in his hand. He died at the age of 180 and was gathered to his people. See Gen. chapters 25 and 35, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapters 26 and 28.

units.la: REBECCA nupsit Isaac anno mundi 2090. ante Christum natum 1872. hæc effecit vt Iacob benedictionem à patre præriperet, quæ Esau promittebatur. Nam cùm feni Isaac oculi caligaret, obtrusit ei Rebecca Iacob indutum vestibus Esau, ac pelliculis hædorum circunfultū manus & collum, interea dum venatum isset Esau, vt pulmētum patri pararet: mox autem rediens Esau, vt audiuit se præuentum, interminatus est mortem fratri Iacob. Id dum rescit Rebecca, mittit Iacob ad Laban, donec furor & indignatio Esau temperetur. Tandem mittens Iacob munera fratri, placatus est. Vide Gene. 27. 32. 33. cap. Iose. lib. Antiq. 1. à cap. 26. ad calcem vsque.
units.tr: REBEKAH married Isaac in the year of the world 2090, before the birth of Christ 1872. She brought it about that Jacob snatched the blessing from his father, which was promised to Esau. For when the eyes of the aged Isaac had grown dim, Rebekah put Jacob, dressed in Esau's clothes, with the skins of kids wrapped around his hands and neck, in front of him, while Esau had gone hunting to prepare a meal for his father. But soon Esau returned, and when he heard that he had been forestalled, he threatened his brother Jacob with death. When Rebekah learned of this, she sent Jacob to Laban, until the fury and indignation of Esau should subside. At last Jacob sent gifts to his brother, and he was appeased. See Gen. chapters 27, 32 and 33, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, from chapter 26 to the end.

units.la: IACOB filius Isaac, fugiens fratrem Efau, ipse in Haran, ab auunculo Laban benignè ac hilariter exceptus est. cúmque mensem vnum apud eum cõmoratus effet, conuenit inter illos vt pro Rachel in vxorem habenda, seruiret Iacob ipsi Laban, patri Rachelis, septem annos: quibus exactis, Lia pro Rachele supposita est: dolúsque consuetudine excusatus: nempe nonlicere vt minor natu prænubat. Seruiit itaq; Iacob pro Rachele alios iterum septem annos. Sícque ambas sorores in vxores habuit: ex his ambabus, atque ex duabus ancillis, filios duodecim sustulit, ac filiam vnam. Natus est ei Ioseph ex Rachel, anno mundi 2200. ante Christum natum 1762. obiit diem annos natus 147. in Aegypto, vbi erat Ioseph, qui patrem accersiuerat durante sterilitate septé annorum. inde asportatus in Hebron, cum patribus sepultus est. Gen. 29. ca. & inde vsque ad calcem. Iosephus lib.r.cap.27.
units.tr: JACOB, son of Isaac, fleeing his brother Esau, was received kindly and cheerfully in Haran by his uncle Laban. When he had stayed with him for one month, they agreed that Jacob should serve Laban, father of Rachel, for seven years in return for having Rachel as his wife. When these years were complete, Leah was substituted for Rachel, and the deceit was excused by custom, namely that the younger should not marry first. So Jacob served another seven years for Rachel. Thus he had both sisters as wives; by these two, and by two maidservants, he begot twelve sons and a daughter. Joseph was born to him by Rachel in the year of the world 2200, before the birth of Christ 1762. He died at the age of 147 in Egypt, where Joseph was, who had summoned his father during the seven years of famine. From there he was carried to Hebron and buried with his fathers. See Gen. chapter 29 and onward to the end. Josephus, book 1, chapter 27.

units.la: LIA fuit vxor Iacob, cuius filij fuere Ruben, Simeon, Leui, Iuda, Iffachar, Zabulon, & Dina fæmella. Zelpha ancilla Liæ, peperit ipsi Iacob Gad, & Afer. Gene. 29. & 30. ca.
units.tr: LEAH was the wife of Jacob, whose sons were Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and the daughter Dinah. Zilpah, Leah's maidservant, bore Gad and Asher to Jacob. See Gen. chapters 29 and 30.

units.la: RACHEL quoque vxor Iacob fuit: huius filij fuere Ioseph & Beniamin, in cuius partu periit. Genef. 29. 30. & 35. cap. Balam ancilla Rachel, peperit item ipsi Iacob, Dan, & Nephthalim. F. IACOB IOSEPH CAST. ASENECH VXOR IOSEPH
units.tr: RACHEL too was a wife of Jacob; her sons were Joseph and Benjamin, in whose birth she died. See Gen. chapters 29, 30 and 35. Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, likewise bore to Jacob Dan and Naphtali. F. JACOB. JOSEPH. CAST. ASENATH, WIFE OF JOSEPH.

units.la: IOSEPH filius Iacob ex Rachel, odiosus erat fratribus, quòd patri esset charissimus: quare ipsi eum in cisternam coniecerunt. At verò consilio fratris sui Iudæ, Ismaëlitis venundatur: ipsi quoque eunucho Pharaonis, Phutiphari, magistro militum, venundant. Post aliquantum temporis falsò accusatus stupri à domina sua, in carcerē detruditur: cùm hæc illum, non ille hanc cōcupissēt, ac pressisset. In carcere dum agit, pincernæ, pistorísque Pharaonis somnia interpretatur. Post hæc è carcere educitur, vt ipsius etiā Pharaonis somnia exponat: qui constituit eum super vniuersam terram Aegypti: vertitque nomen eius, & vocauit eum Saluatorem mundi: anno ætatis suæ 30. anno à mundo condito 2230. ante Christum natum 1732. obiit tandem annos natus 110. Vide Genef. 37. cap. & inde ad calcem vsque. item Iose.lib.antiq.2.à cap.2.ad 9.
units.tr: JOSEPH, son of Jacob by Rachel, was hated by his brothers because he was dearest to their father; so they threw him into a cistern. But at the counsel of his brother Judah, he was sold to the Ishmaelites; they in turn sold him to the eunuch of Pharaoh, Potiphar, commander of the soldiers. After some time, falsely accused of rape by his mistress, he was thrust into prison, although it was she who had desired him, not he her, and had pressed him. In prison, while he was there, he interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker.
