After this he was brought out of prison to interpret the dreams of Pharaoh himself, who set him over the whole land of Egypt; and he changed his name and called him Saviour of the world. In the thirtieth year of his age, in the year 2230 from the creation of the world, before the birth of Christ 1732, he finally died at the age of 110. See Gen. chapter 37 and onward to the end; also Josephus, Antiquities, book 2, chapters 2 to 9.

units.la: ASENETH filia Phutipharis sacerdotis Heliopoleos, fuit vxor ipsius Iosephi, quæ peperit illi Manassen & Ephraim. Hos adoptauit Iacob, benedixitque eis antequam moreretur. Vide Gene.41.& 48.capita. PROMETHEUS (medallion legend, left) ATLAS MAURUS (medallion legend, right)
units.tr: ASENATH, daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis, was the wife of Joseph himself, and she bore him Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob adopted these and blessed them before he died. See Gen. chapters 41 and 48. PROMETHEUS (medallion legend, left) ATLAS OF MAURITANIA (medallion legend, right)

units.la: PROMETHEUS, Iapeti atque Asiæ filius, propterea fertur de luto formasse homines, quia optimus sapientiæ doctor fuisse perhibetur, ut sentit Augustinus. Huic inventionē ferrei anuli tribuebat antiquitas, vinculúmque id, non gestamen intelligi volebat. Lactātius re vera primum omniū simulachrum hominis formasse de pingui & molli luto Prometheum scribit, ab eoque natam primò artem, statuas, & simulachra fingendi. Hic ignem Ioui dicitur furatus, quòd ex ferro, & silice ignem extundere docuerit, servareq; in ferula. Videto Augustinū de civita. Dei lib.18.cap.8. Lactan.lib.2.cap.11. Pli.lib.13.cap.1.
units.tr: PROMETHEUS, son of Iapetus and Asia, is said therefore to have formed men from clay, because he is reported to have been an excellent teacher of wisdom, as Augustine thinks. Antiquity attributed to him the invention of the iron ring, and wished this to be understood as a fetter, not an ornament. Lactantius indeed writes that Prometheus first of all formed the image of a man from fat and soft clay, and that from him the art of shaping statues and images first arose. He is said to have stolen fire from Jupiter, because he taught men to strike fire from iron and flint, and to keep it in a fennel stalk. See Augustine, City of God, book 18, chapter 8; Lactantius, book 2, chapter 11; Pliny, book 13, chapter 1.

units.la: ATLAS, Promethei frater, primus Sphæram Astrologiamq; invenisse dicitur. inde locus fabulæ datus, quòd cœlum humeris fulciret. Vergil.6. Aeneidos,
units.tr: ATLAS, brother of Prometheus, is said to have first invented the sphere and astrology. From this came the occasion for the fable that heupheld the heavens on his shoulders. Virgil, Aeneid 6:

units.la: —Vbi cœlifer Atlas Axem humero torquet, stellis ardentibus aptum.
units.tr: —There where heaven-bearing Atlas turns the axis on his shoulder, fitted with blazing stars.
See Pliny, book 2, chapter 6, and book 7, chapter 56.

units.la: ALTADAS XII. Assyriorum rex, horum temporibus extitit, ut ait Cassiodorus. Hic regnare cœpit anno mundi 2263. ante Christum natum 1699. Huius institutum fuit ut divitiis & gloria, aliena stultitia & miseria à maioribus suis partis, quoad viveret, frueretur. Vide Bero. lib. 5. Huius ætate Galates apud Celtas, & Vandalus apud Thuyscones regnauit.
units.tr: ALTADAS, the twelfth king of the Assyrians, flourished in these times, as Cassiodorus says. He began to reign in the year of the world 2263, before the birth of Christ 1699. It was his practice to enjoy, as long as he lived, the riches and glory that his forebears had largely gained through the folly and misery of others. See Berosus, book 5. In his time Galates reigned among the Celts, and Vandalus among the Teutons.

units.la: CECROPS Diphies Atheniensium rex primus,coepit regnare anno mundi 2408. ante Christum natum 1554. Hic Athenas condidit, vt ait Cassiodorus. De hoc quoq; sic inquit Iustinus lib. 2. Ante Deucalionis tempora Athenienses regem habuere Cecropem,quem,vt omnis antiquitas fabulata est, biformem prodidere, quia primus marem fœminæ,matrimonio iunxit. Sub hoc rege Athenæ vrbs vel instaurata,vel condita fuit. Vide August.lib.de ciui. Dei 18.cap.8.Berosum lib.5.Eufe.in præfa.Chro.
units.tr: CECROPS, son of Diphyes, the first king of the Athenians, began to reign in the year of the world 2408, before the birth of Christ 1554. He founded Athens, as Cassiodorus says. Justin also speaks of him thus, book 2: Before the times of Deucalion, the Athenians had Cecrops as king, whom, as all antiquity has fabled, they described as two-formed, because he first joined a male to a female in marriage. Under this king the city of Athens was either restored or founded. See Augustine, City of God, book 18, chapter 8; Berosus, book 5; Eusebius in the preface to his Chronicle.

units.la: DEVCALION Promethei filius, sed non eius de quo supra,vt supputatio indicat,apud eos regnare coepit, qui circa Parnassum morabantur, anno à mundo condito 2428. ante Christum natum 1534. Hic annos duos & octoginta natus, Thessaliam vidit inundatam.ipse cum vxore Pyrrha in Parnassum montem nauicula delatus,seruatus est. Vide Bero.lib.5.in Sparete rege.Xeno.de æqui.de hoc fabulantur etiã Poëtæ.Cæterùm Archilochus de tempor.& Ioan.Annius,natum Deucalionem scribunt an.2.Spheri,15.Assy.regis,70.an.à diluuio.
units.tr: DEUCALION, son of Prometheus, but not of the one mentioned above, as the calculation shows, began to reign among those who dwelt around Parnassus, in the year 2428 from the creation of the world, before the birth of Christ 1534. He, at the age of eighty-two, saw Thessaly flooded; he himself, with his wife Pyrrha, was carried in a little boat to Mount Parnassus and was saved. See Berosus, book 5, on King Sparetus. Xenophon, On Justice. Poets also tell this story. Moreover, Archilochus, On Times, and Annius of Viterbo write that Deucalion was born in the year 2 of Spherus, the 15th year of the Assyrian king, the 70th year after the Flood.

units.la: IASIVS Ianigena, tempore Deucalionis imperabat Italis,in cuius nuptiis affuit Iö Aegyptia.Vide Bero.lib.5.
units.tr: IASIVS, son of Ianus, ruled over the Italians in the time of Deucalion; Io the Egyptian was present at his wedding. See Berosus, book 5.

units.la: CVRETES & Coribantus circa hæc tempora Gnosson condidere.Hi modulatam & inter se cöcinentem in armis saltationem reperere.
units.tr: The Curetes and Corybas founded Gortyn about this time. They invented a dance in arms, measured and sung in harmony among themselves.

units.la: ASCATADES XVIII. Assyriorum, seu Babyloniorum rex, omnem Syriam suæ ditionis fecit:huius anno 13. vitis inuenta apud Græcos,narratur. Vide Bero.lib.5.
units.tr: ASCATADES, the eighteenth king of the Assyrians, or Babylonians, brought all of Syria under his rule. In his thirteenth year, it is reported, the vine was discovered among the Greeks. See Berosus, book 5.

units.la: MOYSES primus Hebræorum dux fuit, anno mundi 2453. ante Christum natum 1509. quo anno filij Israël ab Aegyptiaca liberati sunt servitute:ac post annum unum atque alterum, Aaron summus creatur Cacerdos, & cōsecratur. Hic Moyses inter Hebræos,Deo atque hominibus charissimus extitit: erat siquidem natura mitis ac candidus. Inter Prophetas summum se historiographum præstitit. Hic decem legis præcepta,digito Dei in duabus lapideis tabulis scripta, in monte Sina sibi tradita,populū Israëliticum docuit, & cæremonias ac ritus veteris legis. Obiit anno ætatis 120. Israël rexit 40. annis, quos per mare rubrum in desertum duxit: huic successit Iosue. Vide Exo.Leui.Nume.Deute.nam omnibus ferè cap.de Moyse tractant.
units.tr: MOSES was the first leader of the Hebrews, in the year of the world 2453, before the birth of Christ 1509, the year in which the children of Israel were freed from Egyptian slavery. One or two years later Aaron was made high priest and consecrated. Moses was the most beloved of the Hebrews, both by God and by men; he was by nature gentle and sincere. Among the prophets he showed himself the greatest historian. He received from God the ten precepts of the law, written with the finger of God on two stone tablets, on Mount Sinai, and taught the Israelite people both the ceremonies and rites of the old law. He died at the age of 120. He ruled Israel for 40 years, during which he led them through the Red Sea into the wilderness; Joshua succeeded him. See Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, for almost all the chapters deal with Moses.

units.la: AARON Moysis frater, inter Hebræos præstans ac disertus extitit,summúsque sacerdos in populo Dei. ad hūc spectabant primitiæ & decimæ à filiis Israël Deo oblatæ. Cum summum sacerdotium gessisset annos 37. obiit, anno ætatis 123. Hoc semel orante pro populo, cessauit plaga incendij cœlitus missi. Videto Nume.16.cap.item Iosep. lib. antiq.4.cap.5. & secundum,diu desideratum ac recèns excusum Iosephum,cap.3. ELEASAR F. AAR SVMM. SACER
units.tr: AARON, the brother of Moses, was outstanding and eloquent among the Hebrews, and the chief priest among the people of God. To him were brought the firstfruits and tithes offered to God by the children of Israel. After he had held the high priesthood for 37 years, he died at the age of 123. When he prayed once for the people, the plague of fire sent from heaven ceased. See Numbers 16; likewise Josephus, Antiquities, book 4, chapter 5, and the second, long-desired and recently printed Josephus, chapter 3. ELEAZAR, SON OF AARON, HIGH PRIEST.

units.la: ELEASAR Aaronis filius, mortuo patre, summus Sacerdos creatur, anno à mundo condito 2491. ante Christum natum 1471. Iste & Iosue terram Chanaan obtinuerunt, quam vocarũt Iudæam. Hæc in duodecim tribus filiorum Israël diuisa est, quarum nomina sunt, Tribus Ruben, Simeon, Leui, Iuda, Issachar, Zabulon, Gad, Aser, Beniamin, Dan, Nephthalim, Manasses. Obiit Eleasar eodem quo Iosue anno. Vide Exo. 6. cap. item Iosue 24.cap.
units.tr: ELEAZAR, son of Aaron, was made high priest after his father's death, in the year of the world 2491, before the birth of Christ 1471. He and Joshua took possession of the land of Canaan, which they called Judea. This land was divided among the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, whose names are: the tribe of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Gad, Asher, Benjamin, Dan, Naphtali and Manasseh. Eleazar died in the same year as Joshua. See Exodus 6; likewise Joshua 24.

units.la: IOSVE, secundus populi Israëlitici dux, anno mundi 2493. ante Christum natum 1469. filios Israël per Iordanem, iuxta præceptum Domini, in terram duxit promissam: Iordanem fluuium, vt Moyses mare rubrum, sine vllo periculo, verbo Dei fretus, pertransiit: obsidione vrbem Iericho cepit, & incendit, attamen Raab cum suis seruauit, minimè ingratus: nam hæc nuntios exploratores receptos, celarat: vrbē quoque Hai succedit Iosue ac Regem suspendit. Dum pro Gabaonitis bellum gerit, sistitur Sol, & prolongatur dies: quinque Reges suspenduntur. In summa 31. reges vicit, victoriq; suo populo Chanaanæorum terrā partitus est. Hic pius, bello & pace clarus, rexit populum annos 28. Obiit diem anno ætatis 110. post eum seniores rexerunt populum annos 17. quibus Othoniel successit. Videto lib. Iosue ab initio ad finem. item Iosep. lib. Ant. 5. cap. 1. 2. 3. 4.
units.tr: JOSHUA, the second leader of the Israelite people, in the year of the world 2493, before the birth of Christ 1469, led the children of Israel across the Jordan, according to the command of the Lord, into the promised land. Trusting in the word of God, he crossed the Jordan river without any danger, as Moses had crossed the Red Sea. He besieged and captured the city of Jericho and burned it, yet he spared Rahab and her household, by no means ungrateful, for she had received and hidden the spies who were sent as scouts. Joshua also took the city of Ai and hanged its king. While he waged war on behalf of the Gibeonites, the sun was made to stand still and the day was prolonged; five kings were hanged. In sum, he conquered 31 kings and, after the victory, divided the land of the Canaanites among his people. He was a pious man, famous in war and in peace, and he ruled the people for 28 years. He died at the age of 110. After him the elders ruled the people for 17 years, after whom Othniel succeeded. See the book of Joshua from beginning to end; likewise Josephus, Antiquities, book 5, chapters 1 to 4.

units.la: PERSEVS Iouis filius ex Danaë, Medusam Gorgonem occidit, anno mundi 2497. ante Christum natum 1465. Hic à Græcia in Asiam transfuectus est: ibi Barbaras gentes graui, diuturnóque bello domuit: & nouissimè victor, nomen superatæ genti dedit:nanque à Perseo Persæ dicti sunt. Vide Orof. lib.1.cap.11. De hoc quoq; sic inquit Herodotus lib.7. Posteaquā Perseus ad Cepheum cōmeauit, & Andromedam eius filiam duxit vxorem,tulit ex ea filium,quem Persen appellauit:eúmque illic reliquit (nam Cepheus carebat virili prole) à quo cognomen sortiti sunt Persæ. De Perseo,Poëtæ multi multa fabulantur. Vide Diodo.lib.1.& 4.
units.tr: PERSEUS, son of Jupiter and Danaë, slew the Gorgon Medusa, in the year of the world 2497, before the birth of Christ 1465. He passed from Greece into Asia, where he subdued the barbarous nations in a grievous and long-lasting war; and finally, as victor, he gave his name to the conquered people, for the Persians were so called from Perses. See Orosius, book 1, chapter 11. Herodotus also says this about him, book 7: "After Perseus had gone to Cepheus and married his daughter Andromeda, he had a son by her, whom he called Perses, and left him there (for Cepheus had no male offspring); from him the Persians received their name." Many poets tell many fables about Perseus. See Diodorus, books 1 and 4.

units.la: ANDROMEDA Cephei regis Aethiopum & Cassiopes filia, vxor fuit Persei, quam scopulo alligatam ac monstro marino, propter matris superbiam, vt aiunt, expositam, liberauit: liberatam in vxorē duxit, occisis Phineo, & reliquis aduersantibus. Acrisiū qui Danaën turri incluserat, occidit Perseus, imprudens tamen. Vide Herodo.lib.7. & Diodorum Siculum multis in locis. ΑΓΕΝ[?] ΦΟΙΝΙΞ ΤΟΥ ΥΟΣ[?] ΚΑΔΜΟΣ ΦΟΙ ΑΔΕΛ[?]
units.tr: ANDROMEDA, daughter of Cepheus, king of the Ethiopians, and of Cassiopeia, was the wife of Perseus. He freed her when she had been bound to a rock and exposed to a sea monster, as they say, on account of her mother's pride; once freed, he took her as his wife, after killing Phineus and the others who opposed him. Perseus, though unwittingly, killed Acrisius, who had shut Danaë up in a tower. See Herodotus, book 7, and Diodorus Siculus in many places. [Greek inscription, damaged: Agenor's son Phoenix and Cadmus, brothers]

units.la: PHOENIX, Agenoris filius,& Cadmi frater fuit. Ambo fratres de Thebis Aegyptiorū in Syriam profecti,apud Tyrum & Sydonem regnauerunt, anno mundi 2506. ante Christum natum 1456. à Phoenice itaque Phoenicia regio dicta. Hic Phoenix Bithyniam condidit: Phoenicibus quasdam literas ad scribendum dedit. Vermiculum instituit,unde fit color puniceus. De Phoenicibus Lucanus,lib.3.sic ait:
units.tr: PHOENIX, son of Agenor, was the brother of Cadmus. The two brothers set out from Thebes of the Egyptians into Syria and ruled at Tyre and Sidon, in the year of the world 2506, before the birth of Christ 1456. The Phoenician region is therefore named after Phoenix. This Phoenix founded Bithynia and gave the Phoenicians certain letters for writing. He introduced the kermes worm, from which the purple colour is made. Lucan, book 3, says of the Phoenicians:

units.la: Phœnices primi,fama si creditur,ausi Mansuram rudibus vocem signare figuris.
units.tr: The Phoenicians, if report be believed, were the first to dare to mark the spoken word, enduring, with rude characters.

units.la: CADMUS frater Phœnicis,è Phœnicia in Græciam literas numero sedecim intulisse fertur, quibus Palamedē Troiano bello adiecisse quatuor, totidémque post eum Simonidem Melicum. Hic quoque lapidicinas,auri metalla,& cōflaturam reperisse dicitur. Plin.lib.7.cap.56.De Cadmo multa Poëtæ fabulantur,præcipuè Ovid.lib.3.&4.Metamorphoseos.
units.tr: CADMUS, brother of Phoenix, is said to have brought sixteen letters from Phoenicia into Greece; Palamedes added four to these during the Trojan War, and Simonides the lyric poet added as many after him. He is also said to have discovered quarries, metal mines and smelting. See Pliny, book 7, chapter 56. Poets tell many fables about Cadmus, especially Ovid, Metamorphoses, books 3 and 4.

units.la: CORAX XVI. Sycioniorum rex hisce temporibus regnare occipit,nempe anno à mundo condito 2507. ante Christum natum 1455.
units.tr: CORAX, the sixteenth king of the Sicyonians, began to reign in these times, namely in the year of the world 2507, before the birth of Christ 1455.

units.la: ROMUS etiam apud Celtas regnat anno mundi 2515.ante Christi nativitatem 1447.Circa hæc quoque tempora Delphicum Apollinis templū Phlegyas incēdit,ob filiam ab Apolline(ut ferunt)compressam. BACCHVS. DIONISIVS LIB. PAT.
units.tr: ROMUS also reigned among the Celts in the year of the world 2515, before the birth of Christ 1447. About this same time Phlegyas burned the Delphic temple of Apollo, because, as they say, Apollo had violated his daughter. BACCHUS, OR DIONYSUS, THE FATHER LIBER.

units.la: DIONYSIVS cognominatus Liber pater, deinde Bacchus,filius fuit Iovis ex Semele, Dionysius ab Iove & Nysa dictus : Nysa autem antrum est in quo à Nymphis nutritus dicitur. Liber pater dictus est,vel à libertate patriæ, quâ armis etiâ tutatus est,vel quòd vinum,cuius inventor extitit, reddat linguas liberas ac faciles. Bacchus dictus est, vel à Bacchantibus mulieribus quæ ipsum sequebatur,vel à baccis, quas in torculari premere docuit. Hic quorum regio vites ferre non posset, docuit potum ex hordeo conficere. In Bœotia iussit,in gratiam patriæ,omnes vrbes liberas esse. Exercitum virorum & mulierum circunducens, nefarios homines merita multavit pœna. In Indiam transcendit, ac militavit, anno mundi 2508. ante Christum natum 1454. triennio post,in Bœotiam multis cum spoliis rediit. Consule Diodorum Siculum de fab.antiq.gestis lib.5.
units.tr: DIONYSUS, surnamed Liber Pater and afterwards Bacchus, was the son of Jupiter and Semele. He was called Dionysus from Jupiter and Nysa; Nysa is a cave in which he is said to have been nursed by the nymphs. He was called Liber Pater either from the liberty of his country, which he also defended with arms, or because wine, of which he was the inventor, makes the tongue free and easy. He was called Bacchus either from the Bacchantes, the women who followed him, or from the berries, which he taught men to press in the wine press. Where a region could not bear vines, he taught people to make a drink from barley. In Boeotia, for the sake of his homeland, he ordered that all cities be free. Leading an army of men and women around, he punished wicked men with the penalties they deserved. He crossed into India and waged war there, in the year of the world 2508, before the birth of Christ 1454. Three years later he returned to Boeotia with much plunder. Consult Diodorus Siculus, Ancient History, book 5.

units.la: DIONYSIVS alter longè illo antiquior, ac ævo prior, à nonnullis Sebasis dictus,filius dicitur Iovis & Proserpinæ: primus hic boves sub iugum misisse fertur ad colendam terram: quare illum cornibus finxerunt. Videto Diodorum Siculum libro quo supra. OTHONIEL ACSAH FIL. CAL. VX. OTHO.
units.tr: ANOTHER DIONYSUS, far older than that one and earlier in age, is by some called Sebasis; he is said to be the son of Jupiter and Proserpina. He is reported to have been the first to put oxen under the yoke to till the land; for this reason they depicted him with horns. See Diodorus Siculus, in the book cited above. OTHNIEL, SON OF KENAZ, ACHSAH'S HUSBAND, CALEB'S BROTHER, OTHNIEL.

units.la: OTHONIEL filius Cenes,& frater Caleb minor natu, de tribu Iuda, iudicauit populum Israël anno mundi 2538. ante Christum natum 1424. In eo fuit spiritus domini:egresfúsq; est ad pugnam,& tradidit dominus in manus eius Chusam-rasathiam Regem Syriæ, cui Israëlitæ seruierant annis octo, & oppressit eum. Hic iudicauit Israële quadraginta annis,& mortuus est. Iudicum 3. Iofe.antiq.lib.5.cap.7.
units.tr: OTHNIEL, son of Kenaz and younger brother of Caleb, of the tribe of Judah, judged the people of Israel in the year of the world 2538, before the birth of Christ 1424. The Spirit of the Lord was upon him; he went out to battle, and the Lord delivered into his hands Cushan-rishathaim, king of Syria, whom the Israelites had served for eight years, and he overcame him. He judged Israel for forty years, and then died. Judges 3; Josephus, Antiquities, book 5, chapter 7.

units.la: AXA filia Caleb fuit, atque uxor Othoniel. Hæc à viro præmonita petiit à patre agrum,ac obtinuit,Iudicum cap.1.
units.tr: ACHSAH was the daughter of Caleb and the wife of Othniel. Admonished by her husband, she asked her father for a field and obtained it. Judges, chapter 1.

units.la: AOD qui & Ehud,filius fuit Gora[?],filij Iemini.hic Israelem iudicauit annos octuaginta à morte Othoniel:primus annorum huius principatus fuit 2578. à creato mundo:& ante Christum natum 1384. Hic populum liberauit à tyrannide Eglon regis Moabitarum,cui seruierat annos decem & octo, propter legis transgressionem.Iudi.3.Iofe.lib.antiq.5.cap.8.
units.tr: EHUD, also called Aod, was the son of Gera, of the sons of Benjamin. He judged Israel for eighty years after the death of Othniel; the first year of his rule was 2578 from the creation of the world, and before the birth of Christ 1384. He freed the people from the tyranny of Eglon, king of the Moabites, whom they had served for eighteen years, because of their transgression of the law. Judges 3; Josephus, Antiquities, book 5, chapter 8.

units.la: SAMGAR,filius Anath,iudicauit populum post Aod annum unum.hic percussit de Philisthiim sexcētos viros vomere, alij legunt stimulo boum.Iudicum 3.
units.tr: SHAMGAR, son of Anath, judged the people for one year after Ehud. He struck down six hundred Philistines with a plowshare; others read "with an ox-goad." Judges 3.

units.la: PELOPS Tantali regis Phrygum filius fuit,qui Hippodamiam Pisæ regis filiam deperibat:atque in uxorem petês eam, à patre virginis elegātissimæ,Oenamao,iniquis propositis conditionibus,est reiectus.quæ res bellum suscitauit : Oenomaus, Myrtilo præfecto suo prodete,victus est.Pelops itaque sumpta in uxore Hippodamia,Pisæregnum tenuit,anno à mundo condito 2617. ante Christum natum 1346. Hic viribus ac prudentia insignis,cum plurimos in Peloponnesum accolas deduxisset,eam patriâ Peloponnesum ab se denominauit.Diod.lib. 5. circa finem. regnauit annis 59.in Pisa,quæ est in Elide,iuxta Archadiam,cuius incolæ eam quæ eiusdem nominis est in Italia,condidere. Vide Strabone lib. Geographiæ 7.&8.item Rapha. Volaterranum lib.34.
units.tr: PELOPS was the son of Tantalus, king of the Phrygians. He was in love with Hippodamia, daughter of the king of Pisa, and when he sought her as his wife he was rejected by the maiden's father, Oenomaus, on unfair conditions. This matter stirred up war; Oenomaus was defeated through the betrayal of Myrtilus, his steward. Pelops, having taken Hippodamia as his wife, then held the kingdom of Pisa, in the year of the world 2617, before the birth of Christ 1346. Distinguished by his strength and wisdom, he led a great many settlers into the Peloponnese and named it after himself, calling it the Peloponnese. Diodorus, book 5, near the end. He reigned for 59 years in Pisa, which is in Elis, next to Arcadia; its inhabitants founded the city of the same name in Italy. See Strabo, Geography, books 7 and 8; likewise Raphael Volaterranus, book 34.

units.la: Hippodamia filia fuit unica,eadémque formosissima Oenomai Elidis regis:hanc à multis procis ambitam , nemini voluit collocare pater:quam tamen Pelops accepit in uxore,victo patre virginis , fraude Myrtili, qui in mare præcipitatus, nomen Myrtoo mari dedisse dicitur. Hinc illa Poëtarum fabula , de Myrtilo auriga , pecunia corrupto , & de curru vitiato,& deficiente. Unde Ouidius epist.8.
units.tr: Hippodamia was the only daughter, and also the most beautiful, of Oenomaus, king of Elis. Her father would not give her in marriage to any of her many suitors. Pelops nevertheless won her as his wife, after defeating her father by the treachery of Myrtilus, who was thrown into the sea and is said to have given his name to the Myrtoan Sea. Hence the poets' fable about Myrtilus the charioteer, bribed with money, and about the chariot being sabotaged and failing. Whence Ovid, Epistles 8:

units.la: Facit autem Ouid. Hermionem loquentem, quæ erat Pelopis proneptis:nam Pelops erat ei proauus.
units.tr: Ovid makes Hermione speak, who was a great-granddaughter of Pelops, for Pelops was her great-grandfather.

units.la: AMPHION Iouis & Antiopes filius, Thebis regnauit anno à mundo condito 2636. ante Christum natum 1326.hic tam insignis musicus[?] extitit, vt testudinem à Mercurio accepisse dicatur:cuius etiam modulamine fingitur à Poëtis saxa ad extruendas Thebas illexisse, ac traxisse:quod sic interpretatur Eusebius in Chro. Fuerunt,inquit,duro corde,&(vt ita dicam)saxei quidam auditores. Cui concinit Horatius in arte Poëtica,dicens,
units.tr: AMPHION, son of Jupiter and Antiope, reigned at Thebes in the year of the world 2636, before the birth of Christ 1326. He was such a distinguished musician that he is said to have received the lyre from Mercury. By the playing of it the poets feign that he drew stones to build Thebes and moved them. Eusebius interprets this in his Chronicle: There were, he says, men of hard heart, and (so to speak) stony listeners. Horace agrees with this in the Art of Poetry, saying:
Sacred interpreter of the gods, he tamed the wild men.
etc., and the rest. A little later he continues:

units.la: Dictus & Amphion Thebanae conditor vrbis, Saxa mouere sono testudinis,& prece blanda Ducere quò vellet. fuit haec sapientia quondam Publica priuatis,secernere sacra profanis, Concubitu prohibere vago,dare iura maritis: Oppida moliri,leges incidere ligno.
units.tr: Amphion too, said to be the founder of the city of Thebes, moved stones with the sound of his lyre and led them by winning prayer wherever he wished. This was once the wisdom: to separate public from private, sacred from profane, to forbid wandering sexual union, to give laws to husbands, to build towns, and to carve laws on wood.

units.la: Hic, vi eloquentiae, suasit rudibus ac sparsim degentibus, in vnum vt conuenirent,ciuitatémque muro cingerent: vel, vt interpretatur Palephatus, lyrae beneficio Thebanum murum construxit.
units.tr: Here, by the power of eloquence, he persuaded rough people living scattered about to come together into one place and surround their city with a wall; or, as Palaephatus explains, he built the Theban wall by the benefit of the lyre.

units.la: NIOBE filia Tantali, soror Pelopis vxórque Amphionis fuit,cui elegantissimae formae filios septe ac filias totidem peperit: vnde se Latonae praetulit: quare indignata Dea hanc in saxum mutauit ( vt fabulantur Poëtae) occisis prius ab Apolline omnibus suis liberis. Ouid.6.lib.Metamorph.Diodor.lib.5.Palephatus inde datu locum fabulae scribit, quòd supra natorum suorum sepulchrum suam ipsius lapideam imaginem Niobe collocarit, eámq; se efferit ipse quoque Palephatus inspexisse imaginem. RA . DELBO [?] BARACH
units.tr: NIOBE, daughter of Tantalus, sister of Pelops and wife of Amphion, bore him seven sons and as many daughters, of most elegant beauty. Hence she preferred herself to Latona. For this the goddess, indignant, changed her into stone (as the poets fable), after Apollo had first killed all her children. Ovid, Metamorphoses book 6; Diodorus, book 5. Palaephatus writes that the occasion for the fable was that Niobe set up her own stone image above the tomb of her children, and Palaephatus himself says he saw the image. RA . DELBO [?] BARACH

units.la: DEBORA Prophetissa, vxor Lapidoth, Israëliticum populum iudicauit anno à mundo condito 2659. ante Christum natum 1303. Hæc Barac exercitui suo præfecit, atque vnà cum eo aduersus Sisaram, ducè exercitus Iabin, Regis Chananæorum, commigrauit: fusa ac prostrata aduersariorum acie, Sisara ipse præceps de curru delapsus, fugam arripuit, atque à muliere Iahel susceptus, & statim epoto lacte obdormiens, defixo per tempora clauo, ab eadem caput cõsuitur, somnóque soporiferum lethum adiicitur. Vide librum Iudicum, capite tertio.
units.tr: DEBORAH, prophetess, wife of Lappidoth, judged the people of Israel in the year of the world 2659, before the birth of Christ 1303. She placed Barak in command of her army and marched with him against Sisera, general of the army of Jabin, king of the Canaanites. When the enemy line was routed and overthrown, Sisera himself fell headlong from his chariot and fled. He was received by the woman Jael, and falling asleep at once after drinking milk, he was struck through the temple with a fixed nail, and his head was pinned down by her, and a deadly sleep was added to it. See the book of Judges, chapter 4.

units.la: BARAC filius Abinoam, de tribu Nepthalim, præfectus fuit exercitui Deboræ, sicuti supra dictũ à me est. hic Dux fortissimus, decem hominum millibus tantùm assumptis, exercitum Sisaræ, longè copiosiorem, imò bis decies ampliorem ad vnum confecit, ac deleuit. Verùm enimuerò, spes ac fiducia in Deum obsirmatissima, præcipua ac potiora erant arma & vires, quibus freti Debora & Barac, insolescētes hostes eneruarunt. Videto lib. Iudicum ca. 4. & Iosephum li. Antiquitatum 5. ca. 9:
units.tr: BARAK, son of Abinoam, of the tribe of Naphtali, was put in command of Deborah's army, as I said above. This most brave leader, taking only ten thousand men, destroyed and annihilated the army of Sisera, far more numerous, indeed twenty times larger. Indeed, hope and trust in God most firmly fixed were the chief and greatest weapons, and relying on these Deborah and Barak wore down the arrogant enemy. See the book of Judges, chapter 4, and Josephus, Antiquities book 5, chapter 9.

units.la: GEDEON, qui & Ierobaal, filius fuit Ioas, de tribu Ma- nasse, iudicauit populum 40. annis, quorum primus, annus erat mundi 2699. ante Christum natum 1263.
units.tr: GIDEON, also called Jerubbaal, was the son of Joash, of the tribe of Manasseh. He judged the people for 40 years, the first of which was the year of the world 2699, before the birth of Christ 1263.

units.la: Hic priusquam aduersus Madianitas contenderet, bis signum à Deo petiit, quò certior fieret se ab eo mitti. duobus itaque miraculis cõfirmatur: prius fuit in holocausto quod totum ignis absumpsit: posterius in vellere primùm humido, deinde sicco. Sic roborata fide, in prælium descendit, ac Oreb & Zeb, Madianitarum Duces, item Zebee (seu Zeba) & Zalmana, cæcidit, ac internitioni dedit, asserens in libertate Israëliticum populum, qui sub illorum iugum ante annos septem missus fuerat. Vide lib. Iudi. cap. 6. 7. & 9. & Iosephum lib. Antiq. 5. cap. 10.
units.tr: Before he marched against the Midianites he twice asked God for a sign, so that he might be more certain that he was sent by him. He was therefore confirmed by two miracles: first, the burnt offering, which fire consumed entirely; second, the fleece, first wet and then dry. With faith thus strengthened, he went down into battle and struck down and put to slaughter Oreb and Zeeb, leaders of the Midianites, and likewise Zebah (or Zeba) and Zalmunna, declaring that the people of Israel, who had been sent under their yoke seven years before, were set free. See the book of Judges, chapters 6, 7 and 9, and Josephus, Antiquities book 5, chapter 10.

units.la: ABIMELECH Gedeonis filius ex Droma concubina, septuaginta fratres suos, depto natu minimo, interfecit: popu- lum administrauit ac iudicauit annos tres, quorum primus, an- nus erat mundi 2739. ante Christum natum 1223.
units.tr: ABIMELECH, son of Gideon by a concubine from Shechem, killed his seventy brothers, except the youngest. He governed and judged the people for three years, the first of which was the year of the world 2739, before the birth of Christ 1223.

units.la: Hic vrbem Sichem expugnauit, incolas occidit, quorum vrbe diruit, ita vt sal in ea euersa spargeret. Ceterum turrim oppidi Thebes dum oppugnat, ostiumque exurere nititur, à muliere, quae illi fragmen molae in caput deiicit, opprimitur: & ne à foemina trucidatus dicatur, quendam ex suis militibus rogat vt gladio transfodiatur: quod & ille perficit. Sic miserè occumbit, qui fratrum suorum caede pollutus, tyrannide principatum arripuerat. Vide Iudi. 9. cap.
units.tr: He stormed the city of Shechem, killed its inhabitants, and destroyed the city, so that he sowed salt on the overthrown site. But while he was attacking the tower of the town of Thebez and trying to set fire to the gate, he was crushed by a woman who dropped a piece of millstone on his head. So that he would not be said to have been slain by a woman, he asked one of his soldiers to run him through with a sword, and this he did. Thus he miserably perished, who, polluted by the slaughter of his brothers, had seized the rule by tyranny. See Judges, chapter 9.

units.la: THOLA de tribu Issachar, iudicauit populum an. 23. post Abimelech. Iudicum cap. 10.
units.tr: THOLA, of the tribe of Issachar, judged the people for 23 years after Abimelech. Judges, chapter 10.

units.la: IAIR Galaadites populum iudicauit ann. 22. post ipsum Thola. Vide vt supra & Iose. lib. Anti. 5. ca. 12. PHENIS EVROPA FIL. MINOS CRE.R.[?]
units.tr: JAIR the Gileadite judged the people for 22 years after Thola himself. See above, and Josephus, Antiquities book 5, chapter 12. PHENIS EVROPA FIL. MINOS CRE.R.[?]

units.la: EVROPA Agenoris Phœnicum regis filia fuit, quam Iuppiter fingitur in formam bouis rapuisse, ac per mare in Cretam trānsuexisse[?]: ex qua tres genuerit liberos, Minoem, Rhadamanthum, Sarpedonem. Vide Diodo.Sicu.lib.5.Ouid.li.2.Metamor. circa finem. Interpretatur fabulam Palephatus de Cretensi quodam, cui nomen erat Taurus, qui Europam captiuam abduxerit.
units.tr: EUROPA was the daughter of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians. Jupiter is feigned to have seized her in the form of a bull and carried her across the sea to Crete, and by her he is said to have had three children: Minos, Rhadamanthus and Sarpedon. See Diodorus Siculus, book 5, and Ovid, Metamorphoses book 2, near the end. Palaephatus interprets the fable as concerning a certain Cretan named Taurus, who carried off Europa as a captive.

units.la: Ab hac Europa, fertur tertia orbis pars denominata, quanquam non assentiat Herodotus, qui neminem cōpertum habere dicat, vnde id tertiæ orbis parti nomen datum. Vide Herodotum lib.4.
units.tr: From this Europa the third part of the world is said to have been named, although Herodotus does not agree, saying that no one has discovered where the name given to the third part of the world came from. See Herodotus, book 4.

units.la: MINOS, Iouis Asterij & Europæ filius, anno à creatione mundi 2710. ante Christum natum 1252. classem comparauit, mare obtinuit, & insularum Cycladū dominus primus, in earū plerisq; colonias posuit, Caribus eiectis, filiósq; suos constituit principes: latrones è mari sustulit. Thucyd.in præfatione historiæ suæ. Hic omnium cōsensu habitus est vir iustus, & probatæ vitæ, tradunt persuasisse primùm scriptis vti legibus, sinxisse autem eas Mercurij datas præcepto, autore Ioue. Diodor. Sicul.lib.2.& 6. De huius Sapientia. vide Diony.Halica.lib.2.in gestis Numæ. Volater.lib.33.sic ait: Minos certè ob summam iustitiam, post mortem iudex apud inferos dictus est, vnà cum Rhadamantho fratre.
units.tr: MINOS, son of Jupiter Asterius and Europa, in the year from the creation of the world 2710, before the birth of Christ 1252, equipped a fleet, gained control of the sea, and was the first lord of the Cyclades islands; he founded colonies on most of them, expelling the Carians, and set up his sons as rulers. He cleared the sea of pirates. Thucydides in the preface to his history. He was held by general consent to be a just man of approved life. They relate that he was the first to persuade people to use written laws, and that he gave out that these laws had been given by the command of Mercury, at the authority of Jupiter. Diodorus Siculus, books 2 and 6. On his wisdom see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2, in the deeds of Numa. Volaterranus, book 33, says: Minos, certainly on account of his supreme justice, after death was called a judge among the dead, together with his brother Rhadamanthus.

units.la: ANDROGEVS, Minoïs filius, præclaræ indolis adolescens, ab Athenien-sibus, quòd in athletica superasset, occiditur: idque causa belli extitit. Volater.lib.33. THEBANVS HERCVLES DEIANIRA
units.tr: ANDROGEUS, son of Minos, a youth of distinguished character, was killed by the Athenians because he had surpassed them in athletics; and this became the cause of war. Volaterranus, book 33. THEBAN HERCULES DEIANIRA

units.la: HERCVLES Iouis & Alcmenæ, Amphitryonis vxoris, (vt fertur) filius, natus est anno mundi 2715. ante Christum natum 1247. vixit annos 52. periit igne, primus è maximis pyratis. autor Manetho. De hoc Hercule quem Græci suum vendicãt, multa ipsi prædicant aut potius fabulantur, quæ nunc locus enarrandi non est: huic suo, omnium aliorum Herculum egregia facinora tribuunt, vt assolet. Huius labores duodecim, qui dicũtur fuisse præcipui, à Diodoro Siculo amplissimè describuntur libr. 5. Hic ab Hispaniis in Italiam venit anno 55. ante aduetum Aeneæ: Cacum interemit: Italis leges tradidit: Ilium cepit: Laomedonta, ob minimè persolutum præmium, interemit: Priamum interempti filium, Troiæ Regem constituit. tandem ob remedium morbi ardentissimi, in ardentes flammas se præcipitem dedit. Sic fato functus est virorum omniũ fortissimus. Diony.Halic.lib.1.dicit optimum hunc duce tyrannis orbem purgasse. Diodor.Herodo.Verg.Ouid. singuli multis in locis multa de Hercule narrant.
units.tr: HERCULES, son (as it is said) of Jupiter and Alcmena, the wife of Amphitryon, was born in the year of the world 2715, before the birth of Christ 1247. He lived 52 years and perished by fire, the first of the greatest pyres; the authority is Manetho. Concerning this Hercules, whom the Greeks claim as their own, they themselves tell, or rather fable, many things, which there is now no place to narrate. To this one they attribute the outstanding deeds of all the other Herculeses, as is customary. His twelve labours, which are said to have been the most important, are described at great length by Diodorus Siculus, book 5. He came from Spain to Italy in the year 55 before the arrival of Aeneas; he killed Cacus; he gave laws to the Italians; he took Troy; he killed Laomedon, because he had not paid the promised reward in full; he made Priam, the son of the slain man, king of Troy. At last, to find relief from a most burning sickness, he threw himself headlong into the blazing flames. Thus he met his end, the bravest of all men. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, says that this best of leaders cleansed the world of tyrants. Diodorus, Herodotus, Virgil and Ovid each narrate many things about Hercules in many places.

units.la: DEIANIRA, Oenei Calydoniæ regis filia, vxor Herculis fuit. Hæc cupiens virum ab alienis amoribus auocare, misit ad illum venenatã tunicam, iuxta Nessi cõsilium: tandem calamitatis mariti certior facta, ipsáq; doli huius minimè cõscia, laqueo vitam finiuit, vt scribit Diodor.lib.5. SIB PERSICA LIBYCA · SIB.
units.tr: DEIANIRA, daughter of Oeneus, king of Calydon, was the wife of Hercules. Wishing to call her husband away from other loves, she sent him a poisoned tunic, on the advice of Nessus. Finally, when she learned of her husband's calamity, and being herself by no means aware of the deceit, she ended her life with a noose, as Diodorus writes, book 5. SIB PERSICA LIBYCA · SIB.

units.la: SIBYLLA Persica,Chaldæa ac Hebrea dicta, sed proprio nomine Sambetha, ad mare rubrum nata est, patre Berosso, matre Erymantha: libros scripsit 84. ac de Christo innumera cecinit, cui cæteræ Sibyllæ concinunt: nam omnium primam fuisse perhibent. huius meminit Nicanor, qui res gestas Alexandri magni scripsit. Vide Lactan.diuina. instit. lib.1. cap.6.& August.de Ciuit. Dei lib.18. cap.23. Huic Sibyllæ hæc tribuitur prophetia: Ecce bestia conculcaberis, & gignetur dominus in orbe terrarum,& gremium virginis érit salus gentium:& pedes eius in valetudine hominum, & inuisibile verbum palpabitur.
units.tr: The Persian Sibyl, also called Chaldean and Hebrew, but whose proper name was Sambetha, was born by the Red Sea, the daughter of Berosus and Erymantha. She wrote 84 books and sang innumerable things about Christ, with whom the other Sibyls agree; for they say she was the first of them all. Nicanor, who wrote the deeds of Alexander the Great, mentions her. See Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 1, chapter 6, and Augustine, City of God, book 18, chapter 23. To this Sibyl the following prophecy is ascribed: Behold, you will be trampled by a beast, and the Lord will be born in the world, and the virgin's bosom will be the salvation of the nations; his feet will be in the weakness of men, and the invisible Word will be touched.

units.la: SIBYLLA Libyca,seu Libyssa, secunda fuisse scribitur à Marc. Varrone, in libris rerum diuinarū, qui Sibyllinos libros ait non vnius tantum fuisse Sibyllæ, sed Sibyllinos appellari, quòd omnes fœminæ vates,Sibyllæ sint à veteribus nucupatæ: vel à consiliis Deorum enuntiandis,iuxta etymologiam, more quidem loquendi Aeolico, σίες[?] enim Deos, ac βουλὴ[?], consilium vocant Aeoles: vel ab vnius Delphidis nomine. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: The Libyan, or Libyssan, Sibyl is written of, by Marcus Varro in his books on divine matters, as the second. He says that the Sibylline books were not the work of one Sibyl alone, but are called Sibylline because the ancients named all women prophetesses "Sibyls": either from the proclaiming of the counsels of the gods, according to etymology, in the Aeolic manner of speaking (for the Aeolians call the gods sies [σίες?] and counsel boule [βουλή?]), or from the name of a single Delphian woman. See above.
To this Sibyl the following prophecy is ascribed:

units.la: Ecce veniet dies , & illuminabit dominus condensa tenebrarum , & nexus synagogæ soluetur, & desinent labia hominum,cùm viderint Regem viuentium: & tenebit illum in gremio virgo domina gentium , & regnabit in misericordia:& vterus matris eius erit statera cunctorum.inde in manus iniquas veniet & dabunt Deo alapas manibus incestis : miserabilis , & ignominiosus erit, miserabilibúsque spem præbebit.
units.tr: Behold, the day will come, and the Lord will light up the thick darkness, and the bonds of the synagogue will be loosed, and the lips of men will fall silent when they see the King of the living; and a virgin, the mistress of the nations, will hold him in her bosom, and he will reign in mercy; and the womb of his mother will be the balance of all things. Then he will come into wicked hands, and they will give blows to God with unclean hands. He will be wretched and dishonoured, yet he will offer hope to the wretched.

units.la: SIBYLLA Delphica, Delphis nata, proprio nomine Themis dicta, ante Troianum excidiū extitisse fertur, cuius etiam versus plurimos operi suo Homerū inseruisse credunt. Sunt tamen interim qui censeant Sibyllæ propriū id illi fuisse nomen, quod in reliquas manarit: vti supra in Libyca Sibylla leuiter attigi. Vide supra in Sibyllis Persica, & Libyca.
units.tr: The Delphic Sibyl, born at Delphi, whose proper name was Themis, is said to have existed before the fall of Troy; and they believe Homer inserted many of her verses into his work. Yet there are some who think that this was her own name, which afterwards spread to the rest; as I touched on lightly above under the Libyan Sibyl. See above under the Persian and Libyan Sibyls.
To her the following prophecy is ascribed:

units.la: Ipsum tuum cognosce dominū, qui verè filius Dei est. Hanc item Chrysippus ait vaticinatam esse, Nasci debere Prophetam absque matris (vel maris) coitu, de virgine.
units.tr: Know your own Lord, who is truly the Son of God. Chrysippus also says that she prophesied the following: A Prophet must be born of a virgin, without the union of a mother (or of a man).

units.la: SIBYLLA Cumæa, ex Cimerio Campaniæ, vicino Cumis oppido, fuit: Italica proinde ac Cimeria dicta. prope Cumas spelunca inhabitauit, vnde oracula edere solita: vt Aeneæ quoque adeuti, futura prædixerit omnia. huius carmina apud Aenā ciuitatem Iuliano imperante cōbusta scribit Am. Marcellinus: quæ sane carmina, quibus Rom. fata conscripta erant, in arcanis apud Rom. habebantur, nec ab vllo nisi à Quindecim viris inspici fas erat: cum aliarum interim Sibyllarū carmina circumferre liceret. audi Verg. Eclog. 4.
units.tr: The Cumaean Sibyl came from Cimmerium in Campania, a town near Cumae; hence she is called Italian as well as Cimmerian. She lived in a cave near Cumae, whence she was accustomed to give oracles; and when she had met Aeneas, she foretold all future events. Ammianus Marcellinus writes that her songs were burned at the city of Aenaria under the emperor Julian. These songs, in which the fates of Rome were written, were kept secret among the Romans, and no one but the Fifteen Men was permitted to inspect them, although at other times it was lawful to circulate the songs of the other Sibyls. Hear Virgil, Eclogue 4:
Now has come the last age of the Cumaean song, etc.

units.la: Scilicet (inquit Viues) tempus etiam quo vaticinium tendebat, certis erat literis insertum: & solitas Sibyllas aliquid per initia versuum significare, scribit Cice. lib. 2. de diuina.
units.tr: Clearly (says Vives), the time to which the prophecy pointed was also set down in fixed letters; and Cicero, in book 2 of On Divination, writes that the usual Sibyls signified something by the initial letters of the verses.
To her the following prophecy is ascribed:

units.la: In prima facie virginis ascendit puella, pulchra facie, prolixa capillis, sedens super sedem stratam: nutrit puerum, dans ei ad comedendū ius proprium, id est lac de cœlo missum.
units.tr: In the first face a virgin ascends, a girl of beautiful face, with long hair, sitting upon a spread throne: she nourishes a child, giving him for food her own broth, that is, milk sent from heaven.

units.la: NICOSTRATA, Euandri Archadis mater,futurorum vaticinatrix fuit,quę à carminibus,quibus Phoebi oracula enūtiabat,Carmentis latinè dicta fuit. Hanc quidam aiunt latinis primùm literas dedisse. Diony.Halicarnafeus lib. quidè 1. Antiq.Rom.scribit ipsos Archades primos literas in Italiam attulisse,qui post Pelasgos venerant. Tit.Liuius Euandrum ipsum, autorem vocat,lib. ab vrbe condita 1. Euāder(inquit)tum ea,profugus ex Peloponnefo,autoritate magis quàm imperio regebat loca,venerabilis vir miraculo literarū,rei nouæ inter rudes artium homines. Huic concinit Cornelius Tacitus,qui tradit Aborigenes ab Euādro Archade didicisse literas. Vide Poly. Verg.li.1.cap.6. Hāc quoque scribit Textor Græcas literas impensè doctam, plerasque ex latinis primùm reperisse: quò coniectare licet mulierē versatili ingenio,variáque doctrina fuisse præditam.
units.tr: Nicostrata, mother of Evander the Arcadian, was a prophetess of future events; from the songs with which she announced the oracles of Phoebus she was called Carmenta in Latin. Some say that she first gave letters to the Latins. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, writes that the Arcadians themselves, who had come after the Pelasgians, first brought letters into Italy. Livy calls Evander himself the author, in book 1 of From the Foundation of the City: Evander (he says) then, an exile from the Peloponnese, ruled the places by authority rather than by command, a venerable man, and a marvel for his letters, a new thing among people rude in the arts. Cornelius Tacitus agrees with this, who relates that the Aborigines learned letters from Evander the Arcadian. See Polydorus Vergilius, book 1, chapter 6. Textor also writes that she was greatly learned in Greek letters, and that most of them were first discovered from Latin ones; from which one may conjecture that the woman was endowed with a versatile mind and varied learning.

units.la: EVANDER huius Nicostratæ, seu Carmentis, filius, cùm patrem imprudes interfecisset,relicta Archadia in Italiam venit,& pulsis Aborigenibus in Palatino monte cōsedit: agróque à Fauno iuniore Aborigenum Rege donatus, collem elegit,qui nunc in medio fermè vrbis est,in quo castellū seu oppidum extruxit,cui Pallantium,seu Pallanteū,nomen dedit, vel à Metropoli Archadię,vel de Pallantis proaui sui nomine circa annum mundi 2725. ante Christum natum 1237.paulò nempe ante quàm Hercules in Italiam ab Hispaniis aduentaret. Pallantium,Rom.postea Palatium dixere. Vide Diony.Halic.lib.1. & Cæli.Rhodi.lib.11.cap.17.& Vergi.lib.Enei.8.vbi sic inquit:
units.tr: Evander, son of this Nicostrata, or Carmenta, having unwittingly killed his father, left Arcadia and came to Italy; and, the Aborigines having been driven out, he settled on the Palatine hill. Given land by Faunus the Younger, king of the Aborigines, he chose the hill which is now roughly in the middle of the city, and there built a fortress or town, which he named Pallantium, or Palanteum, either after the metropolis of Arcadia or after the name of his great-grandfather Pallas, about the year of the world 2725, before the birth of Christ 1237, shortly before Hercules came to Italy from Spain. Pallantium was afterwards called by the Romans Palatium. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, and Caelius Rhodiginus, book 11, chapter 17, and Virgil, Aeneid book 8, where he says:

units.la: Archades his oris,genus à Pallante profectum, Qui Regem Euandrum comites,qui signa secuti, Delegere locum,& posuere in mentibus vrbem, Pallantis proaui de nomine,Pallanteum.
units.tr: The Arcadians came to these shores, a race descended from Pallas, who, following their king Evander, his companions, and his standards, chose a place and in their minds founded a city, named Pallanteum after the name of Pallas their great-grandfather.

units.la: PRIAMVS Laomedontis filius, interfecto patre ab Hercule, Troiaq; vi capta, regnum patris recepit, quod ei Hercules tradidit vt viro iusto, amicoque. Solus enim filiorum patri confuluerat equos diuino femine procreatos (si credere fas est) Herculi, ob liberatam Hesionem promissos, tradendos. Hæc Diod. Sic. lib. 5. Sunt tamen qui scribant Priamū captiuum ab Hercule abductum in Græciā, postea auro à vicinis re-demptum, vnde à redimendo nomen obtinuerit. Habuit filios quinquaginta:vnde Vergi.
units.tr: Priam, son of Laomedon, after his father was killed by Hercules and Troy taken by force, recovered the kingdom of his father, which Hercules handed over to him as to a just man and a friend. For he alone of his sons had advised his father to give to Hercules the horses born of divine seed (if it is right to believe it), which had been promised for the rescue of Hesione. Diodorus Siculus, book 5, relates this. Yet some write that Priam was carried off captive to Greece by Hercules, and afterwards ransomed with gold by his neighbours, whence he obtained the name from ransoming. He had fifty sons, whence Virgil:
Those fifty bridal chambers, such great hope of grandchildren.

units.la: ex his decē & septē sustulit ex iusta vxore Hecuba: inter quos insigniores fuere Hector, Paris, Deiphobus, Helenus, Polites, Polydorus. Capta vrbe à Græcis, interemptus est Priamus senex, à Pyrrho Achillis filio: ídque ad aram Iouis, in sanguine etiam Politæ filij sui. autor Dictys Cretensis. Troiæ Priamus regnat anno mundi 2725. ante Christum natum 1237. quam ita ampliauit & ornauit vt nulli maximarum vrbium ornatu & potentia cederet.
units.tr: Of these he begot seventeen by his lawful wife Hecuba; among them the most distinguished were Hector, Paris, Deiphobus, Helenus, Polites, and Polydorus. When the city was taken by the Greeks, old Priam was slain by Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, at the altar of Jupiter, even in the blood of his son Polites. The authority is Dictys of Crete. Priam reigned over Troy in the year of the world 2725, before the birth of Christ 1237, and he enlarged and adorned it so that it yielded to none of the greatest cities in splendour and power.

units.la: HECVBA Cissei regis Thracum filia, vxor Priami fuit. Hæc cùm Paridem in vtero gestaret, somniauit se parere facem ardentem, quæ patriam exureret. Hanc in canem versam fabulantur, quòd cùm vrbe capta, captiua abduceretur, ac Polydori filij corpus in mare proiectum agnosceret, Græcos inanibus lacessiuerit conuiciis. Vergil. Aen. 10. lib. Ouid. 13. Metamorpho.
units.tr: Hecuba, daughter of Cisseus, king of the Thracians, was the wife of Priam. When she was carrying Paris in her womb, she dreamed that she gave birth to a burning torch which would set fire to her country. They tell the fable that she was changed into a dog, because when the city was taken she was led away captive and, recognising the body of her son Polydorus cast into the sea, she assailed the Greeks with empty reproaches. See Virgil, Aeneid book 10, and Ovid, Metamorphoses book 13.

units.la: HECTOR Priami filiorum fortisimus fuit, quo sospite Troia nunquam potuit à Græcis expugnari. Hic permultos ex Græcis occidit,inter quos Protesilaum & Patroclum : in cuius vltionē ab Achille demum occiditur,à quo bigis alligatus,circum Patrocli sepulchrū trahitur. post 12. dies corpus eius auro à patre redimitur.autor Dares Phrygius.Home.lib.23 Ilia.Ver. lib.1.Aenei.Volaterr.lib.15.
units.tr: Hector was the bravest of the sons of Priam; while he was safe, Troy could never be stormed by the Greeks. He killed very many of the Greeks, among them Protesilaus and Patroclus. In revenge for him he was at last killed by Achilles, by whom he was tied to a chariot and dragged around the tomb of Patroclus. After twelve days his body was ransomed with gold by his father. The authority is Dares the Phrygian. Homer, Iliad book 23; Virgil, Aeneid book 1; Volaterranus, book 15.

units.la: ANDROMACHE, Eetionis Regis Thebarum,quæ in Cilicia sunt,filia,Hectoris vxor castissima , & Astyanactis mater fuit:quem peperit post inchoatū bellum Græcorum, & admodùm paruulum abscōdit:at verò ab Vlysse repertus, de turri ab eodem præcipitatur.mater autē à Pirrho abducta in Græciam,Molossum ex eo parit, deinde Heleno in vxorem datur: eíque regni Epiri portio assignatur. Vide Volaterran. lib. 8. & 13. Strab. lib. 7. Vergil. lib. 3. Aene. Porrò de supputatione annorum facile est cuiuis vel mediocriter docto, rationem inire quo tempore gesta sint nonnulla,quibus annorū numeros non inserui,cùm iidem numeri annorum hinc inde paulùm absint. id te semel monitum volui,candide lector, vt 'ne mihi succenseas , aut vitio vertas, si singulis epitomis aut paginis,supputationem hanc in nonnullis quidem minimè necessariam ( sunt enim multa quæ in idē tempus coincidunt)anxiè non obseruo, nec iterato repono. THESEVS MINOTAVRVS[?]
units.tr: Andromache, daughter of Eetion, king of Thebes in Cilicia, was the most chaste wife of Hector and the mother of Astyanax. She bore him after the Greek war had begun, and while he was still very small she hid him; but he was found by Ulysses and thrown down from a tower by him. The mother, however, was carried off to Greece by Pyrrhus, and bore him Molossus, and was afterwards given in marriage to Helenus, and a portion of the kingdom of Epirus was assigned to her. See Volaterranus, books 8 and 13; Strabo, book 7; Virgil, Aeneid book 3. Moreover, it is easy for anyone who is even moderately learned to work out, from the reckoning of years, at what time some of the events took place, for which I have not inserted the numbers of years, since the same numbers of years differ little here and there. I wished you to be told this once, kind reader, so that you may not be angry with me or find fault if, in the individual epitomes or pages, I do not anxiously observe this reckoning, which in some cases is by no means necessary (for many things coincide in the same time), nor do I repeat it.

units.la: THESEVS Ægei Athenárum Regis filius , ex Æthra Pithei filia, regnauit Athenis anno mundi 2730. ante Christum natum 1232. Hic Herculem imitatus,mare ingressus est: ad ea certamina adiecit animum, quæ laudem & gloriam sibi essent allatura: iuuenis adhuc Creontem tyrannum occîdit: præterea taurum vastantem Atticam, & Minotaurum: item Scyronem,Procruftem,& Schynin latrones, in Attica trucidauit. Cum Hercule aduersus Amazonas strenuè militauit, quarum reginam Hippolyten abduxit, ex qua filium Hippolytum sustulit. Iustin lib.2. Diodor.lib.5.Plutarc. in vita Thesei,Ouid. epist.4.& 10. Hic firmam amicitiam cum Pirithoo iunxit.
units.tr: THESEUS, son of Aegeus, King of Athens, by Aethra, daughter of Pittheus, reigned at Athens in the year of the world 2730, before the birth of Christ 1232. Imitating Hercules, he went out to sea; he applied his mind to those enterprises which would bring him praise and glory. While still a young man, he killed the tyrant Creon; besides, in Attica he slew the bull that laid waste Attica, and the Minotaur, likewise the robbers Sciron, Procrustes and Sinis. He fought vigorously with Hercules against the Amazons, and carried off their queen Hippolyte, by whom he begot a son, Hippolytus. See Justin, book 2; Diodorus, book 5; Plutarch, in the Life of Theseus; Ovid, Epistles 4 and 10. He also formed a firm friendship with Pirithous.

units.la: MINOTAVRVS, filius fuit Pasiphaë, & iuuenis cuiusdam formosissimi,nomine Tauri,qui, morbo laborante Minoë marito Pasiphaës,cum hac concubuit, peperitque Pasiphaë ipsa ex eo concubitu filium,qui inde Minotaurus dictus est,quòd cùm Minoïs filius putaretur , revera tamen Tauri filius esset: quem ideo Minos relegauit,atque insectatus est:ad quem tandem Theseû misit, qui accepto ense ab Ariadne , eum occîdit. Hæc Palephatus libro de non credendis fabulosis narrationibus. De hoc Minotauro multa fabulantur Poëtæ, quòd semiuir, ac semibos fuerit, vnde Ouid.
units.tr: MINOTAUR was the son of Pasiphae and a certain most handsome young man named Taurus, who lay with her while Minos, Pasiphae's husband, was ill. Pasiphae herself bore a son from that union, who was therefore called Minotaur, because although he was thought to be the son of Minos, he was in fact the son of Taurus. Minos therefore banished him and hunted him down; at last he sent Theseus against him, who, having received a sword from Ariadne, killed him. So Palaephatus tells it in his book On Incredible Stories. The poets tell many fables about this Minotaur, that he was half man and half bull, whence Ovid:

units.la: quòd Labyrintho, à Dædalo fabrefacto inclusus , obiectos sibi homines deuorarit. Vergil.lib.6. Ænei.Ouid.epist.10. AMAZ·R· MARTHESIA LAMPEDO AMAZ·R·
units.tr: Because he was shut up in the Labyrinth, built by Daedalus, and devoured the men set before him. See Virgil, Aeneid book 6; Ovid, Epistle 10. AMAZON: MARTHESIA, LAMPEDO, AMAZON

units.la: MARTHESIA, siue Marpesia, & Lampedo, siue Lampeto, Reginæ fuere Amazonum, regnante Theseo Athenis: nempe anno mundi 2734. ante Christum natum 1228. autoribus Iustin. lib. 2. & Oros. lib. 1. cap. 15. & 16. Funccius verò reiicit ad annum mundi 2754. ante Christum natum 1208. hæ in duas partes, exercitu diviso, inclytæ iam opibus, vicissim bella gerebant: & ne successibus deesset autoritas, generatas se Marte prædicabant. Itaque maiore parte Europæ subacta, Asiæ quoque nonnullas civitates occupauere. ibi Ephesum, multásque alias urbes cõdidere: tandem ibi Marthesia incursu barbarorum interficitur, in cuius locum Orithya filia succedit. Iustin. lib. 2. Oros. lib. 1. cap. 15.
units.tr: MARTHESIA, or Marpesia, and Lampedo, or Lampeto, were queens of the Amazons in the reign of Theseus at Athens, namely in the year of the world 2734, before the birth of Christ 1228, on the authority of Justin, book 2, and Orosius, book 1, chapters 15 and 16. Funccius, however, places it in the year of the world 2754, before the birth of Christ 1208. These, having divided their army into two parts, and already famous for their wealth, waged war in turn; and so that their successes might not lack authority, they declared that they were sprung from Mars. Thus, with the greater part of Europe subdued, they also occupied several cities of Asia. There they founded Ephesus and many other cities. At last Marthesia was killed in an incursion of barbarians, and her daughter Orithyia succeeded her. Justin, book 2; Orosius, book 1, chapter 15.

units.la: LAMPEDO, siue Lampeto Amazonum Regina, Epheso multisque aliis urbibus in Asia conditis, domum cum parte exercitus remittitur, ut patria tueatur. Cæterum de huius gestis, & fato nil apud autores reperi, quemadmodum nec ipse etiam Boccacius. De Amazonibus autem in genere pauca dicere lubet. Hæ ex Scythis ortæ, in Cappadociæ ora, ad amnem Thermodoonta consedere: ibi mariti, qui spoliare finitimos consuerant, conspiratione populorum per insidias trucidantur: ipsæ, quarum exilio addebatur orbitas, arma sumunt: remp. sine viris augent: matrimonium seruitutem appellant. tandem pace armis quæsita, ne gens interiret, finitimorum cõcubitum ineunt: si qui mares nascuntur, occidunt: virgines armis exercēt, dextris mammis inustis, ne sagittarum iactus impediatur, unde Amazones dictæ. Iustin. lib. 2. MENALIPPE AMAZO HIPPOL THESEI AΘ[?]
units.tr: LAMPEDO, or Lampeto, queen of the Amazons, after Ephesus and many other cities in Asia had been founded, was sent home with part of the army to defend her homeland. Otherwise, I have found nothing in the authors about her deeds and fate, nor indeed does Boccaccio say anything. I should like, however, to say a few things about the Amazons in general. They were descended from the Scythians, and settled on the coast of Cappadocia, by the river Thermodon. There their husbands, who were accustomed to plunder their neighbours, were butchered by a conspiracy of the peoples through an ambush; the women themselves, to whom widowhood was added by their exile, took up arms; they increased the state without men, and called marriage slavery. At last, having sought peace by arms, so that their race would not perish, they took neighbours as lovers; if any males were born, they killed them; the girls they trained in arms, having branded their right breasts, so that the throwing of arrows would not be hindered; whence they were called Amazons. Justin, book 2. MENALIPPE, AMAZON, HIPPOLYTE, THESEUS, ATHENS

units.la: MENALIPPE,Orithyæ ac Antiopes(hæ ambæ Amazonum reginæ erant)soror,ab Hercule bello superata,captiua abducitur:quam tandem sorori reginæ reddit: & pretium , arma eiusdem reginæ (Baltheum fuisse dicũt)accipit:atque ita mandato functus,ad Regem Eurystheum Hercules ipse,reuertitur. Vide Iustinum libr.2.
units.tr: MENALIPPE, sister of Orithyia and Antiope (both of whom were queens of the Amazons), was overcome in war by Hercules and led away captive; at last he gave her back to her sister the queen, and received as ransom the arms of the same queen (they say it was a belt), and so, having discharged his commission, Hercules himself returned to King Eurystheus. See Justin, book 2.

units.la: HIPPOLYTE, soror Orithyæ, Antiopes, & Menalippes, eodē ipso bello quo soror Menalippe ab Hercule capta,ac abducta est,hæc quoque à Thefeo capitur ac abducitur:Sed tamen eam in vxorē Thefeus accipit, ex eáque gignit Hippolytum,vti iam à me dictum est supra,in Thefeo.Iustin.lib 2.
units.tr: HIPPOLYTE, sister of Orithyia, Antiope and Menalippe, in the very same war in which her sister Menalippe was captured and carried off by Hercules, was also captured and carried off by Theseus. Nevertheless Theseus took her as his wife, and by her begot Hippolytus, as I have already said above, in the account of Theseus. Justin, book 2.

units.la: Nec verò nesciendū est, Hippolytum omnium castissimum fuisse,eundémque venationi deditissimū:de quo multa legere licet apud autores:maximè apud Ouidium li.15.Metamorpho item Heroidum epist.4.
units.tr: Nor indeed must it be unknown that Hippolytus was the most chaste of all and most devoted to hunting; much may be read about him in the authors, especially in Ovid, Metamorphoses book 15, and likewise Heroides, Epistle 4.

units.la: ORITHYA, Marthesiæ filia, Amazonum post matrem Regina, tum ob belli industriam, tum ob perpetuam virginitatem, conspicuam se, ac mirabilem præstitit. Hæc vbi coperit bellum, vim quoque sororibus suis illatam ab Hercule & Theseo, hortatur comites in vltionē, frustráque Ponti sinum & Asiam domitam esse dicit, si Græcorum non tam bellis quàm rapinis pateant. auxiliū à Rege Scytharum capit. Sed ante prœliū dissensione orta, ab auxiliis desertæ Amazones, bellóq; ab Atheniésibus victæ, receptaculum tamen habuere castra sociorum, in regnúmque reuersæ sunt. Iustin. lib. 2.
units.tr: ORITHYIA, daughter of Marthesia, after her mother was queen of the Amazons, distinguished herself and was admired both for her skill in war and for her perpetual virginity. When she began the war, she urged her companions to revenge, and said that the sinus of Pontus and Asia, though subdued, were nothing if the lands of the Greeks lay open not so much to wars as to plundering, and that the injury done to her sisters by Hercules and Theseus must be avenged. She obtained aid from the king of the Scythians. But before the battle a dissension arose, and the Amazons, deserted by their auxiliaries and defeated in war by the Athenians, nevertheless had the camp of their allies as a refuge, and returned to their kingdom. Justin, book 2. ## PENTHESILEA

units.la: PENTHESILEA post Orythiam Amazonis impera- uit. Hæc Troianis aduersus Græcos opem tulit. Verg. lib. Aen. 1.
units.tr: After Orithyia, Penthesilea ruled over the Amazons. She brought aid to the Trojans against the Greeks. Virgil, Aeneid book 1.

units.la: Ducit Amazonidum lunatis agmina peltis Penthesilea furens, mediisque in millibus ardet, Aurea subnectens exerta cingula mamma Bellatrix, audétque viris concurrere virgo.
units.tr: Penthesilea, raging, leads the troops of the Amazons with their crescent shields, and burns in the midst of the thousands, a warrior maiden, fastening a golden belt beneath her bared breast, and dares to fight with men.

units.la: Interfecta demum ab Achille, exercitúque eius absumpto, paucæ quæ remanserant vsque ad tempora Alexandri Magni durauerunt: quem Thalestris, Amazonum Regina, adiit, ad sobolem ex eo generandam. Hunc cum ter centum feminis salutauit, cæteris iussis subsistere, copiam sui fecit ei Alexander per tredecim dies. Hæc coram illi in os ingenuè fassa est se tantum ad suscipiēdos liberos venisse: fœminini sexus se retenturam, marem patri redditurā. reuersa in regnum, breui pòst tempore cum omni Amazonum nomine intercidit. Quint. Curt. lib. 6. Iustin. lib. 2. de hac vide etiam infra in Alexandro. MENELAVS REX SPAR. AGMEMNON REX MYC[?]
units.tr: At last, slain by Achilles and her army destroyed, the few who remained lasted until the time of Alexander the Great, whom Thalestris, queen of the Amazons, approached, in order to beget offspring from him. When she had greeted him with three hundred women, the rest being ordered to stay behind, Alexander granted her his company for thirteen days. She openly and frankly confessed to his face that she had come only to conceive children: she would keep the female sex, and return the male to his father. Returning to her kingdom, after a short time she perished, together with the whole name of the Amazons. Quintus Curtius, book 6; Justin, book 2; concerning her see also below, under Alexander. MENELAUS KING OF SPARTA, AGAMEMNON KING OF MYCENAE

units.la: MENELAVS, Atrei (alij dicunt Plisthenis) & Aeropes filius, in uxorem accepit Helenam formosissimā quidem mulierem, attamē quæ bis rapta est, primùm à Thefeo, postea à Paride. Hic Menelaus regnauit apud Lacedæmonios anno mundi 2758. ante Christum natum 1204. aduersus Troianos bellum gessit pro recuperanda uxore, quam non nisi capta Troia recuperauit. bellum gessit decem fere annis. præterea conscendens nauim in reditu, non nisi post octauum erroris annum patriam attigit. Tantæ molis erat infame reducere scortū. scribit nihilominus Dictys Cretensis non tam animo consternatum fuisse Menelaum ob raptam uxorem, quàm ob Aetram & Clymenam, affines suas. Sustulit ex Helena Hermionem. Dares Phry. Ouid. lib. 11. Metamorp. Cæterùm Menelaum Atrei filium Homerus scribit, Hesiodus autem, Plisthenis.
units.tr: MENELAUS, son of Atreus (others say of Plisthenes) and Aerope, took as his wife Helen, a woman indeed most beautiful, yet one who was carried off twice, first by Theseus, afterwards by Paris. This Menelaus reigned among the Lacedaemonians in the year of the world 2758, before the birth of Christ 1204. He waged war against the Trojans to recover his wife, whom he did not recover until Troy was taken. He carried on the war for about ten years. Moreover, embarking on the ship on his return, he reached his homeland only after the eighth year of wandering. Such was the infamy of bringing back a harlot from so great an enterprise. Nevertheless Dictys of Crete writes that Menelaus was troubled not so much in mind over the rape of his wife as over Aethra and Clymene, his relatives. He begot Hermione from Helen. Dares the Phrygian; Ovid, Metamorphoses book 11. Yet Homer writes that Menelaus was the son of Atreus, while Hesiod says he was the son of Plisthenes.

units.la: AGAMEMNON regnauit Mycœnis anno mundi 2768. ante Christum natum 1194. hic frater fuit Menelai: & omnium consensu Græcorum dux præcipuus aduersus Troianos declaratus est: classem habuit nauium sexaginta supra centum: uniuersa Græcorum classis erat nauium plus mille. Tandem reuersus ab expeditione illa, & bello Troiano confecto, ipse, insidiis Clytemestræ uxoris, ab Aegystho adultero interficitur: Orestésque filius eius hanc iniuriā ulcisci-tur, interfectis adulteris, matre scilicet Clytemnestra ac Aegystho. Euripid. in Oreste, Seneca in Agamemnone. Dares Phrygi. Dictys Cre. PARIS. ALEXAN. HELENA
units.tr: AGAMEMNON reigned at Mycenae in the year of the world 2768, before the birth of Christ 1194. He was the brother of Menelaus, and by the agreement of all the Greeks he was declared the chief leader against the Trojans. He had a fleet of sixty and more than a hundred ships; the whole fleet of the Greeks was more than a thousand ships. At last, returning from that expedition, and the Trojan war being finished, he was killed by Aegisthus, an adulterer, through the treachery of his wife Clytemnestra. His son Orestes avenged this injury, killing the adulterers, namely his mother Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. Euripides, in the Orestes; Seneca, in the Agamemnon. Dares the Phrygian; Dictys of Crete. PARIS, ALEXANDER, HELEN

units.la: PARIS, qui & Alexander dictus, Priami filius fuit & Hecubæ. Hunc pater exponi iussit, quòd mater prægnans somniasset se facem ardentem parere: attamen Hecuba materno assectu ducta, curauit ut in Ida monte à pastoribus nutriretur. Adolescens Oenonem amauit, ex qua Idæum & Daphnidem sustulit. Tandem à parentibus agnitus ac receptus, suscepit legationem in Græciam ad repetendam Hesionem, ubi Helenam rapuit, Troiamque abduxit anno mundi 2768. ante Christum natum 1194. nempe primo anno regni Agamemnonis. Propterea bellum Græcorum aduersus Troianos exarsit. Scribit Herodotus renitentem abduxisse, Spartenque expugnasse, ob id à viro recipi meruisse. Achillē sagitta interemit Paris, vicissim quoq; interemptus est à Pyrrho Achillis filio. Herodo. lib. 2. Dares, Dictys Cretensis.
units.tr: PARIS, also called Alexander, was the son of Priam and Hecuba. His father ordered him to be exposed, because his mother, while pregnant, had dreamed that she bore a burning torch; but Hecuba, moved by maternal affection, arranged for him to be brought up by shepherds on Mount Ida. As a young man he loved Oenone, by whom he begot Ideus and Daphnis. At last, recognised and received by his parents, he undertook an embassy to Greece to demand back Hesione, and there he carried off Helen and led her away to Troy, in the year of the world 2768, before the birth of Christ 1194, namely in the first year of the reign of Agamemnon. For this reason the war of the Greeks against the Trojans broke out. Herodotus writes that he carried her off against her will, and that she had taken Sparta by storm, and for this deserved to be taken back by her husband. Paris killed Achilles with an arrow; in turn he too was killed by Pyrrhus, son of Achilles. Herodotus, book 2; Dares; Dictys of Crete.

units.la: HELENA, Jouis & Ledæ filia, à Thefeo primùm rapta, nec multo post Castori & Polluci fratribus reddita, Menelai uxor fuit, cui Hermionem peperit: hanc Paris seu volentem seu nolentem abduxit, uti dictum à me supra est, ac in uxorem duxit. Hæc proditionis Troiæ cōscia fuisse dicitur, cum Greci armis diffidentes ad dolum se cōuertissent: ac facem, proditionis signum, ex arce sustulisse, & cum priore viro in gratiâ rediisse. De simulachro ac templo Helenæ, in quo mulier ex turpissima, speciosissima facta est, vide Herodotum libr. 6. Capta est Troia deficiente jam vere, 17. diebus ante conuersionem æstiuam, anno mundi 2783. ante Christum natum 1179. Vide Dionys. Halicar. GRECVS ULYSSES. PENELOPE ULY.CON.[?]
units.tr: HELENA, daughter of Jupiter and Leda, was first carried off by Theseus, and not long after was returned to her brothers Castor and Pollux. She became the wife of Menelaus, to whom she bore Hermione. Paris carried her off, whether she was willing or unwilling, as I have said above, and took her as his wife. She is said to have been privy to the betrayal of Troy, when the Greeks, distrusting their arms, turned to trickery; and that she raised a torch from the citadel, as a sign of the betrayal, and afterwards was reconciled with her former husband. Concerning the statue and temple of Helen, in which the woman was made from most shameful into most beautiful, see Herodotus, book 6. Troy was taken when spring was already failing, 17 days before the summer solstice, in the year of the world 2783, before the birth of Christ 1179. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus. GREEK. ULYSSES. PENELOPE. ULY.CON.[?]

units.la: ULYSSES Laërtæ & Anticliæ filius, Solers ac disertus extitit, atque prudentissimus Græcorum, qui in expeditione Troiæ fuerunt. Hic insaniam simulans comitatum negat, nempe irretitus amore iuvenculæ coniugis Penelopes: verùm fraude à Palamede detecta, cogitur cum cæteris in bellum proficisci. Detectus ipse, Achillem vicissim detegit, qui etiam in Troianos contendit, anno mundi 2773.ante Christum natum 1189. Ulysses multa tum fraude tum virtute peregit annis decem in obsidione Troiæ: qua capta, per decennium itidem hac atque illac fluctibus marinis iactatus, tandem ad uxorem in patriam pervenit: procorum iniurias ulciscitur. Postea à Telegono, quem ex Circe susceperat, spina trigonis piscis venenata, incognitus transfigitur. Homer. in Odyss. & Vergil.in Æne. multis in locis.
units.tr: ULYSSES, son of Laertes and Anticlea, was clever and eloquent, and the most prudent of the Greeks who took part in the expedition against Troy. Feigning madness, he refused to join the expedition, being ensnared, as it were, by love for his young wife Penelope; but when his deception was detected by Palamedes, he was forced to set out to war with the others. Having himself been exposed, he in turn exposed Achilles, who also marched against the Trojans, in the year of the world 2773, before the birth of Christ 1189. Ulysses accomplished much during the ten years of the siege of Troy, by both cunning and courage. After Troy was taken, he was likewise tossed for ten years by the sea waves hither and thither, and at last reached his wife and homeland, and avenged the wrongs of the suitors. Later, he was unknowingly pierced by Telegonus, whom he had begotten by Circe, with the poisonous spine of a sting-ray. See Homer, in the Odyssey, and Virgil, in the Aeneid, in many places.

units.la: PENELOPE, Icarij & Peribœæ filia, Ulyssis uxor fuit castissima. Hæc totos viginti annos maritum illibata pudicitia expectavit, nec unquam adduci potuit ut alteri nuberet: quanquam pater Icarius cogeret, & proci valde solicitarent, quos egregio commento fefellit (si credere licet) quanquam aliter de huius pudicitia scribat Lycophron. Vide Ovid. epist. Heroidum prima, quæ nomine Penelopes inscribitur. ACHILES. POLYCENA. F. PRI.
units.tr: PENELOPE, daughter of Icarius and Periboea, was the most chaste wife of Ulysses. She waited for her husband twenty whole years with unblemished chastity, and could never be persuaded to marry another, although her father Icarius pressed her and the suitors pursued her eagerly; these she deceived by a clever device (if we may believe it), although Lycophron writes otherwise of her chastity. See Ovid, the first of the Heroides, which is inscribed with the name of Penelope. ACHILLES. POLYXENA. F. PRI.

units.la: ACHILLES Pelei Thessaliæ regis & Thetidis filius, Græcorum fortissimus fuit. Hic iam adultus inter Lycomedis filias, muliebri indutus ornatu latitauit, opera matris quæ hac arte cavebat ne ad bellum Troianum proficisceretur, unde nō esset reversurus. Nihilominus tamen Ulyssis astu deprehensus, ad bellum perducitur. Hic Deïdamiam Lycomedis filiam compressit, ex qua Pyrrhum sustulit: quinetiam ob ereptam sibi ab Agamemnone Briseïda, pugnare destitit, donec Patrocli amicissimi mors nunciaretur, quam Hectoris morte compensauit. Cæterùm à Paride tum demum interficitur Achilles: tandem & ipse Pyrrhus Polyxenam ad sepulchrum patris immolat. Homer.in Odyss. & Vergil.lib. Eneid.2. & Statius libr. Thebaid.1. item Dares, & Dictys Cretensis.
units.tr: ACHILLES, son of Peleus, king of Thessaly, and of Thetis, was the bravest of the Greeks. Already grown, he hid among the daughters of Lycomedes, dressed in women's clothing, by the efforts of his mother, who by this art sought to prevent him from setting out for the Trojan war, from which he would not return. Nevertheless, he was detected by the cunning of Ulysses and led to the war. Here he lay with Deidamia, daughter of Lycomedes, by whom he begot Pyrrhus. Moreover, because Agamemnon had taken Briseis from him, he ceased to fight, until news came of the death of his dearest friend Patroclus, which he avenged with the death of Hector. But at last Achilles was killed by Paris; and finally Pyrrhus himself sacrificed Polyxena at his father's tomb. See Homer, in the Odyssey, and Virgil, Aeneid book 2, and Statius, Thebaid book 1; likewise Dares and Dictys of Crete.

units.la: POLYXENA Priami & Hecubæ filia speciosissima, ad tumulum Achillis à Pyrrho eiusdem Achillis filio, interficitur, ad placandos Achillis manes. Ouidius lib.13. Metamor.
units.tr: POLYXENA, daughter of Priam and Hecuba, most beautiful, was slain at the tomb of Achilles by Pyrrhus, the son of the same Achilles, to appease the shade of Achilles. Ovid, Metamorphoses book 13.
Polyxena, sacrificed, pleases the shade of Achilles.

units.la: Polyxenam fertur Achilles in mœnibus Troiæ conspectam adamasse, eámque in uxorem petiuisse: Priamus annuit: in Apollinis templum conuenitur, ad ineunda pacis nuptiarúmque fœdera: verum inibi interim Achilles à Paride dolo interficitur. Vide ut supra, & Euripi. Trage. NAVPLIVS EVBOEAE REX PALAMEDES
units.tr: It is said that Achilles, having seen Polyxena within the walls of Troy, fell in love with her and asked for her as his wife; Priam consented; they met in the temple of Apollo to make the covenants of peace and marriage; but meanwhile Achilles was killed there by Paris through treachery.
