See as above, and Euripides, Trojan Women. NAUPLIUS, KING OF EUBOEA. PALAMEDES

units.la: NAVPLIVS, Euboëæ insulæ Rex, quam Nigropontum hodie vocant, Palamedis pater fuit, eius inquam qui Vlyssis commento & fraude, ab exercitu lapidibus est obrutus: Vlysses siquidem oderat Palamedem, mortemque illi dolo machinatus est, quòd technam suam detexisset, cùm illi furorem simulanti, vt ad bellum minimè proficisceretur, filium in sulco obiecit. Nauplius vt filij necem vlciscereretur, vxores principum Græcorum, tum cùm Troiam obsidebant, in iuuenum adulteria pellexit, sperans vt in reditu mutuis se vulneribus confoderent propter vitiatas vxores. Præterea Græcis redeuntibus, ignem ex Caphareo monte ostendit: quò factum est vt bona pars ad ignem, tanquam ad proximum portum adnauigans, inter scopulos naufragium fecerit. tandem doloris impatientia se ipsum in mare præcipitat, quòd Vlysses & Diomedes, quos maximè obrui cupiebat, incolumes euasissent. Vide Homer. Verg. Ouid. multis in locis singulos.
units.tr: NAUPLIUS, king of the island of Euboea, which today they call Negroponte, was the father of Palamedes, the one who, by the contrivance and fraud of Ulysses, was stoned to death by the army. For Ulysses hated Palamedes, and plotted his death by treachery, because Palamedes had exposed his trick, when, as Ulysses feigned madness so that he would not go to the war at all, Palamedes placed his son in a furrow. Nauplius, to avenge his son's death, while the Greek leaders were besieging Troy, enticed their wives into adulteries with young men, hoping that on their return they would stab each other with wounds on account of their defiled wives. Furthermore, when the Greeks were returning, he showed a fire from Mount Caphareus; as a result, a large part of them, sailing toward the fire as to a nearby harbour, were wrecked among the rocks. At last, unable to bear his grief, he threw himself into the sea, because Ulysses and Diomedes, whom he most wanted to be destroyed, had escaped unharmed. See Homer, Virgil, Ovid, passim in many places.

units.la: PALAMEDES Nauplij filius, quatuor dicitur literas inuenisse, præterea ordinem aciei, symbolum bellicum, & vigilias, ad exemplum gruum: item calculorum ludum, atque aleam, & latrunculos, quos scachos vulgò dicimus, & mensurarum ac ponderum rationem, quinetiam annum ad Solis cursum, menses ad Lunæ accommodasse. Hic ab Vlysse falsò proditionis insimulatus, lapidibus obruitur. Vide Ouid. lib. 13. Metamor. Cel. Rhodig. lib. 20. cap. 27. & lib. 7. ca. 31. Huius Palamedis Poemata dicitur Homerus, inuidiæ stimulis agitatus, concerpsisse, aut exussisse[?]. idem Cel. Rhodig. id tradit, lib. 20. ca. 30. Vide item Volat. lib. 18. & Plin. 7. cap. 56. IEPTB[?] ABZAN
units.tr: PALAMEDES, son of Nauplius, is said to have invented four letters; besides this, he arranged the order of battle, the battle signal, and the watches, after the example of cranes; likewise the game of counters and dice, and draughts, which we commonly call chess; and he also devised a system of measures and weights, and moreover adjusted the year to the course of the sun and the months to the moon. He was falsely accused of treason by Ulysses and stoned to death. See Ovid, Metamorphoses book 13; Caelius Rhodiginus, book 20, chapter 27, and book 7, chapter 31. The Homer is said to have torn up, or perhaps burned, the poems of this Palamedes, goaded by the sting of envy; the same Caelius Rhodiginus relates this, book 20, chapter 30. See also Volaterranus, book 18, and Pliny, book 7, chapter 56. JEPHTHAH. ABZAN

units.la: IEPHTE, filius Galaad ex meretrice, iudicauit populum Israël anno mundi 2787. ante Christum natum 1175. Hic pugnauit contra Ammonitas, quos tradidit dominus in manus eius. vouerat autem prius, satis tamen imprudenter, se in holocaustum oblaturū domino eum qui primus de domo sua egrediens, sibi occurreret victori: accidítque vt filia sua vnigenita cum tympanis & choris ei reuertenti occurreret, qua visa scidit ipse sua sibi vestimēta, præ dolore: immolauit tamen filiam post duos menses, quos illa impetrarat ad lugendam virginitatem. Vide lib.Iudi.cap.11.& 12.sex annis iudicauit Iephte Israëlem. Ioseph.lib.Antiq.5.cap.12.
units.tr: JEPHTHAH, son of Gilead by a harlot, judged Israel in the year of the world 2787, before the birth of Christ 1175. He fought against the Ammonites, whom the Lord delivered into his hands. He had previously vowed, rather rashly, that he would offer as a burnt offering to the Lord whoever first came out of his house to meet him as he returned in victory; and it happened that his only daughter met him with timbrels and dances. When he saw her, he tore his garments in grief; yet he sacrificed his daughter after two months, which she had obtained in order to mourn her virginity. See Judges, chapters 11 and 12. Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Josephus, Antiquities book 5, chapter 12.

units.la: ABESAN, de Beth-lehem, mortuo Iephte iudicauit Israël septem annis. Hic habuit triginta filios & totidem filias, quas omnes maritis tradidit, simul filiis omnibus vxores dedit: foras misit filias, filiorum autem vxores domum suam introduxit. Iudi.12. Ioseph.lib.5.cap.12. Rabbi Salomon & Chaldæus paraphrastes hūc Abesan Boos esse dicunt. Post Abesan, Aelon de tribu Zabulon, iudicauit populum annos decem: post quem etiam Abdon de tribu Ephraim, iudicauit Israëlē annos octo. Iudicum cap.12. post hunc Samson iudicauit, cuius meminero postea.
units.tr: IBZAN, of Bethlehem, after the death of Jephthah judged Israel for seven years. He had thirty sons and as many daughters, all of whom he gave in marriage; at the same time he gave wives to all his sons: he sent his daughters out, and brought the wives of his sons into his house. Judges 12. Josephus, book 5, chapter 12. Rabbi Solomon and the Chaldee paraphrast say that this Ibzan is Boaz. After Ibzan, Elon of the tribe of Zebulun judged the people for ten years; after him also Abdon of the tribe of Ephraim judged Israel for eight years. Judges chapter 12. After him Samson judged, of whom I shall speak later.

units.la: LATINUS Laurentum Rex,Fauni & Maricæ, filius fuit. Hic vel bello ab Ænea victus, vel tantùm certior factus quísnam,& unde esset Æneas,antequam signa canerent,ipsi Ænea dextram,fidei signum,dedit:filiam deinde in uxorem tradidit, quanquam prius pacta esset Turno Rutulorum regi.Æneas de nomine uxoris Lauiniæ, Lauinium appellat. Turnus ob præ-reptam Lauiniam sibi pactam , bellum mouet: utrinque summa contentione pugnatum est: inclinauit tamen victoria in Troianos , qui Latinum eo in prælio amisere, anno mundi 2787. ante Christum natum 1175. Titus Liuius lib.1. & Diony. Halicar.lib. item primo.
units.tr: LATINUS, king of Laurentum, was the son of Faunus and Marica. He was either defeated in war by Aeneas, or merely informed of who and whence Aeneas was, before the signs were sung; he then gave his right hand to Aeneas, as a sign of faith, and afterwards gave his daughter to him in marriage, although she had previously been promised to Turnus, king of the Rutulians. Aeneas names Lavinium after the name of his wife Lavinia. Turnus, aggrieved that Lavinia, who had been promised to him, was snatched away, made war; the battle was fought with the greatest intensity on both sides, yet victory inclined toward the Trojans, who lost Latinus in that battle, in the year of the world 2787, before the birth of Christ 1175. Livy, book 1; and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1.

units.la: LAVINIA Latini & Amatæ filia, Æneæ uxor post Creusam fuit. Hæc mortuo Ænea Ascanij tutelam gessit: deinde ab eodem Ascanio, Lauinio, urbe iam florente atque opulenta, donata est:nouā.ipse[?] aliam sub Albano monte condidit, quam ab situ porrectæ in dorso urbis, Longam Albam appellauit. Titus Liuius lib.1. Lauinia Syluium Posthumum peperit tertium regem Latinorum: qui sic dictus est,quòd post patris Æneæ fatum in syluis natus ac educatus sit. Videto ut supra. AENEAS TROIANVS TVRNVS
units.tr: LAVINIA, daughter of Latinus and Amata, was the wife of Aeneas after Creusa. When Aeneas died, she held the guardianship of Ascanius; afterwards she was given by the same Ascanius the city of Lavinium, which was now flourishing and wealthy; he himself founded another city at the foot of Mount Alba, which he called Alba Longa from the position of the city stretched along a ridge. Livy, book 1. Lavinia bore Silvius Posthumus, the third king of the Latins; he was so called because he was born and raised in the woods after the death of his father Aeneas. See above. AENEAS, TROJAN. TURNUS

units.la: ÆNEAS, Anchisæ & Veneris filius, ac Priami gener, pius, probus ac bellicosus à Vergilio in gratiam Augusti describitur: aliter enim scribunt grauissimi autores. Hic patrem humeris impositum Troiano incendio dicitur eripuisse, Creusam uxorem in turba amisisse, in Italiam navigasse, Turnum bello vicisse, Lavîniam duxisse, oppidum condidisse Lavinium, de nomine uxoris sic dictum: Ascanium, qui Albam Longam condidit, genuisse. Aduentum autem Æneæ in Africam, cögressum, societatem aut nuptias cum Didone, ut fabulosa praetereo: neque enim appulisse in Africam scribunt historici probatiores: neque, ut appulerit, Didonem illic potuerit reperisse, cum nondum nata esset. Nauigationem Æneæ sic paucis describit Titus Liuius lib.1. Aeneas, inquit, domo profugus, primo in Macedoniam venit: inde in Siciliam, quaerens sedes, delatus est. Ab Sicilia, classe Laurentem agrum tenuit. Troia & huic loco nomen est. De morte Æneæ nil certi reperi. Constat dum cum Rutulis ac Hetruscis, congreditur, multos utrinque caesos, Aeneæ autem corpus nusquam inuentum. id praelium commissum est postquam treis annos ab obitu Latini soceri sui, regnasset Æneas, anno à capta Troia septimo. Dion. Halicar. lib.1. Titus Liuius lib.1. Verg. in libris Aeneidos. Lavinium vrbem condidit Aeneas anno mundi 2788. ante Christum natum 1174.
units.tr: AENEAS, son of Anchises and Venus, and son-in-law of Priam, is described by Virgil as pious, upright and warlike, to please Augustus; for the most serious authors write otherwise. He is said to have rescued his father from the burning of Troy, lost his wife Creusa in the crowd, sailed to Italy, defeated Turnus in war, married Lavinia, and built the town of Lavinium, so named after his wife; he begot Ascanius, who founded Alba Longa. As for Aeneas's arrival in Africa, his meeting, alliance or marriage with Dido, I pass over these as fables: for the more reliable historians do not write that he landed in Africa, and even if he had landed there, he could not have found Dido there, since she was not yet born. Titus Livy, book 1, describes Aeneas's voyage briefly thus: Aeneas, he says, having fled from home, first came to Macedonia; thence, seeking a settlement, he was carried to Sicily. From Sicily, with his fleet, he held the land of Laurentum. Troy is also the name of this place. Concerning the death of Aeneas I have found nothing certain. It is agreed that while he was fighting with the Rutulians and Etruscans, many were slain on both sides, but the body of Aeneas was never found. This battle was fought after Aeneas had reigned three years following the death of his father-in-law Latinus, in the seventh year after the capture of Troy. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1; Titus Livy, book 1; Virgil, in the books of the Aeneid. Aeneas founded the city of Lavinium in the year of the world 2788, before the birth of Christ 1174.

units.la: TVRNVS, Rutulorum Rex, Amatæ, uxoris Latini, consobrinus fuit. Huic pacta fuerat Lavinia ante aduentum Aeneæ: quare praelatum sibi aduenam ægrè ferens, simul Aneæ Latinóque bellum intulit. Vide ut supra. Victus singulari certamine Turnus ab Aenea, victoriam cum sponsa, rivali Aneæ reliquit. Verg. lib. Eneid. 12.
units.tr: TURNUS, king of the Rutulians, was a cousin of Amata, the wife of Latinus. Lavinia had been promised to him before Aeneas arrived. He took it badly that a foreigner was preferred to him, and so he waged war both on Aeneas and on Latinus. See above. Turnus was defeated by Aeneas in single combat, and left the victory, and his bride, to his rival Aeneas. Verg. Aeneid, bk. 12.

units.la: ORESTES occiso Ægistho imperat Mycoenis, quæ urbs est in Peloponneso, anno mundi 2789. ante Christum natum 1173. Fuit hic Agamemnonis & Clytemnestræ filius: matrem adulteram cum adultero suo Ægistho interemit, quòd patrem suum etiam interemerat. Deinde Pyrrhum quoque interfecit, quòd Hermionem sibi prius desponsatam, quæ & Pyrrhum oderat, rapuisset, víque eam in uxorem sibi retinuisset. Ob hæc scelera furiis agitatus vagabatur: habuit interim Pyladem fidum itineris comitem ac periculorum socium. Pervenit itaque Orestes in regionem Tauricam, ubi inventa sorore Electra, cum ea, jam furore purgatus, migravit in Italiam. Orestes pro Pylade, Pylades pro Oreste, uterque pro altero mori minimè recusavit: sicut nec Nysus pro Eurialo, nec Eurialus pro Nyso, uti est apud Verg. quare numeratur inter insigniora amicorum paria. Vide Sophocl. in Electra, Euripid. in Oreste, Cicer. de amicitia, & lib. 2. de finib. Ovid. Epist. 8. Heroidum.
units.tr: ORESTES, after killing Aegisthus, ruled at Mycenae, a city in the Peloponnese, in the year of the world 2789, before the birth of Christ 1173. He was the son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra. He killed his adulterous mother together with her lover Aegisthus, because they had also killed his father. Then he also killed Pyrrhus, because Pyrrhus had seized Hermione, who had previously been betrothed to Orestes, and had kept her as his wife, though she hated him. Driven mad by the Furies on account of these crimes, he wandered about; in the meantime he had Pylades, a faithful companion on his journey and a sharer in his dangers. So Orestes came to the land of the Taurians, where he found his sister Electra; and, now cleansed of his madness, he went with her to Italy. Orestes would die for Pylades, and Pylades for Orestes; neither refused to die for the other. Nor did Nisus for Euryalus, nor Euryalus for Nisus, as is told in Vergil. For this reason they are counted among the most notable pairs of friends. See Sophocles, in the Electra; Euripides, in the Orestes; Cicero, On Friendship, and On Ends, bk. 2; Ovid, Heroides, letter 8.

units.la: HERMIONE Menelaï & Helenæ filia fuit. Hæc à Tyndaro avo materno primùm pacta est in uxorem Oresti, interea dum pater in bello Troiano militaret: qui etiam eandem Pyrrho, mortuo patre Achille, promittit. Pyrrhus reversus eam rapit, ac retinet invitam: quamobrem indignatus Orestes Pyrrhum in templo Apollinis, ope Macarei sacerdotis interficit, uxorémque suam Hermionem recipit. Videto Vergil. libr. 3. Aeneid. Ovid. epist. 8. supradicta, quæ inscribitur, Hermione Oresti. TROI. ASCANIVS SYLVIVS POS[?]
units.tr: HERMIONE was the daughter of Menelaus and Helen. She was first promised in marriage to Orestes by her maternal grandfather Tyndareus, while her father was away fighting in the Trojan War. Later, after Achilles her father had died, Menelaus also promised her to Pyrrhus. Pyrrhus, on his return, seized her and kept her against her will. Indignant at this, Orestes killed Pyrrhus in the temple of Apollo, with the help of the priest Macareus, and took back his wife Hermione. See Vergil, Aeneid, bk. 3; Ovid, epistle 8, the one mentioned above, which is entitled Hermione to Orestes.

units.la: ASCANIVS Æneæ filius, Latinorum Rex fuit, anno à mundo condito 2789. ante Christum natum 1173. Hic à fluuio Phrygiæ Ascanius dictus est: prætereà Ilus, ab rege Troianorum Ilo: quinetiam Iulus, à prima barbæ Lanugine. Vergil. Æneid.I.
units.tr: ASCANIUS, son of Aeneas, was king of the Latins, in the year from the creation of the world 2789, before the birth of Christ 1173. He was called Ascanius after the river in Phrygia; he was also called Ilus, after Ilus, king of the Trojans; and moreover Iulus, from the first down on his beard. Vergil, Aeneid, bk. 1.

units.la: At puer Ascanius, cui nunc cognomen IuloAdditur, Ilus erat, dum res stetit Ilia regno.
units.tr: But the boy Ascanius, who now has the added name Iulus, was called Ilus while the Ilian kingdom stood.

units.la: Huic puero flammula quædam supra caput apparuit, quæ nec vrebat, nec manibus extingui poterat: hinc sumptum omen est, futurum vt aliquando imperaret: idem narrat de Seruio Tullio Liuius lib.1. Cæterùm Ascanius cum 25. annos in Lauinio regnasset, Longam Albam condidit, ac nouercæ, quæ antea restituta fuerat (nam priuignum Ascanium metuens, in syluas se receperat) Lauinium reliquit: regni hæredem fecit Posthumum fratrem suum ex diuersa matre, cùm nondum esset Iulus eius filius ad regendum idoneus per ætatem. Imperauit Ascanius 38.annis, cùm Lauinio, tum Longæ Albæ. Ab Iulo eius filio Iuliorum familia orta est.Eutrop.auctus.
units.tr: Over this boy a small flame appeared above his head, which neither burned nor could be put out by hand. From this a sign was taken that he would one day rule. Livy, bk. 1, tells the same story about Servius Tullius. Moreover, after Ascanius had reigned for twenty-five years at Lavinium, he founded Alba Longa and left Lavinium to his stepmother, who had been restored earlier (for, fearing her stepson Ascanius, she had withdrawn into the woods). He made his brother Posthumus, from a different mother, heir to the kingdom, since his son Iulus was not yet old enough by age to rule. Ascanius reigned thirty-eight years, both at Lavinium and at Alba Longa. From his son Iulus the family of the Julii arose. Eutropius, augmented.

units.la: SYLVIVS Posthumus Æneæ ex Lauinia filius, regnum Latinorum tenuit post Ascanium, anno mundi 2827. ante Christum natum 1135. Imperauit apud Latinos annis 29. de ratione nominis huius, dictum est supra in Lauinia. huius temporibus agebat Homerus, vt autor est Cassiodor. Vide Diony. Halicarn.& Eutro.lib.1.
units.tr: SILVIUS Posthumus, son of Aeneas by Lavinia, held the kingdom of the Latins after Ascanius, in the year of the world 2827, before the birth of Christ 1135. He ruled among the Latins for twenty-nine years. Concerning the reason for this name, it was said above under Lavinia. In his time Homer lived, as Cassiodorus is the authority for. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Eutropius, bk. 1.

units.la: SAMSON filius Manue de tribu Dan,iudicauit post Abdon, populum Ifraëliticum annos 20. quorum initium fuit anno mundi 2818. ante Christum natum 1144. Hic vir fortissimus leonis catulum sæuum ac rugientem,qui ei occurrebat,in frusta dilacerauit quasi hœdum, nihil omnino gladij habens præ manibus.post aliquot dies inuenit in ore huius leonis examen apum ac sauum mellis. Hic propter ablatam vxorem , segetes Philisthinorum excussit, ligatis facibus ad caudas tercentum vulpium. Maxilla asini mille Philisthinorum interemit: Israëlitas à seruitute eorum liberauit, quibus 40. annis seruierant.in Gaza cùm circundaretur custodibus in porta vrbis stantibus, ipse consurgens circiter medium noctis, apprehendit ambas portæ fores cum postibus & sera, imposuitque humeris suis,& portauit ad verticem montis. Vide Iudi.14.& 15.cap. Iosph. Antiq. lib.5. cap.13. post Samsonem Heli fuit summus sacerdos ac iudex populi per 40. annos, cui successit Samuel, de quo postea mentionem faciemus.
units.tr: SAMSON, son of Manoah, of the tribe of Dan, judged the Israelite people for twenty years after Abdon, the beginning of which was in the year of the world 2818, before the birth of Christ 1144. This most valiant man tore to pieces, as if it were a kid, a fierce and roaring lion's cub that came at him, though he had no sword at all in his hands. Some days later he found in the mouth of this lion a swarm of bees and sweet honey. Because his wife had been taken from him, he burned up the grain of the Philistines, tying torches to the tails of three hundred foxes. With the jawbone of an ass he killed a thousand Philistines. He freed the Israelites from their servitude to them, which had lasted forty years. In Gaza, when he was surrounded by guards standing at the city gate, he rose up about midnight, seized both doors of the gate with their posts and bar, put them on his shoulders, and carried them to the top of a mountain. See Judges, chapters 14 and 15; Josephus, Antiquities, bk. 5, ch. 13. After Samson, Eli was high priest and judge of the people for forty years; he was succeeded by Samuel, of whom we shall speak later.

units.la: DALIDA, siue Dalila ,meretrix fuit, quam amauit Samson. Hæc argento à principibus Philisthinorum accepto corrupta,amasium Samsonem tonsum prodidit, qui ab hostibus captus, erutis oculis in carcerem detrusus est. Postea inde vocatus est vt luderet coram eis,qui excæcato & ligato volebant iludere: at ille cùm venisset, & coram illis luderet, inuocato Domino ait: Domine Deus meus memento mei, & redde mihi nunc fortitudinem pristinam, vt vlciscar me de hostibus meis. Tunc apprehendit columnas ambas ambabus manibus,& cecidit domus, quæ cadendo interfecit ad tria millia vtriusque sexus Philisthinorum,vnà cum ipso.Consulito lib.Iudi.cap.16. BRVTVS IGNOGNE VX·BRVTI
units.tr: DALILAH, or Delilah, was a harlot whom Samson loved. Bribed with money by the princes of the Philistines, she betrayed her lover Samson after he had been shaved. Captured by his enemies, he was blinded and thrust into prison. Afterwards he was summoned from there to perform before them, since they wanted to mock him when he was blinded and bound. But when he came and performed before them, he called upon the Lord and said: "O Lord God, remember me, and give me now my former strength, that I may be avenged on my enemies." Then he took hold of the two pillars with both hands, and the house fell, killing with its collapse about three thousand men and women of the Philistines, together with himself. Consult the book of Judges, chapter 16. BRUTUS, IGNOGNE, WIFE OF BRUTUS

units.la: BRVTVS Ascanij Æneæ filij ex Syluio nepos(quanquam alij censeant Syluium Æneæ filium Posthumum fuisse ) fertur proceros quosdam, atque immanes viros sede sua expulisse: insulamque eam de suo nomine Britanniam cognominasse, quæ prius vocabatur Albion, ab Albina quadam Syriæ regis filia, quæ vna cum 32. sororibus, interfectis ab se viris, à patre expulsa, in hæc loco appulerat. Post annos circiter 50. ab excidio Troiæ, id est circa annum à mundo condito 2832. ante Christum natum 1130. cœpit in ea insula,quam magnam Britanniam vocant, regnare Brutus iste, illicque fertur liberos genuisse tres, qui totidem sibi regna constituerunt: Locrum à quo Locria:Cambrum à quo Cambra, nunc Vuallia: & Albanactum, à quo Albania,quæ Scotia postea dicta est.Locrus fratribus superstes, solus Britannia potitus est: post quem Maddan annos quadraginta regnauit. hæc Raphaël Volaterranus in Geographia,lib.3. de populis ac regibus Britanniæ, quam nunc Angliam vocant. Supputationem annorum potes etiam colligere,ac deprehendere in Ascanio Æneę filio,de quo à nobis dictum est supra,paulò antè, tertia ab hinc pagina.
units.tr: BRUTUS, grandson of Ascanius, son of Aeneas, by Silvius (although others think Silvius was the posthumous son of Aeneas), is said to have driven out certain proud and savage men from their seats. He named the island after himself Britain, which was previously called Albion, after Albina, a daughter of a king of Syria, who, together with 32 sisters, having killed their husbands, had been expelled by her father and had landed at this place. About 50 years after the destruction of Troy, that is around the year 2832 from the creation of the world, and 1130 before the birth of Christ, this Brutus began to reign in the island which they call Great Britain, and there he is said to have begotten three sons, who each established a kingdom for themselves: Locrinus, from whom Loegria; Cambrus, from whom Cambria, now Wales; and Albanactus, from whom Albania, which was later called Scotland. Locrinus, surviving his brothers, alone possessed Britain; after him Maddan reigned for forty years. So writes Raphael Volaterranus in his Geography, book 3, concerning the peoples and kings of Britain, which is now called England. You can also work out and check the reckoning of years from Ascanius, son of Aeneas, of whom we spoke above, a little before, three pages back.

units.la: IGNOGNE Pandrasi Leo-græciæ Regis filia,huius Bruti vxor fuit, ex qua tres, qui supradicti sunt, liberos sustulit. Videto Supplementum Chroni.lib.4. Item Chronica Chronicorum.
units.tr: GUENDOLEN, daughter of Pandrasus, king of Greece, was the wife of this Brutus, and from her he raised the three sons mentioned above. See the Supplement of Chronicles, book 4. Likewise the Chronicle of Chronicles.

units.la: HOMERVS Græcus Poëta percelebris, clarebat circiter annum mundi 2838. ante natiuitatem Christi 1124. secundum Cassiodorum. nam Cornelius Nepos in libris Chronicorum refert ad longè posteriorem ætatem, puta ad annum mundi 3051. ante Christum natum 911. ante Romam conditam 160. annos. Natum itaque Homerum, vt inquit Plutarchus, belli Troiani tempore, eiusdémque spectatorem fuisse, quidam scribunt, alij 100. annis post, alij 150. Mater ad Meletem fluuium eum peperit, ob idque Melesigenes appellatus est: postea cæcus factus, Homeri nomen accepit. Duo præcipua poëmata scripsit, Iliada & Odysseam. Ilias gesta Græcorum & Barbarorum propter Helenæ raptum, sed præcipuè Achillis præclara facinora complectitur. Odyssea verò, Vlyssis ex Troiano bello in patriam reditum. Scribunt eum obiisse præ ingenti mœrore, cùm ænigma à piscatoribus propositum non posset dissoluere: ipsum autem ænigma erat huiusmodi: Quæcunque cepimus, reliquimus: quæ verò non cepimus, habemus. Vide Plutarc. in vita Homeri. HESIODVS Poëta, paulò præcessit Homerum, imò & coætaneus eius, & sanguine illi iunctus fuisse perhibetur. Certè Herodotus scribit Hesiodum atque Homerum 400. non amplius annis ipsum præcessisse: extitit autem Herodotus circiter annum mundi 2520. & ante Christum natum 1442. erat Hesiodus ex Ascra, vico Bœotiæ, vnde & Ascræus dictus. Hic primus ac princeps omniū, de agricultura versibus scripsit, quem imitatus est Verg. in Georgicis. Scribebat in Bœotia Helladis, vt inquit Plin. lib 18. cap. 24. de eius morte misera, cúrque à Locrensibus quibusdam adulescentibus sit occisus, vide Plutarc. in conuiuio septem sapientum. SAMVEL SACERDOS SAVL REX ISRAEL
units.tr: HOMER, the Greek poet, very famous, flourished about the year of the world 2838, before the birth of Christ 1124, according to Cassiodorus. For Cornelius Nepos, in his books of Chronicles, refers him to a much later age, namely the year of the world 3051, before the birth of Christ 911, 160 years before the founding of Rome. Some write that Homer, as Plutarch says, was born at the time of the Trojan War and was a witness of it; others write 100 years after, others 150. His mother bore him by the river Meles, and for that reason he was called Melesigenes; later, having become blind, he received the name Homer. He wrote two principal poems, the Iliad and the Odyssey. The Iliad embraces the deeds of the Greeks and barbarians on account of the abduction of Helen, but chiefly the glorious exploits of Achilles. The Odyssey, however, concerns the return of Ulysses to his homeland from the Trojan War. They write that he died from great grief when he could not solve a riddle proposed to him by fishermen; the riddle was of this kind: "What we caught, we left; what we did not catch, we have." See Plutarch in the Life of Homer. HESIOD the poet came a little before Homer, indeed he is said to have been his contemporary and related to him by blood. Herodotus certainly writes that Hesiod preceded Homer by no more than 400 years; Herodotus flourished around the year of the world 2520 and before the birth of Christ 1442. Hesiod was from Ascra, a village of Boeotia, whence he was also called Ascraeus. He was the first and foremost of all to write verses on agriculture, which Virgil imitated in the Georgics. He wrote in Boeotia of Greece, as Pliny says in book 18, chapter 24. On his wretched death, and how he was killed by certain young men of Locri, see Plutarch in the Banquet of the Seven Sages.

units.la: SAMVEL, Elcanæ filius ex Anna, iudicauit populum Israël post Heli, anno mundi 2878. ante Christum natum 1084. Hunc filium mater diu sterilis, precibus à Deo impetrauit, quem etiam Deo obtulit. Arcam Dei reducunt Philisthini, quam tempore Heli ceperant: iudicauit Samuel annos 11. iuxta Hebræos, puta vsque ad Saul, primum regem. Senex factus Samuel, constituebat filios suos Ioëlem & Abiam iudices in Israël, qui cùm non ambularent in viis Patris, sed declinaret ad auaritiam & munera, peruertentes iudicium, maiores natu Israël petierunt à Samuele regem, qui iudicaret more gentium cæterarum. Itaque Saul à Samuele vngitur in regem, præcipiente Domino. 1. lib. Reg. cap. 1. 2. & 3. ad 9. vsque cap. Ioseph. lib. Antiq. 5. cap. 15. & sequen.
units.tr: SAMUEL, son of Elkanah and Hannah, judged the people of Israel after Eli, in the year of the world 2878, before the birth of Christ 1084. His mother, long barren, obtained this son from God by prayer, and she also offered him to God. The Philistines return the ark of God, which they had taken in the time of Eli. Samuel judged for eleven years according to the Hebrews, that is, until Saul, the first king. When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons Joel and Abijah judges in Israel; but since they did not walk in their father's ways, but turned aside to greed and bribes, perverting judgment, the elders of Israel asked Samuel for a king who would judge them in the manner of the other nations. And so Saul was anointed king by Samuel, at the command of the Lord. 1 Kings chapters 1, 2 and 3 to 9, up to chapter [10]. Josephus, Antiquities, book 5, chapter 15 and following.

units.la: SAVL filius Cis, de tribu Ben-iamin, vnctus est in regem primum Israëlitarum, eodem anno quo Samuel filios suos constituerat iudices: nempe anno mundi 2889. ante Christum natum 1073. Erat Saul altior vniuerso populo à capite ad humeros, quem videns populus clamauit, Viuat Rex. Ammonitas & Philisthæos vicit. At contra præceptum Dei, non expectato Samuele, sacrificans, abiicitur à Deo: item contra præceptum Dei victis Amalecitis, regem eorum Agag & prædam reseruauit: filiam suam Michol Dauidi in vxorem dedit. Tandem victus à Philisthæis, ne viuus in manus eorum veniret, à quibus occideretur, seipsum propriis manibus interfecit. Vide 1. libr. Reg. à fronte ad calcem. hunc lib. sunt qui vocent 1. Samuelis. imperauit Saul annis duobus. Iosep. lib. 6. cap. 4. & sequen. DAVID REX IVDA ET ISR SALOMON REX ISRAEL
units.tr: SAUL, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, was anointed the first king of the Israelites in the same year in which Samuel had appointed his sons judges: namely, in the year of the world 2889, before the birth of Christ 1073. Saul was taller than the whole people, from the shoulders upward, and when the people saw him they shouted, Long live the king. He defeated the Ammonites and the Philistines. But against the command of God, sacrificing without waiting for Samuel, he was rejected by God; likewise, against the command of God, when he had defeated the Amalekites, he spared their king Agag and the spoil; he gave his daughter Michal to David as a wife. At last, defeated by the Philistines, lest he should come alive into their hands and be killed by them, he killed himself with his own hands. See 1 Kings from the beginning to the end. Some call this book 1 Samuel. Saul reigned two years. Josephus, book 6, chapter 4 and following. DAVID, KING OF JUDAH AND ISRAEL; SOLOMON, KING OF ISRAEL.

units.la: DAVID filius Iesse (Iesse vocabatur quoque Isaï) regnauit super tribum Iuda in Hebron, anno mundi 2 8 9 r. ante Christum natum 1 0 7 1. quo tempore etiam Isboseth constituitur Rex super Israelem, regnauit autem Dauid super Iudā & Beniamin in Hebron septem annos, & sex menses: præterea super alias decem tribus, & super totum Israelem annos 3 3. Hic cùm gregem patris pasceret, leonē & vrsum apprehensō mento occidit: quare nec diffidit adfuturum sibi Dei auxilium aduersus Goliath: igitur lapide funda iacto, gigantem interfecit. Propheta Nathan eum homicidij arguit. Præterea proposuit ei Deus per Gad Prophetam tria pœnarum genera, quòd populum numerasset: aut septem annorum famem, aut trium mensium persequente hoste, fugam, aut trium dierum pestilentiā: vltimum elegit, inquiēs melius esse vt in manus Domini inciderent. tunc vsque adeo sæuiit pestis vt 7 0 0 0 0. virorum hac lue perirent, ad ædificationem templi populū & Salomonē filium hortatus, descriptionem ac necessaria ad ædificationem dedit. annos natus 70. moritur, ac sepelitur in Beth-lehem. 2. lib. Reg. 11. cap. & sequen. Ioseph. lib. Antiq. 6. cap. 10. & sequentibus.
units.tr: DAVID, son of Jesse (Jesse was also called Isai), reigned over the tribe of Judah in Hebron, in the year of the world 2 8 9 r [2990?], before the birth of Christ 1 0 7 1. At the same time Ishbosheth was also set up as king over Israel. David reigned over Judah and Benjamin in Hebron for seven years and six months, and afterwards over the other ten tribes and over all Israel for 33 years. When he was feeding his father's flock, he seized a lion and a bear by the beard and killed them; therefore he did not doubt that God's help would be with him against Goliath. So, with a stone thrown from a sling, he killed the giant. The prophet Nathan accused him of murder. Moreover, God set before him through the prophet Gad three kinds of punishment, because he had numbered the people: either seven years of famine, or three months of flight before the pursuing enemy, or three days of pestilence. He chose the last, saying it was better that they fall into the hands of the Lord. Then the pestilence raged so greatly that 70,000 men perished by this plague. He urged the people and his son Solomon to build the temple, and gave the plan and the materials necessary for the building. He died at the age of seventy and was buried in Bethlehem. 2 Kings chapter 11 and following. Josephus, Antiquities, book 6, chapter 10 and following.

units.la: SALOMON filius Dauid ex Beth-sabea, incipit imperare in Israël anno mundi 2 9 3 1. ante Christum natum 1 0 3 1. Hic sapientiam à domino postulauit, & impetrauit. habuit ad ædificationem têpli 70000. qui onera portarent, latomorum 80000. præpositorum 3300. locutus est 3000. parabolas, fuerunt carmina eius 5000. annuus reditus eius erat 666. talentorum auri, excepto vectigali, valebátque talentum auri ad 5000. aureorum. mira potes legere à cap. 4. li. 3. Reg. ad 10. item apud Iosep. lib. 8. vxores habuit quasi reginas 700, & concubinas 300. quæ cùm ex gentibus essent, vt eis gratificaretur, ad idololatriam deflexit: quare decem tribus à filio suo ablatæ. regnauit annos 40.
units.tr: SOLOMON, son of David by Bathsheba, began to reign over Israel in the year of the world 2 9 3 1, before the birth of Christ 1 0 3 1. He asked the Lord for wisdom and obtained it. For the building of the temple he had 70,000 men to carry burdens, 80,000 stonecutters, and 3,300 overseers; he spoke 3,000 parables, and his songs numbered 5,000. His annual revenue was 666 talents of gold, apart from tribute, and a talent of gold was worth 5,000 gold pieces. You may read marvellous things from 1 Kings chapter 4 to chapter 10, and likewise in Josephus, book 8. He had 700 wives, as it were queens, and 300 concubines; since these were from the nations, in order to please them he turned aside to idolatry. Therefore ten tribes were taken from his son. He reigned forty years.

units.la: ROBOAM filius Salomonis ex Naama Pharaonis filia, mortuo patre regnavit super filios Israël qui habitabant in civitatibus Juda, anno mundi 2971.ante Christum natum 991. nam decem tribus ad Jeroboam defecerant.Hic Roboam spreto senum consilio, juvenum consilium amplexatus est, superbissimè respondens populo qui tributorum imminutionem postulabat:quamobrem desciuerunt ab eo decem tribus. ipse autem 80000. virorum congregavit ex tribu Juda & Ben-jamin, ut sub jugum ejus qui filius & hæres Salomonis erat,mitterent has decem tribus quæ ad Jeroboam defecerant: sed ut ne pugnaret prohibuit Dominus, dicens à se factū esse istud, quemadmodum per Ahiam Prophetam prædixerat. Vide 3. Reg. 11. 12.13.14.cap.& 2.Paralipomen.10.11.12.cap. Josephlib. Antiquit. 8.cap.7. & 8.regnavit annos 17, cui successit filius, nomine Abia, sive Abiam.
units.tr: REHOBOAM, son of Solomon by Naamah, the daughter of Pharaoh, reigned over the sons of Israel who dwelt in the cities of Judah after his father's death, in the year of the world 2971, before the birth of Christ 991, for the ten tribes had revolted to Jeroboam. Here Rehoboam, rejecting the counsel of the old men, followed the counsel of the young, answering the people, who asked for a reduction of the taxes, in the most arrogant way; therefore the ten tribes revolted from him. He himself gathered 80,000 men from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, so that they might bring under the yoke of him who was the son and heir of Solomon those ten tribes which had revolted to Jeroboam; but the Lord forbade him to fight, saying that this had been done by himself, as he had foretold through the prophet Ahijah. See 1 Kings 11, 12, 13 and 14 and 2 Chronicles 10, 11 and 12. Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 7 and 8. He reigned seventeen years, and was succeeded by his son, named Abijah or Abijam.

units.la: SESACH rex Ægypti, ascendit in Jerusalem, & tulit thesauros domus Domini,& thesauros regios & universa diripuit, anno quinto regni Roboam. habebat Sesac in exercitu 1200. currus, equitum 60000. Vide ut supra. PROPH. AHIA SILON R. ISRAEL. HIEROBOAM
units.tr: SHISHAK, king of Egypt, went up to Jerusalem and carried off the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal treasures, and plundered everything, in the fifth year of the reign of Rehoboam. Shishak had in his army 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen. See above. THE PROPHET AHIJAH OF SHILOH. KING JEROBOAM OF ISRAEL.

units.la: AHIAS Silonites, Propheta, prædixit ipsi Ieroboam decem tribuum ad se defectionem : nam apprehendens pallium suum nouum quo opertus erat ipsemet Ahias, scidit illud in duodecim partes : & ait ad Ieroboam, Tolle tibi decē scissuras: hæc enim dicit Dominus Deus Israël : Ego scindam regnum de manu Salomonis, & dabo tibi decem tribus. Vide 3. lib. Reg. cap.11. Ioseph.lib.Antiquit.8.cap.7.
units.tr: AHIJAH the Shilonite, a prophet, foretold to Jeroboam himself the revolt of the ten tribes to him; for Ahijah himself took the new cloak with which he was clothed, tore it into twelve pieces, and said to Jeroboam, "Take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the Lord God of Israel: I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give you ten tribes." See 1 Kings chapter 11. Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 7.

units.la: IEROBOAM filius Nabat regnauit in Israël super decem tribus, eodem anno quo Roboam imperauit duabus tribubus, Iudæ scilicet ac Ben-iamin, nempe anno à mundo condito 2971. ante Christum natum 991. Hic Ieroboā fecit duos vitulos aureos ad retinendum populum ne ascenderet, adorandi gratia, in templum Ierosolymitanum, & ne hac forte via deficeret ad regem Roboam, qui Ierosolymis imperabat. Sic falsa religione propter ambitionem & regnandi libidinem, populum imbuit, nam adorandos hos vitulos palàm exhibuit, clamans : Nolite vltrà ascendere in Ierusalem, ecce Dij tui Israel, qui te eduxerunt de terra Aegypti. Hic manum in Prophetam extendit, & aruit, nec potuit eam rex ad se retrahere: at verò orante Prophèta, restituitur in integrum manus arida. Tandem à filio Roboam, Regis Iudæ, vincitur. Rexit Israëlem annis 22. successit Nadab filius eius. Vide 3.lib. Reg.cap.11.12.13.14. Ioseph. lib. Antiq.8. cap.8.9.11.
units.tr: JEROBOAM, son of Nebat, reigned over Israel over the ten tribes, in the same year in which Rehoboam ruled over the two tribes, namely Judah and Benjamin, that is, in the year from the creation of the world 2971, before the birth of Christ 991. Here Jeroboam made two golden calves to keep the people from going up, for the sake of worship, to the temple at Jerusalem, and lest by this way they should perhaps defect to King Rehoboam, who ruled at Jerusalem. Thus, by false religion, from ambition and lust for ruling, he imbued the people; for he openly set up these calves to be worshipped, crying out: Do not go up any longer to Jerusalem; behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Here he stretched out his hand against the prophet, and it withered, and the king could not draw it back to himself; but when the prophet prayed, the withered hand was restored to its wholeness. At last he was conquered by the son of Rehoboam, king of Judah. He ruled Israel for 22 years; his son Nadab succeeded him. See 1 Kings chapters 11, 12, 13 and 14; Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapters 8, 9 and 11.

units.la: ABIA, seu Abiam, filius fuit Roboam, ex Maacha filia Abessalom,& successit patri in regno Iudæ, anno mundi 2988. ante Christum natum 974. Hic prauum se, ac paternorum vestigiorum æmulum præstitit: orantibus tamen Deum suis militibus, vicit ipsum Ieroboam. tunc corruêre 50000. virorum fortium ex Israël, confossi à viris Iuda. Nam diuisæ erant duodecim tribus Hebræorum in duo regna, Iudæorum, & Israëlitarum: præerâtque rex Iudæorum duabus tantùm tribubus, videlicet tribui Iudæ,& Ben-iamin: Rex verò Israëlitarum imperitabat reliquis decem tribubus. Rexit itaque Abia Israëlem tribus ferè annis 3.Reg.15.cap.& 2.lib.Paralip.cap.13.Iosephlib. Antiq.8.cap.11.
units.tr: ABIJAH, or Abijam, was the son of Rehoboam by Maacah, the daughter of Absalom, and succeeded his father in the kingdom of Judah in the year of the world 2988, before the birth of Christ 974. He proved himself wicked and an imitator of his father's footsteps; yet, when his soldiers prayed to God, he defeated Jeroboam himself. Then 500,000 of the brave men of Israel fell, pierced by the men of Judah. For the twelve tribes of the Hebrews had been divided into two kingdoms, that of the Jews and that of the Israelites; the king of the Jews ruled over only two tribes, namely the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, while the king of the Israelites ruled over the remaining ten tribes. So Abijah ruled Israel for about three years. 1 Kings 15 chapter; 2 Chronicles chapter 13; Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 11.

units.la: ASA, filius Abiæ, successit patri in regno Iudæ, anno 20. regni Ieroboam regis Israël, imperauítque annos 41. Fuit Asa rex pius in Deum & homines, subuertit altaria peregrini cultus, confregit statuas, lucos succîdit: & præcepit Iudæ vt quærerêt Dominum Deum patrum suorum,legi diuinæ parëret,& vniuersa mandata impleret. Habuit de tribu Iuda 300000.de Beniamin autem 250000. militum virorum fortissimorum. Egressus est contra eos Zara rex Ethiopum cum decies centenis hominum millibus: hos implorato diuino auxilio, fugauit Asa: fugatos,internecioni dedit. Post hæc iniit fœdus cum Benadab rege Syriæ,timens Baasa regem Israël: quare à Propheta Hanani corripitur, quem in neruum misit. Deinde dolore pedum grauissimo laborans, cùm iam multos occidisset, opem medicorum potius quàm Dei quæsiuit. 3.Reg.15.cap.2. Paralip. 14.& 15.Iosep.lib.8.cap.12. ISRA NADAB R. R. ISRAEL. BAASA
units.tr: ASA, son of Abijah, succeeded his father in the kingdom of Judah in the twentieth year of Jeroboam, king of Israel, and reigned 41 years. Asa was a king pious toward God and men; he overthrew the altars of foreign worship, broke the images, and cut down the groves; and he commanded Judah to seek the Lord God of their fathers, to obey the divine law and to fulfil all the commandments. He had from the tribe of Judah 300,000 and from Benjamin 250,000 men, very brave soldiers. Zerah, king of the Ethiopians, marched out against them with a million men; Asa, having implored divine help, put them to flight, and having put them to flight, gave them over to slaughter. After this he made a covenant with Ben-hadad, king of Syria, fearing Baasha, king of Israel; therefore he was rebuked by the prophet Hanani, whom he put into the stocks. Then, labouring under a very grievous pain in his feet, when he had already lost many men, he sought the help of physicians rather than of God. 1 Kings 15, chapter 2; 2 Chronicles 14 and 15; Josephus, book 8, chapter 12.

units.la: NADAB filius Ieroboam successit patri in regno Israël, anno secundo regni Asa, Regis Iuda: hic impius, genuina patris proles, non diu imperauit: occisus est à Baasa anno tertio Asa Regis Iudæ:& regnum eius occupauit homicida ille Baasa. Vide tertium librū Regum,cap.14. & 15.imperauit anno à condito mundo 2992. ante Christum natum 970.
units.tr: NADAB, son of Jeroboam, succeeded his father as king of Israel in the second year of Asa, king of Judah. He was impious, a true offspring of his father, and did not reign long. He was killed by Baasa in the third year of Asa, king of Judah, and that murderer Baasa seized his kingdom. See the third book of Kings, chapters 14 and 15. He reigned in the year 2992 from the creation of the world, 970 before the birth of Christ.

units.la: BAASA occiso Nadab,regnauit super Israëlem annos 24. homicidio regnum assecutus, homicidia iterum perpetrauit: nam omnem familiam Ieroboam interfecit. fuit huic bellum cum Asa, nam ascenderat Baasa in Iudam, & Rama muro cingebat, vt ne quis à regno Iudæ in regnum Israël penetrare posset: quamobrem perterrefactus Asa, missis muneribus opem Ben-adab Regis Syriæ implorauit: vti dictum iam à me supra est in Asa. Tandem Iehu prædixit ipsi Baasæ sui ipsius suorumque ruinam ob idololatriam, sicuti familiæ Ieroboam. successit Baasæ Ela filius. incepit regnare Baasa anno mundi 2992. ante Christum natum 970. nempe eodem anno de quo supra in Nadab. Vide lib.3.Reg.15.& 16.cap.Iosephlib.Antiq.8.cap.12. ISRAEL ELA R. R. ISRAEL AMRI
units.tr: BAASA, after killing Nadab, reigned over Israel for 24 years. He obtained the kingdom by murder, and he committed murders again, for he destroyed the whole family of Jeroboam. He had war with Asa, for Baasa marched into Judah and fortified Ramah with a wall, so that no one could pass from the kingdom of Judah into the kingdom of Israel. Therefore Asa, greatly alarmed, sent gifts and implored the help of Ben-hadad, king of Syria, as I have already said above under Asa. At last Jehu foretold to Baasa himself the ruin of himself and his household because of idolatry, just as he had foretold for the family of Jeroboam. Ela, the son of Baasa, succeeded him. Baasa began to reign in the year 2992 from the creation of the world, 970 before the birth of Christ, in the same year as I mentioned above under Nadab. See the third book of Kings, chapters 15 and 16, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 12.

units.la: ELA filius Baasæ, defuncto patre imperat Israëlitis anno mundi 3015. ante Christum natum 947.nempe anno 26. Asæ Regis Iudæ: & anno 27. eiusdem ebrius occiditur à Zambri, duce mediæ partis equitum huius Regis Elæ. Itaque Zambri regnum inuadens occidit omnem familiam Baasæ: quod cùm resciuit populus, constituit sibi alterū Regem nomine Ambri, qui obsedit Zambri in Thersa. Porrò cùm videret Zambri expugnandam esse ciuitatem, ingressus palatiū succendit se cum domo regia: sic tyrannide regnum assecutus, septimo etiam die tyrannidem in semetipsum exercuit. Vide lib.3.Reg.cap.16.
units.tr: ELA, son of Baasa, ruled the Israelites after his father's death, in the year 3015 from the creation of the world, 947 before the birth of Christ, that is, in the twenty-sixth year of Asa, king of Judah. In the twenty-seventh year of the same king, while drunk, he was killed by Zimri, commander of half of Ela's cavalry. So Zimri, seizing the kingdom, destroyed the whole family of Baasa. When the people learned of this, they set up for themselves another king named Omri, who besieged Zimri in Tirzah. Then, seeing that the city was about to be taken, Zimri entered the palace and set fire to himself along with the royal house. Thus he obtained the kingdom by tyranny, and after seven days he also turned his tyranny against himself. See the third book of Kings, chapter 16.

units.la: AMRI (Iosephus Amarin vocat) Israëliticum regnum administrauit anno mundi 3016. ante Christum natum 946. nec verò nesciendum est, post Zambri diuisum fuisse populum in duas partes, altera fauebat Thebni, altera Amri: hæc contentio durauit ad aliquot annos: tandem præualuit pars quæ elegerat Amri in Regem, & mortuus est Thebni: sic confirmatum est regnum ipsi Amri, cuius regno etiam adduntur anni huius dissentionis: nam dicitur imperasse in Israël annos duodecim. Hic montem Samariæ emit à Somer (Samarû vocat Iosephus, à quo Samaria dicta) duobus talentis argenti: illic ædificauit Samariam, regniqué sedem constituit, sex annis in Thersa egit reliquos in Samaria. Vide lib.3.Reg.cap.16. & Iosep.lib.Antiq.8. cap.12. Successit ei filius etiam impius Achab. R. ISRAEL ACHAB JEZAB[?]EL REGIN[?]
units.tr: OMRI (Josephus calls him Amarin) governed the kingdom of Israel in the year 3016 from the creation of the world, 946 before the birth of Christ. Nor should it be unknown that after Zimri the people were divided into two parts: one favored Tibni, the other Omri. This contention lasted for some years. At last the party that had chosen Omri as king prevailed, and Tibni died. Thus the kingdom was secured to Omri, and the years of this division are added to his reign, for he is said to have ruled over Israel for twelve years. He bought the mountain of Samaria from Shemer (Josephus calls him Samaru, from whom Samaria was named) for two talents of silver. There he built Samaria and established it as the seat of the kingdom; he spent six years at Tirzah and the rest at Samaria. See the third book of Kings, chapter 16, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 12. He was succeeded by his son, the equally impious Ahab.

units.la: ACHAB regnauit in Israel anno 38.regni Asa Regis Judæ: hic erat annus mundi 3027.ante Christum natum 935. tenuit Achab principatum in Samaria annis 22. omnes priores Reges impietate superauit: duxit vxorem Jezabel Regis Sidoniorum filiam: & posuit aram Baal in templo Baal, quod extruxerat in Samaria, ipsumque Baal adorauit. Prædixit ei Propheta Elias famem, quæ tres annos durauit. posthæc occurrit Achab Eliæ, cui dixit: Tune es ille qui conturbas Israel? respondit Elias: Non ego turbaui Israel, sed tu, & domus patris tui, qui dereliquistis mandata Domini, & secuti estis Baal. Deinde miraculo facto in holocausto Eliæ, eiusdem Eliæ jussu sacerdotes Baal impostores interficiuntur, erant autem 450. Achab semel atque iterum prælio vicit Ben-adab: tertiò contra eundem pugnans mutata etiam veste, sagitta fortuito ad mortem vulneratur. 3.Reg.16.cap.& seq. Josep.lib.Antiq.8.cap.12.&13.
units.tr: AHAB reigned over Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa, king of Judah. This was the year 3027 from the creation of the world, 935 before the birth of Christ. Ahab held the rule in Samaria for 22 years. He surpassed all the earlier kings in impiety. He married Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians, and set up an altar to Baal in the temple of Baal, which he had built in Samaria, and he himself worshipped Baal. The prophet Elijah foretold a famine to him, which lasted three years. Afterwards Ahab met Elijah, and said to him: Is it you who troubles Israel? Elijah answered: I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father's house, who have forsaken the commandments of the Lord and followed Baal. Then, after a miracle at Elijah's sacrifice, at Elijah's command the priests of Baal, who were impostors, were put to death; there were 450 of them. Ahab defeated Ben-hadad once and again in battle. In a third battle against the same man, he changed his clothing, but by chance an arrow struck him and he was mortally wounded. See 3 Kings 16 and following, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapters 12 and 13.

units.la: JEZABEL filia Eth-Baal Regis Sidoniorum, vxor fuit huius supradicti Acab. Impia hæc Pseudoprophetis Baal fauens, Eliæ mortem minitata est: quod cùm resciret Elias, aufugit: præterea ipsi Naboth mortem machinata est, qui lapidibus est obrutus, quòd falsis testibus convicisset ipsa Jezabel, eum Deo ac Regi maledixisse. occasio autem inde manarat, quòd vineam, patrum suorum hæreditatem, Regi Achab non permisisset Naboth. Vide lib.3.Reg.19. & 21.cap.& Josephus lib. Antiq.8. cap.13. Hæc jussu Jehu de fenestra præcipitata est, in Jezrahel: cùm, audiens adventum eius, ornasset se, ac fuco faciem deliniuisset: a spersúsque[?] est sanguine paries, & equorum vngulæ conculcaverunt eam: jussitque eam sepeliri Jehu, quòd filia Regis esset: at cùm sepelirent eam, non invenerunt nisi calvariam, & pedes, & summas manus, juxta prædictionem Eliæ, 4.Reg.9. THES. P. ELIAS PROPH. ELISEVS
units.tr: JEZEBEL, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, was the wife of the Ahab mentioned above. This impious woman, favoring the false prophets of Baal, threatened Elijah with death, and when Elijah learned of it, he fled. Moreover, she plotted the death of Naboth, who was stoned to death because Jezebel herself had accused him, through false witnesses, of cursing God and the king. The occasion for this arose because Naboth would not give his vineyard, the inheritance of his fathers, to King Ahab. See 3 Kings 19 and 21, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 13. At the command of Jehu she was thrown down from a window at Jezreel. When she heard of his arrival, she had adorned herself and painted her face with cosmetics. Her blood splashed the wall, and the hooves of the horses trampled her. Jehu ordered her buried because she was a king's daughter, but when they went to bury her, they found nothing but her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands, in accordance with Elijah's prophecy. See 4 Kings 9.

units.la: ELIAS Thesbites, Propheta fuit clarissimus : floruit temporibus Achab & Ochosiæ, Regum Israël. Vir quidem fuit pilosus,zonáque pellicea accinctus renes:zelo maximo erga Dei cultum affectus, varia edidit miracula quæ vulgatissima sunt (siquidem gratia apud Deum maxima valuit) nam quid commemorem ut in solitudine pastus sit à coruis, deinde ab Angelis ? ut pluviam impetrarit ? ut pseudo prophetas increparit, ac interfecerit ? ut Quinquagenarij duo, cum suis militibus, ad comprehendendum eum ab Rege Ochosia, filio Achab, missi, igne cælitus demisso,subitò consumpti fuerint? ut aquas fluvij Iordanis pallio suo percussas diuiserit? ut denique per turbinem in cœlum raptus fuerit curru & equis igneis ? Legat qui volet 3.lib.Regum à cap.18.ad finem usque.Eccle.48.cap.Iacob. epist. cap.5.item Iosephus[?] lib. Antiquit.8. cap.12. & sequentibus capitibus.
units.tr: ELIJAH the Tishbite was a most famous prophet. He flourished in the times of Ahab and Ahaziah, kings of Israel. He was indeed a hairy man, girded about the loins with a leather belt, and he was filled with the greatest zeal for the worship of God. He performed various miracles, which are very well known (for he was greatly prized in the grace of God). Why should I mention how he was fed in the wilderness by ravens, and then by angels? How he obtained rain? How he rebuked and killed the false prophets? How two captains of fifty, sent with their soldiers by King Ahaziah, son of Ahab, to seize him, were suddenly consumed when fire came down from heaven? How he divided the waters of the Jordan by striking them with his mantle? How at last he was taken up into heaven by a whirlwind, in a chariot and fiery horses? Let him who wishes read the third book of Kings from chapter 18 to the end, Ecclesiasticus 48, James 5, and likewise Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 12, and the following chapters.

units.la: ELISEVS filius Saphat, iubente domino unctus est ab Elia in Prophetam, nempe ut succederet ipsi Eliæ, eíque ministraret. arantem Elisæum reperit Elias: sic ex agricolatione ad Prophetiam vocatur. Hic petiit sibi dari spiritum Eliæ duplicem: filium hospitæ suæ mortuum suscitavit: Naaman Syrum à lepra curavit, præmiáque recusavit. Vitam eius, ac miracula multa quibus claruit, hoc loci non est instituti mei persequi: amplius nosse qui cupit,legat lib.4.Regum à 1.cap.ad 14. Porrò id minimè silentio prætereundum est, quod scribitur in lib. 4. Reg.cap.13. in hæc verba: Quidam sepelientes hominem, viderunt latrunculos,& proiecerunt cadaver in sepulchro Elisei:quod cùm tetigisset ossa Elisei, revixit homo, & stetit super pedes. Vide etiam Iosephum lib.Antiq.9.cad.8. IOSAPHAT REX IVD IORAM REX IVD
units.tr: ELISHA, son of Shaphat, was anointed prophet by Elijah at the Lord's command, namely to succeed Elijah and minister to him. Elijah found Elisha ploughing; thus he was called from farming to prophecy. Elisha asked that a double portion of Elijah's spirit be given to him. He raised to life the son of his hostess; he healed Naaman the Syrian of leprosy, and refused the reward. I am not undertaking here to pursue his life and the many miracles by which he became famous; whoever wishes to know more about them may read the fourth book of Kings, chapters 1 to 14. Furthermore, what is written in 4 Kings chapter 13 in these words must by no means be passed over in silence: Some men burying a man saw a band of robbers, and they threw the corpse into the grave of Elisha. When it touched the bones of Elisha, the man came back to life and stood up on his feet. See also Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 8.

units.la: IOSAPHAT filius Asa, regnare coepit super Iudam anno 4. Achab, regis Israël: hoc est anno mundi 303 r. ante Christum natum 93 r. annorum erat 30. cùm regnare coepisset, &'25. annis regnauit: pietatem coluit, patris Asæ genuinam prolem se præstitit. Classem parauit quæ nauigaret in Ophir ad aurum inde auehendum. Philisthæi munera ei afferebant, & vectigal argenti: Arabes quoque adducebant pecora amplissima. ædificauit in Iuda domos ad instar turrium, vrbésque muratas. Tertio regni anno misit qui circuirent cunctas vrbes Iuda, atque docerent populum, gestantes librum legis Domini. Constituit iudices in singulis vrbibus, quibus dixit: Videte quid faciatis:non enim hominis exercetis iudicium,sed Dei: & quodcunque iudicaueritis, in vos redundabit. Insurrexerunt in eum Ammonitæ & Moabitæ, qui in semetipsos versi, mutuis concidêre vulneribus:ampla spolia legit Iosaphat. Vide 3. lib. Reg. cap. 22. & 2. lib. Para. cap. 17. 18. 19. & 20. & Ioseph. lib. 9. cap. 1.
units.tr: JEHOSHAPHAT, son of Asa, began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab, king of Israel; that is, in the year 3031 from the creation of the world, 931 before the birth of Christ. He was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for 25 years. He cultivated piety and showed himself a true offspring of his father Asa. He prepared a fleet to sail to Ophir to bring back gold from there. The Philistines brought him gifts and tribute of silver; the Arabs also brought very large flocks. He built towers-like houses in Judah and walled cities. In the third year of his reign he sent men to go through all the cities of Judah and teach the people, carrying the book of the Lord's law. He appointed judges in the individual cities, saying to them: Take heed what you do; for you do not exercise judgment for man, but for God, and whatever you judge will fall back upon you. The Ammonites and Moabites rose against him, but they turned upon one another and perished by mutual wounds; Jehoshaphat gathered great spoils. See 3 Kings 22, 2 Chronicles 17, 18, 19 and 20, and Josephus, book 9, chapter 1.

units.la: IORAM filius Iosaphat, successit patri. Hic omnes fratres suos occidit, & quosdam de primoribus Iuda. Athaliam (Gotholiam vocat Iosep.) vxorem duxit, filiam Amri, quæ illum ad cultum idolorum adduxit: quare allatæ sunt ei literæ à Propheta quodam, quæ vltionem diuinam ei prædicebant, quòd imitatus esset Achab, & quòd fratres suos meliores se, occidisset, & declinasset à pietate Iosaphat patris sui. Suscitauit ergo Deus Philisthinos & Arabes, qui terram Iuda vastarunt, domum Ioram diripuerunt, filios eius occiderunt, præter Ioachas minimum natu. Regnauit Ioram tres annos vnà cum patre, & 4. post patrem: successit filius eius Ochosias. fuit alter Ioram filius Achab, rex Israël, de quo pa.sequent. hic verò rex Iudæ. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: JEHORAM, son of Jehoshaphat, succeeded his father. He killed all his brothers and some of the chief men of Judah. He married Athaliah (Josephus calls her Gotholia), daughter of Omri, who led him into the worship of idols. For this reason letters were brought to him from a certain prophet, which foretold divine vengeance upon him, because he had imitated Ahab, had killed his brothers who were better than himself, and had turned away from the piety of his father Jehoshaphat. God therefore stirred up the Philistines and Arabs, who laid waste the land of Judah, plundered the house of Jehoram, and killed his sons, except Jehoahaz, the youngest. Jehoram reigned three years together with his father and four after his father's death. He was succeeded by his son Ahaziah. There was another Jehoram, son of Ahab, king of Israel, of whom I shall speak below; this one was king of Judah. See above.

units.la: OCHOSIA filius Achab, regnare coepit super Israëlem in Samaria anno mundi 3049. ante Christum natum 913. Hic impius, pravus,& utrique parenti persimilis extitit:atque æger ex lapsu, misit consultum Deum Accaron, an conualesceret: reverterentur nuntii,dicentes occurrisse sibi hominem pilosum, renibus accintum zona pellicea, qui dixerit ut reverterentur, renuntiarentque minimè conualituram. Ochosias Eliam esse qui nuntios impediuisset ratus, misit ad eum Tribunum cum quinquaginta militibus,ut eum adducerent,quos omnes ignis coelitus demissus, consumpsit: cùm totidem iterum misisset Ochosias,eodè fato correpti sunt: Tribunus autem qui tertius missus est,supplex Eliam deprecatus est: qui Elias, ab Angelo præmonitus, cum hoc Tribuno ad Ochosiam perrexit. Tandem ab Elia increpatus est Ochosias, apud quem idipsum locutus est,quod per nuntios primùm prædixerat. Itaque ex hac infirmitate obiit, nullis relictis liberis: quare successit ei frater suus Joram. Vide 3.Reg.22.cap.& 4 Reg.1.cap. item Josephus lib. Antiq.9. cap.2. regnauit annos duos. Fuit alter Ochosias filius Jorā Rex Juda,cuius infra meminero:hic verò Rex fuit Israël.
units.tr: OCHOSIAS, son of Ahab, began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the year of the world 3049, before the birth of Christ 913. He was wicked, depraved, and wholly like both of his parents; and when he was sick from a fall, he sent to consult God at Ekron whether he would recover. The messengers returned, saying that a hairy man, girded with a leather belt about his loins, had met them and told them to go back and report that he would not recover. Ochosias, thinking that Elijah was the one who had stopped the messengers, sent a captain with fifty soldiers to bring him; fire sent down from heaven consumed them all. When Ochosias sent the same number again, they were struck by the same fate. The third captain who was sent, however, begged Elijah as a suppliant; Elijah, forewarned by an angel, went with this captain to Ochosias. At last Ochosias was rebuked by Elijah, who spoke to him the very words he had first foretold through the messengers. And so he died of this sickness, leaving no children; therefore his brother Joram succeeded him. See 3 Kings 22 and 4 Kings 1; also Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 2. He reigned two years. There was another Ochosias, son of Joram, king of Judah, of whom I shall speak below; but this one was king of Israel.

units.la: JORAM frater Ochosiæ, & filius Achab, successit prædicto Ochosiæ fratri suo in regno Israël, regnauitque in Samaria duodecim annis. Huius temporibus Rex Syriæ Ben-adab obsedit Samariam, ubi fames magna invaluit, adeò ut venundaretur caput asini octoginta[?] argenteis. Vide 3. lib. Reg. cap.20. Item Josephus lib. Antiq 9. cap.4. huic successit Jehu. Fuit quoque alter Joram filius Josaphat, de quo supra, Rex Juda: hic autem Rex Israël. R.IV. OCHOSIAS ATHALIA IVD REGINA
units.tr: JORAM, brother of Ochosias and son of Ahab, succeeded his brother Ochosias in the kingdom of Israel, and reigned in Samaria for twelve years. In his times Ben-hadad, king of Syria, besieged Samaria, where a great famine took hold, so much so that the head of an ass was sold for eighty pieces of silver. See 3 Kings 20; also Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 4. He was succeeded by Jehu. There was also another Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, of whom I spoke above, king of Judah; but this one was king of Israel. R.IV. OCHOSIAS, ATHALIAH, KING OF JUDAH, QUEEN

units.la: OCHOSIAS filius Ioram Regis Iudæ, non autem eius Ioram qui fuit Rex Israël, successit patri in regno Iudæ anno 12. Ioram filij Achab Regis Israël.annos natus erat 20.cùm regnare cœpisset,& imperauit Ierosolymis anno tātum vno, qui erat annus mundi 3060. ante Christum natum 902. Impiè egit, secutúsq; est domum Achab: iniit societatem cum Ioram filio Achab,de quo supra proximè mentionem feci: & cum eo gessit bellum aduersus Hazael, Regem Syrorum. Iste Ochosias iussu Iehu, qui in Regem vnctus fuerat, interfectus est. Vide lib.4. Reg 8.& 9.cap. item lib 2.Paral.22.ca. Fuit alter Ochosias filius Achab,& frater Ioram,Regum Israël,de quibus supra mentionem fecimus,& nunc quoque commonefactum candidum lectorem voluimus.
units.tr: OCHOSIAS, son of Joram, king of Judah (not that Joram who was king of Israel), succeeded his father in the kingdom of Judah in the twelfth year of Joram, son of Ahab, king of Israel. He was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he ruled at Jerusalem for one year only, which was the year of the world 3060, before the birth of Christ 902. He lived impiously and followed the house of Ahab; he entered into alliance with Joram, son of Ahab, whom I mentioned just above, and with him waged war against Hazael, king of the Syrians. This Ochosias was killed on the orders of Jehu, who had been anointed king. See 4 Kings 8 and 9; also 2 Chronicles 22. There was another Ochosias, son of Ahab and brother of Joram, kings of Israel, whom we have mentioned above, and we have wished to remind the candid reader of them here too.

units.la: ATHALIA, mater huius Ochosiæ,cùm videret mortuum Regem filium suum, interfecit omne semen regium, præter paruulū,nomine Ioas,filium huius Ochosiæ Regis Iuda: quem Iosaba,filia Ioram,Regis Iudæ, patris Ochosiæ proximè suprādicti, abscondērat. Athalia itaque vsurpauit regnum Iudæ, rexítque septem fere annos: nam hoc eodem anno septimo Ioas vnctus est in Regem à Ioiada Pontifice,& occisa est Athalia. Videto lib.4.Reg.cap.11.item Iosephlib.Anti.9.cap.7.vbi hanc vocat Gotholiam. Cæterum quatenus attinet ad annorum supputationem, Athalia hæc,vti apud Chronologos comperio, regnare incepit super Iudam,anno à mundo condito 3061. ante verò Christum seruatorem natum, 901. & imperitauit,vt prædixi, annis fere septem. R. ISRAEL IEHV SV SAC. IOIADA
units.tr: ATHALIAH, mother of this Ochosias, when she saw that her son the king was dead, killed all the royal seed, except for a little boy named Joash, son of this King Ochosias of Judah, whom Jehosheba, daughter of Joram, king of Judah, the father of the Ochosias mentioned just above, had hidden. Athaliah therefore seized the kingdom of Judah and reigned for about seven years; for in this seventh year Joash was anointed king by Jehoiada the high priest, and Athaliah was killed. See 4 Kings 11; also Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 7, where he calls her Gotholia. As for the reckoning of years, Athaliah, as I find among the chronologers, began to reign over Judah in the year 3061 from the creation of the world, but before the birth of Christ the Saviour, 901; and she ruled, as I said before, for about seven years.

units.la: IEHV, Dux exercitus Ioram, Regis Iudæ, imperante in Israël Ioram filio Achab, & Ochosia filio alterius Ioram in Iuda vnctus est in Regem Israël, regnauitque his duobus intersectis, anno mundi quo Athalia, de qua proxima pagina superiore à nobis dictum est. Hic omnem domum Regis Achab exterminauit: Ioram Regem Israël sagitta transfuerberauit. Ochosiam occidit, Iezabel præcipitari iussit. Consulito lib. 4. Reg. ca. 9. & 10. & Iosep. lib. Antiq. 9. cap. 6. Hic sacerdotes Baal occidit, idolum, & templum succendit, in quo loco cloacas fecit: nec tamen à peccatis Ieroboam recessit, nec dereliquit vitulos aureos, qui erant in Bethel, & in Dan. imperauit annos 28. & successit ei Ioachas filius eius.
units.tr: JEHU, captain of the army of Joram, king of Judah, while Joram son of Ahab was reigning in Israel and Ochosias, son of the other Joram, in Judah, was anointed king of Israel; he reigned after the slaying of these two, in the year of the world in which Athaliah lived, of whom we spoke on the preceding page. He utterly destroyed the whole house of King Ahab; he pierced King Joram of Israel with an arrow; he killed Ochosias and ordered Jezebel to be thrown down. Consult 4 Kings 9 and 10; and Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 6. He killed the priests of Baal, burned the idol and the temple, and made a latrine on that site; yet he did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, nor did he abandon the golden calves that were in Bethel and in Dan. He reigned twenty-eight years, and his son Jehoahaz succeeded him.

units.la: IOIADA summum obtinuit apud Iudæos Sacerdotium: hic Ioas Ochosiæ Regis Iudæ filium, in regnum restituit, occisa Athalia, quæ tyrannide regnum invaserat. pepigit Ioiada fœdus cum Ioas, quo fœdere Rex Ioas & ipse populus polliciti sunt obedire Deo, & populus etiam Regi inito hoc fœdere, demoliti sunt aras Baal, idola contriverunt. & Mathan sacerdotem Baal, occiderunt, etiam coram altari. Vide li. 4. Reg. cap. 11. nihilominus tamen mortuo Ioiada, Ioas ipse ad idololatriam deflexit. Vide lib. 2. Paral. 24. cap. & Iosep. lib. Antiq. 9. cap. 7.
units.tr: JEHOIADA held the high priesthood among the Jews. He restored Joash, son of Ochosias, king of Judah, to the kingdom, after Athaliah, who had seized the kingdom by tyranny, was killed. Jehoiada made a covenant with Joash, by which covenant King Joash and the people themselves promised to obey God; and the people too, having entered into this covenant with the king, tore down the altars of Baal and smashed the idols, and they killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, even in front of the altar. See 4 Kings 11. Nevertheless, after Jehoiada died, Joash himself turned aside to idolatry. See 2 Chronicles 24; and Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 7.

units.la: IOAS R. IVD. & R. IVD. AMASIAS
units.tr: JOASH, KING OF JUDAH, AND KING OF JUDAH, AMAZIAH

units.la: IO A S, filius Ochofiæ Regis Iudæ, a anno 7. regni Athaliæ matris, qui erat annus mundi 3067. ante Christum natum 895. à Ioiada pontifice vngitur in Regem Iudæ. De hoc superiori pagina in Athalia dictum est, quòd à Iosaba filia Ioram, sorore Ochosiæ absconditus sit, ne interficeret eum Athalia. hic magnam vim pecuniæ misit ad Regè Syriæ, vt recederet: nam cum exercitu pugnabat contra Iudæos. Templum Domini instaurauit, pius ipse in Deũ & homines. At verò mortuo Ioiada Zachariam Prophetam filium Ioiadæ interemit, beneficiorum Ioiadæ immemor, aut ingratus peccatum vltio secuta est, nec diu moram traxit: nam elapso vix anno ascendit contra Ioas exercitus Syriæ, venitque in Iudam & Ierusalem: primores occiderunt, prædas abegerunt. Denique insurgentes etiam serui in ipsum Ioas, eum occiderunt in lectulo suo, in vltionem fanguinis Zachariæ filij Ioiadæ. 4 Reg. 11. & 12. cap 2. Paralip. 24. & 25. Ioseph. lib. 9. cap. 7. & 8. imperauit annos 40. fuit alter Ioas, filius Ioachas filij Iehu, Rex Israël.
units.tr: JOASH, son of Ochosias, king of Judah, in the seventh year of his mother Athaliah's reign, which was the year of the world 3067, before the birth of Christ 895, was anointed king of Judah by Jehoiada the high priest. Of him it was said on the previous page, in the account of Athaliah, that he had been hidden by Jehosheba, daughter of Joram and sister of Ochosias, so that Athaliah would not kill him. He sent a great sum of money to the king of Syria, so that he would withdraw, for the Syrian king was fighting against the Jews with an army. He restored the temple of the Lord, being devout himself toward God and men. But after Jehoiada died, he killed Zechariah the prophet, son of Jehoiada, forgetful of the kindnesses of Jehoiada, or ungrateful; and punishment followed the sin, and was not long delayed: for within barely a year the army of Syria came up against Joash, and came into Judah and Jerusalem; they slew the chief men and carried off the spoils. At last even his own servants rose up against Joash himself and killed him in his bed, in revenge for the blood of Zechariah, son of Jehoiada. See 4 Kings 11 and 12; 2 Chronicles 24 and 25; Josephus, book 9, chapters 7 and 8. He reigned forty years. There was another Joash, son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel.

units.la: AMASIA filius Ioas, successit patri in regno Iudæ anno mundi 3107. ante Christum natum 855. is erat annus secundus regni Ioas, filij Ioachas Regis Israël. Hic vindex fuit paternæ cædis, in eos qui homicidium perpetrarant: non autem in filios eorum. Idumæos vicit, decem millibus occisis & totidem præcipitatis. Posthæc deos Idumæorum adorauit: quare indignatus Dominus tradidit eum in manus supradicti Ioas, & occisus est anno regni sui 29. 4. Reg. 13. & 14. 2. Paralip. 25. item Ioseph. lib. Anti. 9. ca. 9. successit ei Ozias, qui & Azarias dictus est. SICHE[?] VS. DO[?]
units.tr: AMAZIAH, son of Joash, succeeded his father in the kingdom of Judah in the year of the world 3107, before the birth of Christ 855. This was the second year of Joash, son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel. He was an avenger of his father's murder, against those who had committed the homicide, but not against their sons. He defeated the Edomites, killing ten thousand and throwing as many down from a cliff. Afterwards he worshipped the gods of the Edomites; therefore the Lord, being angered, handed him over into the hands of the Joash mentioned above, and he was killed in the twenty-ninth year of his reign. See 4 Kings 13 and 14; 2 Chronicles 25; also Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 9. He was succeeded by Azariah, who was also called Uzziah. SICHAEUS. DO[?]

units.la: SICHÆVS, Didonis auunculus[?] & vir, Herculis Sacerdos fuit, qui honos secundus à rege erat. Hic opes non tectis, sed terræ crediderat, quam rem etsi homines ignorabant, fama tamen loquebatur: qua incensus Pygmalion, Didonis frater, hunc sacrificiis intentum interfecit, cuius meminit his ver-sibus Vergilius.
units.tr: SICHAEUS, uncle and husband of Dido, was a priest of Hercules, which was the second honour after the king. He had entrusted his wealth not to houses but to the earth; although people did not know this, rumour spoke of it. Pygmalion, Dido's brother, inflamed by this, killed him while he was busy with his sacrifices; Virgil mentions this in these verses.

units.la: Huic coniux Sichæus erat, ditissimus agri Phœnicum: sed regna Tyri germanus habebat Pygmalion, scelere ante alios immanior omnes, Quos inter medius venit furor: ille Sichæum Impius ante aras, atque auri cæcus amore, Clam ferro incautum superat.
units.tr: Her husband was Sichaeus, the richest landowner of the Phoenicians; but the kingdom of Tyre was held by her brother Pygmalion, more monstrous in crime than all the others. Between them came mad fury: that man, impious before the altars and blind with love of gold, secretly struck down Sichaeus, unsuspecting, with the sword.

units.la: Vide Iustin. lib. 18. & Vergil. lib. Ænei. 1. & 4.
units.tr: See Justin, book 18, and Virgil, Aeneid, books 1 and 4.

units.la: DIDO Beli Phœnicum seu Tyriorum Regis filia, Pygmalionis soror, ac Sichæi uxor, occiso marito, astu usa in Africam navigavit, cum thesauris quibus inhiaverat Pygmalion. Carthaginem condidit anno mundi 3076. ante Christum natum 886. ab ædificatione templi Salomonis 143. iuxta Iosephum libro primo contra Apionem. huius castitas, cui notam inurere tentavit Vergilius, eximiè laudatur à Boccacio, atque etiam ab Ausonio: siquidem emori maluit quàm cum Hiarba Rege secundis nuptiis coniungi. hæc proprio nomine Elisa dicta est, Dido autem cognominata à rerum magnitudine, quasi virago. Culta est ut Dea, templis, arisque eius nomini dicatis. Vide Iustin.lib.18.Boc.lib.2.de casibus illustr.
units.tr: DIDO, daughter of Belus, king of the Phoenicians or Tyrians, sister of Pygmalion and wife of Sichaeus; when her husband was killed, she made her escape by cunning to Africa, taking with her the treasures for which Pygmalion had lusted. She founded Carthage in the year of the world 3076, before the birth of Christ 886, 143 years after the building of Solomon's temple, according to Josephus in the first book Against Apion. Her chastity, which Virgil tried to brand with a mark of shame, is highly praised by Boccaccio and also by Ausonius; for she preferred to die rather than be joined in a second marriage to King Iarbas. She was called Elissa by her proper name, but was surnamed Dido from the greatness of her deeds, as if she were a virago. She was worshipped as a goddess, with temples and altars dedicated to her name. See Justin, book 18; Boccaccio, On the Falls of Illustrious Men, book 2.

units.la: IOACHAS filius Iehu, regnauit super Israelem in Samaria anno 23. Ioas filij Ochosiæ Regis Iudæ, qui erat annus à mundo condito 3089. ante Christum natum 873. Hic secutus est impietatem Ieroboam filij Nabat, & peccare fecit Israel: quare iratus Dominus tradidit Israelitas in manu Hazael Regis Syriæ, & Ben-adab filij ipsius Hazael. imperauit annos 16. & successit ei Ioas filius eius. Consulito li. 4. Re. ca. 13. item Iosephum li. Antiquitatum 9. cap. 8.
units.tr: Joachaz, son of Jehu, reigned over Israel in Samaria for 23 years, in the year of Joash son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, which was the year 3089 from the creation of the world, 873 years before the birth of Christ. He followed the impiety of Jeroboam son of Nebat and made Israel sin; therefore the Lord, in anger, delivered the Israelites into the hand of Hazael, king of Syria, and of Ben-hadad, son of Hazael. He ruled 16 years, and his son Joash succeeded him. Consult 4 Kings chapter 13; likewise Josephus, Antiquities book 9, chapter 8.

units.la: IOAS, filius Ioachas, mortuo patre regnauit super Israelem anno mundi 3105. ante Christum natum 857. Hic impiè egit, nec declinauit ab omnibus peccatis Ieroboam: recuperauit vrbes de manu Ben-adab, filij Hazael, quas iure belli de manu Ioachas patris sui ille abstulerat: & tribus vicibus eum vicit: quinetiam contra Amasiam Regem Iuda pugnauit, quem & cepit, & templum Domini diripuit: reuersus tandem in Samariam, obiit: & sepultus est in Samaria cum regibus Israël. Successit ei filius suus Ieroboam. Vide 4. lib. Reg. 13. & 14. cap. item Ioseph. lib. Antiq. 9. cap. 10. imperauit hic Ioas annos sedecim. fuit & alter Ioas filius Ochosiæ & Athaliæ, de quo à me dictum est supra, pagina ab hinc tertia. LYCVRGVS LACEDÆ. DIRCEVS
units.tr: Joash, son of Joachaz, succeeded his father as king over Israel in the year of the world 3105, 857 years before the birth of Christ. He acted wickedly and did not turn aside from any of the sins of Jeroboam. He recovered the cities from the hand of Ben-hadad, son of Hazael, which that king had taken from his father Joachaz by the right of war; and he defeated him three times. Moreover, he fought against Amaziah, king of Judah, whom he captured, and he plundered the temple of the Lord. Returning at last to Samaria, he died and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam succeeded him. See 4 Kings chapters 13 and 14; likewise Josephus, Antiquities book 9, chapter 10. This Joash ruled sixteen years.
