There was also another Joash, son of Ahaziah and Athaliah, of whom I spoke above, three pages back. LYCURGUS OF LACEDAEMON. DIRCEUS.

units.la: LYCVRGVS apud Lacedæmonas leges sanxit, imperante Latinis Aremulo, circiter annum mundi 3090. ante Christum natum 872. alij referunt ad annū mundi 3181. ante Christum natum 781. Primùm omnium 28. seniores instituit, qui Regibus assisterent, & populari principatui repugnarent, rursúsque populi iuribus aduersus tyrannidem faueret. Secundò agros æqualiter diuisit. nummum aureum & argenteum ex vsu sustulit: ferreum solum vtendum imperauit: priuatum luxum inhibuit. Cætera qui cupit noffe, adeat Plutarchum in vita Lycurgi. Fuit oratione breuis: quas tradidit leges, finxit fe ex Apollinis Delphici oraculo tenere, ne reiicerentur, quòd feuerae effent: indotatas iubebat accipi vxores, vt prolis non argenti gratia nuberent viri: tum vt ne puellae pauperes, innuptae relinquerentur. non inuentione legum magis quàm exemplo clarior extitit: siquidem nihil lege vlla in alios sanxit, cuius nõ ipse primus in se documenta daret. Iustinus multis in locis. Auguft.de Ciui.Dei.lib.2.cap.16.& lib.10.cap.13. Plutar.in vita Lycurgi. Xenophon,in Atheniensium politia.
units.tr: Lycurgus gave laws to the Spartans while Aremulus ruled over the Latins, about the year of the world 3090, 872 years before the birth of Christ; others refer it to the year of the world 3181, 781 years before the birth of Christ. First of all, he instituted twenty-eight elders, who would assist the kings and oppose popular rule, and in turn would support the rights of the people against tyranny. Second, he divided the land equally. He abolished the use of gold and silver coinage and ordered that only iron money be used; he restrained private luxury. Whoever wishes to know the rest should consult Plutarch in the Life of Lycurgus. He was brief in speech. Of the laws he handed down, he claimed to hold them from the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, so that they would not be rejected on account of their severity. He ordered that wives be taken without dowry, so that men might marry for the sake of children and not for money, and also so that poor girls would not be left unmarried. He was more distinguished by his example than by his invention of laws, for he imposed no law on others which he did not first give as a lesson in his own person. Justinus, in many places. Augustine, City of God, book 2, chapter 16, and book 10, chapter 13. Plutarch, in the Life of Lycurgus. Xenophon, in the Constitution of the Athenians.

units.la: DIRCEVS, Atheniensis Poëta, deformis quidem, attamen tubæ inuentor fuit. Lacedæmonij etenim cùm responsum accepissent ab Apolline, non alio quàm hoc duce superaturos se aduersarios Messanos, hunc ducem elegerunt, qui in Campano agro clangore tubarum Messanos ita exterruit, vt animo consternati, ac in fugâ versi, facilè victi sint. Vide Mag.Elucida. R. ISRAEL. HIEROBOAM R. ISRAEL. ZACHARIA
units.tr: Dirceus, an Athenian poet, was indeed ugly, yet he was the inventor of the trumpet. For when the Lacedaemonians had received an answer from Apollo that they would conquer their Messenian enemies only under this leader, they chose him, and he, in the Campanian field, so terrified the Messenians with the blast of trumpets that, dismayed in spirit and turned to flight, they were easily defeated. See the Magna Elucidarium.

units.la: IEROBOAM filius Ioas Regis Israël, successit patri anno 15. Amasiæ filij Ioas Regis Iudæ, qui erat annus mundi 3120. ante Christum natum 842. Hic quoque imitatus est impietatem Ieroboam filij Nabat, qui peccare fecit Israël: restituit terminos Israël ab introitu Emath usque ad mare solitudinis, iuxta sermonem Domini, quem locutus est per Ionam filium Amathi Prophetam. 4.Reg.14.cap. Ionas enim huic prophetaverat oportere ut Syros vinceret, & regnum proprium dilataret, in partibus quidem Aquilonis usque ad Hemathi ciuitatem: à meridie vero usque ad Asphaltiten paludem, quod mare mortuum hodie vocatur. Vide 4.lib.Reg.cap.14.& Ioseph.lib.Anti. 9. cap.11. imperauit annos 41. successit ei Zacharias filius eius. Fuit etiam alter Ieroboā filius Nabat, cuius supra meminimus.
units.tr: Jeroboam, son of Joash, king of Israel, succeeded his father in the 15th year of Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah, which was the year of the world 3120, 842 years before the birth of Christ. He too imitated the impiety of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin. He restored the borders of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Wilderness, according to the word of the Lord which he spoke through Jonah, son of Amittai, the prophet. See 4 Kings chapter 14. For Jonah had prophesied to him that he would defeat the Syrians and enlarge his own kingdom, on the northern side as far as the city of Hamath, and from the south as far as the Asphaltite marsh, which is today called the Dead Sea. See 4 Kings chapter 14, and Josephus, Antiquities book 9, chapter 11. He ruled 41 years, and his son Zachariah succeeded him. There was also another Jeroboam, son of Nebat, whom we mentioned above.

units.la: ZACHARIAS filius Ieroboam Regis Israël, successit patri anno 38. Azariæ siue Oziæ Regis Iudæ, qui erat annus mundi 3161. ante Christum natum 801. Hic impiè egit quemadmodum patres eius. Sexto imperij sui mense Sellum filius Iabes, aduersus eum coniurauit: percusitque eum palàm, & interfecit, regnauitque post eum mensem vnum. Consulito lib.4.Regum 15.cap. Fuerunt sanè alij Zachariæ, nempe Zacharias Propheta, filius Ioiadæ, qui à Ioa Rege Iuda occisus est, 2.li. Paralip. cap.24. fuit item alius Zacharias filius Barachiæ, qui populum monuit, ut conuerteretur ad Dominum. Zachar.1. ca. præterea fuit & Zacharias pater Ioannis Baptistæ, Lucæ 1.ca. REX IVD AZARIAS RI IOATHAM
units.tr: Zachariah, son of Jeroboam, king of Israel, succeeded his father in the 38th year of Azariah, or Uzziah, king of Judah, which was the year of the world 3161, 801 years before the birth of Christ. He acted wickedly, as his fathers had done. In the sixth month of his reign, Shallum, son of Jabesh, conspired against him, struck him down openly, and killed him, and he reigned after him one month. Consult 4 Kings chapter 15. Certainly there were other Zechariahs: namely, the prophet Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, who was killed by Joash, king of Judah, 2 Chronicles chapter 24; there was also another Zechariah, son of Berechiah, who admonished the people to turn to the Lord (Zechariah 1); moreover, there was Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, Luke chapter 1.

units.la: OZIAS, qui & Azarias, filius Amasiæ, constitutus est Rex Iudæ ab vniuerso populo, & in locum patris subrogatus annos tantum natus sedecim. Cœpit itaque regnare viuo patre, anno mundi 3124. ante Christum natum 838. imperauit 52. annis: nempe 11. viuo patre, aduersus quem coniuratum fuerat: deinde 41. annos post patrem occisum. Hic initio pius, auxilioque diuino fretus, Philisthæos, Arabes, Ammonitas deuicit, tributarios fecit: ciuitatem Ierusalem restaurauit: tandem ex opulentia in superbiam lapsus, dum sacerdotis munus vsurpat, volens sacrificare atque adolere incensum super altare, dumque sacerdotibus ipsum corripientibus minatur, in lepram incidit: atque à sacerdotibus è templo pellitur: mansitque leprosus ad obitum vsque. successit ei Ioathan. Vide lib.4. Reg.14. & 15.cap. & 2.lib.Paral.26.cap. Item Iosep.lib.Anti.9.cap.11.
units.tr: Uzziah, also called Azariah, son of Amaziah, was made king of Judah by the whole people and appointed in his father's place, being only sixteen years old. He therefore began to reign while his father was still living, in the year of the world 3124, 838 years before the birth of Christ. He reigned 52 years: 11 years while his father was living, against whom a conspiracy had been formed, and then 41 years after his father was killed. At first he was pious, relying on divine help, and he defeated the Philistines, Arabs and Ammonites and made them tributaries. He rebuilt the city of Jerusalem. At last, having fallen into pride through prosperity, he usurped the office of priest, wishing to sacrifice and burn incense upon the altar; when the priests rebuked him and he threatened them, he was struck with leprosy, and was driven out of the temple by the priests, and he remained a leper until his death. His successor was Jotham. See 4 Kings chapters 14 and 15, and 2 Chronicles chapter 26. Likewise Josephus, Antiquities book 9, chapter 11.

units.la: IOATHAN filius Oziæ seu Azatiæ, Regis Iudæ, succef-fit patri, eodem in regno, anno secundo Phaceæ filij Romeliæ Regis Israel: qui erat annus mundi 3176. ante Christum natum 786. Hic pietatem coluit: portam domus Domini excelsam ædificauit: vrbes quoque in montibus Iuda, & in saltibus castella & turres. pugnauit contra Regem filiorum Ammon, quem vicit, fecitque tributarium. imperauit annis 16. & succeffit ei filius eius Achas. Videto vt supra. R.ISRAEL, MANAHEN R. ISRAEL PHASEA F.R.
units.tr: Jotham, son of Uzziah or Azariah, king of Judah, succeeded his father in the same kingdom, in the second year of Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of Israel, which was the year of the world 3176, 786 years before the birth of Christ. He cultivated piety: he built the high gate of the house of the Lord, and also cities in the mountains of Judah, and castles and towers in the woods. He fought against the king of the Ammonites, whom he defeated and made tributary. He ruled sixteen years, and his son Ahaz succeeded him. See above.

units.la: MANAHEN filius Gadi de Thersa, venit in Samariam, & interfecit Sellum, qui mensemunū imperauerat, postquam occiderat Zachariam Regem Israël. Itaque qui tyrannide imperium Israëlitarum invaserat, à tyranno quoque intra mensem oppressus est. Manahen igitur tyrannus, qui tyrannum interemit, regnum Israël occupauit anno mundi 3162. ante Christum natum annis 800. Secutus est hic impietatem Jeroboam filij Nabat. Thapsam civitatem quæ nolebat eum intrò admittere, vsque adeò persecutus est, ut prægnantes quoque eius urbis scinderet. Posthæc Phul Assyriorum rex Thersam obsedit: Manahen mille ei talenta argenti dedit. 4. Reg. 15. cap. imperauit annos decem. Iosep. lib. Antiq. 9. cap. 11.
units.tr: Menahem, son of Gadi, from Tirzah, came to Samaria and killed Shallum, who had reigned one month, after Shallum had killed Zechariah, king of Israel. Thus the one who had seized the rule of the Israelites by tyranny was himself overthrown within a month by a tyrant. Menahem therefore, the tyrant who slew the tyrant, took possession of the kingdom of Israel in the year of the world 3162, 800 years before the birth of Christ. He followed the impiety of Jeroboam, son of Nebat. He so persecuted the city of Tiphsah, which was unwilling to admit him, that he even ripped open its pregnant women. Afterwards Pul, king of the Assyrians, besieged Tirzah; Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver. See 4 Kings chapter 15. He ruled ten years. Josephus, Antiquities book 9, chapter 11.

units.la: PHACEA filius Manahen regnauit super Israël in Samaria anno 50. Azariæ sive Oziæ regis Judæ, qui erat annus mundi 3173. ante Christum natum 789. Hic quoque impiè egit, sequutus vestigia Jeroboam filij Nabat. conjuravit adversus eum Phacea filius Romeliæ dux eius, & percussit eum in Samaria, in turre domus regiæ, & cum eo 50. viros de filiis Galaaditarum, regnavitque post eum. Consulito lib.4.Reg.cap.15. item Iosep. lib.Antiq.9.cap.11.imperauit hic annos duos. R. ISRAEL PHASEA R. ISRAEL HOSEA
units.tr: Pekahiah, son of Menahem, reigned over Israel in Samaria in the 50th year of Azariah or Uzziah, king of Judah, which was the year of the world 3173, 789 years before the birth of Christ. He too acted wickedly, following the footsteps of Jeroboam, son of Nebat. Pekah, son of Remaliah, his captain, conspired against him and struck him down in Samaria, in the tower of the royal house, together with fifty men from the sons of the Gileadites, and he reigned after him. Consult 4 Kings chapter 15; likewise Josephus, Antiquities book 9, chapter 11. This king ruled two years.

units.la: PHACEA, filius Romeliæ, tyrannide regnum Israël obtinuit, occiso Phacea filio Manahen, anno 5 2. Azariæ, siue Oziæ Regis Iudæ: qui erat annus mundi 3175. ante Christum natum 787. Hic quoque impius extitit, nec diuertit à peccatis Ieroboam filij Nabat. huius temporibus Theglat-Phalassar Assyriorum Rex, totam Galaaditen regionem oppressit, ac cepit, incolas in Assyriam abduxit. Hoseas, siue Osee, tandem insidiis aggressus est hunc Phaceam, & interfecit eum, regnumque eius inuasit, cùm iam ille viginti regnasset annos. Vide lib. 4. Reg. 15. cap. & Ioseph. lib. 9. cap. 11.
units.tr: Pekah, son of Remaliah, obtained the kingdom of Israel by tyranny, after killing Pekahiah, son of Menahem, in the 52nd year of Azariah or Uzziah, king of Judah, which was the year of the world 3175, 787 years before the birth of Christ. He too was wicked and did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat. In his times Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, overran and captured the whole region of Gilead and led its inhabitants away into Assyria. Hoshea, or Hosea, at last attacked this Pekah by treachery, killed him, and seized his kingdom, when Pekah had already reigned twenty years. See 4 Kings chapter 15, and Josephus, book 9, chapter 11.

units.la: HOSEA filius Ela, regnauit in Samaria super Israëlem post Phaceam quem occiderat, anno mundi 3195. ante Christum natum 767. anno septimo regni sui, Salmanazar Assyriorum Rex, Samariam obsedit, Hoseamque tributarium fecit. At verò Hoseas dum rebellat, tributáque Assyrio recusat, & dum à Sua Rege Ægypti auxilium petit, à Salmanazare obsessus est, qui vinctum misit in carcerem: Samariam cepit, Israëlitarum regnum perdidit, decémque tribus abduxit: transferens Israël in Assyrios. Itaque ab electione impij Ieroboam filij Nabat, ad quem, post mortem Salomonis, defecerant decem tribus ab Roboam filio Salomonis, afflixit Israëlem Dominus, & tradidit in manus diripientium, ob prævaricationes, præcipuè ob idololatriam. Consule librum 4. Regum cap. 17. & Ioseph. lib. 9. cap. 15. REX IVD ACHAS REX IVD EZECHIAS
units.tr: HOSEA, son of Elah, reigned in Samaria over Israel after Pekah, whom he had killed, in the year of the world 3195, before the birth of Christ 767. In the seventh year of his reign, Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, besieged Samaria and made Hoseas a tributary. But when Hoseas rebelled and refused to pay tribute to the Assyrian, and sought help from So, king of Egypt, he was besieged by Shalmaneser, who sent him in chains to prison. He took Samaria, destroyed the kingdom of Israel, and carried away the ten tribes, transferring Israel to the Assyrians. Thus, from the election of the impious Jeroboam, son of Nebat, to whom the ten tribes had revolted after the death of Solomon from Rehoboam, son of Solomon, the Lord afflicted Israel and gave it into the hands of plunderers, on account of their transgressions, and chiefly on account of idolatry. Consult 4 Kings chapter 17 and Josephus, book 9, chapter 15. KING OF JUDAH: AHAZ. KING OF JUDAH: HEZEKIAH.

units.la: ACHAS filius Joatham Regis Juda, successit patri in eodem regno anno mundi 3192. ante Christum natum 770. hic non est secutus vestigia patris sui, sed Regum Israël: impiissimus etiam filium suum consecrauit, transferens eum per ignem, secundum idola gentium. obsessus est à Phacea, & Rasi Rege Syriæ, nec superatus est. Iniit societatem cum TheglatPhalasar Rege Assyriorum, qui Rasim interfecit, in cuius gratiam ablato Dei cultu, diis Syriæ sacrificauit: imperauit annos sedecim, & successit ei filius suus Ezechias. Vide lib.4.Reg.cap. 16.& Josep.lib.Antiq.9.cap.13.
units.tr: AHAZ, son of Jotham, king of Judah, succeeded his father in the same kingdom in the year of the world 3192, before the birth of Christ 770. He did not follow the footsteps of his father, but those of the kings of Israel. Most impious, he even consecrated his own son, causing him to pass through the fire, according to the idols of the nations. He was besieged by Pekah and Rezin, king of Syria, but was not overcome. He entered into an alliance with Tiglath-Pileser, king of the Assyrians, who killed Rezin; for his sake he abolished the worship of God and sacrificed to the gods of Syria. He reigned sixteen years, and his son Hezekiah succeeded him. See 4 Kings chapter 16 and Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 13.

units.la: EZECHIAS filius Achas successit patri in regno Judæ, anno mundi 3208.ante Christum natum 754.hic pius vestigia Dauid secutus est, dissipauit excelsa, contriuit statuas, succidit lucos, confregitq; serpentem æneum, quem fecerat Moyses, siquidem vsq; ad illud tempus filii Israël adolebant ei incensum. Affuit illi Dominus: nam rebellauit contra regem Assyriorum, & non seruiuit ei: Philisthæos persecutus est: anno sexto regni sui capta est Samaria à Salmanasare, ut in Hosea dictum à me est. Posthæc Sennacherib Assyriorum Rex in Deum blasphemus, Judæam deuastauit, Jerusalem obsedit, miraculo tamen diuinitus liberata est: siquidem Angelus Domini occidit una nocte 180000.hominum in castris Sennacherib, qui inde recessit. Deinde ægrotauit Ezechias, cui mortem prædixit Esaias, attamen oratione & fletu obtinuit à Deo adiici vitæ suæ annos 15. signumque sanitatis ab Esaia accepit in umbra decem linearum, retrograda, in horologio suo. Merodac-Baladan Babyloniorū rex, cum accepisset morbo laborare Ezeciam, misit ei literas & munera. imperauit annos 29. successit ei filius Manasses. Vide 4.lib.Reg.18.19.& 20.cap.& Josep.lib.Antiq.9.& 10. ROMVLVS HERSILIA. SABIN
units.tr: HEZEKIAH, son of Ahaz, succeeded his father in the kingdom of Judah, in the year of the world 3208, before the birth of Christ 754. This pious man followed the footsteps of David: he destroyed the high places, broke the statues, cut down the groves, and broke the bronze serpent which Moses had made, for until that time the children of Israel burned incense to it. The Lord was with him: for he rebelled against the king of the Assyrians and did not serve him; he pursued the Philistines. In the sixth year of his reign Samaria was taken by Shalmaneser, as I have said in Hosea. Afterwards Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, blaspheming against God, laid waste Judea and besieged Jerusalem; yet it was delivered by a miracle from God, for the Angel of the Lord killed 185,000 men in the camp of Sennacherib in one night, and he withdrew from there. Then Hezekiah fell ill, and Isaiah foretold his death to him, but by prayer and weeping he obtained from God that fifteen years be added to his life, and he received from Isaiah a sign of his recovery: the shadow went back ten lines on his sundial. Merodach-Baladan, king of the Babylonians, when he heard that Hezekiah was suffering from illness, sent him letters and gifts. He reigned twenty-nine years, and his son Manasseh succeeded him. See 4 Kings chapters 18, 19 and 20, and Josephus, Antiquities, books 9 and 10. ROMULUS, HERSILIA. SABINE.

units.la: ROMVLVS Romanorum Rex primus, imperauit anno mundi 3212. ante Christum natum 750. filius fuit Rheæ Iliæ Vestalis,quem vnà cum Remo,vnico partu edidit, qui paruuli prope ripam Tyberis expositi, tamen à Faustulo ad Accâ Laurentiam delati sunt: vbi adoleuerunt,collecta pastorum manu, Amulium interfecerunt,& Numitorem auum in regnum restituerunt, qui pulsus fuerat à fratre suo Amulio minore natu. Postea vrbê ædificant vbi fuerant expositi, quæ Roma dicta est à conditoris nomine Romulo:qui Remũ fratrem occidit,quòd ludibrio & quasi per contemptum Romuli, nouos transiluisset muros : cẽtum senatores creat Romulus, qui Patres ab honore, Patricij eorũ progenies appellati.300. armatos ad custodiâ corporis,quos Celeres appellauit,non in bello solùm,sed etiam in pace habuit.ex Sabinis & Rom.vnicam gentem fecit.post subactos Ceninenses, Antemnates, Crustuminos, Fidenates, Veientes, cum ad recensendum exercitum concionem in campo haberet,subitò orta tempestate,cum fragore & tonitribus,tam denso opertus est nimbo , vt conspectum eius concioni abstulerit tempestas , nec deinde in terris sit visus. imperauit annos 37.Vide Tit.Liu.li.1.Diony.Halicar.lib.2. & Eutro.lib.1.
units.tr: ROMULUS, the first king of the Romans, reigned in the year of the world 3212, before the birth of Christ 750. He was the son of Rhea Ilia, a Vestal virgin, and was born together with Remus at a single birth. The infants, exposed near the bank of the Tiber, were nevertheless carried by Faustulus to Acca Laurentia, where, having grown up and gathered a band of shepherds, they killed Amulius and restored their grandfather Numitor to the kingdom, who had been driven out by his brother Amulius, the younger. Afterwards they built the city where they had been exposed, which was called Rome from the name of its founder Romulus; and he killed his brother Remus, because Remus had leapt over the new walls in mockery and, as it were, in contempt of Romulus. Romulus created one hundred senators, who were called Fathers from their honour, and their descendants Patricians. He kept three hundred armed men for the protection of his person, whom he called Celeres, and he kept them not only in war but also in peace. He made one nation out of the Sabines and the Romans. After subduing the Ceninenses, Antemnates, Crustumini, Fidenates and Veientes, when he was holding an assembly in the Campus to review the army, a sudden storm arose with a crash and thunder, and he was covered with so dense a cloud that the storm took him from the sight of the assembly, and afterwards he was not seen on earth. He reigned thirty-seven years. See Titus Livy, book 1; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2; and Eutropius, book 1.

units.la: HERSILIA, vxor fuit Romuli,de qua Ti.Li.1.deca.1.De hac nonnihil fabulatur etiam Ouidius,ad calcem 14.lib.Metamorph. inquiens:
units.tr: HERSILIA was the wife of Romulus, about whom Titus Livy, book 1 of the first decade, says something. Ovid also tells some fabulous things about her at the end of book 14 of the Metamorphoses, saying:

units.la: Flebat vt amissum coniux, cùm regia Iuno Irin ad Herfiliam descendere limite curuo Imperat : & vacuæ sua sic mandata referre: O & de Latio, ò & de gente Sabina Præcipuum matrona d[?]cus, d[?]gnifsima tanti Ante fuisse viri coniux,nunc eff. Quirini, Siste tuos fletus. &c. SIB. ERYTHRAEA SAMIA SIB
units.tr: She was weeping, as a wife for a lost husband, when royal Juno ordered Iris to descend by a winding path to Hersilia, and to deliver to her, who was empty, these commands: O matron, most distinguished glory of Latium and of the Sabine people, wife of a man most worthy of so great a thing, once was, now is the wife of Quirinus; stop your tears. etc. SIBYL OF ERYTHRA. SIBYL OF SAMOS.

units.la: SIBYLLA Erythræa,alias Heriphile,agebat, ut vulgatior est opinio ,antequam à Græcis obsideretur Troia ( quanquam Euseb.in Romuli tepora referat ) nam Apollodorus Erythræus suam esse civem affirmat, eamque Graiis Ilium petentibus vaticinatam, & periturum esse Troiam,& Homerum mendacia scripturum. At Strabo duas facit Erythræas Sibyllas: priscam nempe alteram,item alteram recentiorem,Athenain nomine, tempore Alexadri.Porrò Lactan. Erythræam Babylone natam esse ait, & se Erythræam appellare maluisse, quæ sola nomen suum carmini verum inseruerit: & à Græcis ac Latinis præcipua dicta fit.Vide Lactan.lib.1.cap.6. Divi.insti.& lib.de ira Dei,ca. 22. Fenestella legatos Erythras à Senatu Rom. missos esse referit, ut huius Sibyllæ carmina Romam deportarentur: & ea Coss. Curio & Octavius in capitolio ( quod tunc erat curante Q.Catulo refectum)ponenda curarent. Erythræ autem urbs est Asiæ minoris. Huic Sibyllæ hæc tribuitur prophetia:
units.tr: The Sibyl of Erythra, otherwise called Herophile, lived, as the more common opinion has it, before Troy was besieged by the Greeks (although Eusebius refers her to the times of Romulus). For Apollodorus of Erythrae affirms that she was his fellow citizen, and that she prophesied to the Greeks who were heading for Ilium that Troy would perish, and that Homer would write lies. But Strabo makes two Erythraean Sibyls: one the older, and another, more recent, named Athenais, in the time of Alexander. Furthermore, Lactantius says that the Erythraean was born in Babylon, and that she preferred to be called the Erythraean, since she alone had inserted her own name into her true song; and she was chiefly called so by the Greeks and Latins. See Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 1, chapter 6, and On the Anger of God, chapter 22. Fenestella reports that envoys were sent from the Roman Senate to Erythra so that the songs of this Sibyl might be brought to Rome, and that the consuls Curio and Octavius were to arrange for them to be placed in the Capitol (which at that time had been restored under the care of Quintus Catulus). Erythra is a city of Asia Minor. The following prophecy is attributed to this Sibyl:

units.la: In ultima ætate humiliabitur Deus , humanabitur proles divina, iungetur humanitati divinitas , iacebit in fœno agnus, & puellari officio educabitur Deus & homo. Vide lib.Sibyl.
units.tr: In the last age God will be humbled, the divine offspring will be made human, divinity will be joined to humanity; a lamb will lie in the manger, and God and man will be brought up by the service of a maiden. See the Sibylline books.

units.la: SIBYLLA Samia, Herophila dicta,claruit in Samo insula,autorib.Euseb.Augu.&Cassiod.circiter annū mundi 3297. ante Christum natum 665. Eratosthenes in antiquis Samiorum annalibus se reperisse scribit, hanc dictam fuisse nomine Phyto. Vide ut supra.Hanc sic prophetasse ferunt:
units.tr: The Sibyl of Samos, called Herophila, flourished on the island of Samos, according to Eusebius, Augustine and Cassiodorus, around the year of the world 3297, before the birth of Christ 665. Eratosthenes writes that he found in the ancient annals of the Samians that she was called by the name Phyto. See as above. They say she prophesied thus:

units.la: Tu enim stulta Iudæa Deum tuum non cognouisti,ludentem mortalium mentibus ,sed & spinis coronasti, & horridum fel miscuisti. Item,Ecce veniet dives,& nascetur de paupercula,& bestiæ terrarum adorabunt eum.
units.tr: For you, foolish Judea, did not know your God, who plays with the minds of mortals; but you crowned him with thorns, and you mixed him a bitter gall. Likewise: Behold, the rich one will come, and he will be born of a poor maiden, and the beasts of the earth will adore him.

units.la: SALMANASAR Assyriorum Rex, magno comparato exercitu pugnauit contra Samariam quam cepit, Hoseámque regem Samariæ tributarium fecit.post aliquot annos cum nollet Hoseas amplius tributum persoluere,iterum venit in Samariam Salmanasar, quam post tertium obsidionis annum cepit, ac decem tribus in Assyriam abduxit, anno nono rebellionis Hoseæ.qui erat annus mundi 3213. ante Christum natum 749. hunc finem habuit regnum Israël, quod 242. annos steterat, sub 17.Regibus: si sumas initium à morte Salomonis, & regno Ieroboam filij Nabat,ad quem defecerat decem tribus, desciscentes à Roboam, filio Salomonis. Vide lib. 4. Reg. 17. & 18. cap.Iosephi.lib.9.cap.15. De hoc Salmanasare dictum à me supra est in Hosea.
units.tr: SHALMANESER, king of the Assyrians, having assembled a great army, fought against Samaria, which he took, and he made Hoseas, king of Samaria, a tributary. After some years, when Hoseas no longer wished to pay the tribute, Shalmaneser came again into Samaria; he captured it in the third year of the siege, and carried the ten tribes away into Assyria, in the ninth year of Hoseas's rebellion, which was the year of the world 3213, before the birth of Christ 749. The kingdom of Israel ended here; it had stood for 242 years under seventeen kings, if you take the beginning from the death of Solomon and the reign of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, to whom the ten tribes had revolted, falling away from Rehoboam, son of Solomon. See 4 Kings chapters 17 and 18, and Josephus, book 9, chapter 15. I have spoken of this Shalmaneser above, in Hosea.

units.la: SENNACHERIB Assyriorum Rex, blasphemus in Deum, per nuntios minatus est Ezechiæ Regi Iudæ, & populo, sic exclamantibus nuntiis: Audite verba Regis magni, Regis Assyriorum: hæc dicit Rex, Non vos seducat Ezechias, non enim poterit eruere vos de manu mea: neque fiduciam vobis tribuat super Dominum, dicens, eruens liberabit nos Dominus, & non tradetur civitas hæc in manu Regis Assyriorum. Postea Sennacherib, Iudæam vastavit, Ierosolyma obsedit. At vero tandem ad preces Esaiæ & Ezechiæ, Angelus Domini occidit una nocte 180000. militum Sennacherib, anno mundi 3221. ante Christum natum 741. reuersus itaque cum adoraret in templo Nefroch deum suum, Adramalech & Sarafar, filij eius occiderunt eum. Vide lib. 4.Reg.18. & 19.cap. & lib..2.Paral.cap.32.& Iosep.lib.Antiq.10.cap.1.& 2. De Sennacherib etiam mentionem feci in Ezechia. REX IVD. MANASSES ISAIAS PROPH.
units.tr: SENNACHERIB, king of the Assyrians, blaspheming against God, threatened King Hezekiah of Judah and the people through messengers, who cried out thus: Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians: thus says the king: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you out of my hand; nor let him give you trust in the Lord, saying, The Lord will surely deliver us, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians. Afterwards Sennacherib laid waste Judea and besieged Jerusalem. But at last, at the prayers of Isaiah and Hezekiah, the Angel of the Lord killed in one night 180,000 soldiers of Sennacherib, in the year of the world 3221, before the birth of Christ 741. And so, when he was returning and worshipping his god Nisroch in the temple, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer killed him. See 4 Kings chapters 18 and 19, and 2 Chronicles chapter 32, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 10, chapters 1 and 2. I also made mention of Sennacherib under Hezekiah. KING OF JUDAH: MANASSEH. ISAIAH THE PROPHET.

units.la: MANASSES, Ezechiæ regis Iudæ filius, successit patri in regno, anno mundi 3237. ante Christum natum 725. impius hic ædificauit excelsa quæ dissipauerat Ezechias pater eius, & erexit aras Baal, templum contaminauit, filios Diis immolauit: Ierusalem innocentum sanguine repleuit: quare iratus Deus suscitauit Regem Babyloniæ qui Iudæam inuasit, Manassen cepit, & vinctum catenis, & compedibus, duxit in Babylonem. In captiuitate autem agnoscens Dominum resipuit, pœnitentiam egit, atque regno restitutus idololatriam aboleuit, vitámque reliquam in Dei timore transegit. imperauit annis 55. Vide 4.lib.Reg.21.cap.& lib.2. lib.Paralip.cap.33. item Iosephus lib. Antiq.10. cap.4.& 5.
units.tr: MANASSES, son of King Hezekiah of Judah, succeeded his father in the kingdom in the year of the world 3237, before the birth of Christ 725. This impious king built again the high places which his father Hezekiah had broken down, and erected altars to Baal; he defiled the Temple and sacrificed his sons to the gods, and filled Jerusalem with the blood of the innocent. Therefore God, in anger, raised up the King of Babylon, who invaded Judah, took Manasseh, and led him in chains and fetters to Babylon. In captivity, however, he acknowledged the Lord, repented, and, restored to his kingdom, abolished idolatry and spent the rest of his life in the fear of God. He reigned for 55 years. See 4 Kings 21 and 2 Chronicles 33; also Josephus, Antiquities, book 10, chapters 4 and 5.

units.la: ESAIAS in Ierusalem nobili genere ortus est, ibíque prophetauit, & in Iudæa, necdum decem tribubus in captiuitatem ductis: ac de utroq; regno nunc mixtim, nunc separatim texuit oraculum: & cùm interdum ad præsentem respiciat historiam, & post Babyloniæ captiuitatem reditum populi significet in Iudæam: attamen omnis eius cura de vocatione gentium, & aduentu Christi est: hic sub Manasse Rege sectus in duas partes occubuit. Consulito lib.4.Reg.19. & 20.cap. & Ieronymum in Esaiam. CANDAVLES GYGES.
units.tr: ISAIAH was born of a noble family in Jerusalem, and prophesied there and in Judah, before the ten tribes had been led into captivity. He wove his oracle concerning both kingdoms, now mixed together and now separately; and although at times he looks to the history of his own day, and foretells the return of the people to Judah after the Babylonian captivity, yet all his care concerns the calling of the Gentiles and the coming of Christ. Under King Manasseh he was sawn in two and died. Consult 4 Kings 19 and 20, and Jerome on Isaiah. CANDAULES, GYGES.

units.la: CANDAVLES Lydorum Rex quartus, Lydis imperauit anno mundi 3248. ante Christum natum 714. Hic cùm vxoris suæ pulchritudinem omnibus prædicaret, quasi filetium[?] damnum pulchritudinis esset, ad postremum Gygi sodali suo nudam demonstrauit: quo facto & amicum in adulterium vxoris illectum, hostem sibi fecit, & vxorem veluti tradito alij amore, à se alienauit. nam breui post tempore cædes Candaulis, nuptiarum præmiū fuit. vxor mariti sanguine dotata, regnum viri, & se pariter adultero tradidit. Iusti.li.1. Scribit Herodotus libro primo Gygem, quanquam repugnans & inuitus nudam reginam conspexisset, ab ea accersitum, ab eadémq; hæc verba audiuisse: Aut illum qui ista consuluit interire oportet, aut te qui nudam me es conspicatus. Gyges vbi videt propositam sibi necessitatem aut interficiendi herum Regem, aut seipsum interfectum iri, elegit vt ipse superesset.
units.tr: CANDAULES, the fourth king of the Lydians, reigned over the Lydians in the year of the world 3248, before the birth of Christ 714. When he kept proclaiming to everyone the beauty of his wife, as if it were a loss of beauty not to be seen, at last he showed her naked to his companion Gyges. By this deed he made into an enemy the friend who had been enticed into adultery with his wife, and he estranged his wife from himself, as if she had been handed over to another's love. For shortly afterwards the murder of Candaules was the reward of the marriage. The wife, endowed with her husband's blood, gave both the kingdom of her husband and herself likewise to the adulterer. Justin, book 1. Herodotus writes in book 1 that Gyges, though reluctant and unwilling, had seen the queen naked, was summoned by her, and heard from her these words: "Either he who advised you to this must die, or you who have seen me naked." When Gyges saw the necessity set before him, either of killing his master the King or of being killed himself, he chose to survive himself.

units.la: GYGES imperauit Lydis post Candaulem quem occidit, anno mundi 3265 ante Christum natum 697. postquam imperio potitus est, arma intulit Mileto & Smyrnæ, vrbémque Colophonem vi cepit. Herodotus lib.1. feruntur præterea nescio quæ fabulosa de equo æneo, in cuius lateribus essent fores, & de corpore hominis mortui intus clausi, qui anulum aureum in digito habebat, quem detraxit Gyges: qui huius anuli palam cum ad palmam conuerteret, à nullo videbatur (vt ferunt) itaque huius anuli ope stuprum Reginæ intulisse, Regem occidisse, nec in his facinoribus quenquâ eum videre potuisse. sic repente anuli huius beneficio Regem Lydiæ ipsum fuisse. Cice.3.lib.Offic.
units.tr: GYGES ruled over the Lydians after Candaules, whom he killed, in the year of the world 3265, before the birth of Christ 697. After he had gained the throne, he waged war on Miletus and Smyrna, and took the city of Colophon by force. Herodotus, book 1. There are also reported, besides, certain fabulous things about a bronze horse, in whose sides there were doors, and about the body of a dead man shut up inside, who had a golden ring on his finger, which Gyges drew off; and when he turned this ring toward his palm, he was (so they say) seen by no one. Thus by the help of this ring he is said to have committed the adultery with the queen and to have killed the King, and in these deeds no one could see him. So by the benefit of this ring he suddenly became King of Lydia himself. Cicero, book 3 of On Duties.

units.la: NVMA-POMPILIVS secundus Romanorum Rex, imperat anno mundi 3250. ante Christum natum 712. nam mortuo Romulo res ad interregnum rediit, cùm regerent Senatores annum integrum, creatis decem Decurionibus. Huic Tatius Sabinorum Rex filiam suam unicam in uxore dederat: qua defuncta, relicta ipse Curia, in syluis degebat. ad principatum autem à Romanis post excessum Romuli euocatus, primò contradixit, mansitque diu in sententia, repugnans ne susciperet imperium. ubi verò cohortantes fratres, atque postremò pater, haud æquum censebant tantum honorem ultro oblatum repellere, ut Rex fieret consensit. Bellum nullum quidem gessit Numa, sed non minus ciuitati profuit quàm Romulus: nam legibus moribusque Romanos formauit, qui consuetudine præliorum iam latrones ac semi-barbari putabantur. Duos menses anno addidit, Ianuarium, Februariumque: cùm ante hunc decem tantùm menses apud Romanos fuissent: infinita Romæ sacra, ac templa constituit. morbo decessit 43.imperij anno. Regnante Numa, Glaucus primus ferri interse glutinum excogitauit. Videto Titum Liuium li.I. Deca.I.& Dion.Halic. lib.2.& Eutropium lib.I.
units.tr: NUMA POMPILIUS, the second King of the Romans, reigned in the year of the world 3250, before the birth of Christ 712. For after Romulus died, the state fell back into an interregnum, while the senators governed for a whole year, ten decurions having been created. Tatius, King of the Sabines, had given his only daughter to him in marriage; when she died, he left the Curia behind and lived in the woods. But when he was called by the Romans to the principate after the departure of Romulus, he first refused, and remained for a long time in this opinion, resisting accepting the rule. But when his brothers encouraged him, and at last his father judged it not fitting to reject so great an honour offered of its own accord, he consented to become King. Numa waged no war at all, yet he benefited the state no less than Romulus did: for he formed the Romans by laws and customs, who by the habit of fighting were now thought to be robbers and half-barbarians. He added two months to the year, January and February, whereas before him the Romans had had only ten months. He established countless sacred rites and temples at Rome. He died of disease in the forty-third year of his reign. In the reign of Numa, Glaucus was the first to invent the soldering of iron. See Livy, book 1, decade 1, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2, and Eutropius, book 1.

units.la: ÆGERIA fuit Nimpha siue Dea, quæ fertur fuisse uxor Numæ Pompilij, saltem cum ea nocturnos se congressus habere cominiscebatur Pompilius, cuius etiam monitu quæ acceptissima diis essent sacra instituerat[?]. hanc fabulantur Poëtæ in sontem versam. Vide Oui.li.3.de Fastis,& li.15.Meta.& quos supra citaui autores.
units.tr: EGERIA was a nymph or goddess, who is said to have been the wife of Numa Pompilius, at least Pompilius was reported to have had nightly meetings with her, and at her instruction he had instituted the rites most acceptable to the gods. The poets tell the fable that she was turned into a spring. See Ovid, Fasti book 3, and Metamorphoses book 15, and the authors I cited above.

units.la: Medallion portraits (illustrations): left, "IVDA. AMMON REX"; right, "IOSIAS R. IVDA".
units.tr: Medallion portraits (illustrations): left, "IVDA. AMMON REX"; right, "IOSIAS R. IVDA".

units.la: AMON filius Manasse, successit patri in regno Iudæ, anno mundi 3292. ante Christum natum 670. impius hic vestigia patris etiam impij secutus est. Annorum 22. erat cum regnare cæpisset, & duobus annis regnauit in Ierusalem. hic cunctis idolis quæ Manasses fuerat fabricatus, immolauit, atque seruiuit. coniurarunt aduersus eum serui sui, & interfecerunt eum in domo sua. Vide lib. 4.Reg.21. cap. & lib.2. Paralip.33. cap. & Ioseph.lib.10.cap.4.
units.tr: AMON, son of Manasseh, succeeded his father in the kingdom of Judah, in the year of the world 3292, before the birth of Christ 670. This impious king followed also the impious footsteps of his father. He was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. He sacrificed to and served all the idols which Manasseh had made. His servants conspired against him and killed him in his own house. See 4 Kings 21 and 2 Chronicles 33, and Josephus, book 10, chapter 4.

units.la: IOSIAS filius Amon, successit patri, regnauitque in Ierusalem annos 31. hic iustus, pius, Dauidis vestigia secutus, 12. anno regni sui mundauit Iudam & Ierusalem ab excelsis, & lucis, simulachrisque, & sculptilibus. aras Baalim, & simulachra quæ superposita fuerant, euertit: Templum instaurari iussit: reperit Helcias sacerdos librum legis Domini, qui datus fuerat per manum Moysis: congregato vniuerso populo in domo Domini legit Rex omnia verba libri huius: & stans pro tribunali percussit fœdus coram Domino, adiurauit populum, & celebrauit Phase Domino. Cæterum dum pugnat cum Nechaone Rege Ægypti, qui missis nuntiis indicarat se non parasse bellum in eum, vulneratur sagitta, quo ex vulnere obit. luxerunt eum vniuersus populus, maximè Ieremias qui super eius morte carmen lamentabili modulatione conscripsit, quæ lamentationes vocitantur. Vide lib.4.Reg. 22. & 23.cap. & lib.2. Paralip.34. & 35. cap. & Iosephlib.10.Antiq.cap.5.& 6.
units.tr: JOSIAH, son of Amon, succeeded his father and reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. He was just and pious, following the footsteps of David. In the twelfth year of his reign he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem from the high places, groves, images and carved idols. He overthrew the altars of the Baals and the images that had been set up upon them, and ordered the Temple to be repaired. The priest Hilkiah found the book of the law of the Lord, which had been given through the hand of Moses; and when all the people had been gathered in the house of the Lord, the King read all the words of this book, and standing on a platform he made a covenant before the Lord, bound the people by oath, and celebrated the Passover to the Lord. However, while fighting against Necho, King of Egypt, who had sent messengers to declare that he had not prepared war against him, he was wounded by an arrow, and died from the wound. All the people mourned him, especially Jeremiah, who composed a song of lament in mournful measure about his death, which is called the Lamentations. See 4 Kings 22 and 23, and 2 Chronicles 34 and 35, and Josephus, book 10 of the Antiquities, chapters 5 and 6.

units.la: TVLLVS Hostilius tertius Romanorum Rex, regnauit anno mundi 3293. ante Christum natum 669.Hic primus Romanorum purpura & fascibus usus est: bella reparauit, fiducia bene exercitæ iuuentutis: Albanos vicit sexta congressione: Veientes, Sabinos, & Fidenates itidem. fœdere rupto,de Metio Suffetio supplicium sumit ob violatam fidem. Horatij Curiatios vincūt: Alba solo æquatur:ex Albanis & Romanis unus fit populus. Tradunt volentem Tullum Hostilium commentarios Numæ cùm quædam occulta solennia sacrificia Iouis Elicio facta inuenisset, operatum his sacris se abdidisse: sed non rite initum id sacrum esse: nec solùm nullam ei oblatam cœlestium speciem,sed ira Iouis solicitati praua religione, fulmine ipsum cum domo conflagrasse. Imperauit annos 32. ciuitatem auxit,adiecto Cœlio monte.hoc imperante Byzantium ciuitas condita est à Paufania Rege Spartanorum. Titus Liuius lib.1. Decad.1.Eutrop.lib.1.Diony.Halicarn.lib.3.
units.tr: TULLUS HOSTILIUS, the third King of the Romans, reigned in the year of the world 3293, before the birth of Christ 669. He was the first of the Romans to use the purple and the fasces. He renewed the wars, trusting in his well-trained youth. He conquered the Albans in a sixth engagement; likewise the Veientes, the Sabines and the Fidenates. When the treaty was broken, he exacted punishment from Mettius Suffetius for violated faith. The Horatii overcame the Curiatii. Alba was levelled with the ground, and from Albans and Romans one people was made. They relate that Tullus Hostilius, when he had found in the commentaries of Numa that certain secret solemn sacrifices of Jupiter Elicius had been performed, shut himself away to carry out these rites; but that this sacred rite had not been entered upon properly, and that not only was no heavenly appearance shown to him, but, with Jupiter's wrath stirred up by wrong worship, he was burned together with his house by a thunderbolt. He reigned for 32 years. He enlarged the city, adding the Caelian hill. In his time the city of Byzantium was founded by Pausanias, King of the Spartans. Livy, book 1, decade 1; Eutropius, book 1; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 3.

units.la: ANCVS Martius Numæ ex filia nepos, successit Tullo Hostilio anno mundi 3325. ante Christum natum 637. contra Latinos dimicauit,quos & vicit: Auentinum montem ciuitati adiecit,& Ianiculum.Pontem Subliciù in Tyberi fecit.Ostiam ciuitatem supra mare 16.miliario ab urbe Roma,condidit.Prol. lib.3.cap.1.& Strab.li.5. Huius temporibus Lucumo,cui nomen fuit L.Tarquinius Priscus,cum uxore Tanaquil Romam venit. Anno imperij 24. morbo perit Ancus , quo regnante Epidamnus est condita, quæ nunc Dyrrachium. Vide ut supra.
units.tr: ANCUS MARTIUS, grandson of Numa through his daughter, succeeded Tullus Hostilius in the year of the world 3325, before the birth of Christ 637. He fought against the Latins, whom he also defeated; he added the Aventine hill to the city, and the Janiculum. He built the Sublician bridge over the Tiber. He founded the city of Ostia on the sea, sixteen miles from the city of Rome. Prologue to book 3, chapter 1; and Strabo, book 5. In his times Lucumo, whose name was Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, came to Rome with his wife Tanaquil. In the twenty-fourth year of his reign Ancus died of disease; in his reign Epidamnus, which is now Dyrrachium, was founded. See above.

units.la: SIBYLLA Cumana, nomine Amalthea, à Suida Hierophile vocatur, eámque dicit libros 9. ad Tarquinium Priscum (alij Superbum scribunt) attulisse, ac pro eis 300. aureos postulasse, Regémque mulieris insaniam derisisse: illam coram Rege unum combussisse, ac pro reliquis idem pretiū postulasse: tum Regem multomagis hanc insanire putasse: quæ denuo altero exusto, cùm in eodem precio perseueraret, motū esse Regem, ac residuum 300. aureis emisse. alij singulis vicibus tres combussisse scribunt: at Plin. tres tantùm libros attulisse scribit: duobus autem exustis, tertiū superfuisse. Cæterùm tres residui libri in sacrarium conditi, Sibyllini dicti sunt: ac in Capitolio piè asseruati, à Quindecim viris consulebātur, in rebus dubiis, laborante republ. permanserunt ad usque bellum Marsicum, post verò 173. Olympiadem, tempore Marij incenso templo exusti sunt: alij tamen in eorum locum, iubente Augusto conquisiti, restituto Capitolio, repositi sunt. Hos quoque Stilico, concitaturus in Honorium generum seditionem, exusit. Est autem Cuma unde hæc Sibylla erat, Æolicarum urbium maxima & optima, in Asia minore. Vide Strab. lib.13. Plin. lib.13. cap.13. Aul.Gel.lib.1.cap.19.Chronic. Naucler.genera.52. Huius Sibyllæ hæc fertur prophetia:
units.tr: THE CUMAEAN SIBYL, called Amalthea by name, and by Suidas Herophile, is said to have brought nine books to Tarquinius Priscus (others write Superbus), and to have asked 300 golden coins for them; and the King mocked the woman's madness. She burned one of them in the King's presence, and asked the same price for the remaining ones. Then the King thought her madness much greater; and when, after she had burned a second, she persisted at the same price, the King was moved and bought the remaining 300 golden coins. Others write that she burned three at each time; but Pliny writes that she brought only three books, and that when two had been burned, the third survived. The three remaining books, however, were stored in a sanctuary and called the Sibylline books; and they were kept devoutly on the Capitol, and consulted by fifteen men in doubtful matters, when the commonwealth was in trouble. They remained until the Marsic War, but after the 173rd Olympiad, in the time of Marius, when the temple was set on fire, they were burned. Others, however, were sought out in their place by order of Augustus, and when the Capitol was restored, they were placed there. Stilicho, intending to stir up sedition against his son-in-law Honorius, also burned these. Now Cumae, whence this Sibyl was, was the greatest and best of the Aeolian cities, in Asia Minor. See Strabo, book 13; Pliny, book 13, chapter 13; Aulus Gellius, book 1, chapter 19; Chronicle of Nauclerus, generation 52. The following prophecy is ascribed to this Sibyl:

units.la: Mortis fatum finiet, trium somno suscepto: tunc à mortuis regressus ad lucem lætam veniet, primus resurrectionis initium ostendens.
units.tr: The fate of death will end: after three sleeping in the grave, he will return from the dead to the joyful light, showing the first beginning of the resurrection.

units.la: SIBYLLA Hellespontica, in agro Troiano nata est, vico Marpesso (vel Marmisso) circa oppidum Gergithium (vel Gergetium.) Hanc Heraclides Ponticus scribit Cyri fuisse temporibus. Huic hæc tribuitur prophetia:
units.tr: The Hellespontine Sibyl was born in the Trojan territory, in the village of Marpessus (or Marmissus), near the town of Gergithium (or Gergetium). Heraclides of Pontus writes that she lived in the time of Cyrus. To her is attributed this prophecy:

units.la: De excelso cælorum habitaculo prospexit Deus humiles suos, & nascetur de virgine Hebraa in cunabulis terræ. CHVS. SALEV ZALEVCH[?] FIL.
units.tr: From the lofty dwelling of the heavens God looked down on his humble ones, and he will be born of a Hebrew virgin in the cradle of the earth. CHUS. SALEV ZALEUCH[?] SON.

units.la: ZALEVCVS, vrbe Locrensium (quæ in Græcia est, vel in Calabria, vt alij volunt) à se saluberrimis legibus munita, cùm filius eius, adulterij crimine damnatus, secundum ius ab ipso constitutum, vtroque oculo carere deberet, ac tota ciuitas in honorem patris, pœnam adolescenti remitteret, aliquandiu repugnauit: tandem populi precibus victus, suo prius, deinde filij oculo eruto, vsum vtrique videndi reliquit. Ita debitum supplicij modum legi reddidit: æquitatis admirabili temperamento se inter misericordem patrem, & iustum legislatorem partitus. Videto Valer.Maxi.lib.6.ca.5. hic Zaleucus legumlator clarebat circiter annum mundi 3300. ante Christum natum 660. Hic attendat pius lector quàm diligenter obseruanda sint Christi mandata: cùm ethnicus hic tam mordicus suam obseruarit, ac inuiolatam retinuerit legem, vt nec oculo suo, quæ pars est corporis delicatissima, simul ac præstantissima, pepercerit. Porrò scribit Diog. Laër. Zaleucum edoctum fuisse à Pythagora, cuius postea meminerimus: quæ in re non sat bene conuenit cum Chronica annorum supputatione, quemadmodum nec aliis aliquot in locis.
units.tr: Zaleucus, lawgiver of the city of the Locrians (which is in Greece, or in Calabria, as others hold), who had fortified his city with most wholesome laws, when his son, convicted of adultery, was by the law he himself had established to lose both eyes, and the whole city, out of honour for the father, wished to remit the punishment for the young man, resisted for some time; at last, overcome by the prayers of the people, he had one of his own eyes plucked out, and then one of his son's, leaving them both the use of sight. Thus he rendered to the law the due measure of punishment, dividing himself between a merciful father and a just lawgiver with an admirable balance of fairness. See Valerius Maximus, book 6, chapter 5. This Zaleucus, lawgiver, flourished about the year of the world 3300, before the birth of Christ 660. Let the pious reader consider here how diligently the commands of Christ are to be observed, since this heathen so tenaciously observed his own law and kept it inviolate that he did not spare even his own eye, the most delicate and at the same time the most precious part of the body. Moreover, Diogenes Laertius writes that Zaleucus was taught by Pythagoras, of whom we shall speak later; in this matter it does not agree well enough with the chronological reckoning of the years, as is also the case in several other places.

units.la: ARCHILOCHVS historicus qui scripsit de temporibus, & Simonides, item Aristoxenus Philosophus ac medicus, qui etiam complures libros de Musica scripsit, circa hæc tempora florebant. præterea iisdem his temporibus diruta est Albalonga, quæ 487.annos durauerat. PROPH. HIEREMIAS PROPH. BARUCH
units.tr: Archilochus the historian, who wrote about the times, and Simonides, likewise Aristoxenus, philosopher and physician, who also wrote several books on music, flourished about this time. Moreover, at these same times Alba Longa was destroyed, which had lasted 487 years. PROPHET JEREMIAH, PROPHET BARUCH.

units.la: JEREMIAS Propheta,puer adhuc vaticinari incepit anno 13. regni Josiæ Regis Judæ,qui erat annus mundi 3307.ante Christum natum 655. Hic in Juda tantum & Beniamin prophetauit, iam enim decem tribus Israël Assyrij in Medos transstulerant : civitatis Jerosolymæ ruinas quadruplici planxit alphabeto. Anathothites dictus est à viculo tribus ab Jerosolymis milibus distante:hic sacerdos ex sacerdotibus,& in matris utero sanctificatus est,& ad prophetiam segregatus,quam cum detrectaret,causatus imperitiam,doctrinam, animum quoque à Deo accepit. Tandem apud Taphnas in Ægypto,à populo lapidibus obrutus,occubuit. Vide D.Jero. in Jeremiam. Jeremiæ vitam ac vincula qui cupit amplius nosse, legat eiusdem prophetiam,item Ecclesiast.cap.49.& 2.Machab.2.& Jose.lib. Antiq 10.cap.8.& sequentibus.
units.tr: Jeremiah the prophet began to prophesy while still a boy, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah, king of Judah, which was the year of the world 3307, before the birth of Christ 655. He prophesied only in Judah and Benjamin, for the Assyrians had already carried the ten tribes of Israel into the land of the Medes. He lamented the ruins of the city of Jerusalem in a fourfold alphabet. He was called the Anathothite, from a village three miles distant from Jerusalem; he was a priest of the priests, and was sanctified in his mother's womb, and set apart for prophecy; when he shrank from it, pleading inexperience, God gave him learning and courage as well. At last, at Taphnae in Egypt, he was overwhelmed with stones by the people and died. See St Jerome on Jeremiah. Whoever wishes to know more of the life and imprisonments of Jeremiah should read his prophecy, also Ecclesiasticus chapter 49, and 2 Maccabees 2, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 10, chapter 8 and following.

units.la: BARUCH Propheta, & Jeremiæ scriba fuit, qui librum Jeremiæ scripsit de futuris rebus civitati,populo & templo.fuit quoque Jeremiæ in carcere minister, & in exilio socius, nec eum unquam deseruit. Prophetauit Baruch in Babylonia tempore captiuitatis Judæ, prophetiámque suam legit coram rege Joachin, qui & Jechonias dictus est. multa ac magna mysteria de incarnatione Domini ac de nouissimis temporibus prophetauit. Vide lib.Baruch.Josephlib.[?]Antiq.10.cap.8.& catalogum Sanctorum. IEHOAKIM REX IVD[?] IEHOACIN REX IVD[?]
units.tr: Baruch the prophet was the scribe of Jeremiah, who wrote the book of Jeremiah concerning future events for the city, the people and the temple. He was also Jeremiah's minister in prison and his companion in exile, and never deserted him. Baruch prophesied in Babylon at the time of the captivity of Judah, and read his prophecy before King Jehoiachin, who was also called Jechonias. He prophesied many great mysteries concerning the incarnation of the Lord and the last times. See the book of Baruch, Josephus, Antiquities, book 10, chapter 8, and the catalogue of the Saints. JEHOIAKIM KING OF JUDAH, JEHOIACHIN KING OF JUDAH.

units.la: ELIACIM, qui & Ioacim, filius Iosiæ, cùm imperasset frater nomine Ioachaz annos tres post Iosiam, successit fratri, in regno Iudæ, anno mundi 3326. ante Christum natum 636. nam Pharao Nechao cùm venisset Ierusalem, vinxit Ioachaz, ac captiuum duxit in Ægyptum: constituítque in locum eius Regem hunc Eliacim fratrem eius super Iudam & Ierusalem: & vertit nomen eius vocauítque eum Ioacim: & cõdemnauit terram centum talentis argenti,& talento auri.Impiè egit Eliacim,ideo contra eum ascédit Nabuchodonosor rex Chaldæorum, & vinctum catenis, ut captiuum traduceret Babylonem, interfici iussit: ad quam & vasa Domini transtulit, & posuit ea in templo suo.imperauit annos 11. Consulito li.4.Reg.23. & 24. cap.& lib.2.Paral.36.cap.& Iosep.lib.Antiq.10.cap.8.
units.tr: ELIAKIM, who was also Joakim, son of Josiah. When his brother named Jehoahaz had reigned three years after Josiah, he succeeded his brother in the kingdom of Judah, in the year of the world 3326, before the birth of Christ 636. For Pharaoh Necho, when he came to Jerusalem, bound Jehoahaz and led him away captive into Egypt, and set in his place as king over Judah and Jerusalem this Eliakim, his brother; and he changed his name and called him Joakim; and he laid a tribute on the land of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. Eliakim acted impiously, and therefore Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, came up against him, and ordered him, bound in chains to be led captive to Babylon, to be put to death; and he carried the vessels of the Lord thither and placed them in his own temple. He reigned eleven years. Consult 4 Kings 23 and 24, and 2 Chronicles 36, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 10, chapter 8.

units.la: IOACHIN, qui & Iechonias dictus est, filius fuit supradicti Eliacim:&-successit patri,& regnauit tantum tres menses, imitatus vestigia patris impij.Hic consulente Ieremia Propheta Nabuchodonosori se, cum omni familia dedidit, qui transtulit eos Babylonem,cum primoribus, cum militibus, ac artificibus captiuis ad decem millia: & suffecit Nabuchodonosor in locum eius Mathaniam patruum eius, qui & Sedechias dictus est. Vide lib.4.Reg.24. & lib. 2.Paral.36.cap. & Ioseph. lib. Antiq.10.ca.9. Acta sunt hæc anno à mundo condito 3337.ante Christum natum 625. Post hanc 37. annorum captiuitatem, Euilmerodac, qui Nabuchodonozori successit, Ioachin in libertatem asseruit,qui paulo post genuit Mesezebel, cognomine Salathiel. Vide Iere.cap.32.& 52. & Philonem. NABVCHO DONOSOR M.R.B. ZEDECHIAS R.IVDA
units.tr: JEHOIACHIN, who was also called Jechonias, was the son of the aforesaid Eliakim, and succeeded his father, and reigned only three months, imitating the footsteps of his impious father. At the counsel of the prophet Jeremiah he surrendered himself with his whole household to Nebuchadnezzar, who carried them to Babylon with the nobles, the soldiers and the craftsmen, about ten thousand captives; and Nebuchadnezzar set in his place Mattaniah, his uncle, who was also called Zedekiah. See 4 Kings 24, and 2 Chronicles 36, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 10, chapter 9. These things were done in the year from the creation of the world 3337, before the birth of Christ 625. After this captivity of thirty-seven years, Evil-merodach, who succeeded Nebuchadnezzar, freed Jehoiachin from captivity, who shortly afterwards begot Mesezebel, surnamed Salathiel. See Jeremiah chapters 32 and 52, and Philo.

units.la: NABVCHODONOSOR magnus, qui ab Hebræis Nabucadnezer dicitur, imperauit Babyloniis anno 4. regni Eliacim Regis Iudæ: qui erat annus mundi 3329. ante Christum natum 633. Hic bellum cum Pharaone Necho siue Nechaone, gessit, vicit, & totam Syriam vsque Pelusium, Iudæa adempta, suæ ditioni adiecit: Ioachin seu Eleacim, Regem sibi tributarium fecit, quem postea tributum recusantem, cepit, ligauit vt Babylonem duceret, attamen interim curauit interfici. Iterum Ierusalem tempore Sedechiæ obsedit, habens principem militiæ Nabusardan, filios Sedechiæ occidit coram eo, ipsúmque patrem exoculauit, vinctúmq; catenis abduxit Babylonem: templum succendit, ciuitate capta ac direpta. Tandem regno ob insaniam pulsus, cum feris septé annis in agro egit. Vide apud Danielem huius somnia de quatuor regnis mundi, item de aurea statua quam adorari iussit, vide Iosep.lib.10.ca.7. & sequen.
units.tr: NEBUCHADNEZZAR the Great, who by the Hebrews is called Nebuchadnezzar, reigned over the Babylonians in the fourth year of the reign of Eliakim, king of Judah, which was the year of the world 3329, before the birth of Christ 633. He waged war against Pharaoh Necho, or Nechaon, and conquered him, and, having taken Judaea, added all Syria as far as Pelusium to his dominion. He made Jehoiachin, or Eliakim, a king tributary to himself, whom, when he later refused the tribute, he seized, bound him to lead him to Babylon, and yet meanwhile arranged for him to be put to death. Again he besieged Jerusalem in the time of Zedekiah, having as commander of the army Nebuzaradan; he slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and had the father himself blinded, and led him away bound in chains to Babylon; he set fire to the temple, the city having been taken and plundered. At last, driven from his kingdom on account of madness, he lived for seven years in the field with the wild beasts. See in Daniel his dreams of the four kingdoms of the world, also of the golden statue which he ordered to be worshipped; see Josephus, book 10, chapter 7 and following.

units.la: SEDECHIAS, qui & Mathanias, Iosiæ filius, imperauit Iudæis an.11. à Nabuchodonosore suffectus in locum Ioachin, hac conditione vt tributum ei persolueret, verùm fidem illi fregit, spernens etiam consilia Ezechielis ac Ieremiæ. Quare anno regni eius nono Nabuchodonosor obsedit Ierusalem, quam post 2.an. cepit, Regémque cum populo in Babyloniâ abduxit, anno mundi 3348. ante Christum natum 614. Hæc est illa misera, ac vulgata captiuitas Babylonica annorum 70. Vide lib.4. Reg.24.& 25.cap. & lib.2.Paral.36. cap.Ierem.25.37. & 52.cap. & Ezechi.12.& 21.cap.& Iosephlib.10.cap.9.& 10. Sedechias filios occidi vidit, statimque ipsimet Sedechiæ eruti sunt oculi, vt supra dixi. PROPH. DANIEL PROPH. EZECHIEL
units.tr: ZEDEKIAH, who was also called Mattaniah, son of Josiah, reigned over the Jews for eleven years, appointed by Nebuchadnezzar in the place of Jehoiachin, on this condition, that he should pay him tribute; but he broke faith with him, scorning also the counsels of Ezekiel and Jeremiah. Therefore in the ninth year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, which he took after two years, and led the king with the people away into Babylonia, in the year of the world 3348, before the birth of Christ 614. This is that wretched and well-known Babylonian captivity of seventy years. See 4 Kings 24 and 25, and 2 Chronicles 36, Jeremiah chapters 25, 37 and 52, and Ezekiel chapters 12 and 21, and Josephus, book 10, chapters 9 and 10. Zedekiah saw his sons put to death, and immediately his own eyes were plucked out, as I said above. PROPHET DANIEL, PROPHET EZEKIEL.

units.la: DANIEL Propheta vaticinabatur tempore Iechoniæ, & Ieremiæ. Hic à Nabuchodonofore cum sodalibus captiuus abductus est, anno mundi 3348. ante Christum natum 614. Chaldæorum artes & linguam 3. an. didicit: Somnia Regis Nabucho donosor exposuit, & visionem Baltafaris. in lacum leonum coniectus, atque inde eductus est: Sufannam liberauit. De somnio 4. bestiarum quæ 4. mundi regna signabant: vtque ei 70. hebdo. visionem edisseruerit Gabriel Angelus, & pleraque alia qui cupit nosse, legat huius Danielis librum, & Iofeph. lib. 10. cap. 12. Hic instabat assiduis precibus apud Deū, pro Nabuchodonofore transformato, prædixitque vt formam & regnum recuperaret: quare indidit ei rex Nabuch. nomen Baltasaris filij sui: voluitque eum filiis cohæredem instituere, quod ille recusauit. Vide Epiphan.Obiit Daniel in Babylone, & sepultus est in spelunca regali, honorificè.
units.tr: Daniel the prophet prophesied in the time of Jehoiachin and Jeremiah. He was led away captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar with his companions, in the year of the world 3348, before the birth of Christ 614. He learned the arts and the language of the Chaldeans in three years. He expounded the dreams of King Nebuchadnezzar, and the vision of Belshazzar. He was thrown into the lions' den, and was brought out from there. He freed Susanna. Concerning the dream of the four beasts, which signified the four kingdoms of the world, and how the angel Gabriel explained the vision of the seventy weeks, and many other things, whoever wishes to know should read the book of this Daniel, and Josephus, book 10, chapter 12. He kept urging God with constant prayers for Nebuchadnezzar, when he had been changed, and foretold that he would recover his form and his kingdom; for this reason King Nebuchadnezzar gave him the name Belteshazzar, after his son, and wished to make him co-heir with his sons, which he refused. See Epiphanius. Daniel died in Babylon and was honourably buried in the royal cave.

units.la: EZECHIEL Propheta tempore Ieremiæ, Baruch, & Danielis Prophetarum, extitit: hic adhuc puer cum aliis in Babyloniam captiuus ab-ductus est, vbi prophetare incepit anno mundi 3349. ante Christum natum 613. anno tamen ætatis suæ 30. ait Ieron. in Chaldæa prophetasse Ezechielem: tum cùm Ieremias in Iudæa. eius vide Prophetiam, & Iosef. lib. Antiqui. 10. cap. 9. Et Ecclesiaft. ca. 49. In Babylone iudicauit tribum Dan & Gad: prædixitque culpa earum, non reuersurum populum Hierosolymam, quoad resipiscerent: quare exacerbati diftraxerunt eum equis per crepidines saxorum, & excerebrarūt eum, & sepelierunt in sepulchro Sem & Arphaxad. Vide chro. Guill. [?] TARQVINIVS PRI[?] [?] CVS TANAQVIL TARQVIN
units.tr: Ezekiel the prophet arose in the time of the prophets Jeremiah, Baruch and Daniel. While still a boy, together with others, he was led away captive to Babylonia, where he began to prophesy in the year of the world 3349, before the birth of Christ 613. Yet, in the thirtieth year of his age, Jerome says, Ezekiel prophesied in Chaldea, at the time when Jeremiah was in Judaea. See his prophecy, and Josephus, Antiquities, book 10, chapter 9; and Ecclesiasticus chapter 49. In Babylon he judged the tribes of Dan and Gad, and foretold that, because of their sin, the people would not return to Jerusalem until they repented; therefore, exasperated, they tore him apart with horses over the rough places of the rocks, and beat out his brains, and buried him in the sepulchre of Shem and Arphaxad. See the chronicle of Guillaume [?].

units.la: TARQVINIVS Priscus qui prius Lucumo, Romanorum rex quintus, imperauit Romanis anno mundi 3349. ante Christum natum 613. apud Ancum Martium liberaliter dextréque obeundo officia, in familiarem venit amicitiam, vt publicis ac priuatis consiliis bello,domíque interesset, & per omnia expertus postremo tutor etiam liberis Regis, testamento instituieretur.mortuo Anco, instituit hic vt quàm primum comitia Regi creando fierent,quibus indictis,sub tempus pueros regios venatum ablegauit:& primus petisse ambitiosè regnum & orationem habuisse ad conciliandos plebis animos compositam fertur:maximè verò cùm Tatium Sabinum,etiam ex hoste Regem factum diceret,ac inculcaret,populus eum regnare iussit. numerum Senatorum & equitū duplicauit: Circum Romae aedificauit, ludos Romanos instituit magnificos: Sabinos vicit: Latinos priscos domuit: primus triumphans Romae intrauit:muros & cloacas fecit: Capitolium inchoauit. Tandem à filiis Anci Martij, cui in regno successerat, interfectus est 37. imperij anno. his temporibus Ierusalem à Nabuchodonosore capta ac euersa est:& Massilia condita. Consulito lib.1.Eutrop. Diony.Halicar.lib.3. Titum Liuium lib.1.deca.1.
units.tr: Tarquinius Priscus, who was previously called Lucumo, the fifth king of the Romans, ruled the Romans in the year of the world 3349, before the birth of Christ 613. Having served Ancus Martius generously and well with kindly and skilful duties, he came into his close friendship, so that he took part in his public and private counsels, in war and at home; and, having proved himself in every way, he was finally made tutor to the king's children, and was named in the king's will. When Ancus died, Tarquinius arranged that the assembly for choosing a king should be held as soon as possible; and once it was announced, he sent the royal boys off to hunt at about that time. He is said to have been the first to seek the kingdom with ambition, and to have made a speech composed to win over the hearts of the common people, especially when he said that Tatius the Sabine had also been made king even though he had been an enemy, and kept insisting on it; so the people ordered him to reign. He doubled the number of senators and knights. He built the Circus in Rome, and established the magnificent Roman Games. He defeated the Sabines and subdued the early Latins. He was the first to enter Rome in triumph. He built walls and sewers and began the Capitol. At last he was killed by the sons of Ancus Martius, whose kingdom he had succeeded to, in the thirty-seventh year of his rule. In his time Jerusalem was taken and overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar, and Massilia was founded. See Eutropius, book 1; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 3; and Titus Livius, book 1, decade 1.

units.la: TANAQVIL, Tarquinij Prisci vxor fuit, perita, vt vulgo Etrusci, coelestium prodigiorum mulier. Hæc cùm aquila suspensis demissa leniter alis pileum viri abstulisset, rursúsque velut ministerio diuinitus missa, capiti aptè reposuisset, hæc inquam, virum complexa,alta sperare iussit. id siquidè factum est ipsis primò Romam ingredientibus,antequam regnaret ipse Tarquinius Priscus. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: Tanaquil was the wife of Tarquinius Priscus, a woman skilled, as the Etruscans commonly are, in heavenly portents. When an eagle, swooping down gently with outstretched wings, had taken the cap from her husband's head, and then, as if sent by God to perform a service, had flown back and set it neatly on his head again, she embraced her husband and told him to hope for high things. This happened, indeed, when they were first entering Rome, before Tarquinius Priscus became king. See above.

units.la: SAPPHO Poëtria, Scamandronymi filia fuit, cuius sapientiam admiratur etiam ipse Plato: hæc tamen cum vidua esset, ac filiam etiam ex viro diuite defuncto, Cleiden haberet, Phaonem perditè amauit: nam cum ille in Siciliam discessisset, & hæc ab eo se sperni vereretur, ardens, amorisque impatientissima, statuit etiam capitis periculo furore lenire, demisso in mare corpore ex leucade, Epiri promontorio. amicà etiam habuit Erinnam Poëtriam: de quibus græcum extat epigramma in hunc sensum: Quatò Erinnam in Lyricis Sappho, tantò Sapphus gloriam Erinna hexametris præcellit. Mitylenæi Sapphus imaginem nummis insculpebant. Rhodig.lib.9.cap.24. & lib.10.ca.2. item lib.14.cap.1. Hæc carminis Sapphici inuentrix fuit, cui & nomen dedit: & decima Musa dicta est, unde Ausonius:
units.tr: Sappho the poetess was the daughter of Scamandronymus; her wisdom was admired even by Plato himself. Yet, being a widow, and having a daughter named Cleis by a rich husband who had died, she passionately loved Phaon. When he had gone off to Sicily, and she feared she was being spurned by him, burning and utterly impatient in her love, she resolved to relieve her fury even at the risk of her life: she threw herself into the sea from Leucas, a promontory of Epirus. She also had a female friend, the poetess Erinna, about whom there is a Greek epigram to this effect: "As Sappho surpasses Erinna in lyric verse, so Erinna surpasses Sappho's fame in hexameters." The people of Mytilene stamped Sappho's image on their coins. See Rhodiginus, book 9, chapter 24; book 10, chapter 2; and also book 14, chapter 1. She was the inventor of the Sapphic verse, which also took its name from her, and she was called the tenth Muse, whence Ausonius:
"Sappho, sister of Lesbos, added to the Muses of Pieria."

units.la: extat & Antipatri Sidonij distichon Græcum, in hunc sensum, Mnemosynem matrem Musarum cepit stupor, quādo audiuit dulcisonam Sappho: nunquid decimam Musam (inquit) habet mortales? Fuit sanè in Lesbo altera Sappho, verùm meretrix, hæc autem Poëtria, tempore Tar.Prisci, de quo supra.
units.tr: There is also a Greek couplet of Antipater of Sidon, to this effect: "Mnemosyne, the mother of the Muses, was struck with wonder when she heard the sweet-sounding Sappho; 'Surely,' she said, 'mortals have a tenth Muse?'" There was indeed another Sappho on Lesbos, but she was a courtesan; this one, however, was a poetess, living in the time of Tarquinius Priscus, of whom we spoke above.

units.la: PANTHEA Abradatæ uxor fuit, forma & castitate præcellens: hæc à Cyro maiore capta, Arafpę Mœdo seruanda traditur, qui apud Cyrum affirmat nondum esse ortam hac pulchriorem: nec tamen eam adiit aut accersiuit Cyrus, ne à rebus gerendis auocaretur: quare & ipsa id beneficij, nempe non attentatæ castitatis, rependens, virum Cyro reconciliat, animatque, & armat, ut strenuè pro Cyro pugnet: attamen inter pugnandum occumbit: inque demortui viri pectus impositò hæc se iugulat capite: tres quoque spadones stantes vbi eos iusserat, quod factum erat intuiti, districtis acinacibus ibi se iugulant. Xeno.lib.7.in Cy.Pæ.& Rho.lib.13 cap.33. THALES MILESIUS CHILON LACED.
units.tr: Panthea was the wife of Abradatas, outstanding in beauty and chastity. When she was taken by Cyrus the Elder, she is said to have been entrusted to Araspes the Mede to be kept safe; he told Cyrus that no more beautiful woman had yet been born. Yet Cyrus neither approached her nor summoned her, lest he be distracted from his business. Therefore she, in return for this kindness, namely for her chastity having not been violated, reconciled her husband to Cyrus, and encouraged and armed him so that he would fight bravely for Cyrus. Nevertheless, he fell in the battle. Panthea laid herself on the breast of her dead husband and cut her throat with a sword. Three eunuchs, standing where he had ordered them, seeing what had been done, drew their scimitars and cut their own throats there. See Xenophon, book 7 on the Cyropaedia; and Rhodiginus, book 13, chapter 33. THALES OF MILETUS, CHILON OF LACEDAEMON.

units.la: THALES, primus sapiens & Physicus Philosophus vocatur circiter annum mundi 3325.ante Christum natum 637. principe apud Iudæos Iosia, apud Athenienses Damasia, apud Rom. Anco Mar. Sunt qui ad Ezechiam, & male quidem, referant: nam attigit prima Cyri tempora, cum quo & congressus est: vixitque annos fere centum. Euse.lib.io.præpa.Euang. Hic Mileti ciuis adscriptus est, propheta cum Neleo ex Phœnice, à Cadmo & Agenore originem trahens. Post reip. negocia sese ad contemplandam rerum naturam transtulit. Sunt qui illum immortales animos primùm dixisse asseuerent: & solis cursum reperisse, & annum in 365. dies diuisisse. huius hæc sunt præcipuæ sententiæ: Parce loqui prudentis animi indicium est.
units.tr: Thales, called the first wise man and natural philosopher, lived about the year of the world 3325, before the birth of Christ 637, when Josiah was ruler among the Jews, Damasias among the Athenians, and Ancus Martius among the Romans. Some refer him to the time of Hezekiah, but wrongly: for he reached the early years of Cyrus, with whom he also met; and he lived about a hundred years. See Eusebius, book 10, Preparation for the Gospel. He was enrolled as a citizen of Miletus; a prophet, he was descended from Neleus, who came from Phoenicia, and from Cadmus and Agenor. After dealing with public affairs he turned himself to contemplating the nature of things. Some assert that he first taught the immortality of the soul, and that he discovered the course of the sun and divided the year into 365 days. These are his chief sayings: "To keep silent is a sign of a prudent mind."

units.la: Quæ in aliis damnes, ipse ne feceris. Amicorum præsentium & absentium æquè memores esse debemus. Noli ditari nequiter. Quæ parentibus feceris, eadem ipse à filiis expecta. Male cogitans nedum male agens, Deos haudquaquam latet. Difficile seipsum noscere. Diog.Laër.libr.1. scribit æstu ac siti eum in spectaculis excessisse. Volater.lib.20.
units.tr: "What you condemn in others, do not do yourself. We ought to be equally mindful of friends who are present and of those who are absent. Do not grow rich by wicked means. What you have done to your parents, expect the same from your children. Thinking evil, not to mention doing evil, is never hidden from the gods. It is difficult to know oneself." Diogenes Laertius, book 1, writes that he died of heat and thirst at the games. Volaterranus, book 20.

units.la: CHILO Lacedæmonius, Ephororum ac sapientum vnus, claruit tempore Thaletis, Solonis ac Æsopi, vt ait Plutar.in Solone. Huius hæ sunt selectiores sententiæ: Periti ab imperitis bona spe differunt. Lingua semper, sed in conuiuio præsertim continenda. Proximo non maledicendum, alioquin quæ nobis dolebunt audiemus. Nemini intentandæ minæ, id enim muliebre est. Damnum potius quàm turpe lucrum eligendum. Aurum cote examinatur, auro autem hominum mens. Obiit Pisæ præ lætitia, quòd filius in Olympiis coronatus esset. Vide vt supra. MYTHEL. PITHACVS AENEVS BIAS PRI.
units.tr: Chilon of Lacedaemon, one of the Ephors and one of the wise men, flourished in the time of Thales, Solon and Aesop, as Plutarch says in his life of Solon. These are his more select sayings: "The skilled differ from the unskilled by good hope. The tongue must always be restrained, but especially at a banquet. Do not speak ill of a neighbour, or else we shall hear what will grieve us. Threats should never be made to anyone, for that is womanish. One should choose loss rather than shameful gain. Gold is tested by the touchstone, but men's minds by gold." He died at Pisa from joy, because his son had been crowned at the Olympic games. See above. MYTILENE. PITTACUS OF AENEUS. BIAS OF PRIENE.

units.la: PITTACHVS Mitylenæus Melanchrum Lesbi Tyrannum profligauit: & cùm de agri cuiusdam possessione inter Athenienses & Mitylenæos decerneretur, Dux exercitus ipse cum Phrynone Atheniensium Duce singulari certamine pugnans, rete, quo clypeum texerat, Phrynonem dum non cauet, inuoluit, ipsóque peremptò agrum seruauit anno mundi 3356. ante Christum natum 606. Hic decem annis principatum tenuit, dein sponte se magistratu abdicauit. Agri sibi traditi partem abscidit, dimidiúmque plus toto dixit: cum Croeso, sicut & Solon, pugnauit: cuius & pecunias recusauit, duplo plus quàm vellet, habere se professus. Ebrios duplici incommodo afficiendos statuit. huius hæ sunt inter alias sententiæ: Perdifficile est bonum esse. Principatus virum declarat. Terra fidelis, mare infidum. Prudentis est priusquam aduersa contingant praevidere, atque occurrere: fortis vero cùm obuenerint, æquo animo ferre. Quod facturus es ne prædica, frustratus enim rideberis. Infelicitatem nemini improperâ. Fuit alter Pittacus legislator. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: Pittacus of Mytilene overthrew Melanchrus, tyrant of Lesbos. When a certain field was being decided between the Athenians and the Mytileneans, he himself, as commander of the army, fought in single combat with Phrynon, the Athenian commander; and while Phrynon was not on his guard, Pittacus, who had covered his shield with a net, entangled him in it, and having killed him, saved the field, in the year of the world 3356, before the birth of Christ 606. He held power for ten years, and then of his own accord gave up his office. He cut off part of the field that had been given to him, and said that half was more than the whole. He fought with Croesus, as Solon also did; and he refused the money that was offered him, professing that he had need of twice as much as he wished to have. He decided that drunkards should be punished with a double penalty. Among his other sayings are these: "It is very difficult to be good. Power reveals the man.
