The land is faithful, the sea faithless. It is the mark of a prudent man to foresee adversity before it strikes, and to meet it; of a brave man to bear it with an even mind when it has come. What you are about to do, do not proclaim beforehand, for you will be laughed at if you fail. Reproach no one with his misfortune." There was another Pittacus, a lawgiver. See above.

units.la: BIAS Prienæus, siue Prienensis, capta vrbe, cùm cæteri ita fugerent, vt de suis quisque rebus multa secum asportarent, & admoneretur vt idem faceret: ego verò inquit facio: nam omnia mea mecum porto: (non absimile respondit Demetrio Poliorceti Stilpo) hæc ludibria fortunæ ne sua quidem putauit, quæ nos appellamus bona. huius hæ feruntur sententiæ:
units.tr: Bias of Priene, or Prienensis, when the city was taken, while the others were fleeing and each was carrying off many of his own possessions, and he was urged to do the same, replied: "But I am doing it; for I carry all my possessions with me." (Stilpo answered Demetrius Poliorcetes in much the same way.) He did not even regard as his own those things which we call goods, considering them the playthings of fortune. These sayings are reported as his:

units.la: Infelix næ, qui infelicitatem ferre nequit. Morbus animi est impossibilia amare, & appetere, nec alieni incommodi meminisse. Indignum hominem diuitiarum gratia ne laudaueris. Quicquid boni egeris, in Deos refer. Obiit suaue dormiens in sinu nepotis ex filia. Vide vt supra. LINDIUS CHILEBOULUS PERIANDER REX COR[?]
units.tr: "Wretched indeed is he who cannot bear wretchedness. It is a sickness of the mind to love and desire impossible things, and not to remember another's misfortune. Do not praise an unworthy man for the sake of his riches. Whatever good you have done, refer it to the gods." He died peacefully, sleeping in the lap of his grandson by his daughter. See above. LINDIUS, CHILEBOULUS, PERIANDER, KING COR...

units.la: CLEOBULUS Lindius, è septem quoque Græciæ sapientibus, cunctos suæ ætatis, viribus & forma antecelluit: hic fertur id ænigmatis edidisse:
units.tr: Cleobulus of Lindus, also one of the seven wise men of Greece, surpassed all men of his age in strength and beauty. He is said to have produced this riddle:

units.la: Est genitor, proles cui sit bissena: sed horum Cuius triginta nata, sed dispare forma: Hæ niueis totæ, fuscis sed vultibus illæ: Atque immortales cum sint, moriuntur ad unam.
units.tr: "There is a father whose offspring are twelve; and of these, thirty are born of his daughters, but of unlike form. Some of them are wholly snowy, others have dark faces; and though they are immortal, they all die at once."

units.la: Est autem annus. Sunt & eiusdem hæ sententiæ: Amicos beneficiis foue, vt amiciores sint: ex inimicis autem amicos fac. Audiendi magis quàm loquendi, auidum esse oportet. Cum muliere neque blandiciis agendum, neque præsentibus extraneis iurgandum:illud vecordē, hoc vesanum arguit. Diog. Laër. lib.1. huic fuit Cleobulina filia, insignis vates ænigmatum heroicis versibus conscriptorum.
units.tr: The riddle's answer is the year. There are also these sayings of his: "Cherish friends with kindnesses, so that they may become closer; and make friends out of enemies. One ought to be more eager to listen than to speak. One should not flatter a woman, nor quarrel with her in front of strangers: the first shows folly, the second madness." Diogenes Laertius, book 1. He had a daughter, Cleobulina, a notable poetess of riddles written in heroic verse.

units.la: PERIANDER Corynthius, è septem Græciæ sapientibus, claruit eadem ferè ætate qua priores illi: nam id in cõfesso est septem illos nomine sapientiæ insignes viros in eadem tempora incidisse. Porrò sunt qui hunc eundem putant cum illo Periandro tyranno, qui agebat tempore Sedechiæ, sed aberrât: nam diuersos, hoc est duos fuisse Periādros Ælianus autor est, sapientia illum illustrem, hunc tyrannide. Vide Rhod. lib. 21. cap.37. huius sapientis hæ sunt potiores sententiæ: Bona res quies, ac periculosa temeritas. Turpe lucrum. Voluptates fluxæ sunt: honores immotales. Inter secundas res esto moderatus, inter aduersas prudens. Amicis felicibus & infelicibus, eundem te præbe. Inter loquendum caue ne secreta pronunties. Diog.Laër.lib.1. Cæterùm de Solone dicemus inferius, nam adiunctus est Croeso. SERVIVS TVLLIVS ROM. R UX. PUBL. CORN. CORNI[?] CRESA[?] M. SER. TVL[?]
units.tr: Periander of Corinth, one of the seven wise men of Greece, flourished at about the same time as those earlier men. For it is agreed that those seven, famous for their wisdom, lived in the same period. Some think that this same man is the Periander the tyrant who reigned in the time of Zedekiah, but they are mistaken: Aelian is the authority that there were two Perianders, distinct persons, one famous for wisdom and the other for tyranny. See Rhodiginus, book 21, chapter 37. The most notable sayings of this sage are these: Quiet is a good thing, but rashness is dangerous. Gain obtained by shame is base. Pleasures are fleeting; honours are not lasting. In prosperity be moderate, in adversity be prudent. Show yourself the same to friends whether they are fortunate or unfortunate. When you are speaking, take care not to disclose secrets. Diogenes Laertius, book 1. As for Solon, we will speak of him below, since he was associated with Croesus. SERVIUS TULLIUS, ROMAN KING, PUBLIC PROPERTY, CORNELIUS CORNI... [illegible in the scan]

units.la: SERVIVS Tullius Romanorum Rex sextus ac penultimus, successit Tarquinio Prisco anno à mundo condito 3387. ante Christum seruatorem natum 575. hic ex nobili fœmina Corniculana, captiua tamen & ancilla, genitus est: cui adolescentulo dormienti caput ardere uisum est: quod prodigium Tanaquil uxor Regis Tarquinij Prisci cùm uidisset, eum inter liberos suos educauit: omen enim sic interpretabatur, fore ut aliquando imperaret, quod & contigit: simile etiam de Ascanio supra narrauimus pag. 56. Hic Tarquinij Prisci cum esset gener, eo mortuo, Rex à patribus, hinc à plebe designatur. Sabinos subegit, Veientes fregit, montes Quirinalem, Viminalem & Esquilinum urbi adiunxit, fossas circum murum duxit: primus omnium censum ordinauit, rem saluberrimam tanto futuro imperio, ut inquit Liuius. Sub eo Roma omnibus in censum delatis, habuit capita 84. millia ciuium Romanorum, cum his qui in agris erant, occisus est 44. imperij anno, scelere generi sui Tarquinij superbi, filij eius Regis cui ipse successerat, & impulsu Tulliæ filiæ suæ. Videto Tit.Liu. libr.1. Decad. 1. & Dionys.Hali.lib.4.ac Eutrop. lib.1.
units.tr: Servius Tullius, the sixth and second-to-last king of the Romans, succeeded Tarquinius Priscus in the year 3387 from the creation of the world, 575 years before Christ the Saviour was born. He was born of a noble woman of Corniculum, yet a captive and a slave. While he was sleeping as a boy, his head was seen to burn. When Tanaquil, the wife of King Tarquinius Priscus, saw this portent, she brought him up among her own children, for she interpreted the omen to mean that he would someday rule, which indeed came to pass. We related something similar about Ascanius above, on page 56. Since he was the son-in-law of Tarquinius Priscus, when that king died he was designated king by the Fathers and then by the common people. He subdued the Sabines, broke the Veientes, joined the Quirinal, Viminal and Esquiline hills to the city, and dug ditches around the wall. He was the first of all to establish a census, a most salutary measure for so great a future empire, as Livy says. Under him, when all had been enrolled in the census, Rome had 84,000 citizens, not counting those who were in the countryside. He was killed in the 44th year of his reign, through the crime of his son-in-law Tarquinius the Proud, the son of that king to whom he himself had succeeded, and at the instigation of his daughter Tullia. See Livy, book 1, decade 1, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 4, and Eutropius, book 1.

units.la: OCRISIA, uxor Publij Corniculæ, supradicti Seruij Tullij mater fuit, & Tanaquilis Reginæ ancilla captiua. Videto ut supra. Cæterum Plin. lib.36.cap.27. mira narrat de Ocrisia, qua via conceperit Seruium Tullium. AESO PVS PHRYGIVS RHODO PE. MER.
units.tr: Ocrisia, the wife of Publius Cornicula, was the mother of the aforesaid Servius Tullius, and a captive slave of Queen Tanaquil. See above. Moreover, Pliny, book 36, chapter 27, tells wonderful stories about Ocrisia, in what way she conceived Servius Tullius.

units.la: ÆSOPVS Phrygius, facie quidem & corpore deformis fuit: at verò iocis & fabulis omnium facetissimus. Conditione etiam fuit seruus, tempore Croesi Lydorū Regis (de quo pagina sequēte) autor fuit quidem fabularum, quem citare non dedignatur Aristoteles 2.li.Rhetoricorum: & Plato in 1. Phædri : & Apuleius de deor. fom. fabulas ac vitam eius non est hic locus recensendi, & vulgatiora sunt quàm ut recitatione aut cōmendatione egeant. legat qui volet Volaterranum li.13. & 38. praeterea Æsopi vitam à Maximo Planude descriptam Græcè, atque etiam latinam factā, quæ præponitur eiusdem fabulis. Hic furti falsò Delphis accusatus, de rupe insons præcipitatur.
units.tr: Aesop the Phrygian was indeed deformed in face and body, but in jokes and fables he was the most witty of all. He was also a slave by condition. He lived in the time of Croesus, king of the Lydians (of whom more on the following page). He was indeed the author of fables, which Aristotle does not disdain to cite in book 2 of his Rhetoric, and Plato in the first book of the Phaedrus, and Apuleius in On the God of Socrates. It is not the place here to recount his fables or his life, and they are too widely known to need recital or commendation. Let whoever wishes read Volaterranus, books 13 and 38. Besides, there is the life of Aesop written in Greek by Maximus Planudes, and also translated into Latin, which is prefixed to his fables. Falsely accused of theft at Delphi, he was thrown from a cliff, though innocent.

units.la: RHODOPE, siue Rhodopis meretrix fuit famosissima, ex Thracia, Æsopi aliquandiu conserua, postea à Charaxo, siue Coraxe, Sapphus Poëtriæ fratre, qui eius amore tenebatur, ingēti pecunia redempta: cuius sic meminit Sappho apud Ouid. 21. & ultima epistola: Arsit inops frater, victus meretricis amore, Mixtáque cum turpi damna pudore tulit. Factus inops, agili peragit freta cærula remo: Quásque male amisit, nunc male quærit opes. Me quoque, quòd monui bene multa fideliter, odit: Hoc mihi libertas, hoc pia lingua dedit.
units.tr: Rhodope, or Rhodopis, was a most famous courtesan from Thrace, for a time a fellow-slave of Aesop. Afterwards she was bought for a great sum by Charaxus, or Caraxus, the brother of the poetess Sappho, who was enslaved by love for her. Sappho recalls this in Ovid, letter 21 and the last letter: My brother burned, beaten by love for a courtesan, and bore his losses mixed with shameful disgrace. Made a pauper, he sails the blue seas with a nimble oar, and now seeks wealth badly, which he lost badly before. He hates me too, because I faithfully warned him of many things: my freedom, my loyal tongue, gave me this.

units.la: Scribit Plinius lib.36.cap.12. Rhodopen tantas opes meretricio quæstu cumulasse, vt insignem turrim, siue pyramidem, suis sumptibus extruxerit.
units.tr: Pliny writes, book 36, chapter 12, that Rhodope amassed such great wealth from her harlot's gains that at her own expense she built a famous tower, or pyramid.

units.la: CROESVS Lydorum Rex, imperauit ipsis Lydis anno mundi 3402. ante Christum natum 560. hic opibus & diuitiis praepotens, auxilium tulit Babyloniis aduersus Cyrum: verumtamen victus, iamque de se solicitus, in regnum regreditur. At vero post victoriam compositis in Babylonia rebus, bellum transfert Cyrus in Lydiam: vbi, perculsum iam fortuna prioris belli, Croesi exercitum, nullo negotio fundit. Croesum capit, vinctúmque super ingentem lignorum struem imponit, & circa eum14. Lydorū filios, vt viui exurerentur. Tunc ingemiscens Croesus ter clara voce exclamauit, O Solō, Solon, Solon. quod intelligens Cyrus, voluit rescire quamobrem id exclamaret: retulit Croesus, se tunc meminisse Solonis, qui aliquando illi dixerat, neminem in hac vita beatum ante mortem: Itaque Cyrum poenituit, cùm se quoque hominem esse agnosceret: iussitque ignem iam incensum celerrimè extingui. Posthac summo in honore habuit Croesum Cyrus, atque à consiliis praecipuum. Vide Herod.lib.i.& Iusti.lib. item i.
units.tr: Croesus, king of the Lydians, reigned over the Lydians themselves in the year 3402 from the creation of the world, 560 years before Christ was born. Mighty in resources and riches, he brought aid to the Babylonians against Cyrus. But when he was defeated and was anxious about his own position, he returned to his kingdom. Yet after the victory, when affairs in Babylon were settled, Cyrus carried the war into Lydia, where he easily routed Croesus' army, already shaken by the fortune of the earlier war. He captured Croesus, bound him, and placed him on a huge pile of wood, and around him he set fourteen sons of the Lydians, to be burned alive. Then Croesus, groaning, cried out three times in a loud voice, "O Solon, Solon, Solon." Cyrus, understanding this, wished to know why he cried out so. Croesus replied that he then remembered Solon, who once told him that no one in this life is blessed before death. Cyrus was moved to repentance, recognising that he himself was a man, and ordered the fire, already lit, to be quickly put out. Afterwards Cyrus held Croesus in the highest honour and made him his chief counsellor. See Herodotus, book 1, and Justin, book 1, likewise.

units.la: SOLON, inter septem Graeciae sapientes clarus, Atheniensibus leges dedit: & quas Draco instituerat abrogauit, praeterquam quae de caede erant. Pisistrati propinqui sui tyrannidi latenter obrepenti semper obstitit: quę vbi inualuit, in Aegyptum abiit sapientiae operam daturus, impetrata prius ab Atheniensibus decem annorum peregrinatione. Vocatus à Croeso intuitúsque omnes eius opes, eas coram, pro nihilo duxit: inquiens, non esse beatum quempiam nisi post funera. Plutar. in Solone. ad huius leges describendas, legati à Roma Athenas missi sunt, anno mundi 3510. ante Christum natum 452. Liui.lib.3. obiit Rhodi anno natus 80.
units.tr: Solon, famous among the seven wise men of Greece, gave laws to the Athenians. He repealed those which Draco had instituted, except those concerning homicide. He always opposed the tyranny of his kinsman Pisistratus, which was creeping in secretly; when that tyranny took hold, Solon went off to Egypt to pursue wisdom, having first obtained from the Athenians a ten-year absence. Summoned by Croesus, he looked upon all his riches and, in their presence, counted them as nothing, saying that no one is blessed except after death. Plutarch, in the Life of Solon. To draw up his laws, envoys were sent from Rome to Athens in the year 3510 from the creation of the world, 452 years before Christ was born. See Livy, book 3. He died at Rhodes at the age of eighty.

units.la: CYRVS Perfarũ Rex primus, imperauit apud Persas anno mundi 3403. ante Christũ natum 559. rexitque annos 30. hic filius fuit Cambyfæ, & Mandanes, quæ filia erat Astyagis Medorum Regis. A filiis pastorum, Rex appellatus est per ludum, cum esset annorũ 12. Nam iusserat eum occidi Astyages, ob somnium, quòd viderat ex genitalibus filiæ vitem enasci, quæ totam Asiam occuparet: attamen ab vxore Mitradatis, seruatus & enutritus est, cui vxori nomen erat Cyno, quod Græcè canem significat. hic consilio Harpagi aduersus Astyagem exercitũ duxit, eúmq; superauit prodente Harpago, vlciscente mortem filij, quem in e[?]ulium[?] paratum, ei edendum dederat Astyages, ob seruatum Cyrum. Cum Cyro regnauit Cyaxares Astyagis filius apud Medos, anno 20. antequam Cyrus Babyloniam caperet, vt ait Xenophon lib.8. Cyrus iste à Daniele vocatur Darius, item ab Esdras, 3.Esdræ 3. De Cyro vide Herodo. lib.1. & Iustin.lib.item 1.Oro.lib.2.cap.6. & 7.
units.tr: Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, reigned among the Persians in the year 3403 from the creation of the world, 559 years before Christ was born, and ruled for 30 years. He was the son of Cambyses and Mandane, who was the daughter of Astyages, king of the Medes. He was called king by the sons of shepherds in a game when he was twelve years old. For Astyages had ordered him to be killed because of a dream in which he had seen a vine sprout from his daughter's genitals, which would cover all Asia. However, he was saved and brought up by the wife of Mitradates, whose name was Cyno, which in Greek means dog. Through the counsel of Harpagus, he led an army against Astyages and defeated him, Harpagus betraying him, avenging the death of his son whom Astyages had given him to be eaten, having been prepared, because Cyrus had been saved. Cyaxares, son of Astyages, reigned with Cyrus among the Medes, for 20 years before Cyrus captured Babylon, as Xenophon says in book 8. This Cyrus is called Darius by Daniel, and likewise by Esdras, 3 Esdras 3. About Cyrus, see Herodotus, book 1, and Justin, book 1, and Orosius, book 2, chapters 6 and 7.

units.la: TOMYRIS, regina Massagetarum in Scythia, cum Cyro pugnauit, vicit, omnémque eius exercitum internecioni dedit: erant autem militum 20000. Sic vlta est filij mortem, quem Cyrus per bellicas insidias cum suis interfecerat: nã amisso hęc exercitu quem præmiserat, & vnico filio, orbitatis dolore non in lachrymas effudit, sed in vltionis solatia intendit: hostésque recenti victoria exultantes, pari insidiarum fraude circûdedit: quippe simulata diffidentia, Cyrum vsq; ad angustias perduxit: ibi compositis in montibus insidiis, exercitum cum Rege trucidauit, neq; nuncius tantæ cladis vllus superfuit. Cyri caput in vtrem demisit, quem humano cruore cõpleuerat, cum hac exprobratione crudelitatis, Satia te sanguine(inquit)quem sitisti. Herod.li.1. Iust.li.1. acta sunt an.mun.3432. ante Christũ natum 530. D.IVD. ZOROBABEL IESVM. SACER IEHOSVA
units.tr: Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae in Scythia, fought with Cyrus, won, and gave his whole army over to slaughter; there were 20,000 soldiers. Thus she avenged the death of her son, whom Cyrus had killed with his men by a warlike ambush. For, having lost the army she had sent ahead and her only son, she did not pour herself out in tears from the grief of bereavement, but turned her mind to the consolations of revenge. Exulting in their recent victory, she surrounded the enemy with the same deceit of ambush: feigning distrust, she led Cyrus into a narrow place; there, with ambushes laid in the mountains, she slaughtered the army together with the king, and no messenger of so great a disaster survived. She plunged Cyrus' head into a wineskin which she had filled with human blood, with this reproach of cruelty: "Sate yourself with the blood you thirsted for." Herodotus, book 1; Justin, book 1. These things were done in the year 3432 from the creation of the world, 530 years before Christ was born.

units.la: ZOROBABEL, filius Salathiel, Iudæorum Dux fuit anno à mũdo condito 3418. ante verò Christum natum 544. Hic Regis Iechoniæ in directa (quam vocât) linea, nepos erat: qui cum Iehofua, siue Iesu, Sacerdote summo, in Iudæam remigrauit, & cum multis Iudæorum millibus: templi Hierosolymitani fundamenta iecit, permittente Cyro Persarum Rege, qui Babyloniam ceperat, regnúmque & monarchiam ad Persas transtulerat, Rege Baltazaro interempto, iuxta Prophetiam ac prædictionem Danielis, imperante apud Romanos Seruio Tullio Rege sexto: quanquam Orosius lib.2.cap.6. sentiat regnante Tarquinio superbo, septimo atque vltimo Romanorum Rege, captam fuisse à Cyro Babyloniam. At vero Baltazar imperitabat Chaldæis tempore Seruij Tullij: sub quo Baltazare Daniel scripturam mysticam legit & interpretatus est: autore Eutropio, lib.1. Cæterum quatenus attinet ad historiam sacram de Salathiele & Iehofua, consulito lib.1. Esdræ cap.1. & sequentibus. item Aggæum & Zachariã Prophetas, & Ecclesiasticum, cap.49. ipsum denique Iosep. lib.Antiq.10.cap.1. ac Ioan. Cario. cron.lib.2.
units.tr: Zorobabel, son of Salathiel, was leader of the Jews in the year 3418 from the creation of the world, 544 years before Christ was born. He was a grandson in the direct line, as they call it, of King Jechoniah. He returned to Judaea from the Babylonian captivity with Jehoshua, or Jesus, the high priest, and with many thousands of Jews, and laid the foundations of the temple of Jerusalem, with the permission of Cyrus, king of the Persians, who had captured Babylon, and had transferred the kingdom and monarchy to the Persians, King Belshazzar having been slain, according to the prophecy and prediction of Daniel, while Servius Tullius, the sixth king, reigned among the Romans. Although Orosius, book 2, chapter 6, holds that Babylon was taken by Cyrus during the reign of Tarquinius the Proud, the seventh and last king of the Romans. But Belshazzar ruled the Chaldeans in the time of Servius Tullius, and under this Belshazzar Daniel read and interpreted the mystical writing, according to Eutropius, book 1. As for the sacred history concerning Salathiel and Jehoshua, consult 1 Esdras chapter 1 and following, likewise the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, and Ecclesiasticus, chapter 49, and finally Josephus, Antiquities book 10, chapter 1, and John Carion, Chronicle, book 2.

units.la: IEHOSVA, qui & Iosue, & Iesus dictus est, summum gessit apud Iudæos sacerdotium, temporibus Zorobabelis supradicti, cuius & in remigratione ex captiuitate Babylonica comes fuit. Vide vt supra. Hic (vt Philo refert) historiam Iudith & Hester conscripsit. Fuit alter eiusdem nominis Iosue (ne erres) Israëlitici populi post Moysen Dux, qui cum Caleb in terram à Deo promissam tandem peruenit.
units.tr: JEHOSHUA, who is also called Joshua and Jesus, held the high priesthood among the Jews in the time of the aforesaid Zerubbabel, and was a companion of his when they returned from Babylonian captivity. See above. He (as Philo reports) wrote the history of Judith and Esther. There was another Joshua of the same name (lest you be mistaken), leader of the Israelite people after Moses, who together with Caleb at last reached the land promised by God.

units.la: HIPPONAX, Iambicus Poëta fuit insignis fœditate vultus: quamobrem imaginem eius sculptores Bupalus & Anthermus publicè deridendam proposuerunt. quod indigne ferens Hipponax tam amarum carmen in eos distrinxit, vt à nonnullis credatur eos ad suspendium compulisse. Scazõtem, carminis iambici genus, fertur inuenifle Hipponax, quod ab eius nomine Hipponacticum, seu Hipponacteū, vocatur. Plin. lib.36.cap.5.huius meminit.Clarebat autem Hipponax circiter annum mundi 3424. ante Christum natum 538.
units.tr: HIPPONAX, the iambic poet, was notable for the ugliness of his face. For this reason the sculptors Bupalus and Anthermus exhibited his image to be publicly mocked. Hipponax, taking this badly, attacked them in so bitter a poem that some believe they were driven to hang themselves. The scazon, a kind of iambic verse, is said to have been invented by Hipponax, and for that reason it is called Hipponactic, or Hipponacteum. Pliny mentions him in book 36, chapter 5. Hipponax flourished about the year of the world 3424, before the birth of Christ 538.

units.la: BVPALVS & Anthermus filij fuerunt Anthermi Chij, qui in arte sculpendi clarissimi extitere. ij feruntur sculpsisse Hipponactis deformis Poëtæ imaginem, de qua hîc supra mentionem feci: reiicit tamen Plinius vt falsum, quod ad laqueum adacti fuerint à Poëta: complura enim (inquit) in finitimis insulis fimulachra postea fecere, sicut in Delo, quibus subiecerunt carmen, non vitibus tantùm censeri Chium, sed & operibus Anthermi fi'iorum. In ipsa Chio narrata est operis eorum Dianæ facies in sublimi posita, cuius vultum intrantes tristem, exeuntes exhilaratum putant. Consulito Plin.lib 36.cap.5.vt supra citaui.nec est hîc repetenda à me annorum supputatio quam supra inserui, cùm iisdem vixerint temporibus sculptores hi, cum Hipponacte Poëta prædicto, vbi habes annorum rationem. L. TARQVIN SVPERBVS TVLLIA VXOR L.S
units.tr: BUPALUS and Anthermus were the sons of Anthermus of Chios, who became most famous in the art of sculpture. They are said to have carved the image of the deformed poet Hipponax, which I mentioned above. Pliny, however, rejects this as false, that they were driven to the noose by the poet: "For (he says) they later made many statues in the neighbouring islands, as in Delos, and added verses to them, to the effect that Chios was valued not only for its vines but also for the works of the sons of Anthermus." On Chios itself it is recorded that a statue of Diana by their hand stands on a high place, and that those who enter think her face sad, while those who leave think it cheerful. Consult Pliny, book 36, chapter 5, as I cited above. Nor should I repeat here the reckoning of years that I inserted above, since these sculptors lived in the same times as the aforesaid poet Hipponax; where you have the chronology.

units.la: L. TARQVINIVS Superbus, septimus ac vltimus Romanorum Rex, regnare incepit anno mundi 3431. ante Christum natum 531. primus vincula excogitauit, fustes, carceres, compedes, catenas, exilia, atque metalla. Volscos vicit: oppida valida in Latio, Gabios, Suefsámque Pometiam subegit: cum Thufcis pacé fecit, templú Ioui in Capitolio ædificauit. verùm Ardeam oppugnás, imperiú perdidit. nam omnibus cùm effet exosus, accepta occasione ex violatione Lucretiæ, quâ Sextus Tarquinius filius eius armatus noctu cõstuprarat, Romani eum cum suis omnibus eiecerunt. defecit ab eo exercitus qui ciuitatem Ardeä decem & octo miliaribus ab vrbe Roma distantem, oppugnabat: atque etiam Romam veniēs Rex ipse, portis exclusus est. ita Romę septem regnarunt Reges annos 244. qui vix ad decimum quintum vrbis miliarium possidebant. postea crearunt Romani Consules. Titus Liu. lib. 1. Diony. Hali. lib. 4. Eutro. lib. 1. Plutar. in Bruti vita.
units.tr: L. TARQUINIUS Superbus, the seventh and last king of the Romans, began to reign in the year of the world 3431, before the birth of Christ 531. He first devised chains, rods, prisons, fetters, exile and the mines. He conquered the Volsci, subdued the strong towns in Latium, Gabii and Suessa Pometia; he made peace with the Etruscans and built the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol. But while besieging Ardea he lost his empire. For, being hated by all, he was given an opportunity by the violation of Lucretia, whom his son Sextus Tarquinius had violated at night under arms; the Romans expelled him with all his people. The army that was besieging the city of Ardea, eighteen miles from the city of Rome, deserted him; and when the king himself came to Rome, he was shut out of the gates. Thus seven kings reigned at Rome for 244 years, who scarcely held more than fifteen miles around the city. Afterwards the Romans appointed consuls. See Livy, book 1; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 4; Eutropius, book 1; Plutarch in the Life of Brutus.

units.la: TVLLIA vxor fuit L. Tarquinij Superbi, filiáque Seruij Tullij. hæc hoccifo[?] patre, cuius cædis conscia erat, carpento in forum inuecta, nec reuerita coetum virorum, euocauit virum è Curia, primáque Regem appellauit: deinde, redeundo, per patris demortui corpus carpentum egisse fertur. Diony. Halicar. & Titus Liuius vt supra. PERS. REX. CAMBISES HOLOFERNES[?]
units.tr: TULLIA was the wife of L. Tarquinius Superbus and daughter of Servius Tullius. She, with her father, whose murder she was privy to, was carried into the forum in a chariot, and not ashamed of the gathering of men, she called her husband out of the Curia and first greeted him as king. Then, returning, she is said to have driven the chariot over the body of her dead father. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Livy, as above. PERS. KING. CAMBYSES. HOLOFERNES[?]

units.la: CAMBYSES Persarum Rex secundus, successit Cyro, anno mundi 3433. ante Christum natum 529. Is dicitur Artaxerxes, 1. Esdræ 4. cap. qui templi & ciuitatis ædificationem prohibuit, quam Cyrus, pater permiserat. Sub hoc Hebræi historiam Hester factam asserunt: alij in tempora Darij, Hystaspis filij, reiiciunt. Is Ægyptum suo regno adiecit, sed offensus illorum superstitionibus, Apidis, cæterorumque deorum ædes dirui iussit. Ad Ammonis quoque templum expugnandum exercitum misit, qui in Libya deserta arenis obrutus, vniuersus interiit. Smerdin fratrem ex vtroque parente, interfici iussit, liuore commotus, quòd solus ille arcum duobus traheret digitis, quod nemo alius è Persis poterat: præterea eo in Persidem profecto, somniarat sibi nuntiari in regio sedentem fratrem Smerdin solio cœlum vertice tangere: quare metuens ne se necato, à fratre occuparetur imperium, Prexaspem ad illum occidendum misit: Sororem quam in vxorem duxerat, interfecit. Cæterùm Actabanem obsidens, proprio se interemit gladio, anno regni 8. fuit quoque alter Cambyses, mediocris dignitatis Persa, huius auus, Cyri pater, ac Mandanes maritus. Vide Herodo. lib. 3. Iusti. lib. 1. Iofeph. lib. 11. cap. 2.
units.tr: CAMBYSES, the second king of the Persians, succeeded Cyrus in the year of the world 3433, before the birth of Christ 529. He is called Artaxerxes in 1 Esdras, chapter 4, and he forbade the building of the temple and the city, which Cyrus his father had permitted. Under him the Hebrews place the history of Esther; others place it in the times of Darius, son of Hystaspes. He added Egypt to his kingdom, but, offended by their superstitions, he ordered the temples of Apis and of the other gods to be torn down. He also sent an army to storm the temple of Ammon, which, buried in the sands of the Libyan desert, perished entirely. Moved by envy, because he alone could draw the bow with two fingers, which no other Persian could do, he ordered his brother Smerdis, born of the same parents, to be killed; moreover, when he had set out for Persia, he dreamed that his brother Smerdis was being announced to him as sitting on the royal throne and touching the heavens with his head; therefore, fearing that the empire would be seized by his brother if he himself were killed, he sent Prexaspes to kill him. He killed his sister whom he had taken as his wife. But while besieging Actabanes, he killed himself with his own sword, in the eighth year of his reign. There was also another Cambyses, a Persian of moderate rank, the grandfather of this one, father of Cyrus, and husband of Mandane. See Herodotus, book 3; Justin, book 1; Josephus, book 11, chapter 2.

units.la: HOLOFERNES Dux exercitus Cambysæ supra dicti, missus est ab eo aduersus prouincias quæ suo ipsius nolebant subdi imperio. Hic Bethuliam obsedit, ciues ad extremam redacti sitim se dedere volebant: at consilio, atque insigni facinore Iudith liberantur. Vulgatior est Iudith historia, quàm vt hîc ad vnguem referri consentaneum sit. Vide librum Iudith.
units.tr: HOLOFERNES, commander of the army of the aforesaid Cambyses, was sent by him against the provinces that were unwilling to be subjected to his rule. He besieged Bethulia, and the citizens, reduced to extreme thirst, were willing to surrender; but they are freed by the counsel and remarkable deed of Judith. The story of Judith is too well known to be fitting to recount here in every detail. See the book of Judith.

units.la: EPIMENIDES Poëta Cretensis, Atheniensibus pestilentia laborantibus dixit ciuitatem purgari oportere: eò cùm rogatus venisset: iussit oues albas atque nigras apud Areopagũ immolari. inde recedens domum, purgatis Athenis, ab Atheniensibus pecuniam recusauit (nam etiam Poëtas haud facilè auaros videas.) Hic,iuuenis in agrum ad custodiendum pecus missus ab Agiasarcho patre,in quodam antro obdormisse dicitur annos 75. hinc manauit prouerbium, Epimenidis somnum dormire. Fertur primus domos atque agros expiasse, delubráque erexisse. expiauit itaque Athenas anno mundi 3368. ante Christum natum 594. Vide Dioge. Laër.lib.1. Plato.1. & 3. de legibus Apule.lib.2. Floridorum.
units.tr: EPIMENIDES, the Cretan poet, when the Athenians were suffering from a plague, said that the city had to be purified. When he had come there at their request, he ordered white and black sheep to be sacrificed at the Areopagus. Then, departing home after Athens was purified, he refused money from the Athenians (for you would scarcely find poets greedy either). He, as a young man sent into the field by his father Agiasarchus to guard the flock, is said to have fallen asleep in a certain cave for 75 years; hence the proverb, "to sleep the sleep of Epimenides." He is said to have been the first to purify houses and fields, and to have erected shrines. He thus purified Athens in the year of the world 3368, before the birth of Christ 594. See Diogenes Laertius, book 1; Plato, the first and third books of the Laws; Apuleius, book 2 of the Florida.

units.la: PYTHAGORAS Samius, Mnesarchi anulorum sculptoris filius clarebat circa annum mundi 3439. ante Christum natum 523. hic primus, amicorum omnia communia, dixit, amicitiamque æqualitatem: cuius etiam discipuli facultates omnes in vnum deponebant,& quinquennium silebant. Animatis abstinere iussit, assuefaciès homines ad faciliorem victum. fertur primus Græcis pondera & mesuras inuexisse, primúmque, vesperum atq; Luciferum idem sydus dixisse. sequuntur aliquot eius symbola: Ignis gladio nonsodiendus. Statera non translilieda. Cor non edendum. Verso ad Solem vultu non mingendum. Extra publicam viam non eundum. A fabis abstinendum. Sunt & alia quæ referuntur latiùs à Diog.Laër.lib.8. DARIVS HIST[?]ASPIS FIL. REX PERS. IIII SOPIRVS NOB. PER.
units.tr: PYTHAGORAS of Samos, son of Mnesarchus, a seal-engraver, flourished about the year of the world 3439, before the birth of Christ 523. He was the first to say, "The goods of friends are common," and spoke of friendship as equality; his disciples too deposited all their property into one fund and kept silent for five years. He ordered abstinence from living creatures, accustoming men to a simpler diet. He is said to have been the first to introduce weights and measures to the Greeks, and the first to say that the evening star and the morning star are the same planet. Several of his symbols follow: "Do not stir the fire with a sword. Do not step over the balance. Do not eat the heart. Do not urinate facing the sun. Do not walk outside the public road. Abstain from beans." There are also others, which Diogenes Laertius, book 8, reports more fully. DARIUS, SON OF HYSTASPES, KING OF PERSIA, FOURTH. SOPIRUS, NOBLE PERSIAN.

units.la: DARIVS Hystaspis filius, hinnitu equi rex declaratus est anno mundi 3441. ante Christum natum 521. Smerdis & Patizithes qui regnum usurparant, occisi sunt antequam imperaret hic, qui etiam Smerdin occidit, detecta per Otanem eius fraude: nam Smerdis hic, se Cambysis fratrem dicebat, quòd illi de facie ac nomine similis esset: attamen ab aurium mutilatione dolus deprehensus est. Porrò Darius hic, Atossam Cyri filiam uxorem duxit, ex qua liberos sustulit, inter quos Xerxes fuit: hanc atossam putant nonnulli fuisse Hester. hic permisit Judæis remigrare in Judæam ac templum reædificare: vasa & thesauros templi restituit. Provincias viginti constituit, earúmque singulis præsides præfecit, taxato quod penderetur tributo. etenim sub Cyro & Cambyse nihil dum fuerat circa tributa institutum, sed munera afferebatur. hic Geras subegit, Thraces se dedidere: at Scythæ hunc in fugam adegêre. Vide Herod.lib.3. nam Justit.lib.1. Smerdin, sive Smerdem, de quo supra, Oropastem vocat.
units.tr: DARIUS, son of Hystaspes, was declared king by the neighing of a horse in the year of the world 3441, before the birth of Christ 521. Smerdis and Patizithes, who had usurped the kingdom, were killed before this man reigned; he also killed Smerdis, the fraud having been detected by Otanes. For this Smerdis claimed to be the brother of Cambyses, because he was similar to him in face and name; yet the deceit was caught by the mutilation of his ears. Moreover, this Darius took Atossa, daughter of Cyrus, as his wife, and had children by her, among whom was Xerxes; some think this Atossa was Esther. He permitted the Jews to return to Judea and to rebuild the temple; he restored the vessels and treasures of the temple. He established twenty provinces and set governors over each of them, with a tribute fixed to be paid. For under Cyrus and Cambyses nothing had yet been established concerning tributes, but gifts were brought. He subdued the Geras; the Thracians surrendered; but the Scythians drove him into flight. See Herodotus, book 3; for Justin, book 1, calls the Smerdis mentioned above Oropastes.

units.la: ZOPYRVS, præcisis de industria, labiis, naso, auribus, nomine tranfugæ Babylonem profectus, corpus populo laniatum ostendit: constituitur dux omnium suffragio adversus Darium, qui Babylonem iandiu frustra obsidebat, cui tandem creditum sibi exercitum prodidit: sicque Babylonem quæ defecerat, & ab Assyriis occupabatur, recuperavit Darius, memorabili hoc quidem facto Zopyri: cui fuit etiam Megabizus filius, dux exercitus Darij in Europa, qui & Thraciam subegit. Herod.lib.3.Justit.lib.1.
units.tr: ZOPYRUS, having deliberately had his lips, nose and ears cut off, went to Babylon under the name of a deserter, and showed the people his mangled body. He was appointed commander of all by common vote against Darius, who had been besieging Babylon in vain for a long time; to whom at last he betrayed the army entrusted to him; and thus Darius recovered Babylon, which had revolted and was held by the Assyrians, by this memorable deed of Zopyrus. He also had a son Megabyzus, commander of Darius's army in Europe, who also subdued Thrace. See Herodotus, book 3; Justin, book 1.

units.la: TARQUINIUS Collatinus Lucretiæ maritus, cœnabat cum regiis iuuenibus & aliis primoribus in statiuis obsidionis Ardeæ, cùm incidit de vxoribus mentio: suam quisque mirè laudat:hoc certamine contentionis accenso, negat Collatinus verbis opus esse: paucis id quidem horis posse sciri quantum cæteris sua præstet Lucretia: vxores inuisunt. certamine laudem retulit Lucretia.Ibi mala libido Lucretiæ stuprandæ Sextum Tarquinium capit: post aliquot dies stricto gladio ad dormientem Lucretiam venit, marito in castris agente: vi potitur. vltio breui crimen sequitur: deturbatur regno Tarquinius Superbus: Sextus Tarquinius eius filius, Gabios profectus, interficitur. Titus Liuius lib.i.
units.tr: Tarquinius Collatinus, the husband of Lucretia, was dining with the royal youths and other leading men in the camp during the siege of Ardea, when the talk turned to wives. Each man praised his own wife extravagantly. When this rivalry grew heated, Collatinus said there was no need for words: within a few hours they could learn how far his Lucretia surpassed the others. They went to visit their wives, and Lucretia carried off the prize for the contest. Then an evil lust to ravish Lucretia seized Sextus Tarquinius. Some days later he came to the sleeping Lucretia with a drawn sword, while her husband was away at the camp, and he took her by force. Punishment soon followed the crime: Tarquinius Superbus was driven from the kingdom, and his son Sextus Tarquinius, having gone to Gabii, was killed. Titus Livy, book 1.

units.la: LUCRETIA Spurij Lucretij filia, fœminam certè Romanam atque exemplar totius coniugalis castitatis se præstitit. hæc siquidem vi à Sexto Tarquinio constuprata, mœsta nuntium ad patrem atque ad virum mittit, vt cum amicis veniant: ita facto maturatóque opus esse, rem atrocem incidisse: veniunt cum L. Iunio Bruto: his corpus violatum fatetur, animam verò insontem morte ipsa testatur. Brutus viro patríque luctu occupatis, cultrum ex vulnere Lucretiæ extrahens, Per hunc inquit castissimum sanguinem iuro, me Tarquinium Superbum cum scelerata coniuge, & omni liberorū stirpe, ferro, igni, quacunque vi possim exaćturum. Vide Tit.Liu. lib.i. Sic exaćto rege res Romana rediit ad Consules, anno mundi 3456. ante Christum natum 506. PA TRO. CORIOLANVS VETVRIA CORIO MAT.
units.tr: Lucretia, daughter of Spurius Lucretius, showed herself certainly a Roman woman and an example of complete conjugal chastity. For when she had been ravished by Sextus Tarquinius, she sent a grieving message to her father and her husband, asking them to come with their friends: it was necessary to act quickly, since a dreadful thing had happened. They came with Lucius Junius Brutus. She confessed to them that her body had been violated, but her death itself bore witness that her soul was innocent. Brutus, while the husband and father were occupied with grief, drew a knife from Lucretia's wound and said: "By this most chaste blood I swear that I will pursue Tarquinius Superbus, with his wicked wife and every offspring of his line, with fire and sword and by whatever force I can." See Titus Livy, book 1. Thus, with the king expelled, the Roman state returned to the consuls, in the year of the world 3456, before the birth of Christ 506. PATRO. CORIOLANVS VETVRIA CORIO MAT.

units.la: Patricius Romanus ab Romanis exactus est, quòd Consulatum arroganter ambiret, & Tribunis Plebis aduersaretur, ac proinde suspectus esse populo ob nimium factum ac potentiam.quare cum iam ante pro Romanis pugnans,Coriolos vrbem,Volscorum ciuitatem,vnde Coriolanus dictus est,expugnasset, ad ipsos Volscos contendit iratus, à quibus auxilia contra Romanos accepit anno mundi 3 4 7 5. ante Christum natum 4 8 7. Romanos saepe vicit: vsque ad quintum miliarium vrbis accessit, expugnaturus etiam patriam suam(legatis qui pacem petebat repudiatis) nisi ad eum mater Veturia & vxor Volumnia, ex vrbe venissent: quarum precibus remouit exercitum, quem submouere armis Roma non poterat.Vide Titum Liuium lib.2.& Eutro. lib.1.Foeminae item preces ac lachrymae vxoris Meleagri, ad arma pro patriae tutela capessenda Meleagrum compulerunt.Ouid.epi.3.
units.tr: A Roman patrician was expelled by the Romans, because he sought the consulship arrogantly, opposed the tribunes of the plebs, and for this reason was suspected by the people because of his excessive influence and power. Therefore, having earlier fought for the Romans and captured the city of Corioli, a city of the Volsci, from which he took the name Coriolanus, he went in anger to the Volsci themselves, and from them received auxiliaries against the Romans, in the year of the world 3475, before the birth of Christ 487. He often defeated the Romans, and advanced as far as the fifth milestone from the city, intending to storm his own homeland as well, after he had rejected the envoys who sought peace; unless his mother Veturia and his wife Volumnia had come to him from the city. By their prayers he withdrew the army, which Rome could not drive away by arms. See Titus Livy, book 2, and Eutropius, book 1. Likewise, the prayers and tears of Meleager's wife compelled Meleager to take up arms in defence of his country. Ovid, Epistles 3.

units.la: C.M. Coriolani mater fuit, ad quam adierunt matronae Romanae, quae in discrimine patriae periuicerunt[?] vt Veturia magno natu mulier, & Volumnia Coriolani vxor, duos paruulos ex Coriolano ferentes secum,in castra hostium irent:& quam armis viri defendere vrbem non possent,mulieres precibus lachrymisque defenderent: quod praestiterunt. nam fractus precibus ac fletibus matris Veturiae ac vxoris Volumniae Coriolanus,castra retro ab vrbe mouit.Titus Liuius li. 2.Dion.Halic.lib.7.& 8. Statuit Senatus vt foemineum extrueretur templum Diuae Fortunae, vbi foeminae singulis annis, eadem qua liberata fuerat vrbs die, sacra peragerent: idque in foeminarum honorem, ac huius facti, & velut miraculi, monimentum perpetuum. PORSENAC[?] C.T.R. CLOELIA VIR.R.
units.tr: C.M. Veturia was the mother of Coriolanus. To her came the Roman matrons, who, in the peril of their country, [?] persuaded that Veturia, an elderly woman, and Volumnia, the wife of Coriolanus, should go with two little children of Coriolanus into the enemy camp; and what the men could not defend the city with arms, the women should defend with prayers and tears. This they accomplished. For Coriolanus, broken by the prayers and weeping of his mother Veturia and his wife Volumnia, moved his camp back from the city. Titus Livy, book 2; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, books 7 and 8. The Senate decreed that a temple of Fortuna Muliebris should be built, where the women should celebrate rites every year on the same day on which the city had been delivered, and this was to be a perpetual monument in honour of the women, and of this deed, as if of a miracle. PORSENAC[?] C.T.R. CLOELIA VIR.R.

units.la: PORSENA Hetruriæ Rex, bellum Rom.intulit, in gratiam Tarquinij Superbi, tripúsque continuis annis trepidam urbē terruit : quam audax Scævolæ facinus ab hoste liberavit: nam scribam pro Rege interfecit,dum timet sciscitari uter Porsena effet. Tit. Livi. lib.2. Halicar. lib.5. Eutrop. lib.1. Porrò de Porsena & Scævola elegans hoc apud Martialem lib. 1. extat epigramma:
units.tr: Porsena, king of Etruria, made war on the Romans, on behalf of Tarquinius Superbus, and for three successive years terrified the trembling city; the bold deed of Scaevola freed it from the enemy. For he killed the secretary instead of the king, while he was afraid to ask which one was Porsena. Titus Livy, book 2; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 5; Eutropius, book 1. Moreover, concerning Porsena and Scaevola, there is an elegant epigram in Martial, book 1:

units.la: Dum peteret Regem decepta satellite dextra, Iniecit sacris se peritura focus: Sed tam sæua pius miracula non tulit hostis, Et raptum flammis iussit abire virum. Vrere quam potuit contempto Mutius igne, Hanc spectare manum Porsena non potuit. Maior deceptæ fama est, & gloria dextræ: Si non errasset, fecerat illa minus.
units.tr: While he sought to strike the king, his right hand deceived by the attendant, he threw himself onto the sacred fire, about to die. But the pious enemy did not bear such a fierce marvel, and ordered the man snatched from the flames to depart. Mucius endured the fire with contempt, as far as he could burn; Porsena could not bear to watch that hand. The fame of the mistaken hand is greater, and the glory of it; had it not erred, it would have done less.

units.la: CLOELIA, Romana virgo, una ex obsidibus, cum castra Hetruscorum forte haud procul ripa Tyberis locata essent, frustrata custodes dux agminis virginum inter tela hostium Tyberim tranavit, sospitesque omnes Romam ad propinquos restituit anno mundi 3457. ante Christum natum 505.iratus Porsena Cloeliam obsidem per oratores deposcit: deinde in admirationem versus, supra Coclites & Mutios id facinoris esse dicebat : restituta hæc apud Regem Hetruscum,non tuta solum, sed honorata,partéque obsidum donata est. Romani novam in fœmina virtutem novo genere honoris, statua equestri donavere: in summa sacra via fuit posita virgo insidens equo. Livius lib.2. XERXES PERS. REX CIMON D. ATHENIEN
units.tr: Cloelia, a Roman maiden, one of the hostages, when the camp of the Etruscans happened to be placed not far from the bank of the Tiber, deceived the guards, and as leader of the girls swam across the Tiber amid the enemy's weapons, and restored all of them safe to their relatives in Rome, in the year of the world 3457, before the birth of Christ 505. Angry, Porsena demanded Cloelia back as a hostage through envoys; then, turned to admiration, he said that such a deed had been done by Horatius Cocles and the Mucii. Cloelia was returned to the Etruscan king, not only safe but honoured, and was given a part of the hostages as a gift. The Romans, to honour a new kind of virtue in a woman with a new kind of honour, set up an equestrian statue for her: on the Sacred Way at the top, the maiden was placed sitting on a horse. Livy, book 2. XERXES PERS. REX CIMON D. ATHENIEN

units.la: XERXES quintus Persarum Rex, Darij Hystaspis filius, successit patri in regno Persarum anno mundi 3477. ante Christum natum 485. fuit nonnihil controuersiae inter hunc & maiorem natu fratrem Artabarzanem: attamen res facile componitur ut Xerxes, Atossae secundae Darij uxoris filius, quae Cyri filia erat, regno potiretur. Primùm Ægyptios qui defecerant subegit: posthaec maximam in Græciam expeditionem fecit: tantaéque feruntur eius fuisse copiae ut fluuios exiccarent: quod de Scamádro fluuio (qui & Xanthus dictus est) legimus. Græciam uastauit, Athenas, urbésque vicinas combussit. tandem à Leonida ac Themistocle pulsus, uno die etiam duo vulnera accepit: nauicula piscatoria aufugit. Cæterùm is cum filio Dario ab Artabano, spe adipiscendi regni interficitur: Artabanum autem Artaxerxes gladio transuerberauit, ut dicturi sumus inserius. consulito Iusti.lib.1.2.&3. Præterea Plut. in vita Themist. & Agesil. item Hero.li.7.
units.tr: Xerxes, the fifth king of the Persians, son of Darius Hystaspis, succeeded his father in the kingdom of the Persians in the year of the world 3477, before the birth of Christ 485. There was some dispute between him and his elder brother Artabazanes; yet the matter was easily settled, so that Xerxes, son of Atossa, the second wife of Darius, who was a daughter of Cyrus, gained the kingdom. First he subdued the Egyptians who had revolted; afterwards he made his greatest expedition into Greece. And his forces are said to have been so great that they dried up rivers; we read this of the river Scamander (which is also called Xanthus). He laid waste Greece and burned Athens and the neighbouring cities. At length, driven off by Leonidas and Themistocles, he was even wounded twice in one day; he fled away in a little fishing boat. Yet he, together with his son Darius, was killed by Artabanus in hope of obtaining the kingdom; but Artaxerxes ran Artabanus through with a sword, as we shall relate further below. Consult Justin, books 1, 2 and 3. Also Plutarch in the lives of Themistocles and Agesilaus, and likewise Herodotus, book 7.

units.la: CIMON Athenien-sium dux præstantissimus, semel atque iterum Xerxis exercitu uno die fudit: primò pugna nauali, deinde terrestri: præterea Asiae minoris partem cepit: inimicorum exuuiis opulëtus factus, pauperibus bonam partem distribuit, mensasque dapibus instructas, pauperibus ac peregrinis publicè parauit. Vide Plutar. in Cimone.
units.tr: Cimon, the most outstanding leader of the Athenians, twice routed the army of Xerxes in a single day: first in a naval battle, then on land; besides, he took a part of Asia Minor. Enriched by the spoils of his enemies, he distributed a good portion to the poor, and at public expense prepared tables laden with food for the poor and for strangers. See Plutarch in the life of Cimon.

units.la: Clarebant his temporibus Æschylus, Sophocles, & Euripides, Poëtæ Tragici, quinetiam Zeuxis pictor insignis. ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΘΕΜΙΣΤΟΚΛΗΣ STESILEA
units.tr: At this time the tragic poets Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides flourished, and moreover the painter Zeuxis, famous. ATHENAIOS THEMISTOKLES STESILEA

units.la: THEMISTOCLES, Atheniensium dux fortissimus ac prudentissimus,ingenti gloriæ studio tenebatur.hic fusis,sugatísque Persis,atq; eorum Rege Xerxe,Athenas reædificauit, muro cinxit, Pyreúmque ciuitati iunxit,anno mundi 3492. à Christo nato 470. nec tamen inuidia caruit, dicere solitus se neque honoribus ab Atheniensibus affici,neq; apud eos in admiratione esse,sed procella vexatos imminente periculo, ad se veluti platanû subterfugere,reddita autem serenitate,euellere atque deiicere.Suffragiis è ciuitate eiectus,eiusq; dignitate ac nimiis opibus depressis,grauis fortuna inimico patriæ supplicë esse coegit.Nec tamen,iussus à rege Persarum,ad quë desciuerat, Græcis bellû inferre,ira in ciues suos eum cöcitare potuit: nec maximi honores atque opes ad patriam bello lacessendam impulerunt:fortasse quidë ratus opus maius quàm vt à se confici posset,præclaris tum ducibus abundâte Græcia, præsertim Cimone.Itaque fertur epoto taurino sanguine,venenóque infuso,in Magnesia diem obiisse,annos natus 65.Plutarc. in Themisto. Thucy. li. 1. huius etiam Themistoclis meminit Eras. in apophth.li.5.&8.
units.tr: Themistocles, the bravest and most prudent leader of the Athenians, was held by a great passion for glory. He, having routed and put to flight the Persians and their king Xerxes, rebuilt Athens, surrounded it with a wall, and joined the Piraeus to the city, in the year of the world 3492, from the birth of Christ 470. Yet he did not escape envy; he used to say that he was neither honoured by the Athenians nor esteemed among them, but that, like a plane tree, they took refuge under him when tossed by a storm and threatening danger, yet when the calm returned they plucked him up and cast him down. Expelled from the city by votes, and with his dignity and excessive wealth brought low, he was forced by grievous fortune to be a suppliant to the enemy of his country. Nevertheless, though ordered by the king of the Persians, to whom he had gone over, to wage war on the Greeks, he could not be driven by anger to attack his fellow citizens; nor did the greatest honours and wealth impel him to provoke his country with war, perhaps thinking the task too great to be accomplished by himself, since Greece abounded with excellent leaders, especially Cimon. And so it is said that, having drunk bull's blood with poison poured in, he died at Magnesia, at the age of 65. Plutarch in Themistocles; Thucydides, book 1. Erasmus also mentions this Themistocles in the Apophthegms, books 5 and 8.

units.la: STESILEA, eleganti forma mulier,amata fuit ab Aristide ac Themistocle:inde fortasse cöflato liuore,perpetuo flagrarunt inter se odio:quâquam vitæ ac morum dissimilitudo,non parum auxisse odium dicatur: nam Aristidë cöntraria in repub. sententia aduersarium semper habuit Themistocles. Vide Plutar.in Themistocle. LONGIM. PERS. R. ARTHAXERXES[?] ESDRAS SCRIBA ET SACER
units.tr: Stesilea, a woman of elegant beauty, was loved by Aristides and Themistocles; from this, perhaps, envy having been kindled, they burned with perpetual hatred for each other, although it is said that the difference of their life and manners did not a little increase the hatred: for Themistocles always had Aristides as an opponent, because of opposing views on the state. See Plutarch in Themistocles. LONGIM. PERS. R. ARTHAXERXES[?] ESDRAS SCRIBA ET SACER

units.la: ARTAXERXES Xerxis filius, cognomèto Longimanus, quòd manum dextram sinistra longiore haberet, Artabanum cum filiis occidit, de patris nece vindictam sumens. imperauit Persis anno mundi 3497. ante Christum natum 465. hic à Metasthene Darius, ab Esdra Darius & Artaxerxes vocatur indifferenter. nam Persæ his duobus nominibus promiscuè utuntur, sicut & nos imperatores nostros Cæsares & Augustos, sine discrimine vocamus. Astu Artabanū, juvenis ad huc, gladio transfodit: nam finxit se arma velle commutare, si inermem aggressus egregio in juvene commento, inimicum ense traiecit. Just.li.3.&10.Hero.lib.7.Plutar.in Artaxerxe. imperauit annos 40. Vide item Esdr.1.lib.ca.4.&7.
units.tr: Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes, surnamed Longimanus because he had a right hand longer than his left, killed Artabanus with his sons, taking vengeance for his father's murder. He ruled over the Persians in the year of the world 3497, before the birth of Christ 465. He is called Darius by Metasthenes, and Artaxerxes by Ezra, indifferently; for the Persians use both names interchangeably, just as we call our emperors Caesars and Augustuses without distinction. Being still a young man, he pierced Artabanus with a sword: for he pretended that he wished to exchange weapons, and so, attacking an unarmed man with a clever stratagem, he ran his enemy through with his blade. Justin, books 3 and 10; Herodotus, book 7; Plutarch in the life of Artaxerxes. He reigned forty years. See also Ezra, book 1, chapters 4 and 7.

units.la: ESDRAS Propheta fuit temporibus Artaxerxis, quē adiit, ab eóque petiit ut liceret Judæis reverti Jerusalem: & obtinuit. missus est igitur Esdras Jerosolymam, cum reliquiis vasorum Domini à Nabuchodonosore in Babyloniam abduc-torum, acceptis ab Artaxerxe privilegiis ut liceret ei constituere judices ac præsides in populo Judæ, ac Jerusalē, collapsámque Judæorum remp. instaurare. Consulito 1. lib. Esdræ, 7. cap. hinc incipiunt septem Danielis hebdomades.
units.tr: Ezra was a prophet in the time of Artaxerxes, whom he approached and asked that the Jews be permitted to return to Jerusalem; and he obtained it. Ezra was therefore sent to Jerusalem with the remnant of the vessels of the Lord that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off to Babylon, having received from Artaxerxes privileges that allowed him to appoint judges and governors among the people of Judah and Jerusalem, and to restore the fallen commonwealth of the Jews. See the first book of Ezra, chapter 7. From here begin the seven weeks of Daniel.

units.la: L. QVINTIVS Cincinnatus in opere, arans inuentus, sudore deterso ab aratro accersitus ad fasces, togam prætextam accepit, Dictatórque est creatus anno mundi 3506. ante Christum natum 456. hic mox sumpto honore, instructóque exercitu, cæsis hostibus victor exercitum Romanum liberauit. Nam Minutius Consul ab Equis & Volscis superatus, fugerat, ac fame ferróque cingebatur, actúmque infœliciter foret, ni Quintius ipse, qui iugum boum Equis imposuit, victoriámque quasi stiuam tenens, subiugatos hostes præ se primus egit. Romæ triumphauit. Castris hostium receptis, plenis rerum omnium (nudos hostes emiserat) prædam omnem suo tantum militi dedit: Consularem exercitum, ipsúmque Consulem increpans, carebis, inquit, prædæ parte miles ex eo hoste cui propè prædæ fuisti. Titus Liuius lib.3. Eutropius lib.1. Romæ quidem hic L.Quintius Cincinnatus ob egregiam hanc partam victoriam merito triumphum egit. tandem Dictatura (qui erat summus honos) se abdicauit, rursúsque rus ad agriculturam diuertit.
units.tr: Lucius Quintius Cincinnatus was found ploughing in his field; having wiped the sweat from his brow, he was called from the plough to the fasces, received the purple-bordered toga, and was created Dictator in the year of the world 3506, before the birth of Christ 456. Soon after taking up the office and raising an army, he defeated the enemy and freed the Roman army. For the consul Minucius had been overcome by the Aequi and the Volsci and had fled; he was surrounded by hunger and the sword, and the affair would have ended unhappily had not Quintius himself, who had put a yoke of oxen on the Aequi, holding victory as if it were a plough-handle, been the first to drive the conquered enemy before him. He triumphed at Rome. When the enemy camp was taken, full of everything (he had sent the enemy out naked), he gave all the booty to his own soldiers alone, rebuking the consular army and the consul himself: You will go without a share of the booty, soldiers, because of that enemy whom you almost were the booty of. Titus Livy, book 3; Eutropius, book 1. At Rome this same Lucius Quintius Cincinnatus rightly celebrated a triumph for this splendid victory. At last he laid down the dictatorship (which was the highest honour) and again turned aside to the countryside and farming.

units.la: RACILIA uxor fuit L.Quintij Cincinnati. hæc togam properè è tugurio viro postulanti protulit: cùm mandata Senatus,togatus ut audiret rogaretur à legatis, qui eum operi agresti intentum nomine Senatus salutabant. Titus Liuius lib.3. SOCRATES S ATHENIENSIS XANTIPES UX.SO
units.tr: Racilia was the wife of Lucius Quintius Cincinnatus. When her husband was asked by the envoys, who found him busy with farm work and greeted him in the name of the Senate, to hear the commands of the Senate in his toga, she quickly brought the toga out of the hut to him. Titus Livy, book 3. SOCRATES OF ATHENS, HIS WIFE XANTIPPE.

units.la: SOCRATES Sophronisci statuarij & Phanaretæ obstetricis filius fuit. clarebat anno mundi 3531. ante Christum natum 431. hic veram Philosophiam esse prædicabat, seipsum cognoscere, talemque esse debere hominem, qualis vellet videri. Philosophiam naturalem deseruit, vt moralem amplexaretur. Constantissimus ille, nec tristior nec iucundior vnquam visus est. pauperculus quidem extitit, at vero ab Apolline omnium sapientissimus dicitur iudicatus. In huius signo sculptum erat, hominis amicum esse, idipsum sapere: inimicum autem, desipere. Inuidia non caruit: accusatus est ab Anyto diuite, Melito Poëta, Lycone oratore, quòd male de iis sentiret. Intrepidus coram iudicibus stabat, nec voluit quam ei parauerat orationem Lysias, orator percelebris, ad sui defensionem, pronuntiare: quinimo ad bibêdam cicutam damnatus, eam sumpsit intrepidè. Athenienses tandem delatores eius occiderunt: æneámque statuam ei erexerunt, quam in templo collocarunt. Cice.li.1.de Orato. Aelianus, Plin.lib.7. Augusts[?].de ciui.Dei, lib.8.cap.3.
units.tr: Socrates was the son of Sophroniscus, a sculptor, and of Phaenarete, a midwife. He flourished in the year of the world 3531, before the birth of Christ 431. He taught that true philosophy was this: to know oneself, and that a man ought to be such as he wishes to appear. He abandoned natural philosophy in order to embrace moral philosophy. He was most constant, and was never seen sadder or merrier than usual. He was indeed very poor, yet he is said to have been judged by Apollo the wisest of all men. On his statue was carved: to be a friend of man is to be wise in the same thing; but to be an enemy is to be foolish. He was not spared envy: he was accused by Anytus, a rich man, by Meletus, a poet, and by Lycon, an orator, for holding bad opinions about them. He stood fearless before the judges, and did not wish to deliver the speech that Lysias, a very famous orator, had prepared for his defence. Indeed, condemned to drink hemlock, he drank it fearlessly. The Athenians at last put his accusers to death, erected a bronze statue to him, and placed it in a temple. Cicero, On the Orator, book 1; Aelian; Pliny, book 7; Augustine, On the City of God, book 8, chapter 3.

units.la: XANTIPPE, uxor fuit Socratis, quæ cùm molestissima esset, atque aliquando post nimios clamores & iurgia, sordidam aquam in caput illi iecisset, haud ægrè ferens respondit, Sciebam post tonitru venturam pluviam, interrogatus ab Alcibiade Socrates cur tam acerbam uxorem domo non exigeret, quoniam, inquit, cum talem domi perpetior, insuesco vt aliorum foris iniuriam feram. Vide Gel.li.1.cap.17. & Apophtheg.Eras. ASPA SIA MILESIA PERICLES ATHEN.
units.tr: Xanthippe was the wife of Socrates. She was most troublesome, and once, after excessive shouting and quarrelling, she poured dirty water over his head. He bore it without distress and replied: I knew that after thunder there would come rain. When Socrates was asked by Alcibiades why he did not drive so bitter a wife out of his house, he answered: since I endure such a wife at home, I accustom myself to bear the wrongs of others outside. See Aulus Gellius, book 1, chapter 17, and Erasmus' Apophthegms.

units.la: ASPASIA mulier, consuetudinem amatoriam cum Pericle habuit,quam vnicè adamauit: nam cùm exiret domo, & cùm ingrederetur, eam osculabatur. hanc nomine & gloria clatuiffe ferunt. Quæ autem in bello cõtra Samios gesta sunt, decreto Periclis ob Milesios, rogatu Aspasiæ facta dicuntur. Vxorem Pericles alteri dedit, cùm ingrata vtrique vitæ consuetudo foret, hanc autem Aspasiam superinduxit. Plutarc. in Pericle.
units.tr: Aspasia was a woman who had a love affair with Pericles, whom alone she loved passionately; for whenever he went out and came in, he kissed her. They say she was famous for her name and glory. What was done in the war against the Samians is said to have been done at the decree of Pericles, on behalf of the Milesians, at the request of Aspasia. Pericles gave his wife to another man, since the living arrangement was unpleasant to both of them, and took Aspasia in as his wife. Plutarch, in the life of Pericles.

units.la: PERICLES Atheniensium dux, cum Sophocle Poëta tragico,missus est aduersus Lacedæmonios, qui diuerso exercitu, Lacedæmoniorum agros vastauerunt, & multas Achaiæ ciuitates Atheniensium imperio adiecerunt. his malis fracti Lacedæmonij in annos triginta pepigerunt pacem: sed tam longum ocium inimicitiæ non tulerunt. Quare intra quindecim annos,fines Atticos populantur,hostes ad prælium vocât: verùm Athenienses Periclis consilio iniuriam differunt in tempus vltionis.Deinde interiectis aliquot diebus naues confcendunt,& nihil sentientibus Lacedæmoniis, totam Spartam deprædantur, multóque plura auferunt quàm amiserant. Post hæc nauali prælio victi Lacedæmonij, fugerunt: pacem in annos quinquaginta fecerunt, quam non nisi sex annos inuiolatam obferuarunt. hæc facta sunt temporibus Artaxerxis, anno scilicet à mundo condito 3536. ante Christum natum 426.Iusti.lib.3.Plutar.in Periclis vita.bellum intestinum,quod Peloponnefiacum dicitur, tunc incepit, quod durauit annis 27.de quo Thucy. & Xeno.De Pericle mentionem quoque facit Eraf,in apoph.lib.5.& 8.
units.tr: Pericles, leader of the Athenians, was sent against the Lacedaemonians together with Sophocles, the tragic poet. With a divided army they laid waste the fields of the Lacedaemonians and added many cities of Achaea to the empire of the Athenians. Broken by these calamities, the Lacedaemonians made a peace for thirty years; but such a long leisure did not suit their enmity. So, within fifteen years, they ravaged the Attic territory and called the enemy to battle. But the Athenians, on Pericles' advice, deferred their revenge to a later time. Then, after some days had passed, they boarded ships and, while the Lacedaemonians suspected nothing, plundered all of Sparta, carrying off far more than they had lost. After this the Lacedaemonians, defeated in a naval battle, fled; they made peace for fifty years, which they kept unbroken for only six years. These things happened in the time of Artaxerxes, namely in the year of the world's creation 3536, before the birth of Christ 426. Justin, book 3; Plutarch, in the life of Pericles. The internal war called the Peloponnesian War then began, which lasted twenty-seven years; concerning it, see Thucydides and Xenophon. Erasmus also makes mention of Pericles in his Apophthegms, books 5 and 8.

units.la: ALCIBIADES Atheniensium Dux, ad bellum Siculum missus est anno mundi 3548. ante Christum natum 414.hic erat aetatis flore, formae venera tione, nec minus eloquentia insignis:sed in conciliandis amicitiarum studiis quàm in retinendis vir melior. Siculi itaque belli concitator & Dux Alcibiades, Athenis insimulatur:reuocatus à bello ad iudicium, siue conscientiam, siue indignitatem rei non ferens, tacitus in exilium Elidem proficiscitur:deinde Lacedaemona se confert.Lacedaemoniorum Regem aduersus Atheniensis impellit: sed huius virtus plus inuidiae quàm gratiae apud Lacedaemonios contraxit: quare praemonitus à Tinaea vxore Regis, quam adulterio cognouerat,sibi tendi insidias, ad Tisafernem Darij praefectum profugit. Circa haec tempora Atheniensis Lacedaemonios vicerunt ad Arginusas.Alcibiades ad Chalcedonem victoria est potitus: Byzantium per proditionem obtinuit : Lacedaemonios vicit,Pharnabazum fudit.Vide Xenoph. li.2.de reb.Graec.Tandem Atheniensium iussu vulneribus multis confossus occubuit. Iustin.lib.5.Plut.in Alci.Thuci.li.6. hic in Lacedaemoniorum gratiam à Pharnabazi militibus occisus dicitur: alij à quibusdam familiaribus,quando cum eorum sorore congressum haberet.
units.tr: Alcibiades, leader of the Athenians, was sent to the Sicilian war in the year of the world 3548, before the birth of Christ 414. He was distinguished by the bloom of youth, by the admiration for his beauty, and no less by his eloquence; but he was a better man in winning friendships than in keeping them. So Alcibiades, the instigator and leader of the Sicilian war, was accused at Athens. Recalled from the war to trial, unable to bear either the verdict of his conscience or the disgrace of the affair, he went silently into exile at Elis, and then betook himself to Lacedaemon. He stirred up the king of the Lacedaemonians against the Athenians; but his excellence brought him more envy than favour among the Lacedaemonians. Therefore, warned by Timaea, the king's wife, whom he had known in adultery, that snares were being laid for him, he fled to Tissaphernes, the governor of Darius. About this time the Athenians defeated the Lacedaemonians at Arginusae. Alcibiades obtained victory at Chalcedon; he got Byzantium by treachery; he defeated the Lacedaemonians and routed Pharnabazus. See Xenophon, book 2, On the Affairs of Greece. At last, by the order of the Athenians, he fell, pierced by many wounds. Justin, book 5; Plutarch, in the life of Alcibiades; Thucydides, book 6. He is said to have been killed by soldiers of Pharnabazus to win the favour of the Lacedaemonians; others say by some of his close associates, when he had an encounter with their sister.

units.la: TIMANDRA meretrix fuit quam deperibat Alcibiades, cui haec Timandra funus satis amplum atque magnificum pro suis facultatibus curauit faciendum. huius Timandrae filiam fuisse dicunt Laidem, quam Corynthiam appellabant: Sic matrem sequitur sua proles. Vide Plutarchum in Alcibiade. CONON DUX ATHENIEN. LYSANDER LACEDAE. DUX.
units.tr: Timandra was a courtesan whom Alcibiades loved to distraction, and for whom Timandra arranged a funeral, quite large and magnificent for her means. They say that Laïs, whom they called the Corinthian, was the daughter of this Timandra: so the offspring follows the mother. See Plutarch, in the life of Alcibiades. CONON, GENERAL OF THE ATHENIANS. LYSANDER, GENERAL OF THE LACEDAEMONIANS.

units.la: CONON Athenīensis dux in locum Alcibiadis suffectus est.hic classem maxima industria adornat, anno mundi 3 5 5 3. ante Christum natum 4 0 9. Sed navibus exercitus deerat, fortissimis quibusque in Asiæ populatione amissis: armantur tamen senes aut impuberes pueri, & numerus militum sine robore exercitus expletur. non magnam bello moram ætas facit. Omnibus captis aut occisis, cum dux Conon superfuisset solus,crudelitatem civium metuens, ad Regem Cyprium contendit. Athenienses 3o.rectores accipiunt,quos triginta Atheniensium tyrannos vocant. Lacedæmonij formandas Lysandro Athenas tradunt: repletur Græcia Atheniensium exulibus. Tandem Pharnabazus cum Conone classe comparata, Laconicas maritimas civitates incommodis affecit: pugnatur: vicit Conon. Videto Iustinum lib.5.& 6.
units.tr: Conon, the Athenian general, was appointed in place of Alcibiades. He equipped the fleet with the greatest diligence, in the year of the world 3553, before the birth of Christ 409. But the army lacked ships, since the bravest men had been lost in the ravaging of Asia; nevertheless old men and boys not yet of age were armed, and the number of soldiers was filled up without the strength of an army. Age was no great hindrance to the war. When all had been captured or killed and only the general Conon was left alive, fearing the cruelty of his fellow citizens, he hurried to the king of Cyprus. The Athenians received thirty rulers, whom they called the thirty tyrants of Athens. The Lacedaemonians handed over Athens to Lysander to be reshaped; Greece was filled with Athenian exiles. At last Pharnabazus, with a fleet equipped together with Conon, harmed the maritime cities of Laconia; there was fighting, and Conon won. See Justin, books 5 and 6.

units.la: LYSANDER Lacedæmoniorum dux factiosus, Alcibiadem in capitis adduxit periculum: totius Græciæ odium in Lacedæmonios concitauit. hoc duce Conon navali prælio victus est. paulò post tamen duce Conone victi sunt terrestri prælio Lacedæmonij, in quo occisus etiam est ipse Lysander. Tunc restituta est per Cononem terrestri prælio Atheniensibus libertas, per quem antea amissa maritimo prælio fuerat. Videto ut supra,& Plutar.in eius vita.
units.tr: Lysander, a factious general of the Lacedaemonians, brought Alcibiades into mortal danger and stirred up the hatred of all Greece against the Lacedaemonians. Under his leadership Conon was defeated in a naval battle. Shortly afterwards, however, under the leadership of Conon, the Lacedaemonians were defeated in a land battle, in which Lysander himself was also killed. Then through Conon liberty was restored to the Athenians in a land battle, by the same man through whom it had been lost in a sea battle before. See above, and Plutarch in his life.

units.la: THRASYBVLVS à triginta Atheniensium tyrannis in exilium actus, audendum aliquid pro patria ac salute communi, etiam cum periculo ratus, adiunctis sibi exulibus, reditum in patriam manu comparauit, lato prius Plebiscito de iniuriis vltro citróque obliterandis. sic Tyrannis victis popularis status restituitur eius opera, anno mundi 3558. ante Christum natum 404. Xeno. rerum Græcarum lib. 4. Iustin. lib. 5. Plutarc. in Pelopida, Cicer. in Philip.
units.tr: Thrasybulus, driven into exile by the thirty tyrants of Athens, thought that something had to be attempted for his country and the common safety, even at risk; having joined the exiles to himself, he secured a return to the homeland by force, after first passing a plebiscite that the injuries done on both sides should be wiped out. Thus, through his work, with the tyrants defeated, the popular government was restored, in the year of the world 3558, before the birth of Christ 404. Xenophon, Greek History, book 4; Justin, book 5; Plutarch, in the life of Pelopidas; Cicero, Philippics.

units.la: EPAMINONDAS Thebanorum dux fortissimus, claruit circa annum mundi 3590. ante Christum natum 372. fuit vestium tenuitate, cibi moderatione, laborum tolerantia, atq;, in fungendo imperatorio munere, synceritate singularis ac præstantissimus: huic soli ex amicis nunquam vt quicquam acciperet, potuit persuadere Pelopidas. hic dum non ducis tantùm, verumetiam fortissimi militis officio fungitur, grauiter vulneratur. fuit incertum, vírne melior an dux esset. honores ita gessit vt ornamentum non accipere, sed dare ipsi dignitati videretur: literis & Philosophia vsqueadeo clarus, vt mirum esset vnde tam insignis militiæ scientia homini inter literas nato. Saucius ac semianimis quæsiuit num cadenti sibi scutum ademisset hostis, quod sibi allatum velut laborum gloriaæque socium, osculatus est: iterum quæsiuit vtri vicissent: vt Thebanos audiuit, velut gratulabundus patriæ expirauit, apud Mantineam cum Lacedæmoniis congressus. Iustin. lib. 6. Plutar. in vita Pelopidæ, Cicer. in epist. ad Luceium. DIOGENES. THEBAN. CRATES
units.tr: EPAMINONDAS, the most valiant leader of the Thebans, flourished around the year of the world 3590, before the birth of Christ 372. He was singular and outstanding in the slenderness of his clothing, the moderation of his diet, his endurance of toil, and, in discharging his commander's office, in integrity. Pelopidas alone of his friends could never persuade him to accept anything. While performing the duty not only of a general but of the bravest soldier, he was severely wounded. It was uncertain whether he was the better soldier or the better commander. He held his offices in such a way that they seemed to receive lustre from him rather than to confer it on him. He was so distinguished in letters and philosophy that it was remarkable how a man born among books came to have such outstanding knowledge of warfare. Wounded and half dead, he asked whether the enemy had taken away the shield of him as he fell; when he was told that it had been brought to him, he kissed it as a companion in his labours and his glory. He asked again which side had won. When he heard that the Thebans had, he died, as if rejoicing for his country, after the battle with the Lacedaemonians at Mantinea. Justin, book 6; Plutarch, in the Life of Pelopidas; Cicero, in the letter to Lucceius. DIOGENES. THEBAN. CRATES

units.la: DIOGENES, Philosophus Cynicus, palliolum duplex ad frigus arcendum habuit, peram pro cellario, baculum pro corporis sustentatione. habitans in portarum vestibulis & porticibus civitatum, cibum emendicabat. cùm se contorqueret in dolio, volubilem domum se habere iocabatur, & se temporibus immutante: frigore enim os dolij vertebat in Meridiem, æstate in Septentrionem. Cum Alexandrum cæteri Philosophi adiissent, Alexander hunc adiit: ad solem apricantem offendit, rogat Alexander reíne[?] cuiuspiam egeat: cui Diogenes, parumper inquit à sole mihi secedas. Adeò hoc responso delectatum & admiratum ferunt Alexandrum, ut eo discedente, cùm amici irriderent, ac per iocum morderent, dixerit: Ego prosecto nisi Alexander essem, Diogenes esse vellem. Fertur cùm aliquando videret puerum manu aquam haurientem, ac bibentem, vasculum quod ad bibendum gestabat, ab se abiecisse, cùm natura manu tanquam ad bibendum instrumento, providisset. Vixit fermè nonagenarius. Plutar. in Alex. Dioge. Laër. hic ex ficu poma aliquando legebat: at custode dicente, huic ante paucos dies homo suspesus[?] est, ego, inquit, illam purgabo. fuerunt autem Diogenes quinque. supputationem temporum non est quòd hic inferam, cùm constet fuisse tempore Alexandri, de quo vide inferius.
units.tr: DIOGENES, the Cynic philosopher, had a double cloak to keep off the cold, a wallet for his store, and a staff to support his body. Living in the porches and colonnades of the city gates, he begged for his food. When he curled himself up in a tub, he joked that he had a house that could be rolled about, and that he changed it with the seasons: in winter he turned the mouth of the tub towards the south, and in summer towards the north. When the other philosophers went to Alexander, Alexander went to him. He found him sunning himself and asked whether he needed anything. Diogenes replied: "Only that you stand a little out of my sunlight." They say Alexander was so delighted and impressed by this answer that, as he left, when his friends laughed and mocked, he said: "Truly, if I were not Alexander, I would wish to be Diogenes." It is said that once, seeing a boy drinking water from his hands, he threw away the little cup he carried for drinking, since nature had provided the hand as an instrument for drinking. He lived almost to ninety. Plutarch, in the Life of Alexander; Diogenes Laertius. Once he gathered apples from a fig tree, and when the keeper said, "A man was hanged on this tree a few days ago," he replied, "Then I will purify it." There were five Diogeneses. It is not worth my while to set out the chronology here, since it is established that he lived in the time of Alexander, of whom see below.

units.la: CRATES Thebanus, ut Philosophiæ vacare posset, magnum auri pondus in mare proiecit, Abite, inquiens, pessum malæ cupiditates: ego vos mergam, ne ipse mergar à vobis. Neque putauit, se posse virtutes & opes simul amplecti. Cic. in Paradox.
units.tr: CRATES of Thebes, so that he might be free for philosophy, threw a great weight of gold into the sea, saying: "Begone, you evil desires, to the bottom; I will drown you, lest I be drowned by you." Nor did he think it possible to embrace virtue and wealth together. Cicero, in the Paradoxes.

units.la: PLATO Philosophus Ariftone Patricio inter Athenienfes ciue,& Periεtiona fiue Prona natus est.claruit circa annum mundi 3575. ante Christum natum 387. à corporis habitu egregio, Plato dictus est, aut ab orationis vbertate & mira amplitudine, cùm prius Ariftocles ex aui nomine diceretur: 20.annos natus, Poëticam miro complexus est ingenio: celebratas Tragœdias, atque alia carmina scripsit, suauíque vocis sono pronuntiauit,nisi quòd ad gracilitatem tenderet. Postea Philosophiam amplexatus, Poëticam reliquit: Socratis discipulus fuit, & Ariftotelis ac Xenocratis præceptor. Ter militauit,egregiúmque militem fe præstitit.
