Ter in Siciliam navigauit: tertiò rediens,venundatus,atque à Dionysio Tyranno extrema penè passus est. In Ægypto didicit quæcunq; illic magna habebantur. Philosophiam in moralem,naturalem,& rationalem distribuit. Varia de eius morte scribuntur. Vixit annos 8o. Vide Dioge.Laër.libr.3. Auguft.de ciuit.Dei lib.8.ca.4. & Plutar.in eius vita.
units.tr: PLATO, a philosopher, was born among the Athenians, the son of the patrician Ariston and of Perictione, or Prone. He flourished around the year of the world 3575, before the birth of Christ 387. He was called Plato either from the excellence of his bodily build or from the richness and remarkable breadth of his oratory, having previously been called Aristocles after his grandfather's name. At twenty years of age he took up poetry with remarkable talent; he wrote celebrated tragedies and other poems, and recited them in a sweet voice, except that it tended to thinness. Afterwards he embraced philosophy and gave up poetry. He was a pupil of Socrates, and the teacher of Aristotle and Xenocrates. He served in the army three times and proved himself an outstanding soldier. Three times he sailed to Sicily; on the third return he was sold, and at the hands of the tyrant Dionysius he suffered almost the worst. In Egypt he learned whatever was held great there. He divided philosophy into moral, natural and rational. Various accounts of his death are written. He lived eighty years. See Diogenes Laertius, book 3; Augustine, City of God, book 8, chapter 4; and Plutarch in his Life.

units.la: ARISTOTELES patre Nicomacho medico,natus est in obscuro oppido Stagira: vbi adoleuit, Athenas studiorum gratia missus est. Platonem audiuit annos 2 o.Deinde in Macedoniam euocatus à Philippo, & Alexandro filio in difciplinam tradito, maximam autoritatem in regno promeruit. huius scripta extant quàm plurima, quæ vel ad eloquentiam spestant, vel ad ciuilem, moralémque disciplinam, vel ad fecreta naturæ. Dioge.Laër.lib.5.Plutar.in eius vita. BRENNVS GAL. SEN. D. M. FVRI. CAMIL. DICTA.
units.tr: ARISTOTLE was born in the obscure town of Stagira, to his father Nicomachus, a physician. When he had grown up, he was sent to Athens for the sake of his studies. He heard Plato for twenty years. Then, summoned into Macedonia by Philip, and handed over to be taught his son Alexander, he earned the greatest authority in the kingdom. Very many of his writings survive, some relating to eloquence, some to civil and moral learning, and some to the secrets of nature. Diogenes Laertius, book 5; Plutarch in his Life. BRENNUS, the Gaul, Senone, D. M., Furius Camillus, the Dictator.

units.la: BRENNO,seu Brennus,Gallorum Sanonum Dux fortis. collecto exercitu in Italiā irrupit(nec tamen primus,nam ante 200. an.Galli Italiam inuaserant(cumque vrbem Clusium obsedisset,dimissa obsidione,totis viribus Romam contendit, quem Fabius cum exercitu excepit,nec tamen obstitit: quin potius impetus ille hostilis Romanos quasi aridas segetes succidit:testatur hanc Fabij cladem fluuius Allia,patentem Romam capit Brenno,(nam metu perculsi Rom.in Capitolium se receperant)eam depraedatur ac exurit:Capitolii obsidet:pacta pecunia obsidionem soluit: cum aurum penderetur, additur etiam a Gallo duce ponderi gladius,anno mundi 3576. ante Christum natum 386. Tit. Li. 5. Eutro.lib.1.Oro.lib.2.ca.19.Ab hoc,seu ab alio eiusde nominis, extructam ferunt Brenonam, quae postea Verona dicta est:nam post an. centum Brennus quidam,Gallorum qui Graeciam inuaserunt dux, Softhenem fudit: at contra Delphos infeliciter pugnans, pugione seipsum confodit.Iustin.lib.24.Porro Galli cum Nicomedi Bithyniae Regi opem aduersus Zibaeam tulissent, parta victoria, regionem partiti sunt:inde Gallograecia dicta.Tit.Liu.li.8. Deca.4. Iustin lib. 25. qui etiam scribit Gallos sedibus Thuscos expulisse, ac Mediolanum,Comum, Brixiam, Veronam, Bergomum,Tridentum,& Vicentiam in Italia condidisse.
units.tr: BRENNO, or Brennus, a brave leader of the Gallic Senones. Having gathered an army, he burst into Italy (though not first, for the Gauls had invaded Italy about 200 years before). When he had besieged the city of Clusium, he gave up the siege and pressed on with all his strength to Rome. Fabius met him with an army but did not stop him; rather, that hostile onslaught cut down the Romans like dry crops. The river Allia bears witness to the defeat of Fabius. Brennus took undefended Rome (for the Romans, struck with fear, had retreated to the Capitol), plundered and burned it, and besieged the Capitol. He ended the siege by a payment of money. When the gold was being weighed, the Gallic leader added his sword to the weight. This was in the year of the world 3576, before the birth of Christ 386. Livy, book 5; Eutropius, book 1; Orosius, book 2, chapter 19. From him, or from another of the same name, they say the town of Brenona was built, which was later called Verona. For about a hundred years after, a certain Brennus, leader of the Gauls who had invaded Greece, routed Softhenes; but fighting unsuccessfully against Delphi, he stabbed himself with a dagger. Justin, book 24. Moreover, when the Gauls had brought help to Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, against Zibaeus, and the victory was won, they divided the territory among themselves, and it was called Gallograecia. Livy, book 8; Decade 4; Justin, book 25, who also writes that the Gauls drove the Tuscans from their seats and founded Milan, Como, Brescia, Verona, Bergamo, Trento and Vicenza in Italy.

units.la: M.FVRIVS Camillus nobilis Roman. Dictaturam quin quies gessit,triumphum quater egit.hic ob praedā Veientanam, in exilium abiit, deos orans , ut si insonti ea sibi iniuria fieret, statim desiderium sui ingratae ciuitati facerent:quod contigit: nam paulò post Dictator creatus, Brennum vincit, aurum reportat,vt inquit Liuius:nam Drusum potius sunt qui censeant aurum extorsisse.Sueto.in Tibe.Plutar.in Camil. REX CAR. MAVSOS[?] ARTEMISIA R. HAL. VX. MA[?]
units.tr: M. FURIUS Camillus, a noble Roman, held the dictatorship five times and celebrated four triumphs. On account of the plunder of Veii he went into exile, praying to the gods that if this injury was done to him though he was innocent, they should make his ungrateful city long for him at once. This came to pass, for soon afterwards he was created dictator, defeated Brennus, and recovered the gold, as Livy says. Some, however, think that it was rather Drusus who extorted the gold. Suetonius, in Tiberius; Plutarch, in the Life of Camillus. REX CAR. MAUSOLUS, ARTEMISIA, R. HAL., WIFE, MA...

units.la: MAUSOLUS Cariæ regulus, quæ est in Asia minore, obiit anno mundi 3586. ante Christum natum 376. huic Artemisia uxor fuit, quæ illum usqueadeo amauit, ut illius demortui cineres vino mixtos biberit, alij dicunt aqua odoribus mixta: præterea sepulchrum illi extruxit, quod ab Oriente cælauit Scopas, à Septentrione Bryaxis, à meridie Timotheus, ab occasu Leochares: priusquam id operis perageret, obiit Artemisia: nec tamen recesserunt nisi absoluto iam, id gloriæ ipsorum, artisque monumentum iudicantes. Plin.li.36.ca.5.
units.tr: MAUSOLUS, a petty king of Caria, which is in Asia Minor, died in the year of the world 3586, before the birth of Christ 376. His wife was Artemisia, who loved him so intensely that she drank his dead ashes mixed with wine; others say mixed with scented water. Besides this, she built him a tomb, which Scopas carved on the east side, Bryaxis on the north, Timotheus on the south, and Leochares on the west. Artemisia died before she could finish the work, yet the artists did not leave until it was completed, judging it a monument to their glory and their art. Pliny, book 36, chapter 5.

units.la: ARTEMISIA, Mausoli uxor, molita est, conseruandæ mariti memoriæ causa, sepulchrum memoratissimū, dignatum que numerari inter septem omniū terrarum spectacula. Id monumentū Artemisia cum diis Manibus, sacris Mausoli dicaret, agona, id est certamen laudibus eius dicundis fecit: proposuit præmia pecuniæ, aliarumque rerum amplissima. Ad eas laudes decertadas venisse dicuntur pleriq; diserti viri, inter quos Isocrates ac Theopompus, quem vicisse iudicatum est. Aul.Gel. lib.10.ca.18.Boc.& Herodo.li.7.
units.tr: ARTEMISIA, the wife of Mausolus, had a most famous tomb built to preserve her husband's memory, which was deemed worthy to be counted among the seven wonders of the whole world. Artemisia dedicated this monument to the spirits of the dead and to the rites of Mausolus, and held a contest, that is, a competition in praising him. She offered prizes of money and other very rich things. Many eloquent men are said to have come to compete in these praises, among them Isocrates and Theopompus, and Theopompus was judged the winner. Aulus Gellius, book 10, chapter 18; Boccaccio; and Herodotus, book 7.

units.la: PHILIPPVS, Amintæ filius, apud Macedones imperauit anno mundi 3603. ante Christum natum 359. In Athenienses primò bellum mouit: vicit: modestissimè victoria vsus est. deinde aduersus Illyricos mouit, multáque horum milia, cecidit. hinc Thessaliâ non prædæ cupiditate, sed quòd exercitui suo Thessalorum equitum robur adiungere gestiebat, improuisus expugnat. Cùm Methonam vrbem oppugnaret, de muris sagitta iacta dextrum Regis Philippi oculum effodit: quo vulnere nec segnior ad bellum, nec iracundior aduersus hostes factus est: adeò vt pacem deprecantibus dederit, mitisque aduersus victos fuerit. Tandem totius Græciæ Imperator factus, parabat bellum in Persas, cùm à Pausania occiditur, ob priuatam iniuriam: creditum quoque est immissum ab Olympiade Alexandri matre fuisse, nec ipsum Alexandrum ignarum paternæ cædis extitisse, cùm ipse vereretur ne hæres regni institueretur frater natu minor, ex Cleopatra nouerca susceptus. Consulito Iustin.li.7. & 8.& Diod.de gestis Philippi. Imperauit Macedoniæ annos 25. vixit 47.
units.tr: PHILIP, son of Amyntas, ruled over the Macedonians in the year of the world 3603, before the birth of Christ 359. He first made war on the Athenians and conquered them, using victory with great moderation. Then he turned against the Illyrians and slew many thousands of them. From there he took Thessaly by surprise, not out of greed for plunder, but because he was eager to add the strength of the Thessalian cavalry to his own army. When he was besieging the city of Methone, an arrow shot from the walls pierced the right eye of King Philip. He was not made slower to war or more savage against his enemies by this wound; indeed, he gave peace to those who begged for it and was mild towards the conquered. At last, made commander of all Greece, he was preparing war against the Persians when he was killed by Pausanias for a private wrong. It was also believed that the deed was instigated by Olympias, the mother of Alexander, and that Alexander himself was not ignorant of his father's murder, since he feared that his younger half-brother, born of his stepmother Cleopatra, would be appointed heir to the kingdom. See Justin, books 7 and 8, and Diodorus, on the deeds of Philip. He ruled Macedonia for 25 years and lived 47.

units.la: OLYMPIAS Regis Molossorum filia, vxor fuit supradicti[?] Philippi Macedoniæ Regis, & Alexandri mater. hæc dolens se ob adulteria repudiatam, prælatámque sibi Cleopatram, parauit necem viro, vnà cum filio regni æmulo, qui fratrem ex nouerca susceptum, timebat. Videto Iustinum vt supra. DEMOSTHENES LAIS CORIN[?]
units.tr: OLYMPIAS, daughter of the king of the Molossians, was the wife of the aforesaid Philip, king of Macedonia, and the mother of Alexander. Grieved at having been put away because of his adulteries, and at Cleopatra being preferred to her, she plotted the death of her husband, together with her son, a rival for the kingdom, who feared the brother born to them by the stepmother. See Justin, as above.

units.la: DEMOSTHENES orator facundissimus, clarebat circa annum mundi 3615. ante Christum natum 347.hic patrem habuit gladiorum fabrum, satis opulentum, qui obiit, filium relinquens septennem: patrimonium a tutoribus male administratum, dum in iudicio repetit Demosthenes, dumque in causa propria disertus esse studet, etiam in alienis causis disertus esse discit. Nec mens eius primum satis poterat intelligi, cum lingua,vocéque laboraret:verùm studio ac exercitatione incredibili, actionem hanc ingratam in suauissimam commutauit. Dubium fuit ingenio plúsne an doctrina valuerit. plus olei quàm vini consumpsisse dictus est.Sæpe duos vel tres menses continuos non cessabat motum corporis fingere, vocem exercitare, chartis impallescere, abrasa etiam parte capitis, ut exeundi facultatem sibiipsi præriperet. Propositum eius in republ. maximè fuit, omnibus Philippi Macedoniæ regis conatibus obsistere. hoc etiam autore ciuitates Græciæ post mortem Philippi conspirauere. postea exulauit,sub obitum Alexandri, cuius cognita morte, rursus ciuitates Græciæ conspirauerunt, Antipatro in Lamia urbe a Leosthene fortiter obsesso. Tandem accersitus ab Antipatro per nuntium Archiam Tragœdum,qui identidem repetebat, fore ut ab eo humanissimè susciperetur, venenum è calamo hausit. Plutar.in Demost.Iuuena.Saty.10.
units.tr: DEMOSTHENES, the most eloquent orator, flourished around the year of the world 3615, before the birth of Christ 347. His father was a sword-maker, fairly wealthy, who died leaving a son of seven. His patrimony was badly managed by his guardians; Demosthenes sought to recover it in court, and in pleading his own case he was eager to speak well, and so learned to speak well in the cases of others too. At first his mind could hardly be understood, since his tongue and voice were defective; but by incredible study and practice he turned this ungrateful task into a most pleasant one. It was doubtful whether his success owed more to natural talent or to learning. He is said to have consumed more oil than wine. He often for two or three months in a row would not cease practising movements of the body, exercising his voice, and growing pale over his papers; he even shaved half his head so that he would have no excuse to go out. His chief aim in public affairs was to resist all the attempts of Philip, king of Macedonia. Under his influence the cities of Greece conspired after Philip's death. Later he went into exile, but near the death of Alexander, when that death became known, the cities of Greece again conspired, while Antipater was bravely besieged at Lamia by Leosthenes. At last, summoned by Antipater through a messenger, the tragic actor Archias, who kept repeating that he would be received very kindly by him, Demosthenes drank poison from a reed. See Plutarch on Demosthenes; Juvenal, Satire 10.

units.la: LAIS, meretrix fuit nobilis,Corynthi habitans,quam Demosthenes clanculum adiit,hac autem noctis pretium 10000. drachmarũ petente,discedens Demosthenes, Pœnitere (inquit) tanti non emo. Gel.lib.1.cap.8.Macro.in Satur.lib.2.
units.tr: LAIS, a noble courtesan living at Corinth, whom Demosthenes visited secretly. When she asked a price of 10,000 drachmas for a night, Demosthenes, leaving, said: "I do not buy repentance at such a price." Gellius, book 1, chapter 8; Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 2.

units.la: M. VALERIVS adolescens Trib.militum, adversus Gallum provocatorem solus, omnibus territis, processit: corvus repente galeae eius insedit: dictu mirabile, quoties certamen initu est, levans se alis, os, oculosque hostis, rostro & unguibus appetiit: donec territum prodigij talis visu, oculisque simul ac mete turbatum, Valerius obtruncat, anno mundi 3617. ante Christum, natum 345. Consul laudatum Valerium decem bobus, aureaq; corona donat: inde Corvinus dictus, summo populi favore annos natus 23. Consul renuntiatur. Ti. Li. li. 7. c. 1. Dec. Eut, li. 2. Oro. li. 3. ca. 6. Au. Gel. li. 9. ca. 11. Statuam Corvino Augustus erexit, in cuius capite corvi effigies erat, pugnae monimentum. Vixit Corvinus centum annos, interque primum & sextum consulatum intercesserunt anni 46. Valer. li. 8. ca. 14.
units.tr: MARCUS VALERIUS, a young tribune of the soldiers, advanced alone against a Gallic challenger, all the others being terrified. Suddenly a crow settled on his helmet. Wonderful to tell, whenever the fight began, it rose on its wings and attacked the enemy's mouth and eyes with its beak and claws, until the Gaul, terrified by the sight of such a portent and his eyes and mind confused, was cut down by Valerius, in the year of the world 3617, before Christ 345. As consul he gave the praised Valerius ten oxen and a golden crown; thereafter he was called Corvinus (Crow). Chosen consul by the highest favour of the people at the age of twenty-three. Livy, book 7, chapter 1; Decades; Eutropius, book 2; Orosius, book 3, chapter 6; Aulus Gellius, book 9, chapter 11. Augustus erected a statue to Corvinus, on whose head was the image of a crow, a memorial of the battle. Corvinus lived a hundred years, and between his first and sixth consulships there were 46 years. Valerius Maximus, book 8, chapter 14.

units.la: M. CVRIVS Dentatus Consul Rom. Samnium diruit funditus, anno mundi 3673. ante Christum natum 289. tunc bellum 49. annis cum Samnitibus gestum, finitum est: neque ullus hostis intra Italiā fuit, qui Ro. antea usque adeo fatigaverit. Huic Samnites magnum auri pondus publice missum attulerunt, qui in agresti scamno, assidens foco, ac ligneo catino coenans, vultumque risu soluens, Superuacuæ, inquit, legationis ministri, narrate Samnitibus, M. Curium malle locupletibus imperare, quam ipsum fieri locupletem: & mementote me nec acie vinci, nec pecunia corrumpi posse. Idem Curius Italia Pyrrhum regem exegit: atque ex praeda regia, qua exercitum urbemque ditauerat, nil attigit. Eutro. lib. 2. Valer. lib. 4. cap. 3. & Pli.lib.8.cap.6.de elephantis primum Romae visis.
units.tr: MARCUS CURIUS Dentatus, Roman consul, utterly destroyed Samnium in the year of the world 3673, before Christ 289. The war waged for forty-nine years with the Samnites was then ended; and no enemy within Italy had ever so wearied Rome before. The Samnites sent him a great weight of gold publicly; he received the envoys sitting by the hearth on a rustic stool, eating his dinner from a wooden dish, and, relaxing his face into a smile, said: "Servants of a superfluous embassy, tell the Samnites that Marcus Curius prefers to rule the rich rather than to be rich himself; and remember that I can be conquered neither in battle nor corrupted by money." The same Curius drove King Pyrrhus out of Italy; and from the royal spoil, with which he enriched the army and the city, he touched nothing. Eutropius, book 2; Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 3; and Pliny, book 8, chapter 6, on the elephants first seen at Rome.

units.la: TIMOLEON, nobilis Corynthius, missus est cum paucis triremibus in Siciliam anno mundi 3618. ante Christum natum 344. idque ad liberandas à Dionysij tyrannide Syracusas. hic quinquagesimo postquam appulisset die, vrbem cepit: deinde arcem obsidens, Dionysium ad deditionem compulit, & cum paucis in exilium Corynthum misit: arcem solo æquauit: Syracusanis libertate restituit: miserā Corynthi vitā priuatámque Dionysius duxit. Ex Græcia coloni noui in Siciliam habitatum missi, benignè Timoleon suscepit: deinde leges Syracusanis dedit. Cùm itaque ciuitas reuiresceret, & ciuibus vndiq; confluentibus oppleretur, cupiens vniuersam Siciliam in libertatem asserere, & ad vnum tyrannos excindere, ad cæteras vrbes exercitum duxit, & Icetem à Carthaginensibus deficientem vt arces demoliri promitteret, & apud Leptinos priuatè viueret, coégit, Leptinum tyrannum Corynthum misit: nam Siciliæ tyrános in exilio & calamitate Corynthi degere pulchrum ducebat speƈtaculum Timoleon. Consulito Plutar. in Timoleontis vita.
units.tr: TIMOLEON, a noble Corinthian, was sent with a few triremes to Sicily in the year of the world 3618, before Christ 344, to free Syracuse from the tyranny of Dionysius. Fifty days after landing he took the city; then, besieging the citadel, he forced Dionysius to surrender, and sent him into exile at Corinth with a few men; he levelled the citadel with the ground, and restored Syracuse to liberty. Dionysius lived a wretched and private life at Corinth. New colonists sent from Greece to inhabit Sicily were kindly received by Timoleon, and then he gave laws to the Syracusans. When the city was thus reviving and was filled with citizens flocking in from every side, he, wishing to assert the liberty of all Sicily and to root out tyrants altogether, led his army against the other cities. He compelled Icetes, who had revolted from the Carthaginians, to promise to demolish his citadels, and forced Leptines, who lived as a private man among the Leptinians, to be sent to Corinth as a tyrant. For Timoleon thought it a fine spectacle that the tyrants of Sicily should live in exile and misery at Corinth. See Plutarch, Life of Timoleon.

units.la: DIONYSIVS Siciliæ Tyrannus, patre eiusdem nominis genitus, militum fauore patri succedēs, initio tria captiuorum millia libertate donat, tributa triennio remittit, vt populū sibi conciliet. At verò sublatis quos metuebat, in cæteros quoque grassatus, ob crudelitatem inuisus expugnatur, fugatur: redit: Syracusas proditione recipit. Iterum, Corynthiorum auxilio obsessus, deposito imperio Corynthi exulat, puerófq; in triuiis docet. Vide Iusti.li.21.Cice.li.Tuscu.4.Vale.li.6.ca.11.meminit eiusdem idem Valer. de neglecta religione, li. 1. ca. 2. & de exquisita custodia, li.9.ca.14.
units.tr: DIONYSIUS, tyrant of Sicily, son of the man of the same name. Succeeding his father by the favour of the soldiers, at first he granted freedom to three thousand captives and remitted taxes for three years, to win the people to himself. But then, having removed those he feared, he raged against the rest as well; hated for his cruelty, he was overthrown and put to flight, returned, and recovered Syracuse by treachery. Again, besieged with the help of the Corinthians, he laid down his power and went into exile at Corinth, where he taught boys in the streets. See Justin, book 21; Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book 4; Valerius Maximus, book 6, chapter 11. The same Valerius mentions him, on neglect of religion, book 1, chapter 2, and on exquisite guarding, book 9, chapter 14.

units.la: ALEXANDER, cognominatus magnus, successit patri Philippo in regno Macedoniæ, anno mundi 3 6 2 8. ante Christum natum 334. anno ætatis 20:hic conspecta Asia, summo desiderio obtinendę accensus, ac spe eximia, patrimonium omne suum quod in Macedonia Europaque habebat, amicis diuidit, sibi Asiam sufficere præfatus. Persis dictitans longa iam satis & matura imperia contigisse, quorumque tepus esset vices excipere melius acturos. Sed neque alia quàm regis animorum, exercitus præsumptio fuit: nam obliti omnes coniugum liberorumque, & longinquæ à domo militiæ, Persicum aurum, & totius orientis opes, iam quasi suam prædā ducebāt, nec belli periculorum, sed diuitiarum meminerant. milites à populatione Asiæ prohibuit, parcedum suis rebus præfatus, nec perdenda ea quæ possessuri venerant. In exercitu habuit peditum 3 2 0 0 0. equitum 4500. naues 182. Milites elegit veteranos, vt magistros militiæ magis quàm milites electos putares. Dariū vicit. Persarum peditum 2 0 0 0 0. occidit: equitum 1 5 0 0. mater, vxor, filiæ Darij captæ sunt. Babyloniā cepit, Persepolim diripuit, Indiam ad Gangem vsque obtinuit. Imperauit annos 12. Vide Plutar. in eius vita, & Iusti. multis in locis.
units.tr: ALEXANDER, surnamed the Great, succeeded his father Philip in the kingdom of Macedonia in the year of the world 3628, before Christ 334, at the age of twenty. Having seen Asia, he was fired with the greatest desire and the highest hope of obtaining it, and divided among his friends all the patrimony he had in Macedonia and Europe, declaring that Asia was enough for himself. He kept saying to the Persians that they had enjoyed long and ripe enough empires, and that those whose time it was to yield would act better by giving way. But there was nothing behind this except the presumption of the king's spirit and army; for all of them, forgetting wives and children and a military service far from home, already counted the Persian gold and the wealth of the whole East as their own booty, and remembered not the dangers of war but the riches. He forbade the soldiers to plunder Asia, saying that their own property must be spared, and that what they had come to possess must not be destroyed. In his army he had 32,000 infantry, 4,500 cavalry, and 182 ships. He chose veterans, so that you would think them masters of the art of war rather than chosen soldiers. He conquered Darius. He killed 20,000 Persian infantry and 1,500 cavalry; the mother, wife and daughters of Darius were captured. He took Babylon, plundered Persepolis, and held India as far as the Ganges. He reigned twelve years. See Plutarch in his life, and Justin in many places.

units.la: THALESTRIS, Amazonum regina, Alexandrum adiit, concubitum ad prolem suscipiendam petiit, & obtinuit. Vide Iusti.li. 2. & 12. Quin.Cur.lib.6. Oro.li.3.ca.18. de hac vide etiam supra in Penthesilea.
units.tr: THALESTRIS, queen of the Amazons, came to Alexander, asked for intercourse to have offspring, and obtained it. See Justin, books 2 and 12; Quintus Curtius, book 6; Orosius, book 3, chapter 18. On her, see also above under Penthesilea.

units.la: XENOCRATES Platonis auditor fuit, tardus quidem ingenio, quem Plato Aristoteli conferens, alterum freno, alterum dicebat egere calcaribus: item, cui equo quem asinum iungo? fuit tamen tantæ seueritatis, atque integritatis, tantaque illius verbis fides habita, vt cùm nullius iniurati testimonium admitteretur, huic soli remiserint Athenienses iusiurandum: tantæ cōtinentiæ, vt Phryne ac Laïs, insignia scorta, nullis eum vnquam blādimentis allicere potuerint, quinetiā statuam non hominem esse dixerint: tantæ frugalitatis, vt maximas pecuniæ summas sibi ab Alexandro, itémq; ab Antipatro missas recusauerit: tantæ erga præceptorē Platonem obseruantiæ, atque amicitiæ, vt cùm Platoni Dionysius diceret, Caput tibi quisquām tollet, hic suũ oftendes, Nullus, inquit, id prius quàm istud abscindet. Vide Diog. Laer. li. 4. S. Aug. de ciui. Dei li. 8. ca. 12. & Vale. Max. li. 4. ca. 3.
units.tr: XENOCRATES was a hearer of Plato. He was indeed slow of wit, and Plato, comparing him with Aristotle, said that the one needed the bridle and the other the spurs; likewise, "What horse or what donkey shall I yoke him to?" Yet he was of such severity and integrity, and such trust was placed in his word, that when the testimony of no man under oath was admitted, the Athenians remitted the oath to him alone. He was of such self-control that Phryne and Lais, notorious courtesans, could never entice him with any allurements; indeed they said he was a statue, not a man. He was of such frugality that he refused the very large sums of money sent him by Alexander and likewise by Antipater. He had such reverence and affection for his teacher Plato that, when Dionysius said to Plato, "Who will cut off your head?" "This man will show you his," Xenocrates said, and the answer was: "No one, before he cuts off that one." See Diogenes Laertius, book 4; Augustine, City of God, book 8, chapter 12; and Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 3.

units.la: EPICURUS Neoclis filius, tempore Xenocratis Athenas adiit. Is vulgò dicitur summũ bonum in voluptate constituisse. verùm sic suam explanat mentem in epistola ad Menicaeum:Cùm voluptatem finem esse dicamus, non eam quæ in gustu & ingluuie est posita, vt quidam ignorantes, aut male accipientes arbitrantur, sed non dolere corpore, animoque tranquillum esse dicimus: virtutes iucundæ vitæ coniunctæ sunt, iucundaque vita separari à virtutibus nequit. Diog. Laert. lib. 10. agnitus est Epicurus circa annum mundi 3635. ante Christum natum 327. LAG.F.R.AEG. PTOLOMEVS BERONICE[?] PTOLOM.
units.tr: Epicurus, son of Neocles, went to Athens in the time of Xenocrates. He is commonly said to have placed the highest good in pleasure. But he explains his own view in his letter to Menoeceus: "When we say that pleasure is the end, we do not mean the pleasure that lies in taste and gluttony, as some do who through ignorance or misunderstanding suppose; we mean not being in pain in the body and being calm in the mind. Virtues are bound up with a pleasant life, and a pleasant life cannot be separated from the virtues." Diog. Laert. book 10. Epicurus is held to have lived about the year of the world 3635, 327 years before the birth of Christ. LAG.F.R.AEG. PTOLOMEVS BERONICE[?] PTOLOM.

units.la: PTOLEMAEVS Lagi filius, mortuo Alexandro Magno, ab equitibus primùm, deinde communi omnium consensu Ægypti rex declaratur, anno mundi 3640. ante Christum natum 322.huic Africæ, Arabiæque pars cum Aegypto forte venit: ex gregario milite eum Alexander virtutis causa evexerat. In Ægypto folerti industria magnas opes paravit: Ægyptios insigni moderatione in favorem sui solicitavit, & reges finitimos obsequiis devinxit: terminos imperij, urbe Cyrene ampliavit:tantúsq; factus est, ut non tam hostes timeret, quàm timendus ipse hostibus esset. Demetrium Antigoni filium bello vicit:captiuos,omnémq; prædam dimisit: se propter dignitatem,non propter prædam pugnasse dictitans. Posthæc victor ipse à victo navali prælio vincitur: filium & fratrem atque amicos Ptolemæi captos, Demetrius pari antea munere provocatus, in Ægyptum remittit: donísque inter ipsa bella contendunt:tanto honestius tunc bella gerebantur, quanto nunc amicitiæ coluntur. Vide Justin.lib.13.14.&15. Legatos ex Alexandria misit Romam conciliandæ amicitiæ gratia: imperavit annis 40. Cyprum & Phoeniciam tenuit: ab hoc omnes alij reges Ægyptiaci, vocati sunt Ptolemæi.
units.tr: Ptolemy, son of Lagus, after the death of Alexander the Great, was first declared king of Egypt by the cavalry and then, by the common consent of all, in the year of the world 3640, 322 years before the birth of Christ. To him fell, by chance, part of Africa and Arabia along with Egypt; Alexander had raised him from a common soldier because of his courage. In Egypt, by skilful industry, he amassed great wealth. By remarkable moderation he won the goodwill of the Egyptians and bound the neighbouring kings to him by favours. He enlarged the boundaries of his realm, including the city of Cyrene, and became so powerful that he feared his enemies less than he was feared by them. He defeated Demetrius, son of Antigonus, in war; he released the captives and all the booty, saying that he had fought for honour, not for plunder. Afterwards, he himself was defeated in a naval battle by the man he had defeated, and Demetrius, who had earlier been offered the same favour, sent back to Egypt the son, brother and friends of Ptolemy whom he had captured. They then vied with each other in gifts even in the midst of war; the wars were waged the more honourably then, the more friendship is cultivated now. See Justin, books 13, 14 and 15. He sent envoys from Alexandria to Rome to secure friendship. He reigned for 40 years and held Cyprus and Phoenicia. From him all the other kings of Egypt were called Ptolemies.

units.la: BERENICE uxor fuit Ptolemæi prædicti, de cuius nomine Philadelphus eius filius, quam in sinu Arabico extruxit urbem, appellavit. Fuit & altera Berenice, Philadelphi & Arsinoes filia, quæ Ptolemæo Euergeti nupsit, cuius crines in cœlum relati feruntur, autore Conone mathematico.
units.tr: Berenice was the wife of the aforesaid Ptolemy, and her son Philadelphus named after her the city he founded on the Arabian Gulf. There was also another Berenice, daughter of Philadelphus and Arsinoe, who married Ptolemy Euergetes; her hair is said to have been carried up to heaven, according to the mathematician Conon.

units.la: CASSANDER Antipatri filius, post cædem Philippi (qui & Aridæus) fratris Alexandri Magni, imperium tenuit apud Macedones, anno mundi 3647. ante Christum natum 315 hic Pictuam urbem obsedit: Olympias longæ obsidionis tædio,pacta salute,ei se tradidit:nihilominus tamen eam interfici iusit: hæc erat Alexandri magni mater. Herculem quoq; huius Alexandri filium una cum matre Barsine occidi curauit. hic Abderitis,à ranis & muribus patria pulsis, agros in Macedoniæ finibus dedit, sibi ab illis timens. huius filius Antipater matrem Thessalonicen occidit,quòd fratri Alexandro in partitione regni propensior esse videretur. Vide Iusti.lib.15. & 16. regnauit annis 19.
units.tr: Cassander, son of Antipater, after the murder of Philip (also called Arrhidaeus), brother of Alexander the Great, held power among the Macedonians, in the year of the world 3647, 315 years before the birth of Christ. He besieged the city of Pydna; Olympias, weary of the long siege, surrendered to him on terms of safety, but he nonetheless ordered her to be put to death. She was the mother of Alexander the Great. He also arranged for Hercules, the son of this Alexander, to be killed together with his mother Barsine. He gave fields within the borders of Macedonia to the people of Abdera, who had been driven from their homeland by frogs and mice, fearing them. His son Antipater killed his mother Thessalonice, because she seemed to favour his brother Alexander in the division of the kingdom. See Justin, books 15 and 16. He reigned for 19 years.

units.la: SELEVCVS Nicanor, Antiochi & Laodice filius, vir clarus,cum Alexandro Magno ad bellum Persicum profectus est:quo mortuo Castris eius præfuit. urbem condidit,quam de patris nomine Antiochiam vocavit: Regnum Syriæ occupauit anno mundi 3652. ante Christum natum 310.multa in Oriente post diuisionem,inter socios, regni Macedonici, bella gessit. principio Babyloniam capit:inde auctis ex victoria viribus, Bactrianos expugnat: transitum deinde in Indiam facit, quæ post mortem Alexandri velut iugo ceruicibus excusso, præfectos occiderat: autorque libertatis Sandrocottus fuerat, qui tunc Indiam posidebat: cum quo facta pactione Seleucus, compositisque in Oriente rebus, in bellum Antigoni descendit. Iusti.lib.13.& 16.regnauit in Syria annis 32.
units.tr: Seleucus, son of Nicanor, of Antiochus and Laodice, a man of distinction, set out with Alexander the Great for the Persian war; after Alexander's death he commanded his camp. He founded a city, which he called Antioch after his father's name, and seized the kingdom of Syria in the year of the world 3652, 310 years before the birth of Christ. After the division of the Macedonian kingdom he waged many wars in the East against his fellow-partners in it. At first he took Babylon; then, his forces strengthened by victory, he overcame the Bactrians. Next he made a crossing into India, which, after Alexander's death, had shaken off the yoke from its necks and killed its governors; the author of its liberty had been Sandrocottus, who then held India. With him Seleucus made a treaty, and, having settled affairs in the East, he descended to war against Antigonus. See Justin, books 13 and 16. He reigned in Syria for 32 years.

units.la: ANTIGONVS, inter Alexandri Primores clarus, forte tenuit Phrygiam maiorem, mortuo Alexadro: verumtamen post sex annos Asiam occupat, regnatque in ea annos 18. quorum initium fuit annus a mundo condito 3645. ante Christum natum 317. Contra Eumenem pugnauit, fugauit, obsedit: obsidionem soluit, ob auxilia ab Antipatro ad Antigonum missa. Altero bello vicit Eumenem cum Argyraspidibus: qui ignaris ducibus legatos ad Antigonum mittunt, vt sua reddi iubeat: redditurum se pollicetur, si Eumenem sibi tradant: Eumenes fugere tentat, concursu multitudinis retrahitur: retractus facultatem orandi petit: orat: cum non obtinet, milites suos devouet: hi produnt eum, quem verecundia prioris amicitiae in conspectum suum venire prohibet Antigonus, & custodibus assignari praecipit. tandem dum in belli praedam, in cuius periculum solus descenderat, socios Ptolemaeum, Cassandrum, & Lysimachum admissurum se negat Antigonus, ab eisdem bello victus occiditur. Vide Iusti.lib.13.14.& 17.
units.tr: Antigonus, distinguished among Alexander's leading men, held Greater Phrygia by chance after Alexander's death; but after six years he seized Asia and reigned there for 18 years, the beginning of which was the year 3645 from the creation of the world, 317 years before the birth of Christ. He fought against Eumenes, defeated him, and besieged him; he lifted the siege because of the auxiliaries sent to Antigonus by Antipater. In a second war he defeated Eumenes together with the Argyraspides, who, with their leaders unaware, sent envoys to Antigonus asking that their own property be returned to them; he promised to return it if they handed Eumenes over to him. Eumenes tried to flee but was pulled back by a crowd of people. Once dragged back, he asked for the chance to speak; he spoke, and when he did not prevail, he devoted his soldiers to the gods. They betrayed him. Antigonus, out of respect for their former friendship, would not allow him to come into his sight, and ordered him to be assigned to guards. At last, when Antigonus refused to admit his allies Ptolemy, Cassander and Lysimachus to the share of the booty, into whose danger he alone had descended, he was defeated by these same men and killed. See Justin, books 13, 14 and 17.

units.la: DEMETRIVS, qui & Polyorcetes, successit Antigono patri in regno Asiae, anno mundi 3663. ante Christum natum 299. hic a Ptolemaeo victus est, deinde Ptolemaeum vicit, vt in Ptolemaeo diximus. Cleonymum fudit, Thebas cepit: Macedoniae regnum sex annis tenuit, Philippo & Alexandro, Cassandri filiis, prius a se per insidias occisis. Pyrrhus victo Demetrio Macedoniae regnum occupat. Demetrius Seleuco se tandem cum Asiae regno dedidit. Vide Iusti.li.15.16.17. & Plutar.in Pyrrho & Demetrio.
units.tr: Demetrius, who was also called Poliorcetes, succeeded his father Antigonus in the kingdom of Asia, in the year of the world 3663, 299 years before the birth of Christ. He was defeated by Ptolemy, and then defeated Ptolemy, as we said under Ptolemy. He routed Cleonymus and took Thebes. He held the kingdom of Macedonia for six years, after first killing by treachery Philip and Alexander, the sons of Cassander. Pyrrhus, after defeating Demetrius, seized the kingdom of Macedonia. Demetrius at last surrendered himself and the kingdom of Asia to Seleucus. See Justin, books 15, 16 and 17, and Plutarch in the lives of Pyrrhus and Demetrius.

units.la: LYSIMACHVS illustri quidem Macedoniæ loco natus, sed virtutis ornamentis omni nobilitate clarior extitit.hic animi magnitudine, Philosophia, virium gloria, omnes per quos Oriens domitus est,vicit. A Callisthene,quamuis truncato auribus, naribus, ac labiis, præcepta Philosophiæ accipere non erubuit.hunc ferocissimo leoni obiecit Alexander:leonis linguam hic statim avulsit: chariorem inde habuit eum Alexander,quem imprudens cùm in fronte vulnerasset, diadema sibi demptum Rex alligandi vulneris causa, capiti eius imposuit, quod auspicium primum regalis maiestatis Lysimacho fuit. Regnavit itaque in Macedonia anno mundi 3676. ante Christum natum 286. Post mortem Alexandri cùm inter successores provinciæ dividerentur, Thraces,& Pontici, ferocissimæ gentes, illi quasi omnium fortissimo assignatę sunt. De cuius morte ac filiorum eius 15. vide Justin.lib.17. Lysimachiam condidit, quæ terræ motu corruit.
units.tr: Lysimachus, indeed born of a noble Macedonian family, became more famous than any nobility through the adornments of virtue. He surpassed, in greatness of spirit, in philosophy and in the glory of his strength, all those by whom the East was subdued. Although his ears, nostrils and lips had been cut off, he was not ashamed to receive the precepts of philosophy from Callisthenes. Alexander threw him to a very fierce lion; he at once tore out the lion's tongue. Alexander held him all the dearer from then on. When Alexander had wounded him in the forehead by accident, the king took the diadem from his own head to bind up the wound and placed it on Lysimachus's head; this was the first omen of royal majesty for Lysimachus. He therefore reigned in Macedonia in the year of the world 3676, 286 years before the birth of Christ. After Alexander's death, when the provinces were divided among the successors, the Thracians and the Pontic peoples, most ferocious tribes, were assigned to him as to the strongest of all. For the account of his death and that of his sons, see Justin, book 17. He founded Lysimachia, which was destroyed by an earthquake.

units.la: ANTIGONVS Gonatas , Demetrij Asiæ regis filius, apud Macedones regnat anno mundi 3686. ante Christum natum 276. Pyrrhus Antigonum fugat: Macedoniam occupat:post cuius mortem Peloponnesij Antigono traduntur: tandem multiplici bello pressus, in speciem castrorum parua manu adversus cæteros relicta, totis viribus in Gallos contendit, quos vicit. Interim Alexander Rex Epiri in ultionem mortis Pyrrhi patris sui, Macedoniam depopulatur, & capit: Demetrius Antigoni filius eam recipit, regnóque Epiri Alexandrum spoliat. Cosulito Justi. lib.25.& 26. ac Plutar.in Pau.Aemi.
units.tr: Antigonus Gonatas, son of Demetrius, king of Asia, reigns among the Macedonians in the year of the world 3686, 276 years before the birth of Christ. Pyrrhus put Antigonus to flight and seized Macedonia; after his death the Peloponnesians were handed over to Antigonus. At last, hard pressed by many wars, he left a small force behind in what was in effect a camp, to face the rest, and with all his strength advanced against the Gauls, whom he defeated. Meanwhile Alexander, king of Epirus, in revenge for the death of his father Pyrrhus, laid waste Macedonia and captured it; Demetrius, son of Antigonus, recovered it and stripped Alexander of the kingdom of Epirus. Consult Justin, books 25 and 26, and Plutarch in the life of Paulus Aemilius.

units.la: PYRRHVS, patre Epirotarum Rege in exilium acto, furtim subtractus ad Illyricos bimus defertur, vbi Rex eum adoptat, protegitque aduersus Cassandrum Macedoniæ Regem. his rebus moti Epirotæ, odio in misericordiam verso, eum in regnum reuocant. Adolescens multa bella gesit, tantóq; successu, ut Tarentinos solus aduersus Romanos tueri posse videretur. Romanos elephantis primum visis territos, vincit, vulneratus ipse: ducentos captiuos milites gratis Romam remittit. Syracusas veniens, multas ciuitates dum subigit, Rex Siciliæ sicut Epiri appellatur: filiis, Heleno, Siciliæ, Alexandro, Italiæ regnum destinat: postea bella aliquot feliciter cum Carthaginensibus gerit. tandem ex Sicilia abiens, dixisse fertur, O qualem Carthaginensibus & Romanis pro hac insula palæstram relinquimus! A Pœnis nauali prælio victus, ab Antigono, de quo supra, auxiliares milites petit: non obtinës, repente Antigonum vincit, fugat, Macedoniam capit, anno mundi 3 6 7 6. ante Christum natû 286. Iam Græciæ, Asiæque regna meditatur: nec illi maior ex imperio quam ex bello voluptas: à Spartanis tamen, maximè a mulieribus, non fortius quàm verecundius victus, recedit: Ptolemæum filium amittit. Pulsus à Spartanis Argos petit, vbi Antigonum oppugnans, atque inter confertissimos hostes fortissimè dimicans, saxo de muris iactato, occiditur. Vide Iustin. lib. 17. 18. 23. 25. Plutar. in Pyr. & Oro. lib. 4. cap. 1. 2. 3.
units.tr: Pyrrhus, whose father, king of the Epirots, had been driven into exile, was secretly carried off and taken as a two-year-old to the Illyrians, where the king adopted him and protected him against Cassander, king of Macedonia. Moved by these events, the Epirots turned their hatred into pity and recalled him to the kingdom. As a young man he waged many wars with such success that he alone seemed able to defend the Tarentines against the Romans. He defeated the Romans, who were first terrified by the sight of elephants, and was himself wounded; he sent back to Rome two hundred captured soldiers without ransom. On his way to Syracuse, while subduing many cities, he was called king of Sicily as he was of Epirus. He designated his sons, Helenus for Sicily and Alexander for Italy, to rule these kingdoms. Afterwards he fought several wars successfully against the Carthaginians. At last, leaving Sicily, he is said to have remarked: "What a wrestling-ground we leave to the Carthaginians and Romans for this island!" Defeated by the Carthaginians in a naval battle, he asked for auxiliary troops from Antigonus, of whom we spoke above; not obtaining them, he suddenly defeated Antigonus, put him to flight and seized Macedonia, in the year of the world 3676, 286 years before the birth of Christ. Now he planned the kingdoms of Greece and Asia; yet his pleasure was no greater in ruling than in war. From the Spartans, and especially from the women, he withdrew, defeated not more bravely than shamefully, and lost his son Ptolemy. Driven out by the Spartans, he made for Argos, where, attacking Antigonus and fighting most bravely among the thickest of the enemy, he was killed by a stone hurled from the walls. See Justin, books 17, 18, 23 and 25, Plutarch in the life of Pyrrhus, and Orosius, book 4, chapters 1, 2 and 3.

units.la: ALEXANDER, Pyrrhi filius, ulcisci patris mortem cupiens, Macedoniæ fines populatur: Antigonus transsitione militum destitutus, regnum cum exercitu amittit. Iusti. lib. 26.
units.tr: ALEXANDER, son of Pyrrhus, desiring to avenge his father's death, lays waste the borders of Macedonia. Antigonus, deserted by the defection of his soldiers, loses both his kingdom and his army. Justin, book 26.

units.la: M.CL.MARCELLUS Romæ Consul fuit, anno mundi 3676. ante Christum natum 286. natura vir ad bellum propensus extitit, & quod illius certamina declarant, acer ac strenuus: ad cæteras vitæ partes humanus atque modestus. Græcæ vero disciplinæ ac dicendi studiis addictus, quæ tamen per bellorum occupationes, non usque adeo illi assequi licuit. Briomatum Gessatarum Regem singulari certamine vicit. Tunc prædam & arma secum auferens, ad collegam Cornelium regreditur, per id tempus adversus Gallos infœliciter dimicantem: ut venit, Mediolanum, ac collegam obsidione liberat: posthæc decretus est à senatu soli Marcello triumphus. Syracusas cepit, opulentissimam ac florentissimam Siciliæ urbem: cuius subiectam oculis magnificentiam ac splendorem circunspiciens, diu illachrymasse dicitur: fatúmque Archimedis Geometri ægerrimè tulisse. Cum Annibale post Cannensem cladem congredi ausus est, quem & Nola expulit. Annos supra 60. natus, quintum agens consulatum, inter pugnandum lata transfigitur lancea. Eius clarissima progenies ad Marcellum usque Cæsaris nepotem propagatur, quem Octauia Cæsaris soror, ex C. Marcello suscepit. Plutar.in Augusti, Marcelli & Annibalis vita: Titus Liuius Deca. 3. lib. 3. 4. 5. 6. & 7.
units.tr: M. CLAUDIUS MARCELLUS was consul at Rome in the year of the world 3676, before the birth of Christ 286. By nature he was inclined to war and, as his campaigns show, keen and energetic; in the other parts of life he was humane and moderate. He was devoted to Greek learning and the study of oratory, though the demands of war allowed him little opportunity to pursue these. He defeated in single combat the king of the Gaesatae, Viridomarus. Then, carrying off the spoils and the arms, he returned to his colleague Cornelius, who at that time was fighting unsuccessfully against the Gauls. On arriving at Milan, he freed his colleague from siege. Afterwards the senate decreed a triumph to Marcellus alone. He took Syracuse, the richest and most flourishing city of Sicily; surveying its magnificence and splendour spread out before his eyes, he is said to have wept for a long time, and he took very badly the death of Archimedes the geometer. After the defeat at Cannae he dared to engage Hannibal, whom he also drove out of Nola. Though over sixty years old and in his fifth consulship, he was pierced by a lance thrown in the fighting. His most illustrious descendants were carried on down to Marcellus, the nephew of Caesar, whom Octavia, Caesar's sister, bore to Gaius Marcellus. Plutarch, in the lives of Augustus, Marcellus and Hannibal; Titus Livy, decades 3, books 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7.

units.la: A.POSTHUMIUS Albinus Consul Romæ fuit cum Luctatio Catulo, anno mundi 3721. ante Christum natum 241. Luctatius Hannonem vicit: anno sequente Tyberis exundatio, atque incendium Romam prope absumpserunt. Consulito Eutr. lib. 2. atque Oro. lib. 4. cap. 11. & 12. PTOLOMAEVS ELEAZARVS[?]
units.tr: A. POSTHUMIUS Albinus was consul at Rome with Lutatius Catulus, in the year of the world 3721, before the birth of Christ 241. Lutatius defeated Hanno. In the following year a flood of the Tiber and a fire nearly destroyed Rome. See Eutropius, book 2, and Orosius, book 4, chapters 11 and 12. PTOLEMY ELEAZAR[?]

units.la: PTOLOMAEVS Philadelphus, superioris Ptolomæi filius iunior, successit patri in regno Ægypti, anno mundi 3680. ante Christum natum 282. hic Stratonis discipulus doctissimus fuit:Bibliothecam insignem parauit Alexandriæ. Iudæos qui in Ægypto erant, liberos esse permisit, & vasa Eleazaro summo sacerdoti Ierosolymorum, votiua transmittens, diuinas scripturas in Græcam linguam per septuaginta interpretes verti curauit. Huius frater maior natu, qui Seleucum vita regnoque Macedoniæ priuauerat, amicitiam, pacemque ac concordiam per epistolas deprecatur, professus deponere se offensam erepti paterni regni, neque amplius à fratre quæsiturum quod honestius à paterno hoste percepisset. Eutr.lib.2. Iusti.lib.17.D.Epipha.in lib.de ponde. & mensuris.Iose. lib.Antiqui.12.cap.2. Titus Liu.Deca.5.lib.4.&5.
units.tr: PTOLEMY Philadelphus, the younger son of the earlier Ptolemy, succeeded his father in the kingdom of Egypt, in the year of the world 3680, before the birth of Christ 282. He was a most learned pupil of Strato. He assembled a notable library at Alexandria. He allowed the Jews who were in Egypt to be free, and, sending votive gifts to Eleazar, the high priest of Jerusalem, he saw to it that the divine Scriptures were translated into the Greek language by the seventy interpreters. His elder brother, who had deprived Seleucus of life and of the kingdom of Macedonia, begged for friendship, peace and concord by letters, professing that he would put aside his resentment over the seizure of their father's kingdom and would no longer ask of his brother what he had received more honourably from a hostile father. Eutropius, book 2; Justin, book 17; Epiphanius, On Weights and Measures; Josephus, Antiquities, book 12, chapter 2; Titus Livy, decade 5, books 4 and 5.

units.la: ELEAZARVS, patri Oniæ, cognominato iusto, successit in pontificatu Iudæorum, anno mundi 3691. ante Christum natum 271. Ad hunc scripsit Ptolemæus Philadelphus, hic quoque ad illum: extant utriusque epistolæ apud Iosephum lib.Antiquit.12.cap.2. Misit hic ad Ptolemæum libros Mosaicæ legis, atque ex unaquaque tribu senos viros interpretes, Hebraicè Græcéque peritissimos. Consulito D.Augustin.[?]lib.de ciuit.Dei 18.cap.42. BITHYNIE PRVSIAS REX ANNIBAL CAR.D.
units.tr: ELEAZAR, son of Onias, surnamed the Just, succeeded to the high priesthood of the Jews in the year of the world 3691, before the birth of Christ 271. Ptolemy Philadelphus wrote to him, and he in turn to Ptolemy; both letters are extant in Josephus, Antiquities, book 12, chapter 2. He sent to Ptolemy the books of the Mosaic law, and from each tribe six men, most skilled in Hebrew and Greek, as interpreters. See Augustine, The City of God, book 18, chapter 42. BITHYNIA: PRUSIAS, KING; HANNIBAL; CARTHAGE.

units.la: PRVSIAS Bithyniæ Rex fuit,ad quem, post memorabilem pugnam ad Magnesiam commissam,confugit Annibal,ab Antiocho à Romanis debellato discedens:tandem Prusias Q. Flaminio Romanorum legato Annibalem prodidit: custodiis ac militibus Regis vallatam domum vt sensit Annibal, venenum sumpsit. Postea proditor ille Prusias consilium capit occidendi filij sui,dum minoribus filiis quos ex nouerca susceperat, quos & Romæ habebat,fauet:verum à filio præuentus, ille ipsemet occiditur. Vide Plutar.in Annibal.& Iustin.li.31. & 34.
units.tr: PRUSIAS was king of Bithynia. To him Hannibal fled after the memorable battle fought at Magnesia, when he was leaving Antiochus, who had been defeated by the Romans. At last Prusias betrayed Hannibal to Quintus Flamininus, the Roman legate. When Hannibal perceived that his house was surrounded by the king's guards and soldiers, he took poison. Afterwards that same treacherous Prusias formed a plan to kill his own son, while he favoured the younger sons whom he had by a stepmother and who were living at Rome; but he was forestalled by his son, and was himself killed. See Plutarch, in the life of Hannibal, and Justin, books 31 and 34.

units.la: ANNIBAL Amilcaris filius, Carthaginensium dux præclarissimus, nisi auariciam & sæuiciam in eo culpes ,rem Romanam mirè afflixit. Primùm annos natus viginti ,Saguntum Romanis amicam,debellauit: congregatis 150000. peditum, & 20000.equitum, exercitum deinde per alpes in Italiam traduxit: Titum Sempronium, item Flaminium fudit, cæsis 15000. Romanorū.Sed tamen eius vires à Fabio attritæ sunt: quibus collectis ac resumptis, maxima clade Cannensi Romanos affecit:nam equitum 2700.peditum 40000. occidit:tres anulorum modios Carthaginem misit:cumque vrbem capere posset,in Campaniam reuertitur. Tandem victus à Marcello, iterumque à P.Scipione,item ab Eumene Antiocho etiam superato,qui illi opem tulerat,ad Prusiam fugit: vbi fidem Prusiæ suspectam habens,hausto veneno,volens obit,anno mundi 3774.ante Christum natum 188. Vide Eutr.li.3.Flo.li.2.Plutar. in Annibal. In Italiam adduxit elephantos 37. Polyb.lib.2. &3. Tit.Li.li.1.Deca.3. Auguft.lib.de ciuit.Dei.3.cap.20.
units.tr: HANNIBAL, son of Hamilcar, the most distinguished general of the Carthaginians, if you do not blame him for greed and cruelty, dealt the Roman state a terrible blow. At the age of twenty he subdued Saguntum, a city friendly to the Romans. Having gathered 150,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry, he then led his army across the Alps into Italy. He routed Titus Sempronius and likewise Flaminius, with 15,000 Romans slain. But his strength was worn down by Fabius; yet, having gathered and renewed his forces, he dealt the Romans a most severe blow at Cannae, for he killed 2,700 cavalry and 40,000 infantry. He sent three bushels of rings to Carthage. And although he could have taken the city, he returned to Campania. At last he was defeated by Marcellus and again by Publius Scipio, and also by Eumenes; Antiochus too, who had brought him help, was overcome. He fled to Prusias, and, suspecting Prusias's faith, he drank poison and died of his own will, in the year of the world 3774, before the birth of Christ 188. See Eutropius, book 3; Florus, book 2; Plutarch, in the life of Hannibal. He brought thirty-seven elephants into Italy. Polybius, books 2 and 3; Titus Livy, book 1, decade 3; Augustine, The City of God, book 3, chapter 20.

units.la: P. CORNELIVS SCIPIO, dictus Africanus maior, ab Africa devicta, annos natus 2 4. vir Romanorum omnium & sua ætate, & posteriori tempore ferè primus, quasi novâ integràmque provinciâ ultor patris, & patrui invadit, Carthaginê Hispaniæ capit, in qua omne aurum & argentum, & belli apparatum Afri habebant: nobilissimos obsides, Magonem etiam Annibalis fratrem, ibi capit, quem Romã cum aliis mittit. Non contentus Pœnos expulisse, stipendiariâ Romanis provinciam facit: omnem citra ultráq; Iberum subiecit imperio: primúsque Romanorum ducum victor ad Gades pervenit: plus etiam provinciam retinere quàm facere studuit. Hispanorū obsides patrẽtibus reddidit: quare omnes ferè Hispaniæ ad eum trâsierunt. Asdrubalem, Annibalis fratrẽ victum fugavit, prædámque maximam cepit. Senex tandẽ invidiæ cedens, Linternum exulat, ubi sepultus creditur. Vide Eutr. li. 3. & Flor. li. 2. exulavit anno à mundo condito 3777. ante Christum natum 185.
units.tr: P. CORNELIUS SCIPIO, called Africanus the Elder, having conquered Africa, at the age of twenty-four, the man of all the Romans, both in his own age and nearly first in later times, like a new and untouched province, as an avenger of his father and uncle, attacked Spain and took New Carthage, in which the Africans had all their gold and silver and their war supplies. There he captured the most noble hostages, including Mago, the brother of Hannibal, whom he sent to Rome with the others. Not content to have driven out the Carthaginians, he made the province tributary to the Romans; he brought all of it on this side of and beyond the Ebro under his rule. He was the first of the Roman commanders to reach Gades as victor; he strove to keep the province more than to make conquests. He returned the Spanish hostages to their parents, and for this almost all of Spain went over to him. He routed and put to flight Hasdrubal, the brother of Hannibal, and took very great booty. At last, yielding to envy in his old age, he went into exile at Liternum, where he is believed to have been buried. See Eutropius, book 3, and Florus, book 2. He went into exile in the year from the founding of the world 3777, before the birth of Christ 185.

units.la: TERENTIA Æmylia, Scipionis Africani uxor, præter uxorum morem, cùm videret senem maritũ ancillulam deperire, ne eius dignitas imminueretur, reticuit, constantíque animo pertulit: quinetiam eo mortuo, ad tollendam suspicionem, ancillam manumisit, libertóque suo in matrimonium collocauit. Vide Supplemen.chro. [illegible, ~6 letters] AS SAC. MATATHI CHABEVS IVDAS MA
units.tr: TERENTIA Aemilia, wife of Scipio Africanus, contrary to the custom of wives, when she saw her elderly husband falling in love with a maidservant, kept silent, so that his dignity would not be diminished, and bore it with a steady mind. Moreover, after his death, to remove suspicion, she freed the maidservant and married her to her own freedman. See the Supplementum chronicorum [illegible, about six letters] ... AS, SAC. MATATHIAS, CHABEUS, JUDAS MA[CHABEUS]

units.la: MATATHIAS sacerdos,vir pietate clarus,Iudæũ quemdam idolis palàm sacrificantem iuxta mandatum impij Antiochi,zelo Domini accensus,occidit ad altare ipsum,quod & diruit:ac mox etiã interfecit Antiochi Regis legatum præcipientem idolis immolare : hũc Regis Antiochi iudicẽ, Apollonium vocat Iosephus,li.Anti. 12.ca.7.Hic Matathias autor fuit pugnã di Iudæis,etiã die sabbati,cùm iam mille occubuissent,religiosè nimis obseruantes hunc diem. Multi itaque Iudæorum adiunguntur Matathiæ,& illum sibi iudicem creant, qui & Sabbatis eos docet pugnare:quod si non feceritis, inquit, vobismetipsis eritis hostes, in illo die contra vos venientibus inimicis.Sic arma corripiês,patrias leges aduersus Antiochi Duces vindicauit,præfuitque populo annum vnum,anno scilicet mundi 3795. ante Christum natum 167.vide li.1.Macha.ca.2.Ioseph.li.12.ca.7.
units.tr: MATTATHIAS, a priest, a man renowned for piety, kindled with zeal for the Lord, killed a certain Jew who was openly sacrificing to idols in obedience to the command of the impious Antiochus, and he killed him at the very altar, which he also pulled down. Soon afterwards he also slew the legate of King Antiochus who was ordering him to sacrifice to idols. Josephus calls this man Apollonius, the judge of King Antiochus; Josephus, Antiquities, book 12, chapter 7. This Mattathias was the author of the Jews' fighting even on the sabbath, when already a thousand had perished, because they observed that day too scrupulously. Many of the Jews therefore joined Mattathias and made him their judge, and he taught them to fight even on the sabbaths, saying: "If you do not do so, you will be your own enemies, since your enemies will come against you on that day." Thus, taking up arms, he defended the ancestral laws against the commanders of Antiochus, and he led the people for one year, in the year of the world 3795, before the birth of Christ 167. See 1 Maccabees, chapter 2; Josephus, book 12, chapter 7.

units.la: IVDAS Machabeus,Matathiæ filius,rebus & populo præest in locum patris suffectus,qui iuuantibus prono animo quatuor suis fratribus,cæterisque piis,qui patri suo adhæserãt hostes profligat:Apollonium Ducẽ,alterum à priore,qui primus contra Machabæũ in aciem descendit,cum suis copiis partim cæsis partim fugatis,interficit: Seron quoque Syriæ inferioris ducem superat: deinde Gorgiam à Lisia exercitui præfectum, ipsum quoque postea Lisiam,ac Nicanorem fundit,fugat,superat,mira celeritate,ac victoria: post hæc templum purgat ac instaurat,altare Domino dedicat:pro mortuis sacrificiũ offert. Antiochus cum eo fœdus init: fidem frangit,templum spoliat: à populo summus sacerdos creatur Iudas,anno mundi 3805. ante Christum natum 157.Prefuit annis 12.fœdúsque cum Romanis init: obit in prælio. z. D. IVD.[?] IONATHAS s. D. IVD.[?] SYMON
units.tr: JUDAS Maccabeus, son of Mattathias, succeeded his father and governed the affairs and the people. Helped with ready hearts by his four brothers and the other pious men who had clung to their father, he routed the enemies: he killed Apollonius, the general, another than the earlier one, who first came into battle against the Maccabeus with his forces, some slain and some put to flight; he also defeated Seron, the commander of Lower Syria; then he routed, defeated and overcame Gorgias, the officer set over the army by Lysias, and afterwards Lysias himself and Nicanor, with remarkable speed and victory. After these things he purified and restored the temple and dedicated an altar to the Lord; he offered a sacrifice for the dead. Antiochus made a covenant with him, then broke faith and plundered the temple. Judas was created high priest by the people, in the year of the world 3805, before the birth of Christ 157. He governed for twelve years and made a covenant with the Romans; he died in battle. See 1 Maccabees. ... JONATHAN ... SIMON

units.la: IONATHAS fratre Iuda Machabæo interfecto Dux populi constituitur anno mundi 3808.ante Christum natum 154. Hic statim Bacchidem,cum quo pugnās occubuerat Iudas,ad Iordanē vicit. Tertio posthæc anno, collecto ingenti exercitu iterum in Iudæam venit Bacchides, Ionathã cum Simone fratre obsedit,tandémque commissa cum Bacchide pugna,fusus est Bacchides ipse:qui rebus accisis,coactúsque pacē amplecti, iurauit se nunquam in Ionathã quicquam moliturũ. Alexander Epiphanes, Antiochi filius,audiēs Ionathæ famā, amicitiæ fœdera cum eo sanciuit. Demetrij præfectum Apollonium Ionathas bello fundit ac fugat,multásque vrbes capit:octo hostium millia occidit:templum Dagon , quod erat in Azoto,vnà cum vrbe incēdit.Posthæc aduersus alienigenas qui Iudæam vastabant,mouit , atque eos tota Iudæa expulit:& cum Romanis ac Spartiatis amicitiæ fœdera renouauit.Tandem Tryphon simulata amicitia eum circumuentum cum suis interfecit.Vide li.1. Macha.ca.9.10.11.& 12.rexit an.15.
units.tr: JONATHAN, after his brother Judas Maccabeus was killed, was appointed leader of the people in the year of the world 3808, before the birth of Christ 154. He at once defeated Bacchides, with whom Judas had fallen while fighting, at the Jordan. Three years later, Bacchides again came into Judaea with a huge army, and besieged Jonathan with his brother Simon. At last, in the battle joined with Bacchides, Bacchides himself was put to flight; he, his forces cut down and compelled to embrace peace, swore that he would never attempt anything against Jonathan. Alexander Epiphanes, son of Antiochus, hearing of Jonathan's fame, ratified a treaty of friendship with him. Jonathan defeated and put to flight Apollonius, the prefect of Demetrius, in war, and captured many cities; he killed eight thousand enemies; he set fire to the temple of Dagon, which was in Azotus, together with the city. Afterwards he moved against the foreigners who were laying waste Judaea, and drove them out of all Judaea; and he renewed the treaties of friendship with the Romans and the Spartans. At last Tryphon, by feigned friendship, surrounded him and killed him with his men. See 1 Maccabees, chapters 9, 10, 11 and 12. He ruled for fifteen years.

units.la: SIMON occiso fratre Ionatha, Dux populi creatur anno mundi 3823. ante Christum natum 139. Hic Gazam vrbem, quā cepit,ab idolis purgauit : fœdus cum Romanis ac Spartiatis redintegrauit. Cendebæum Antiochi præfectū fudit, fugauítque. At verò,vt sunt hominū fata in temerè fortunæ variantis arbitrio,tandē cum filiis duobus atq; aliquot seruis, in conuiuio,atque à Ptolemæo genero suo dominium affectante,qui ei cōuiuium apparárat,interficitur. vide li.1.Macha.ca.13.14.15.16.& Iose.li.Anti.13.ca.9.10.11.12.rexit an.8. D. IVD. HIRCANVS ARISTOBO LVS D. IVD.
units.tr: SIMON, after his brother Jonathan was killed, is made leader of the people in the year of the world 3823, before the birth of Christ 139. He cleansed the city of Gaza, which he had taken, from idols, and renewed the covenant with the Romans and the Spartans. He routed and put to flight Cendebaeus, the commander of Antiochus. But, since human fates are subject to the whim of a fickle fortune, he was at last killed at a banquet, along with his two sons and several servants, by Ptolemy his son-in-law, who was aspiring to rule and had prepared the banquet for him. See 1 Macc. chs. 13, 14, 15, 16, and Josephus, Antiquities bk. 13, chs. 9, 10, 11, 12. He reigned 8 years. D. IVD. HIRCANUS ARISTOBULUS D. IVD.

units.la: HYRCANVS, qui & Ioannes, supradicti Simonis filius, patri succeßit, Dúxque populi fuit anno mundi 3831. ante Christum natum 131. Hic summa cum laude populo praefuit, vitae suae insidiātes, à Ptolemaeo missos, occidit. Antiochus Soter, qui & Pius, Hircanum Ierosolymis obsedit, accepta tandem pecunia obsidionem soluit. Hyrcanus Dauidis sepulchrum aperuit, ingentes thesauros reperit, quibus Iudaeorum caepit peregrinos alere. Cum Rom. foedus renouauit. Cognita Antiochi morte, Samariam, quae rursum à Iudaeis defecerat, obsedit, ac post annum captam, solo aequauit. magnas opes cumulauit (nam à Regibus Syriae, qui inter se certabat, liber factus, nullum iis vectigal ab Antiochi morte pendebat) quinetiam ciuitates Idumaeae domuit. Vide 1. lib. Macha. ca. 16. Iose. lib. Antiqui. 13. à ca. 13. ad 18. Fuit Hyrcanus Dux, summus sacerdos, ac Propheta: rexit an. 25. Iose. ait 31.
units.tr: HYRCANUS, also called John, son of the aforementioned Simon, succeeded his father and was leader of the people in the year of the world 3831, before the birth of Christ 131. He governed the people with great praise, and killed those sent by Ptolemy to lie in wait for his life. Antiochus Soter, also called Pius, besieged Hyrcanus in Jerusalem, and at last, having accepted money, lifted the siege. Hyrcanus opened the tomb of David, found immense treasures, and with them began to feed foreigners who came to Judea. He renewed the covenant with the Romans. When the death of Antiochus became known, he besieged Samaria, which had again revolted from the Jews, and after a year, having captured it, razed it to the ground. He amassed great wealth, for, freed from the kings of Syria, who were fighting among themselves, he paid no tribute to anyone after the death of Antiochus; moreover he subdued the cities of Idumea. See 1 Macc. ch. 16; Josephus, Antiquities bk. 13, chs. 13 to 18. Hyrcanus was leader, high priest and prophet. He reigned 25 years; Josephus says 31.

units.la: ARISTOBVLVS Hyrcani filius, mortuo patre principatum & sacerdotium suscepit, anno mundi 3857. ante Christum natum 105. Hic Magistratum ad regiam dignitatem transtulit, primúsque, post captiuitate Babylonicam, diadema sibi imposuit. Crudelis, fratres in vinculis tenuit & matrem quâ penuria cõsumpsit: fratrem Antigonû nefariè occidi curauit, ad turrim Stratonis clam collocatis sicariis. Ituraeos subegit, plurimámq; eorum prouinciam Iudeis adiecit. Corruptis postquam annum imperat, visceribus, copiámque sanguinis euomens, decidit in eundem locum qui sanguine fratris aspersus erat, ibíque fraternos manes, miserè moriens, placat. Iose. li. Anti. 13. ca. 18.
units.tr: ARISTOBULUS, son of Hyrcanus, on his father's death assumed the leadership and the high priesthood, in the year of the world 3857, before the birth of Christ 105. He transferred the magistracy to royal dignity, and was the first, after the Babylonian captivity, to place a diadem upon his own head. He was cruel: he kept his brothers in chains and starved his mother to death; he had his brother Antigonus secretly murdered, by assassins stationed at the tower of Strato. He subdued the Ituraeans and added a large part of their territory to the Jews. After he had ruled for a year, his bowels became corrupted, and, vomiting a quantity of blood, he fell in the same place that had been sprinkled with his brother's blood, and there, dying miserably, appeased the spirit of his brother. Josephus, Antiquities bk. 13, ch. 18.

units.la: TIB. GRACCHVS Tribunus plebis, certauit de lege agraria pro egenis aduersus diuites,quo tēpore Africanus Scipio apud Numantiam pugnabat. Nam Romani quantum vicini agri hostibus adimebant,partim venundare,partim in publicum redigere, ac egenis ciuibus pro modica pensione vtendum tradere cōsueuerant:sed diuitibus pensiones augentibus, pauperēsque excludentibus , lata est lex,quæ supra quingenta agri iugera ciuem Romanū possidere vetabat. Hæc lex paucos annos aduersus locupletes auxilio fuit. Nam primò conductis personis fraus legi fiebat : deinde apertè iam per seipsos occupare agros diuites cœperant. Pauperum itaque partes fouens Gracchus,diuitum inuidia contraxit:in ipsoque tumultu dum fugere tentat , toga retentus , pede subsellij caput percutitur à P.Saturnino,vno ex principibus,&,cum aliis triginta, fustibus & lapidibus mactatur:quorum corpora fuerunt proiecta in Tyberim,anno mundi 3831.ante Christum natum 131. Plut.in vita Grac.Appi.li.1.Eutr.li.4.
units.tr: TIBERIUS GRACCHUS, tribune of the plebs, contended over the agrarian law on behalf of the poor against the rich, at the time when Scipio Africanus was fighting at Numantia. For the Romans had customarily sold off, partly, the land they took from the enemies, and partly reduced it to public ownership and handed it over to needy citizens to be used for a modest rent. But as the rich increased their rents and shut out the poor, a law was passed forbidding any citizen to possess more than five hundred iugera of land. This law gave some help to the poor for a few years against the wealthy. For first, the law was evaded by means of hired persons; then, openly, the rich had begun to occupy the fields themselves. Gracchus, therefore, favouring the cause of the poor, incurred the hatred of the rich; and in the very tumult, while trying to flee, he was caught by his toga, and was struck on the head with a footstool by P. Saturninus, one of the leaders, and was beaten to death with clubs and stones together with about thirty others; their bodies were thrown into the Tiber, in the year of the world 3831, before the birth of Christ 131. Plutarch, Life of Gracchus; Appian, bk. 1; Eutropius, bk. 4.

units.la: CORNELIA Africani filia,Tiberij & Caij Gracchorum mater, marito vidua hos sic educauit,vt cum magnitudine indolis cæteros omnes anteirent, doctrina tamen quàm natura prævaluisse viderentur.hæc relicta cum duodecim filiis,Ptolemaei regis nuptias respuit : cum ille regni & diadematis communicationem offerret. Deinde decem ex filiis obierunt, supradictis duobus relictis : filiam Africano minori collocauit. Plutar.in Tibe.& Ca.Gracchis.
units.tr: CORNELIA, daughter of Africanus, mother of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, widowed by her husband, brought up these sons in such a way that they outstripped all others in the greatness of their talent, though their learning seemed to have prevailed over their nature. She, left with twelve children, refused the marriage of King Ptolemy, when he offered her a share of his kingdom and diadem. Then ten of her sons died, leaving the two aforementioned; she married her daughter to the younger Africanus. Plutarch, Life of Tiberius and of Gaius Gracchus.

units.la: IVGVRTHA, Micipsæ Numidarum regis adoptiuus hæres, Hiempsalis capite potitus, in Adherbalem se conuertit (hi erant fratres regni cohæredes.) Adherbal Romā profugit (nam in Romanorum fide ac clientela regnum Numidicū erat) missa itaque pecunia primò in sententiā suam senatum trahit Iugurtha: deinde missis à senatu, qui regnum diuiderent, inchoatum nefas perficit, pacem emit. Accersitus posthæc Romā, publica interueniente fide, vbi venit, auro omnibus corruptis aut attentatis, omnia dissentionibus permiscet: discedénsque dicit, O Urbem venalem, & citò perituram, si emptorem inveniat. Placet deinde Senatui bello hunc parricidam persequi, Sp. Albinus in eum mittitur, cuius exercitū auro etiam corrumpit Iugurtha. Assurgit Metellus, qui eum duobus præliis vincit: cumque iam bello finé impositurus effet, successit C. Marius, qui Bocchum Mauritaniæ regem Iugurthæ socerum superat: Bocchus precium fœderis atque amicitiæ, regem Iugurtham facit: quem catenis opertum in triumpho populus Romanus aspexit. Eutr. li.4. Flo.li.3. Sall. Plutar. in Mar. & Syl. Romæ in scrobe demissus post sextum diem fame ac frigore atteritur, anno mundi 3857. ante Christum natum 105.
units.tr: JUGURTHA, adopted heir of Micipsa, king of the Numidians, seized the throne after Hiempsal and turned against Adherbal (these were the brothers who were co-heirs of the kingdom). Adherbal fled to Rome (for the Numidian kingdom was under the protection and clientship of the Romans). Jugurtha, therefore, having sent money, first drew the Senate to his own opinion; then, when the Senate sent men to divide the kingdom, he carried through the crime he had begun and bought peace. Afterwards summoned to Rome under a public guarantee of safe conduct, when he arrived, having corrupted or tried to corrupt everyone with gold, he threw everything into confusion through dissensions; and as he left he said, "O city ready for sale, and soon to perish, if it finds a buyer!" The Senate then decided to pursue this parricide in war; Spurius Albinus was sent against him, but Jugurtha bribed his army with gold too. Metellus took up the command, and defeated him in two battles; and when he was about to bring the war to an end, Gaius Marius succeeded him, and defeated Bocchus, king of Mauretania and Jugurtha's father-in-law. Bocchus, as the price of the treaty and friendship, handed over King Jugurtha; the Roman people saw him in a triumph, covered with chains. Eutropius, bk. 4; Florus, bk. 3; Sallust; Plutarch, Life of Marius and Sulla. Lowered into a pit at Rome, he was worn down by hunger and cold after six days, in the year of the world 3857, before the birth of Christ 105.

units.la: C. MARIVS cum Q. Catulo aduersus Cymbros missus, victoriam reportat, anno mundi 3863. ante Christum natum 99. Hic affectauit ut ad bellum Mithridaticū mitteretur: quare Sylla commotus, Marium urbe fugat: inde perniciosissimum bellum ciuile exortum. Eutr. li.5. Appi.li.1.ca.8. Flo.li.3.ca.3. fuit septies Consul: victus à Sylla, in palude latuit: in vincula inde coiectus, immissum percussorem, autoritate vultus terruit, & scapha in Africam traiecit: fertur voluntaria morte obiisse. IANNEVS D. IVDEOR. ALEXANDRA
units.tr: GAIUS MARIUS, sent with Quintus Catulus against the Cimbri, won a victory, in the year of the world 3863, before the birth of Christ 99. He aspired to be sent to the Mithridatic war; for this reason Sulla, roused to anger, drove Marius from the city, and from this there arose a most destructive civil war. Eutropius, bk. 5; Appian, bk. 1, ch. 8; Florus, bk. 3, ch. 3. He was consul seven times. Defeated by Sulla, he hid in a marsh; then he was cast into chains, and when an assassin was sent against him, he terrified him by the authority of his countenance, and crossed to Africa by boat. He is said to have died by his own will.

units.la: IAMNEVS, qui & Alexander, Aristobuli frater, Rex Iudæis constituitur à Salome, siue Alexãdra, eiusdem Aristobuli uxore relicta, quæ mariti fratres, inter quos erat is Iamneus, statim è vinculis liberat anno mundi 3858. ante Christum natum 104. Iamneus fratē regni æmulum occidit. cōtra Ptolemaidem & Gazam, quæ à Iudæis rursus defecerat, mouit: cladēque maximā à Ptolemæo Lathyro accepit ad Iordanē. A cleopatra Ægypti Regina, Ptolemæi huius matre, opem implorat, quæ ne filius subacta Iudæa in Ægyptū irrumperet, valida eum manu in Cyprum abire cogit. Maxima populi multitudo ab Alexādro defecit, sed adiutos etiam à Demetrio Rege Syriæ, vicit: quorum potentissimos octingentos, dum cum cōcubinis cœnat, crucifigi iubet, liberosque & uxores eorum corā ipsis adhuc viuentibus, mactari. post hæc Iamneus hic, siue Alexander, crapulæ indulgens, in morbū incidit, quartanáque febri postquàm tribus annis laborauit, obiit anno regni 27. Vide Iose.li.13.ca.19.20.& 21.
units.tr: JANNAEUS, also called Alexander, brother of Aristobulus, was set up as king of the Jews by Salome, or Alexandra, the widow of that same Aristobulus, who immediately freed Jannaeus, the brothers of her husband, among whom he was, from their chains, in the year of the world 3858, before the birth of Christ 104. Jannaeus killed his brother, a rival to the kingdom. He moved against Ptolemais and Gaza, which had again revolted from the Jews, and received a very great defeat from Ptolemy Lathyrus at the Jordan. He implored help from Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt, mother of this Ptolemy, who, lest her son, after subduing Judea, should break into Egypt, forced him with a strong army to go off to Cyprus. A very great multitude of the people revolted from Alexander, but he, aided also by Demetrius, king of Syria, defeated them; he ordered eight hundred of their most powerful men to be crucified, while he was dining with his concubines, and their children and wives to be slaughtered before their own eyes while they were still alive. After this Jannaeus, or Alexander, indulging in drunkenness, fell ill, and after suffering for three years from a quartan fever, died in the twenty-seventh year of his reign. See Josephus, bk. 13, chs. 19, 20 and 21.

units.la: ALEXANDRA, quæ & Salome, Aristobuli prædicti ac Iamnei postea uxor, ut certum cum filiis regnum tutaretur, Regis morte, ex eiusdem Regis Iamnei mandatis, militibus celat, usquequo castellum cepisset: præterea Pharisæorū beneuolentiam captat, in quos omnem potestate transfert, nomen tātum regium ipsa retinet annos nouem, incipiētes anno mundi 3885. ante Christum natum 77. Iofe. li. Antiqui. 13. ca. 22. Hæc summum sacerdotem Hyrcanum creauit. REX . PONT . MITHRIDATE HYPSICRATEA . . . MITHR[?]
units.tr: ALEXANDRA, also called Salome, later the wife of the aforementioned Aristobulus and of Jannaeus, in order to keep the kingdom safe for her sons, on the king's death, by the orders of the same king Jannaeus, concealed the death from the soldiers until she had taken the stronghold; besides, she courted the goodwill of the Pharisees, to whom she handed over all power, herself keeping only the royal title for nine years, beginning in the year of the world 3885, before the birth of Christ 77. Josephus, Antiquities bk. 13, ch. 22. She appointed Hyrcanus high priest. KING OF PONTUS, MITHRIDATES; HYPSICRATEA ... MITHRIDATES

units.la: MITHRIDATES Rex Ponti, diffidentibus Romanis primùm sociali bello,deinde ciuili, Cappadociam occupat,ex eáque Ariobarzane Regè, amicum populi Romani fugat:mox etiam Bithyniam inuadit, & Paphlagoniá, quorum Reges expellit,anno mundi 3876.ante Christũ natum 86. Inde ad Ephesum contendit,& per omnê Asiam literas mittit,vt vbicunque inuenirentur ciues Romani,vnico die trucidarentur : quod & factum est : nam vno die octuaginta Romanorũ ciuium millia occisa sunt.Causam belli praetenderat, attrectari terminos suos à Nicomede Bithyniæ Rege, populi Romani amico. Mittit ad Achaiam Archelaum ducê suum cum hominum 120.millibus, tam equitũ quàm peditum , per quem Græcia occupata est.
