In summa fuit hoc bellum Mithridaticũ omniũ longè maximum: nam cùm anni quatuor Pyrrho, 17. anni Annibali suffecerint, hic Mithridates per 40.annos restitit,donec tribus ingentibus bellis subactus,felicitate Syllæ, virtute Luculli , magnitudine Pompeij eneruaretur. Cõsulito Eutr.li.5.& Flor.li.3.item Appi. li.Mithridatico.
units.tr: MITHRIDATES, king of Pontus, when the Romans first distrusted him in the Social War and then in the civil war, seized Cappadocia and drove out Ariobarzanes, the king who was a friend of the Roman people; soon he also invaded Bithynia and Paphlagonia, expelling their kings, in the year of the world 3876, before the birth of Christ 86. From there he hastened to Ephesus, and sent letters throughout all of Asia that wherever Roman citizens might be found they should be slaughtered on one day; and this was done, for on a single day eighty thousand Roman citizens were killed. As the pretext for war he had alleged that his boundaries were being encroached upon by Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, a friend of the Roman people. He sent his general Archelaus into Achaea with 120,000 men, both horse and foot, by whom Greece was occupied. In sum, this Mithridatic war was by far the greatest of all: for while four years sufficed for Pyrrhus and seventeen years for Hannibal, this Mithridates held out for forty years, until, subdued by three huge wars, he was weakened by the good fortune of Sulla, the valour of Lucullus and the greatness of Pompey. See Eutropius, bk. 5, and Florus, bk. 3; also Appian, Mithridatic War.

units.la: HYPSICRATEA, pellex,siue,vt alij valunt,Mithridatis vxor,viri Persici habitum gerés,aderat Mithridati etiã tum cùm à Pompeio victus , à suis etiam,praeterquã à duobus,sociis relictus est summo in discrimine. Vide Plutar.in Pompeij vita. SYLLA COS C MARIVS COS.
units.tr: HYPSICRATEA, the concubine, or, as others have it, the wife of Mithridates, wearing the dress of a Persian man, was with Mithridates even at the time when he was defeated by Pompey and deserted by his own men, all but two companions, in the greatest danger. See Plutarch in the life of Pompey. SYLLA CONSUL, C. MARIUS CONSUL.

units.la: SYLLA Romanus Patricius, Consul, mittitur à Senatu adversus Mithridatē. Archelaum Mithridatis ducē obsidet, vincit, ita ut ex 120.hominū millibus vix decem superessent millia Archelao. Athenas capit Sylla anno mundi 3877. ante Christum natum 85. Mithridates 70.hominum millia lectissima Archelao in subsidium mittit: uno atque altero prælio has omnes Mithridatis copias delet Sylla: Archelaus triduo nudus in palude latet. Mithridates pacē postulat: non daturū se respondet Sylla, nisi relictis quæ occuparat, in regnū redeat. Interim Sylla Dardanos, Scordiscos, Dalmatas & Mœsos partim vincit, partim in fidē accipit. Ecce autē interea Romæ Marius & Cor. Cinna nobilissimos ex Senatu interficiunt, multos proscribunt: Syllę domum evertunt: universus reliquus Senatus ex urbe sugiens, ad Syllam in Græciā venit: atq; ut patriæ subveniat, precatur. In Italiam ille traiicit, Marianam factionem dissipat: adversariorum exercitus delet, fundit, obruit. Eutr. li.5. Appi. li.1. Flo. li 3. Dictaturam gerens, ea se abdicavit, ruríque agens morbo obiit pediculari.
units.tr: SYLLA, a Roman patrician and consul, is sent by the Senate against Mithridates. He besieges and defeats Archelaus, the general of Mithridates, so that of the 120,000 men, scarcely ten thousand were left to Archelaus. Sylla takes Athens in the year of the world 3877, before the birth of Christ 85. Mithridates sends 70,000 picked men to Archelaus as reinforcements; in one or two battles Sylla destroys all these forces of Mithridates. Archelaus hides naked in a marsh for three days. Mithridates asks for peace; Sylla replies that he will not grant it unless Mithridates gives up what he has occupied and returns to his kingdom. Meanwhile Sylla partly conquers and partly takes into his protection the Dardanians, Scordiscans, Dalmatians and Moesians. But meanwhile at Rome Marius and Cornelius Cinna put to death the most noble men of the Senate and proscribe many; they overthrow Sylla's house. The whole remaining Senate, fleeing from the city, comes to Sylla in Greece and begs him to come to the aid of his country. He crosses into Italy, breaks up the Marian faction, and routs, scatters and crushes the armies of his opponents. See Eutropius, book 5; Appian, book 1; Florus, book 3. Holding the dictatorship, he laid it down, and living in the country he died of lice.

units.la: MARIUS, C. Marij filius, Romæ consulatum gerens infeliciter contra Syllam dimicat, 20000. ex suis perdit: Præneste fugit, obsessus ad mortem compellitur. Eutro. lib.5. Porrò Flo. li. 3. scribit hunc apud Catuli sepulchrum, oculis, manibus, cruribúsque defossis, aliquandiu servatum, ut per singula membra moreretur. Q METEL PIVS CLAVDIA METEL
units.tr: MARIUS, son of C. Marius, while consul at Rome, fights unsuccessfully against Sylla and loses 20,000 of his own men; he flees to Praeneste, and being besieged is driven to death. See Eutropius, book 5. Florus, book 3, further writes that he was kept alive for some time beside the tomb of Catulus, with his eyes, hands and shins buried, so that he might die limb by limb.

units.la: QVINTVS Metellus, Pius dictus est, quòd patrem Metellum Numidicum, qui de Numidiæ rege Iugurtha triumpharat, assiduis precibus ac lachrymis ab exilio reuocarit. Hic Prætor bello sociali Marsorum ducem interemit: Consul in Hispania Herculeos fratres cōpreffit, Sertorium expulit, qui redeunte à bello Mithridatico Sylla, in Hispaniâ aufugerat, quòd partium Marianarum fuisset. Adolescens Metellus in petitione prætura & Pontificatus, consularibus viris Prælatus est. huius adolescentia priscos vidit mores, senectus autem nouam exorsa est luxuriam, ut Valerij verbis utar. Hic inter proscriptos à Sylla, cum ad posticum uxoris suæ Bastiæ, clam capite adoperto accessisset, nec admitteretur, quia illum proscriptum diceret uxor, ibidem se trâsuerberans, fores sanguine respersit. Cæcilius, Liuius in epito.lib. 89. Vale. lib. 9. cha. 1. hic Consul fuit anno mundi 3884. ante Christum natum 78. palmata veste conuiuia celebrauit in Hispania, demissaque lacunaribus aureas coronas velut cœlesti capite recepit: aris, thure, Attalicisque aulæis læto animo excipi passus est, & lautis epulis apparatos ludos interponi.
units.tr: QUINTUS Metellus was called Pius because by constant prayers and tears he recalled his father Metellus Numidicus, who had triumphed over Jugurtha, king of Numidia, from exile. He, as praetor in the Social War, killed the leader of the Marsi; as consul in Spain he subdued the Herculean brothers and expelled Sertorius, who had fled to Spain when Sylla returned from the Mithridatic war, because he had been on the Marian side. As a young man Metellus, in seeking the praetorship and the pontificate, was preferred over men of consular rank. In his youth he saw the ancient customs; but his old age began a new luxury, to use the words of Valerius. Among those proscribed by Sylla, he came secretly with his head covered to the back door of his wife Bastia, and when he was not admitted, because his wife said he was a proscribed man, he stabbed himself there and sprinkled the doors with blood. See Caelius, Livy in the epitome of book 89, Valerius, book 9, chapter 1. He was consul in the year of the world 3884, before the birth of Christ 78. Wearing the palm-embroidered robe he held banquets in Spain, and letting down golden crowns from the ceilings he received them as if on a heavenly head; he allowed altars, incense and Attalic hangings to be received with a glad heart, and games prepared with lavish feasts to be interposed.

units.la: CLAVDIA, Q. Metelli Pij supradicti fuit filia. Circa hæc tempora locutus esse dicitur gallus gallinaceus in Ariminensi agro, in villa Galerij. Plinius li.10.ca.21.id miraculi, in annalibus relatum, editum est (si credere fas est) anno à mundo condito 3887. ante Christum natum 75. nempe M. Æmy. Lepido, & Q. Luctatio Catulo Romæ Consulibus. Tribunatus plebi restituitur.
units.tr: CLAUDIA, daughter of the above-mentioned Q. Metellus Pius. Around this time a rooster is said to have crowed in the territory of Ariminum, in the villa of Galerius. Pliny, book 10, chapter 21, that this marvel was recorded in the annals and published (if it is right to believe it) in the year from the founding of the world 3887, before the birth of Christ 75, namely when M. Aemilius Lepidus and Q. Lutatius Catulus were consuls at Rome. The tribunate of the plebs is restored.

units.la: ANTIPATER à C. Cæsare Iudææ Procurator designatur anno mundi 3919. ante Christum natum 43.
units.tr: ANTIPATER was appointed procurator of Judaea by C. Caesar in the year of the world 3919, before the birth of Christ 43.

units.la: HYRCANUS Iamnei filius post matrem Alexandram apud Iudæos regnat non ita diu, nam frater eius Aristobulus minor natu, eum fugat: convenit tandem inter ipsos ut Hyrcanus privatum, Aristobulus Regem vivat. verum post an.6.à Pompeio Hyrcanus restituitur: & partim solus, partim cum Antipatro Herodis patre, administrat:tandē ei aures dentibus præcidit Antigonus.Iose.lib.14.ca.1.& 22.
units.tr: HYRCANUS, son of Jannaeus, after his mother Alexandra reigned among the Jews, not for long, for his younger brother Aristobulus drove him out; at last it was agreed between them that Hyrcanus should live as a private man and Aristobulus as king. But after six years Hyrcanus was restored by Pompey, and governed partly alone and partly with Antipater, the father of Herod; at last Antigonus cut off his ears with his teeth. See Josephus, book 14, chapters 1 and 22.

units.la: ARISTOBULUS itaque regnat apud Iudæos anno mundi 3895. ante Christum natum 67. sed enim Hyrcanus tandem ad Pompeium Magnum confugiens,ab eodem iuvatur, cognita superbia ac iniuria Aristobuli: qui cum bellum Romanis inferre statueret,à Pompeio Ierosolymis prævetus, obsidetur:ad quē supplex egreditur,pecuniamq; promittit: quā cum primores dare recusarent,relicto Rege Aristobulo apud Pompeium,urbem claudūt,eósque introitu arcent.æstuas ira Pompeius, Aristobulum ligat:atq; urbē magnis viribus dum oppugnat,hæc ab iis qui Hyrcano fauebant,Pompeio traditur:templúmq; tertio postquam obsederat mēse oppugnat Pompeius, M. Tullio Cicerone,& M. Antonio Romæ Cos. Hircanum summum Sacerdote appellat: Aristobulum cum duabus filiabus filio uno(alter enim filius Alexander effugerat)vinctos Romam abducit.tum primùm Romanis subiiciuntur Iudæi.Iosephi.li.Anti.14.à 1.cap.ad 9.& de bel.Iud.li.1.cap.5.Post annum ausugit Aristobulus à Roma in Iudæam, & regnū iterum affectans, à Gabinio captus, & secundò Romam vinctus missus est: tandem à Cæsare liberatus,præmisúsq; in Iudæam,à Pompeianis veneno necatur.Ægesip.li.1.
units.tr: ARISTOBULUS therefore reigned among the Jews in the year of the world 3895, before the birth of Christ 67. But Hyrcanus, fleeing at last to Pompey the Great, was aided by him, since Pompey had recognised the arrogance and injustice of Aristobulus. When Aristobulus resolved to make war on the Romans, he was forestalled by Pompey and besieged at Jerusalem; he went out to him as a suppliant and promised money. When the leading men refused to give this, they left King Aristobulus with Pompey and closed the city, keeping them from entering. Pompey, inflamed with anger, bound Aristobulus, and while he attacked the city with great forces, it was handed over to Pompey by those who favoured Hyrcanus; and Pompey, after he had besieged the temple for three months, stormed it, when M. Tullius Cicero and M. Antonius were consuls at Rome. He named Hyrcanus high priest; he led Aristobulus, bound, to Rome with his two daughters and one son (for the other son, Alexander, had escaped). Then for the first time the Jews were made subject to the Romans. See Josephus, Antiquities, book 14, chapters 1 to 9, and the Jewish War, book 1, chapter 5. Afterwards, a year later, Aristobulus escaped from Rome to Judaea, and again aiming at the kingship, was captured by Gabinius and sent back to Rome in chains a second time; at last, freed by Caesar and sent ahead into Judaea, he was killed with poison by the Pompeians. See Hegesippus, book 1.

units.la: P. CLODIVS vir claris parentibus ortus,iuuenis quidē audax,incestuosus ac seditiosus,cūm amore Pompeiæ Cæsaris coniugis flagraret,clam eius domū ingreditur,vestem ac habitum psaltriæ indutus:spéq; latēdi mulieres abductus ob adolescentiæ formam,genāsque nondū pubentes turbæ earum,quæ tum in ædeCasaris sacrum inacessum viris agebant,immistus, ad Pompeiam ingreditur:deprehensus ac agnitus,etiā Cicerone teste,accusatur:verūm iudices tū metu,tum largitione,tum fauore eum absoluunt. fit deinde Tribunus plebis, & factione sua Ciceronē in exilium agit, anno à mundo cōdito 3906. ante Christum seruatorē natum 56.cuius domum ac villas incendit: reliqua bona hastæ subiicit:attamē emit nemo. Tandem à Milone Clodius occiditur, accusatur Milo, patronúmque habet Ciceronē, iam antè ab exilio reuocatum. Vide Plutar.in Cice. & Cæs.item Appi.de ciui.Ro.bel.li.2.
units.tr: P. CLODIUS, a man born of distinguished parents, was indeed a bold young man, incestuous and seditious. Since he burned with love for Pompeia, the wife of Caesar, he secretly entered her house, dressed in the clothing and garb of a female harpist; and, drawn by the hope of hiding among women because of his youthful beauty and his cheeks not yet bearded, he mingled with the crowd of women who were then performing the rites of the goddess in Caesar's house, which were forbidden to men, and entered to Pompeia. Discovered and recognised, he was accused, even with Cicero as witness; but the judges, partly from fear, partly from bribery, partly from favour, acquitted him. He then became tribune of the plebs and by his faction drove Cicero into exile in the year from the founding of the world 3906, before the birth of the Saviour 56. He set fire to Cicero's house and villas, put the remaining goods up for auction, but no one bought them. At last Clodius was killed by Milo; Milo was accused, and had Cicero as his advocate, who had already been recalled from exile. See Plutarch in the life of Cicero and of Caesar; also Appian, On the Civil Wars, book 2.

units.la: FVLVIA, uxor P. Clodij, quæ postea M. antonio nupsit, non muliebres artes, non familiam regere curabat,nec priuatum hominem superare contendebat, sed magistratus gerere, & imperatibus imperare,vt sibi magnas gratias deberet Cleopatra, quod institutum ab ea Antonium acceperit. hæc clam noctu profecta, Ciceroni Catilinæ detexit insidias, eúmque cōmonefecit vt Cethegum,eiusque comites præcaueret. Plut. in Cice. & Anto. L. CAESAR. C. CAES. DICTAT. PATER. AVRELIA MATER. C. CAES. DICTATORIS.
units.tr: FULVIA, wife of P. Clodius, who afterwards married Mark Antony, did not care for women's arts or for managing a household, nor did she strive to surpass a private man, but to hold the offices of magistrates and to command generals, so that Cleopatra should owe her great thanks, since Antony had adopted this custom from her. She, secretly departing at night, revealed the plots of Catiline to Cicero, and advised him to be on his guard against Cethegus and his companions. Plutarch in the life of Cicero and of Antony. L. CAESAR. C. CAESAR DICTATOR. PATER. AURELIA MOTHER. C. CAESAR THE DICTATOR.

units.la: L. IVLIVS Cæsar,C.Iulij Cæsaris Dictatoris pater , Prætura perfunctus,nullis euidétibus causis obiit Pisis,exanimatus derepéte,dum matutino calceatur. Vide Pli.li.7.ca.52. Fuit hic quoque L.Iulius Cęsar Consul cum Antonio,anno præcedéte Consulatum Ciceronis,qui erat annus à mundo condito 3900. ante verò Christum natum 62. Præturam gessit anno ab hinc quarto:Prætórque Iberos,hoc est Hispanos, ad Oceanũ usque subigit,ac paulò post emoritur. Vide Appi.li.2.
units.tr: L. JULIUS Caesar, father of C. Julius Caesar the dictator, having held the praetorship, died at Pisa for no evident cause, suddenly struck down while being shod in the morning. See Pliny, book 7, chapter 52. This L. Julius Caesar was also consul with Antony, in the year before the consulship of Cicero, which was the year from the founding of the world 3900, but before the birth of Christ 62. He held the praetorship four years earlier; as praetor he subdued the Iberians, that is the Spaniards, as far as the Ocean, and soon after died. See Appian, book 2.

units.la: AVRELIA uxor L. Iulij Cæsaris , & mater C. Cæsaris Dictatoris fuit. Vide Sueto.in Cæsaris vita. Porrò Aurelia familia,Romæ olim percelebris,à Sabinis, si Festo credimus,oriunda,Aurelios nobiles Romanos tulit : qui primùm Aufelij dicti sunt:quemadmodum & Valesij & Papyfij,postea Valerij & Papyrij sunt vocitati.
units.tr: AURELIA was the wife of L. Julius Caesar and mother of C. Caesar the dictator. See Suetonius in the life of Caesar. Moreover, the Aurelian family, once very famous at Rome, came from the Sabines, if we believe Festus, and produced the noble Romans Aurelii, who were first called Aufelii, just as the Valesii and Papyisii were afterwards called Valerii and Papyrii.

units.la: C. IVLIVS Cæsar primus Romæ imperat anno mundi 3917. ante Christum natum 44.huic Consuli decreta est Gallia & Illyricum cum legionibus decem.Nam Asia Pompeij manibus subacta,reliqua quæ restabat in Europa,fortuna in hunc transtulit. Restabant autem immanis. gentium, Galli, atque Germani:& quamuis toto orbe diuisa,habuit qui vinceret,Britannia. Primò vicit Heluetios:deinde vincendo per bella graujs. vsque ad Oceanum Britannicum accesit. Domuit autem fere annis nouem omnè Galliam quæ inter Alpes, flumè Rhodanum, Rhenum & Oceanum est. Britannos victos (hi Angli sunt) quibus ante ne nomen quidè Romanum cognitum erat, obsidibus acceptis stipendiarios fecit. Germanos etiam trans Rhenum aggressus, immanis. præliis vicit.Inter tot successus ter,nec amplius, malè illi successum est: in Britannia (Anglia nunc dicitur)vi tempestatis classe penè absumpta,& in Gallia ad Gergouiam legione fusa: & in Germanorū finibus legatis per insidias cæsis. E Gallia victor rediēs, poscit alterū consulatum, contradicitur ei à Marcello,à Bibulo,à Pompeio,à Catone, iubetūrque dimisso exercitu Romā redire. Hinc manat bellum ciuile lachrymabile. Aduersum ille patriā cum exercitu venit: fugit ex vrbe cum Pōpeio Senatus omnis in Græciā. Pompeio duce contra Cæsarē bellum parat Senatus,primò prælio vincit Pompeius, deinde in Thessalia vincit Cæsar. rediens vincit Pharnacē Cæsar: item in Africa nobiles Rom. cum Iuba rege: & in Hispaniis filios Pompeij, vbi primo congressu in tantum discrimē venit,vt se voluerit occidere. Tandē omnium victor, dum Romæ insolentius agit, coniurant in eum 60. senatores, equitesque. Senatus die in curia 24.vulneribus macfatur, post assumptum imperium an.3.alij dicunt 4.vixit annos 56. Consulito Sueto. in Cæs.Plut.item in Cæsaris vita.
units.tr: C. JULIUS Caesar first ruled at Rome in the year of the world 3917, before the birth of Christ 44. To this consul were assigned Gaul and Illyricum with ten legions. For Asia had been subdued by the hands of Pompey, and fortune transferred to him what remained in Europe. There remained the huge nations of the Gauls and the Germans; and although the world was divided, there was one who would conquer it, Britain. First he conquered the Helvetii; then, by conquering through many wars, he advanced to the British Ocean. He subdued almost all of Gaul, which lies between the Alps, the river Rhone, the Rhine and the Ocean, in about nine years. The Britons, whom he conquered (these are the English), and to whom the Roman name had not even been known before, he made tributary after receiving hostages. He also attacked the Germans beyond the Rhine and conquered them in huge battles. Amid so many successes, three times and no more, things went badly for him: in Britain, when his fleet was nearly destroyed by a storm; in Gaul, when his legion was routed at Gergovia; and in the territory of the Germans, when his legates were cut down by an ambush. Returning victorious from Gaul, he demanded a second consulship; Marcellus, Bibulus, Pompey and Cato opposed him, and he was ordered to dismiss his army and return to Rome. From this a lamentable civil war broke out. He came against his country with his army; the whole Senate fled from the city with Pompey to Greece. The Senate prepared war against Caesar under Pompey's leadership: first Pompey won in battle, then Caesar won in Thessaly. Returning, Caesar overcame Pharnaces; likewise in Africa he overcame the Roman nobles with King Juba, and in Spain the sons of Pompey, when in the first encounter he came into such danger that he wanted to kill himself. At last, victor over all, while he behaved more arrogantly at Rome, sixty senators and knights conspired against him. On the Ides of March in the Senate house he was pierced with twenty-four wounds; after assuming power he reigned three years (others say four) and lived fifty-six years. See Suetonius on Caesar; Plutarch also in the life of Caesar.

units.la: COSSUTIA, quæ familia equestri, admodum diues fuit, prætext ato C. Iulio Cæsari nupsit, quam postea dimisit. Sueton. in Cæsa.
units.tr: COSSUTIA, a family of the equestrian order and very wealthy, married Gaius Julius Caesar while he was still a praetextate boy; he later divorced her. Suetonius, in the Life of Caesar.

units.la: CORNELIA, Cinnæ quartùm Cõ sulis filia, secunda Cæsaris uxor fuit, ex qua mox Iuliam suscepit. hanc ut repudiaret cõpelli à Dictatore Sylla nullo modo potuit: quamuis & sacerdotio, & uxoris dote, & gentiliciis hæreditatibus multaretur. Quæstor Cæsar Iuliam amitam, uxorémque Corneliam defunctas, laudauit è more pro rostris.
units.tr: CORNELIA, daughter of Cinna, four times consul, was Caesar's second wife, and by her he soon had Julia. Dictator Sulla could in no way compel him to repudiate her, although he was punished by the loss of his priesthood, his wife's dowry, and his ancestral inheritances. When Caesar, as quaestor, delivered the funeral oration from the Rostra for his aunt Julia and his wife Cornelia, who had died, he praised them according to custom.

units.la: POMPEIA, terrtia Cæsaris uxor fuit, Q. Pompeij filia, L. Syllæ neptis, cum qua diuortium fecit, adulteratam opinatus à P. Clodio: dicebatque, Cæsaris thorum non tantum crimine, sed & criminis suspitione carere debere. Sueto. & Plutar. in Cæsar.
units.tr: POMPEIA, Caesar's third wife, was the daughter of Quintus Pompeius and granddaughter of Lucius Sulla. He divorced her, believing she had been defiled by Publius Clodius. He said that Caesar's bed ought to be free not only of crime but also of the suspicion of crime. Suetonius and Plutarch, in the Life of Caesar.

units.la: CALPHURNIA L. Pisonis filia, fuit quarta Cæsaris uxor, cùm in Cõsulatu ei successurus esset ille L. Piso. hæc post viri necem omnē pecuniam ad M. Antoniū tulit. Suet. in Cæs.
units.tr: CALPHURNIA, daughter of Lucius Piso, was Caesar's fourth wife, when Lucius Piso, who was to succeed him in the consulship, was still alive. After her husband's death she carried all her money to Marcus Antonius. Suetonius, in the Life of Caesar.

units.la: POMPEIVS, parta ingenti felicitate,& celeritate de piratis victoria, mox bellum contra Mithridatem suscepit anno mundi 3897. ante Christum natum 65. quem in Armenia minore nocturno prælio vicit,ac 40000.eius militum occisis, 30.tantum de exercitu suo perdidit:Mithridates cum vxore & duobus ex suis fugit.Tigranes maioris Armeniæ rex Pōpeio se dedidit,ad genua eius procubuit, in cuius manus diadema collocauit,quod ei reposuit Pompeius.Orodē Albanorum regem vicit:rogatus,veniam ei ac pacem cōceffit.Iberiæ quoq; regem acie vicit. Armeniam minorem Deiotaro Galatiæ regi dedit, quòd opem tulisset ei aduersus Mithridatē. Attalo & Pylemeni Paphlagoniam tradidit. Ariftarchum Colchis regem impofuit.Mox Iturǣos & Arabes vicit.Seleucia Antiochiæ vicinam, libertate donauit, quòd Tigranem non recepisset:Antiochēsibus obsides reddidit. Inde ad Iudæam transgressus, Ierosolymam tertio mense capit:12000.Iudæorum occidit, reliquos in fidem accipit. Post aliquot annos exarsit bellū ciuile(commune potius,ac plus quàm bellum vocat Florus)omniū turbulentiss.ac pestilentiss. inter Pompeiū & Cæsarem. Primo congressu victus & fugatus Cæsar,euasit:quia noćte interueniēte Pompeius sequi noluit:dixitque Cæsar, nec Pompeium scire vincere:& illo tantùm die se potuisse superari.Deinde apud Pharsaliam pugnatur,vtrinque summa contentione : victus tamen Pompeius ad Ptolemæum,cui tutor à senatu datus fuerat,fugit. is fortunam magis quàm amicitiā secutus,Pompeium occidit anno mundi 3917. ante Christum natum 45. Vide Eutro. libr. 6. Plutar. in Pom.Appia li.2.Iosep.lib.14.cap.8.
units.tr: POMPEY, having gained enormous good fortune and speed in his victory over the pirates, soon undertook war against Mithridates in the year of the world 3897, before the birth of Christ 65. He defeated him in Lesser Armenia in a night battle, with 40,000 of his soldiers killed, while he lost only thirty from his own army. Mithridates fled with his wife and two of his men. Tigranes, king of Greater Armenia, surrendered to Pompey, fell at his knees, and placed the diadem in his hands, and Pompey returned it to him. He defeated Orodes, king of the Albanians, and, when asked, granted him pardon and peace. He also defeated the king of Iberia in battle. He gave Lesser Armenia to Deiotarus, king of Galatia, because he had brought him aid against Mithridates. He handed Paphlagonia to Attalus and Pylaemenes. He set Aristarchus over Colchis as king. Soon afterwards he defeated the Ituraeans and the Arabs. He granted liberty to Seleucia, near Antioch, because it had not received Tigranes, and he returned hostages to the people of Antioch. From there he crossed into Judea and in the third month took Jerusalem, killing 12,000 Jews and taking the rest into his protection. Some years later a civil war broke out, which Florus calls the most turbulent and destructive of all wars (rather a common war, or more than a war), between Pompey and Caesar. Caesar, defeated and put to flight in the first encounter, escaped, because Pompey, with night intervening, would not pursue him. Caesar said that Pompey did not know how to win, and that he had only been able to be defeated on that one day. Then the battle was fought at Pharsalus, with great effort on both sides; nevertheless Pompey, defeated, fled to Ptolemy, to whom the senate had given him a guardian. Following fortune rather than friendship, Ptolemy killed Pompey in the year of the world 3917, before the birth of Christ 45. See Eutropius, book 6; Plutarch, in the Life of Pompey; Appian, book 2; Josephus, book 14, chapter 8.

units.la: IVLIA C. Cæsaris & Corneliæ filia, Pompeij fuit vxor, quæ dum filiam parit,emoritur.
units.tr: JULIA Julia, daughter of Gaius Caesar and Cornelia, was the wife of Pompey; she died while giving birth to a daughter.

units.la: M. POR. CATO, cognominatus Vticensis, quòd post Pharsalicam pugnā Vticæ seipsum interfecerit, Catonis maioris, qui Cēsorius dictus est, pronepos fuit. Hic relictus parētum orphanus, cum fratre Cæpione & sorore Portia, apud Liuium Drusum auunculum educatur. Romæ Tribunus plebis fuit anno mundi 3903.ante Christū natum 59.fuit quo quę tribunus militum, item Prætor audacia, fortitudine ac decore, nihilo antiquo illo Catone proauo inferior apparuit. Consulatū petens, victus à competitoribus, non ægrè tulit repulsam, nec erubuit, erubescētibus interim amicis: quinimò sequēti die sine calceis & tunica in forū vt solebat, iuit: cum familiaribus ambulauit: sese adsuefaciens non nisi turpibus rebus erubescere. Tandem deuicto Pompeio, cuius partes secutus fuerat, Vticæ, quæ vrbs in Africa est, gladio se trâsfixit, bis perlecto prius (vt ferūt) libro Platonis de animæ immortalitate. hic Cato minor dictus est: nam alter fuit dictus maior. Horum duorum Catonū innocentia, & sapientia in prouerbium abiit: vnde Iuuen.
units.tr: Marcus Porcius Cato, surnamed Uticensis because he killed himself at Utica after the battle of Pharsalus, was the great-grandson of the elder Cato, who was called the Censor. Left an orphan by his parents, he was brought up with his brother Caepio and his sister Portia by his uncle Livius Drusus. At Rome he was tribune of the plebs in the year of the world 3903, before the birth of Christ 59. Earlier he had been military tribune and praetor, and in boldness, courage and dignity he appeared in no way inferior to his ancient forebear Cato. When he sought the consulship and was defeated by his rivals, he bore the rejection without distress and did not blush, although his friends blushed in his place; indeed on the following day he went into the forum without shoes or tunic, as was his custom, and walked about with his companions, accustoming himself to blush only at shameful things. At last, when Pompey, whose party he had followed, was defeated, he ran himself through with a sword at Utica, a city in Africa, having first read (as they say) Plato's book on the immortality of the soul twice. He was called the younger Cato, for the other was called the elder. The innocence and wisdom of these two Catos passed into a proverb; whence Juvenal:
A third Cato has fallen from heaven.

units.la: Huius cognita morte exclamauit Cæsar, Inuideo morti tuæ Cato, nam & tu gloriæ meæ pro salute tua inuidisti, filiúmque eius vita donauit. Vide Plutar. in eius vita. & Apoph.Eraf[?].li.5[?].& 8.item D. Augusti.li.de ciuitate Dei,1.ca.23.
units.tr: When his death became known, Caesar exclaimed: "I envy you your death, Cato, for you too envied me my glory by seeking your own safety," and he pardoned his son. See Plutarch in his Life, and the Apophthegms of Erasmus, book 5 and 8; also Augustine, On the City of God, book 1, chapter 23.

units.la: IVBA Mauritaniæ Rex, Pōpeij partibus fauens, Curionem à Cæsare in Africam missum cum copiis deleuit, anno mundi 3916.ante Christum natum 46. hic victo Pompeio, cum Scipione copias iunxit. Victi à Cæsare Iuba & Petreius, cùm nec sugam nec salutem sperarēt, inedia vulneribúsque se adinuicem tandem confecere. Vide Appi.li.2.& Plut.in Cæs. PORTIA BRVTI VXOR MARTIA.CAT FILIA
units.tr: JUBA, king of Mauretania, favouring Pompey's side, destroyed Curio, whom Caesar had sent into Africa with troops, in the year of the world 3916, before the birth of Christ 46. After Pompey was defeated, he joined his forces with Scipio's. Juba and Petreius, defeated by Caesar, having no hope of flight or safety, at last wore each other out by hunger and by wounds on each other. See Appian, book 2, and Plutarch in the Life of Caesar. PORTIA, WIFE OF BRUTUS, DAUGHTER OF CATO

units.la: PORTIA Catonis Vticensis filia, vxórque Bruti fuit: hæc accepta viri morte, cùm ipsa quoque mori statuisset, nec diu superesse viro quem tantopere diligebat, nemo amicorum assentiebatur: quinimo diligenti cura cùm id prohiberent, hæc ex igne ardentes prunas corripiens, in os sibi coniecit, deinde os, diémque clausit. Plutar. in vita Bruti. Vale. lib. 3. & 4. ca. 2. & 6. Appi. lib. 15. De hac sic scribit Martialis, lib. Epigrammatum primo:
units.tr: Portia, daughter of Cato Uticensis and wife of Brutus, when she received news of her husband's death and had herself decided to die too, since she could not long survive the husband whom she loved so much, was opposed by none of her friends. Indeed, when they prevented her with careful vigilance, she seized burning coals from the fire, put them into her mouth, and so closed her mouth and her life. Plutarch, in the Life of Brutus; Valerius, book 3 and 4, chapters 2 and 6; Appian, book 15. Martial writes thus about her, in the first book of his Epigrams:

units.la: Coniugis audisset fatum cum Portia Bruti, Et subtracta sibi quaereret arma dolor: Nondum scitis (ait) mortem non posse negari: Crederam satis hoc vos docuisse patrem.
units.tr: When Portia, Brutus's wife, heard of her husband's fate, and grief sought weapons withheld from her, she said: "You do not yet know that death cannot be denied. I thought I had taught you this well enough, father."

units.la: Dixit, & ardentes avido bibit ore fauillas: I nunc, & ferrum, turba molesta, nega.
units.tr: She spoke, and drank the burning embers with eager mouth. Go now, and deny her the sword, you troublesome crowd.

units.la: MARTIA, Catonis filia minor fuit, quæ cùm interrogaretur, cur demortuo marito priore, alteri non nuberet, respōdit se non inuenire virum qui se magis vellet quàm sua.quo responso ostēdit diuitias magis in vxoribus eligi solere quàm pudiciam. Quæsitū est iterum ab ea quis esset illi extremus dies lugendi mariti:is(respondit hæc) qui & extremus vitæ dies mihi erit. Vide Eras.Apoph.li.8.
units.tr: MARCIA, the younger daughter of Cato, when asked why, after her first husband had died, she did not marry another, replied that she could not find a man who wanted her more than his own riches. By this answer she showed that wives are commonly chosen for their wealth rather than their chastity. She was asked again what would be the last day of mourning for her husband; she replied that it would be the last day of her life. See Erasmus, Apophthegms, book 8.

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] (medallions: M. TVLLI[?]VS CICERO and LVTIVS MVNATIVS PLANCVS; the medallion portraits are pictures, not text)
units.tr: [illegible, about six letters] (medallions: M. TULLIUS CICERO and LUTIUS MUNATIUS PLANCUS; the medallion portraits are pictures, not text)

units.la: CICERO, Ro.oratorum facilè princeps, obscuro satis loco natus, ingenio atq; eloquentia nobilè se præstitit. honorum desiderio forensibus causis se obtulit: in pronunciado primùm laborauit, sicut & Demosthenes: in iocando nimius, plerosque acriter offendit. Difficilem Roscij causam cum laude sustinuit: vnde & odiũ Syllæ conflauit: cui cedens in Græciã abiit: philosophos ac oratores Athenis audiuit. Vim opum parua licet, sed sumptibus suis cum satis concinnam haberet, admirationi est habitus, quòd neque mercedes, neque nummorum quicquam in actionibus forensibus caperet. Catilinæ conatibus tam diligenter ac prudẽter obstitit, vt primus pater patriæ diceretur. In P. Clodium testis fuit. Ab eodem Clodio Tribuno plebis aqua & igni interdictus est, ac in exilium actus: vnde post aliquot mẽses cum omnium plausu, atq; etiã laudibus ornatus, rediit Proconsul, in Ciliciam exercitum 12000. peditum, 2600. equitum traiecit: munera à Regibus sibi oblata renuit. Tandem cum Cæsari aduersus M. Antonium fauisset, ab hoc Antonio miserè côtrucidari iubetur, anno mundi 3922. ante Christũ natum 40. Plutar. in Cice. Cæsarem post Pharsalicam victoriam pertimescebat (Pompeianarũ fiquidẽ partium fuerat) Cicero, attamen Cæsar illi occurrens, eum præsalutauit, atque in honore habuit.
units.tr: CICERO, easily the prince of Roman orators, born in a rather obscure place, made himself famous for his talent and eloquence. Driven by desire for honours, he devoted himself to forensic cases. At first he struggled with delivery, as Demosthenes did; he was excessive in joking, and offended many sharply. He undertook the difficult case of Roscius with praise, and so drew upon himself the hatred of Sulla; yielding to him, he went to Greece and heard philosophers and orators at Athens. Though his means were small, he had a fairly comfortable estate from his own resources, and he was admired because he took neither fees nor any sum of money for his pleadings in court. He opposed the attempts of Catiline so diligently and prudently that he was called "the first father of his country." He gave testimony against Publius Clodius. By that same Clodius, as tribune of the plebs, he was banished from fire and water and driven into exile; afterwards, a few months later, he returned as proconsul to general applause and even praise, adorned with honours. He led an army of 12,000 foot and 2,600 horse across into Cilicia; he refused gifts offered him by kings. At last, because he had favoured Caesar against Marcus Antonius, he was shamefully murdered on Antony's orders, in the year of the world 3922, before the birth of Christ 40. See Plutarch, in the Life of Cicero. Cicero feared Caesar after the victory at Pharsalus (for he had been of Pompey's party), but Caesar, meeting him, greeted him first and held him in honour.

units.la: L. MVNATIVS Plancus Romæ Consul fuit eodẽ anno quo Cicero interfectus est. Is dum Galliã Comatã regit, Lugdunum condit, aut (vt alij volunt) instaurat: item Rauricam, quæ nunc est Basilea. Huius sententia. Octauio Augusto, Augusti cognomen inditum est, cum alij Romulum potius dici cêserent. Sueto.in Aug. Volater.li.18. ꝑD. PARTH. [?] PACORVS ꝑD. IVD. [?] ANTIGONVS
units.tr: LUCIUS MUNATIUS PLANCUS was consul at Rome in the same year in which Cicero was killed. While governing Gallia Comata, he founded Lugdunum, or (as others prefer) restored it; likewise Raurica, which is now Basel. His opinion was the reason why the name Augustus was given to Octavian Augustus, although others thought he should rather be called Romulus. Suetonius, in the Life of Augustus; Volaterranus, book 18. PACORUS, KING OF THE PARTHIANS. ANTIGONUS, KING OF THE JEWS

units.la: PACORVS Parthorum Rex, Antigono fauens, Hierusalem venit, prætextu cõponēdæ seditionis obortæ inter Iudæos, partim Phaselo & Hyrcano, partim Antigono fauentibus: re vera autē principatum Antigono traditurus: itaque per dolum Phaselum ad Barzafarnē, Persarum satrapam, mittit: Phaselus cum Hyrcano ligatus à Parthis est, quibus talēta mille, ac mulieres quingētas pollicitus erat Antigonus. hac via Iudææ Rex à Pacoro cõstitutus Antigonus, Hyrcano sibi à Parthis tradito, dentibus aures præscidit, ne quando summum obiret sacerdotium: nam lex integros tantùm admittebat. Phaselus autē, cùm se occidendum sciret, maluit præuenire, saxóque caput allidēs, emori: porrò Herodes Phaseli frater, fuga salutē quærit: atque à Senatu Ro. ob patris beneficia, Iudææ Rex declaratur. huius Pacori pater, Crassum Ro. dolo circunuētum interfecerat, quā maculam Ventidius Bassus, M. Antonij legatus, deleuit, Pacorum cum exercitu ad internecionē cædens. Vide Aegesip. li.1. & Iosefli.14.ca.22.& 23.
units.tr: Pacorus, king of the Parthians, favouring Antigonus, came to Jerusalem, under the pretext of settling a sedition that had broken out among the Jews, some supporting Phasael and Hyrcanus, others Antigonus; in truth, however, he meant to hand the principate over to Antigonus. So, by trickery, he sent Phasael to Barzapharnes, satrap of the Persians. Phasael, together with Hyrcanus, was bound by the Parthians, to whom Antigonus had promised a thousand talents and five hundred women. In this way Antigonus, appointed king of Judaea by Pacorus, and with Hyrcanus handed over to the Parthians, cut off his ears with his teeth, so that he could never assume the high priesthood, for the law admitted only those who were whole. Phasael, however, knowing he was to be killed, preferred to forestall it, and dashing his head against a rock, died. Herod, brother of Phasael, sought safety in flight; and by the Roman Senate, on account of his father's services, he was declared king of Judaea. The father of this Pacorus had treacherously ensnared and killed Crassus of Rome; this stain was wiped out by Ventidius Bassus, legate of Mark Antony, who cut Pacorus down with his army to utter destruction. See Aegesippus, book 1, and Josephus, book 14, chapters 22 and 23.

units.la: ANTIGONVS Ariftobuli filius, Pacori, vt dixi, auxilio Iudæam occupat, anno mundi 3924. ante Christum natum 38. eodem ferè tempore. Herodes antipatri filius, ac Phaseli frater, qui cum Antigono, prius cõgressus, eum vicerat, nunc autem à Pacoro fugatus, Romam peruenerat, à Senatu Iudæorum Rex designatur: ac post an. 4. ipse cum Sosio Romano Hierusalem capit: Antigonum Sosius ad M. Antonium mittit, à quo securi percutitur. Vide Iofe.li.14.ca.vltimo. C. CASSIVS COS M. BRVTVS
units.tr: Antigonus, son of Aristobulus, with the help of Pacorus, as I have said, seized Judaea in the year of the world 3924, about 38 years before the birth of Christ, at roughly the same time. Herod, son of Antipater and brother of Phasael, who had earlier engaged Antigonus in battle and defeated him, but was now driven out by Pacorus and had reached Rome, was designated king of the Jews by the Senate. And after four years he himself, together with the Roman Sosius, took Jerusalem. Sosius sent Antigonus to Mark Antony, by whom he was beheaded. See Josephus, book 14, the last chapter.

units.la: C. CASSIVS, vir Bruto familiaris, sed tamen dissimili ingenio, ac varius & impurus fuit, omnisq; autoritatis, potestatis, ac tyrannidis adversarius: testis sit Faustus ab eo, adhuc adolescente, in maxillam percussus, quòd Syllam patre nimis commendaret, taliq; patre gloriaretur. In summa ferus & truculentus ille, odia privata cum Cæsare exercuit: priórq; super insidiis & parricidio in Cæsarem, Brutum conuenit, quem inflámauit, impulitque, privatè [illegible, ~2 letters]gis inimicus Cæsari, quàm publicæ tyrannidi. Dicitur enim Brutus dominationem grauiter tulisse, sed Cassius odisse dominantem. Itaque conspiratione facta, Cassius comite Bruto, Cæsarem in curia opprimit. Cassius, deinde cum Bruto, ab Augusto & Antonio victus, desperata salute, eodem quo Cæsarem interfecerat gladio, seipsum interfecit anno mundi 3 9 2 2. ante Christum natum, 40. Vide Plut. in Cæs. & Bruto.
units.tr: Gaius Cassius, a man familiar with Brutus but of a different disposition, was restless, dishonest and an enemy of all authority, power and tyranny. Let Faustus be a witness: while still a young man, he was struck on the cheek by Cassius for praising Sulla too highly as a father and boasting of such a father. In sum, that man was savage and fierce; he pursued private hatreds against Caesar. Earlier, he met Brutus about plots and the murder of Caesar, whom he inflamed and urged on, being an enemy of Caesar more in private grievance [illegible] than out of hatred for public tyranny. For Brutus, it is said, bore the domination heavily, but Cassius hated the one who dominated. So, after a conspiracy was formed, Cassius, with Brutus as companion, cornered Caesar in the senate-house. Cassius afterwards, together with Brutus, was defeated by Augustus and Antony; having given up hope of safety, he killed himself with the same sword with which he had slain Caesar, in the year of the world 3922, about 40 years before the birth of Christ. See Plutarch in the lives of Caesar and Brutus.

units.la: BRVTVS bonarum artium disciplina & philosophiæ studiis imbutus, mores suos natura graues & humiles, ciuilibus negotiis excitans, ad bonum & æquum modestissimè ferri visus est. Pompeij partes secutus est, cuius causam quàm Cæsaris iustiorem æstimabat. Valuit primò gratia apud Cæsarem, atque quátü voluit impetrabat, sed hinc eum sodales Cassij abstraxere, ipsumque plane in perniciem adduxere. Nihilominus tamè bello ciuili Cæsar suis militibus iussit ut caueret eum occidere, sed eum volentem ad se adducerent, nolentem, liberum abire sinerent. Tandè multis ab eo acceptis beneficiis, cum parricidij illius conscius & cófors cum Cassio fuisset, eodem quo Cassius fato periit. Plut. in Bru. & Appi. li. 2.
units.tr: Brutus, steeped in the discipline of the liberal arts and the pursuits of philosophy, whose character by nature was grave and humble, and who, when engaged in civic affairs, was seen to act with the greatest moderation in matters of good and right, followed the side of Pompey, whose cause he judged more just than Caesar's. At first he had great favour with Caesar and obtained as much as he wished; but then the associates of Cassius drew him away and brought him plainly into ruin. Nevertheless, in the civil war Caesar ordered his soldiers to take care not to kill him, but, if he were willing, to bring him to himself, and if unwilling, to let him go free. At last, having received many benefits from him, and being a party to and accomplice of that murder together with Cassius, he perished by the same fate as Cassius. See Plutarch in the life of Brutus, and Appian, book 2.

units.la: HERODES Magnus,dictus Ascalonita,Antipatri Iudææ Procuratoris filius, primus fuit Iudæorum Rex ex alienigenis (nam erat Idumæus)anno mundi 3927. ante Christum natum 35. iam aliquot ante annos à Ro. Senatu Iudæorum Rex fuerat designatus.hic diligebatur ab Augusto,qui regnum eius auxit, adiecta Samaria,atque aliquot aliis vrbibus ac castellis. Herodes vicissim in honorem eius templum atque vrbem extruxit, quam de nomine eius Cæsaream vocauit. Alexandrum atque Aristobulü filios,Romæ erudiedos curauit. Arabes vicit. Templum funditus deposuit, summáq; magnificentia aliud secundum,figuram primi,construxit.Huius temporibus terrę motus in Iudæa,30000. hominum peremit. Vide Iosep.de bel.Iud.li.1.[?] ca.14.Crudelis hic,vxorem,filios,amicos, occidit, legis etiam interpretes,ac statim post Christum natum Beth-lehemitas infantes puerulos,innocentes interfecit,non redeuntibus Magis, quibus abeundi potestatem fecerat, ad Christum seruatorem nuper natum disquiredum,non tamen ex animo. Vide Matth. ca.2.& Iofe.li.Antiq.14.15.& 16.
units.tr: Herod the Great, called the Ascalonite, son of Antipater, procurator of Judaea, was the first king of the Jews of foreign origin (for he was an Idumaean), in the year of the world 3927, about 35 years before the birth of Christ; some years earlier he had already been designated king of the Jews by the Roman Senate. He was esteemed by Augustus, who enlarged his kingdom, adding Samaria and several other cities and fortresses. Herod in turn built a temple and a city in honour of Augustus, which he called Caesarea after his name. He had the sons Alexander and Aristobulus educated at Rome. He conquered the Arabs. He tore down the temple to its foundations and built another in its place, of the greatest magnificence, following the figure of the first. In his time an earthquake in Judaea destroyed 30,000 people. See Josephus, The Jewish War, book 1, chapter 14. This cruel man put to death his wife, his sons, his friends, and even the interpreters of the law, and immediately after the birth of Christ he killed the little infants of Bethlehem, innocent children, when the Magi did not return, to whom he had granted leave to depart, after they had been sent to seek out the Saviour Christ, recently born, though not with a sincere heart. See Matthew, chapter 2, and Josephus, Antiquities, books 14, 15 and 16.

units.la: MARIAMNE, filia Alexandræ,vxórque supradicti Herodis fuit,quam ille ob pulchitudinem valdè dilexit. hæc cùm casta esset,animo tamen interim satis rigido ac præfracto, meridie quadam recusauit viri amplexus, quinetiam improperauit ei parricidium. Id ægerrimè tulit Rex:quod sentiens Regis soror Salome, pincernam regium instruit qui persuadeat Regi Mariamnem ei confecisse potionem. quare indignatus Rex, de vxore supplicium sumit. Vide Iosep. lib. Antiq. 15. ca. 3.& 9. item.lib.18.cap.11.
units.tr: Mariamne, daughter of Alexandra, was the wife of the aforementioned Herod, whom he loved greatly on account of her beauty. Although she was chaste, yet her spirit was meanwhile rather unyielding and obstinate; at midday on one occasion she refused her husband's embraces, and moreover reproached him with murder. The king took this very badly. Perceiving this, Salome, the king's sister, arranged for a royal cupbearer to persuade the king that Mariamne had prepared a drink for him. Therefore the king, indignant, took punishment on his wife. See Josephus, Antiquities, book 15, chapters 3 and 9; likewise book 18, chapter 11.

units.la: C. MECOENAS à regibus Thuscis originem trahens, iuuenis poëmata scripsit. perfugium fuit Poëtarum atque oratorū: huius munificentia Vergiliū, Horatiū atq; alios cōplures ditauit, vnde Mecoenates hodie quoq; vocamus qui Poëtis faiuent. Ortos Romę habuit amœnis. vbi versari consueuit, & de liberalibus disciplinis cū amicis disceptare. ad hos sæpe diuertit Octauius, quòd à curis liberū haberet animū in eo quietis se cessu. taciturnus fuit, nec tamē interim monere ac reprehēdere Augustū dubitauit. Hic vrbis custodiis præpositus, vbi res exigeret, sanè ex somniis, resurrecturi belli ciuilis restinxit initiū, oppresso M. Lepido iuuene, forma quàm mēte meliore, qui de Augusto interficiēdo cōsilia inierat. Vide Velleiū Pat. Cri. & Su.
units.tr: Gaius Maecenas, descended from Tuscan kings, wrote poems in his youth. He was a refuge for poets and orators, and by his generosity he enriched Virgil, Horace and many others; hence we still today call those who favour poets "Maecenases." He had gardens in Rome, amoenis ortos, where he was accustomed to spend his time and to debate the liberal arts with his friends. Octavius often turned aside to these gardens, because there in quiet retreat his mind was freed from the cares of state. He was taciturn, yet he did not hesitate from time to time to advise and rebuke Augustus. Set over the city's guards, when the situation required it, he quenched, by means of dreams, the beginning of a civil war that was about to rise again, when the young M. Lepidus was put down; he was a man of handsome appearance rather than of better mind, who had planned to kill Augustus. See Velleius Paterculus and Suetonius.

units.la: VERGILIVS natus est in Vico Ande, nō procul à Mantua, parētibus sat obscuris anno mundi 3895. ante Christ. nat. 67. nec vagisse nascēdo ferūt. tam probus extitit, vt Parthenias dictus sit. valuit gratia apud Augustū, tū ob mores, tum ob poëma, vt nil vnquā ei denegarit petenti: quinimo bona cuiusdam exulis offerente Augusto recusauit Vergilius. Bucolica tribus an. Georgica 7. Aeneid. 10. an. cōscripsit. huius eclogā cūm per cantores recitatā intellexisset Cicero, dixit, magna spes altera Romæ: quæ verba postea Aeneidi inseruit Verg. Ro. populus auditis aliquādo in theatro eius versibus, surrexit vniuersus, & spectare Vergilii, veneratus est sic quasi Augustū. Porro Aeneidos tāta fuit fama, vt scriberet Prop. Cedite Rom. scriptores, cedite Graij: Nisi o quid maius nascitur Iliade. Hanc tamen Aeneida vrere voluit, & testamēto mādauit: hoc tādē ipse sibi epitaphiū fecit:
units.tr: Virgil was born in the village of Andes, not far from Mantua, of rather obscure parents, in the year of the world 3895, before the birth of Christ 67. They say he did not even cry when he was born. He was so upright that he was called Parthenias. He had great influence with Augustus, both because of his character and because of his poem, so that Augustus never refused him anything he asked; indeed, when Augustus offered him the goods of a certain exile, Virgil declined. He wrote the Bucolics in three years, the Georgics in seven, and the Aeneid in ten. When Cicero had heard one of his eclogues recited by singers, he said: a second great hope for Rome; these words Virgil later inserted into the Aeneid. The Roman people, having once heard his verses in the theatre, all rose and, as if they were looking at Augustus, paid reverence to Virgil. Moreover, the fame of the Aeneid was so great that Propertius wrote: Make way, Roman writers, make way, Greeks: something greater than the Iliad is being born. Nevertheless, Virgil wished to burn this Aeneid and commanded it in his will; he himself at last composed this epitaph for himself:

units.la: Mantua me genuit: Calabri rapuere: tenet nunc Parthenope: cecini pascua, rura, duces. Vide Cor. Tac. & Crini. Ex Augusti & amicorum munificentia possedit propè centies Sester. hoc est 2500000. aureorum. Budæ. de Asse li. 3. SIB. PHRYGIA. TIBVRTINA. SIB.
units.tr: Mantua bore me, Calabria took me, Parthenope holds me now; I sang of pastures, fields and leaders. See Cornelius Tacitus and Crinitus. From the generosity of Augustus and his friends he possessed nearly a hundred sestertii, that is, 2,500,000 gold coins. Budé, On the As, book 3.

units.la: SIBYLLA Phrygia, Ancyrae vaticinata dicitur: est autem Ancyra Asiae minoris vrbs, inter Paphlagoniā & Galatiam. Vide Lactan. li.1.ca.6. at verò de nominis Sibyllae origine sic apud Caelium Rhodig. li.14.ca.1. scriptum reperi: Dardanus ex Samo profectus, Teucrorū Regis filiā, nomine Neso, duxit vxorem, ex qua nata illi filia vaticina, nomine Sibylla, ex qua in vaticinatrices omnes propagatum sit nomen, ob theophoriae cognationem quandā. Huius Sibyllae Phrigiae haec fertur prophetia:
units.tr: The Phrygian Sibyl is said to have prophesied at Ancyra; now Ancyra is a city of Asia Minor, between Paphlagonia and Galatia. See Lactantius, book 1, chapter 6. But I have found written about the origin of the name Sibyl, as follows, in Caelius Rhodiginus, book 14, chapter 1: Dardanus, having set out from Samos, took as his wife a daughter of the king of the Teucrians, named Neso; from her a prophetic daughter was born to him, named Sibyl, and from her the name has been passed on to all female prophets, because of some kinship with the divine (theophoria). To this Phrygian Sibyl the following prophecy is attributed:

units.la: Tuba de caelo vocem luctuosum emittet, tartari[?] unque choas ostendet dehiscentibus terra: veniet ad tribunal Dei Reges omnes: Deus ipse iudicabit pios simul, & impios: demum impios in ignem mittet: qui autē pietatem coluerunt, iterum viuent. Item: flagellabit Deus potentes terra ex olympo excelsus veniet.
units.tr: A trumpet from heaven will send out a mournful voice; it will show the chaos of Tartarus as the earth opens up. All kings will come to the judgment seat of God; God himself will judge the righteous and the wicked together; at last he will send the wicked into fire, but those who have cultivated piety will live again. Likewise: God will scourge the powerful of the earth; he will come down from high Olympus.

units.la: SIBYLLA Tyburtina, siue Tyburs, proprio nomine Albunea, Tyburi olim vt Dea culta est, iuxta ripas Anienis, in cuius gurgite simulachrum eius inuentū esse dicitur, habens prae manibus librū: cuius Sibyllae sacra, Senatus Rom. in Capitoliū transtulerit. Vide Lactan. vt supra. Caeterum Sibyllarum trium statuas iuxta rostra positas, ad suam vsque aetatē perdurasse, autor est Pli. li.34.ca. 5. quaenam illae sint, non constat: attamen liceat coniicere hanc ex illis tribus vnā fuisse, cuius extaret effigies. Huic haec tribuitur prophetia:
units.tr: The Tiburtine Sibyl, or Tiburs, whose proper name was Albunea, was once worshipped at Tibur as a goddess, beside the banks of the Anio; in its whirlpool her image is said to have been found, holding a book in her hands. The Roman Senate transferred the rites of this Sibyl to the Capitol. See Lactantius, as above. Moreover, the author Pliny, book 34, chapter 5, states that statues of three Sibyls, placed beside the Rostra, survived down to his own age. Which ones they were is not certain; yet it may be conjectured that this was one of those three, whose likeness still existed. To her the following prophecy is ascribed:

units.la: Nascetur Christus in Beth-lehem, & annuntiabitur in Nazareth, regente Tauro pacifico fundatore quietis: O felix illa mater, cuius vbera ipsum lactabunt. C·OCTAVIVS PATER·AVG ACCIA·OCTAVI·AVG·MATER
units.tr: Christ will be born in Bethlehem, and will be announced in Nazareth, under the reign of the Bull, the peaceful founder of rest. O happy mother, whose breasts he will suckle. GAIUS OCTAVIUS, FATHER OF AUGUSTUS; ACCIA, MOTHER OF AUGUSTUS

units.la: C. OCTAVIVS, pater Augusti, à principio ætatis, & re & æstimatione magna fuit: amplis innutritus opibus, honores & adeptus est facilè, & egregiè administrauit. Prætor Macedoniæ, fugitiuos, reliquam Spartaci & Catilinæ manum, in itinere deleuit. Prouinciæ præfuit non minore iustitia quàm sortitudine: nam Bessis ac Thracibus magno prælio fusis, ita socios tractauit, ut epistolæ Ciceronis extét, quibus Quintum fratre, eodem tempore parum secunda fama Procōsulatum Asiæ administrantem, hortatur & moner ut imitetur in promerendis sociis, vicinum suum, hunc inquam, Octauium. Decedens Macedonia priusquam confiteri se cādidatum Consulatus posset, morte obiit repetina, superstitibus liberis, Octauia maiore, quā ex Ancharia, & Octauia minore, item Octauio, nondum Augusto, quos ex Accia suscepérat. Cōsulito C. Suetonium Tranquillum in Augusti vita.
units.tr: Gaius Octavius, father of Augustus, was from the beginning of his life great both in wealth and in esteem; brought up amid ample resources, he easily obtained honours and administered them with distinction. As praetor of Macedonia, he destroyed on his march the fugitives, the remnant of the band of Spartacus and Catiline. He governed the province with no less justice than courage: for after the Bessi and Thracians were routed in a great battle, he treated his allies so well that there survive letters of Cicero in which he urges and advises his brother Quintus, who at that same time was administering the proconsulship of Asia with little favourable repute, to imitate in winning over his allies his neighbour, this man, I mean, Octavius. Departing from Macedonia before he could declare himself a candidate for the consulship, he died a sudden death, leaving surviving children: Octavia the elder, whom he had by Ancharia, and Octavia the younger, and also Octavius, not yet Augustus, whom he had by Accia. Consult Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus in the Life of Augustus.

units.la: ACCIA, C. Octauij patris Augusti vxor, M. Accio Balbo, & Iulia, sorore C. Cæsaris, genita est. Balbus paterna stirpe Aricinus, multis in familia Senatoriis imaginibus clarus, à matre Magnum Pompeium arctissimo contingebat gradu: functúsque honore prætūrae, inter 20. viros agrum Campanum plebi, Iulia lege, diuisit. Suet. in Aug. fuit hæc Accia imperatoris Augusti mater.
units.tr: Accia, wife of Gaius Octavius, father of Augustus, was born of Marcus Accius Balbus and Julia, sister of Gaius Caesar. Balbus, on his father's side, was from Aricia, and was famous in his family for many senatorial images; through his mother he was connected by a very close degree to Pompey the Great. Having held the office of praetor, he divided the Campanian land among the plebs, among twenty men, by the Julian law. Suetonius, in the Life of Augustus. This Accia was the mother of the emperor Augustus.

units.la: OCTAVIVS Augustus, C. Cæsaris auunculi hæres, Romæ imperat anno mundi 3921. ante Christum natum 41. Hic primùm cum M. Antonio, Marcóq; Lepido, dein tantùm cum Antonio 12. ferè annos, nouissimè verò 44. solus remp. tenuit. Antonium vicit nauali pugna apud Actium. Deinde Romano adiecit imperio Ægyptum, Cantabriam, Dalmatiam, sæpe antè victam, sed penitus tunc subactam: Pánoniam: Aquitaniã, Illyricum: Rhetiam, Vindelicos, & Salassos in Alpibus: omnésque Ponti maritimas ciuitates. Armeniã à Parthis recepit: obsides, quod nulli antea, Persæ ei dedérùt: quin etiam signa Romana, quæ Crasso victo ademerant reddiderunt. Scythæ & Indi, quibus antea Romanorum nomen incognitum fuerat, munera & legatos ad eum miserunt. Galatia sub hoc prouincia facta est, cùm antea regnum fuisset. Multi Reges ad eum ex regnis suis venerunt, ut ei obsequerëtur. Hic in bello felix, in pace moderatus, in cunctos liberalis, in amicos fidus extitit, quos tantis euexit honoribus ut penè fastigio suo æquaret. Nullo tempore res Romana magis floruit. Ab initio principatus eius ad finem usque 56. anni numerantur:anno autem 42. imperij huius, natus est Dominus noster Iesus Christus. Vide Euang. Lucæ 2. cap. item Sueto. in August. & Eutro. li 7:
units.tr: Octavius Augustus, heir of his uncle Gaius Caesar, ruled at Rome in the year of the world 3921, before the birth of Christ 41. He first held power together with Marcus Antonius and Marcus Lepidus, then with Antonius alone for about twelve years, and at last, for 44 years, he governed the state alone. He defeated Antony in a naval battle at Actium. Then he added to the Roman empire Egypt, Cantabria, Dalmatia, which had often been conquered before but was then thoroughly subdued, Pannonia, Aquitania, Illyricum, Raetia, the Vindelici and the Salassi in the Alps, and all the maritime cities of the Pontus. He recovered Armenia from the Parthians; the Persians gave him hostages, which they had given to no one before; indeed they also returned the Roman standards which they had taken when Crassus was defeated. The Scythians and the Indians, to whom the name of the Romans had previously been unknown, sent gifts and envoys to him. Galatia was made a province under him, though before it had been a kingdom. Many kings came to him from their kingdoms to pay him homage. He was fortunate in war, moderate in peace, generous to all, and faithful to his friends, whom he raised to such great honours that he nearly equalled them to himself. At no time did the Roman state flourish more. From the beginning of his rule to its end, 56 years are counted; and in the forty-second year of his reign our Lord Jesus Christ was born. See the Gospel of Luke, chapter 2; also Suetonius in the Life of Augustus, and Eutropius, book 7.

units.la: CLAVDIA priuigna Antonij, Fuluiæ ex P. Clodio filia, uixdum nubilis, uxor fuit Augusti, quam dimisit[?] intactã adhuc & virginë, exorta simultate cum Fuluia socru: móxque Scriboniam accepit.Sueto.in Aug. SCRIBONIA AVGVSTI VXOR LIVIA DRVSILLA AVGVSTI VXOR
units.tr: Claudia, stepdaughter of Antony, daughter of Fulvia by Publius Clodius, scarcely of marriageable age, was the wife of Augustus; he sent her away still untouched and a virgin, after a quarrel had arisen with Fulvia, her mother-in-law; and soon he took Scribonia. Suetonius, in the Life of Augustus. SCRIBONIA, WIFE OF AUGUSTUS; LIVIA DRUSILLA, WIFE OF AUGUSTUS

units.la: SCRIBONIA Imperatoris Augusti vxor fuit, postquàm ille dimisisset supradictâ Claudiam, quæ illi in matrimonium pacta fuerat, sicuti diximus. Porrò Scribonia hæc nupserat ante duobus Consularibus, & ex altero quoque mater fuerat: cum hac etiâ diuortium fecit Augustus, pertæsus (vt scripsit) morum eius peruersitatem: ex hac filiam Iuliam suscepit. Vide C. Suetonium Tranquillum in vita Octauij Augusti, Romanorum imperatoris secundi.
units.tr: Scribonia was the wife of the emperor Augustus, after he had put away the aforementioned Claudia, who had been betrothed to him in marriage, as we have said. Moreover, this Scribonia had previously been married to two men of consular rank, and by the second she had also become a mother; Augustus also divorced her, being weary (as he wrote) of the perversity of her character; by her he had a daughter, Julia. See Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus in the Life of Octavius Augustus, the second Roman emperor.

units.la: LIVIA Drusilla vxor quoque fuit Augusti, quam matrimonio Tiberij Neronis, Imperatoris Tiberij patris, & quidem prægnantem abduxit, dilexitque ac probauit vnice ac perseueranter. Ex hac nullos suscepit liberos, cùm maximè cuperet: infans (is est Drusus Tiberij Imperatoris frater, ac Claudij Cæsaris, qui Tiberio successit, pater) qui conceptus erat, immaturus est editus. in oculis Liuiæ, & in hac voce defecit Augustus: Liuia, nostri coniugij memor viue, ac vale: sortitus exitum facilem, & qualem semper optauerat. Vide Suetonium Tranquillum in Octauio Augusto, & secudi libri huius operis paginâ quintam.
units.tr: Livia Drusilla was also a wife of Augustus; he took her away from her marriage to Tiberius Nero, the father of the emperor Tiberius, and indeed while she was pregnant; he loved and approved of her alone and constantly. By her he had no children, though he most earnestly desired them; the infant who had been conceived was born prematurely (this is Drusus, brother of the emperor Tiberius and father of Claudius Caesar, who succeeded Tiberius). In the sight of Livia, and with these words, Augustus died: Livia, mindful of our marriage, live on and farewell; he met with an easy end, and such as he had always wished for. See Suetonius Tranquillus in the Life of Octavius Augustus, and the fifth page of the second book of this work.

units.la: SIBYLLA Europa, siue Europea, vulgò vndecima inter Sibyllas, hoc est fatidicas, & Deo plenas, consiliíque diuini participes mulieres annumeratur. De hac non memini me vsquam quidquam apud autores legisse, nisi quòd libellus ille vetus, qui de Sibyllarum vaticiniis est, Sibyllæ huic hanc tribuit prophetiam:
units.tr: The European Sibyl, or Sibylla Europea, is commonly counted eleventh among the Sibyls, that is, the women who prophesied, who were filled with God and shared in the divine counsel. I do not recall having read anything about her anywhere in the authors, except that the old little book on the prophecies of the Sibyls attributes to this Sibyl the following prophecy:

units.la: Veniet ille, & transfibit montes & colles, & latices Syluarum olympi: regnabit in paupertate, & dominabitur in silentio: & egredietur de vtero virginis.
units.tr: He will come, and will pass over mountains and hills, and the streams of the woods of Olympus; he will reign in poverty, and rule in silence; and he will come forth from the womb of a virgin.

units.la: SIBYLLA Ægyptia, quam supradictus libellus Sibyllam Agrippa vocat, ab Æliano inter quatuor Sibyllas enumeratur: quæ sunt hoc ordine, Erythræa, Samia, Ægyptia, & Sardiana. Sibyllas porrò in iis quæ de Christo, aut aliis ad humanā salutem spectatibus, sunt vaticinatæ, probabile habet D. Augu.(seu bonæ fuerint seu malæ) à Deo edoctas fuisse: nā prophetiæ donum bonis esse commune ac malis. Vide S. August. de ciui. Dei li.18.ca.23. & Cæl. Rhodig. li.21.ca.37. nec me fugit de quadam Sibylla mentionem fecisse Diod.Sicu.lib.5. Huius Ægyptiæ Sibyllæ hæc circunfertur prophetia:
units.tr: The Egyptian Sibyl, whom the aforementioned little book calls the Sibyl Agrippa, is listed by Aelian among four Sibyls, which are in this order: the Erythraean, the Samian, the Egyptian, and the Sardian. Holy Augustine holds that the Sibyls, in what they prophesied about Christ or about other matters pertaining to human salvation, were taught by God (whether their prophecies were good or bad), for the gift of prophecy is common to good and bad alike. See Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 18, chapter 23, and Caelius Rhodiginus, book 21, chapter 37. Nor am I unaware that Diodorus Siculus, book 5, made mention of a certain Sibyl. The following prophecy is circulated under the name of this Egyptian Sibyl:

units.la: Inuisibile verbum palpabitur, & germinabit ut radix, & siccabitur ut folium, & non apparebit venustas eius. &c.
units.tr: The invisible Word shall be touched, and shall sprout like a root, and shall wither like a leaf, and its beauty shall not appear. &c.

units.la: M. AGRIPPA. L. F. COS. III [?]
units.tr: M. AGRIPPA, SON OF L., CONSUL FOR THE THIRD TIME [?]
JULIA, DAUGHTER OF AUGUSTUS, WIFE OF M. AGRIPPA [?]

units.la: M. AGRIPPA in pedes dicitur ex vtero matris egressus, vnde nomen auspicatus sit vnico felicitatis exēplo, quanquam ille plurima sit passus, duabus susceptis Agrippinis: quibus C. Caligula & Nero, principes, totidem generis humani faces geniti sunt. Hic gener fuit Augusti, coronaque nauali ab eo donari meruit bello Actiaco, anno mundi 3930. ante Christum natum 32. de quo Verg.lib.8.Æne.
units.tr: Marcus Agrippa is said to have come out of his mother's womb feet first, whence he took his name as the one unique example of good fortune; although he suffered very many things, having married two Agrippinas, by whom were born the emperors Gaius Caligula and Nero, two torches of the human race. He was son-in-law of Augustus, and deserved to be given the naval crown by him in the war at Actium, in the year of the world 3930, before the birth of Christ 32. Concerning him, Virgil, Aeneid book 8:
On the other side Agrippa, with the winds and the gods favorable.

units.la: Altera Agrippinarum, nempe filia Agrippæ huius, nupsit Germanico, quæ peperit C.Caligulâ altera verò, neptis ex filia, Domitio Neroni primum nupsit, ex quo Neronē peperit, deinde Claudio Cæsari, quem postea boleto sustulit. Hic M. Agrippa aquam Marciam, omniū salubérrimâ, Romæ restituit: compluraque alia præstitit, de quibus vide Plinium li.31.ca.3. atque aliis in locis, maximè li.16.ca.4. & lib.7.ca.8. Fuerunt alij Agrippæ, vt Menenius, item filius Aristobuli, à Tiberio coniectus in carcerem, & à C. Caligula liberatus, Rexque Iudææ factus: de quo vide in 2.huius operis parte, pag.14.
units.tr: The other of the Agrippinas, namely the daughter of this Agrippa, married Germanicus, and bore Gaius Caligula; the other, a granddaughter through a daughter, first married Domitius Ahenobarbus, by whom she bore Nero, and then married the emperor Claudius, whom she later removed with a mushroom. This M. Agrippa restored the Marcian aqueduct at Rome, the most healthful of all waters, and accomplished many other things, about which see Pliny, book 31, chapter 3, and elsewhere, especially book 16, chapter 4, and book 7, chapter 8. There were other Agrippas, such as Menenius, and also the son of Aristobulus, who was thrown into prison by Tiberius, freed by Gaius Caligula, and made king of Judea; on him see in the second part of this work, page 14.

units.la: IVLIA Augusti & Scriboniæ filia, quæ primùm pacta fuerat Marcello adulescenti vt is obiit, M. Agrippæ supradicto nupsit: quo defuncto, Tiberio, Augusti priuigno, nupsit, qui coactus est ab Augusto prægnatem uxorē, & ex qua iam pater erat, dimittere: ut in Tiberio dicemus. Hanc omnibus probris contaminatam, relegauit Augustus per quinquennium: usum vini, & delicatiorem cultum ei ademit: neque adiri à quoquam nisi se consulto permisit. hæc Agrippinam peperit, quam Germanico uxoris suæ nepoti collocauit Augustus, ex quo Agrippina secundam alteram Agrippinam peperit, Neronis matrē. Sueto, in Augusto. Vide item secundam huius operis partem, pag. sexta & undecima. M. ANTONIVS ΚΛΕΟΠΑΤΡΑ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΙΑ [?]
units.tr: JULIA, daughter of Augustus and Scribonia, who was first betrothed to the young Marcellus, and after his death married the aforementioned M. Agrippa; when he died, she married Tiberius, stepson of Augustus, who was compelled by Augustus to dismiss his wife, who was already pregnant and by whom he was already a father, as we shall say under Tiberius. Augustus banished her, stained with every disgrace, for five years; he took from her the use of wine and her more refined way of life, and did not permit anyone to approach her unless he had consented. She bore Agrippina, whom Augustus gave in marriage to Germanicus, the grandson of his wife; from this Agrippina came another Agrippina, the second, the mother of Nero. Suetonius, in Augustus. See also the second part of this work, pages 6 and 11. M. ANTONIUS, CLEOPATRA, QUEEN [?]

units.la: M. ANTONIVS Consul, partiu Cæsaris, ciuilibus bellis opprimere Cęsaris interfectores, quibus Senatus fauebat, conabatur: turbata hic rep. multáq; scelera cõmittes, à Senatu hostis iudicatus est. missi sunt aduersus eum Cos. Pása [?] & Hircius & Augustus 18. annorum: vincitur, sed Lepido operâ dáte, cum Augusto pacè facit: diuiditur respub. Antonius Asiam, Pōtum, orienté sortitur: deinde repudiata sorore Augusti, Cleopatram vxorem ducit, ex qua suscipit vnico partu Solè & Lunam: (sic enim vocauit gemellos, marem & femellam.) cõtra Persas pugnat, vincit. Cleopatra itaq; muliebri cupiditate optás Romæ quoque regnare, Antoniũ ad suscipiendũ bellum ciuile cogit: vincitur ab Augusto nauali pugna, apud Actium, in Epiro: fugit in Ægyptum, seipsum interimit. Cleopatra aspidem admittit, cuius veneno extinguitur, anno mundi 3 9 3 4. ante Christum natum 28. Vide Eutr.li.7.Suet.in Octa.
units.tr: M. ANTONIUS, consul, as partner of Caesar, tried to crush by civil wars the assassins of Caesar, whom the Senate favored; disturbing the commonwealth and committing many crimes, he was declared a public enemy by the Senate. The consuls Pansa [?] and Hirtius were sent against him, and Augustus, aged eighteen. He was defeated, but through the work of Lepidus he made peace with Augustus; the commonwealth was divided. Antony received Asia, Pontus, and the East by lot; then, having put away the sister of Augustus, he married Cleopatra, by whom in a single birth he had a son and a daughter, the Sun and the Moon (for so he named the twins, a male and a female). He fought against the Persians and conquered them. Cleopatra, then, driven by a womanly desire to rule at Rome too, forced Antony to undertake a civil war; he was defeated by Augustus in a naval battle at Actium, in Epirus; he fled to Egypt and killed himself. Cleopatra admitted an asp, by whose poison she died, in the year of the world 3934, before the birth of Christ 28. See Eutropius, book 7; Suetonius, in Augustus.

units.la: CLEOPATRA Ægypti regina, non vsqueadeo eleganti forma præstitit: verùm moribus suauis. ac facundia, forma adiuta, omnes in admirationem trahebat. lingua sua velut instrumento plurium chordarum, apud quasuis gentes promptè vtebatur: paucis nationibus per interpretem loquebatur. Hæc anno mundi 3 9 2 3. ante Christum natum 39. ad Antonium incredibili pompa per Cydnum amnem nauigauit: erat enim aurea puppis, vela purpurea pandebantur, remi argentei ad fistulæ tibiæque modos agitabantur: ipsa regina sub tentorio aurato requiescens, ad similitudinem Veneris ornata erat: pueri vtrinque collocati pictis Cupidinibus persimiles: puellæ insignes, Nereidum & Gratiarũ stolis, gubernaculis incumbebãt, rudentibus annitebantur: ancillæ ornatis. omnes ripas fluuij complebant vaporibus.Plu.in.Anto. M·MARCELLVS [?] OCTAVIA AVG.SOR [?]
units.tr: CLEOPATRA, queen of Egypt, did not excel in beauty to such a degree, but was pleasant in her manners and eloquent; her beauty, aided by her eloquence, drew everyone into admiration. She used her tongue, like an instrument of many strings, readily among all nations; she spoke through an interpreter with only a few peoples. In the year of the world 3923, before the birth of Christ 39, she sailed to Antony along the river Cydnus with incredible pomp: for her barge was golden, purple sails were spread, silver oars were moved to the tones of pipes and flutes; the queen herself, reclining under a golden canopy, was adorned like Venus; boys were placed on either side, very like painted Cupids; attractive girls, dressed as Nereids and Graces, leaned on the rudders and tugged at the ropes; attendants stood by in ornate dress. All the banks of the river were filled with perfumes. Plutarch, in Antony. M. MARCELLUS [?], OCTAVIA, SISTER OF AUGUSTUS [?]

units.la: C. MARCELLVS, Octauiæ,sororis Augusti vir, ex ea Marcellū suscepit, qui ab Augusto adoptatus est,anno 16.ætatis,incidítque in valetudiné,ac 18.obiit, cum ædilitatē gereret. huic tantum pueritiā egresso(vt inquit Suet.)Augustus Iuliam suam filiā ex Scribonia nuptui dedit,deinde,vt is obiit, Marco Agrippæ.Huius adolescentis generosam indolē describit Vergilius 6.Æneidos,deflens immaturū eius obitum aliquot versibus,quos recitauit coram Augusto & Octauia:sed vbi tandē ad nomē Marcelli ventū est,perculsa dolore filij demortui mater, decidit,quasi intermortua,filetióq; imperato,iussit pro singulis versibus dena sestertia numerari,quæ valent ducentos aureos. in summa 5000.aureorum pro 18.versibus reportauit,qui sic incipiunt apud Verg.li.6.Æne.ad calcem:
units.tr: GAIUS MARCELLUS, husband of Octavia, sister of Augustus, had by her a son Marcellus, who was adopted by Augustus; in his sixteenth year he fell ill and died at eighteen, while he was holding the office of aedile. Augustus, as Suetonius says, gave his daughter Julia, whom he had by Scribonia, in marriage to this youth, when he had just passed out of boyhood; then, after he died, to Marcus Agrippa. Virgil describes the noble character of this youth in book 6 of the Aeneid, lamenting his untimely death in several verses, which he recited in the presence of Augustus and Octavia. But when at last the name of Marcellus was reached, the mother, struck with grief for her dead son, fell down as if she had died; and with silence ordered, she commanded that for each single verse ten thousand sesterces be counted out, which amount to two hundred gold pieces. In all, for the eighteen verses she received 5000 gold pieces. The verses, which begin in Virgil, Aeneid book 6, near the end, are these:

units.la: Atque hic Aeneas(unà namque ire videbat Egregium forma iuuenem,& fulgentibus armis)&c.
units.tr: And here Aeneas (for he saw a youth walking with him, remarkable in form and in shining arms) &c.

units.la: Multum sanè abest ut tam officiosos ac munificos se hodie in Musas præstêt principes viri, quàm se erga Verg. præstitit Octauia, quæ etiam in filij memoriâ ac decus,bibliothecâ extruxit: Augustus verò theatrū huius Marcelli nomine inscripsit. Vide Sue. in Aug. & Plut. in M.Cl.Marcello, de quo diximus supra pag.138.cuius progenies ad hunc C.Marcellum propagatur.
units.tr: Surely it is far from true that the men of rank today show themselves so dutiful and generous toward the Muses as Octavia showed herself toward Virgil; she even built a library in memory and honor of her son. Augustus, however, inscribed the theatre with the name of this Marcellus. See Suetonius, in Augustus, and Plutarch, in the life of M. Claudius Marcellus, of whom we spoke above on page 138, whose line descends to this Gaius Marcellus.

units.la: OCTAVIA Augusti soror,non ex eadē matre(hæc enim ex Ancharia, ille ex Tatia natus est)forma, moribus, ingenio præstans, nupsit Antonio (mortuo C.Marcello piore marito) quam susceptis etiam ille ex ea liberis, dimisit,superinducta Cleopatra. Vide Plutar.in Anto. TIAVRVS[?] IVBRE[?] VARVS QVINTILIVS
units.tr: OCTAVIA, sister of Augustus, not from the same mother (for she was born of Ancharia, he of Tatia), outstanding in beauty, character and talent, married Antony (after the death of her first husband, Gaius Marcellus); although she had children by him too, he dismissed her, having taken Cleopatra as a new wife. See Plutarch, in Antony. TAURUS [?], IUBRE [?], VARUS QUINTILIUS

units.la: TAVRVS Cæsaris Augusti præfectus,totâ pene Siciliam ferro perterritam,in fidem recepit.44.legiones sub unius tunc imperio Augusti erát:milites multitudine ferociores quosdam pro ambiendis agris tumultus excitauerunt, sed Cæsar animo ingens,20000. militum exautorauit,30000. seruorum dominis restituit,6000. quorum domini non extabant,in crucem egit. Vide Suet.in Augusto.Id factum est circa annum mundi 3932. ante Christum natum 30. Cæterùm de ratione legionum Romanarum Consule Vegetium, & Budæum de Asse,li.3.
units.tr: TAURUS, prefect of Caesar Augustus, received almost the whole of Sicily, terrified by the sword, into his protection. At that time 44 legions were under the sole command of Augustus; certain soldiers, more fierce in their numbers, stirred up disturbances in order to seize lands; but Caesar, of great spirit, dismissed 20,000 soldiers, restored 30,000 slaves to their masters, and crucified 6000 whose masters could not be found. See Suetonius, in Augustus. This took place about the year of the world 3932, before the birth of Christ 30. Concerning the organization of the Roman legions, see Vegetius, and Budé, On the As, book 3.

units.la: QVINTILIVS Varus nobilis Romanus fuit, qui Dux expeditionis Germanicæ(perfecerat siquidem illum tribus legionibus Augustus) ab Arminio dolo circunuentus, cum suis legionibus est interfectus: qua clade pene exitiali, usqueadeo cōsternatum ferunt Augustum,ut per cōtinuos menses,barba, capilloque summisso,caput interdum foribus illideret,vociferans, Quintili Vare,legiones redde:diémque cladis quotanis mœstum habuerit,ac lugubre. Is Varus fuit Vergilij amicus, cuius meminit Ecloga 6.& 9.honorificè,his,atque aliis versibus.
units.tr: QUINTILIUS VARUS was a noble Roman, who was commander of the German expedition (for Augustus had indeed entrusted him with three legions); surrounded by deceit by Arminius, he was killed with his legions.
