The disaster was almost ruinous, and they say Augustus was so dismayed that for months on end, with beard and hair unkempt, he would sometimes beat his head against the doors, crying out, "Quintilius Varus, give back my legions!" and he kept the day of the defeat every year as a sad and mournful day. This Varus was a friend of Virgil, whom Eclogues 6 and 9 mention honorably, with these and other verses.

units.la: Vare tuum nomen (superet modo Mantua nobis: Mantua, væ miseræ, nimium vicina Cremonæ) Cantantes sublime ferent ad sydera cygni.
units.tr: Varus, your name (if only Mantua remains to us: Mantua, alas for the wretched, too close to Cremona) the singing swans will raise to the stars on high.

units.la: Cæsus est cum suis legionibus Varus à Germanis anno mundi 3972.decem annis post Christum natum. Sueto.in Augusti.ipse Varus infelici dextera mortem sibi consciuit.Cor.Taci.li.1.
units.tr: Varus, with his legions, was slain by the Germans in the year of the world 3972, ten years after the birth of Christ. See Suetonius, in Augustus. Varus himself, with an unlucky right hand, brought death upon himself. See Cornelius Tacitus, book 1.

units.la: Hactenus huius operis pars prior : sequetur subinde posterior.
units.tr: So far the first part of this work; the second part will follow in due course.

NATIVITAS D. NOSTRI SALVATORIS IESV CHRISTI PLANE est praenuntiata, ac praedicta ab ipsis Prophetis, e quibus nonnulla quae sequuntur de- cerpsimus.
units.tr: THE NATIVITY OF OUR SAVIOUR JESUS CHRIST has been clearly foretold and predicted by the Prophets themselves, from whom we have excerpted some of the passages that follow.

units.la: Non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, nec Dux de femore eius, donec veniat qui mittendus est: & ipse erit expectatio Gentium. Genes.cap. 49.
units.tr: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a ruler from between his feet, until he come who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the Gentiles. Gen. ch. 49.

units.la: Ecce Virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabitur nomen eius Emanuel: quod est interpretatum, nobiscum Deus. Isa. cap.7. & Matthaei cap.1.
units.tr: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us. Isa. ch. 7. and Matt. ch. 1.

units.la: Paruulus natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis. Isa.9.cap.
units.tr: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given. Isa. ch. 9.

units.la: Exulta, & lauda habitatio Sion: quia magnus in medio tui Sanctus Israel. Isa.cap.12.
units.tr: Rejoice and sing, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in the midst of thee is the Holy One of Israel. Isa. ch. 12.

units.la: Et tu Beth-leem terra Iuda, nequaquam minima es in principibus Iuda: ex te enim exiet Dux, qui regat populum meum Israel. Micheae cap.5. & Matth. 2.
units.tr: And thou, Bethlehem, land of Judah, art not the least among the princes of Judah, for out of thee shall come a ruler who shall govern my people Israel. Mic. ch. 5. and Matt. 2.

units.la: Sic Deus dilexit mundum ut filium suum unigenitum daret: ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Ioan.cap.3.
units.tr: For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. John ch. 3.

units.la: Lauda, & laetare filia Sion: quia ecce ego venio, & habitabo in medio tui, ait Dominus. Zachariae cap.2.
units.tr: Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the Lord. Zech. ch. 2.

units.la: SALVATOR noster Jesus CHRISTUS, verus atque unicus Dei filius secundum essentiam divinam, natus est ex Maria virgine, quemadmodum ei in Nazareth Angelus Gabriel praedixerat, anno mundi 3962. imperij Augusti 42. ab urbe Roma condita, 752. Olympiade 194. anno regni Herodis Ascalonitae 35. Natus est autem cooperante Spiritu sancto, in Beth-leem, civitate Judaeae. Porro simulatque natus est Christus, pannis eum involuit virgo mater, & reclinavit in praesepio, quia non erat ei locus in diversorio. Et pastores erant in regione eadem vigilantes, & custodientes vigilias noctis super gregem suum. Et ecce Angelus Domini astitit iuxta illos, & claritas Dei circumfulsit illos, & timuerunt timore magno: & dixit illis Angelus, Nolite timere: ecce enim evangelizo vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit omni populo: quia natus est vobis hodie Salvator qui est Christus Dominus, in civitate David. & hoc vobis signum: Invenietis (inquit) infantem pannis involutum, & positum in praesepio. finita legatione, subito facta est cum Angelo multitudo militiae coelestis, laudantium Deum & dicentium, Gloria in altissimis Deo, & in terra pax hominibus. Porro ut discesserunt ab eis Angeli in coelum, pastores locuti sunt adinvicem: Transeamus usque Beth-leem & videamus quae nuntiata sunt: statim itaque profecti, invenerunt puerum cum Maria matre positum in praesepio: & omnes qui haec audierunt, mirati sunt. Maria autem conservabat omnia verba haec, conferens in corde suo. Et reverti sunt pastores glorificantes & laudantes Deum. Luc. 1. & 2. cap. Haec autem facta sunt anno 42. imperij Octavij Augusti, ut praedictum à me est. R.[?]IVD ARCHELAVS GLAPHIRE
units.tr: Our SAVIOUR Jesus CHRIST, the true and only Son of God according to the divine essence, was born of the virgin Mary, as the angel Gabriel had foretold to her in Nazareth, in the year of the world 3962, the 42nd year of the reign of Augustus, 752 years from the founding of the city of Rome, in the 194th Olympiad, in the 35th year of the reign of Herod the Ascalonite. He was born, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, in Bethlehem, a city of Judea. Moreover, as soon as Christ was born, the virgin mother wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for him in the inn. And there were shepherds in the same region, watching and keeping the night watches over their flock. And behold, the angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone round about them, and they feared with great fear. And the angel said to them, Fear not, for behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be for all the people; for today in the city of David there is born to you a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord. And this shall be a sign to you: you will find (he says) an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger. When the message was finished, suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men. And when the angels had gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, Let us go over to Bethlehem and see these things which have come to pass; so they went at once and found the child with Mary his mother, lying in the manger. And all who heard these things marvelled. But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God. Luke chs. 1 and 2. These things happened in the 42nd year of the reign of Octavius Augustus, as I have said before. R.[?]IVD ARCHELAUS GLAPHYRA

units.la: ARCHELAVS magni Herodis Ascalonitæ filius, succesit patri in regno Iudæorum anno mundi 3964. post Christum natum 2. Augustus imperator Archelaum Idumææ, Iudææ,& Samariæ: Antipam, qui & Herodes, Galilææ: Philippum Gaulanitidis, Trachonitidis, Bathaniæ, & Paneados Tetrarchas ex testamento Herodis designauit. Hic Archelaus in ipsis regni auspiciis modestus admodum, noluit Rex appellari, donec confirmaretur ab Imperatore, apud quem ab Antipatro fratre accusatus, absoluitur. Confirmatus Tetrarcha, male administrauit. Accusatus iterum apud Imperatorem, exilio damnatur, & relegatur in Galilæam: postea Cyrenius ac post eum Pilatus Romanorum nomine Iudæam administrant. Iose. lib. Antiq. 17. cap. 10. vsque ad finem 17. & lib. 2. de bel. Iudæa.cap. 4. Regnauit Archelaus annis nouem, & desiit regnum Iudæorum: nam [?]Iudæa in prouinciam redacta, Syriæ tunc iuncta est. Iose. lib. 17. Antiq. ca. 19.
units.tr: ARCHELAUS, son of Herod the Ascalonite the Great, succeeded his father in the kingdom of the Jews in the year of the world 3964, two years after Christ's birth. The Emperor Augustus appointed Archelaus over Idumaea, Judea and Samaria; Antipas, also called Herod, over Galilee; and Philip over Gaulanitis, Trachonitis, Batanaea and Paneas, as tetrarchs, according to the will of Herod. This Archelaus, very modest at the outset of his reign, did not wish to be called king until he should be confirmed by the Emperor; accused before him by his brother Antipater, he was acquitted. Confirmed as tetrarch, he governed badly. Accused a second time before the Emperor, he was condemned to exile and banished to Gaul; afterwards Cyrenius, and after him Pilate, administered Judea in the name of the Romans. Josephus, Antiquities book 17, chapter 10 to the end of 17, and Jewish War book 2, chapter 4. Archelaus reigned nine years, and the kingdom of the Jews ceased; for Judea was reduced to a province and then joined to Syria. Josephus, Antiquities book 17, chapter 19.

units.la: GLAPHYRA Alexãdri Cappadocum regis filia, nupsit primùm Alexandro fratri Archelai supradicti, deinde Iubæ Maurorum Regi, deinde ipsi etiam Archelao, qui contra legem Mariam priorem vxorem dimisit. præterea susceperat ex Glaphyra filios Alexander, huius Archelai frater: quare apparuit vxori in somnis exprobrans ei in hæc verba: Nunc confirmas prouerbium, fidem mulieribus non habendam: nonne mihi iureiurando constricta es, & iugali fœdere virgo sociata? post susceptos etiam filios (chara pignora) amoris nostri oblita es, iterum nubens, imò tertiò, atque cum meo fratre: nunquam tamen ego tui obliuiscar: quin liberabo te opprobriis,& efficiam vt mea, sicut fuisti, in perpetuum sis.ac post paucos dies hæc obiit.Iose. lib. 17. ca. 19.
units.tr: GLAPHYRA, daughter of Alexander, king of the Cappadocians, first married Alexander, brother of the aforesaid Archelaus, then Juba, king of the Mauritanians, and then Archelaus himself, who against the law had put away his former wife Mariamne. Moreover, she had borne Alexander, Archelaus's brother, sons by him; wherefore he appeared to her in her sleep, reproaching her in these words: "Now you confirm the proverb that women are not to be trusted. Were you not bound to me by oath, and joined to me in marriage as a virgin by a bond of wedlock? After we had even had children, dear pledges, you forgot our love, marrying again, and a third time, and with my brother. Yet I will never forget you; rather I will free you from disgrace and make you mine, as you once were, for ever." And a few days later she died. Josephus, Antiquities book 17, chapter 19.

units.la: CL. TIBERIUS pater Tiberij Cæsaris, Quæstor sub C. Cæsare, Alexandrino bello classi præpositus, plurimum ad victoriam cōtulit: quare & pontifex in locum P. Scipionis substitutus, & ad deducēdas in Galliā colonias, in queis Narbona & Arelate erat, missus est. Cæsare occiso, cunctis turbarum metu abolitione facta: decernentibus, etiā de præmiis tyrānicidarum referendum cēsuit. Tandē indignē ferens nec statim se in conspectum Sexti Pompeij admissum, & fasciūm usu prohibitū, ad M. Antonium traiecit in Achaiam: cum quo breui, reconciliata inter omnes pace, Romam rediit, uxoremq; Liviam Drusillam, & tunc grauidā, & antè iam apud se Tiberium enixam, petenti Augusto concessit: nec multò post diem obiit, utroq; liberorum superstite, Tiberio, Drusoque Neronis. Sueto. in Tiber.
units.tr: CL. TIBERIUS, father of the Emperor Tiberius Caesar, quaestor under Gaius Caesar, placed in command of the fleet in the Alexandrine war, contributed greatly to the victory; wherefore he was also substituted as pontifex in the place of P. Scipio, and was sent to conduct colonies into Gaul, among which were Narbo and Arelate. After Caesar was killed, an amnesty was declared for all because of fear of disturbances, and when the decrees concerning rewards for the tyrannicides were being passed, he thought the matter should be referred back. At last, resenting that he had not been admitted at once into the presence of Sextus Pompeius, and that the use of the fasces was forbidden him, he crossed over to Achaia to Mark Antony; with whom, after a peace had soon been restored among all, he returned to Rome, and yielded his wife Livia Drusilla, who was then pregnant and had already borne him Tiberius, to Augustus, who asked for her. Not long after he died, leaving two surviving children, Tiberius and Drusus Nero. Suetonius, Tiberius.

units.la: LIVIA Drusilla Cl. Tiberij supradicti uxor, Tiberij imperatoris mater fuit, de qua dictū à nobis est in fine prioris partis huius operis. hanc prægnantem abduxit Augustus: porrò qui cōceptus erat, infans, immaturus est editus: is est Drusus Tiberij Imperatoris frater minor natu, ac Claudij Cæsaris, qui Caligulæ successit, pater: fuit alter Drusus Agrippinæ & Tibe. Impe, filius. Cæterum in osculis Liviæ, & in hac voce defecit Augustus, Livia nostra coniugi memor vive, ac vale.
units.tr: LIVIA Drusilla, wife of the aforesaid Cl. Tiberius, was the mother of the Emperor Tiberius, of whom we spoke at the end of the first part of this work. Augustus took her away while she was pregnant; and the child that had been conceived was born prematurely. This is Drusus, the younger brother of the Emperor Tiberius, and the father of the Emperor Claudius, who succeeded Caligula; there was another Drusus, son of Agrippina and of the Emperor Tiberius. Moreover, at the kisses of Livia, and with these words, Augustus expired: Livia, remember our marriage, live and farewell.

units.la: CL. TIBERIVS Nero Imperator Romanorum tertius, succedens Augusto, imperauit anno mûdi 3977. post Christum natum, an. 15. Hic principatu diu recusauit impudentissimo animo, nunc adhortates amicos increpans, vt ignaros quanta belua esset imperium: nunc precante Senatu, & procumbente sibi ad genua, ambiguis responsis, & callida cunctatione suspendes. Tandem quasi coactus, & querens miseram & onerosam sibi iniungi seruitutem, habenas rerum suscepit: nec tamen aliter quam vt depositurû se quandoq; spem faceret. Ad Orientê exercitum duxit: regnû Armeniae Tigrani restituit: signa quae Crasso ademerant Parthi, recepit. Comatâ Galliam anno fere rexit: Rheticum, Vindelicum, Pannonicum ac Germanicû bellum gessit, Germanico bello 40000. dediticiorum traiecit in Galliam, iuxtaq; ripâ Rheni sedibus assignatis collocauit: quas ob res ouans Romae antequam imperaret triumphauit. adulationes initio auersatus est: huius quoque vox illa est, bonus pastor pecus tondet, non devorat. Ipse demum ingenti socordia & tyrannide imperiû administrauit: quosdâ Reges per blandicias euocatos, non remisit. Luxuriae itaq; ac caedibus vacans, Caligulae nepotis astu periit, anno aetatis 78. imperij 23. huius imperij anno 18. Seruator noster Iesus Christus à Iudaeis cruci affixus est. Suetonin Tiber. Hic Christianorum persecutoribus periculum interminatus est.
units.tr: CL. TIBERIUS Nero, third Emperor of the Romans, succeeding Augustus, reigned in the year of the world 3977, after Christ's birth the 15th year. He refused the principate for a long time with the most shameless spirit, now exhorting his friends with reproaches, as if they did not know what a beast empire was; now, with the Senate praying and falling at his knees, he held them in suspense with ambiguous replies and crafty delay. At last, as if compelled, and complaining that a wretched and burdensome servitude was being laid upon him, he took up the reins of affairs; yet he did so only with the hope of laying them down at some time. He led an army to the East: he restored the kingdom of Armenia to Tigranes; he recovered the standards which the Parthians had taken from Crassus. He ruled Gaul for almost a year; he waged war in Raetia, Vindelicia, Pannonia and Germany. In the German war he brought 40,000 surrendered men across into Gaul and settled them on the bank of the Rhine, assigning them lands; for these deeds he triumphed in Rome in ovation before he became emperor. At the beginning he shunned flattery; this saying is also his: A good shepherd shears the flock, he does not devour it. At last he administered the empire with great sloth and tyranny; some kings who had been summoned by flattery he did not let go. Given over therefore to luxury and slaughter, he perished by the plot of his grandson Caligula, in the 78th year of his age, the 23rd of his reign, the 18th year of his reign in which our Saviour Jesus Christ was affixed to the cross by the Jews. Suetonius, Tiberius. He threatened the persecutors of the Christians with danger.

units.la: AGRIPPINA M. Agrippae filia, vxor fuit Tiberij Imperatoris, ex quo Drusum iuniore peperit: hac rursum grauidam dimittere coactus est, ac Iuliam Augusti filiâ vxorem ducere, quanquam Agrippina valde amaret Tiberius maritus, & Iuliae mores improbaret. Sueto.in Tiber.
units.tr: AGRIPPINA, daughter of Marcus Agrippa, was the wife of the Emperor Tiberius, by whom she bore Drusus the Younger. Tiberius was forced to send her away while she was pregnant with another child, and to marry Julia, the daughter of Augustus, although Tiberius, her husband, loved Agrippina very much and disapproved of Julia's morals. Suetonius, in the life of Tiberius.

units.la: CAIPHAS, Iudæorum Pontifex fuit anno mundi 3983. post Christum natum 21. Aiunt hunc cum Anna socero Pontificatum emisse, atque eodem anno ambos rexisse: nam Cæsarū procuratores pro auaricia & libidine sacerdotiū tunc conferebant. hunc Vitellius Syriæ præfectus post 17. annos sacerdotio priuauit. Hic est ille Caiphas qui scidit vestimenta sua ad responsionem Christi: in cuius etiam domo illusus, consputus & colaphis cæsus est D. noster: vbi etiam Petrus Dominum negauit, ab vna atque altera ancilla conterritus. Mat. 26. cap. Iose. lib. Antiq. 18. cap. 8. hic cùm esset Pontifex, prophetauit, expedire vt vnus homo moriatur pro populo, quàmsi tota gens pereat[?]. Ioan. 21.
units.tr: CAIAPHAS, High Priest of the Jews, held the office in the year of the world 3983, 21 years after the birth of Christ. They say he bought the high priesthood together with his father-in-law Annas, and that the two of them ruled in the same year; for at that time the procurators of the Caesars conferred the priesthood for the sake of greed and lust. Vitellius, prefect of Syria, deprived him of the priesthood after seventeen years. This is that Caiaphas who tore his garments at Christ's answer; in his house too our Lord was mocked, spat upon and struck with blows, and there Peter denied the Lord, terrified by one maidservant and then another. Matthew 26; Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 8. While he was high priest he prophesied, "It is expedient that one man should die for the people, rather than the whole nation perish" [?]. John 11.

units.la: PILATVS Iudææ præfuit an. 9. incipientes anno mundi 3988. post Christū natum 26. Hic statuas Cæsaris Ierosolymis collocauit, mortem etiam cōminatus Iudæis nisi quieuissent: at illi mortem se potius subituros quàm legis suæ cōstitutiones transgressum iri, profitebātur. Tum Pilatus demiratus Iudæorū in sua lege obfirmationem, imagines auferri præcipit. de Christiano dogmate ad Tiberiū retulit: & Tiberius ad Senatū: sed Christianos vrbe eliminandos Senatus statuit: & Tiberius edicto, morte accusatoribus Christianorū interminatus est. Tert. in Apolog. cap. 5. Oro. li. 7. ca. 4. Coràm Pilato Christus criminatus est à Iudæis quòd populū auerteret, quòd tributū Cæsaris prohiberet, quoq; se regē faceret: quē cùm aliquoties interrogasset, cupit: hoc se iudicio eximere, & absolutū dimittere: verùm vbi Iudaica rabies inualuit, importunitate ac minis fractus Pilatus, Christū illis ad arbitriū vt crucifigeret tradidit: præfatus tamē lotis quoq; manibus, se innocētē esse à sanguine eius. Iof. li. ant. 18. c. 5. 6. 7. Vide etiā Eufe. Hic tandē tēporibus Caligulæ sibi propria manu morte cōsciuit. Eufe. li. 2. c. 7. Pilatū scribit Phi. Berg. li. 7. è Lugduno ortū, vbi etiam exul seipsum interfecerit.
units.tr: PILATE governed Judea for nine years, beginning in the year of the world 3988, 26 years after the birth of Christ. He set up statues of Caesar in Jerusalem, and threatened the Jews with death unless they kept quiet; but they declared that they would rather undergo death than see the decrees of their law transgressed. Then Pilate, amazed at the Jews' obstinacy in their law, ordered the images removed. He reported the Christian doctrine to Tiberius, and Tiberius to the Senate; but the Senate decided that the Christians should be expelled from the city, and Tiberius, by edict, threatened death to the accusers of the Christians. Tertullian, Apology, chapter 5; Orosius, book 7, chapter 4. Christ was accused before Pilate by the Jews, for turning the people away, for forbidding the tribute to Caesar, and for making himself king. Though Pilate questioned him several times, he wished to release himself from this judgment and let him go free; but when the Jewish rage prevailed, Pilate, worn down by their importunity and threats, handed Christ over to them to be crucified as they pleased, yet first, having washed his hands, he declared that he was innocent of his blood. Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapters 5, 6, 7. See also Eusebius. Finally, in the time of Caligula, he took his own life with his own hand. Eusebius, book 2, chapter 7. Philippus writes that Pilate was born at Lugdunum, where he also, while in exile, killed himself.

units.la: HERODES Antipas Tetrarcha Galilææ, superuixit fratri suo Archelao,de quo à nobis dictum est supra. Hic primùm vocabatur tantùm Antipas,sed mortuo fratre, nomè Herodis aflumpfit. Hic Philippi fratris fui vxorem, fratre viuo, qui etiā ex ea liberos susceperat,abduxit, ac in matrimonium accepit: ex sapientibus Israelitis complures occidit. D. Ioann em Baptiftam obtruncauit anno mundi 3993.post Christum natum 31. tum quòd eum flagitij coargueret,propter abductā fratris vxorem, tum quòd vereretur ne forte doctrinæ eius perfuafione, populi à suo regno deficerent:nam frequens populus ad Ioannem confluebat. Hic etiam Christum Dominum noftrū fpreuit,ac illusit,indutúmque veste alba remisit ad Pilatum. Tandem accusatus Antipas coram C.Cæsare Calicula,Lugdunum in exilium agitur:eiúsque tetrarchia Agrippæ regno adiicitur. Iofeph.lib.Anti.18.cap.10.& 14.attamen idem Iofe.lib.2. de bel. Iuda.cap.8. scribit hunc Herodem fugisse in Hispaniam, vbi etiam cum vxore ait decessisse.
units.tr: HEROD Antipas, Tetrarch of Galilee, survived his brother Archelaus, of whom we have spoken above. At first he was called only Antipas, but after his brother's death he took the name Herod. While his brother Philip was still alive, he led away Philip's wife, who had even borne him children, and took her as his own wife. He killed many of the wise men of Israel. He beheaded St John the Baptist in the year of the world 3993, 31 years after the birth of Christ; partly because John rebuked him for his crime, in taking his brother's wife, and partly because he feared that through John's teaching the people might fall away from his kingdom, for a great crowd flocked to John. He also despised and mocked Christ our Lord, and sent him back to Pilate clothed in a white robe. At last Antipas was accused before Gaius Caesar Caligula, and was sent into exile at Lugdunum; his tetrarchy was added to the kingdom of Agrippa. Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapters 10 and 14. Yet the same Josephus, in The Jewish War, book 2, chapter 8, writes that this Herod fled to Spain, where he also, he says, died with his wife.

units.la: HERODIAS filia Ariftobuli,soror Agrippæ maioris,nupfit primùm Philippo Tetrarchæ patruo, cum quo diuortium fecit,adiunxítque fe Herodi Antipæ,quem & in exilium fecuta est:nec obstitit libertas sibi ab Imperatore cōceffa, quòd efset Agrippæ,quem Imp.diligebat,soror: hæc enim respondit Imperatori,non æquum esse, vt quem in prospera fortuna fecuta effet,in aduersa relinqueret:Lugduni itaq; cum viro exul obiit:extátque etiam nunc memorabile horum sepulturæ monimentum,pyramis lapidea, quam vulgus duorum amantium Pyramidem vocat. Vide Comestorem, & 1.part.hifto. D. Antonini Archie.to.6.cap.21.§.4. huius filia saltauit coram Herode, quæ caput D.Ioannis petiit.Marci 6.cap.
units.tr: HERODIAS, daughter of Aristobulus and sister of Agrippa the Elder, first married Philip the Tetrarch, her uncle, from whom she divorced, and joined herself to Herod Antipas, whom she followed into exile. Nor did the freedom granted to her by the Emperor stand in the way, although she was the sister of Agrippa, whom the Emperor loved; for she answered the Emperor that it was not right to abandon in adversity the man whom she had followed in prosperity. So she died in exile at Lugdunum with her husband; and their tomb, a stone pyramid which the common people call the Pyramid of the two lovers, still stands today as a memorial. See Comestor, and part 1 of the History. Antoninus, Archbishop, vol. 6, chapter 21, §4. Her daughter danced before Herod and asked for the head of St John. Mark 6.

units.la: CHRISTVS REX VENIT IN PACE DEVS HOMO FACTVS EST. [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters]
units.tr: CHRIST THE KING COMES IN PEACE, GOD BECAME MAN. [illegible] [illegible]

units.la: IESVS Christus Dominus noster, verus Deus ac verus homo,natus ex muliere virgine,factus sub lege, vt eos qui sub lege erant redimeret,passus est, mortémque in cruce pro vita & salute nostra oppetiit anno suae aetatis 33. anno mundi 3994. anno imperij Tiberij 18. ac post tres dies resurrexit, nempe vt qui mortem nostram moriendo destuxerat[?], vitam quoque resurgendo repararet:mortuus est enim propter peccata nostra, & resurrexit propter iustificationem nostram : vt nos peccatis mortui,iustitiae viuamus,per bona opera certam facientes vocationem nostram. Quadragesimo autem die à morte ascedit in coelum:quinquagesimo, misit spiritum sanctum, quemadmodum suis fuerat pollicitus:& venturus est iudicare viuos & mortuos in consummatione seculi:beati serui illi quos paratos & vigilantes offendet. Euangelia,epistolae D.Pauli,Petri,Ioannis,Iacobi proponunt nobis ob oculos isthaec omnia, Christi vitam, mortem, resurrectionem, ascensionem, spiritus sancti missionem, mundi conflagrationem extremam,extremum quoque venturi eiusdem Christi iudicium, vitam aeternam, & supplicium aeternum.
units.tr: JESUS Christ our Lord, true God and true man, born of a virgin woman, made under the law that he might redeem those who were under the law, suffered and underwent death on the cross for our life and salvation, in the thirty-third year of his age, in the year of the world 3994, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius; and on the third day he rose again, so that he who had destroyed our death by dying might also restore our life by rising. For he died because of our sins, and rose again because of our justification, that we, dead to sin, might live to righteousness, making our calling sure by good works. On the fortieth day after his death he ascended into heaven; on the fiftieth he sent the Holy Spirit, as he had promised his own; and he will come to judge the living and the dead at the end of the age: blessed are those servants whom he finds watching and ready. The Gospels and the epistles of Paul, Peter, John and James set before our eyes all these things: the life, death, resurrection and ascension of Christ, the sending of the Holy Spirit, the final burning of the world, the last judgment of the same Christ to come, eternal life, and eternal punishment.

units.la: JUDAS Iscariotes unus ex duodecim Apostolis Domini fuit,qui cum loculos gestaret,fur & auarus erat : nec æquo potuit animo pati unguenti pretiosi effusionem in corpus Christi. Hic Dominum suum,ac nostrum, pretio triginta denariorum prodidit, signo osculi dato Judæis ut Christum cognoscerent. tandem pœnituit,& pecuniâ retulit,ex qua emptus est ager figuli in sepulturam peregrinorū: veruntamen amens & exspes laqueo se suspendit,mediúsque crepuit, & diffusa sunt omnia viscera eius,cùm desperaret de obtinenda venia à piisimo ac, ut ita dicam,misericordissimo Deo,ac in Judæ locum subrogatus est Mathias.Porrò quod attinet ad rationem denariorum, singuli valebát tres asses,siue solidos, & dimidium (autore Budæo in libro de Asse) si quidem erant denarij Romani ac vulgares:cuiuscunque autem formæ aut metalli fuerint, feruntur fuisse similes huic qui vobis hic utrinque effigiatus est, ac expressus.Matt.27.Ioan.12. Act.1. GERMANICVS CAES P.C. CAES AUG[?] AGRIPPINA M F GERMANICI CAES[?]
units.tr: JUDAS Iscariot was one of the twelve Apostles of the Lord; he carried the money-bag, and was a thief and a covetous man; nor could he bear with an equal mind the pouring out of precious ointment on the body of Christ. For thirty pieces of silver he betrayed his Lord and ours, giving the Jews a sign of a kiss so that they might know Christ. At last he repented and brought back the money, with which the potter's field was bought as a burial place for strangers; yet, mad and hopeless, he hanged himself with a noose, and, bursting in the middle, all his bowels were poured out, since he despaired of obtaining pardon from the most pious and, so to speak, most merciful God. In Judas' place Matthias was substituted. As for the value of the denarii, each was worth three asses, or a solidus and a half (according to Budaeus, in his book on the As), provided they were Roman and common denarii; but whatever their form or metal, they are said to have been like this one, which is stamped and impressed here on both sides for you. Matthew 27; John 12; Acts 1. GERMANICUS CAESAR, PUBLIC CONSENT, CAESAR AUGUSTUS, AGRIPPINA, DAUGHTER OF MARCUS, OF GERMANICUS CAESAR [?]

units.la: GERMANICUS C.Cæsaris Caligulæ pater, à Tiberio patruo adoptatus, quæsturam quinquénio ante quàm per leges liceret, ac post eam Consulatum statim gessit. Missus ad exercitum in Germaniam, excessu Augusti nūtiato, legiones universas imperatorē Tiberiū pertinacissimè recusantes, & sibi summam reip. deferentes, incertū constàtia an pietate maiore compescuit: atque hoste mox devicto triumphauit. Armeniæ Regē devicit: Cappadociam in provinciæ formam redegit. Diutino morbo Antiochiæ obiit anno ætatis 3 4. non sine veneni suspicione, fraude Tiberij, ministerio & opera Cn. Pisonis, qui sub idem tempus Syriæ præpositus erat. Sueto.in C.Cæsare Caligula. moritur hic Germanicus anno mundi 3 9 8 1. post Christum natum 19.
units.tr: GERMANICUS, father of Gaius Caesar Caligula, was adopted by his uncle Tiberius; he held the quaestorship five years before the law allowed it, and afterwards the consulship immediately. Sent to the army in Germany, when the death of Augustus was announced, he restrained all the legions, which most obstinately refused to recognise Tiberius as emperor and offered him the supreme power of the state, though it is uncertain whether by greater firmness or by greater loyalty. Soon after, having defeated the enemy, he celebrated a triumph. He conquered the King of Armenia, and reduced Cappadocia to the form of a province. He died of a lingering illness at Antioch, in his thirty-fourth year, not without suspicion of poison, by the treachery of Tiberius and the service and work of Gnaeus Piso, who was at about the same time placed over Syria. Suetonius, in the life of Gaius Caesar Caligula. This Germanicus died in the year of the world 3981, 19 years after the birth of Christ.

units.la: AGRIPPINA M. Agrippæ & Iuliæ filia, Germanici supradicti uxor, C. Cæsarē, qui Caligula dictus est, peperit, atque Agrippinam Neronis matrem, item alios complures liberos. Hæc virum in Syriam comitata est: Pisonem judicio persecuta, ad spontaneam necem adegit. tandē apud Tiberiū in invidiam adducta, mortem sibi inedia cōscivit. Vide Suet. ut supra.hanc Augustus vix anniculā Tiberio privigno despondit, quā postea dimittere coëgit, ut Iuliam assumeret, sicuti supra in Tiberio diximus. Vide etiam Cor. Nepotem. C.CAES.AVG.GERMANICVS.PON.M.TR.POT. IVNIA CLAVDIL.C.CAES IMP.IX [?]
units.tr: AGRIPPINA, daughter of Marcus Agrippa and Julia, wife of the above-mentioned Germanicus, bore Gaius Caesar, who was called Caligula, and Agrippina, the mother of Nero, and several other children. She accompanied her husband into Syria; having prosecuted Piso in a case, she drove him to a voluntary death. At last, brought into hatred before Tiberius, she took her own life by starvation. See Suetonius, as above. Augustus had betrothed her, scarcely a year old, to Tiberius, his stepson, whom he later compelled to send her away so that he might take Julia, as we said above in the life of Tiberius. See also Cornelius Nepos. GAIUS CAESAR AUGUSTUS GERMANICUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, TRIBUNICIAN POWER, JUNIA CLAUDIA, GAIUS CAESAR IMPERATOR IX [?]

units.la: C. CÆSAR, Caligula cognominatus, Germanici filius, & Drusi, priuigni Augusti, & ipsius Tiberij nepos, Romæ imperauit anno mundi 4000 post Christum natum 38. Hic veneno Tiberium, cui successit, aggressus esse dicitur, quinetiam manu sua spirantis adhuc fauces oppressisse liberto, qui ob atrocitate facinoris exclamauerat, confestim in cruce acto. Initio imperij popularem se ostendit, dein monstrum se exhibuit, luxu, incontinentia, atrocitate. Dictu est de eo, nec meliore ab initio principem, nec peiore postea fuisse. vnam ceruicem populo Romano optauit, quo facilius vno ictu abscindi posset: dixitq;, oderint dū metuant. cum omnibus sororibus suis stupri consuetudinem fecit: has etiam sæpe exoletis suis prostrauit: quo facilius eas condenauit, quasi adulteras, & insidiarum aduersus se conscias. Multos honesti ordinis, deformatos prius stigmatum notis, ad metalla & munitiones viarum, aut ad bestias condenauit: aut bestiarum more quadrupedes cauea coercuit: aut medios ferra diffecuit: nec omnes grauibus ex causis: verum male de munere suo opinatos, aut quod nunquam per genium suum deierassent. Palam queri solebat nullis calamitatibus publicis tempora sua insigniri, tam flagitiosus ac funestus, vt etiam Tiberij dedecora purgauerit. Bellum contra Germanos suscepit: & ingressus Sueuiam, nihil strenuè gessit. Tandē cum aduersus cunctos ingenti auaricia, libidine, crudelitate sæuiret, interfectus est in palatio. Imperauit annos 4. vixit 29. Suet. in vita C. Cæ. Caligulæ. dictus est autem Caligula, vt inquit Aur. Victor, cognomentum calceamenti militaris, id est Caligulæ sortitus, quia natus in exercitu fuerat.
units.tr: Caius Caesar, called Caligula, son of Germanicus and of Drusus (stepson of Augustus), and grandson of Tiberius himself, ruled at Rome in the year of the world 4000, the thirty-eighth year after the birth of Christ. It is said that he attempted to poison Tiberius, his predecessor, and moreover that he smothered with his own hand a freedman who was still breathing, because the freedman cried out at the atrocity of the deed; the man was immediately crucified. At the beginning of his reign he showed himself popular, but afterwards he revealed himself a monster of luxury, lewdness and cruelty. It is said of him that he was neither a better prince at the start nor a worse one afterwards. He wished the Roman people had one neck, so that it could be cut off with a single blow, and he said: let them hate me, so long as they fear me. He kept up a habit of debauchery with all his sisters, and often gave these same sisters to his male favourites; the more easily he condemned them as adulteresses and as conspirators against him. Many men of honourable rank, first branded with marks of infamy, he condemned to the mines and the road works, or to the beasts; or he shut up four-footed beasts in cages in the manner of beasts; or he cut others in two with the sword. Nor were all of these punished for serious causes; rather, some were punished for having thought poorly of his office, or because they had never sworn by his divine spirit. He used to complain openly that his times were not marked by any public calamities, so shameful and deadly was he, so that he even purged the disgraces of Tiberius. He undertook war against the Germans, and having entered Suevia, he accomplished nothing vigorous. At last, since he raged against everyone with immense greed, lust and cruelty, he was killed in the palace. He reigned four years and lived twenty-nine. Suetonius, in the life of Caius Caesar Caligula. Caligula was called, as Aurelius Victor says, from the nickname of a military boot, that is, he received the name Caligula because he had been born in the army.

units.la: IVNIA Claudilla, M. Syllani nobilissimi viri filia, nupsit C. Cæsari Caligulæ, quam amisit ex partu, etiā antequā imperaret ipse, nēpe viuo Tiberio, cui successit. Sue. in C. Cæf. Cali.
units.tr: Junia Claudilla, daughter of Marcus Silanus, a most noble man, married Caius Caesar Caligula; she died in childbirth, even before he himself ruled, namely while Tiberius, his predecessor, was still alive. Suetonius, in the life of Caius Caesar Caligula.

units.la: LIVIA Horestilla C. Pisoni cùm nuberet, iussa est ad C. Caesarem Caligulam deduci. hanc Caligula intra paucos dies repudiauit,ac biennio post relegauit,quod repetiisse usum prioris mariti tempore medio videbatur.Suet. in Caligula.
units.tr: When Livia Orestilla was about to marry Caius Piso, she was ordered to be brought to Caius Caesar Caligula. Caligula divorced her within a few days, and two years later banished her, because she seemed to have resumed the marriage relations of her earlier husband in the meantime. Suetonius, in the life of Caligula.

units.la: LOLLIA Paulina, C. Memmij Consularis, ac exercitus Ducis uxor fuit. hanc quoque, facta mentione auiae eius, ut quondam pulcherrimae, subito ex prouincia euocauit C. Caesar Caligula: ac perductam à marito iunxit sibi, breuíque missam fecit, interdicto cuiuscquam in perpetuum coitu. Vide ut supra.
units.tr: Lollia Paulina was the wife of Caius Memmius, a consular and commander of an army. Caius Caesar Caligula also summoned her suddenly from her province, after mention had been made of her grandmother, who had once been very beautiful; he had her brought from her husband and joined her to himself, and soon dismissed her, forbidding anyone to have intercourse with her for ever. See above.

units.la: CAESONIA neque facie insigni, neque ætate integra, matérque iam ex alio viro trium filiarum, sed luxuriæ ac lasciuiæ perditæ, & ardentius & constantius amata est à C.Caesare Caligula:quam sæpe chlamyde peltáque & galea armatam, & iuxta adequitantem militibus ostédit, amicis verò etiam nudam, quam enixam uxorio nomine dignatus est, uno atque eodem die professus & maritum se eius, & patrem infantis ex ea natæ: nec ullo firmiore indicio sui seminis esse credebat infantem hanc, quàm feritatis, quæ illi quoque tanta iam tunc erat, ut infestis digitis ora & oculos simul ludentium infantium incesseret. periit cum viro Caesonia, gladio à Centurione confossa,cuius etiam filia parieti est illisa. Vide ut supra. HERODES AGRIP AGRIPPA IVN. [?]
units.tr: Caesonia, neither remarkable in face nor in full youth, and already the mother of three daughters by another husband, but abandoned to luxury and lasciviousness, was loved by Caius Caesar Caligula more ardently and more constantly. He often showed her to his soldiers, armed with a cloak, shield and helmet, and riding beside them; to his friends he showed her even naked. When she had given birth, he deigned to name her by the title of wife, and on one and the same day he declared himself both her husband and the father of the infant born of her. He believed that this infant was of his own seed by no firmer proof than its savagery, which was already then so great that it attacked with its hostile fingers the faces and eyes of the infants who were playing with it. Caesonia perished together with her husband, stabbed with a sword by a centurion; her own daughter was also dashed against a wall. See above. Herod Agrippa, Junia.

units.la: HERODES Agrippa Aristobuli filius, ac magni Herodis Ascalonitæ nepos ex filio, Romæ agens, Tiberij nepotis cuiam suscipit: verum ab Eutycho liberto accusatus, iussu Tiberij in vincula coniicitur: quo Imperatore defuncto, statim è vinculis liberatur, diadematéque [?] regio à C. Caligula, cuius curam gesferat, donatur: nam Rex Tetrarchiæ Philippi ac Lysaniæ designatur anno mundi 4000. à Christo nato 38. Quinetiam Claudius, qui Caligulæ successit, Agrippæ huius regnum ratum habuit, omne Herodis quoque Antipæ exulis Imperium addens: atque Herodem fratrem (nam Antipas patruus erat) Chalcidis Regem creat. Hic est Herodes ille qui Iacobum maiorem obtruncauit ac D. Petrum in carcerem trusit, & ab Angelo percussus; à vermibus post diem quintum erosus est. Vide Acta Apost. cap. 12. Sed ut ad Agrippam nostrum redeam, hic Herodiadem sororem, eiusque virum Antipam, contra ipsum nonnihil molientes, prævenit: exiliíque eorum occasione præbuit, misso ad Caligulā Fortunato liberto cum literis. Vide Iose. li.18.ca.12.13. & 14. Variat autores in hoc Agrippa & fratre prædicto, alij alia huic, alia illi tribuentes: sunt & qui unum tantum ex his duobus faciant, quem Herodem Agrippam vocitant.
units.tr: Herod Agrippa, son of Aristobulus and grandson, through his son, of Herod the great, the Ascalonite. While living at Rome, he was a companion of the grandson Tiberius; but accused by Eutychus, a freedman, he was thrown into chains by order of Tiberius. When that emperor died, he was immediately freed from his chains, and was given a royal diadem by Caius Caligula, whose care he had taken; for he was designated king of the tetrarchy of Philip and of Lysanias in the year of the world 4000, the thirty-eighth year after the birth of Christ. Moreover, Claudius, who succeeded Caligula, confirmed the kingdom of this Agrippa, adding to it the whole realm of Herod Antipas, the exile. He also made Herod, his brother (for Antipas was their uncle), king of Chalcis. This is that Herod who put James the greater to death and threw Peter into prison, and who, struck by an angel, was eaten by worms after the fifth day. See Acts, chapter 12. But to return to our Agrippa: he forestalled his sister Herodias and her husband Antipas, who were plotting something against him, and furnished the occasion for their exile, by sending the freedman Fortunatus to Caligula with letters. See Josephus, book 18, chapters 12, 13 and 14. Authors vary about this Agrippa and the brother just mentioned, some ascribing this to one and that to the other; and there are some who make only one of these two, whom they call Herod Agrippa.

units.la: AGRIPPA iunior prædicti filius, seu nepos, defuncto Herode Chalcidis Rege prædicto, Chalcidis Rex designatur, à Cl. Tiberio, qui Caligulæ successerat, nempe anno mundi 4011. à Christo nato 49. Fuit hic ultimus Iudæ Rex, prudens, Hebræa Latinaque lingua doctus. Hoc Rege Titus Hierusalem captam exussit 17. agebat annum, moriente patre, seu avo, cum Romæ à Cæsare aleretur. Porrò Cæsar Cuspium Fadum huius immaturi loco, Iudææ præfecit: cui successit Felix, & huic rursus Portius Festus. Vide Iosephi Hebr. diu desi. lib. 5. cap. 46. DRVSVS.CAESAR.TIB.AVG.FR. ANTONIA IVNIOR.GER.MAT.
units.tr: Agrippa the younger, son or grandson of the aforesaid, when Herod, king of Chalcis, had died, was designated king of Chalcis by the Emperor Claudius, who had succeeded Caligula, namely in the year of the world 4011, the forty-ninth year after the birth of Christ. This man was the last king of Judea, prudent and learned in the Hebrew and Latin languages. In his reign Titus burned Jerusalem after capturing it. He was seventeen years old when his father, or grandfather, died, and he was being brought up at Rome by Caesar. Moreover, Caesar placed Cuspius Fadus in charge of Judea in place of this immature king; Felix succeeded him, and after him Porcius Festus. See Josephus, the Hebrew History (?), book 5, chapter 46.

units.la: DRVSVS, Claudij Cæsaris pater, olim Decimus, mox Nero prænomine, ex Liuia Drusilla natus est, intra mensem tertium quàm grauida abducta essset ab Augusto, ex contubernio ac matrimonio Tiberij patris Imperatoris: fuitque suspicio ex vitrico per adulterij consuetudinem procreatum Drusum. Is in Quæsturæ Præturæque honore, dux Rhetici, deinde Germanici belli, Oceanum Septentrionalem primus Romanorum ducum nauigauit: tránsque Rhenum fossas noui & immensi operis effecit, quæ Drusianæ vocatæ sunt: hostem frequenter cæsum in intimas solitudines egit. Inito consulatu, atque expeditione repetita, obiit diem in æstiuis castris, quæ ex eo scelerata sunt appellata. Hunc Augustus tantopere & viuum dilexit, vt cohæredem semper filiis instituerit: & defunctum ita pro concione laudauerit, vt deos precatus sit similes ei Cæsares suos facerent: sibíque tam honestum quandoque exitum darent quàm illi dedissent. nec contentus elogium tumulo eius, versibus à se compositis insculpsisse, etiam vitæ memoriam prosa oratione composuit. Vide Suet.in C.Clau. Cæ.
units.tr: Drusus, father of the Emperor Claudius, formerly called Decimus, and afterwards Nero by his praenomen, was born of Livia Drusilla, within the third month after she had been taken away from her husband by Augustus; she was in the intimacy and marriage of Tiberius, his father, the emperor. And there was a suspicion that Drusus was begotten by his stepfather through a habit of adultery. He, in the honours of the quaestorship and praetorship, as commander in the Rhaetian war and then in the German war, was the first of the Roman commanders to sail the northern Ocean. He made ditches of a new and immense work across the Rhine, which were called the Drusian ditches; he often drove the enemy, cut down, into the inmost wildernesses. Having entered upon his consulship and resumed the campaign, he died in the summer camp, which for that reason was called accursed. Augustus loved him so greatly while he lived that he always named him co-heir with his sons; and when he was dead he praised him before the assembly so highly that he prayed the gods to make his own Caesars like him, and to give them as honourable an end as they had given him. Not content with inscribing an epitaph on his tomb in verses composed by himself, he also wrote a memoir of his life in prose. See Suetonius, in the life of the Emperor Claudius.

units.la: ANTONIA minor, Drusi supradicti vxor fuit, ex qua liberos complures suscepit, verùm tres omnino reliquit, nempe Germanicum, Liuillam, & Claudium, qui postea imperauit. Hæc Antonia M. Antonio, & Octauia genita est, quæ sororem habuit maiorem eiusdem nominis, Domitij Aenobarbi vxorem. Vide Plutar. in M.Antonio.
units.tr: Antonia the younger, the wife of the aforementioned Drusus, had by him several children, but she left only three in all: Germanicus, Livilla and Claudius, who afterwards ruled. This Antonia was born of Mark Antony and Octavia; she had an elder sister of the same name, the wife of Domitius Ahenobarbus. See Plutarch, in the life of Mark Antony.

units.la: CLAVDIVS, Drufi Germanici ex minore Antonia filius, Liuillæ & alterius Drufi frater, Romæ post Caligulam imperat anno mundi 4004. à Christo nato 42. Hic Lugduni natus est, quem mater portentum hominis dictitabat: auia Augusta pro despectis. semper habuit: soror Liuilla, cum audisset imperaturum, tam iniquam fortem pop. Ro. palam detestata est. Fortunæ ludibrio ad imperium, cum latitaret extrema pertimescens, interfecto Caligula, venit: quod non minore socordia quàm crudelitate per annos ferè 14. vexauit. Britanniæ bellum intulit, eámque in deditionem accepit. Orcades insulas Ro. imperio addidit. Hic Messalina uxore sua uixdum supplicio affecta, quòd C. Silio nupsisset, Agrippinam Germanici fratris filiam, nouo exemplo, liberis duobus nouercam superinduxit: cùm paulò ante pro concione confirmasset, quatenus sibi male cederent matrimonia, in cœlibatu se permansurum, ac nisi permansisset, non recusaturum confodi manibus ipsorum. Præterea Britannico filio priuignum Neronem antepofuit: cuius insidiis, & Agrippinæ matris, veneno in boleto dato periit, anno ætatis 64. imperij 4. exortus crinitæ stellæ, tactúmque de cœlo monumentum Drufi patris, præsagia mortis eius præcipua fuere: & in ultima cognitione pro tribunali accessisse se ad vitæ terminum semel atque iterum pronuntiauit. Vide Sueto.in Claud.Cæs.
units.tr: Claudius, son of Drusus and of Germanicus' younger Antonia, brother of Livilla and of another Drusus, ruled at Rome after Caligula in the year of the world 4004, the forty-second year after the birth of Christ. He was born at Lyons, and his mother used to call him a monstrous birth; his grandmother Augusta always held him in contempt. His sister Livilla, when she heard that he would become emperor, openly cursed so unjust a lot for the Roman people. He came to power as the plaything of Fortune, hiding in fear of the worst, after Caligula had been killed; and he harassed the state for almost fourteen years with no less sloth than cruelty. He waged war on Britain and received that land into surrender. He added the Orkney islands to the Roman empire. He, having barely executed his wife Messalina because she had married Gaius Silius, brought in as a stepmother over two children, in an unprecedented manner, Agrippina, daughter of his brother Germanicus; although a little earlier he had declared before the assembly that, as far as marriages went, things had turned out badly for him, and that he would remain unmarried, and that if he did not remain so, he would not refuse to be stabbed by their own hands. Besides, he preferred his stepson Nero to his son Britannicus; through the plots of Nero and of his mother Agrippina, he perished by poison given in a mushroom, in the sixty-fourth year of his life and the fourth of his reign. The appearance of a comet and the striking of his father Drusus' monument by lightning were the chief omens of his death; and at the final hearing, before the tribunal, he declared once and again that he had come to the end of his life. See Suetonius, in the life of the Emperor Claudius.

units.la: AEMILIA Lepida, Augusti proneptis, Pauli AEmilij Censoris filij, & Iuliæ, neptis Augusti, filia, prima omnium desponsata est Claudio: sed eam, quòd parentes eius Augustum offenderant, virginem adhuc repudiauit. Sueto.in Clau.
units.tr: Aemilia Lepida, great-granddaughter of Augustus, daughter of Paullus Aemilius Censorinus and of Julia, Augustus's granddaughter, was the first woman betrothed to Claudius; but because her parents had offended Augustus, he broke off the engagement while she was still a virgin. Suetonius, in Claudius.
LIVIA MEDULLINA, WIFE OF THE EMPEROR CLAUDIUS
PLAUTIA HERCULANIA [?], WIFE OF THE EMPEROR CLAUDIUS

units.la: LIVIA MEDULLINA, cognomine Camilla, è genere antiquo Dictatoris M. Furij Camilli (cuius meminimus in priori huius operis parte pag.125.) eo ipso die qui erat nuptiis Claudij Imp. atque huius Medullinæ destinatus, morbo periit. Vide Sueto. in Claud.
units.tr: Livia Medullina, also called Camilla, of the ancient family of the Dictator Marcus Furius Camillus (whom we mentioned in the earlier part of this work, p. 125), died of illness on the very day that had been set for her marriage to the Emperor Claudius. See Suetonius, in Claudius.

units.la: PLAUTIA HERCULANILLA, triumphali patre nata, eidē Claud. Imp. nupsit, cum qua diuortiū ille fecit, ob libidinū probra, & homicidij in virum fuspitionē. ex hac Claudiam suscepit, & Drusum, quem puberē amisit, pyro per lusum in sublime iactato, & haitu [?] oris excepto strangulatum, cui & filiam Seiani desponderat. Vide ut supra. Cæterum de Seiano homine præpotente ac prædiuite, cui tandem fortuna nouercā se præstitit, vide Iuvenalem Satyra 10. nam huius exēplo nimias opes, potentiam ac fastum multis exitio esse ostēdit Iuvenalis, his versibus.
units.tr: Plautia Herculanilla, daughter of a man of triumphal rank, was also married to the Emperor Claudius; he divorced her because of her shameful debauchery and a suspicion that she had murdered her husband. By her he had a daughter, Claudia, and a son, Drusus, whom he lost while still a boy: he was strangled when, playing a game, he tossed a pear into the air and caught it in his open mouth, where it stuck. Claudius had also betrothed him to a daughter of Sejanus. On Sejanus himself, a man of great power and very great wealth, to whom fortune at last showed herself a stepmother, see Juvenal, Satire 10; for Juvenal shows, in these verses, through the example of this man, that excessive wealth, power and pride are the ruin of many.

units.la: Quosdam præcipitat subiecta potentia magna / Invidia, mergit longa, atque insignis honorum / Pagina, descendunt statuæ, restémque sequuntur. / Ipsas deinde rotas bigarum impacta securis / Cadit, & immeritis franguntur crura caballis: / Jam stridunt ignes, jam follibus atque caminis / Ardet adoratum populo caput, & crepat ingens / Seianus, deinde ex facie toto orbe secunda, / Fiunt urceoli, pelues, sartago, patella. / Pone domi lauros, duc in capitolia magnum / Cretatúmque bouem, Seianus ducitur unco / Spectandus: gaudent omnes. &c.
units.tr: Some the great power that lies beneath envy casts down; the long and distinguished page of their honours sinks, their statues come down and follow the rope. Then the axe, driven into the very wheels of the chariot, falls, and the legs are broken of horses that did no wrong. Now the fires hiss; now the head once worshipped by the people blazes on the hearths and in the furnaces, and loud crashes Sejanus, and then from that face, once second to none in the whole world, little jugs, basins, a frying pan and a dish are made. Put laurels at home, lead the great white bull up to the Capitol: Sejanus is dragged along by a hook, to be looked at. Everyone rejoices. etc.

units.la: ÆLIA Petina Consulari patre nata, mox, repudiata Plautia Herculanilla, nupsit Claudio Imp. cum qua item diuortium fecit, ob leuiculas offensas. ex hac Antonia suscepit quam Cneo Pompeio magno, deinde Fausto Sylle collocauit, quorum alter à Pompeio magno, alter à Fausto Sylla, Syllæ Felicis filio originem trahebat. Vide Sueto.in Clau.
units.tr: Aelia Petina, daughter of a consular father, was afterwards divorced by Claudius after Plautia Herculanilla, and was married to him; he divorced her too, for trifling offences. By her he had a daughter, Antonia, whom he gave in marriage first to Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus and then to Faustus Sulla; one of these traced his descent from Pompey the Great, the other from Faustus Sulla, son of Sulla Felix. See Suetonius, in Claudius.

units.la: VALERIA MESSALINA Claud. quoque Imp. nupsit: hanc cum coperisset vir, super cætera flagitia atq; dedecora, se absente, Caio Silio, iuuetutis Romanæ pulcherrimo, etiam nupsisse, dote inter Auspices cosignata, curauit interfici. Vide Cor. Taci. li. II. ad calcem. De hac item sic scribit Iuue. Saty. 6.
units.tr: Valeria Messalina was also married to the Emperor Claudius. When her husband learned of her many crimes and disgraces, and in particular that, in his absence, she had married Gaius Silius, the most handsome young man of Roman youth, with the dowry signed before the augurs, he had her put to death. See Cornelius Tacitus, Book 11, at the end. Juvenal also writes about her in the same way, Satire 6:
—when her husband was asleep, his wife
dared to prefer a mat to the palace bed:
the Augusta, a whore, took up a hooded cloak for the night,
and left, with no more than one maidservant for company,
and, hiding her dark hair under a yellow wig,
went into the warm brothel, a patched-up old blanket over her,

units.la: Et cellam vacuam, atque suam: tunc nuda papillis
units.tr: into its empty cubicle, her own: there she stood, naked, her nipples gilded,
She welcomed in the men as they entered with coaxing words, and asked for their money.
And when she was worn out by men, but not yet satisfied, she left.
Dirty, with her cheeks darkened by the smoke of the lamp,
she carried the foul smell of the brothel back to the pillow.

units.la: ex hac Messalina Clau. Octauiâ, & quem primò Germanicum, mox Britannicum cognominauit, suscepit. Vide vt supra. PRAEFECT. FELIX · IVD[?] DRVSILLA · FEL. V[?]
units.tr: By this Messalina, Claudius had Octavia and a son whom he first named Germanicus and then Britannicus. See above. Prefect Felix; Drusilla, Felix.

units.la: FELIX constitutus est ab Imperatore Claudio praeses, siue procurator Iudaeae, Samariae quoq; & Galilaeae, & regionis quae dicitur trans Iordanē, anno mundi 4015. post Christū natum 53. Tertullus coram hoc praeside Paulum accusauit, Paulus vicissim pro se contra Tertullū causam dixit: quibus auditis distulit iudicium Felix in aduentum tribuni Lysiae. Hic Felix frequenter accersens Paulum, loquebatur cum eo, & audiuit ab eo fidē quae est in Christum Iesum. Disputante autem Paulo de iudicio futuro, tremefactus Felix noluit vltra attendere, sed distulit in alium diē: simul sperabat quōd pecunia ei daretur a Paulo. De huius auaritia, & factione cum Ventidio, qua, glisceret pernicie, arsisset bello prouincia, ni Quadratus Syriae rector subuenisset, vide Cor. Taci. li. Anna. 12. item quatenus ad alia, vide Act. 24. ca. Eusc. li. 2. ca. 20 Iosc. li. Antiq. 20. cap. 9.
units.tr: Felix was appointed by the Emperor Claudius as governor, or procurator, of Judaea, and also of Samaria and Galilee, and of the region called beyond the Jordan, in the year of the world 4015, which was 53 after the birth of Christ. Tertullus accused Paul before this governor; Paul in turn pleaded his cause against Tertullus. After hearing both, Felix put off judgement until the arrival of the tribune Lysias. Felix often sent for Paul and talked with him, and heard from him about the faith that is in Christ Jesus. But when Paul discoursed on future judgement, Felix was alarmed and would not listen any further, but put him off to another day; at the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. On his greed, and his faction with Ventidius, by which the province, flaming up to its destruction, would have burned in war had not Quadratus, governor of Syria, come to its aid, see Cornelius Tacitus, Annals, Book 12. For other matters, see Acts 24; Eusebius, Book 2, chapter 20; Josephus, Antiquities, Book 20, chapter 9.

units.la: DRVSILLA Agrippae soror, Aziazi Emesorū siue Amazorū Regis vxor cūm esset, & pulchritudine caeteris praestaret, Felix eam cocupiuit: quare misso nuntio, eam in suam partem flexit: nam haec spōte relicto priore marito, huius nuptias secuta est. Vide. Ioseph. li. Antiq. 20. cap. 9. ANTONIA MAIOR NERONIS [?] IMP [?] LEPIDA DOMITIA NERONIS IMP [?]
units.tr: Drusilla, sister of Agrippa, was the wife of Azizus, king of the Emesenes or Amazenes, and since she excelled the others in beauty, Felix desired her. He therefore sent a messenger and won her over: for she, of her own accord, left her former husband and followed his marriage. See Josephus, Antiquities, Book 20, chapter 9. Antonia the Elder, [wife] of Nero [?]; Emperor [?]; Lepida; Domitia, [mother] of the Emperor Nero.

units.la: ANTONIA Marci Antonij & Octauiæ sororis Augusti filia maior, Domitio Aenobarbo nupsit, ex quo matrimonio natus est Cneus Domitius Neronis pater, omni parte vitæ detestabilis, vt inquit Suetonius, in Nerono Imperatore Romanorum 6. de quo mox tractabimus.
units.tr: Antonia, the elder daughter of Marcus Antonius and of Octavia, the sister of Augustus, married Domitius Ahenobarbus, and from this marriage was born Gnaeus Domitius, father of Nero, a man detestable in every part of his life, as Suetonius says in his Life of Nero, the sixth of the Roman emperors, of whom we shall soon speak.

units.la: LEPIDA DOMITIA Cnei Domitij Aenobarbi patris Neronis soror fuit. Consulito Caium Suetonium Tranquillum in Neronis Imperatoris 6. vita, si initium sumas à Caio Iulio Cæsare, quod vbique factitamus. Cæterùm quod attinet ad Aenobarbi cognomentum, atque huius vocabuli (quod sub obscurum est) rationem siue interpretationem, visum est quod scriptum reperi edere. Cùm, itaque, Castor & Pollux Helenæ fratres, Domitio victoriam aliquando nuntiarent, ipseq; narrantibus minimè crederet, malas, barbamque manibus attrectarunt, atq; eam contrectando (si credere dignum est) ex fusca flauam effecerunt: vnde à rutilo, æneoque barbæ colore, Aenobarbi cognomen accepit Domitius, quod postea in familiam transiit, virisque ex ea ortis peculiare id nominis fuit. Vide Ludovicum Cælium Rhodiginum, lib. antiquarum [?]tionum le 29.cap.autem 8. CN·DOMIT·[?] NERO IMP[?] AGRIPPINA AVGVSTA
units.tr: Lepida Domitia was the sister of Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, the father of Nero. Consult Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, in his Life of the Emperor Nero, chapter 6, beginning from Gaius Julius Caesar, as we do everywhere. As for the surname Ahenobarbus, and the reason or explanation of this word, which is obscure, it seemed right to publish what I have found written. When Castor and Pollux, the brothers of Helen, once brought Domitius news of a victory, and he did not believe what they told him, they touched his cheeks and beard with their hands, and by handling them (if it is worth believing) turned them from dark to yellow; whence Domitius received the surname Ahenobarbus, from the reddish, bronze colour of his beard, a name which afterwards passed into the family, and was peculiar to the men born of it. See Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, Book 29 of Antiquarum lectionum, chapter 8.

units.la: CNEVS Domitius Ænobarbus, Neronis pater,ex Antonia maiore,uti dictū est,natus,omni parte vitæ detestabilis,primùm occidit libertum,quòd potare quàtum jubebatur recusarat:deinde in viæ Appiæ vico, repentè puerum citatis jumētis haud ignarus obtriuit:& Romæ medio foro cuidam equiti Ro. liberius jurgāti oculum eruit.Perfidiæ atque avaritiæ maximæ fuit:argentarios pretiis rerum coëmptarū,aurigarios mercede palmarum fraudauit. Maiestatis quoque,& adulteriorū, incestíque cum sorore Lepida sub excessu Tiberij reus, mutatione temporū euasit. Decessit morbo aquæ intercutis, suscepto,ex Agrippina Germanico genita, Nerone,malo ouo ex malo corvo.Suet.in Nerone.
units.tr: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, the father of Nero, born of Antonia the Elder as has been said, was a man detestable in every part of his life. First he killed a freedman because he had refused to drink as much as he was ordered; then, in a village on the Appian Way, he suddenly ran down a boy with a team of horses, without the least concern; and at Rome, in the middle of the Forum, he tore out the eye of a Roman knight who had spoken to him rather freely. He was extremely treacherous and greedy: he cheated the money-changers over the prices of goods he had bought, and the charioteers over their winnings. He was also accused of treason, of adultery, and of incest with his sister Lepida under the close of Tiberius's reign, but he escaped through the change of times. He died of dropsy, having had by Agrippina, daughter of Germanicus, a son Nero, a bad egg from a bad crow. Suetonius, in Nero.

units.la: AGRIPPINA Germanici filia,ac Neronis mater,quem ex Domitio suscepit, nupsit secundò Claudio Cæsari patruo suo,quem blanditiis illexit,quémque tādem boleto sustulit,ut viam filio Neroni ad imperiū faceret.cæterū ipsa quoque ab eodē filio immissis percussoribus occiditur,exclamans percussori,Feri ventrem qui tam ferum monstrum tulit. Suet. in Nerone Cor.Taci.li.14. NERO CLAVD.CAES.AVG.GER.P.M.TR.P.M.P.P. OCTAVIA.CL.IMP.F.NERONIS.VXOR
units.tr: Agrippina, daughter of Germanicus and mother of Nero, whom she had by Domitius, married secondly Claudius Caesar, her uncle; she won him over with flattery, and at last removed him with a poisoned mushroom, so as to make the way to empire for her son Nero. But she herself was also killed by the same son, who sent assassins; crying out to the murderer, "Strike the belly that bore such a savage monster." Suetonius, in Nero; Cornelius Tacitus, Book 14. NERO CLAUDIUS CAESAR AUGUSTUS GERMANICUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, TRIBUNICIAN POWER, FATHER OF THE COUNTRY. OCTAVIA, DAUGHTER OF THE EMPEROR CLAUDIUS, WIFE OF NERO.

units.la: CLAV. DOMI. Nero, Domitio & Agrippina Germanico genita, genitus est. Hic adoptatus à Claudio Imperatore, successit ei in imperio, anno mundi 4017. à Christo nato 55. Orsus à pietatis ostentatione, ex Augusti præscripto imperaturum se professus est: liberalitatis, clemétiæ, comitatis exhibendæ nullam omisit occasionem. grauiora vectigalia aut aboleuit, aut minuit. tandem Caligulæ nepoté se præstitit, auunculo suo simillimus: meritóq; fax orbis altera cum Claudio dictus est. Bonam partem Senatus interfecit, & præceptoré Senecam, bonis omnibus hostis. fratrē, vxorem, matrem denique interfecit, cuius etiam cōcubitum appetiisse dicitur. Primus Christianū sanguinem, Petro & Paulo interfectis, hausit. tāto se dedecore prostituit, vt saltaret & cantaret in sena. Romā incendit, vt spectaculi eius imaginē cerneret, quali olim Troia capta arserat. Hic Britanniam pené amisit. Armeniam Parthi sustulerūt. Duæ tamen prouinciæ sub eo factæ sunt, Pontus, & Alpes. In Achaia Isthmum perfodere aggressus, primus rastello humum effodit, & corbulæ congestam, humeris extulit. Tandē ab omnibus destitutus, & à Senatu hostis iudicatus, cum quæreretur ad pœnā, è palatio fugit, nec fortiter perire potuit, adiutus alterius, adigendo ferro, manu: anno ætatis 32. imperij 14. Sueto.in Clau. Eutr.lib.7.Egna.lib.1.
units.tr: Claudius Domitius Nero, born of Domitius and of Agrippina, daughter of Germanicus, was adopted by the Emperor Claudius and succeeded him in the empire, in the year of the world 4017, which was 55 after the birth of Christ. At first, through a show of piety, he professed to rule according to the prescription of Augustus; he let no occasion for showing generosity, mercy and courtesy pass. He abolished or reduced the heavier taxes. Finally he showed himself a grandson of Caligula, very like his uncle, and so he was rightly called, together with Claudius, a second torch of the world. He had most of the Senate killed, and his tutor Seneca, an enemy of all good men. He killed his brother, his wife, and finally his mother; he is said even to have sought her bed. He was the first to drink Christian blood, when Peter and Paul were put to death. He prostituted himself to such disgrace that he danced and sang on the stage. He set fire to Rome, so that he might see an image of that spectacle, such as Troy had once blazed like when it was taken. Under him Britain was almost lost. The Parthians seized Armenia. Yet two provinces were made under him, Pontus and the Alps. In Achaia he undertook to pierce the Isthmus; he was the first to break the ground with a mattock, and carried away the earth heaped in baskets on his shoulders. At last, abandoned by all and declared an enemy by the Senate, when search was made for him to be punished, he fled from the palace, and could not die bravely, helped by another's hand, which drove the sword home. He was in the thirty-second year of his life and the fourteenth of his reign. Suetonius, in Claudius; Eutropius, Book 7; Aegnatius [?], Book 1.

units.la: OCTAVIA, Claudij & Messalinæ filia, vxor fuit Neronis, cuius consuetudinē citò aspernatus est, occidirq; eam sub crimine falso adulterij: cùm antea sæpe frustra strangulare meditatus, dimisisset eam vt sterilem, respondiséque corripientibus amicis, sufficere ei debere vxoria ornamenta. POPPEA SABINA NERO. IMP. VXOR STATILIA MESSALINA[?] NERO. IMP. VXOR
units.tr: Octavia, daughter of Claudius and Messalina, was the wife of Nero. He soon grew tired of her company and had her put to death on a false charge of adultery. Earlier he had often planned to strangle her, but he dismissed her as barren; and when his friends rebuked him, he replied that the trappings of a wife should be enough for her. POPPEA SABINA, WIFE OF NERO EMPEROR. STATILIA MESSALINA[?], WIFE OF NERO EMPEROR.

units.la: POPPÆA Sabina, Tito Olio Quæstorio patre nata, Neronis vxor fuit, quam duodecimo die post diuortium Octauiæ in matrimonium accepit. hanc dilexit vnicè: & tamen ipsam quoque ictu calcis occidit, quòd se ex aurigatione serò reuersum grauida & ægra conuiciis incesserat. hæc antea nupserat Rufo Crispino Equiti Romano. huic Poppeæ omnia alia fuere præter honestum animum: sermo comis, nec absurdum ingenium: modestiam præferebat, & lasciuia tamen vtebatur: famæ nunquam pepercit, maritos & adulteros non distinguens. Vide Sueto.in Nerone. hæc luxu supramodum diffluebat, autore Plin.lib.34.cap II.in hæc verba: Nostra ætate Poppæa coniux Neronis principis, delicatioribus iumentis suas soleas ex auro quoque induere solebat.
units.tr: Poppaea Sabina, daughter of Titus Olius Quaestorius, was the wife of Nero, whom he took in marriage on the twelfth day after his divorce from Octavia. He loved her alone, and yet he also killed her with a kick, because she, pregnant and ill, had reproached him with abuse when he came home late from driving his chariot. She had previously been married to Rufus Crispinus, a Roman knight. Poppaea had every quality except an honest mind: her conversation was pleasant, and her wit was not dull. She had a show of modesty, yet she indulged in wantonness; she never spared her reputation, distinguishing neither husbands from adulterers. See Suetonius in Nero. She lived in great luxury, as Pliny says in book 34, chapter 11, in these words: "In our age Poppaea, the wife of the emperor Nero, used to have her slippers made even of gold, for the sake of the more pampered beasts of burden." [Pliny's words are a little garbled in the text; the sense is that she had even her shoes made of gold.]

units.la: STATILIA Messalina (altera quidem à Valeria illa Messalina Claudij vxore, de qua à nobis dictum est supra) vxor quoque fuit Neronis: hac vt potiretur, virum eius Atticū Vestinum Consulem in honore ipso trucidauit. Hæc erat Statilij Tauri bis Consulis, ac triumphalis, abneptis. Taurus hic temporibus Augusti amphitheatrum Romæ extruxerat. fuit alter eiusdem nominis, huius, vt opinor, Messalinæ frater, qui ob opes & hortos egregios, quibus Agrippina inhiabat, accusatus, vim vitæ suæ attulit. Sueton.in Nerone. PETRUS APOSTOLUS PAULUS APOST. DOCT. GEN.
units.tr: Statilia Messalina (a different person from that Valeria Messalina, the wife of Claudius, of whom we spoke above) was also a wife of Nero. In order to gain him, she had her husband Atticus Vestinus, a consul, murdered in the very office he held. She was the great-granddaughter of Statilius Taurus, who was consul twice and held a triumph. This Taurus had built an amphitheatre at Rome in the time of Augustus. There was another of the same name, who, I suppose, was the brother of this Messalina; he was accused on account of his wealth and his splendid gardens, which Agrippina coveted, and he took his own life. See Suetonius in Nero. PETER THE APOSTLE, PAUL THE APOSTLE, TEACHER, GENTILES.

units.la: S. PETRUS inter Apostolos præcipuus, frater fuit Andreæ etiã Apostoli. Ambo ex vico Galilææ, Bethsaida, ambo à Christo simul vocati sunt, cùm iacerent rete in mare, erát enim piscatores: quibus dixit, Venite post me, & faciam vos fieri piscatores hominum, at illi continuò relictis retibus secuti sunt eum. Matth. 4. huic Christus resurgens dixit, Pasce oues meas. Ioã 21. Antiochiæ præses fuit: euangelium dispersos Iudæos in Pōto, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia & Bithynia docuit. Diony. Corynt. Epis. scripsit S. Petrum & Paulum eodem die Romæ iussu Neronis passos. Petrus capite ad terrā verso, fertur crucifixus, asserens se indignũ ut crucifigeretur sicut Dominus suus. epistolas complures scripsere, quas habes in novo testameto. vide item Euse. li. 3. ca. 1. & 2. D. Iero. scripsit Petrum ad expugnādum Simonem Magum, Romæ perrexisse, ibíque pōtificatum 25. annis tenuisse, usq; ad ultimum Neronis annum.
units.tr: S. Peter, the foremost among the apostles, was the brother of the apostle Andrew also. Both were from the village of Bethsaida in Galilee, and both were called by Christ together, when they were casting their net into the sea, for they were fishermen. To them he said, "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men"; and at once they left their nets and followed him. Matt. 4. To Peter, when he rose again, Christ said, "Feed my sheep." John 21. He was president at Antioch; he taught the gospel to the Jews scattered in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia. Dionysius of Corinth, in his letter, wrote that S. Peter and S. Paul suffered on the same day at Rome, by order of Nero. Peter, with his head turned towards the ground, is said to have been crucified, declaring that he was unworthy to be crucified as his Lord had been. They wrote several epistles, which you have in the New Testament. See also Eusebius, book 3, chapters 1 and 2. Jerome wrote that Peter went to Rome to confront Simon the Magician, and there held the papacy for 25 years, down to the last year of Nero.

units.la: S. PAULUS de tribu Beniamin, & oppido Iudæ Giscalis fuit, quo à Romanis capto, cum parētibus suis Tarsum Ciliciæ cōmigrauit: à quibus ob studia legis missus Ierusalem, à Gamaliele eruditus est. Cùm autē interfuisset neci D. Stephani, & acceptis à Pōtifice tēpli epistolis, ad Christianos persequēdos, Damascum pergeret, reuelatione ad fidem, ac miraculo velut cōpulsus, vas electionis de persecutore factus est. Docuit gentes Euāgelium annos 21. duobus annis Cefareæ tantundémque Romæ in carcere fuit: at Romæ è carcere exibat quò vellet, sub custodia tamen. hinc liberatus atq; absolutus, cùm causam ipse suam coram Nerone egisset, liberè denuo docuit Euangelium decem annis. at, iterum in carcerem cõiectus, capite truncatur, anno mundi 4030. à Christo nato 68. SERGIVS GALBA GALBAE IMP. PA[?] NVMMIA ACHAIA GAL. IMP. MAT.
units.tr: S. Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin, and of the town Giscala in Judea; when it was taken by the Romans, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus in Cilicia. Sent from there to Jerusalem on account of his study of the law, he was taught by Gamaliel. When he had been present at the death of S. Stephen, and had received letters from the high priest of the temple to persecute the Christians, and was travelling to Damascus, he was, by a revelation and a miracle, as it were compelled to faith, and from a persecutor became a chosen vessel. He taught the Gentiles the gospel for 21 years; for two years he was in prison at Caesarea, and as long a time at Rome; yet at Rome he went out of prison wherever he wished, though under guard. Then, freed and acquitted, after he had himself pleaded his cause before Nero, he taught the gospel freely again for ten years. But, cast into prison a second time, he was beheaded in the year of the world 4030, from the birth of Christ 68. SERGIUS GALBA, FATHER OF THE EMPEROR GALBA. PA[?]. NUMMIA ACHAIA, MOTHER OF THE EMPEROR GALBA.

units.la: SERGIVS Galba, Galbæ Imperatoris pater, Romæ Consulatu functus, quamquam breui corpore, atque etiam gibber, modicæque in dicendo facultatis, causas tamen industriè actitauit. Hic vxores habuit Mummiam Achaiam, item Liuiam Ocellinam, ditem admodum & pulchram: à qua tamen nobilitatis causa appetitus vltro existimatur, & aliquanto enixius, postquàm subinde instanti, vitium corporis secretò posita veste detexit, ne quasi ignaram fallere videretur. Crati quoque Thebano idem contigit, cùm Hipparche eum maritum optaret. Vide quatenus ad Sergium, Sueto. in Galba.
units.tr: Sergius Galba, father of the emperor Galba, held the consulship at Rome. Although he was short of body and even hunchbacked, and of only modest ability in speaking, he pleaded cases diligently. He had as wives Mummia Achaia, and also Livia Ocellina, a very rich and beautiful woman; yet he is thought to have been sought by her of her own accord, on account of his nobility, and rather eagerly. Later, when she kept pressing him, he secretly took off his garment and showed her his bodily defect, lest he seem to deceive her as one who was ignorant of it. The same thing happened to Crates of Thebes, when Hipparchia wished him as her husband. See how far this applies to Sergius; Suetonius in Galba.

units.la: MVMMIA Achaïa neptis Catuli, proneptisque L. Mummij qui Corinthum excidit, vxor Sergij Galbæ fuit, ex qua Caium & Sergium procreauit: quorum maior Caius attritis facultatibus vrbe cessit, prohibitúsque à Tiberio sortiri anno suo Proconsulatum, voluntaria morte obiit: Sergius verò post Neronem imperauit. Vide Sueto. in Galba. SER. GALBA IMP. SAES [?] AVG. LEPIDA GALBAE IMP VXOR.
units.tr: Mummia Achaia, granddaughter of Catulus and great-granddaughter of L. Mummius, who destroyed Corinth, was the wife of Sergius Galba, and by her he had Caius and Sergius. The elder, Caius, having exhausted his resources, left the city; and when Tiberius forbade him to take up the proconsulship in his year, he died by his own hand. Sergius, however, ruled after Nero. See Suetonius in Galba. SERGIUS GALBA, EMPEROR. SAES[?] AUGUSTA. LEPIDA, WIFE OF THE EMPEROR GALBA.

units.la: SERGIVS Sulpitius Galba, Romæ post Neronē imperat anno mundi 4030. à Christo nato 68. Hic nullo gradu Cæsares contingebat, nam horum familia, siue progenies in Neronē defecerat: nobilissimus tamen erat, magnáq; & vetere prosapia. Antequàm imperaret mula fertur peperisse. Hic cùm Prætor esset, elephantos funambulos edidit ludis Floralibus. Maiore ab initio fauore quàm læto successu, septimestre imperium tenuit annos natus circiter 80. priuata eius vita insignis fuerat militaribus & ciuilibus rebus. Tandem auarum, sæuum, pigrum se præstitit: atque inuisus omnibus, in medio foro, insidiis Othonis iugulatur: nam cùm subinde iactaret se legere militem, uon emere consuesse, eo nomine omnes milites exacerbauit. Sed maximè fremebat superioris Germaniæ exercitus fraudari se præmiis: quare statim legationem ad prætorianos cum mandatis destinant: displicere inquiunt Imperatorem in Hispania factum, eligerent ipsi quem cuncti exercitus probarent. Quamobrem ascitus Otho eum trucidari curauit. Vide Sueto.in Galba, Eutro.lib.7. Bap.Egna.lib.1.
units.tr: Sergius Sulpicius Galba ruled at Rome after Nero, in the year of the world 4030, from the birth of Christ 68. He was related to the Caesars by no degree of kinship, for their family, or line, had died out in Nero; yet he was of the most noble birth, and of a great and ancient lineage. Before he became emperor, a mule is said to have given birth. When he was praetor, he presented elephant tightrope-walkers at the Floralia games. He held the imperial power for seven months, at first with greater favour than successful outcome, being about 80 years old. His private life had been distinguished in military and civil affairs. At last he showed himself greedy, cruel and sluggish; and hated by all, he was slain in the middle of the forum by the plots of Otho. For when he kept saying that he chose soldiers, and did not buy them, he angered all the soldiers on that account. But the army of Upper Germany especially complained that it was defrauded of its rewards; so they at once sent a deputation with instructions to the praetorian guard, saying that it displeased them that an emperor had been made in Spain, and that they themselves should choose whomever all the armies approved. Accordingly, Otho, who had been taken into their favour, saw to it that Galba was slaughtered. See Suetonius in Galba, Eutropius book 7, and Baptista Egnatius book 1.

units.la: LEPIDA vxor fuit Galbæ Imperatoris, qua amissa, duobúsque ex ea filiis, remansit in cœlibatu: neque solicitari vlla conditione amplius potuit, ne Agrippinæ quidem matris Neronis, viduatæ morte Domitij Aenobarbi, quæ maritum quoq; adhuc, necdum cœlibem Galbam, adeò omnibus solicitauerat modis, vt in conuentu matronarum correpta iurgio, atq; etiam manu pullata sit à matre Lepidæ. Sueto.in Gal.
units.tr: Lepida was the wife of the emperor Galba.
