After she was lost, and her two sons by him, she remained unmarried; nor could she be solicited any more on any terms, not even by Agrippina, the mother of Nero, widowed by the death of Domitius Ahenobarbus, who had so pressed her, even Galba being still unmarried, by every means, that in a gathering of matrons she was caught in a quarrel and even had her hair pulled by the mother of Lepida. Suetonius in Galba.

units.la: L. OTHO, Imperatoris Othonis pater, materno genere præclaro, multarúmque & magnarum propinquitatum, tam charus,támq; non absimilis facie Tiberio principi fuit,ut plerique procreatū ex eo crederent.Hic urbanos honores,Proconsulatum Africæ,& extraordinaria imperia seuerissimè administrauit. Senatus hunc honore rarissimo,statua in palatio posita, prosecutus est: & Claudius allectum inter Patricios collaudās hunc amplissimis verbis,hæc quoq; adiecit:Vir,quo meliores liberos habere ne opto quidem. Sueton.in Othone.
units.tr: L. Otho, father of the emperor Otho, of illustrious maternal descent and of many great connections, was so dear to the emperor Tiberius, and so not unlike him in appearance, that most people believed he had been begotten by him. He discharged the urban offices, the proconsulship of Africa, and extraordinary commands with the greatest severity. The Senate honoured him with a very rare distinction, setting up a statue of him in the palace; and Claudius, having admitted him among the patricians, praised him in the most generous terms and also added these words: "A man, than whose better children I do not even wish to have." Suetonius in Otho.

units.la: ALBIA Terentia splendidissima fœmina,L.Othonis uxor fuit,quæ peperit illi L. Titianum,siue Terentianū,& minorem Marcum,cognominem patri,Othonémq; appellatum,qui post Galbam imperavit:peperit quoq; filiam, quam nondum nubilem Drufo Germanici filio despōdit, Consulito Suetonium in Othone.
units.tr: Albia Terentia, a most distinguished woman, was the wife of L. Otho. She bore him L. Titianus, or Terentianus, and the younger Marcus, named after his father, called Otho, who afterwards ruled after Galba; she also bore a daughter, whom, not yet marriageable, he betrothed to Drusus, son of Germanicus. Consult Suetonius in Otho.

units.la: MARC. S. Otho octauus, Galbæ succedens, Romanis imperat anno mundi 4031. à Christo nato 69. A prima adolescentia prodigus, procax, & mollis extitit, Neroni etiā familiaris. die quem Nero necandæ matri destinarat, ad avertendas suspitiones cœnā utrique exquisitissimè comitatis dedit. Speraverat fore ut adoptaretur à Galba:sed Pisone prælato ad vim conversus est, instigante, super animi dolorem, etiam magnitudine æris alieni. Neque enim dissimulabat, nisi principem se stare non posse, nihilque referre, ab hoste in acie, an in foro sub creditoribus caderet. Quare missis qui Galbam, & Pisonem trucidarent, ea ipsa die qua Galbā mane salutarat, osculo etiam ut consueuerat exceptus, Imperator salutatur. Ad conciliandos pollicitationibus animos nihil magis pro cōcione testatus est, quàm id demum se habiturum quod sibi milites reliquissent. Dicitur noctu per quietem pavefactus, gemitus maximos edidisse, repertúsque à concursantibus humi ante lectū jacens, à quo manes Galbæ eum deturbarant: quod fatebatur ipsemet vidisse. Hic levi prælio victus à Vitellii ducibus, sinistram sibi papillam pugione transfixit: cùm tamen complures adhuc copias haberet, & petentibus militibus ne tam citò de belli eventu desperaret, dixisset, se tanti non esse, ut propter eum ciuile bellum oriretur. Vixit annos 38. imperavit menses treis: adeò militibus charus ut multi ad eius exemplum, ante mortui pedes se interfecerint.•Suet.in Othone. VITELLIVS VITELLI IMP GERM [?] SEXTILIA VITELLI IMP MATER
units.tr: M. S. Otho, the eighth, succeeding Galba, ruled over the Romans in the year of the world 4031, from the birth of Christ 69. From his earliest youth he was prodigal, insolent and effeminate, and he was also a close friend of Nero. On the day which Nero had appointed for killing his mother, in order to avert suspicion, he gave a very elaborate dinner to both of them. He had hoped to be adopted by Galba; but, Piso being preferred, he turned to violence, incited, besides the bitterness of his spirit, by the great size of his debts. For he did not conceal that he could not remain a prince unless he did so, and that it made no difference whether he fell by an enemy in battle or in the forum under his creditors. Accordingly, sending men to slaughter Galba and Piso, on the very day on which he had greeted Galba in the morning and been received with a kiss, as was his custom, he was saluted emperor. To win over men's minds with promises, he gave no greater assurance in the assembly than that he would keep whatever the soldiers left him. It is said that at night, terrified in his sleep, he uttered very great groans, and was found by those running together lying on the ground before his bed, where the ghosts of Galba had thrown him down; this he himself admitted he had seen. Defeated in a slight battle by the leaders of Vitellius, he pierced his left breast with a dagger; yet, although he still had many troops, and the soldiers begged him not to despair so quickly of the outcome of the war, he said that he was not worth so much that a civil war should arise on his account. He lived 38 years and ruled for three months; so dear was he to the soldiers that many, following his example, killed themselves at his feet before he died. Suet. in Otho. VITELLIUS, FATHER OF THE EMPEROR VITELLIUS, GERMANICUS[?]. SEXTILIA, MOTHER OF THE EMPEROR VITELLIUS.

units.la: L. VITELLIVS, A. Vitellij Imperatoris pater , Syriæ præpositus,Artabanum Parthorũ Regem summis artibus non modò ad colloquium suum, sed etiam ad veneranda legionũ Signa pellexit.Mox cum Claudio principe duos insuper ordinarios Consulatus,Censuramque gesit. Curam quoque Imperij sustinuit absente eo,expeditione Britannica : vir innocès [?] & industrius,sed amore libertinæ perinfamis.Idem miri in adulando ingenij,primus C.Cęsarem Caligulam adorari ut Deum instituit,primúsque adorauiti [?], non aliter adire aulus , quàm capite velato circunvertens se,deinde procumbens. Hic à Valeria Messalina petiit ut ei pedes præberet excalceandos: detractúmque socculum dextrum inter togam tunicámque gestauit assiduè, nõnnunquam osculabundus, ídque factitabat, ut nulla non via,atque arte, principem uxori addictū demererētur. Decessit paralysi altero die quàm correptus est. Sueton.in Vitellio.
units.tr: L. Vitellius, father of the Emperor Aulus Vitellius, was placed in charge of Syria. By the greatest skill he persuaded Artabanus, king of the Parthians, not only to come to a conference with him but also to venerate the standards of the legions. Soon afterwards, with the Emperor Claudius, he held two ordinary consulships in succession and also the censorship. He also bore the care of the empire in the absence of Claudius on the British expedition. He was a blameless and industrious man, but he was notoriously given over to love of a freedwoman. He had a marvellous talent for flattery: he was the first to institute the worship of Gaius Caesar Caligula as a god, and he was the first to approach him with his head veiled, turning himself about, and then prostrating himself. He once asked Valeria Messalina to offer him her feet to be unshod; he took off her right slipper and carried it constantly between his toga and tunic, sometimes kissing it, and he did this so that by every road and every art he might win the emperor, who was devoted to his wife. He died of paralysis the day after he was seized by it. Suetonius, in Vitellius.

units.la: SEXTILIA, probatissima, nec ignobilis fœmina, Lucij Vitellij prædicti uxor fuit,quæ ei peperit duos filios , quos eodem anno ambos Consules,cum maiori minor in sex menses successisset,uterque parens vidit.Alter ex his filius, Aulus Vitellius,post Othonem imperavit:cuius genituram, sive nativitatem,aut natalis horæ inspectionem, à Mathematicis prædictam ita exhorruerunt parentes , ut pater magnopere contenderit ne qua ei provincia vivo se committeretur:mater&missum ad legiones,& appellatum Imperatorem, pro afflicto statim lamentata sit. Vide Sueton.in Vitel. prædixerant Mathematici Aulum Vitellium futurum quidem Imperatorem : sed in imperio per vim cruciabiliter periturum.
units.tr: Sextilia, a most virtuous woman of no mean family, was the wife of the aforesaid Lucius Vitellius. She bore him two sons, and both parents saw them both made consuls in the same year, the younger having succeeded the elder after six months. One of these sons, Aulus Vitellius, ruled after Otho. His parents were so horrified by the prediction of the mathematicians about his horoscope, that is, the casting of his nativity or the inspection of the hour of his birth, that his father strenuously insisted that no province be entrusted to him while he lived; and his mother, when he was sent to the legions and hailed as emperor, lamented as if he were already ruined. See Suetonius, in Vitellius. The mathematicians had foretold that Aulus Vitellius would indeed become emperor, but that in his rule he would perish miserably by violence.

units.la: AVLVS Vitellius, à Galba in inferiorem Germaniā missus est. Aduentantem, male animatus erga principē exercitus, libens ac supinis manibus excipit, velut dono Deūm oblatum III.Conf.filiū, ætate integra, facili ac prodigo animo. hāc de se veterē persuasione auxerat, tota ipse via milites obuios exosculatus, pérq; diuersoria comis, manè singulos iámne ientassent sciscitatus, séque fecisse, rustu quoque ostédens. nil cuiquā negauit, atq; etiā vltro reis sordes, dānatis supplicia dēpsit: Quare vixdū mense transacto, subitò à militibus è cubiculo raptus, vt erat, in veste domestica, Imperator consalutatur anno mundi 4031.à Christo nato 69. Hic in ientacula, prādia & cœnas, facilè omnibus sufficiebat vomitandi cõsuetudine. Cœna ei data est aduentitia à fratre, in qua, super cæteros sumptus, 2000.lectissimorū pisciū 7000.auium apposita sunt. hāc quoque exuperauit ipse, dedicatione patinæ, quam clipeum Minervæ dictitabat.Sæuus fuit, nam & eius hæc vox est, optimè olere occisum hostē, & melius ciuem. Vespasiano principe declarato, cœno fimóque iactatus, vestéque discissa in forum tractus, subiecto ad mentū gladio, tandem minutis.ictibus excarnificatus, vnco trahitur in Tyberim.Suet.in Vitell.vixit an.57.rexit menses 8.
units.tr: Aulus Vitellius was sent by Galba into Lower Germany. The army, which was ill-disposed towards the emperor, received him gladly and with open hands, as if a gift of the gods had been offered: a son of Lucius, the consul of the third time, in the full vigour of his age, of an easy and lavish spirit. He increased this old opinion of himself by kissing the soldiers he met along the whole road, and by asking, in the lodgings where he stayed, whether each of them had already eaten breakfast, showing himself to have done so too, even in his belching. He refused nothing to anyone; and, moreover, he willingly remitted the penalties of the guilty and the punishments of the condemned. Therefore, scarcely a month having passed, he was suddenly dragged from his bedchamber by the soldiers, just as he was, in his house clothes, and was hailed as emperor, in the year of the world 4031 and of the birth of Christ 69. He was able, at breakfasts, lunches and dinners, to satisfy everyone easily, by the habit of vomiting. A dinner was given to him by his brother as a gift for the arrival, at which, besides the other expenses, 2,000 choice fish and 7,000 birds were served. He himself surpassed even this, at the dedication of a platter which he used to call the shield of Minerva. He was cruel, for this saying of his is also recorded: that a slain enemy smells excellent, and a slain citizen still better. When Vespasian had been declared emperor, he was battered with mud and dung, dragged in torn clothing into the forum with a sword placed at his chin, and at last was butchered with small blows and dragged with a hook into the Tiber. Suetonius, in Vitellius. He lived 57 years and reigned 8 months.

units.la: PETRONIA Consularis viri filia, Vitellij vxor prior, Petronianū altero captum oculo peperit, quem pater interemisse creditur, insimulatum parricidij, post matris obitum.
units.tr: Petronia, daughter of a consular man, was the first wife of Vitellius. She bore him Petronianus, who was born blind in one eye; his father is believed to have killed him, having accused him of parricide after the death of his mother.

units.la: GALERIA Fundana, A.Vitellij vxor, Prætorio patre nata, liberos vtriusque sexus tulit, sed marem titubantia oris prope mutum.Suet.in Vitell.
units.tr: Galeria Fundana, wife of Aulus Vitellius, was born of a praetorian father. She bore children of both sexes to him, but the male was almost mute, stammering in his speech. Suetonius, in Vitellius.

units.la: T. FL A. Sabinus, Vespasiani imperatoris pater, Tit. Flau. Petronio municipe Reatino natus est, eo, inquâ, qui bello ciuili Pompeianarum partium Centurio fuit, ac ex acie Pharsalica domum se contulit, vbi venia, & missione impetrata, coactiones argentarias factitauit. Porrò Sabinus Vespasiani, vt dixi, pater (nâ de auo Principis quæ prælibauimus, dicta sunt) expers militiæ (etsi quidam eum Primipilarē, nōnu lli cùm adhuc ordines duceret, sacramēto solutū per causam valetudinis tradūt) publicanū quadragesimę in Asia egit, fuerúntq; imagines à ciuitatibus ei sub hoc titulo positę, Rectè vectigalia exigēti. postea fœnus apud Heluetios exercuit, ibíque diē obiit, superstitibus uxore Vespasia Polla, & duobus ex ea liberis, Sabino videlicet, altero ab illo priore Principis patre, & Vespasiano: horum maior Sabinus, Principis frater, ad præfecturam vrbis, minor verò Vespasianus, ad imperium euectus est. Vide Suetonium in Vespasiano Imp.
units.tr: T. Flavius Sabinus, father of the Emperor Vespasian, was born at Petronium, a citizen of Reate, the same man, I say, who was a centurion of the Pompeian party in the civil war, and who, after the battle of Pharsalus, withdrew home, where, having obtained pardon and discharge, he carried on the business of money-changing and collecting. Moreover, Sabinus, the father of Vespasian, as I have said (for what has been touched upon about the grandfather of the prince has been told), had no military service (although some hand down that he was a chief centurion, and some, when he was still leading the ranks, that he was discharged from his oath on account of ill health). He was a tax-farmer of the fortieth in Asia, and statues were set up to him by the cities under this inscription: "To the man who collects the taxes rightly." Afterwards he carried on usury among the Helvetians, and there he died, leaving behind his wife Vespasia Polla and two sons by her: Sabinus, namely, and, the other, Vespasian, the father of the prince being the earlier by another marriage. The elder, Sabinus, the brother of the prince, was raised to the prefecture of the city; the younger, Vespasian, was raised to the empire. See Suetonius, in Vespasian.

units.la: VESPASIA Polla T. Flauij Sabini vxor, superstes fuit viro cum duobus ex eo liberis, quorum maior Sabinus ad præfecturam vrbis, minor Vespasianus ad principatum vsq; processit. Hæc Polla Nursiæ honesto genere orta patrem habuit Vespasium Pollionem, ter Tribunum militum, præfectúmque castrorum, fratrémque Senatorem prætoriæ dignitatis. Sueton. in Vespasiano.
units.tr: Vespasia Polla, wife of T. Flavius Sabinus, survived her husband with two sons by him, of whom the elder, Sabinus, advanced to the prefecture of the city, and the younger, Vespasian, to the principate. This Polla, sprung from an honourable family of Nursia, had as her father Vespasius Pollio, three times a military tribune and prefect of the camp, and a brother who was a senator of praetorian rank. Suetonius, in Vespasian.

units.la: IMP CAES VESPASIAN AVG P M TR P P P COS[?]
units.tr: IMP. CAES. VESPASIAN. AVG. P.M. TR. P. P.P. COS.

units.la: FLA. VESPASIANVS natus est in Sabinis vltra Reaten, vico modico, cui nomen est Phalacrine, quinquennio antequàm Augustus obiret. Claudio principe, legatus legionis in Germaniam missus est: inde in Britannia translatus, tricies cum hoste conflixit. Duas validis. gentes, superque 20. oppida, & insulam Vecten, Britanniæ proximam, in deditionē redegit. Missus ad comprimēdos Iudæos de Ierusalem cum filio triumphauit. Mortuo Othone hic à Mœsiaco exercitu Imperator creatur, posthæc qui erat Ægypri præfectus, primus in verba Vespasiani legiones adegit, post paucos dies Iudaicus exercitus apud ipsū iurauit anno mundi 4032. à Christo nato 70. Misso itaq; exercitu aduersus Vitellium, in Alexandriam transiit, vt claustra Ægypti obtineret: statimq; venēre literæ fusas apud Cremonam Vitellij copias, ipsum in vrbe interfectum nuntiantes. Romam igitur reuersus Vespasianus, afflictam prope, nutantémq; remp. stabiliuit primò, deinde ornauit. Cum adolescens vnguēto fragrās pro impetrata præfectura gratias ei ageret, maluissem, inquit allium oboluisses, literásque reuocauit. Achaiam, Lyciam, Rhodum, Byzantium, Samū libertate adēpta, item Tracheam, Ciliciā, & Comagenē, ditionis regiæ vsq; ad id tempus, in prouinciarum formā redegit. Modestiam retinuit & comitatem: iustis supplicis illachrymauit, offensarū minimè memor: ingenia & artes maximè fouit: Sola culpatur auaritia. Tandē septuagenarius ac stans obiit inter manus subleuantium, Imperatorem dicens stantem mori oportere. imperauit annos 10. Sueto. in. Vespa.
units.tr: T. Flavius Vespasianus was born among the Sabines beyond Reate, in a small village called Phalacrine, five years before Augustus died. Under the emperor Claudius he was sent into Germany as legate of a legion; thence he was transferred to Britain, where he fought thirty battles with the enemy. He reduced two powerful peoples, more than twenty towns, and the island of Vectis, next to Britain, to surrender. Sent to put down the Jews, he triumphed with his son over Jerusalem. After Otho's death he was created emperor by the Moesian army; afterwards he, who was prefect of Egypt, was the first to bind the legions to the oath to Vespasian, and a few days later the Jewish army swore allegiance to him, in the year of the world 4032 and of the birth of Christ 70. Having therefore sent an army against Vitellius, he himself crossed into Alexandria, in order to hold the gates of Egypt; and immediately letters came announcing that the forces of Vitellius had been routed at Cremona and that he himself had been killed in the city. Vespasian, returning to Rome, first stabilised the state, which was nearly ruined and wavering, and then adorned it. When a young man, fragrant with ointment, thanked him for a prefecture that had been obtained for him, Vespasian said, "I would rather you had eaten garlic," and he revoked the letters. He reduced to the form of provinces Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium and Samos, having taken away their freedom, likewise Thrace, Cilicia and Commagene, which until then had been under royal sway. He kept moderation and courtesy; he wept over the just pleas of suppliants, and was very little mindful of offences; he chiefly fostered talents and the arts. Only avarice was blamed in him. At last he died at the age of seventy, standing, in the arms of those who supported him, saying, "An emperor ought to die standing." He reigned ten years. Suetonius, in Vespasian.

units.la: Vespasiani vxor, peperit ei Titum, Domitianum & Domicillam: vxorem & natam priuatus adhuc amisit Vespasianus. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: Wife of Vespasian, who bore him Titus, Domitian and Domicilla. Vespasian lost his wife and daughter while still a private citizen. See above.

units.la: TITVS Vespasianus Romæ post patrē imperat anno mundi 4042. à Christo nato 80. Hic amor & deliciæ humani generis dictus est:facudus,bellicosus,moderatus fuit,clemens ac liberalis:quas virtutes per totum principatū magis cōmendauit & vitæ anteactę licētia,& sub initia luxuriæ & auaritię suspicio, vt Neronis tyrannidē pleriq; augurarētur.Sed mutatus,adepto imperio,in melius, declarauit eiusdē esse ingenij & pesima & optima interdū ferre. Amicos elegit reip.necessarios:Berenicē statim ab vrbe dimisit,inuitus inuitam.nulli ciuium quicquam ademit:ac ne confessas quidē,ac solitas collationes recepit,nec tamen eum quisquam munificētia prævertit:recordatúsq;aliquando super cœnam,se nil in quenquā toto die contulisse,dixit: Amici,diem perdidi.huius etiā & hæc vox est,Neminem oportere à sermone principis tristem discedere.Dedit nauale prelium,atque vno die 5000.omne genus ferarū exhibuit. Ad perdomandam Iudææ à patre relictus 12.propugnatores totidem sagittarū confecit ictibus,cepitque Ierusalē natali filiæ suæ,tāto militū gaudio, vt eum Imperatorem cōsalutarint. hic matres etiam filios in edulium pararunt. Fratrem insidiantem,nec occidit,nec relegauit:sed vt à primo imperij die, consortem successoremque testari perseuerauit. Cæterum obiit febre eadē qua pater villa, ætatis an.41.impe rij 2. Vide Suetonium.
units.tr: TITUS Vespasian became emperor at Rome after his father, in the year of the world 4042, from the birth of Christ 80. He was called the darling and delight of the human race. He was eloquent, warlike, moderate, merciful and generous, and he commended these virtues more and more throughout his whole reign. His earlier life had been licentious, and at the beginning of his rule there were suspicions of luxury and avarice, so that most people feared he would be a tyrant like Nero. But once he had gained the empire, he changed for the better, and showed that he was of such a character that he could sometimes bear both the worst and the best. He chose as friends men necessary to the state. He sent Berenice away from the city at once, though she was unwilling and he was unwilling to send her. He took nothing from any citizen, and did not even accept the customary gifts and contributions that had been regularly offered, yet no one surpassed him in generosity. Once, recalling at dinner that he had given nothing to anyone the whole day, he said: "Friends, I have lost a day." This is also his saying: "No one should leave the emperor's presence sad." He gave a naval battle, and in a single day exhibited five thousand beasts of every kind. To subdue Judea, which his father had left unfinished, he raised twelve champions and, with that many archers, cut them down with arrows; he took Jerusalem on his daughter's birthday, to such joy of the soldiers that they hailed him as emperor. Here mothers, too, prepared their sons as food. He neither killed nor banished his brother, who was plotting against him, but persisted in naming him partner and successor from the first day of his reign. He died of the same fever his father had died of, at the age of 41, in the second year of his reign. See Suetonius.

units.la: ARRICIDIA, Tertullo patre Equite Romano nata,Titi vxor fuit.
units.tr: ARRICIDIA, daughter of Tertullus, a Roman knight, was the wife of Titus.

units.la: MARTIA Fuluia splēdidi generis, Tito quoque, mortua Arricidia, nupsit: cum qua,suscepta filia, diuortium fecit. Sueto. in Tito.
units.tr: MARTIA Fulvia, of a distinguished family, also married Titus after Arricidia died. He divorced her after she had borne him a daughter. See Suetonius, in Titus.

units.la: FLA. DOMITIANVS, post fratrem Titum Romæ imperat anno mundi 4044. à Christo nato 82. Adolescentiam cum infamia,& paupertate transfegit.Expeditionē in Galliam & Germanias non necessariam inchoauit,tantum vt fratri se & operibus & dignatione adæquaret.Patre defuncto,iactare non dubitauit,relictum se principem imperij,sed fraude testamento adhibitam.Initio principatus sui,secretum horarium quotidie sumebat,nec quicquâ amplius quàm muscas captabat,ac stylo præacuto configebat:vt non absurdè responderit Vibius Crispus,ne muscam quidem cum Cæsare esse. Varium se præstitit aliquandiu,mixtura quadâ inæquabili virtutum ac vitiorū:donec virtutes quoq; in vitia deflexit, super ingenij naturam , inopia rapax,metu sævus. De Cattis,Dacisq; post varia prælia duplicē triumphum egit:de Sarmatis lauream Capitolino Ioui retulit. Superbus hic,tandem Dominum & Deum se appellari coëgit: nullam sibi nisi auream & argenteam statuam poni passus est. crudelis etiam consobrinos,item nobilis.ex Senatu interfecit. Per hæc terribilis cunctis & inuisus,multis vulneribus cōfoditur,fuorū,vxoris quoq; coniuratione,anno ætatis 45.imperij 15. Funus eius per vespillones cum ingenti dedecore exportatur, & ignobiliter sepelitur:radendū eius nomen Senatus decernit, omniaque eius acta rescindit.Sueto. in Domiti.Eutr.li.7.
units.tr: FLAVIUS DOMITIAN became emperor at Rome after his brother Titus, in the year of the world 4044, from the birth of Christ 82. He spent his youth in disgrace and poverty. He began an unnecessary expedition into Gaul and the Germanies, only so that he might match his brother in achievements and in honour. After his father's death he did not hesitate to boast that he had been left as ruler of the empire, but that this had been brought about by fraud in the will. At the beginning of his reign he took a private hour each day, and did nothing more than catch flies and stab them with a sharp stylus, so that Vibius Crispus fittingly replied, "There is not even a fly with Caesar." For a while he showed himself changeable, with an uneven mixture of virtues and vices, until finally his virtues too turned into vices, beyond the nature of his talent: he was greedy through poverty and cruel through fear. After various battles against the Catti and the Daci he celebrated a double triumph, and over the Sarmatians he brought the laurel to Jupiter of the Capitol. This proud man at last compelled people to call him Lord and God, and he allowed no statue of himself to be set up except of gold and silver. He was also cruel, and put to death his cousins, and likewise noble men from the Senate. Hated and feared by all for these things, he was stabbed with many wounds, through a conspiracy that included his own freedmen and wife, in the forty-fifth year of his life and the fifteenth of his reign. His body was carried out by gravediggers with great dishonour and buried without ceremony; the Senate decreed that his name be erased and annulled all his acts. See Suetonius, in Domitian; Eutropius, book 7.

units.la: DOMITIA Longina Ælio Lamiæ nupta, à Dom itiano abducitur,ante quàm imperaret.hanc Paridis histrionis amore deperditam,repudiauit:intráque breue tempus impatiês diffidij,quasi efflagitante populo,reduxit.
units.tr: DOMITIA Longina was married to Aelius Lamia, and was taken away by Domitian before he became emperor. When she was lost through love of the actor Paris, he divorced her, but within a short time, being unable to endure the separation, and as if the people were demanding it, he took her back.

units.la: COCCEIUS Nerva, Romæ post cædē Domitiani, Imperator designatur, anno mundi 4059. à Christo nato 97. Et hactenus Romæ seu per Italiam orti imperium rexere: hinc advenæ. unde compertum, urbem Romā externorum virtute crevisse: quod aurea gibba Domitiano post ceruicem in somnis enata, portendit. Hic quicquid antea pœnæ nomine, tributis accesserat, indulsit: afflictas civitates releuavit: puellas, puerósq; natos parentibus egenis, sumptu publico per Italiæ oppida alii iussit. Quæ in aula reperta sunt, ex bonis quæ Domitianus per vim abstulerat, restitui curavit. Servi & libertorū plurimi, dominis atque patronis insidias fecerat, hos ad unū occidi imperavit. Ad sustentandam civium vitam plus 100000 aureorum erogavit, & quosdam Senatorii ordinis delegit qui agros emeret, eósque egenis diuideret. Pecuniæ inops factus, vestes primum & vasa aurea & argentea, siue sua propria siue publica forent auctioni subiecit: agros, item ingētes domos, & omnia demum præter admodum necessaria vēdidit. Nihil unquam de suo arbitrio statuit, sed primarios viros in cōsilium semper adhibuit. Cùm ob senectam contemptui esset, Traianum Hispanum, publicæ utilitati societatem sanguinis postponens, præteritis cognatis propriis, adoptavit. in coniuratores clemens fuit. obiit ferè septuagenarius, sudore correptus dū voce quàm maxima, cōtra quēdam inclamaret suggerēte ira, tunc Solis deliquium factum est. imperavit anno uno, & mēsibus 4. Dion Cass. Aurel. Vict. Bap. Egna. lib. i. Eutro. li. 8.
units.tr: COCCEIUS Nerva was designated emperor at Rome after the murder of Domitian, in the year of the world 4059, from the birth of Christ 97. Up to this point those born at Rome or in Italy had ruled the empire; from now on it was foreigners. From this it is evident that the city of Rome had grown by the valour of outsiders, as the golden hump that grew in dreams on Domitian's neck foretold. Nerva remitted whatever had been added beforehand under the name of punishment, in the form of taxes; he relieved the afflicted cities; he ordered that girls and boys born to needy parents be maintained at public expense in the towns of Italy. He saw to it that what was found in the palace from the goods Domitian had seized by force was restored. Many slaves and freedmen had plotted against their masters and patrons, and he ordered that these be put to death, every one. To sustain the lives of citizens he spent more than 100,000 gold pieces, and he chose some men of senatorial rank to buy fields and distribute them to the needy. Having become short of money, he first put up for auction the clothes, gold and silver vessels, whether they were his own private property or public property; he sold fields, likewise huge houses, and in short nearly everything except what was absolutely necessary. He never decided anything by his own will alone, but always took the leading men into his council. When, on account of his old age, he had become an object of contempt, he adopted Trajan, a Spaniard, placing the public good above ties of blood, and passing over his own relatives. He was merciful toward the conspirators. He died at nearly seventy years of age, seized by a sweat while shouting with all his might against a certain man, urged on by anger; then an eclipse of the sun took place. He reigned one year and four months. See Dio Cassius, Aurelius Victor, Bapt. Egnatius, book 1; Eutropius, book 8.

units.la: M. VLPIVS Traianus Hispanus, optimus omnium princeps, externorum primus, Romae imperat anno mundi 4060. à Christo nato 98. Hic Daciam provinciam fecit, victo rege Decebalo:lapideum pontem in Istro fecit, Parthos superavit, superatis Regè dedit. Transtigritanas provincias imperio adiecit: Armeniam atque Arabiam peruastauit: Amicitias, simplicia ac erudita ingenia coluit, ipse à literis & Musis non abhorrens. De hoc Cæsare scribit Juvenalis Satyra 7.
units.tr: M. ULPIUS Trajan, a Spaniard, the best of all princes, the first of the foreigners, became emperor at Rome in the year of the world 4060, from the birth of Christ 98. He made Dacia a province after defeating King Decebalus. He built a stone bridge over the Danube. He overcame the Parthians, and after overcoming them gave them a king. He added the provinces beyond the Tigris to the empire. He laid waste Armenia and Arabia. He cultivated friendships and simple and learned minds, himself not averse to letters and the Muses. Juvenal writes about this emperor in Satire 7:

units.la: Et spes,& ratio studiorum in Cæsare tantum: Solus enim tristes hac tempestate Camœnas Respexit,&c.
units.tr: And the hope and the reason of study rest on Caesar alone: for he alone in these gloomy times has looked upon the sorrowing Muses, etc.

units.la: Hic Armeniam, Assyriam, Mesopotamiam, postea Arabiam provincias fecit. in mari rubro classem instituit, ut per eam Indiæ fines vastaret. Gloriam tamen militarem civilitate & moderatione superavit: liberalis in omnes fuit: immunitates civitatibus tribuit. amicis culpantibus quòd nimis circa omnes comis esset, respondit, Talem se Imperatorem esse priuatis, quales esse sibi Imperatores priuatus optasset[?]. in summa, Deo proximus habitus est. E Perfide rediens profluvio vetris obiit anno ætatis 62. imperij ferè 20. Eutr. lib. 8. Aure. Vict. fuit paululum cibo, vinoque deditus.
units.tr: He made Armenia, Assyria and Mesopotamia, and afterwards Arabia, into provinces. He established a fleet in the Red Sea, so that through it he might lay waste the borders of India. Yet he surpassed his military glory by courtesy and moderation. He was generous toward all; he granted exemptions to cities. When his friends blamed him because he was too affable to everyone, he replied: "I am such an emperor to private citizens as I would have wished private citizens to be to me, when I was one." In sum, he was considered next to God. Returning from Persia, he died of a flux of the bowels at the age of 62, in about the twentieth year of his reign. He was somewhat given to food and wine. See Eutropius, book 8; Aurelius Victor.

units.la: PLOTINA Traiani vxor fuit, quæ tam modestè & sanctè in summa se potestate gesit, ut de ea nullus iure conqueri potuerit. huius factione Tatianus Traiani Procurator, Adrianū Imperatorem declaravit, cum sine liberis excessisset Traianus, & hæc Adriani amore flagraret, qui vicinus & potens erat. Dion Cassius. AEL.HADRIANVS. HADR.IMP.PA[?] DOMITIA PAVL. HADR.IMP.M.
units.tr: PLOTINA was the wife of Trajan. She conducted herself so modestly and piously in the highest power that no one could rightly complain of her. Through her influence Tatianus, Trajan's procurator, declared Hadrian emperor, since Trajan had died without children, and Hadrian was burning with love for her, being near at hand and powerful. See Dio Cassius. AEL. HADRIAN. HADR. IMP. PA[?] DOMITIA PAUL. HADR. IMP. M.

units.la: ÆLIVS Adrianus, cognomento Afer, Adriani Imperatoris pater fuit, ac Traiani consobrinus: huius origo vetustior à Picentibus, posterior ab Hispanensibus manat: siquidem Adria ortos maiores suos apud Italiam Scipionum temporibus resedisse, in libris vitæ suæ Adrianus ipse commemorat. est autem Adria, seu Hadria, oppidum agri Piceni, quod etiā mari Adriatico nomen dedisse nonnulli censent: attamen huic refragatur opinioni Plin.li.3.cap.16.ab Atria Thuscorum oppido, Atriaticum mare dictum censens, quod post mutatione vnius tantùm literæ Adriaticum dici cæpit. Cæterùm quatenus attinet ad Ælium Adrianum, vide Ælium Spartianum, & Sex. Aurelium Victorem. Sunt qui Hadrianum cum H, scribant: sunt qui sine H. Porrò quod ad Adriam attinet, vide Strabonem li.5. & 7. Geographiæ, & Plinium lib.3.cap.16.
units.tr: AELIUS Hadrian, surnamed Afer, was the father of the emperor Hadrian and a cousin of Trajan. His origin, the older one, derives from the Picentes, the later from the people of Hispania: for Hadrian himself records in the books of his life that his ancestors, who came from Hadria, had settled in Italy in the times of the Scipios. Hadria, or Hadria, is a town in the territory of Picenum, which some think also gave its name to the Adriatic Sea; yet Pliny, book 3, chapter 16, opposes this opinion, holding that the sea was called Atriaticum from the Etruscan town of Atria, and that after the change of a single letter it began to be called Adriaticum. However, as far as Aelius Hadrian is concerned, see Aelius Spartianus and Sextus Aurelius Victor. Some write Hadrianus with an H, some without an H. Moreover, as far as Hadria is concerned, see Strabo, books 5 and 7, Geography, and Pliny, book 3, chapter 16.

units.la: DOMITIA Paulina supradicti Ælij Adriani uxor, Imperatorisque Adriani mater fuit. erat hæc Gadibus orta. Vide Ælium Spartianum.
units.tr: DOMITIA Paulina, wife of the aforesaid Aelius Hadrian, was the mother of the emperor Hadrian. She was born at Gades. See Aelius Spartianus.

units.la: ÆLIVS Adrianus Romæ post Traianum imperat anno mundi 4080. à Christo nato 118. hunc,quanquam cõsobrinæ filium,viuēs noluerat adoptare Traianus,subindicaratq; se talem nolle successorem habere:attamen Plotinæ Traiani vxoris opera,Imperator est designatus: vti iā in Plotina dixi. hic velut Traiani gloriæ inuidens , statim prouincias tres reliquit, quas Traianus addiderat,Assyriam,Mesopotamiam, & Armeniam: reuocauit exercitus,ac finē Imperij voluit esse Eufratem.Idem de Dacia facere conatū,amici deterruerunt,ne multi ciues Ro. barbaris traderentur: nam Traianus victa Dacia , eò infinitas Ro.copias transtulerat , ad agros & vrbes colendas. miserabili tandē fato consumptus est, vt insemetipsum sæuire potuerit,si per domesticos licuisset. Imperauit annos 21. vixit 62. inuisum eum fecere viri illustres , non pauci sub eius exitum exilio aut morte multati. Eutro. li. 8. Egnat. li.1.Literas coluit,doctorum nunc irrisor,nunc fautor.
units.tr: AELIUS Hadrian became emperor at Rome after Trajan, in the year of the world 4080, from the birth of Christ 118. Although he was the son of a cousin, Trajan while alive had refused to adopt him, and had indicated that he did not wish to have such a successor; nevertheless, through the work of Plotina, Trajan's wife, he was designated emperor, as I have already said under Plotina. He, as if envious of Trajan's glory, at once gave up the three provinces Trajan had added, Assyria, Mesopotamia and Armenia; he recalled the armies and wished the Euphrates to be the limit of the empire. When he tried to do the same with Dacia, his friends dissuaded him, lest many Roman citizens be handed over to the barbarians; for after Dacia was conquered, Trajan had transferred there an infinite number of Roman troops to cultivate fields and cities. At last he was consumed by a wretched fate, so that he could have raged against himself, had it been permitted by those at home. He reigned twenty-one years and lived sixty-two. Illustrious men, not a few, were punished with exile or death toward the end of his reign, and they made him hated. See Eutropius, book 8; Egnatius, book 1. He cultivated letters, sometimes mocking the learned, sometimes favouring them.

units.la: SABINA Adriani vxor fuit , quam si priuatus vixisset , vt morosam, & adulterij suspectā dimisisset:nec sine rumore dati ab eo veneni,obiit hæc. Vide Æl.Spartianum.
units.tr: Sabina, the wife of Hadrian, was (had he lived as a private citizen) the sort of woman he would have divorced as ill-tempered and suspected of adultery. She died, and not without rumour that poison had been given her by him. See Aelius Spartianus.

units.la: ANTINOVS iuuenis formisiss.[?] ex Cithynide quā Claudiopolim vocarunt, vrbe Bithyniæ,ortus,in Nilo periit:hunc Adrianus muliebriter fleuit,ac coluit:vrbem ad Nilum de nomine eius condidit: statuas ei per orbem terrarū erexit:templum quoq; & sacerdotes ei apud Mantineam instituit. Hunc Græci volente Adriano cõsecrarunt,oracula per eum dari asserêtes,quæ Adrianus ipse edidisse iactatur. Vide Ælium Spar. & Dionē Cassium in Adriano:& Eusc.li.3.ca.8.& li.7.ca.2. AUREL. FULVIUS AN. PII PAT. ARRIA FATIDIA AN. PI. MAT.
units.tr: Antinous, a youth of remarkable beauty, was born in Cithynia, a city of Bithynia which they called Claudiopolis, and perished in the Nile. Hadrian mourned him womanishly and cherished him. He founded a city on the Nile named after him, erected statues of him throughout the world, and also established a temple and priests for him at Mantinea. The Greeks, at Hadrian's wish, consecrated him, claiming that oracles were given through him, which Hadrian himself is boasted to have published. See Aelius Spartianus and Dio Cassius in the life of Hadrian, and Eusebius, book 3, chapter 8, and book 7, chapter 2. AUREL. FULVIUS, father of Antoninus Pius. ARRIA FATIDIA, mother of Pius.

units.la: AURELIUS Fulvius Antonini Pij Imperatoris pater, è Gallia Trāfalpina fuit oriundus: Consulatū gessit, homo tristis & æger.huius pater Titus Aurel.Fulvius, Imperatoris avus, per honores diversos ad secundum Consulatum, & Præfecturam urbis pervenit. Julius Capitolin. in Antonino Pio.
units.tr: Aurelius Fulvius, father of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, was born in Transpadane Gaul. He held the consulship, a gloomy and sickly man. His father, Titus Aurelius Fulvius, the emperor's grandfather, rose through various offices to a second consulship and the prefecture of the city. Julius Capitolinus, in the life of Antoninus Pius.

units.la: ARRIA Fadilla Aurelij Fulvij uxor,& Antonini Pij Imperatoris mater extitit. huius Arriæ pater fuit Arrius Antoninus bis Consul,homo sanctus,& qui Nervam miseratus esset,quòd imperare cœpisset. Julius Capitolinus in Antonino Pio. ANTONINVS AVG. PIVS PP TRI COS. IIII. FAVSTINA DIVA
units.tr: Arria Fadilla, wife of Aurelius Fulvius, was the mother of the Emperor Antoninus Pius. Her father was Arrius Antoninus, twice consul, a holy man, who pitied Nerva for having begun to rule. Julius Capitolinus, in the life of Antoninus Pius. ANTONINUS AUGUSTUS PIUS, FATHER OF THE COUNTRY, TRIBUNICIAN POWER, CONSUL FOR THE FOURTH TIME. FAUSTINA THE DIVINE.

units.la: TI. AV. FVL. BO. Antoninus Pius imperat post Adrianum anno mundi 4101. à Christo nato 139. fuit genere claro, sed non admodũ vetere:vir insignis,& qui merito Numæ Ponpilio comparatur:Romulo item,& Traiano æquatur. Barbarorum plurimæ nationes depositis armis, ad eũ cõtrouerfias suas litéfq; deferētes,sententiæ eius paruerunt. Nullum sub eo bellum fuit. Amor ac timor gentium in eo certarunt:bellũ mouere timebant aduersus principem,quẽ vt numen aliquod venerarentur:nec ille gloriæ ita cupidus,vt per aliorum damna, cædésque eam appeteret. Nam & à coniuratis vim omnem abftinuit,&in conscios quæri vetuit,ne plures inuēti , odium augerent. Hic ante Imperiũ ditissimus opes suas ftipēdiis militum, & liberalitate in amicos minuit : nihilominus tamen ærarium opulentũ reliquit.febre obiit vitæ anno 78.Imperij.22.Eutr.li.8. hunc Adrianus adoptarat in locũ demortui Ceionij,hac conditione vt eiusdem filium cum M.Antonino adoptaret, quod & fecit:deinde ambo vnà adoptati,vnà item imperarunt.
units.tr: Titus Aurelius Fulvius Boionius Antoninus Pius became emperor after Hadrian, in the year of the world 4101, from the birth of Christ 139. He was of a distinguished family, though not very ancient: an outstanding man, rightly compared with Numa Pompilius, and likewise equated with Romulus and Trajan. Very many barbarian nations, laying down their arms, brought their disputes and petitions to him and obeyed his judgment. There was no war under him. The love and the fear of the nations contended in him: they feared to make war against a prince whom they revered as a kind of divinity. Nor was he so eager for glory that he sought it through the losses and slaughter of others. For he abstained from all violence against the conspirators, and forbade inquiry into their accomplices, lest the discovery of many increase hatred. Before his reign he was very wealthy, but he diminished his resources by paying soldiers and by generosity to friends; nevertheless he left the treasury full. He died of fever in the seventy-eighth year of his life, the twenty-second of his reign. See Eutropius, book 8. Hadrian had adopted him in place of the deceased Ceionius, on the condition that he should in turn adopt Marcus Antoninus, the son of Ceionius; and so he did. Then both, adopted together, also ruled together.

units.la: ANNIA FAVSTINA, Annij Veri filia,vxor fuit Antonini Pij,ex qua duos mares , duásq; femellas suscepit:harum maior Lamiæ Syllano, minor , M. Antonino Philosopho, qui postea imperat,nupsit.De Fauftina hac multa dicta sunt ob nimiam libertate, quæ Antoninus Pius cum animi dolore compressit.Iul.Capitolin.in Anto. Pio. obiit Fauftina anno Imperij viri tertio.
units.tr: Annia Faustina, daughter of Annius Verus, was the wife of Antoninus Pius, by whom she bore two sons and two daughters. The elder daughter married Lamia Silanus, the younger married Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, who afterwards became emperor. Much has been said about this Faustina because of her excessive freedom, which Antoninus Pius suppressed with grief of mind. Julius Capitolinus, in the life of Antoninus Pius. Faustina died in the third year of her husband's reign.

units.la: ANNIVS Verus, pater Marci Antonini Philosophi Imperatoris,in Prætura decessit: cuius etiam pater, Imperatoris auus,iterū Consul & Præfectus vrbi, adscitus est in Patricios à principibus Vespasiano & Tito, Censoribus. Huius familia in originem recurrens,à Numa probatur originē trahere: vt Marius Maximus docet:item à rege Salentino Malennio,Dasummi filio,qui Lupias condidit.Iul.Capitolin.
units.tr: Annius Verus, father of the Emperor Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, died while serving as praetor. His grandfather, the emperor's great-grandfather, was again consul and prefect of the city, and was admitted among the patricians by the princes Vespasian and Titus, who were censors. His family, tracing its origin back, is shown to derive its descent from Numa; as Marius Maximus teaches, also from the Salentine king Malennius, son of Dasumus, who founded Lupiae. Julius Capitolinus.

units.la: DOMITIA Caluilla,Caluisij Tulli bis Consulis filia, Annij Veri vxor, & M. Antonini Philosophi Imperatoris mater fuit. hic Antoninus Philosophus , de quo statim amplius dicemus , patrimonium paternum totū sorori cōcesfit:ac vbi cumperit se ab Imperatore adoptatū,magis est deterritus quàm lætatus:iussufq; in Adriani priuatā domum migrare, inuitus de maternis hortis recessit.Cùm ab eo domestici quęreret cur tristis in adoptionem regiam transiret , disputauit quæ mala in se cōtinet imperiū. Anno ætatis 18.adoptatus,in secundo Consulatu AntoniniPij,iam patris fui,per adoptionē, Adriano serente,gratia seu dispēsatione ætatis facta, Quæstor est designatus. Posthæc Faustinam duxit vxorem , relicta filia Ceionij quæ illi pacta fuerat,sed impar ætate. Tribunitia potestate donatus est, suscepta filia ex Faustina,atq; Imperio extra vrbem Proconsulari:tantúmq; apud Pium valuit,vt nunquā quenquam sine eo facile promouerit.Iulius Capitoli.in M.Antonino Philosopho: de quo etiam pagina sequente,plura suo loco dicemus.
units.tr: Domitia Calvilla, daughter of Calvisius Tullus, twice consul, was the wife of Annius Verus and mother of the Emperor Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher. This Antoninus the Philosopher, of whom we shall speak more fully straight away, yielded his entire paternal inheritance to his sister. When he found that he had been adopted by the emperor, he was more dismayed than glad, and when ordered to move into Hadrian's private house he left his mother's gardens reluctantly. When his household asked him why he went sadly into the imperial adoption, he argued what evils the empire contains within it. He was adopted at the age of eighteen, in the second consulship of Antoninus Pius, by which time he was already a father through adoption; with Hadrian arranging it, an exception was made to his age, and he was designated quaestor. Afterwards he married Faustina, having put away the daughter of Ceionius, who had been promised to him but was not equal in age. He was granted tribunician power, and after a daughter was born to him by Faustina, he received proconsular imperium outside the city. He held such influence with Pius that he never readily advanced anyone without him. Julius Capitolinus, in the life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher; of whom also, on the following page, we shall say more in its place.

units.la: MARC. Antoninus Verus Philosophus,post Antoninum Pium imperat, anno mundi 4123. à Christo nato 161. Is fratrem & generū L. Anto. Verum ad Imperij partem nouo beneuolētiæ genere asciuit:tum primum duo hi æquo iure Imperiū administrarunt. M. Antoninū mirari facilius quis,quàm laudare possit:à principio vitæ tranquillissimus fuit,adeò vt in infantia quoque vultum nec ex gaudio,nec ex mœrore mutaret. hic vita, moribus, & eruditione Philosophus,tantæ admirationis fuit adhuc iuuenis,vt eum succeßorē parauerit Adrianus relinquere:adoptato tamē Antonino Pio,generum eidem Antonino idcirco hunc esse voluit,vt hoc ordine ad Imperiū peruenire t. Contra Germanos eo principe res feliciter gestæ sunt. Bellum ipse vnum gessit Marcomannicū, sed quantum nulla memoria fuit,adeò vt Punicis conferatur: quòd eò grauius est factum,quòd pestilentia,post victoriam Persicam,Italiam peruaserat,& maxima hominū pars, militum verò omnes ferè copiæ langore defecerant. Marcomannos igitur,& cum his Quados, Vādalos,Sarmatas,Sueuos fudit:multa millia interfecit. ærario exhausto pretiosam suam supellectile hastæ subiecit: Pānonias Marcomānorum seruitio liberauit:Romæ cum filio triumphauit periit morbo,anno ætatis 61. Imperij 19. Eutro.li.8.
units.tr: Marcus Antoninus Verus the Philosopher became emperor after Antoninus Pius, in the year of the world 4123, from the birth of Christ 161. He took his brother and son-in-law, Lucius Antoninus Verus, into a share of the empire by a new kind of favour; these two, for the first time, administered the empire with equal right. Marcus Antoninus is easier to admire than to praise. From the beginning of his life he was most tranquil, so much so that even in infancy he did not change his expression either for joy or for grief. He was a philosopher in life, character and learning, and while still a young man was of such admiration that Hadrian chose to leave him as his successor; yet, when Antoninus Pius had been adopted, Hadrian wished Antoninus to be his son-in-law for this reason, that he might come to the empire by this order. Under this prince, things were successfully done against the Germans. He himself waged one war, against the Marcomanni, but of a size that no memory matched, so that it is compared with the Punic wars. This was made the more grievous because a plague, after the Persian victory, had spread through Italy, and the greater part of the population, and almost all the army, had been worn down by sickness. So he routed the Marcomanni and with them the Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians and Suevi, and killed many thousands. With the treasury exhausted, he put his valuable household furniture up for auction; he freed the Pannonias from servitude to the Marcomanni; he triumphed at Rome with his son, and died of disease in the sixty-first year of his life, the nineteenth of his reign. See Eutropius, book 8.

units.la: FAVSTINA Antonini Pij & Faustinæ filia, M. Anton. Philosophi vxor fuit,ex quo Commodum,qui postea imperat, suscepit,non sine magna adulterij suspitione,& Lucillā filiam. Iulius Capitolin. AEL. VERVS CAES. HADR. IMP. DOMITIA CAL. AEL. VER. XX [?]
units.tr: Faustina, daughter of Antoninus Pius and Faustina, was the wife of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher; by him she bore Commodus, who afterwards became emperor, not without great suspicion of adultery, and a daughter Lucilla. Julius Capitolinus. AELIUS VERUS CAESAR, HADRIAN IMPERATOR. DOMITIA CALVILLA. AELIUS VERUS, 20 [?]

units.la: L. CEONIVS Commodus, qui & Ælius Verus, ab Adriano æuo iam ingrauescēte,morbísq; tristioribus presso,adoptatus est , anno mundi 4098. à Christo nato 136. hic tantùm Cæsar est appellatus,& ab Adriano in Æliorum familiam ascitus,hoc est in Adriani transcriptus:Prætor factus est,& Pannoniis dux ac rector impositus,mox etiā Consul creatus.hic solus omnia quæ cuperet, vel per literas,impetrabat ab Adriano:cui (ut aiunt)acceptior forma quàm moribus fuit:attamē reip.non omnino inutilis fuit,etsi delicatè vixurit. nam lectum mollem ac voluptarium extruxit: minuto reticulo undique inclusum, eminentibus quatuor anaclinteriis,eúmque foliis rosæ,quibus demptum esset album,replebat,iacénsque cum cōcubinis, velamine de liliis facto se tegebat,unctus odoribus perficis : præterea accubationes ac mēsas de rosis ac liliis,& quidē purgatis fecit,quæ etsi non decora , non tamen ad publicam perniciem sunt. libros amorū Ouidij in lecto semper habuit : Martialem, Vergilium suum dixit. Cursoribus suis exemplo Cupidinum, alas sæpe apposuit,ventorúmq; nominibus vocitavit,indefessè faciens eos cursitare. Vxori cōquerenti de extraneis voluptatibus,dixit : Patere me per alias,exercere cupiditates meas,vxor enim dignitatis nomen est,non voluptatis.hic tandē valetudinarius obiit, superstite etiam Adriano:sepultúsque est imperatorio funere Iuli.Capi.in Ceionio.
units.tr: Lucius Ceionius Commodus, who was also called Aelius Verus, was adopted by Hadrian when the old man's age was now weighing heavily on him and he was pressed by more grievous illnesses, in the year of the world 4098, from the birth of Christ 136. He was called only Caesar, and was taken by Hadrian into the family of the Aelii, that is, transferred into the adoption of Hadrian. He was made praetor, placed in command and governance of Pannonia, and soon afterwards was even created consul. He alone obtained by letter from Hadrian whatever he desired; he was (as they say) more pleasing in appearance than in character, yet he was not wholly useless to the state, though he lived in a self-indulgent way. For he built a soft and voluptuous couch, enclosed on all sides with fine netting, with four raised cushions, and he filled them with rose petals from which the white part had been removed; and lying with his concubines he covered himself with a canopy made of lilies, anointed with Persian perfumes. Besides, he made couches and tables of roses and lilies, though purified; these, though not decorous, were not ruinous to the public. He always kept the books of Ovid's Loves in bed; he called Martial and Virgil his own. He often fastened wings on his couriers, after the example of the Cupids, and gave them the names of winds, making them run about tirelessly. When his wife complained to him about his outside pleasures, he said: "Allow me to indulge my desires with other women; for 'wife' is a title of dignity, not of pleasure." At last he died of illness, while Hadrian was still alive, and was buried with imperial funeral rites. Julius Capitolinus, in the life of Ceionius.

units.la: DOMITIA Caluilla uxor L.Ceionij,peperit L. Annium Antonin.qui cum M.Antonin.Philosopho imperavit. IMP.CAESL.AVRE.VERVS.AVGAR. [?] FAVSTINA AVG.ANTONINI [?] AVG.PII FIL.
units.tr: Domitia Calvilla, wife of Lucius Ceionius, bore Lucius Annius Antoninus, who ruled together with Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher. IMPERATOR CAESAR LUCIUS AUREL. VERUS AUGUSTUS. FAUSTINA AUGUSTA. ANTONINUS [?] AUGUSTUS, SON OF PIUS AUGUSTUS.

units.la: L. ANNIVS, Antoninus, Verus, alias etiam dictus L. Ælius commodus, Verus, qui cum fratre & socero M.Anton. Philosopho,eiusdē fratris benignitate,imperauit, neque inter bonos,neq; inter malos principes ponitur.hic contra Parthos a fratre missus,qui tum primum post victoria Traiani rebellaverant,Antiochiae & circa Armeniā agens,multa per duces,& ingentia patravit. Seleuciam Assyriae urbem nobilissimam cum 5ooooo.hominum cepit: Parthicum triumphum revexit:cum fratre,eodemq; socero,triuphauit. Deinde cum fratre ad Marcomannicum bellū profectus,in itinere periit apoplexia, sedes cum fratre in vehiculo. Ingenij fuit parū civilis,reverentia tamen fratris nihil unquā atroxausus. erat enim solus frater Imperator à Senatu dictus. obiit anno Imperij fratris, & fui, 11. tunc M. Antoninus solus tenuit Imperium:ij autem fratres dicuntur,non quòd sint iisdē parētibus prognati,sed,quatenus licet mihi ex autoribus historicis colligere, quòd M.Antoninus sorori huius primùm nupserit:tum etiā quòd ambos adoptarat Imperator Antoninus Pius: vel potius quòd ex eadem matre nati sint.Iul.Capi.
units.tr: Lucius Annius Antoninus Verus, also called Lucius Aelius Commodus Verus, who ruled together with his brother and father-in-law Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, by the kindness of his brother, is placed neither among the good nor among the bad princes. Sent by his brother against the Parthians, who had then for the first time rebelled since the victory of Trajan, he acted at Antioch and around Armenia, and accomplished many great things through his generals. He took Seleucia, the most noted city of Assyria, with 500,000 men; he brought back a Parthian triumph, and triumphed together with his brother and his father-in-law. Then, setting out with his brother against the Marcomannic war, he died on the journey of apoplexy, while seated with his brother in a carriage. He was of a character little inclined to civility, yet out of reverence for his brother he never dared anything outrageous. For he alone was called "Imperator" by the Senate, along with his brother. He died in the eleventh year of his own reign and his brother's; then Marcus Antoninus held the empire alone. These are called brothers not because they were born of the same parents, but, as far as I can gather from historical authors, because Marcus Antoninus first married this man's sister, and also because the emperor Antoninus Pius had adopted both; or rather because they were born of the same mother. Julius Capitolinus.

units.la: LUCILLA, filia M. Antonini Philosophi,nupsit L. Annio Antonino supradicto:quāquam ex voluntate Imperatoris Adriani debebat hic L.Annius Anto.in uxorē accipere Faustinam, Antonini Pij filiam:verùm cùm minimè congrueret amborum ætas, nupsit potius Faustina M. Antonino Philosopho. Iul.Cap.in vita Veri principis,qui unus & idem est cum hoc L. An.Ant.Vero,cuius nunc meminimus:qui filius fuit L.Ceionij Commodi,de quo paulò ante tractavimus. IMP COMMODVS ANT P FELIX AVG BR CRISPINA AVGVSTA C V
units.tr: LUCILLA, daughter of M. Antoninus the Philosopher, married L. Annius Antoninus mentioned above. Although by the will of the Emperor Hadrian this L. Annius Antoninus ought to have taken Faustina, daughter of Antoninus Pius, as his wife, since their ages did not agree at all, Faustina instead married M. Antoninus the Philosopher. Julius Capitolinus, in the life of the emperor Verus, who is one and the same as this L. Annius Antoninus Verus, whom we now mention and who was the son of L. Ceionius Commodus, of whom we treated a little earlier. IMP COMMODVS ANT P FELIX AVG BR CRISPINA AVGVSTA C V
L. ANTONINUS, or Aurelius Commodus, succeeded.

units.la: P. ÆLIVS, siue Heluius, Pertinax,Commodo succesfsit, coactúsque imperauit Læti opera, ac decreto Senatus, anno mundi 4155.à Christo nato 193.hic dum renuit Imperium suscipere,tale Pertinacis cognomen sortitus est:quauis Capitolinus aliam huius nominis originē tradat. Libertino fuit genitus patre apud Ligures, genere quidē humili, virtute autē atque innocētia summa.Militia clarus Pertinax,in ea ad summas dignitates euectus est,vnde & Pilæ ludus est dictus.Summā de se expectationem omnibus cùm daret,Læti insidiis,qui imperium illi astruxerat,& militari factione,Iuliano,qui ei successit, non insscio, imò conscio, periit,anno ætatis 71.Imperauit vix menses tres:cuius caput ab vrbe delatū est in castra. Nam cùm omnia in pristinū statū reducere conatur, à praetoriis cohortibus odio habitus, interimitur:acclamatū est adusq; defectum, Pertinace imperante securi viximus,neminem timuimus:patri pio, patri Senatus, patri omniū bonorum. hic ex Senatusconsulto imperare iussus fuerat. Eutro.li.8.Bap. Egna.li.1.Sex. Aure. Vict. huius vitam vide fusius apud Iulium Capitolinum & Herodianum li.2.
units.tr: P. AELIUS, or Helvius, Pertinax, succeeded Commodus. He was compelled to rule by the work of Laetus and by the decree of the Senate, in the year of the world 4155, from the birth of Christ 193. Here, while he refused to take up the empire, he acquired the cognomen Pertinax in such a way, although Capitolinus gives another origin for this name. He was born of a freedman father among the Ligurians, of humble birth indeed, but of the greatest virtue and innocence. Pertinax became famous in the army, and was raised to the highest dignities through it, whence the saying the game of ball was coined. When he had given everyone the highest expectations of himself, he perished through the plots of Laetus, who had built up his power, and by the military faction, with Julian, who succeeded him, not ignorant of it, indeed with his full knowledge, in the seventy-first year of his life. He ruled barely three months. His head was carried from the city to the camp. For when he tried to restore all things to their former state, he was hated by the praetorian cohorts and was put to death. The cry was raised even to the point of exhaustion: Under Pertinax we lived safely, we feared no one: a dutiful father, a father of the Senate, a father of all good men. He had been ordered to rule by a decree of the Senate. See Eutropius, book 8; Bapt. Egnatius, book 1; Sext. Aurelius Victor. For his life see more fully in Julius Capitolinus and Herodian, book 2.

units.la: FLAVIA Titiana Ælij Pertinacis vxor fuit. hanc Senatus nomine Augustæ donauit:filiúmque eius nomine Cæsaris, quos titulos etiā recusabat pater,tanta præditus erat modestia. porrò Flauia palàm cytharœdū amauit:Pertinax vicissim,cùm vxoris pudicitiā non vsqueadeò curaret, Cornificiam perditè, & ad infamiam vsque deperisse dicitur.Iulius Capitolinus. IMP.M.DID.IVLIAN.AVG. MALLIA SCAN.FIL.DIDIA.AVG.
units.tr: FLAVIA Titiana was the wife of Aelius Pertinax. The Senate granted her the name of Augusta, and granted his son the title of Caesar, which titles the father himself refused, so great was his modesty. Moreover, Flavia openly loved a harpist, and Pertinax in turn, though he did not care very much about his wife's chastity, is said to have loved Cornificia shamelessly and to the point of infamy. Julius Capitolinus. IMP.M.DID.IVLIAN.AVG. MALLIA SCAN.FIL.DIDIA.AVG.

units.la: DIDIUS Iulianus,qui & Saluius dictus est,Mediolanensis,imperium quod per scelus,necis imperatoriae conscius ipse, primus etiam licitatus esse dicitur,intra tertium mensem à nece Pertinacis,cum vita simul amisit.Nam Severo,ab exercitu Imperatore appellato,à Iuliano omnes defecerunt,qui ab eodem Severo victus,tandē in palatio etiam iussu Senatus interficitur. neque enim militi gratus erat, ob non integrū donatiuum datum:& populo etiā invisus erat, ob perfidiam in principē optimum. fuit Didius factiosus,praeceps,regni auidus, nobilis,iure peritissimus,nepósq; Saluij Iuliani, qui sub Adriano perpetuū cōposuit edictum.educatus est apud Domitiā Lucillam, Marci Anton. Philosophi matrem. Imperium illi iussu Senatus abrogatum est,paulò ante necem.Eutro.li.8.Egna.li.1.Aure. Vict. & Hero.li.2.Vixit annos 56.
units.tr: DIDIUS Julianus, who was also called Salvius, a native of Milan, is said to have been the first to bid for the empire, which he obtained through crime, being himself a party to the emperor's murder; he lost his life together with his rule within three months of Pertinax's death. For when Severus was proclaimed emperor by the army, all deserted Julian, and he, conquered by the same Severus, was at last killed in the palace by order of the Senate. For he was not pleasing to the soldiers, because the promised gift had not been paid in full, and he was also hateful to the people on account of his treachery against the best of princes. Didius was factious, rash, greedy for power, of noble birth, most skilled in law, and grandson of Salvius Julianus, who under Hadrian composed the perpetual edict. He was brought up by Domitia Lucilla, the mother of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher. His rule was revoked by order of the Senate shortly before his death. Eutropius, book 8; Egnatius, book 1; Aurelius Victor; and Herodian, book 2. He lived fifty-six years.

units.la: MALLIA Scantilla vxor,& Didia Clara filia Didij Iuliani fuit.ambae edicto Senatus Augustae appellatae,& in Palatium à viro & patre vocatae,trepidae,& quasi invitae introierunt,velut iam iam imminens exitium praesagiret.Filiam,potitus imperio pater,dato patrimonio emāciparat, quod ei cum Augustae nomine obtruncato patre,statim sublatum est. Vide Ælium Spartianum in Didio Iuliano. L SEPTIMIVS SEVERVS PERTINAX AVG IMP VII MARTIA OTACIL SEVERA AVG
units.tr: MALLIA Scantilla, the wife, and Didia Clara, the daughter of Didius Julianus, were both by decree of the Senate called Augusta, and summoned into the palace by their husband and father; they entered trembling and as if unwilling, as though foreseeing imminent destruction. When their father had seized power, he emancipated his daughter, having given her a dowry, which was taken away again immediately, together with the title of Augusta, when her father was beheaded. See Aelius Spartianus, in the life of Didius Julianus. L SEPTIMIVS SEVERVS PERTINAX AVG IMP VII MARTIA OTACIL SEVERA AVG

units.la: L. SEPTIMIVS Seuerus post Iulianum imperat anno mundi 4156. à Christo nato 194. Hic primus Afer ad imperij fastigium euectus, ab Illyrico exercitu Imperator dicitur, hinc à Senatu. Pertinacem se appellari voluit in honorem eius qui à Iuliano fuerat occisus. Parcus fuit, sæuus [?], bellicosus. Pescennium Nigrum in Oriente, Clodiū Albinum apud Lugdunū deuicit: erant siquidem hi Imperatores ab exercitibus dicti. Orientem, Parthis, Arabibus, Adiabenis deuictis, Romano restituit imperio: Britannos tumultuates cōpescuit, vallo à mari ad mare per 32000. passuum ducto: vbi etiam septuagenarius morbo articulari decessit, anno imperij 18. Philosophiae ac dicedi studiis deditus, latronū ubiq; hostis, vitam suam priuatam, publicā que composuit ad fidem: solū tamen vitium crudelitatis excusauit. De hoc Senatus ita iudicauit, aut non nasci debuisse, aut non mori. Eutro.lib.8.Egna.lib.1.Aur. Vict.
units.tr: L. SEPTIMIUS Severus succeeded Julian as emperor in the year of the world 4156, from the birth of Christ 194. He was the first African raised to the summit of power; he is said to have been made emperor by the Illyrian army, and then by the Senate. He wished to be called Pertinax in honour of the man who had been killed by Julian. He was sparing, [harsh?], warlike. He defeated Pescennius Niger in the East and Clodius Albinus near Lyons; for these men had been called emperors by their armies. Having conquered the Parthians, Arabs and Adiabenians, he restored the East to the Roman empire. He checked the rebellious Britons, having built a rampart from sea to sea over 32,000 paces; there, too, he died of a joint disease in his seventieth year, in the eighteenth year of his reign. Devoted to philosophy and to the study of law, an enemy of brigands everywhere, he arranged his private and public life in good faith; he alone excused himself for the vice of cruelty. Of him the Senate judged thus: he ought either not to have been born, or not to die. Eutropius, book 8; Egnatius, book 1; Aurelius Victor.

units.la: MARTIA, L. Septimij Seueri uxor fuit tum cum Tribunatum plebis, Marco Imperatore decernete, promeruit: de qua tacuit in historia vitae priuatae: ei tamen postea, cum imperaret ipse, statuas collacauit: ex hac Bassianū, qui postea imperat, suscepit. Deinde Iuliæ nupsit, quā, domi minus cautus, adulteriis famosam tenuit, etiam coniurationis conscium: ex Iulia Getam quoque filium suscepit. Ælius Spart. in Seuero.
units.tr: MARTIA, the wife of L. Septimius Severus, was when he earned the tribunate of the plebs, as Marcus the emperor decreed; she is passed over in silence in the history of her private life. Yet later, when he himself was emperor, he set up statues to her. By her he had a son Bassianus, who later became emperor. Then he married Julia, whom, being less careful at home, he kept, infamous for adulteries, even as a party to a conspiracy. By Julia he also had a son, Geta. Aelius Spartianus, in the life of Severus.

units.la: M. AVREL. Antoninus Bassianus, dictus Caracalla, Severo patri succedit, imperátque anno mundi 4174. à Christio nato 212. hic Lugduni genitus est, dictúsque Bassianus ex aui materni nomine: Caracalla autem, quòd cùm è Gallia vestem plurimam deuexisset, talarésq; caracallas fecisset, coëgerit plebem ad se salutandū talibus indutā caracallis. Antoninus porrò dictus est in honoré M. Antonini Imperatoris. Hic simulatque imperauit, fratrem ex patre, Getam nomine, falsò criminatum occidit ipse in gremio matris eius. Papinianum etiā Iurisconsultissimum occidi à militibus iussit, complurésque alios. In summa, nullo in pretio apud populū fuit, etiamsi vestes dedisset, & thermas nominis sui, id est Antonianas, eximiè fabrefactas, extruxisset. fuit patre duro crudelior, in eúmq; contumax, cibi & vini auidus, præter milites prætorianos omnibus castris exosus, Alexandri Magni admirator, quem, collo in lœuum humerū detorto, reddere, & eius nomine vocari cuperet. Alexandrinorum dicacitatē vltus est ingenti eorum cæde: Persas dolo magis quàm virtute fudit. Cùm Carris iter faceret, apud Edessam secedēs ad onus ventris leuandū, à milite, qui quasi ad custodiam sequebatur, occisus est anno imperij 6. ætatis 43. Herodian. lib. 4. Egna. li. i. Eutr. lib. 9. Aurel. Vict. Ælius Spart.
units.tr: M. AUREL. Antoninus Bassianus, called Caracalla, succeeded his father Severus, and ruled in the year of the world 4174, from the birth of Christ 212. He was born at Lyons, and was called Bassianus after his maternal grandfather; he was called Caracalla because, having imported a great quantity of clothing from Gaul and made long hooded tunics (caracallae), he forced the common people to greet him wearing such tunics. Moreover he was called Antoninus in honour of the emperor Marcus Antoninus. As soon as he began to rule, he killed his brother Geta, whom he falsely accused, in the lap of their mother himself. He also ordered the most learned jurist Papinian to be killed by soldiers, and many others. In sum, he was held in no esteem among the people, even though he had given clothing and built baths of his own name, the Antonian, most splendidly constructed. He was more cruel than his harsh father, and obstinate towards him, greedy for food and wine, hated by all the camps except the praetorian guards, an admirer of Alexander the Great, whose neck he wished to resemble by twisting his own head to the left shoulder, and to be called by his name. He took revenge on the wit of the Alexandrians by a great slaughter of them. He defeated the Persians more by treachery than by valour. While he was travelling to Carrhae, he stopped at Edessa to relieve the needs of his belly, and was killed by a soldier who followed him as if to guard him, in the sixth year of his reign, in his forty-third year of life. Herodian, book 4; Egnatius, book 1; Eutropius, book 9; Aurelius Victor; Aelius Spartianus.

units.la: IVLIA, quæ erat Caracallæ nouerca, eiusdem etiam vxor fuit. nam cùm esset pulcherrima, & quasi per negligētiā se maxima corporis parte nudasset, dixit Caracalla, Vellem, si liceret: at respondit hæc, Si libet, licet: an nescis te Imperatorem esse, & leges dare, non accipere? tunc nuptias celebrat, eíque copulatur, in cuius gremio, eiusdémque filium nuper confoderat. Æl. Spartian.
units.tr: JULIA, who was Caracalla's stepmother, was also his wife. For when she was very beautiful and had, as if out of carelessness, exposed the greater part of her body, Caracalla said, I would wish it, if it were allowed; but she replied, If you wish, it is allowed; or do you not know that you are emperor, and give laws, not receive them? Then he celebrated the wedding and was united to her, in whose lap he had lately slain her son. Aelius Spartianus.

units.la: OPILIUS Macrinus obscuris parentibus ortus, Maurusij generis, proditor, & necis Caracallae conscius, imperat anno mundi 4180. à Christo nato 218. unà cum Diadumeno filio formosissimo. hic Artabano Parthorū Regi graviter necè suorum ciuium vindicati, quos occiderat Caracalla, primò restitit: postea missis legatis petiit pacè, eam libenti animo, interfecto Caracalla Parthus concessit. Inde cum se Antiochiam recepisset, ac luxuriae operâ daret, iustam causam necis suae praebuit exercitui, ac Bafsiani, ut putabatur, filium sequedi, id est Heliogabalum. fugiés itaque cum filio in vico quodâ Bithiniae occiditur: caput eius ablatū ad Heliogabalum perfertur. Iul. Capito. Æl. Lam. vixit annos 50. imperauit menses 14. cuius caput amputatum ad Heliogabalum est perlatum.
units.tr: OPILIUS Macrinus, born of obscure parents, of Moorish race, a traitor and an accomplice in the murder of Caracalla, ruled in the year of the world 4180, from the birth of Christ 218, together with his son Diadumenus, a most handsome youth. He first resisted Artabanus, king of the Parthians, who gravely demanded vengeance for the slaughter of his citizens whom Caracalla had killed; afterwards, having sent envoys, he sought peace, and the Parthian granted it willingly, Caracalla having been killed. Then, when he had withdrawn to Antioch and given himself to luxury, he gave the army a just reason for his own death, and it was said that he was following the son of Bassianus, that is, Heliogabalus. Thus fleeing with his son, he was killed in a certain village of Bithynia; his head was carried to Heliogabalus. Julius Capitolinus; Aelius Lampridius. He lived fifty years and ruled fourteen months; his head, cut off, was carried to Heliogabalus.

units.la: M. AURE. Anto. Bafsianus Varius, Heliogabalus, victo Opi. Macrino imperat anno mundi 4181. à Christo nato 219. fuit hic impurus, superbus, crudelis: honores & dignitates cōtulit in aurigas, mimos, histriones. cum omnia sordidè ageret, iniretúrque à viris, statim milites facti poenituit: quare in Alexandrum, Heliogabali cōsobrinum inclinauere animos: tandemq; Heliogabalum, cum matre & satellitibus, interficiunt, operam etiam dante Alexādri matre, quae militibus clam pecunias dabat. tractum est cadauer per Circi spatia priusquam in Tiberim praecipitaretur. Æl. Lamp. in Helioga. Herodianus li.5. vixit annos 18. imperauit 4. IMP. ALEXANDER PIVS AVG IVLIA MAMEA AVGVSTA
units.tr: M. AUREL. Antoninus Bassianus Varius, Heliogabalus, after defeating Opilius Macrinus, ruled in the year of the world 4181, from the birth of Christ 219. He was impure, arrogant and cruel. He conferred honours and dignities on charioteers, mimes and actors. When he did everything basely, and was thought of by men as a fool, soon the soldiers regretted having made him emperor; therefore they turned their minds to Alexander, the cousin of Heliogabalus. At last they killed Heliogabalus, together with his mother and attendants, with the help also of Alexander's mother, who secretly gave money to the soldiers. His corpse was dragged through the length of the Circus before being thrown into the Tiber. Aelius Lampridius, in the life of Heliogabalus; Herodian, book 5. He lived eighteen years and ruled four. IMP. ALEXANDER PIVS AVG IVLIA MAMEA AVGVSTA

units.la: AVREL. Alexander Seuerus,ab Heliogabalo adoptatus, post eum imperauit anno mundi 4185. à natiui. Christi 223. à prima pueritia bonis artibus imbutus,pius,mãsuetus & liberalis extitit:Christianis fauit:vetuit ne mulieres vulgato corpore matrem illius Mammeã salutarent.in pretio habuit Vlpianum, & tãquam tutorem. bonorum principũ vitam versibus descripsit.Fures valde persecutus est,quos inimicos reipu.dictitabat. cum solus accumberet, librũ ad mensam habebat:quãdo conuiuas habebat,aderat Vlpianus atq; aliquot alij,quorum doctis sermonibus ac disceptationibus recreabatur inter epulas. aduersus Parthos , quos vicit,exercitũ duxit,habès milites tantæ grauitatis & modestiæ,vt quacũque iter faceret,Senatores esse dicerentur,non milites. Ad Alexandri magni mores sese coponebat,cũ eiusdem nominis esset,imò & exuperare satagebat, inquiens multum interesse debere inter Romanum [?]Alexandrum, & Macedonem.clamabat sæpe,atq; per præconẽ proclamari iubebat, cũm aliquẽ emendaret, Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris. Tandem factione militari vnà cum matre in tentorio necatur.vixit annos 29.imperauit 13.ÆI.Lampri.& Herodi.li.6.
units.tr: AVREL. Alexander Severus, adopted by Heliogabalus, reigned after him in the year of the world 4185, from the birth of Christ 223. Imbued with good arts from his earliest boyhood, he was pious, gentle and generous. He favoured the Christians. He forbade women to greet his mother Mammaea by the common name of the body (?). He held Ulpian in high esteem, as though he were his guardian. He described the lives of good princes in verse. He pursued thieves very harshly, whom he used to call enemies of the commonwealth. When he dined alone he kept a book at the table; when he held banquets, Ulpian and several others were present, and he was refreshed during the feast by their learned talk and debates. He led an army against the Parthians, whom he defeated, and his soldiers were of such gravity and modesty that wherever he marched they were said to be senators, not soldiers. He modelled himself on the manners of Alexander the Great, since he had the same name, and even strove to surpass him, saying that there ought to be a great difference between the Roman Alexander and the Macedonian. He often cried out, and had it proclaimed through a herald, whenever he corrected someone: What you do not want done to you, do not do to another. At last, through a military faction, he was killed together with his mother in a tent. He lived 29 years and reigned 13. Ael. Lampr. and Herodian, book 6.

units.la: MAMMEA, mater Alexandri Seueri,à quibusdam dicitur Christiana fuisse,& ab Origene edocta. hæc filiũ eò coegerat,vt quæ mensæ superessent edulia,quãuis permodica,altera vice apponerentur.Aurel. Vict.Ab.Vrsper.Eufe.li.6.cap.16.
units.tr: MAMMEA, mother of Alexander Severus, is said by some to have been a Christian, and to have been taught by Origen. She had compelled her son that the food left over from his table, however very scanty, should be served up again on another occasion. Aurel. Vict. Ab. Vrsper. Euseb. book 6, chapter 16.

units.la: IVLIVS Maximinus Thrax,è militaribus imperauit cum filio eiusdem nominis,coactus à militibus,post Aurel.Alexandrum anno mundi 4198.à Christo nato 236.altus fuit pedes 8.& digitum:tam validus vt Hercules,Achilles,Aiax,Milo,Antæus vocitaretur:tam ferox vt Cyclops,Busiris,Sciron,Phalaris,Typhon,Gyges diceretur. hūc vsq; adeò reformidauit Senatus,vt vota in templis publicè fierét ne vnquam vrbem ingrederetur. érat ei persuasum nisi crudelitate imperiū non teneri.simul verebatur ne propter humilitatè generis sperneretur[?](fuerat siquidem in prima pueritia pastor)quare ignobilitatis tegédæ causa, omnes cōscios generis interemit. Aduersus hunc Senatus Pupienum & Balbinū Imperatores declarauit.Hic verò in Italiam statim cum exercitu descendit:Aquileiaq; frustra obsessa,à suis militibus penuria oppressis,cum filio discerpitur, conclamatibus cunctis militari ioco,Ex pessimo genere ne catulum quidè habendum. horū capita Romam perlata sunt. imperauit annos 3.vixit pater 50.filius 20.Herodi.li.7.& 8.Iul.Cap.Aur.Vict.
units.tr: IVLIVS Maximinus the Thracian, from the soldiery, reigned with his son of the same name, forced to it by the soldiers, after Aurelius Alexander, in the year of the world 4198, from the birth of Christ 236. He was eight feet and a finger tall, so strong that he was called a Hercules, an Achilles, an Ajax, a Milo, an Antaeus, and so fierce that he was called a Cyclops, a Busiris, a Sciron, a Phalaris, a Typhon, a Gyges. The Senate so greatly feared him that public vows were made in the temples that he would never enter the city. He was persuaded that he could not hold the empire except by cruelty. At the same time he feared that he would be scorned on account of the lowliness of his birth (for he had indeed been a shepherd in his earliest boyhood), and so, to hide his low birth, he put to death all who were aware of his origin. Against him the Senate declared Pupienus and Balbinus emperors. He immediately descended into Italy with an army, and when Aquileia had been besieged in vain, he was torn to pieces by his own soldiers, who were oppressed by shortage, together with his son, with everyone shouting in soldiers' jest: One should not even keep a puppy from a worst breed. Their heads were carried to Rome. He reigned 3 years; the father lived 50, the son 20. Herodian, books 7 and 8. Julius Capitolinus. Aurel. Vict.
