units.la: GORDIANVS senior ab exercitu Africano, ipse Proconsul Africæ, Imperator factus vnà cum filio eiusdē nominis, à Senatu approbatus est: ídque in odium Iulij Maximini anno mundi 4200. à Christo nato 238. At Capelianus, Mauritaniæ procurator, in gratiâ Maximini bellum Gordiano mouet,vincit occumbit Gordiani filius:pater laqueo se suspēdit. imperarunt annum & sex menses, quo tempore etiam imperabat Iul. Maximinus. Vide Iulium Capit.
units.tr: GORDIAN the elder, made emperor by the African army, being himself proconsul of Africa, was approved by the Senate together with his son of the same name, and this was out of hatred for Julius Maximinus, in the year of the world 4200, from the birth of Christ 238. But Capelianus, procurator of Mauretania, out of favour with Maximinus, made war on Gordian; he conquered, and Gordian's son perished. The father hanged himself with a noose. They reigned a year and six months, during which time Julius Maximinus was also reigning. See Julius Capitolinus.

units.la: DIVI IMP. MC PIPIENVS ET BALBINVS AV[?]
units.tr: DIVI IMP. MC PIPIENVS ET BALBINVS AV[?]

units.la: MAX. PVPIENVS, & Clodius Balbinus,siue Albinus, à Senatu Imperatores creati sunt, & Gordianus iunior Cæsar electus est : idq; aduersus Iulij Maximini innatā crudelitatem. anno mundi 4201. à Christo nato 239. Albinus in vrbe manet ad componendam rempublicam, Pupienus foris Iulium Maximinum vincit. tandem ambo Romæ à militibus occiduntur, cùm parum cõcordi inter se animo rempublicam administrarent: erat præterea odio militibus, quòd à Senatu Imperatores facti essent. Imperarunt annum vnum ab obitu Maximini. Iulius Capit. Bap. Egn.li.i.
units.tr: MAX. PUPIENUS and Clodius Balbinus, or Albinus, were created emperors by the Senate, and Gordian the younger was chosen Caesar, and this against the innate cruelty of Julius Maximinus. In the year of the world 4201, from the birth of Christ 239. Albinus remained in the city to settle the commonwealth, while Pupienus conquered Julius Maximinus abroad. At last both were killed at Rome by the soldiers, since they administered the commonwealth with little harmony between them; moreover the soldiers were hostile to them because they had been made emperors by the Senate. They reigned one year from the death of Maximinus. Julius Capitolinus, Bap. Egn. book 1.

units.la: GORDIANVS 13. annos natus Romæ cum supradictis Imperatoribus, Maximo Pupieno,& Clodio Balbino,siue Albino,imperauit.hic Senatui, populo & militibus charus,tum ob claritatem generis, tum ob peculiares animi dotes, cùm bellum aduersus insolescentes Persas per Misitheum confecissiet, Philippi præfecti dolo interficitur. nec tamen fuit inulta optimi principis cædes:quicunque in eum coniurauerant,crudelibus afflicti suppliciis interierunt.huius successibus cùm posset Persicum nomen deleri, Philippi insidiæ obstiterunt. fuit hic maioris Gordiani ex filia nepos. imperauit annos sex,quinque solus,vnum cum Pupieno & Balbino. dixit aliquando,miserum esse Imperatorem, nempe apud quem vera fere reticeantur. Consulito Iul. Capitol.
units.tr: GORDIAN, 13 years old, reigned at Rome with the aforesaid emperors, Maximus Pupienus and Clodius Balbinus, or Albinus. He was dear to the Senate, the people and the soldiers, both on account of the distinction of his family and because of his particular gifts of mind; when he had brought the war against the insolent Persians to an end through Misitheus, he was killed by the treachery of the prefect Philip. Nor was the death of this best of princes left unavenged: all who had conspired against him perished, afflicted with cruel punishments. Under his successes the Persian name could have been destroyed, but the plots of Philip stood in the way. He was a grandson of the elder Gordian through a daughter. He reigned six years, five alone and one with Pupienus and Balbinus. He once said that it was a wretched thing to be an emperor, since with him the truth is almost always kept back. Consult Julius Capitolinus.

units.la: M. IVL. Philippus, occiso Gordiano iuniore, ab exercitu Imperator declaratus, ad Senatum scripsit de morte Gordiani (nepe graui eum morbo periisse) & de suaipsius electione, postulans ut confirmaretur. Senatus, rem non plane intelligens, eum Imperatorem confirmat, anno mundi 4 2 0 7. à Christo nato 2 4 5. fuit hic Arabs, humillimo ortus loco, patre nobilis latronum ductore. Misitheū primum veneno sustulerat, Gordiani socerū, virum modestū ac frugi, cuius consilio Imperium augebatur: deinde Gordianum occidit. Huius tempore Scythae desciuerunt, cōtra quos Marinum misit, qui à militib. Imperator factus, ab eisdē occiditur: atq; iterum ab iis Decius Imperator creatur. Aduersus quē Philippus furēs tendit, atq; à militibus occiditur Veronæ, medio capite supra ordines dentiū praecifo: filius annorum 12. Romæ necatur, qui à quinquenio nunquam risisse dicitur. Imperarunt annis 5. sunt qui hunc primum Imperatorem Christianum fuisse tradant, at perfidi mores obstant. Bap.Egn.Capi.in Gordiano iuniore.
units.tr: M. IVL. Philip, after the younger Gordian was killed, was declared emperor by the army; he wrote to the Senate about the death of Gordian (saying that he had died of a severe illness) and about his own election, asking that it be confirmed. The Senate, not fully understanding the matter, confirmed him as emperor, in the year of the world 4207, from the birth of Christ 245. He was an Arab, born of the very lowliest station, his father a noble leader of brigands. He first removed Misitheus by poison, Gordian's father-in-law, a modest and thrifty man, by whose counsel the empire had been enlarged; then he killed Gordian. In his time the Scythians revolted, against whom he sent Marinus, who was made emperor by the soldiers and was killed by them; and then Decius was created emperor by them again. Philip marched furiously against him, and was killed by the soldiers at Verona, his head cut off at the middle above the row of teeth; his son, aged 12, was put to death at Rome, who is said never to have laughed from the age of five. They reigned 5 years. Some hand down that he was the first Christian emperor, but his perfidious manners stand in the way. Bap. Egn. Capitolinus, in Gordian the younger.

units.la: DECIVS missus à Philippo ad coprimendos motus Moesiacos, ut primum provinciam attigit, Imperator omnium consensu dicitur anno mundi 4 2 1 2. à Christo nato 2 5 0. Hic civiles in Gallia motus sedauit, prius quam ad urbem rediret. Ad versus Scythas ad liberādas Thracias cum filio profectus, una cum filio perit, & loco, & fato adversantibus, equo sedēs ne in manus hostium veniret, in paludē insiliit: nec cadaver usquam inventum est. imperauit annis duobus. vixit quinquaginta. inter optimos annumeraretur, si à cruciatibus Christianorū temperasset. Pompo.Letus, Euse.li.6.ca.29.
units.tr: DECIUS, sent by Philip to suppress the Moesian disturbances, as soon as he reached the province, was declared emperor by universal consent, in the year of the world 4212, from the birth of Christ 250. He quelled the civil disturbances in Gaul before he returned to the city. Setting out against the Scythians to free Thrace, together with his son, he perished along with his son; the place and fate being against them, to avoid falling into the hands of the enemy, he leapt into a marsh while on horseback, and his body was never found anywhere. He reigned two years, and lived fifty. He would have been counted among the best if he had refrained from the tortures of the Christians. Pomponius Laetus, Eusebius, book 6, chapter 29.

units.la: VIBIVS, seu Virius Gallus Hostilianus post Decium Imperator à militibus creatus est, anno mundi 4214. à Christo nato 252. hic cum Scythis fœdus pepigit, non sine Romani nominis ignominia, tributum eis annuum pendens. tunc primùm respublica Romana iugũ Scythicæ seruitutis accepit. hinc Barbari insolentiores facti, nec tributo contenti, ingenti exercitu comparato, terra marique sæpius irrumpūt: & Dardaniam, Thraciam, Thessaliam, Macedoniam, & Helladam infestant. Scytharum exemplo alij hostes insurgunt: iam viscera Syriæ penetrāt Parthi, & Armenias fugato rege Tyridate occupāt. Interim per nitiosa pestis orbem peruasit, quæ ex Æthiopia orta, per annos 15. terras prope omnes exhausit. prouenisse ex infelicibus Galli auspiciis visa est, vt qui proditione Imperium arripuisset, Christiani etiā dogmatis hostis erat. Ita Imperium Galli infaustum, rerum gestarum monimentis obscurum, clade generis humani memoriæ traditum est. Hic cùm aduersus Æmilianum in Mœsia Imperatore factum proficiscitur, prælio victus, à suis militibus vnà cum filio Volusiano occiditur, annos natus 47. imperauit annos 2. Pom.Læ.Bap.Egna.Eutro.li.9.Orosi.li.7.ca.21.
units.tr: VIBIUS, or Virius Gallus Hostilianus, after Decius, was created emperor by the soldiers, in the year of the world 4214, from the birth of Christ 252. He made a covenant with the Scythians, not without the disgrace of the Roman name, paying them an annual tribute. Then for the first time the Roman commonwealth received the yoke of Scythian servitude. Hence the barbarians became more insolent, and, not content with tribute, having gathered a huge army, they repeatedly burst in by land and sea and laid waste Dardania, Thrace, Thessaly, Macedonia and Hellas. Following the example of the Scythians, other enemies rose up: now the Parthians penetrated the heart of Syria and, with king Tiridates driven out, seized Armenia. Meanwhile a deadly pestilence spread over the world, which arose from Ethiopia and for fifteen years exhausted almost all lands. It seemed to have come from the unhappy auspices of Gallus, since he who had seized the empire by treachery was also an enemy of the Christian doctrine. Thus the empire of Gallus, unfortunate and obscure in the records of his deeds, was handed down to the memory of mankind by the calamity of the human race. When he set out against Aemilianus, who had been made emperor in Moesia, he was defeated in battle and killed by his own soldiers together with his son Volusianus, aged 47; he reigned two years. Pomponius Laetus, Baptista Egnatius, Eutropius, book 9, Orosius, book 7, chapter 21.

units.la: VOLVSIANVS, Galli filius, à patre Imperij consors factus, mortis item consors & socius fuit.
units.tr: VOLUSIANUS, son of Gallus, was made a partner in the empire by his father, and likewise shared his death.

units.la: ÆMILIANVS Libycus,dux limiti Sarmatico in Mœsia à Decio præpositus est,nec à Gallo submotus. is itaq; cum Scythæ ,solertissimū latrocinandi genus,contenti tributo non essent , id pro cōcione suis militibus pollicitus est, si hostes vicissent. Præmio accensi vicerunt.reversus in Mœsiam Æmilianus præmia persoluit. Hoc successu adeò gratus victori exercitui fuit,ut ab eo sit Imperator appellatus. ad hos motus opprimendos Gallus cum filio profectus non profecit. Æmilianus ad Senatum scribit se Imperatorem lectum,promittit se Mesopotamiam,& Armenias recuperaturum , depulsurū undique hostes.At vero priusquàm opus aggrederetur,qui in Alpibus erat milites Valerianum Imperatorem faciunt. tunc qui sub Æmiliano erant , ne civili bello , & cognato sanguine se inficerent, eum ob humilitatem generis trucidant: Valeriano,ob generis nobilitatem,& laudatiss. mores , sese dedunt. vixit Æmilianus annos 40. imperauit menses 3.Pom. Læ. Eutro. lib. 9. Bap.Egn. Aur. Vict.
units.tr: AEMILIANUS the Libyan, a commander of the Sarmatian frontier in Moesia, was appointed by Decius, and was not removed by Gallus. Since the Scythians, the most skilled kind of robbers, were not content with the tribute, he promised this to his soldiers in an assembly, if they should defeat the enemy. Inflamed by the reward, they conquered. On returning to Moesia, Aemilianus paid the rewards. By this success he became so pleasing to the victorious army that he was hailed emperor by them. Gallus set out with his son to put down these disturbances, but accomplished nothing. Aemilianus wrote to the Senate that he had been chosen emperor, and promised that he would recover Mesopotamia and Armenia and drive the enemies off on every side. But before he could undertake the task, the soldiers who were in the Alps made Valerian emperor. Then those who were under Aemilianus, so as not to stain themselves with civil war and kindred blood, slaughtered him on account of his lowly birth; they surrendered to Valerian, on account of his noble birth and most praiseworthy manners. Aemilianus lived 40 years and reigned 3 months. Pomponius Laetus, Eutropius, book 9, Baptista Egnatius, Aurelius Victor.

units.la: VALERIANVS, maioris spei quàm fortunæ, imperavit anno mundi 4216. à Christo nato 254. hic duplici nomine calamitosissimus extitit: tum quòd à Sapore Persarū Rege victus acie(sive dolo suorum,sive eius imprudētia id acciderit) in captivitate consenuit: tum quòd Gallienum filium reliquit, qui Caligulæ ac Viteliis simillimus, Imperium contaminavit. Vixit Valerianus annos 70. imperavit 4. ante captivitatem suam unà cum filio. Quandiu captivus vixit, Rex Sapor incuruato eo,pedem cervici eius imponens,equum ascēdere solitus est. Aurel. Vict.
units.tr: VALERIANUS, of greater promise than fortune, reigned in the year of the world 4216, from the birth of Christ 254. He was made most unfortunate in two respects: first, because he was defeated in battle by Sapor, King of the Persians (whether this happened through the treachery of his own men or through his own imprudence), and grew old in captivity; second, because he left behind a son Gallienus, who, most like Caligula and Vitellius, polluted the empire. Valerian lived 70 years and reigned 4 years, including the time before his captivity, together with his son. While he lived in captivity, King Sapor was accustomed to mount his horse by having him bowed down and placing his foot on his neck. Aurel. Vict.

units.la: GALLIENVS Romæ à Senatu Augustus creatus est, quando & pater Valerianus ab exercitu in Rhetia. Ab initio Imperium non infeliciter administrauit : at postea in luxum & socordiam lapsus, mirum in modum afflixit : externis hostibus adeò insultantibus ut fœminæ Imperium in eius contemptum occuparint, & tyrani 3o. ex ipso & in ipsum quoq; insurrexerint Imperiū. Græcia, Macedonia, Pontus, Asia uastata est à Gothis: Pannonia à Sarmatis, Quadisq; depopulata est. Germani usque ad Hispanias penetrarunt, & ciuitatem nobilem Tarraconem expugnauerunt, opulentissimam, ut inquit Pomponius Mela. Parthi Mesopotamia occupata, Syriā sibi cœperunt vendicare. Dacia, quæ à Traiano ultra Danubiū fuerat adiecta, tum amissa est: quòd si Posthumus in Occidente, Odenatus in Oriente Imperium non fustētassent, actum de Rom. Imperio esset. Gallienus nouissimè aduersus Aureolū profectus, à militibus suis, commento Aureoli, ad Mediolanum obsessi, unà cum fratre Valeriano occiditur. Annos uixit 5o. imperauit 15. tam cum patre quàm solus. Eutro. lib. 9. Aurel. Vict. Bap. Egna. li. i. Pom. Le Trebel. Pol.
units.tr: GALLIENUS was created Augustus at Rome by the Senate, at the same time as his father Valerian was created by the army in Rhaetia. At first he administered the empire not unsuccessfully, but afterwards he fell into luxury and sloth and afflicted it wonderfully. With foreign enemies attacking so boldly that women seized the empire in contempt of him, and thirty tyrants rose up both from his own ranks and against him as well, Greece, Macedonia, Pontus and Asia were laid waste by the Goths; Pannonia was depopulated by the Sarmatians and the Quadi. The Germans penetrated as far as Spain and captured the famous city of Tarraco, very wealthy, as Pomponius Mela says. The Parthians occupied Mesopotamia and began to claim Syria for themselves. Dacia, which had been added beyond the Danube by Trajan, was then lost. And if Postumus in the West and Odenathus in the East had not sustained the empire, it would have been all over with the Roman Empire. Gallienus, setting out last against Aureolus, was besieged at Milan by his own soldiers through a stratagem of Aureolus, and was killed together with his brother Valerian. He lived 50 years and reigned 15, both with his father and alone. Eutrop. book 9. Aurel. Vict. Bap. Egnat. book 1. Pomp. Le Trebel. Pol.

units.la: SALONINA natione, & Pipa nomine, siue Pipara, Marcomannorum Regis filia fuit, quam per pactionē concessa parte superioris Pannoniæ, matrimonij specie accepit Gallienus: ex hac Salonianum alterum filium suscepit, quæ in locum defuncti Cornelij filij sui, qui fuerat Cæsar creatus, subrogauit. Consulto Trebellium Pollionem, & Sextum Aurelium Victo.
units.tr: SALONINA was of the Marcomanni by birth and was called Pipa, or Pipara; she was the daughter of a king of the Marcomanni. Gallienus took her in marriage, in a kind of wedlock, after a part of Upper Pannonia had been ceded by treaty. By her he had another son, Salonianus, whom he put in the place of his son Cornelius, who had been made Caesar and had died. I have consulted Trebellius Pollio and Sextus Aurelius Victor.

units.la: SEQUUNTUR triginta tyrannorum imagines, subiectis illorum vitiis[?] per compendium, ex Trebellio Pollione illis fere contemporaneo. hi siquidem tyranni Imperium invaserunt partim vi, partim dolo, temporibus Valeriani & Gallieni Imperatorum: quare & tyranni dicuntur, non quod tyrannicè, hoc est iniquè, se gesserint, (nam nonnulli etiam inter eos optimi innocentem vitam duxerunt) sed quòd Imperium usurparint, nonnulli etiam coacti, seque Cæsares & Augustos appellari passi sint. Porrò, dubium est magisne Ro. Imperium labefactarint, an asseruerint: ne, diffluēte luxu & lasciuia Gallieno, ac patre eius Valeriano, bello Persico occupato, quinetiā à Persis victo & capto, omnino illa ipse miserā Ro. resp. pessum iret: dum undiquaque ab ingruentibus hostibus premeretur. Cæterum Titus & Censorinus, qui in hac tyranorum serie ultimi duo habentur, extiterunt, alter Iulio Maximino, alter verò Fl.Claudio imperate, qui Gallieno successit. Fuerunt alij vulgati 30. Athenis Tyranni, Lysandri temporibus, qui paulò post arreptam Tyrannidem à Thrasybulo victi sunt, & popularis status tunc restitutus est: sicuti diximus in priori huius operis parte, pagina 122. Porrò eadem phrasi, imò iisdem pene verbis usus sum, quibus autor meus Trebellius Pollio: qui si haud ita purè latinè loquatur, ipse viderit: institutum meum fuit eius orationè ac metem persequi: quemadmodum & aliorum quorum ego in hoc opere cito autoritates.
units.tr: THERE FOLLOW images of the thirty tyrants, with their vices briefly set beneath them, taken from Trebellius Pollio, who was almost their contemporary. These tyrants seized the empire partly by force, partly by trickery, in the times of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus; and they are called tyrants, not because they conducted themselves tyrannically, that is, unjustly (for some among them even led blameless lives and were very good men), but because they usurped the empire, and some, even though forced to it, allowed themselves to be called Caesars and Augusti. Moreover, it is doubtful whether they weakened the Roman Empire or rather asserted it: since Gallienus was dissolute in luxury and wantonness, and his father Valerian was occupied with the Persian war, and indeed was defeated and captured by the Persians, the wretched Roman state itself would have gone to ruin, while it was pressed on every side by the attacking enemies. The last two in this series of tyrants are considered to be Titus and Censorinus; the one was in the time of Julius Maximinus, the other in the time of Claudius, who succeeded Gallienus. There were also the thirty commonly reported tyrants at Athens, in the time of Lysander, who were defeated by Thrasybulus shortly after they had seized the tyranny, and the popular government was then restored; as I said in the earlier part of this work, page 122. Moreover, I have used the same phrasing, indeed almost the same words, as my author Trebellius Pollio; if he does not speak quite purely in Latin, let him see to it himself. My intention was to follow his language and meaning, just as I have cited the authorities of others in this work.

units.la: CYRIADES primus è 30. Tyrannorum numero fuit: eorum inquā qui temporibus Valeriani & Gallieni Imperatorum imperarunt. hic dum luxuria sua & moribus perditis sanctum senem eiusdem nominis patrem grauaret, direpta magna parte auri & argenti, Persas adiit: atq; Sapori regi coniunctus, hortator belli Romanis inferendi fuit. Antiochia capta & Cæsarea, Cæsarianū nomen accepit: atque inde vocatus Augustus, cùm omnem Orientem vel virium audacia, vel terrore quateret, patrem etiā interemit: ipse quoque per insidias suorū, cùm Valerianus iam ad bellum Persicum iret, interemptus est. Cōsulito Trebellium Pollionem, in horum 30. Tyrannorum vitis, ut semel te candide lector, commonefaciam.
units.tr: CYRIADES was the first of the thirty tyrants, that is, of those who ruled in the times of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. While, by his luxury and corrupt manners, he burdened his aged and holy father of the same name, he carried off a large part of the gold and silver and went over to the Persians; and, joined to King Sapor, he urged him to wage war on the Romans. Antioch and Caesarea were taken, and he received the name Caesarianus; and then, called Augustus, while he shook all the East either by the boldness of his forces or by terror, he also put his father to death. He himself was killed by the treachery of his own men, when Valerian was already setting out for the Persian war. I have consulted Trebellius Pollio concerning the vices of these thirty tyrants, so that I may remind you of them once, kind reader.

units.la: POSTHVMVS vir fuit bello fortissimus, atque in pace constantissimus, in omni quoq; vita grauis, usqueadeo ut Saloninum filium suum eidē Gallienus in Gallia positum crederet, quasi custodi vitæ, morum, & actuum Imperialium institutori. Sed ut pleriq; afferunt (quod eius non conuenit moribus) postea fide fregit, & occisio Salonino sumpsit Imperium. Ut autem verius plerique tradiderunt, cùm Galli vehemētissimè Gallienum odissent, puerū autē apud se imperare ferre non possent, eum qui commissam regebat Prouinciam, Imperatore appellarunt, misisque militibus adolescente interfecerunt. Sic omnibus Gallis acceptissimus, Gallias per annos septem instaurauit, submotis omnibus Germanicis getibus. Sed cùm se grauissimè gereret, Lolliani opera interemptus est.
units.tr: POSTUMUS was a man most brave in war and most steadfast in peace, serious in every part of his life, so much so that Gallienus trusted his son Saloninus to him while he was posted in Gaul, as a guardian of his life, a teacher of his morals and of imperial conduct. But, as many relate (which does not agree with his character), he later broke faith and, after Saloninus was killed, took the empire. However, as most have more truly handed down, since the Gauls hated Gallienus most violently, and could not bear a boy to rule over them, they proclaimed as emperor the man who governed the province entrusted to him, and, sending soldiers, they killed the young man. Thus, most acceptable to all the Gauls, he restored the Gallic provinces for seven years, all the German tribes having been driven out. But since he conducted himself very severely, he was killed through the work of Lollianus.

units.la: POSTHVMVS iunior, supradicti Posthumi filius, à patre appellatus est Cæsar, ac deinceps in eius honore Augustus. Hic cum patre dicitur intereptus, tum cum Lollianus in locum Posthumi subrogatus, delatū sibi à Gallis sumpsisset Imperium. fuit ita in declamando disertus, vt eius controuersiæ & declamationes inter Quintiliani declamationes dicantur insertæ.
units.tr: POSTUMUS the younger, son of the aforesaid Postumus, was named Caesar by his father, and afterwards Augustus in his honour. He is said to have been killed along with his father, at the time when Lollianus was put in the place of Postumus and took the empire offered to him by the Gauls. He was so eloquent in declamation that his controversies and declamations are said to have been inserted among the declamations of Quintilian.

units.la: LOLLIANVS fuit quidem vir fortissimus, sed rebellionis gratia minorem apud Gallos authoritate de suis viribus tenuit. attamen nonnihil reip. profuit: nam plerasq; Galliæ ciuitates, nonnulla etiam castra Posthumus per septem annos in solo barbarico ædificauerat, quæ ipso interfecto Posthumo, subita irruptione Germanorum, & direpta fuerat, & incensa: hæc Lollianus instaurauit, deinde à suis militibus, quòd in labore nimius esset, occisus est: idque factione Victorini, Victorinæ, seu Victoriæ, filij quæ postea Mater castrorum appellata est, & Augustæ nomine affecta, cùm ipsa per se fugiens tanti ponderis molem, primùm in Marium, deinde in Tetricum atque eius filium contulisset imperia. Ita Gallieno perdente rempub. in Gallia primùm Posthumus, deinde Lollianus, Victorinus deinceps, postremò Tetricus affectatores Romani nominis extiterunt. Lolliani autem vita in multis obscura est, vt & ipsius Posthumi: sed priuata virtute clari, non nobilitatis authoritate vixerunt. Vide Trebe.Pol.
units.tr: LOLLIANUS was indeed a very brave man, but because of his rebellion he held less authority among the Gauls for his own strength. Yet he did the state some service, for he restored most of the cities of Gaul and some fortresses which Postumus had built in hostile territory over seven years, and which, after Postumus himself was killed, had been plundered and burned in a sudden invasion of the Germans. Then he was killed by his own soldiers, because he was too demanding of their labour; and this was brought about by the faction of Victorinus, the son of Victorina, or Victoria, who was afterwards called the Mother of the Camps and was given the title of Augusta, since she herself, fleeing the burden of so great a weight, had transferred the power first to Marius, then to Tetricus and his son. Thus, while Gallienus was ruining the state, in Gaul first Postumus, then Lollianus, then Victorinus, and finally Tetricus, became the usurpers of the Roman name. The life of Lollianus is obscure in many respects, as is that of Postumus himself; but they lived renowned for private virtue, not through the authority of noble birth. See Trebellius Pollio.

units.la: VICTORINVS militaris industriæ vir à Posthumo seniore in partem vocatus est imperij, & cum eodem cōtra Gallienum conflixi:cúmq; adhibitis non paucis Germanorum auxiliis, diu bella traxissent,victi sunt. Tunc,interfecto etiā Lolliano, Victorinus in Imperio remansit:qui & ipse, quòd matrimoniis militum & militarium corrumpendis operam daret, à quodam actuario,cuius vxorem stuprauerat,factione Agrippinæ,percussus est,Victorino filio Cæsare appellato,ab ipsa, auia Victorina,seu Victoria,quæ Mater castrorum dicta est : hic autem Victorinus filius, adhuc puerulus,statim est interemptus, cùm apud Agrippinam pater eius esset occisus.De hoc Victorino Iulius Aterianus sic scriptū reliquit, Victorino qui Gallias post iuniorem Posthumum rexit,neminē existimo præferendum:Non in virtute Traianū,non Antoninum in clemētia,non in grauitate Neruam,non in gubernando ærario Vespasianum,non in censura totius vitæ, ac seueritate militari Pertinacē,vel Seuerum. Sed omnia hæc,libido in mulieres insana sic obliterauit,vt nemo audeat virtutes eius literis mădare,quem constat omnium iudicio condignas voluptatis pœnas luisse.
units.tr: VICTORINUS, a man of military diligence, was called by the elder Postumus to share in the empire, and with him fought against Gallienus; and, although they employed no small number of German auxiliaries and carried on the war for a long time, they were defeated. Then, after Lollianus was also killed, Victorinus remained in power. He too, because he set about corrupting the marriages of soldiers and of soldiers' wives, was struck down by a certain clerk, whose wife he had debauched, through the faction of Agrippina; his son Victorinus, named Caesar by his grandmother Victorina, or Victoria, who was called the Mother of the Camps, was at once killed, since his father had been slain among Agrippina's people. Concerning this Victorinus, Julius Atherianus left this written judgment: "I think no one should be preferred to Victorinus, who ruled the Gauls after the younger Postumus: not Trajan in virtue, not Antoninus in clemency, not Nerva in gravity, not Vespasian in managing the treasury, not Pertinax or Severus in the censorship of his whole life and military severity. But all these things were so obliterated by his insane lust for women that no one dares to commit his virtues to writing, since he is known to have paid, by the judgment of all, the punishments due to his pleasure."

units.la: VICTORINVS iunior, Victoriæ nepos, Victorini supradicti filius fuit:hic & à patre & ab auia,sub eadem hora qua ipse pater Victorinus interemptus est,Cæsar est nuncupatus,ac statim à militibus occisus. diceres iram diuinā de paternis flagitiis etiam in hoc puero supplicium ac vindictam sumpsisse. AVGVSTVS MARIVS IMPERATOR T. INGENVS
units.tr: Victorinus the younger, grandson of Victoria and son of the Victorinus mentioned above, was the one who, at the same hour his father Victorinus was killed, was named Caesar both by his father and by his grandmother, and was at once slain by the soldiers. One would say that the wrath of God, for the father's crimes, took its punishment and vengeance even upon this boy. AUGUSTUS MARIUS IMPERATOR T. INGENUUS MARIUS

units.la: MARIVS, interemptis Victorino, Lolliano & Posthumo, triduo tantum imperauit: vir quidem strenuus, ac militaribus vsq; ad Imperiū gradibus euectus. Antea opifex fuerat ferrarius, cuius manus vel ad feriendum, vel ad impellendū robustissimæ fuerunt: nam fortissimos quosq; vno digito sic afflixit, vt quasi ligni vel ferri ictu percusi dolerent. Huius concio prima fuit, Scio, cōmilitones, posse mihi obiici artem pristinam, cuius omnes testes estis: sed dicat quisque quod vult, vtinam semper ferrum exerceam: Non vino, non floribus, nō muliercula, nō popinis, vt facit Gallienus, indignus patre suo, & sui generis nobilitate, depereā. Ars mihi obiiciatur ferraria, dum me exterae gentes ferrum attrectasse suis cladibus recognoscant. Occisus est à quodā milite, quem dedignari ac spernere videbatur, cum tamen eius quondam miles ille operarius in fabrili officina fuisset, dixisseq; fertur inter occidēdum, Hic est gladius quem ipse cudisti.
units.tr: Marius, after Victorinus, Lollianus and Posthumus had been killed, ruled for only three days. He was indeed a vigorous man, raised to imperial power through the military ranks. Before this he had been a blacksmith, and his hands were most powerful both for striking and for pushing: for he could crush the bravest men with a single finger, so that they groaned as if struck by a blow of wood or iron. His first sermon to the soldiers was this: "I know, fellow soldiers, that my former trade can be thrown at me, and you are all witnesses to it. But let each man say what he likes; I wish I might always be working with iron. Not with wine, not with flowers, not with women, not with taverns, as Gallienus does, unworthy of his father and of the nobility of his family, does I despair. Let my smithy's craft be thrown in my face, so long as foreign nations recognise from their defeats that I have handled iron." He was killed by a certain soldier, whom he seemed to disdain and scorn, although that soldier had once been a workman in his forge; and it is reported that during the killing he said, "This is the sword which you yourself forged."

units.la: INGENVVS, qui Pannonias regebat, à Mœsiacis legionibus Imperator dictus est: neq; in quoquam melius cōsultum reip. à militibus videbatur, quàm quòd instatibus Sarmatis creatus est Imperator, qui fesis rebus mederi sua virtute posset. Sed Gallienus (vt erat nequam & perditus, ita etiam, vbi necessitas coëgisset, velox, fortis, vehemens & crudelis) Ingenuum bello vicit: eóq; occiso in omnes Mœsiacos tam milites quàm ciues, ita sæuiit, vt in plerisq; ciuitatibus viros à medio tolleret.fertur Ingenuus expugnata à Gallieno ciuitate, ne in tyranni veniret potestatem, domum intrasse, in qua se pugione transfodit. REGILLIANVS IMP. IMP. AVREOLVS
units.tr: Ingenuus, who ruled Pannonia, was proclaimed emperor by the legions of Moesia. Nothing seemed to have been better decided for the commonwealth by the soldiers than that he was made emperor when the Sarmatians were pressing, since he could by his own valour heal a ruined state. But Gallienus (who was as worthless and dissolute as he was swift, brave, vehement and cruel when necessity forced him) defeated Ingenuus in war; and after Ingenuus was killed he raged against all the Moesian soldiers and citizens alike, so that in most of the cities he removed the men altogether. It is reported that when Gallienus had captured a city, Ingenuus, lest he fall into the power of the tyrant, went into a house and pierced himself with a dagger. REGILLIANUS IMP. IMP. AUREOLUS

units.la: REGILLIANVS Illyrico Præfectus, militari ioco ad imperiū vocatus est,autoribus Mœsiacis legionibus.Nam cum milites cum eo quidam cœnaret,agitata est quæstio , vnde Regilliani nomē?cui responsum est,credimus quòd à regno.Tum aliquis cœpit quasi grāmaticaliter inflectere,rex,regis,regi,Regillianus. Milites itaque(vt est hominum genus pronum ad ea quæ cogitant)hoc omine sumpto,postridie ipsum vt Imperatorem salutarunt.Fuit vir in re militari semper probatus , & Gallieno iam ante suspectus,quòd dignus videretur imperio:nec à Gallieno promotus erat,sed à patre eius Valeriano,quèadmodum & Claudius,Macrianus,Ingenuus , Posthumus & Aureolus,qui omnes in imperio interempti sunt, cùm mererētur imperium.Mirum sanè fuit in Valeriano,quòd omnes quoscunq; duces fecit,postea militū testimonio ad Imperiū peruenerunt. sed fortuna cum Valeriano & bonos principes tulit, & Gallienum diutius quàm oportebat,reip.reseruauit.Cæterùm Regillianus cùm multa fortiter contra Sarmatas gesisse , autoribus Roxolanis,consentientibúsque militibus,& timore prouincialium,ne iterum Gallienus graviora faceret,interemptus est.
units.tr: Regillianus, prefect of Illyricum, was called to the throne by a military joke, at the instigation of the Moesian legions. For when some soldiers were dining with him, a question arose: whence is the name Regillianus? It was answered, "We believe it comes from regnum, kingdom." Then someone began to inflect it, as if grammatically: rex, regis, regi, Regillianus. The soldiers, therefore (since mankind is inclined to act on what it is thinking), took this omen and the next day saluted him as emperor. He was always proved in military affairs, and he had already been suspected by Gallienus, because he seemed worthy of empire; nor had he been advanced by Gallienus, but by his father Valerian, as were Claudius, Macrianus, Ingenuus, Posthumus and Aureolus, all of whom were killed while in power, though they deserved the empire. It was indeed remarkable in Valerian that all the commanders he made were afterwards, by the testimony of the soldiers, raised to the throne. But fortune, while it bore good emperors under Valerian, also kept Gallienus over the commonwealth longer than was fitting. Regillianus, however, having fought bravely against the Sarmatians on many occasions, was killed at the instigation of the Roxolani, with the soldiers consenting, and from fear among the provincials that Gallienus would again act more harshly.

units.la: AVREOLVS quoque Illyricianos exercitus regens , in contemptum Gallieni,vt omnes eo tepore,coactus à militibus, sumpsit Imperium:cumq; Gallienus frustra tetasset eum expugnare,pacem cum eo,cōtra Posthumū pugnaturus,fecit.Hunc Claudius,interfecto iam Gallieno,conflictu habito, apud eum ponte interemit qui inde pons Aureoli dictus est. Trebel. Pol. SEN.AVG MACRIANVS NVS[?] IMP MACRIA
units.tr: Aureolus also, commanding the Illyrian armies, out of contempt for Gallienus (as everyone was at that time), was compelled by the soldiers and took the empire. And when Gallienus had tried in vain to overcome him, he made peace with him, since he was about to fight against Postumus. Claudius, after Gallienus had already been killed, held a battle and slew him at the bridge there, which for that reason was called the Bridge of Aureolus. Trebellius Pollio. SEN. AUG. MACRIANUS NUS[?] IMP. MACRIA

units.la: MACRIANVS,Gallieno & Aureolo usurpate imperium, factus est Imperator,cum duobus filiis suis,Macriano & Quieto:idque consilio & opera ducis Balistae, ac omnium militum assensu.Hic cum statim contra Gallienum veniret,ac 45000.militum secum duceret,in Illyrico,vel Thraciarum finibus, congressus cum Aureolo, victus & cum Macriano filio intereptus est: triginta denique milia militum in Aureoli potestate concedere. Domitianus aute eum vicit,dux Aureoli fortissimus,& vehementissimus,qui se origine diceret a Domitiano Imperatore trahere,atq; a Domicilla. De hoc sic scripsit Valerianus ad senatum e Persidis finibus:Ego P.C.bellum Persicu gerens Macriano totam rempub. credidi,quod a parte militari ille vobis fidelis,ille mihi devotus, illu & amat & timet miles:nec noua vel inopinata nobis sunt:pueri eius virtus in Italia,adolescetis in Gallia,iuuenis in Thracia,senescentis denique in Illyrico & Dalmatia comprobata est, cum in diuersis proeliis ad exemplu fortiter faceret: huc accedit quod habet iuuenes filios Romano dignos collegio,nostra dignos amicitia.
units.tr: Macrianus, having usurped the empire after Gallienus and Aureolus, was made emperor together with his two sons, Macrianus and Quietus; and this was done by the counsel and effort of the commander Balista, and with the assent of all the soldiers. He immediately marched against Gallienus, and leading 45,000 soldiers with him, he met Aureolus in Illyricum or on the borders of Thrace; defeated, he was killed together with his son Macrianus, and finally thirty thousand soldiers surrendered to Aureolus's power. But Domitianus, the most brave and vehement commander of Aureolus, who said he descended in origin from the emperor Domitian and from Domitilla, defeated him. Concerning him Valerian wrote thus to the senate from the borders of Persia: "Conscript Fathers, while waging war against Persia I entrusted the whole commonwealth to Macrianus, because he is faithful to you from the military side, devoted to me, and loved and feared by the soldiers. Nor are these things new or unexpected to us: his valour was proved as a boy in Italy, as a youth in Gaul, as a young man in Thrace, and finally as an old man in Illyricum and Dalmatia, since in various battles he acted bravely as an example. Add to this that he has young sons worthy of the Roman college and of our friendship."

units.la: MACRIANVS iunior una cum patre factus est Imperator,una ite cum patre cuius merito imperare coeperat, a Domitiano victus,triginta, ut superius dictum est,milibus militum spoliatus est. De hoc multa dicuntur quae ad fortitudine pertinent iuuenilis aetatis. fuit matre nobili, patre tantum forti & militia claro. Trebel.Pol.
units.tr: Macrianus the younger was made emperor together with his father, and together with the father by whose merit he had begun to rule; defeated by Domitianus, he was stripped of thirty thousand soldiers, as was said above. Many things are told of him which pertain to courage of youthful age. He had a noble mother and a father strong and famous in war. Trebellius Pollio.

units.la: QVIETVS cum patre & fratre, Balistæ iudicio, Imperator est factus. Sed vbi cœperit Odenatus, qui olim iam Orientem tenebat, ab Aureolo Macrianum patre, Quietū & eius fratrem Macrianum victos, militésque Macriani, in Aureoli potestatem concessisse, quasi Gallieni partes vindicaret, adolescentem Quietū cum Balista, præfecto dudum, interemit. Idē quoque adolescens, Ro.dignus Imperio fuit, ut vera Macriani proles. Porrò Macrianorum familia speciale semper habuit, ut viri in auro & argento, mulieres in reticulis & dextrocheriis, & in anulis, & in omni ornamentorum genere Alexandri magni effigiem gestarent. Trebel. Pollio.
units.tr: Quietus, with his father and brother, was made emperor by the judgement of Balista. But when Odenathus, who had long held the East, learned that Aureolus had defeated Macrianus the father, Quietus and his brother Macrianus, and had taken the soldiers of Macrianus into his power, he, as if avenging the cause of Gallienus, killed the young Quietus together with Balista, the prefect of long standing. This youth too was worthy of empire, as the true offspring of Macrianus. Moreover the family of the Macriani always had a particular habit: the men wore the image of Alexander the Great on gold and silver, the women on hairnets and bracelets and rings, and in every kind of ornament. Trebellius Pollio.

units.la: ODENATVS, princeps Palmyrenorum, capto Valeriano, fessis reipub. viribus, nisi sumpsisset Imperium, in Oriete res perditæ essent. Nam hic collecto exercitu contra Persas prosectus est, cum uxore Zenobia & filio maiore, cui nomen erat Herodes. Nisibin primum & Orietis pleraque cum omni Mesopotamia in potestate recepit: deinde ipsum Regem, victum sugere coegit, Saporem & eius liberos bello lacessiuit, captis concubinis, capta etiam magna præda. Macriano interepto, filium eius Quietū, interfecit. Copofito itaq; magna ex parte Orientis statu, a consobrino suo Maeonio, qui & ipse Imperium sumpserat, intereptus est, cum filio suo Herode, qui & ipse post reditu è Perfide cum patre Imperator est appellatus. Fuit Odenatus bellicosus: præterea capiedis leonibus, pardis & ursis a prima ætate assuefactus, iniuriarū cœli pertolerantis. Cuius etiam uxor non minus viro fortis extitisse perhibetur: huius uxoris postea meminerimus pagina 75.
units.tr: Odenathus, prince of the Palmyrenes, after Valerian was taken, when the strength of the commonwealth had failed, would have had affairs in the East utterly lost had he not taken up the empire. For he gathered an army and set out against the Persians, with his wife Zenobia and his elder son, whose name was Herodes. He first recovered Nisibis and most of the East, together with all Mesopotamia, into his power; then he forced the king himself to flee defeated, and attacked Sapor and his children in war, capturing his concubines and also a great booty. After Macrianus was killed, he put to death his son Quietus. Having thus settled the state of the East for the most part, he was killed by his cousin Maeonius, who had himself also assumed the empire, together with his son Herodes, who after returning from Persia had also been called emperor with his father. Odenathus was warlike; moreover, from earliest youth he was accustomed to catching lions, leopards and bears, and he endured the injuries of the sky. His wife is also said to have been no less brave than her husband; we shall mention this wife later, on page 75.

units.la: HERODES, non Zenobia matre, sed priore Odenati uxore genitus, cum patre accepit Imperiū, homo omnium delicatissimus, ac prorsus Orientalis, & græcæ luxuriæ, cui erant figillata tentoria, & aurati papiliones, & omnia Persica. Denique ingenio eius usus Odenatus, regias Saporis cōcubinas, & quascunq; gemmas ac diuitias cepit, huic filio suo Herodi tradidit paterna motus indulgentia. Oderat illum Zenobia nouercali animo, quare cōmendabiliorem eum patri fecerat. Consulito Trebellium Pollionem.
units.tr: Herodes, born not of Zenobia as mother but of Odenathus's earlier wife, received the empire together with his father. He was a man most delicate of all, and altogether Oriental, and given to Greek luxury: he had embroidered tents and gilded pavilions and everything Persian. Finally Odenathus, having used his talent, took the royal concubines of Sapor and whatever gems and riches he had captured, and, moved by paternal indulgence, handed them over to his son Herodes. Zenobia hated him with a stepmother's spirit, and for that reason had made him more commendable to his father. Consult Trebellius Pollio.

units.la: MÆONIVS Odenati consobrinus inuidia extimulatus Imperatorem optimum, eundémque consobrinum suum interemit, cùm ei nihil aliud obiiceretur, præter filij Herodis delicias. Dicitur autem primùm cum Zenobia conspirasse, quæ ferre non poterat ut priuignus suus Herodes princeps diceretur, atque autoritate præiret eius filios, Herennianum & Timolaum. Hic Ipurcissimus[?] fuit, quare Imperator appellatus per errorē, breui à militibus pro suæ luxuriæ meritis interemptus est. Videto ut supra.
units.tr: Maeonius, the cousin of Odenathus, goaded by envy, killed the best emperor, and his own cousin, when nothing else was charged against him except the luxuries of Herodes his son. It is said that he first conspired with Zenobia, who could not bear that her stepson Herodes should be called prince and, by his authority, go before her sons Herennianus and Timolaus. This man was most impure, and was called emperor by mistake; soon afterwards he was killed by the soldiers as his luxury deserved. See above.

units.la: BALISTA utrum imperarit ambigitur: sunt qui dicant Quieto per Odenatum occiso, Balistæ veniam datam: attamen eum imperasse, quòd nec Gallieno, nec Aureolo, nec Odenato se crederet. Alij asserunt priuatum in agro suo interemptum. Multi & sumpsisse illũ purpuram, & more Romano imperasse, ac exercitum duxisse. Fuit vir quidem insignis, valuit consilio: expeditionibus & prouisione annonaria singularis. Gratias egit Balistæ Valerianus per epistolã, in qua docet sibi præcepta gubernandæ reipub. ab hoc data, gaudens quòd eius consilio nullum adscriptitium, id est vacãtem haberet, & Tribunũ nullum stipatorem qui non verè pugnaret. Hic nihilominus in tetorio[?] suo cubans, à quodã gregario milite Odenati, in Gallieni gratiam dicitur interemptus. Vide Treb. Pol.
units.tr: It is uncertain whether Balista ever ruled: some say that after Quietus had been killed by Odenathus, pardon was granted to Balista, but that he nevertheless ruled, since he believed he could trust neither Gallienus, nor Aureolus, nor Odenathus. Others assert that he was killed in private on his own estate. Many also say that he assumed the purple and ruled in the Roman manner and led an army. He was indeed an outstanding man and strong in counsel; singular in expeditions and in the provisioning of the grain supply. Valerian gave thanks to Balista by letter, in which he records that the precepts for governing the commonwealth had been given to him by this man, rejoicing that by his counsel he had no vacant post of an enlisted man, and no tribune as a bodyguard who did not truly fight. Nevertheless he, while lying on his couch, is said to have been killed by a certain common soldier of Odenathus, to win the favour of Gallienus. See Trebellius Pollio.

units.la: VALENS, militaris vir, simul etiam ciuilium virtutũ gloria pollens, Proconsulatũ Achaiæ, dato à Gallieno tunc honore administrabat: quem Macrianus vehementer reformidans, misso Pisone interfici præcepit. At valens sibi diligentissimè cauens, nec aliter sibi posse subueniri existimãs, sumpsit Imperiũ, & breui à militibus interemptus est. Fuit & alter Valens, huius auunculus, sed par in ambobus fuit fortuna: nã & ille cũ paucis diebus Illyrico imperasset, occisus est. Vide vt supra. IMP. PISO FRVGI P.F.AVG AEMILIANVS
units.tr: Valens, a military man who also excelled in the glory of civic virtues, was administering the proconsulship of Achaea, an office given to him by Gallienus at that time. Macrian, greatly fearing him, sent Piso and ordered him to be killed. But Valens, taking the greatest care of himself and thinking that he could be helped in no other way, assumed the imperial power, and was soon killed by the soldiers. There was also another Valens, the uncle of this one, but the fortune of both was the same: for he too, after ruling Illyricum for a few days, was killed. See above. IMP. PISO FRUGI P.F. AVG. AEMILIANUS

units.la: PISO ad interficiendum Valentem missus, ubi eum providum futurorū imperare cognovit, in Thessaliam concessit, atq; illic paucis sibi cōsentientibus sumpsit Imperiū, Thessalicúsque appellatus, interemptus est, vir frugi, & summæ sanctitatis, dictus ducere originē ab illa Pisonū familia, cui se Cicero nobilitandi causa sociaverat. Ipse quoq; Valens, qui ad eum percussores misisse perhibetur, dixisse fertur, Non sibi apud Deos inferos constare rationem, quòd quamuis hostem suum, Pisonem tamen iussisset occidi, virum cui similem Romana respublica non haberet.
units.tr: Piso, sent to kill Valens, when he learned that Valens was ruling prudently for the future, withdrew into Thessaly, and there, with a few supporters, assumed the imperial power, was called Thessalicus, and was killed. He was a man of virtue and of the highest integrity, said to derive his descent from that family of the Pisos with which Cicero had allied himself for the sake of ennobling himself. Valens himself, who is said to have sent assassins against him, is also reported to have said that he could not account for himself before the gods below, since, although Piso was his enemy, he had ordered him to be killed, a man whom the Roman commonwealth would not have another like.

units.la: ÆMILIANVS coactus sumpsit Imperium, cùm alioquin videret ob seditionē obortam undecunque sibi pereundum. Consenserunt ei Ægyptiacus exercitus, maximè in Gallieni odium. Nec ei ad regendam rempublicam animus defuit. Nam Thebaidem, totámque Ægyptum peragravit: & quatenus potuit, barbarorum gentes armis ac auctoritate submovit. Denique Alexander, vel Alexandrinus, virtutum merito vocatus est. At cùm contra Indos pararet expeditionem, misso Theodoto duce, Gallieno iubente, dedit pœnas: siquidem strangulatus in carcere, captivorū veterum more, perhibetur.
units.tr: Aemilianus was forced to assume the imperial power, since he saw that he was bound to perish from every side because of a sedition that had arisen. The Egyptian army joined him, chiefly out of hatred for Gallienus. Nor did he lack the spirit to govern the commonwealth. For he travelled through the Thebaid and all of Egypt, and as far as he was able, he drove the tribes of the barbarians back by arms and authority. Finally, he was called Alexander, or the Alexandrine, by merit of his virtues. But when he was preparing an expedition against the Indians, Gallienus commanded that Theodotus, a leader, be sent, and he paid the penalty: for he is reported to have been strangled in prison, after the manner of the old captives.

units.la: Vide Trebel. Pol. IMP. SATVRNINVS IMP. TETRICVS P F AVGVSTVS
units.tr: See Trebellius Pollio. IMP. SATURNINUS IMP. TETRICUS P.F. AUGUSTUS

units.la: SATVRNINVS, optimus ducum,à Valeriano dilectus fuit.hic cùm dissolutione Gallieni pernoctantis in publico,ferre non posset,& milites non Imperatoris exemplo, sed suo regeret, ab exercitibus Imperator designatur:vir sanè prudens, gravis, omnibus gratus,atque adeò victoriarū barbararum insignis. qua die à militibus peplo Imperatorio est amictus, concione adhibita, dixisse fertur: Commilitones bonum ducem perdidistis,& malum Imperatorem creastis. Cùm multa strennuè in Imperio gessisset,tādem quòd esset severior, & gravior militibus, ab iis ipsis à quibus creatus Imperator fuerat, interemptus est. Vide Trebel.Pollio.
units.tr: Saturninus, the best of commanders, was beloved by Valerian. When he could not bear the debauchery of Gallienus, who spent the nights in public, and when he ruled the soldiers not by the example of the emperor but by his own, he was designated emperor by the armies: a man truly prudent, serious, pleasing to all, and indeed distinguished for his victories over the barbarians. On the day he was clothed in the imperial robe by the soldiers, he is reported to have said, after calling an assembly: "Fellow soldiers, you have lost a good general and have created a bad emperor." Although he had performed many feats with vigour in the empire, at last, because he was too severe and too stern for the soldiers, he was killed by those very men by whom he had been made emperor. See Trebellius Pollio.

units.la: TETRICVS, senior, pop. Rom. Senator, cùm præses in Gallia esset, ad capessendum Imperiū instigatus est à Victoria, sive Victorina. Augustum itaque eum appellari fecit,filiúmque eius Cæsarē nuncupauit,mortuo Victorino eiúsque filio. Tandem cùm multa feliciter gessisset,diúq; imperasset,ab Aureliano victus, militum suorum impudentiam & procacitatem vix ferēs, gravissimo principi,simul ac severissimo volens se dedit, Aureliano inquam:cui & statim scripsisse fertur,
units.tr: Tetricus the elder, a senator of the Roman people, while he was governor in Gaul, was urged to take up the imperial power by Victoria, or Victorina. He therefore caused himself to be called Augustus and named his son Caesar, after Victorinus and his son had died. At last, after he had carried on many affairs successfully and had ruled for a long time, he was defeated by Aurelian. Scarcely enduring the shamelessness and insolence of his own soldiers, he gave himself up to a most severe prince who was at the same time most strict, namely to Aurelian; and he is also reported to have written to him at once:
"Rescue me, unconquered one, from these evils."

units.la: Sed tamen severus ille Aurelianus hunc virum Senatorē,Consularem,Galliarum præsidē,in triumphum duxit,quo tempore & Zenobiam.pudore deinde victus,eum quem triumphauerat toti Italiæ præfecit,nec solùm vivere,sed etiā in summa dignitate esse passus est,sæpe collegam,nonnunquā commilitonem, aliquando etiam Imperatorem eum nuncupans. Vide ut supra.
units.tr: Yet that stern Aurelian led this man, a senator, a consular, and governor of the Gauls, in his triumph, at the same time as Zenobia. Then, overcome by shame, he set over all of Italy the man whom he had led in triumph, and he allowed him not only to live but also to be in the highest dignity, often calling him his colleague, sometimes his fellow soldier, and at other times even naming him emperor. See above.

units.la: TETRICVS iunior, superioris Tetrici filius, appellatus est Cæsar(vt dixi)à Victoria,cùm illa Mater castrorum ab exercitu nuncupata esset. hic vnà cum patre in triúpho ductus postea omnibus Senatoriis honoribus functus est illibato patrimonio, quod quidem ad suos posteros transmisit. Narrabat auus Trebellij Pollionis hunc sibi familiarem fuisse neq; quenquam illi ab Aureliano, aut Postea ab aliis principibus esse prælatum Vide Trebel. Pollionem.
units.tr: Tetricus the younger, son of the elder Tetricus, was named Caesar (as I said) by Victoria, when that woman had been named Mother of the Camps by the army. He was led in triumph together with his father, and afterwards, having held all the senatorial offices, he kept his patrimony intact, which he passed on to his descendants. The grandfather of Trebellius Pollio used to relate that this man had been a friend of his, and that no one had been preferred to him by Aurelian or afterwards by other emperors. See Trebellius Pollio.

units.la: TREBELLIANVS factus est in Isauria princeps, ipsis Isauris sibi ducem quærentibus: quem cùm alij archipiratam vocassent, ipse se Imperatorem appellauit: monetā etiam cudi iussit: in intima Isaurorum loca se contulit: munitúsque locorum difficultatibus & montibus, aliquandiu apud Cilicas regnauit: sed per Gallieni ducē Caufisoleum, natione Ægyptium, fratrem Theodoti, qui Æmilianum ceperat, in campum deductus, victus & occisus est. Neque tamen postea Isauri, timore ne in eos Gallienus sæuiret, ad obseruantiam, ac præstandam fidem quauis principum humanitate allici vnquam potuerunt. Denique post Trebellianum pro barbaris habentur. Non sunt statura decori, non virtute graues, non instructi armis, non consiliis valentes, sed hoc solo securi, quòd in editis positi, adiri nequeunt. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: Trebellianus was made prince in Isauria, the Isaurians themselves seeking a leader for themselves. Though others called him an archpirate, he called himself emperor and ordered coins to be struck. He withdrew into the innermost regions of the Isaurians, and, fortified by the difficulties of the places and the mountains, he reigned for some time among the Cilicians. But he was lured into the open field by Caufisoleus, a general of Gallienus, an Egyptian by nation, brother of Theodotus who had captured Aemilianus, and was defeated and killed. Nor could the Isaurians afterwards, for fear that Gallienus would rage against them, ever be attracted to obedience and to keeping faith by any kindness of the princes. Finally, after Trebellianus, they are regarded as barbarians. They are not graceful in stature, not weighty in virtue, not equipped with arms, not strong in counsel, but secure in this alone, that, being placed in high places, they cannot be approached. See above.

units.la: HERENNIANVS, & Timolaüs , Odenato patre nati sunt , quos moriens superstites reliquit pater. horum nomine Zenobia mater vsurpauit Imperium,ac rempub.administrauit diutius quàm fœminâ decuit : paruulos Ro. Imperatorio habitu ostendit purpuratos,eosdémque adhibuit concionibus quas illa quasi vir sæpe ad populum habuit,Didonẽ,Semiramidem, & Cleopatram sui generis principẽ inter cætera prædicans.De horum exitu incertũ est:aiunt nonnulli ab Aureliano interemptos , alij morte sua extinctos : nam & Zenobiæ posteri etiam Romæ inter nobiles agebant tempore Trebellij Pollionis, qui horum vitas descripsit.
units.tr: Herennianus and Timolaus were born to Odenathus their father, whom their father left behind as survivors when he died. In the name of these boys Zenobia their mother seized the imperial power and administered the commonwealth longer than became a woman. She displayed the little boys to the Romans in imperial dress, clothed in purple, and she brought them to the assemblies which she, acting like a man, often held before the people, proclaiming among other things Dido, Semiramis and Cleopatra, princes of her own kind. Concerning the end of these boys it is uncertain: some say they were killed by Aurelian, others that they died a natural death. For also the descendants of Zenobia were living among the nobles at Rome in the time of Trebellius Pollio, who described their lives.

units.la: TIMOLAUS,supradicti Herenniani frater,breui Grammaticam cõsecutus esse dicitur:fratri fuit haud absimilis, eum tamen ingenio longè anteuertit.nam potuisse Timolaüm summum etiam Latini sermonis Rhetorẽ instituere tradunt. Consulito quem supra citaui autorem.
units.tr: Timolaus, brother of the Herennianus mentioned above, is said to have soon attained the study of grammar. He was not very unlike his brother, though he far surpassed him in talent; for they relate that Timolaus could have been trained as the greatest orator even in the Latin tongue. Consult the author I cited above.

units.la: CELSVS peplo deæ cœlestis ornatus, appellatus est Imperator ab Afris, autore Vibio Passieno Proconsule Africæ, & Fabio Pöponiano duce limitis Libyci. Hic priuatus ex Tribunis, in Africa positus, in agris suis degebat: sed ea iustitia & corporis magnitudine, vt dignus videretur Imperio. At verò per quandam mulierem Gallienam nomine, consobrinâ Gallieni, 7. Imperij die interēptus, atq; adeò etiā inter obscuros principes vix relatus est. corpus eius à canibus laniatum est: nouóq; iniuriæ genere imago eius in crucem sublata est, persultante populo quasi patibulo ipse Celsus videretur affixus.
units.tr: Celsus, adorned with the robe of the heavenly goddess, was called emperor by the Africans, on the authority of Vibius Passienus, proconsul of Africa, and Fabius Poponianus, commander of the Libyan frontier. He was a private man, formerly a tribune, living in Africa, and he dwelt on his own lands; but he was of such justice and bodily size that he seemed worthy of empire. Yet he was killed on the seventh day of his rule through a certain woman named Galliena, a cousin of Gallienus, and so he was scarcely recorded even among the obscure princes. His body was torn to pieces by dogs; and by a new kind of insult his image was raised on a cross, the people mocking as though Celsus himself had been fixed to a gibbet.

units.la: VICTORIA, seu Victorina, vbi filium ac nepotem ex filio Victorinos, inquâ, à militibus vidit occisos, ac Posthumū, deinde Lollianum, Mariumetiam, quem principē milites nuncuparant, interfectos, Tetricū, cuius supra memini, ad Imperiū adhortata est, vt virile semper facinus tētare auderet. insignita est præterea hoc titulo, castrorū mater, sicq; ab exercitu vocitabatur. Cusi sunt eius nummi ærei, aurei, & argentei. Non diu vixit: nam Tetrico imperāte, vt pleriq; aiunt, occisa, vt alij asserunt, fato suo extincta est. Itaque dum Gallienus popinatur, ac inter lenones & meretrices degit, partes Gallicanæ, orientales item, Ponti, Thraciarū & Illyrici occupatur: mulieres denique imperant, nempe Zenobia & Victoria: de Zenobia meminerimus statim, quam cum Aureliano collocauimus: nam illam vicit, ac triumphauit. IMP TITVS AVGVST. T. CENSORINVS
units.tr: Victoria, or Victorina, when she saw her son and her grandson, the sons of Victorinus, I say, killed by the soldiers, and Postumus, then Lollianus, and Marius also, whom the soldiers had named prince, all killed, urged Tetricus, whom I mentioned above, to take up the empire, so that he would always dare to attempt manly deeds. She was furthermore distinguished by this title, Mother of the Camps, and was so called by the army. Her coins were struck, of bronze, gold and silver. She did not live long: for while Tetricus was emperor, she was killed, as most say, though others assert that she died by her own fate. And so, while Gallienus feasted and spent his time among pimps and prostitutes, the Gallic provinces, the eastern ones as well, of Pontus, Thrace and Illyricum, were occupied; women finally held power, namely Zenobia and Victoria. Of Zenobia we shall remember shortly, whom we have placed with Aurelian, for he defeated her and triumphed over her. IMP. TITUS AUGUST. T. CENSORINUS

units.la: TITVS Tribunus Maurorum, qui à Maximino inter priuatos relictus fuerat,invitus,atq; à militibus coactus, imperauit:atque intra paucos dies, post vindicatam defectione quam Magnus, vir consularis, Maximino parauerat,à suis militibus interemptus est. imperauit mēses 6.domi forisque fortunatus, sed Imperio parum felix. huic fuit vxor Calphurnia nomine, sancta & venerabilis fœmina,de genere Censorinorum, id est Pisonum. Hæc uniones Cleopatræ habuisse perhibetur,& lancem 100.librarum argenti, cuius plerique poëtæ meminerunt, in qua maiorum eius expressa visebatur historia.
units.tr: Titus, tribune of the Moors, who had been left as a private man by Maximinus, was made emperor against his will and under compulsion from the soldiers. Within a few days, after avenging the revolt which Magnus, a man of consular rank, had prepared against Maximinus, he was killed by his own soldiers. He ruled for six months, fortunate at home and abroad, but not very fortunate in empire. He had a wife named Calpurnia, a holy and venerable woman, of the family of the Censorini, that is, of the Pisos. She is said to have had the pearls of Cleopatra, and a platter of one hundred pounds of silver, which many poets mention, on which the history of her ancestors was seen engraved.

units.la: CENSORINVS, vir plane militaris,atq; antsquæ[?] in curia autoritatis, cùm post omnes honores ( nam multis functus fuerat)in agro suo degeret senex ( atque uno pede claudicans, eo vulnere quod bello Persico Valeriani temporibus acceperat)factus est Imperator, & scurrarum ioco Claudius quasi claudicans appellatus est. Hic cùm se gravissimè gereret, neque à militibus ob disciplinam censoriam ferri posset, ab his ipsis à quibus Imperator fuerat designatus, interemptus est. extabat tempore Trebellij eius sepulchrum, in quo grandiusculis literis iuxta Bononiam incisi erant omnes eius honores, ultimo tamen versu adscripto.
units.tr: Censorinus, a man altogether military, and indeed of great authority in the senate, when after all his honours (for he had held many) he was living in his country estate as an old man, limping on one foot from the wound he had received in the Persian war in the time of Valerian, was made emperor; and by the jest of buffoons he was called Claudius, as if limping. Since he conducted himself very severely, and could not be borne by the soldiers on account of his censorial discipline, he was killed by those very men by whom he had been designated emperor. His tomb still stood in the time of Trebellius, on which all his honours were cut in rather large letters near Bologna, with a final line added.

units.la: Hactenus de iis qui Imperiū usurparūt à Gallieno ad Fla.Claudium:de quo mox tractabimus,persequentes ipsorū Rom. Imperatorum seriem.
units.tr: So far concerning those who usurped the empire from Gallienus to Flavius Claudius, of whom we shall soon treat, following the series of the Roman emperors themselves.

units.la: FLA. CLAVDIVS post Gallienum imperauit anno mundi 4231. à natiuitate Christi 269. Hic Sarmatas, Getas, Scythas, & Quados deuicit: Daciâ recuperauit: Aureolum vicit, ac Imperio exuit. Alemannorû tam multa millia cæcidit, vt vix media pars exercitus eorum superesset. Imperator optimus remp. bene administrauit. Senatus aureum illi statuâ in Capitolio posuit. A plerisque Gordiani, cuius supra meminimus, filius existimatus est. Hic Gallieni morientis sententia Imperator designatus est, ad quem etiam regia misit ornamenta. bienniû imperauit: & Diuus est appellatus: moriens Aurelianum cõmendauit, quasi suffragium ferês, vt post se ille imperaret. Consulito: Aur. Vict. Pomp. Læ. Bap. Egna. li.1. atque Eutro. li.9.
units.tr: FLAVIUS CLAUDIUS reigned after Gallienus, in the year of the world 4231, from the birth of Christ 269. He conquered the Sarmatians, Getae, Scythians and Quadi; he recovered Dacia; he defeated Aureolus and deprived him of the empire. He slew so many thousands of the Alemanni that scarcely half their army survived. As emperor he administered the commonwealth well and excellently. The Senate set up a golden statue of him on the Capitol. By many he was thought to be a son of Gordian, whom we mentioned above. He was designated emperor by the dying wish of Gallienus, to whom he also sent the royal insignia. He reigned two years, and was called Divus; dying, he commended Aurelian, as if giving his vote, that he should reign after him. See Aurelius Victor, Pomponius Laetus, Baptista Egnatius, book 1, and Eutropius, book 9.

units.la: AVRELIVS Quintillus Flauij Claudij frater fuit: hunc Senatus, nunciata Claudij morte, Cæsarem Augustum appellauit: at exercitus interea Aurelianum Imperatorem lêgit. Postquàm nuntium ad vrbẽ peruênit, illius conatibus se imparem cùm videt, venas sibi soluit, & pòst paulò decessit, 17. Imperij die. fuit hic ante Imperium Italici præsidij dux. Videto Pomponium Lætum, in Claudio. IMP.C.M.AVRELIANVS P.AVG. SENOBIA ORIENT. DNA
units.tr: AURELIUS Quintillus was the brother of Flavius Claudius. When the death of Claudius was announced, the Senate named him Caesar Augustus; but meanwhile the army chose Aurelian as emperor. When the news reached the city, seeing that he was unequal to Aurelian's undertakings, he opened his veins and a little later died, on the seventeenth day of his rule. Before his rule he had been commander of the Italian guard. See Pomponius Laetus, under Claudius. IMP. C. M. AVRELIANVS P. AVG. SENOBIA ORIENT. DNA.

units.la: VALE. AVRELIANVS imperauit post Quintillum anno mundi 4233. à Christo nato 271. Hic quanquam patre colono inter Daciam & Macedoniam genitus, haud dissimilis fuit Magno Alexandro, nam Ro. urbem triennio ab inuasoribus receptauit, cùm Alexander annis 13. ad Indiam peruenerit. Hic Sueuos & Sarmatas vicit: Marcomannos, qui Mediolanum vastarant, attriuit: Imperiū ad antiquos fines perduxit: validioribus muris urbem sepsit. Sæuus ac sanguinarius hic, atiã sororis filium interfecit: ipse itidem fraude serui, inter Constātinopolim & Heracleam occisus est. imperauit an.5.menses 6.primus apud Ro. diadema capiti innexuit, gemmisque & aurata veste usus est. Vide Aure.Vict.Bap.Egna.lib.1.& Eutro.lib.9.
units.tr: VALE. AVRELIAN reigned after Quintillus, in the year of the world 4233, from the birth of Christ 271. Although he was born of a peasant father between Dacia and Macedonia, he was not unlike Alexander the Great: for he recovered the city of Rome from invaders in three years, whereas Alexander reached India in thirteen years. He defeated the Suevi and Sarmatians; he crushed the Marcomanni, who had laid waste Milan; he brought the empire back to its ancient borders; he surrounded the city with stronger walls. Cruel and bloodthirsty, he killed the son of his own sister; he himself was killed by treachery of a slave, between Constantinople and Heraclea. He reigned five years and six months. He was the first at Rome to bind a diadem on his head, and he used gems and gold-embroidered clothing. See Aurelius Victor, Baptista Egnatius, book 1, and Eutropius, book 9.

units.la: ZENOBIA, bellicosa mulier, quæ se de Cleopatrarum Ptolemæorúmq; gente iactabat, nomine filiorum an.8. imperauit, vixque tandē ab Aureliano victa & triumphata, cōcessit in iura Romana. Cùm illam Aurelianus cepisset, interrogauit exprobrâs, Quid, ò Zenobia, ausa es insultare Romanis Imperatoribus? at respondit hæc, Imperatorē te esse agnosco, qui vincis. fuit castis.[?] vocem habuit claram & virilem, oculo nigros ac vigentes: dentes tam candidos vt plerique margaritas putarent: ingenium diuinum. venusta fuit, seuera, atq; etiam clemens vbi oportuit: in triumphum ducta, sub gemmarum pondere anhelas sæpe restitit, alioqui fortissima: collum, manus, pedes aureis vinculis ac catenis, irretiebatur. huic agrum dedit Aurelianus: vixitque hæc more matronæ Ro. Vide Trebel. Pollio.
units.tr: ZENOBIA, a warlike woman, who boasted that she was of the race of the Cleopatras and the Ptolemies, ruled for eight years in the name of her sons; at last, scarcely conquered and led in triumph by Aurelian, she yielded to Roman law. When Aurelian had captured her, he asked her, reproachfully, What made you, O Zenobia, dare to insult Roman emperors? But she answered, I acknowledge you as emperor, you who conquer. She was chaste. She had a clear and manly voice, eyes black and lively, teeth so white that most thought them pearls; her intellect was divine. She was graceful, stern, and even merciful when it was fitting. Led in triumph, she often stopped, gasping under the weight of her gems, though otherwise most courageous; her neck, hands and feet were bound with golden chains and fetters. Aurelian gave her an estate, and she lived in the manner of a Roman matron. See Trebellius Pollio.

units.la: AN. TACITUS post Aurelianum imperauit anno à mundo condito 4238. à Christo nato 276. Siquidem Aureliano interempto,7.menses vacauit Imperium:interim milites ad Senatum,Senatus ad milites Imperatoris eligendi prærogatiuam deferebant. Tandem Senatus hunc Senatorij ordinis Augustum dixit. Quàm verò amplissimi ordinis iudiciū à militari tumultu distet,Taciti electio ostendit,cùm in curia testatum sit,neminem aut iustius quàm grauem virum,aut prudêtius quàm doctū imperare posse. Verùm hic tantus vir sexto imperij sui mese obiit. Vide Orof.lib.7.cap.24.Hic ducentesimo Imperij die, ut inquit Aurelius Victor, apud Tarsum febre periit: at 6. mense postquâ imperare cœperat, militari scelere periisse scribit Bap. Egna.lib.1.Aurel.Vict.
units.tr: AN. TACITUS reigned after Aurelian, in the year from the creation of the world 4238, from the birth of Christ 276. For, Aurelian having been killed, the empire stood vacant for seven months; meanwhile the soldiers granted to the Senate, and the Senate to the soldiers, the prerogative of choosing an emperor. At last the Senate proclaimed this man, of senatorial rank, Augustus. But how far the judgment of the most distinguished order is from military tumult the election of Tacitus shows, since it was declared in the senate house that no one could rule more justly than a grave man, or more wisely than a learned one. Yet this great man died in the sixth month of his reign. See Orosius, book 7, chapter 24. Here, as Aurelius Victor says, on the two hundredth day of his rule he died of fever at Tarsus; but Baptista Egnatius, book 1, writes that he perished by military crime six months after he had begun to rule. See Aurelius Victor.

units.la: FLORIANUS,Taciti frater,cùm suo iudicio ad tantam velut hæreditatem mortuo fratre properaret,Imperium & invasit,& arripuit. Itaque cùm vix duobus mensibus præfuisset, quasi per ludum Imperio usus,& ad ludibriū fortunæ eueētus[?] esset,à militibus occisus est, aut ad Probi imperantis nuntium, solutis sibi venis,expirauit.Consulito autores quos supra.
units.tr: FLORIANUS, brother of Tacitus, when his brother died, hastened, in his own judgment, to take up so great an inheritance, and seized and grasped the empire. Thus, having scarcely presided for two months, and having used the empire as if in a game, and been carried away to the mockery of fortune, he was killed by the soldiers, or, on the news of the approach of the emperor Probus, his veins were opened and he expired. Consult the authors mentioned above.

units.la: AVRE. PROBVS, verè probus, mortuo Tacito, ac Floriano fratre, ex alio patre, imperauit anno mundi 4239. à Christo nato 277. patrem habuit agrestem Dalmatici sanguinis: sed nec genus humile, nec qui praecesserat Florianus obstitit quominus omnium consensu Imperator diceretur, vir omnium amantissimus. pacis, belliqúe artibus clarissimus. Hic Gallias à barbaris occupatas, ingenti praeliorum felicitate asseruit: ita se & in toga & in militia gessit, ut res ipsa nomen sequeretur. Saturninum in Oriente, Proculum & Bonosum Agrippinę Imperium usurpantes oppressit: Sarmatas contudit: tyrannos omnes sustulit: pacem orbi restituit. Pace terra marique parta, dicere solebat milites minimè necessarios fore, cùm desunt hostes, quos nusquam virtute sua futuros, mox sibi promittebat: quae vox invidiam sibi apud milites conflauit. In Smirnensi agro, natali suo dum moram trahit, tumultu militari occisus est, anno Imperij 6. Pompo.Læ.Eutro.lib.9.Egna.li.1.
units.tr: AVRE. PROBUS, truly upright, reigned in the year of the world 4239, from the birth of Christ 277, after the death of Tacitus and of his brother Florianus, who was of another father. He had a rustic father of Dalmatian blood; but neither his lowly birth nor the fact that Florianus had preceded him stood in the way of his being called emperor by the consent of all, a man most beloved by all, most famous for the arts of peace and of war. He recovered Gaul, occupied by barbarians, with remarkable success in battles, and he conducted himself so well both in civil and in military affairs that the reality followed the name. He crushed Saturninus in the East, and Proculus and Bonosus, who had usurped power in Agrippina; he subdued the Sarmatians; he destroyed all the tyrants; he restored peace to the world. With peace won on land and sea, he used to say that soldiers would be quite unnecessary when there were no enemies, and he promised that soon they would be nowhere, by their valour. This saying stirred up hatred against him among the soldiers. While he lingered in the district of Smyrna, his birthplace, he was killed by a military uprising, in the sixth year of his reign. See Pomponius Laetus, Eutropius, book 9, and Egnatius, book 1.

units.la: CARVS Narbonæ genitus, ab exercitu Imperator dictus est anno mundi 4245. à Christo nato 283. filios suos, Carinum & Numerianum, Cæsares dixit. Hic dum bellum Sarmaticum gerit, nuntiato Persarum tumultu, ad Orientem profectus est cum filio Numeriano Cæsare, doctis.iuvene: bellum itaque Persicum, quod Probus paraverat, aggressus, Mesopotamiâ cepit, Ctesiphonte usque pervenit. quod si fulmina ictus non fuisset, dum ad Tigrim fluvium castrametaretur, regnum Persicum subvertisset. Aure.Vict.Oro.lib.6.cap.24. imperarunt hic, & duo proximè sequentes, annos duos.
units.tr: CARUS, born at Narbo, was named emperor by the army in the year of the world 4245, from the birth of Christ 283. He called his sons, Carinus and Numerian, Caesars. While he was waging war against the Sarmatians, news came of a Persian uprising, and he set out for the East with his son Numerian, a Caesar, a learned young man. Taking up the Persian war, which Probus had prepared, he captured Mesopotamia and reached as far as Ctesiphon. Had he not been struck by lightning, while he was encamped by the river Tigris, he would have overthrown the Persian kingdom. See Aurelius Victor and Orosius, book 6, chapter 24. These men, and the two who immediately followed, reigned two years in all.

units.la: CARINUS, Cæsar à patre dictus, omnibus se sceleribus inquinavit: plurimos innoxios fictis criminibus occidit: matrimonia nobilium corrupit. Ad extremū trucidatur, eius præcipuè tribuni opera, & dextera, cuius dicebatur coniugē polluisse. Consulito Aur.vict.Eutr.li.9.imperavit annos duos.
units.tr: CARINUS, Caesar named by his father, polluted himself with every crime: he killed many innocent people on invented charges, and he corrupted the marriages of the nobles. At last he was slaughtered, chiefly by the work of his tribune and his right hand, whose wife he was said to have defiled. Consult Aurelius Victor and Eutropius, book 9. He reigned two years.

units.la: NUMERIANUS Cæsar Carini frater, Carino tamen longè absimilis fuit. hic nempe adolescens tum probitatis, tum eruditionis eximiæ, maximè verò ad poëticen natus erat, atque etiam ad arma. hic itaque miles, orator, poëta, dum oculis æger in occlusa lectica ferretur, confecto bello Persico, unà cum patre, ab Apro socero, Imperiū invadere cupiēte occiditur. Nec eius mors inulta est, concionante Aprū Diocletianus manu propria confodit. Imperarunt hi tres, Carus, Carinus & Numerianus, annis duobus. Pomp.Lætus. IMP DIOCLETIANVS PF AVG IMP C MAXIMIANVS PF AVG
units.tr: NUMERIAN, Caesar, brother of Carinus, was yet by no means like Carinus. For this young man was, at that time, of outstanding integrity and learning, and was born especially for poetry, and also for arms. Thus he was a soldier, orator and poet; while, sick in his eyes, he was carried in a closed litter after the Persian war was finished, together with his father, he was killed by Aper, his father-in-law, who was desiring to seize the empire. Nor was his death unavenged: Diocletian stabbed Aper with his own hand while he was addressing the soldiers. These three reigned, Carus, Carinus and Numerian, for two years. See Pomponius Laetus. IMP. DIOCLETIANVS P. F. AVG. IMP. C. MAXIMIANVS P. F. AVG.

units.la: DIOCLETIANVS Dalmata, Amilini Senatoris Libertinus,matre atq; oppido nomine Dioclea, vnde & Diocles dictus,imperauit anno mundi 4247. à nat.Christi 285.hic Carinum omnibus odiosum prælio vicit:at 2.Imperij an.cùm tãtam molê grauiore animaduerteret quàm vt vnus esse vniuersæ par posset, Maximianû Herculium Augustum creat,ac in consortem Imperij legit.anno 6.Constantium Chlorum,& Galerium Maximianû siue Maximum,cognomento Armentariû, Cæsares creat in Ægypto:Alexandriam 8. mensibus obsessam cepit: Achilleum Alexandriæ imperiû affectantem feris obiecit. anno Imperij 22.principatu se abdicat Nicomediæ,& Herculius Maximianus Mediolani eodem die:cumque in propriis agris consenescens, ab Herculio atq; Galerio ad recipiedum Imperium rogaretur,tanquam pestem aliquâ detestans, respondit:Vtinam Salonæ possetis visere olera nostris manibus insita, profecto nunquam istud tentandum iudicaretis:sicque per decé annos priuatus,& Imperij mole exoneratus vixit. Attamen adorari aliquâdo voluit: Christianos etiâ afflixit. vixit annos 78. imperauit 22. obiit vel alienatione mentis,vel hausto veneno,dum veretur Licinium ac Constantinum.
