He ordered that a third of the church's revenues be given to him; the archbishop of Tours opposed this gift freely and bravely, prophesying that the king would be despoiled of his kingdom if he diminished or took away the goods of the poor. He had his son Chramn, who had been subdued in war, burned together with his wife, children and whole household. For Chramn, not obeying his father, had inflicted many losses on Gaul, first at the instigation of his uncle Childebert, and then with the duke of Aquitaine, his father-in-law, defending his cause. Conobus the Briton received him and protected him. The king had almost destroyed that father-in-law, and had shortly before killed the Briton's son. The king died at Compiègne in the fifth year of his reign. Paulus Aemilius, book 1; Robert Gaguin, book 2.

units.la: CHEREBERTVS, qui & Aribertus, patri Clotario succedit anno mundi 4527. à Christo nato 565. nam ei, diuisa inter fratres hæreditate paterna, parisij forte obuenere: Chilperico Suesionum regnum, Guntrano Aurelianesium, Sigiberto Metesium. Fertur Cherebertus paucos annos vixisse, muliere quauis corruptior, scortationi & luxui addictissimus: cõputantur tamen in chronicis anni nouem administrationis huius Childeberti. Pau.Æmy.lib.1.Ro.Ga.lib.2.
units.tr: CHERIBERT, who is also called Aribert, succeeded his father Clotaire in the year of the world 4527, from the birth of Christ 565; for when the paternal inheritance was divided among the brothers, Paris fell to him by chance: Chilperic received the kingdom of the Soissonnais, Guntram that of Orléans, Sigebert that of Metz. It is said that Cheribert lived only a few years, more corrupt than any woman, devoted above all to debauchery and luxury; yet the chronicles reckon nine years of this Childebert's rule. Paulus Aemilius, book 1; Gaguin, book 2.

units.la: IVSTINVS Iunior , filius filiæ Iustiniani Imperatoris, post auuum imperat Constantinopoli anno mundi 4529. à Christo nato 567: Hic æmulus Iustini,atque perinde ac filius à Iustiniano in regia semper enutritus,facili admodum ingenio fuit,atque ad promerendam,ex liberalitate,hominum gratiam accŏmodato.Cum Persis fœdus pepigit,tributo, quod Romani annuum his penderent,sublato. Porrò Narses cùm post Gothicam victoriâ Italiæ præesset,accusatur apud Iustinum,malæ administrationis:hic per literas se purgat. Sophia Iustini vxor, scripsit ad Narsetem vt ad pensa muliebria rediret, eunuchus enim erat Narses,quare eum oderat.tunc Lŏgobardi, Germanica gens,qui in Pannonia erant,à Narsete indignato vocati,in Italiam irrumpunt, quâ ab Alboino Rege ad Desiderium , per 204.annos in principatus diuisam tenuere:responderat vtique Sophiæ Narses,se talem texturū telam, quam ipsa discutere & diuellere nequiret : obiit graui pedū dolore Iustinus anno imperij II.Pom.Læ.Egna.lib.2.Longinus , primus Rauennæ exarcha fuit anno mundi 4533. à Christo nato 571.
units.tr: JUSTIN the Younger, son of the daughter of the emperor Justinian, after his uncle reigned at Constantinople in the year of the world 4529, from the birth of Christ 567. He was a rival of Justin and, just as if he were his son, had always been brought up at court by Justinian; he was a man of very easy temper and well suited to win people's favour by generosity. He made a treaty with the Persians, abolishing the tribute which the Romans had paid them every year. Furthermore, when Narses, after his Gothic victory, was governing Italy, he was accused before Justin of bad administration; he cleared himself by letter. Sophia, the wife of Justin, wrote to Narses to return to women's work, for Narses was a eunuch, and therefore she hated him. Then the Lombards, a German people who were in Pannonia, were called in by Narses, who was indignant, and they burst into Italy; from there, under King Alboin, and then under Desiderius, for 204 years they held the land divided into principalities. Narses had certainly answered Sophia that he would weave such a web that she could not unravel or tear it apart. Justin died of severe pain in his feet in the second year of his reign. Pompon. Laetus; Egnatius, book 2. Longinus was the first exarch of Ravenna, in the year of the world 4533, from the birth of Christ 571.

units.la: TIBERIVS Constantinus adoptatus à Iustino , rem per septennium satis feliciter administrat, Persas sæpe profligatos, intra suos fines compellit, recepta Mesopotamia. Longobardi rupto fœdere vrbē Romam graui obsidione premunt : sed eos iniuria decidētium imbrium depellit:nihil hoc principe fortunatius , si res vt in Oriente , ita in Occidente successisset. vixit summa cum pietatis & liberalitatis opinione.Pomp.Læt. Egn. lib.2.Diac.lib.8. IMP.MAVRITIVS.AVGVST VXOR.MAVRICI.CONSTANTIA
units.tr: Tiberius Constantine, adopted by Justin, administered affairs fairly successfully for seven years. He often routed the Persians and drove them within their own borders, and recovered Mesopotamia. The Lombards, breaking the treaty, pressed the city of Rome with a severe siege, but a violent downpour of rain that fell upon them drove them off. Nothing was more fortunate under this prince, if affairs had gone as well in the West as they did in the East. He lived with a high reputation for piety and generosity. Pomp. Læt., Egn. bk. 2; Diac. bk. 8. EMPEROR MAURICE AUGUSTUS. WIFE OF MAURICE: CONSTANTINA.

units.la: MAVRICIVS, Cappadox, Tiberij Constantini gener fuit: à Socero successor declaratur, imperatque ann.mun.4547. à Christo nato 585. Hic imperium sub initia Persis victis, Scythis afflictis, Longobardis repressis, ac Hunnis è patrio solo in solitudines pulsis, feliciter administrauit. Mox tamen cùm præ auaricia, stipendia aut nulla aut rara daret, cõiuratur in eum ab exercitu cui præerat Phocas imminēs Sarmatiæ. Tandem cùm frustra Phocæ insidias, somnio etiā admonitus præcauet, cúmque miles stipēdio fraudatus, seditiosius agit, ab eodem Phoca imperio & vita priuatur Mauricius anno ætatis 66. imperij 20. vxor, liberi, omnísq; eius prosapia cum eo sublata est. Turcaicum nomen tunc primùm Asiæ auditum. Pom. Læ.Egna.lib.2. Hic Mauricius Childeberto Frácorum Regi summam argenti misit vt Longobardos Italia exturbaret.Pau. Diac.li.8.mirū est sanè in hoc Imperatore opum cumulandarum cupiditatē eius oculos ita excæcasse, cum præsertim notarius primùm fuisset, deinde miles, postea præfectus vigilum, deinde Imperatoris gener, postea Augustus. Discant itaque Principes auaritiam non tātùm illos dedecere, sed & damno & exitio interim illis esse: (exemplo sint Imperatores Pertinax & Mauricius) contrà verò maximum esse Principis ornamentum liberalitatem.
units.tr: Maurice, a Cappadocian, was the son-in-law of Tiberius Constantine; he was declared successor by his father-in-law and ruled in the year of the world 4547, from the birth of Christ 585. Early in his reign he administered affairs happily: the Persians were defeated, the Scythians afflicted, the Lombards held back, and the Huns driven from their native soil into the wastelands. Soon, however, since out of avarice he paid the soldiers either nothing or rarely, a conspiracy was formed against him by the army which Phocas, living on the border of Sarmatia, commanded. At last, when he had in vain guarded against Phocas's plots, and was even warned by a dream, the soldiers, cheated of their pay, acted more mutinously; Maurice was deprived of empire and life by this same Phocas, in the sixty-sixth year of his age and the twentieth of his reign. His wife, children and whole family were destroyed with him. Then for the first time the name Turk was heard in Asia. Pom. Læt., Egn. bk. 2. This Maurice sent a great sum of silver to Childebert, King of the Franks, so that he might drive the Lombards out of Italy. Paulus Diaconus, bk. 8. It is indeed remarkable that a lust for amassing wealth so blinded this emperor's eyes, especially since he had first been a clerk, then a soldier, afterwards prefect of the watch, then the emperor's son-in-law, and finally Augustus. Let princes therefore learn that avarice not only disgraces them, but meanwhile brings loss and ruin to them (let the emperors Pertinax and Maurice be examples); on the contrary, generosity is the greatest ornament of a prince.

units.la: CONSTANTINA, Tiberij Imperatoris filia, Mauricij vxor fuit, ex quo liberos suscepit, qui vnà cum patre & matre cæsi sunt, vti dictum est. Vide autores quos supra. R. FRAN. 9 CHILPERICVS F. REX IO CLOTARIVS
units.tr: Constantina, daughter of the emperor Tiberius, was the wife of Maurice; from her he had children, who were slain together with their father and mother, as has been said. See the authors cited above. R. FRAN. 9. CHILPERIC, SON OF KING. 10. CLOTHAIRE.

units.la: CHILPERICVS, post fratre Cherebertum apud Francos imperat anno mundi 4536. à Christo nato 574. Initio Chilpericus neque omnia tenebat, neq; fortior erat. Inter fratres de regno lis est. Sigiberto in Germania trans Rhenū occupato, Remorū oppidū quod ditionis Sigiberti erat, nonnullâq; in Campania loca Chilpericus adoritur: parátque bellū quantum potest maximū cum filio Theodeberto. Sigibertus redit: Suesfsionum deditione facta, Theodebertum capit, quê statim ad Chilpericum remittit, iureiurâdo tamen prius astrictū, vt ne vnquâ bellū aduersus eum susciperet. Attamê iussu patris, violato iureiurando, côtra patruū dimicans occiditur Theodebertus. Rebus accisis Chilpericus Tornacum se recipit. Sigibertus magna põpa cum vxore Brunechilde Parisios ingreditur: atq; post paucos dies cûm statuisset fratri ne vitam quidê saluâ iri, à duobus percussoribus, quos Fredegûda Chilperici vxor immiserat, trucidatur: Hæc tandê etiam cum adultero Landrico, virum, regê, noctu à venatione redeunte, cædi curauit: ad Calam Parisiorū vicum. huius item imperio nouercæ, puer regius Clodoueus, natu postremus, iam ante necatus fuerat. rexit annis 14. Sepultus est in æde D. Germani à Pratis, iuxta Lutetiam. Æmy.lib.1.Gaguin lib.2.
units.tr: Chilperic, after his brother Charibert, ruled among the Franks in the year of the world 4536, from the birth of Christ 574. At first he held neither all things nor was he the stronger. There was a dispute over the kingdom between the brothers. While Sigebert was occupied in Germany beyond the Rhine, Chilperic attacked the town of Reims, which was under Sigebert's control, and some places in Champagne; and he prepared a war as great as he could with his son Theodebert. Sigebert returned; after the surrender of the Soissonnais he captured Theodebert, whom he immediately sent back to Chilperic, though first bound by an oath never to wage war against him. Yet, at their father's command, Theodebert broke his oath, fought against his uncle, and was killed. With his affairs broken, Chilperic withdrew to Tournai. Sigebert entered Paris with great pomp, with his wife Brunhilda; but a few days later, when he had decided that his brother should not even be spared his life, he was slain by two assassins whom Fredegund, Chilperic's wife, had sent. She also arranged for her lover Landry to kill her husband, the king, as he returned at night from hunting, at Calais, a village of Paris. By her command too, her stepson, the royal boy Clovis, the youngest, had been killed earlier. He reigned fourteen years. He was buried in the church of St. Germain-des-Prés, near Lutetia. Æmilius bk. 1; Gaguin bk. 2.

units.la: CLOTARIVS, huius nominis secundus, Francorū Rex 10. Chilperico patri puer admodū successit, anno mundi 4549. à Christo nato 587. Tutor à Guntrano patruo ei datur Landricus: apud matrem Fredegundam educatur. Cruetam de Saxonibus victoriam reportat Clotarius: rexit annos 44. in æde D. Germani sepultus est. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: Clotaire, the second of that name, King of the Franks, succeeded his father Chilperic as a very young boy, in the year of the world 4549, from the birth of Christ 587. Landry was given to him as guardian by his uncle Guntram; he was brought up by his mother Fredegund. Clotaire won a bloody victory over the Saxons. He reigned forty-four years and was buried in the church of St. Germain. See above.

units.la: PHOCAS in eius Imperatoris,& Domini fui,locu succedit, quę nuper imperio & vita priuarat:nec tamen ipse ab auaricię vicio tęperauit,cūm causam ei auaricia Mauricij prębuifset coniurandi in caput illius:quin longę studiosius corradędæ pecuniæ incubuit:& omnia ex Persicæ seruitutis instituto egit. Hic Romanum Pontifice[?] primarium omnium declarauit sollicitatus à Bonifacio 3. Cætera adeò socors & ignauus, & frequentibus adulteriis infamis,ut cūm Ro.imperium undiq; barbari vastarent,starętque solùm eius nominis umbra, conspiratum fit in illum ab Heracliona,Heraclio & Prisco,qui captum inertissimum hominem prius interfecere quàm ferte ei suppetias eius milites potuerint,omnémq; stirpem impuriffimi principis sustulēre. cœpit imperare anno mundi 4567. à Christo nato 605. imperátque annis 8.Egna.lib.2.
units.tr: Phocas succeeded in the place of that emperor and lord whom he had recently deprived of empire and life; yet he himself was not free of the vice of avarice, although avarice had given Maurice cause to conspire against his head; indeed he applied himself far more eagerly to hoarding money, and conducted everything on the Persian model of slavery. He was the first to declare the Roman Pontiff the head of all, at the urging of Boniface III. In other respects he was so careless and lazy, and infamous for frequent adulteries, that while the barbarians were laying waste the Roman empire on every side, and only the shadow of that name remained, a conspiracy was formed against him by Heraclion, Heraclius and Priscus; they killed the most inept man, once captured, before his soldiers could bring him aid, and destroyed the whole line of that most impure prince. He began to rule in the year of the world 4567, from the birth of Christ 605, and reigned eight years. Egn. bk. 2.

units.la: HERACLIVS, qui in Phocam coniurarat, à militibus primùm Imperator pronunciatur: populus dein & Senatus ingenti acclamatione probant:accepto itaq; diademate à Sergio Constantinopolitano patriarcha,Persicum bellum parat,legatis antea missis pro induciis impetrandis. Ludibrio habitus à Persis,adeò excanduit ut differre non potuerit: respondebant enim impij hostes non prius fe Romanis pacem daturos,quàm Christum abnegaffet Imperator.Perfide igitur omni, in ultionem,igni ferróque vastata, lignũ salutiferæ crucis recepit..Celebris adhuc est nobis dies festus,argumentũ victoriæ insignis: Tigris factus est inter utrosque limes:nouo tandem morbi genere obiit Heraclius,anno imperij 30.Pom.Læ.Egna.li.2. Tunc Mahomethes insanus emersit.
units.tr: Heraclius, who had conspired against Phocas, was first proclaimed emperor by the soldiers; the people and the Senate then approved him with great acclamation. Having received the diadem from Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, he prepared a Persian war, after first sending envoys to obtain a truce. Mocked by the Persians, he was so inflamed that he could not delay; for the impious enemies replied that they would not give peace to the Romans until the emperor had renounced Christ. Therefore, in vengeance, he ravaged Persia with fire and sword and recovered the wood of the saving cross. The feast day, a sign of that remarkable victory, is still celebrated by us. The Tigris became the boundary between the two sides. At last Heraclius died of a new kind of disease, in the thirtieth year of his reign. Pom. Læt., Egn. bk. 2. Then the madman Mahomet emerged.

units.la: MAHOMETVS ex stirpe Ismaëlis oriundus, in Arabia humili loco natus, inops, ac orphanus, captus est ac venditus mercatori cuidam diuiti, qui eum mercimoniis praeposuit. Hero mortuo uxor eius uidua ac vetus nupsit Mahometo robusto iuueni: qui à Sergio monacho haeretico praua imbutus opinione, diuinitatem quandam inde sibi adstruxit, quam leuissimo hominum generi facilè persuasit: cumq; epilepsia laboraret, cospectum se Angeli Gabrielis minime ferre posse cominiscebatur: sunt etiā qui prodant assuefacta columbam ei ad aurem aduolasse, grana in aure captatura, metitumq; eum hanc esse spiritum sanctū. Hic vinū lege prohibuit: plures uxores permisit: paradisum etiam voluptarium constituit: legem suam armis tutari sanxit. Hic itaque rerum successu elatus, Syriā, vastat, Damascum expugnat: in Persas mouet: à quibus victus Scenitas Arabes, Romanae assuetos militiae, ab Heraclio, ob negata stipendia deficientes, adiungit. Sic stabilito paulatim imperio, an. aetatis 40. veneno, ut aiunt, à cognatis ad quos uxoris hereditas spectabat, inter epulas immixto, interiit spurcissimus ille: cuius tandē superstitio Romanorum principū ignauia, eò credit, ut iam non Asiam solum, & Africam, sed bonam Europae partē infecerit. Vide Egn. lib.2. Pom. Laet. Blon. lib. 9. Deca.1. Chro. Antonini. titu. 13. cap.3. hunc Turci vocant Mehemet, alij autem Muhamet.
units.tr: Mahomet, descended from the stock of Ishmael, born in Arabia of humble station, poor and orphaned, was captured and sold to a certain rich merchant, who placed him over his wares. When his master died, his widow, an old woman, married Mahomet, a strong young man; he, imbued with a perverse opinion by Sergius, a heretical monk, claimed for himself a certain divinity drawn from this, which he very easily persuaded upon the most foolish kind of men. Since he suffered from epilepsy, he pretended that he could not bear the sight of the angel Gabriel; there are also those who report that a tame dove flew to his ear, to peck grains from his ear, and he declared that this was the Holy Spirit. He prohibited wine by law; he permitted many wives; he also established a voluptuous paradise; he sanctioned that his law be defended by arms. Elated by such success, he laid waste Syria and took Damascus by storm; he moved against the Persians, and, when defeated by them, he joined the Scenite Arabs, accustomed to Roman military service, who had revolted from Heraclius over withheld pay. Thus, with his power gradually established, he died that most filthy man at the age of forty, poisoned, as they say, by his kinsmen, to whom his wife's inheritance belonged, the poison being mixed into a feast. His superstition, by the sloth of the Roman princes, has so prevailed that it has now infected not only Asia and Africa but a good part of Europe. See Egn. bk. 2; Pom. Læt.; Blondus bk. 9; Decade 1; Chronicle of Antoninus, title 13, chapter 3. The Turks call him Mehemet, others Muhamet.

units.la: CADIGA, seu Tadiga Mahometi hera, cũ vidua effet quinquagenaria, ac diues nupsit seruo suo Mahometo, à Sergio monacho, ut censet Pom. Læ. persuasa. Hic Mahometus primò Cadigæ camelis ad negotiādū utebatur: cumq; veniret in Palæstinam cum Iudæis & Christianis versatus, religionémq; eorum edoctus, ex his duabus doctrinis mixtis, unam quandā tertiā ac nouā cōfinxit circa ann.mun.4586. à Christo nato 624. Vide Ab. Vrsper. in Heraclio Imper. & Volater. lib. Geographiæ 12.
units.tr: Cadiga, or Tadiga, Mahomet's mistress, when she was a widow of fifty and rich, married her slave Mahomet, having been persuaded, as Pom. Læt. thinks, by the monk Sergius. This Mahomet at first used camels of Cadiga for trading; and when he came into Palestine and mixed with Jews and Christians, and learned their religion, from these two doctrines mixed together he fashioned a certain third and new one, around the year of the world 4586, from the birth of Christ 624. See Abulfeda's (Ab. Vrsper.) account under Emperor Heraclius, and Volaterranus, Geography bk. 12.

units.la: HERACLIVS, qui & Constantinus iunior, & nouus Constantinus dictus est, Heraclii ex Fabia Eudoxia filius fuit: admodū adolescens erat tum cum à patre imperiali diademate donatus est.Hic verae pietatis cultor,cum nondum annum imperasset,Martinae nouercae insidiis,quae Heraclionae filio imperium astrueret,veneno sublatus est. Vide Baptistam Egna. li. 2. Pom.Læt.Succedit Heraclionas Heraclio anno mundi 4604. à Christo nato 642.
units.tr: Heraclius, who was also called Constantine the Younger and the New Constantine, was the son of Heraclius and Eudoxia Fabia. He was quite young when his father gave him the imperial diadem. Being a cultivator of true piety, before he had ruled a full year he was removed by poison, through the plots of his stepmother Martina, who wanted to secure the empire for her son Heracleon. See Baptista Egn. bk. 2; Pom. Læt. Heracleon succeeded Heraclius in the year of the world 4604, from the birth of Christ 642.

units.la: HERACLION, siue Heraclionas,imperauit Constantinopoli cum Martina matre,quæimperium inuaserat venefica: hæc cum esset filia fratris Heraclii prioris Imperatoris,fuit item illi Heraclio uxor,suscepitque ex eo hunc Heraclionē siue Heraclionam. Cum imperium male partum vix biennio tenuissent mater,& filius decennis, in exilium à Senatu in Cappadociam mittuntur:mulieri lingua praeciditur,ne oratione,qua plurimū valebat,populos commoueret:puero nasus abscinditur,ne decor aut gratia vultus in miseratione populum flecteret. Senatus tunc sine militibus Imperatorem Constantem fecit, quod raro contigit, vel ante vel post Tacitum. Pomponius Lætus,in progenie Heraclii.
units.tr: Heracleon, or Heraclionas, ruled at Constantinople together with his mother Martina, who had seized the empire by poisoning; she was the daughter of the brother of the earlier emperor Heraclius, and was likewise the wife of that Heraclius, and by him she had this Heracleon or Heraclionas. When the mother and her ten-year-old son had held the ill-gotten empire for barely two years, they were sent into exile by the Senate to Cappadocia: the woman had her tongue cut out, so that she could not stir up the people by her speech, in which she was very powerful; the boy had his nose cut off, so that his beauty or grace of face would not move the people to pity. The Senate then, without soldiers, made Constans emperor, which happened rarely, either before or after Tacitus. Pomponius Læt., in the lineage of Heraclius.

units.la: DAGOBERTVS huius nominis primus,ac Francorum Rex vndecimus succedit patri Clotario,huius nominis secundo,anno mundi 4593. à Christo nato 631. Hic viuo adhuc patre, pædagogo barbam vulsit, virgísq; eum cædi iussit:pro miraculo habetur,patris iram vitare potuisse. Fratri Ariberto Aquitaniæ regnum in partem hæreditariam dedit:Sclauos adhuc idololatras debellauit. Effeminatus Dagobertus ,scortorū & pellicum agmen secum traxit:& variis in locis formosarū collegia instituit,quæ vt Reginæ adornarentur: D.Amandus,id flagitij corripiés,in exilium mittitur.Rex Iudæos omnes qui Christum ampleāti nollent,edicto expulit. Templum D. Dionysij,ad Parisios,à fundametis erexit:ex aliis vndequaque corrasit,quò id vnū ditaret, nec quisquā ante eum patrimonij reditus annuos templis tam profusè donauit.Vascones rebelles in fidem recepit. Tandem profluuio ventris obiit anno regni 14. Pau. Emyl. lib.1.Gag.lib.3.
units.tr: DAGOBERTUS, the first of that name and the eleventh king of the Franks, succeeds his father Clotaire, the second of that name, in the year of the world 4593, from the birth of Christ 631. While his father was still alive, he had his tutor's beard plucked out and ordered him beaten with rods; it is regarded as a marvel that he was able to escape his father's anger. He gave the kingdom of Aquitaine as a hereditary portion to his brother Aribert. He crushed the Slavs, who were still idolaters. Dagobert, being effeminate, dragged a crowd of whores and concubines about with him, and set up in various places colleges of beautiful women, who were to adorn the queen. Saint Amandus, rebuking this disgrace, was sent into exile. The king expelled by edict all the Jews who would not accept Christ. He built from the foundations the church of Saint Denis at Paris, scraping together gifts from every quarter so that it alone might be enriched; and no one before him had given the yearly revenues of his estates to churches so lavishly. He received the rebellious Gascons back into his allegiance. At last he died of a flux of the bowels in the fourteenth year of his reign. Paulus Aemilius, book 1; Gagnier, book 3.

units.la: CLODOVEVS, huius nominis secundus, Francorum Rex duodecimus,succedit patri Dagoberto anno mun.4607. à Christo nato 645. cùm Sigibertus natu maior Austrasia contentus esset. Clodoeus & Ludouicus idem nomē est Germanicè.Sigibertus,nulla prole suscepta,Ildebertū filiū Grimoaldi adoptat:verùm mox nascitur illi filius Dagobertus:quem Grimoaldus valde puerū,& tonsum, & monachum in Scotiā mittit,patre Sigiberto defuncto:& eundem Ildebertum Austriæ Regem creat. Clodoeus hanc perfidiā minimè fert.Ildeberto in bello occisio,Grimoaldus captus, Parisiis in carcere vitā miserè finiit. Fames maxima Galliā inuadit:cui vt succurrat Clodoeus,thesauros & opes,quibus ædem D.Dionysij Dagobertus pater ornarat,aufert,obiítque anno regni 17.
units.tr: CLODOVEUS, the second of that name, the twelfth king of the Franks, succeeds his father Dagobert in the year of the world 4607, from the birth of Christ 645, since the elder son Sigebert was content with Austrasia. (Clodoveus and Ludovicus are the same name in German.) Sigebert, having no offspring, adopted Hildebert, the son of Grimoald; but soon a son, Dagobert, was born to him. Grimoald, when the father Sigebert had died, sent this boy, very young and tonsured and made a monk, into Scotland, and appointed the same Hildebert king of Austrasia. Clodoveus could not bear this treachery. Hildebert was slain in battle, and Grimoald, taken prisoner, ended his life miserably in prison at Paris. A great famine invaded Gaul; to relieve it Clodoveus took away the treasures and riches with which his father Dagobert had adorned the church of Saint Denis, and he died in the seventeenth year of his reign.

units.la: CONSTANS, qui & Constantinus, Heraclij Constantini supradicti ex Gregoria, filia Nicetæ Patricij, filius, imperio potitur adnitente Senatu, uti dictū à me est, qui Martinæ scelus execrabatur. Hic dicitur etiam Constantinus tertius, qui valde dilectus ab auo Heraclio, Phocæ succeßsore, magnísque honoribus functus, auitæ tandem impietatis hæres, Martinum Ro. Pontificem sibi aduersantem comprehendi iubet, in exilióque mori cogit. A Saracenis victus aufugit. Biennij ab eisdem induciis impetratis, Italiam petit, ut eam à Longobardis liberet: à quibus etiam victus, in suos conuertit iram, laminas argenteas, quibus Pantheon tegebatur, & alia quædam pretiosa, reliquias hostilium prædarum atque incendiorum aufert: plúsque ornamentorum intra quintū diem urbi detrahit, quàm barbari per tot annos: quicquid Romæ antiqui operis, signorúmue fuit, in Siciliam secum asportat: ubi cum sextū annum agit, & auarè ac crudeliter tributū exigit, in balneis, à ministris, autore Mazefe, interficitur, anno imperij 27. coepit anno mundi 4605. à Christo nato, 643. Pom. Læt. Diaco. lib. 8. Egna. lib. 2.
units.tr: CONSTANS, who is also called Constantine, son of the aforementioned Heraclius Constantine by Gregoria, daughter of the patrician Nicetas, gained the empire with the support of the Senate, as I have said, the Senate which execrated the crime of Martina. He is also called Constantine the Third. He was greatly loved by his grandfather Heraclius, the successor of Phocas, and held great honours, but at last became the heir of his grandfather's impiety. He ordered Pope Martin of Rome, who opposed him, to be arrested, and forced him to die in exile. Defeated by the Saracens, he fled. Having obtained a truce of two years from them, he made for Italy to free it from the Lombards; but he too was defeated by them, and turned his anger on his own people. He took away the silver plates with which the Pantheon was covered, and other precious things, the remnants of the plunder and burnings of the enemy; and he carried away more of the ornaments from the city within five days than the barbarians had in so many years. Whatever ancient work or statues there were in Rome he took with him to Sicily, where, after spending six years there, he exacted tribute greedily and cruelly, and was killed in his bath by his servants, at the instigation of Mezezius, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign. He began his reign in the year of the world 4605, from the birth of Christ 643. Pomponius Laetus, Diaconus, book 8; Egnatius, book 2.

units.la: CONSTANTINVS, natu maximus Constantis prædicti, post patrem imperat. Hic in Siciliam venit, ultúsque Mizizium, siue Mazefen, tyrannum, & cædis paternæ conscios, bellum in Saracenos annos septem terra marique feliciter gessit: vnico congressu 30000. cæcidit: tributarios fecit. Ignis sub aqua ardet, Callinici inventum: quo valde terrentur hostes Arabes. Bulgari trans Danubium derepête bellum ostentant: inhonesta pace, Mysia ad inhabitándum datur, cum annuo tributo. imperat annis 17. Pogonatus dictus, id est barbatus, quòd barbatus è Sicilia rediisset. Egn. lib. 2. Dia. lib. 8. hic è palatio præcipitatus interiit.
units.tr: CONSTANTINE, the eldest son of the aforementioned Constans, reigned after his father. He came to Sicily, avenged himself on Mizizius, or Mezezius, the tyrant and accomplice in his father's murder, and for seven years waged war successfully against the Saracens by land and sea: in a single encounter he cut down 30,000 of them, and he made them tributaries. Fire burns under water: this was the invention of Callinicus, by which the Arab enemies were greatly terrified. The Bulgarians suddenly threatened war across the Danube; by a dishonourable peace, Mysia was given to them to settle, with an annual tribute. He reigned for seventeen years. He was called Pogonatus, that is, the bearded, because he had returned from Sicily bearded. Egnatius, book 2; Diaconus, book 8. He was thrown headlong from the palace and died.

units.la: CLOTARIVS, huius nominis tertius, Francorum Rex decimus tertius, succedit patri Clodoueo secundo, tanquam ma- ximus natu filius, anno mundi 4624. à Christo nato 662.
units.tr: CLOTAIRE, the third of that name, the thirteenth king of the Franks, succeeds his father Clodoveus the second, as the eldest son, in the year of the world 4624, from the birth of Christ 662.

units.la: Hic egregij nihil præstitit. Theodoricus huius frater Childerico minor, post hunc, Ebroini Magistri equitum opera regnat: sed ob incontinentiam & scelera regno pellitur: & cum suo Ebroino in cœnobium truditur Theodoricus. Childericus frater, qui in Austrasia imperabat accersitus, Rex creatur. Tunc inertes Reges toti se Magistris equitū permittebāt, in deliciis clam voluptabantur: tātum in publicū prodibant Calēdis Maij, cūm pompa & regio apparatu. Ferè Parisij & Neustriæ regnum erat vniuersæ eorū ditiones: reliquum Galliæ in cōtrouersia erat, quàm plurimis ab eorū imperio deficientibus, dum penes Magistros equitum summa rerū esset, apud quos stetit ad Pipinū vsque, id est annis ferè cētum: vixit, ex quo patri in regno successit Clotarius ann. 4. regio magis ornatus nomine, quàm Regem agēs, sicuti nec qui ad Pipinum vsque ferè sunt. Æmy. lib. 1. Gag. lib. 3. obiit nullis relictis liberis.
units.tr: He achieved nothing remarkable. His brother Theodoric, younger than Childeric, reigned after him through the work of Ebroin, the mayor of the palace; but on account of his incontinence and crimes he was driven from the kingdom, and Theodoric was shut up in a monastery together with his Ebroin. Childeric, his brother, who had been reigning in Austrasia, was summoned and created king. At that time the idle kings gave themselves entirely over to the mayors of the palace and secretly indulged in pleasures; they appeared in public only on the first of May, with pomp and royal display. Almost Paris and Neustria was the kingdom, and all their territories; the rest of Gaul was in dispute, with very many revolting from their rule, while the chief power of affairs was in the hands of the mayors of the palace, whose power lasted until Pepin, that is, for nearly a hundred years. Clotaire lived, after succeeding his father in the kingdom, for four years, more adorned with the royal name than acting as king, as also were nearly all those up to Pepin. He died leaving no children. Aemilius, book 1; Gagnier, book 3.

units.la: CHILDERICVS, huius nominis secundus accersitus ex Austrasia, vti dictum est, creatur Rex, in locum Theodorici prædicti anno mundi 4629. à Christo nato 667.
units.tr: CHILDERIC, the second of that name, summoned from Austrasia, as has been said, was made king in place of the aforementioned Theodoric, in the year of the world 4629, from the birth of Christ 667.

units.la: Crudelis hic in suos, insignem virum Bodillum, palo alligatum flagris cædi iubet. Bodillus in vindictam inter venādum Regem adortus eum occidit 12. regnante annum, atque vnà cum eo Reginam Blitildem, vterum feretem. Sepultus est ad fanum D. Germani à pratis. Consulito autores quos supra. R. FRAN. 15 THEODORICVS R. FRAN. 16 CLODOVEVS
units.tr: He was cruel towards his own people: he ordered the distinguished man Bodillus to be tied to a stake and beaten with rods. Bodillus, in revenge, attacked the king while hunting and killed him, in the twelfth year of his reign, and together with him Queen Blitilda, who was pregnant. He was buried at the church of Saint Germain-des-Prés. Consult the authors cited above. FRANKISH KINGS: 15, THEODORIC; 16, CLODOVEUS.

units.la: THEODORICVS, huius nominis primus,ac Francorum Rex decimusquintus,qui iam post Clotariū tertium, ferè annum regnarat,& ob scelera in monasterium detrusus fuerat, perempto Childerico, è monastica vita revocatus,à Francis in solium reponitur,anno mundi 4641. à Christo nato 679. Lendesius,Ercembaldi filius,Magister equitum creatur. Ebroinus, tandē relicto monachatu,ingenti sceleratorum manu collecta, inopinātes hostes magna celeritate opprimit.Gaza capta, Rex ægrè effugit initiō:mòxq; se Ebroino cōmittit, Magistro equitum ab se dicto, & periculorū socio:medio in colloquio trucidatur Lendesius ab Ebroino. Ita sublato adversario, Ebroinus unus rebus, Regíque præest:sæuítq; in eos quos sibi in calamitate insultasse sentit,nec dignitati,nec sanctitati cuiusquā parcit. Pipini dein,& Martini,fratrū, Austrasianorū Ducum acies fundit Ebroinus,contráq; fidem datam Martinum occidit.tandémque occiditur ipse,ab Ermēfredo in Martini ultionē. Moritur Rex anno regni 14.qui à Pipino victus, fugatúsque fuerat ante paucos annos:tum Pipinus Palatij curā suscipiēs,multum res Francorum auxit. Vide Gag. lib. 3. Æmy.lib.1.Rex Atrebatibus sepelitur in D.Vedasti æde.
units.tr: THEODORIC, the first of that name, and the fifteenth king of the Franks, who, after Clotaire the third, had reigned for nearly a year already, and because of his crimes had been thrust into a monastery, was recalled from monastic life when Childeric had been killed, and was restored to the throne by the Franks, in the year of the world 4641, from the birth of Christ 679. Lendesius, son of Ercembald, was created mayor of the palace. Ebroin, at last giving up the monastic life, gathered a great band of criminals and with great speed crushed the unsuspecting enemies. Gaza was taken; the king at first barely escaped, but soon he entrusted himself to Ebroin, the mayor of the palace he had named and his companion in dangers: in the midst of a conference Lendesius was butchered by Ebroin. Thus, with his opponent removed, Ebroin alone ruled affairs and the king; and he raged against those whom he felt had insulted him in his distress, sparing neither dignity nor holiness of anyone. Then Ebroin routed the army of Pepin and Martin, brothers and dukes of the Austrasians, and contrary to the pledge given he killed Martin. At last he himself was killed by Ermenfred in revenge for Martin. The king died in the fourteenth year of his reign; he had been defeated by Pepin and put to flight a few years before. Then Pepin, taking up the care of the palace, greatly increased the power of the Franks. See Gagnier, book 3; Aemilius, book 1. The king was buried at Arras in the church of Saint Vedastus.

units.la: CLODOVEVS,huius nominis tertius,Francorum Rex 16.succedit patri Theodorico anno mundi 4655.à Christo nato 693. Hic brevis æui,moriens post annos quatuor,fratrem suum Childebertum regni successorē habuit. Claret venerabilis Beda.Frisij,Rabodo eorum Duce superato, in Christianismum à Pipino inducūtur:apud quos Vullibrotus,quem nonnulli Clementem Papam vocant,frequētes de Christi verbo conciones habuit,eósque instituit. Vide Chro.Reg.Fran.
units.tr: CLODOVEUS, the third of that name, the sixteenth king of the Franks, succeeds his father Theodoric in the year of the world 4655, from the birth of Christ 693. Short-lived, he died after four years, and left his brother Childebert as successor to the kingdom. The venerable Bede is clear on this. The Frisians, their leader Rabodo having been overcome, were brought to Christianity by Pepin; among them Willibrord, whom some call Pope Clement, gave frequent sermons on the word of Christ and instructed them. See the Chronicle of the Frankish Kings.

units.la: IVSTINIANVS huius nominis secundus, qui etiā Iustinus quartus dicitur, Heraclianæ stirpis vltimus, imperat post patrem anno mundi 4648. à Christo nato 686. hunc pater Constantinus 4. imperij hæredē reliquerat, & fratribus minoribus, ne ad imperium aspirarent, nares absciderat. Praui hic ingenij, synodum aduersus sextam à patre celebratā indixit: aduersantem Papam cōprehendi iussit, quòd hanc synodū minimè probarer. Bellum in Arabas & Bulgaros cōtra fœdus mouit, vtrunque infeliciter gessit. Ammirathus Saracenorū Rex cum eo fœdus icit, Africámque restituit. Tum crudelitate in suos inuisior factus, imperio deturbatur anno imperij 10. & relegatur Chersonā, nare prius abscissa: opera Bulgarorum post annos sex restitutus in hostes sæuit: Tiberiū qui Leoncio successerat, fugat: Callinicum exoculat: ac quoties truncas nares mungit, vnū aliquem ex iis qui Leontio fauerāt trucidat. Post annos sex restitutionis, Chersonā euertere studens, à Philippico, quem exilio dānauerat cum Tiberio filio, bello superatur, & occiditur. Egn. lib. 2. Pau. Diac. lib. 8. Ab. Vrsper.
units.tr: JUSTINIAN, the second of that name, who is also called Justinus the Fourth, the last of the Heraclian line, reigns after his father in the year of the world 4648, from the birth of Christ 686. His father Constantine the Fourth had left him as heir to the empire, and had cut off the noses of his younger brothers, lest they aspire to the throne. Of a depraved disposition, he called a synod against the Sixth, which his father had celebrated; he ordered the Pope who opposed him to be arrested, because he did not approve of this synod. He waged war against the Arabs and Bulgarians contrary to the treaty, and conducted both unsuccessfully. Ammirathus, king of the Saracens, made a treaty with him and restored Africa. Then, having become more hated for his cruelty towards his own people, he was deposed from the empire in the tenth year of his reign and relegated to Cherson, his nose having first been cut off. Through the work of the Bulgarians, after six years he was restored, and raged against his enemies: he drove out Tiberius, who had succeeded Leontius; he gouged out the eyes of Callinicus; and as often as he wiped his mutilated nose, he butchered one of those who had favoured Leontius. After six years of his restoration, while trying to overthrow Cherson, he was defeated in war by Philippicus, whom he had condemned to exile together with Tiberius his son, and he was killed. Egnatius, book 2; Paulus Diaconus, book 8; Abbot Ursperg.

units.la: LEONTIVS, qui & Leo secundus, adnitente Callinico Patriarcha Constātinopolitano, Iustinianum imperium deturbat, imperiúmque inuadit, anno mundi 4658. à Christo nato 696. itaque ab Heraclio, qui Phocā occidit, in vna gente imperatum est annis plus 80. quod vix vlli priorum contigit: fuit Iustinianus sextus continua serie ab Heraclio Imperator, traditūmque est imperium velut per manus Heraclianæ stirpi, quæ defecit in hoc Iustiniano. Porrò Leontius itidem cum infecta re ab expeditione Africana rediret imperio pellitur à Tiberio Absimaro, post annos tres, nasóque mutilatur, & in carcerem truditur. Egna. lib. 2. Diac. lib. 8.
units.tr: LEONTIUS, who is also called Leo the Second, with the support of Callinicus, Patriarch of Constantinople, overthrows Justinian, seizes the empire, in the year of the world 4658, from the birth of Christ 696. Thus from Heraclius, who killed Phocas, the empire was held by one family for more than 80 years, which scarcely happened to any of the earlier emperors. Justinian was the sixth emperor in unbroken succession from Heraclius, and the empire was passed on, as it were, from hand to hand within the Heraclian line, which came to an end with this Justinian. Afterwards Leontius, returning from the African expedition with the business unaccomplished, was likewise driven from the throne by Tiberius Absimarus after three years, had his nose cut off, and was thrust into prison. Egnatius, book 2; Diaconus, book 8.

units.la: ABSIMARVS,qui & Tiberius tertius,ab exercitu Imperator eligitur,cum Leontius ingëti classe parata aduersus Arabas Africam occupantes,infecta re rediret,anno mundi 4661. à Christo nato 699. Hic Arabas,opera fratris,repressit. Philippicum nobilitatis præcipuæ Chersonā relegauit, quòd aquila caput obumbrasse videbatur Philippico dormienti.Cæterùm septimo post anno,reuerso tandem Iustiniano,qui pulsus fuerat, ab eóq; captus, vnà cum Leontio interimitur:calcato prius eorum collo,à Iustiniano in solio sedente,vniuersáque plebe clamante : Super aspidem & basilicum ambulasti,& leonem, draconémque conculcasti. id etiā fecit Papa Friderico primo, vt infra dicetur. Vide Ab. Vrsper.Egna.lib.2.Diac.lib.8.
units.tr: ABSIMARUS, who is also called Tiberius the Third, was chosen emperor by the army, when Leontius, returning with his great fleet prepared against the Arabs who were occupying Africa, had failed in his task, in the year of the world 4661, from the birth of Christ 699. He held the Arabs in check through the work of his brother. He banished Philippicus, a man of the highest nobility, to Cherson, because an eagle seemed to have shadowed his head while Philippicus was asleep. But seven years later, when Justinian, who had been driven out, returned at last, Absimarus was taken by him and executed together with Leontius. Justinian first trampled their necks, while he sat on the throne and the whole populace shouted: "You have walked upon the asp and the basilisk, and have trodden down the lion and the dragon." Pope Frederick the First also did this, as will be said below. See Ab. Ursperg.; Egnatius, book 2; Diaconus, book 8.

units.la: PHILIPPICVS, cognomento Bardanes,quem acriter insectatus fuerat Iustinianus, quémque relegarat Absimarus, vita& imperio Iustinianum,secundò imperantem priuat,prius à se victum:ab exercitu etiā Iustiniani Imperator dicitur, anno mundi 4674. à Christo nato 712. Hic sextæ synodi decreta, altera synodo infirmare cōtendit,gratificaturus monacho, qui imperaturū illum prædixerat,id prædictionis præmium petenti. Huic cum sermonis multū, sapientiæ parum inesset,opésque imperij iampridem congestas dissiparet,passus etiam Bulgaros Thraciā depraedari,post annos ferè duos, ab Anastasio in ordinem redigitur,oculisq; pridie Pentecostes priuatur,& sequenti die Arthemius Imperator designatur. Vide Pau.Diaco.lib.8. Egna.lib.2. FRANC.R.17. CHILDEBERTUS F.REX 18. DAGOBERTUS
units.tr: PHILIPPICUS, surnamed Bardanes, whom Justinian had bitterly persecuted and whom Absimarus had exiled, deprived Justinian, who was emperor for the second time, of his life and rule, having first defeated him. He was also proclaimed emperor by Justinian's own army, in the year of the world 4674, from the birth of Christ 712. He tried to overturn the decrees of the Sixth Synod by another synod, wishing to do a favour to a monk who had foretold that he would become emperor and asked for this as the reward of his prediction. He had much eloquence but little wisdom, and he squandered the imperial wealth that had long been amassed. He also allowed the Bulgarians to plunder Thrace. After about two years he was removed from office by Anastasius and blinded on the day before Pentecost, and on the following day Artemius was appointed emperor. See Paulus Diaconus, book 8; Egnatius, book 2; Franc. R. 17; Childebert, King 18; Dagobert.

units.la: CHILDEBERTUS huius nominis secundus Francorum Rex 17.fratri Clodoueo tertio succedit anno mundi 4659. à Christo nato 697. De huius gestis, quasi nil commendatione vel memoria dignum gessisset, nil scriptum reperi. Pipinus regnum administrans, D.Lambertum Traiectetium Episcopum, ab Ebroino, virtutum hoste, sede pulsum, in pristinum locum restituit: qui cum non dubitat Pipinum adulterij arguere, à Dodone pellicis fratre interficitur. percussor & conscij intra annum pereunt.Obiit Pipinus crassus 27. Magisterij anno, cum iam instituisset Austrasianorum ducem Carolum, à viribus Martiis cognomento Martellum, ex Alpaide concubina natum: quem Plectrudis[?] Pipini vidua in carcerem coniicit, sperans cum Theobaldo nepote summa rerum potiri. Anni regni huius Childeberti numerantur 18. Sepultus est apud D. Stephanum in oppido Canciaco. Vide Guag.lib.3.
units.tr: CHILDEBERT the Second of this name, King 17 of the Franks, succeeded his brother Clovis the Third in the year of the world 4659, from the birth of Christ 697. Of his deeds, as though he had done nothing worthy of praise or memory, I have found nothing written. Pepin, governing the kingdom, restored to his former place Bishop Lambert of Utrecht, who had been driven from his see by Ebroin, an enemy of virtue. But when Lambert did not hesitate to accuse Pepin of adultery, he was killed by Dodo, the brother of the mistress. The killer and his accomplices perished within a year. Pepin the Fat died in the twenty-seventh year of his rule as mayor of the palace, after he had already appointed Charles, surnamed Martel, the duke of the Austrasians, son of the concubine Alpaida, to succeed him. Plectrudis, Pepin's widow, threw Charles into prison, hoping to gain control of the government together with her grandson Theobald. The years of this Childebert's reign are counted as 18. He was buried at St. Stephen's in the town of Quierzy. See Guaguin, book 3.

units.la: DAGOBERTUS, huius nominis secundus, qui & Clodoueus à Sigiberto dicitur, succedit patri Childeberto anno mundi 4677. à Christo nato 715 In Francia tunc maxima fuit rerum perturbatio, quousque genus hoc regum extingueretur, & regni administratio ad Martelli familiam deuolueretur. Theobaldus Magister equitum Dagoberti, & Ramanfredus Magister equitum Chilperici prœliantur acerrime ad syluam Cociam. Theobaldus multis suorum millibus prostratis effugit. Interea obiit Dagobertus anno regni sui quarto: quo mortuo, à victoribus Rex salutatur Chilpericus, quem Austrasiani dicebant Danielem vocatum monachum,in coenobio adolefcentiam egisse. Pau. Æmy.lib.1.
units.tr: DAGOBERT the Second of this name, who is also called Clovis by Sigebert, succeeded his father Childebert in the year of the world 4677, from the birth of Christ 715. In France at that time there was great upheaval, until this line of kings was extinguished and the government of the kingdom passed to the family of Martel. Theobald, master of the horse to Dagobert, and Ramanfred, master of the horse to Chilperic, fought very fiercely at the Cotian forest. Theobald, after many thousands of his men had been struck down, escaped. Meanwhile Dagobert died in the fourth year of his reign. When he died, the victors hailed Chilperic as king, whom the Austrasians used to call Daniel, saying that he had spent his youth as a monk in a monastery. See Paulus Aemilius, book 1.

units.la: ARTEMIVS, qui & Anastasius secundus, ab exercitu Imperator creatus, in Philippicum, uti dictum est, insurrexit, regno oculisque eum priuauit, nec tamen occidit. Hic imperium adeptus est anno mundi 4676. à Christo nato 714. Cum optime quæ ad pietatem attinent instituisset, classem ingentē aduersus Arabes in Alexandriam misit. Verùm classiarij quidam contumacius agentes, qui illum oderant, domum reuersi, Theodosium ignobilem alioqui virum Imperatorem creant: captaque Constantinopoli, monasterio Anastasium includunt, annos tres Imperantem. Vide Pau. Diac. lib. 8. Egna. lib. 2. Ab. Vrsp.
units.tr: ARTEMIUS, who is also called Anastasius the Second, was created emperor by the army. As has been said, he rose against Philippicus, deprived him of his kingdom and his eyes, but did not kill him. He obtained the empire in the year of the world 4676, from the birth of Christ 714. Having organized matters of piety very well, he sent a great fleet against the Arabs at Alexandria. But some of the sailors, acting more stubbornly, who hated him, returned home and created Theodosius, a man otherwise of no distinction, emperor. They captured Constantinople and shut Anastasius up in a monastery; he had reigned for three years. See Paulus Diaconus, book 8; Egnatius, book 2; Abbas Ursperg.

units.la: THEODOSIVS Atramitenus coactus à militibus sumpsit imperium, anno mundi 4679. à Christo nato 717. Hic ad Niceam graui prælio Artemium vicit: obscuro licet loco natus, non pœnitedum Imperatore egisset, si diutius illi per Leonem & Cononem, Orietis præfectos, imperare licuisset. Verùm cùm Leonem exercitus Imperatorem dixisset, pertæsus belli ciuilis Theodosius cessit imperio, monasticam vitam amplexatus. Vide Diac. lib. 8. Egna. lib. 2. Ab Vrsper. hic annum imperat.
units.tr: THEODOSIUS Atramyttenus, compelled by the soldiers, took up the empire in the year of the world 4679, from the birth of Christ 717. He defeated Artemius in a severe battle at Nicaea. Though born in an obscure place, he would not have repented of having ruled as emperor, had he been allowed to rule longer through Leo and Conon, prefects of the East. But when the army proclaimed Leo emperor, Theodosius, weary of civil war, gave up the empire and embraced the monastic life. See Diaconus, book 8; Egnatius, book 2; Abbas Ursperg. He reigned for one year.

units.la: LEO Isaurus sceleratus, imperat post Theodosiū. huius temporibus Saraceni triénali obsidione terra mariq; Constantinopolim obsident: verùm peste fameque cōfecti, à Bulgaris etiam sæpe victi, classe magna ex parte igne sub aquis ardēte cōsumpta, numinis iram sensere: nec minori interim clade in urbe sæuitum, trecenta & amplius ciuium millia peste fameque consumpta sunt. Hic, in gratia duorum Iudæorum, imagines sanctorum deiecit atque incendit. imperauit annis 24. Vide Diac. lib. 8. Egna. lib. 2. REX 19. CLOTARIVS REX FRAN. 20. CHILPERICVS
units.tr: LEO the Isaurian, a wicked man, reigned after Theodosius. In his time the Saracens besieged Constantinople by land and sea for three years. But worn down by plague and famine, and often defeated by the Bulgarians, and with a great part of their fleet destroyed by fire burning under the water, they felt the anger of the divine power. Meanwhile no less a slaughter raged in the city, and three hundred thousand citizens and more were consumed by plague and famine. This emperor, at the instigation of two Jews, pulled down and burned the images of the saints. He reigned for 24 years. See Diaconus, book 8; Egnatius, book 2. KING 19. CLOTAIRE, KING OF THE FRANKS 20. CHILPERIC.

units.la: CLOTARIVS, huius nominis quartus, Francorum Rex extitit. Nam cum Carolus Martellus è custodia nouercæ Pleftrudis elapsus esset, Chilpericum Danielē, Regem à morte Dagoberti statim creatum, persequitur, & magna tandem clade castigat ad Vinciacum Samarobrinesium iterumque eundem cum Eudone Aquitaniæ duce, quem in auxilium aduocarat Chilpericus, fugat: & Ramanfredum Andegaui assequitur. Tunc Martellus Regem salutat Clotarium quendam (nonnulli scribunt fuisse Dagoberti secundi fratrem, alij autem auunculum aut patruum) qui annos duos regnat: sepultus Cāciaci cum Childeberto & Dagoberto.
units.tr: CLOTAIRE, the Fourth of this name, was King of the Franks. For when Charles Martel had escaped from the custody of his stepmother Plectrudis, he pursued Chilperic Daniel, who had been made king immediately after the death of Dagobert, and at last punished him with a great defeat at Vinci near Samarobriva, and again put to flight that same man together with Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, whom Chilperic had called in as an ally. He also overtook Ramanfred at Angers. Then Martel hailed as king a certain Clotaire (some write that he was a brother of Dagobert the Second, others that he was an uncle or a paternal uncle), who reigned for two years. He was buried at Quierzy with Childebert and Dagobert.

units.la: CHILPERICVS huius nominis secundus, Francorum Rex vicesimus, qui antea & Daniel vocatus & monachus fuisse dicitur, siue vera Clodouei magni soboles, siue falsa, mortuo Clotario, ex Vasconia à Martello reuocatur: quē reddidit Eudo cum parte gazæ. Vt venit Chilpericus, Regem sibi facit eum Martellus anno mundi 4683. à Christo nato 721. regnat Chilpericus hic, qui & Daniel, annos quinque, deinde moritur, & sepelitur Nouioduni. Vide Chro. Regum Francorum.
units.tr: CHILPERIC the Second of this name, the twentieth King of the Franks, who is said earlier to have been called Daniel and to have been a monk, whether a true offspring of Clovis the Great or a false one, was recalled from Gascony by Martel after the death of Clotaire; Eudo gave him back together with part of the treasure. When Chilperic came, Martel made him king, in the year of the world 4683, from the birth of Christ 721. This Chilperic, who was also called Daniel, reigned five years, then died and was buried at Noyon. See the Chronicle of the Kings of the Franks.

units.la: CAROLVS Martellus,gloriæ suæ augendæ, opibúsque Francorum tutandis incumbens,Saxones, arma parátes finitimósque solicitantes,antequā maius exoriretur bellum,ad ossicium redire cogit,Bauaros debellat. Alemanis vi armorū perterritis recipit,reducítq; Plectrudem vnà cum Sonichilde eius neptc,quæ profugerat illuc,sibi à Martello metuentes. Interea Eudo Aquitaniæ Dux multa hostilia in Francos ausus est. Celerius omniū opinione reuersus Martellus, primùm omniū conuentū vniuersæ Fraciæ habuit:ab eoq; iam non Magisterequitum,sed altiore fastigio princeps Francorum salutatus est,anno mundi 4686.à Christo nato 724.Tum noua nominis nobilitate inclytus,Aquitanicum bellum suscipit,aduersus Eudonem qui Saracenos ex Africa exciuerat:quo in bello ad 370000.barbarorum cecidere:ex Francis 1500.tātum.exteri rerū scriptores de nobis hoc literis prodiderūt,cum magna lætitiæ significatione quòd gens legis ac religionis tam impiæ,penè occidione occiderit. Obiit Martellus Carisiaci ad Isaram:conditus in Mausoleo Dionysiaco in ordine Regum. Clotarium quartum vt dixi, Martellus Regem creauit,deinde Danielē Chilpericum vocatum,postea Theodoricum secundum. Vide Æmy.li.2.Gag.li.3.
units.tr: CHARLES MARTEL, intent on increasing his glory and on defending the riches of the Franks, compelled the Saxons, who were preparing arms and stirring up their neighbours, to return to their duty before a greater war broke out, and defeated the Bavarians. The Alemanni, terrified by the force of arms, he received back, and he brought back Plectrudis together with her granddaughter Sonichild, who had fled there, fearing Martel for themselves. Meanwhile Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, dared many hostile acts against the Franks. Martel returned more quickly than anyone expected, and first of all held an assembly of the whole of France. From then on he was hailed as prince of the Franks, no longer as master of the horse but at a higher height of dignity, in the year of the world 4686, from the birth of Christ 724. Then, made famous by the new distinction of his name, he undertook the war in Aquitaine against Eudo, who had driven the Saracens out of Africa. In that war about 370,000 barbarians fell, and only 1,500 of the Franks. Foreign writers of history have recorded this in their books with great signs of joy, because a nation of such impious law and religion had been nearly wiped out. Martel died at Quierzy on the Oise and was buried in the Mausoleum of St. Denis among the kings. As I said, Martel made Clotaire the Fourth king, then Daniel, called Chilperic, afterwards Theodoric the Second. See Aemilius, book 2; Gaguin, book 3.

units.la: THEODORICVS secundus,Dagoberti item secundi filius, post Chilpericum qui & Daniel dictus est,apud Francos imperat anno mundi 4688. à Christo nato 726. Huic fuit cognomentum Cala, qui in cœnobio, educatus fuit: imperauit Martelli opera, nec præter nomen, regium quicquam habuit, cum summa rerum,penes vnicum principem Martellum esset: qui,hoc rege,Abdiramam,atque Athinum,Saracenorum Reges, variis præliis strenuè debellauit. Obiit Theodoricus hic, anno regni 15. (eodem anno etiam obiit Martellus.) atque in æde D.Dionysij sepultus est. Vide vt supra. FRAN.R.22 CHILDERICVS F.REX 23 PIPINVS
units.tr: THEODORIC the Second, likewise son of Dagobert the Second, after Chilperic who was also called Daniel, reigned among the Franks in the year of the world 4688, from the birth of Christ 726. He had the surname Cala, and was brought up in a monastery. He reigned through the work of Martel and had nothing royal beyond his name, since the whole government lay in the hands of one prince, Martel, who, while this king was on the throne, vigorously subdued in various battles Abdirrahman and Anthymus, kings of the Saracens. This Theodoric died in the fifteenth year of his reign (in the same year Martel also died) and was buried in the church of St. Denis. See as above.

units.la: CHILDERICVS, huius nominis tertius, dictus stupidus,ob ignauiā, fratri suo Theodorico secūdo supradicto,succedit in regno Franciae anno mundi 4703. à Christo nato 741. hoc principe,Gripho hæreditate Martelli patris priuatus,Laudunum arce belli occupauerat,mox fratribus in fide se permittere cogitur. Carolomanus eius frater Roma rediens, abiectis omnibus fortunis,in cœnobium secessit:deinde in monte Cassinum migrauit,tonsu,habituq; monachi.Childericus anno regni nono,cum regio nomine indignus ac solij dehonestamentum videretur,opera Pipini consilióque Zachariæ, Pontificis, regno pellitur:conuentu præterea habito,mira procerum consensione Pipinus ipse salutatur Rex:Childericus fit monachus. Vide Æmy.lib.2.Chroni.Reg.Franc.Gag.lib.3.defecit primum in hoc Childerico masculea Regum Francorum progenies.
units.tr: CHILDERICUS, the third of that name, called the Simple (stupidus) on account of his sloth, succeeded his brother Theodoric the Second, mentioned above, in the kingdom of France in the year of the world 4703, from the birth of Christ 741. In this prince's reign Grifo, deprived of the inheritance of his father Martel, had seized the citadel of Laon by force of arms, but was soon compelled to entrust himself to his brothers in good faith. Carloman, his brother, returning from Rome, abandoned all his fortunes and withdrew to a monastery; then he moved to Monte Cassino, where he took the tonsure and the monk's habit. In the ninth year of his reign Childeric, who seemed unworthy of the royal name and a disgrace to the throne, was driven from the kingdom through the efforts of Pipin and the counsel of Zacharias, the Pontiff. Moreover, an assembly having been held, Pipin himself was hailed as king by the remarkable agreement of the nobles, and Childeric became a monk. See Aimoin, book 2; Chronicle of the Kings of the Franks; Gaguin, book 3. In Childeric the male line of the kings of the Franks first failed.

units.la: PIPINVS Breuis, Francorum Rex dicitur anno mundi 4712. à Christo nato 750. Pipini præsidium contra Aistulfum Longobardorum Regem Papa implorat:coscripto exercitu Pipinus Italiā intrat: Aistulfum Papiæ obsidet, atque ad deditionem cogit. Papæ exarchatum Rauennatem dono dat, monitis etiā Constantini Copronymi Imperatoris neglectis. Vide Blon. lib.1.Dec.2.Æmy.li.2. Aistulfus Longobardorum Rex inter venandum obiit. Rex Pipinus Parlamentū in Frācia instituit:Pariliis[?] obiit anno regni 18. relictis filiis Regibus, Carolo Magno & Carolomano:succedit ei in Franciae regno Carolus Magnus anno mundi 4730. à Christo nato 768. qui imperat Romae anno mundi 4763. de quo,vt Imperatore,suo loco meminerimus: à Pharamundo ad Pipinum sunt anni 331. à Meroueo 302. à Clodoueo Christiano 252. IMP. CONSTANTINVS P.F. AVG. IIII[?] IMPERATOR LEO III P.F. AVG.[?]
units.tr: PIPIN the Short, is said to be king of the Franks in the year of the world 4712, from the birth of Christ 750. The Pope implores Pipin's protection against Aistulf, king of the Lombards. Pipin, having raised an army, enters Italy, besieges Aistulf at Pavia and forces him to surrender. He gives the exarchate of Ravenna to the Pope as a gift, the admonitions of the emperor Constantine Copronymus being disregarded as well. See Blondus, book 1, Decade 2; Aimoin, book 2. Aistulf, king of the Lombards, died while hunting. King Pipin instituted a parliament in France. He died at Paris in the eighteenth year of his reign, leaving behind sons who were kings, Charlemagne and Carloman. Charles the Great succeeded him in the kingdom of France in the year of the world 4730, from the birth of Christ 768; he ruled at Rome in the year of the world 4763, of whom we shall speak in his place as emperor. From Pharamond to Pipin are 331 years; from Merovech 302; from Clovis the Christian 252.

units.la: CONSTANTINVS huius nominis quintus Leonis Isauri filius, impio patri scelestissima proles succedit, imperatq; Constantinopoli anno mundi 4704. à Christo nato 742. Hic dictus est Copronymus, quòd infans dum baptizatur, ventrem purgat. Sanctorum imagines non tantùm, sed & reliquias aut contemnit, aut comburit: nobilissimum quenq; è medio tollit. Constantinopolitanos antistites duos grauiter excruciatos capite plectit. Bulgaricum, variante fortuna, bellum, terra marìque gerit. Artabasdum Imperatorem creatum oculorum vsu cum liberis priuat. Grauissimam hyemem, vti Pontus, Bosphorúsq; Thracius perglaciauerit expertus, post infinita flagitia exquisitissimo cruciatu, nempe lepra consumptus, obiit anno imperij 35. Consulito Egna. lib.2.
units.tr: CONSTANTINE the Fifth of that name, son of Leo the Isaurian, a most wicked offspring succeeded his impious father and ruled at Constantinople in the year of the world 4704, from the birth of Christ 742. He was called Copronymus because, as an infant during his baptism, he defiled the font. He not only despised but also burned the images of the saints, and even their relics; he removed the most noble men from the midst of the people. He had two bishops of Constantinople severely tortured and beheaded. He waged war against the Bulgarians, by land and sea, with changing fortune. He deprived Artabasdus, who had been made emperor, of his sight, together with his children. Having experienced a most severe winter, when the Black Sea and the Thracian Bosporus were frozen solid, after countless crimes he died, consumed by leprosy, in the thirty-fifth year of his reign, after the most exquisite torment. Consult Zonaras? See Egnatius, book 2.

units.la: LEO quartus, succedit patri Constantino Copronymo anno mundi 4739. à Christo nato 777. Hic paterni sceleris atque imperij hæres extitit, idque minimè assentiente matre, pia quidem ac proba muliere. Coronam à Mauricio principe Deo dicatam, nefario capiti imponēs, captus gemmarū & auri splendore, breui pœnas luit. In Saracenos, Syriam inhabitantes, imperium fecit. Imperauit annos quinque, relinquens ex Irene coniuge, proba, & speciosa, filium Constantinum, qui post patrem imperat. Vide Egna. lib.2..
units.tr: LEO the Fourth succeeded his father Constantine Copronymus in the year of the world 4739, from the birth of Christ 777. He became the heir of his father's crime and of his rule, and this without the approval of his mother, a truly pious and upright woman. Placing on his wicked head the crown dedicated to God by the emperor Maurice, and captivated by the splendour of the jewels and gold, he soon paid the penalty. He waged war on the Saracens who inhabited Syria. He reigned five years, leaving from his wife Irene, a virtuous and beautiful woman, a son Constantine, who reigned after his father. See Egnatius, book 2.

units.la: CONSTANTINVS, huius nominis sextus, succedit patri, Leoni quarto, imperatq; cum matre apud Constantinopolim, anno mundi 4744. à Christo nato 782. Hic & mater eius, persuasi consilio Therasij Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani, septimam synodum in Nicea urbe 350. Episcoporum celebrarunt, in qua sanctorum imagines templis restitutę sunt. Nec multò post tamen, Constantinus iam adultus, matre haud amplius passus imperare, imperio deiicit, eiectâmque in ordinē redigit. Nicephorum, in quę suffragia multorum tacitè inclinabant, oculorum & linguæ vsu priuat. Et ne quid sceleris deesset, Maria vxore monasterio obtrusa, quæ filia erat Caroli magni, Theodoram concubinam superinduxit: idque etiam matris consilio, vt filium inuisum omnibus faceret: vnde mox rerum sola potita, filium in potestatem redactum excæcat. Consulito Blondum & Baptistam Egna. lib.2.
units.tr: CONSTANTINE, the sixth of that name, succeeded his father Leo the Fourth, and ruled together with his mother at Constantinople, in the year of the world 4744, from the birth of Christ 782. He and his mother, at the urging of Tarasius, Patriarch of Constantinople, celebrated the seventh synod at the city of Nicaea, with 350 bishops, in which the images of the saints were restored to the temples. Not long afterwards, however, Constantine, now grown up, no longer willing to suffer his mother to rule, deposed her from power and reduced her to a private station. He deprived Nicephorus, toward whom the votes of many secretly inclined, of the use of his eyes and tongue. And lest any crime be lacking, he thrust his wife Maria, who was a daughter of Charlemagne, into a monastery, and took in Theodora as a concubine, and this also on the advice of his mother, in order to make her son hateful to everyone. Thereupon she alone seized the government, and when her son had been brought under her power, she blinded him. Consult Blondus and Baptista; Egnatius, book 2.

units.la: IRENE, Attici sanguinis mulier, Leonis quarti vxor, atque huius Constantini mater imperauit cum filio puero admodum, annis nouem: deinde à filio deiicitur. Verùm exacto circiter anno deiectionis septimo, iterum, sed sola quatuor annos imperat. Postea à Nicephoro pulsa, in Lesbum insulam relegatur. Hac principe, Carolus Magnus à Leone tertio huius nominis Romano Pontifice, Imperij Romani corona donatur, virtutis ac pietatis gratia. Vide Egna. lib.2.
units.tr: IRENE, a woman of Athenian blood, wife of Leo the Fourth and mother of this Constantine, ruled together with her son, who was a mere boy, for nine years; then she was deposed by her son. Indeed, after about seven years of deposition, she again ruled for four years, but alone. Afterwards, driven out by Nicephorus, she was banished to the island of Lesbos. Under this empress, Charlemagne was crowned with the Roman imperial crown by Leo the Third, Roman Pontiff, on account of his virtue and piety. See Egnatius, book 2.

units.la: NICEPHORVS Patricius, relegata Irene, Constantinopolitanum imperiũ invadit anno mundi 4764. à Christo nato 802. Hic fœdus cum Carolo magno icit. Nemo maiore opinione hominum ad imperium venit, dum singulos aut muliebris impotentiæ, aut flagitiosi principis tædet: nemo tamen avarius aut crudelius administravit: quorũ scelerum mox pœnas meritas luit. A Bulgaris enim paulò ante à se victis, improviso noctis assultu oppressus, ipse cum toto exercitu ad internecionem cæditur. Stauracius filius saucius evadit, qui cum patre imperarat, & post patrem Imperator ab amicis salutatus, non multò post à Michaële Curoplate, qui sororem eius in vxorem duxerat, imperio deturbatur, & monasterio includitur. Vide Blon. lib.2. Egn. lib. 2. Stauracius in hac Imperatorum serie minimè à nobis inseritur, quòd paucis diebus post Nicephorum patrem imperitarit.
units.tr: NICEPHORUS the Patrician, after Irene was banished, seized the imperial power of Constantinople in the year of the world 4764, from the birth of Christ 802. He made an alliance with Charlemagne. No one came to the throne with greater popular esteem, since people were weary of each one either through the weakness of a woman or the shamefulness of a prince; yet no one governed more avariciously or cruelly, and soon he paid the deserved penalty for these crimes. For, having been attacked by surprise at night by the Bulgarians, whom he had conquered shortly before, he himself was cut down with his whole army to the last man. His son Staurakios escaped wounded; he had ruled together with his father, and after his father was hailed emperor by his friends, but not long afterwards he was thrown from power by Michael Kouropalates, who had married his sister, and was shut up in a monastery. See Blondus, book 2; Egnatius, book 2. Staurakios is in no way included by us in this series of emperors, since he ruled for only a few days after his father Nicephorus.

units.la: MICHAEL Curoplates, Rangabe cognomento, imperarat, qua dixi via, Constantinopoli anno mundi 4773. à Christo nato 811. hic melior pacis artibus & pietate, quàm bellicis rebus administrandis, ad unam adversam cum Bulgaris pugnam, ita deiecit animũ, ut accepto nuntio de Leonis imperio, qui post eum Constantinopoli imperat, monasterio sese abdiderit: habenas imperij facilè relinquens post annum alterum imperij. Hic quemadmodum Nicephorus, legaris ad Carolum magnum missis pacem fecit, hac conditione ut Veneti suis legibus ac iure viverent: immunitate his servata, quam ad eam diem retinuerant. Egn.lib.2.
units.tr: MICHAEL Kouropalates, called Rangabe, had ruled, by the way I have described, at Constantinople in the year of the world 4773, from the birth of Christ 811. He, better at the arts of peace and in piety than at managing warlike affairs, was so discouraged by a single unfortunate battle with the Bulgarians that, on receiving news of the rule of Leo, who afterwards ruled at Constantinople, he hid himself in a monastery, easily relinquishing the reins of empire after the second year of his reign. He, like Nicephorus, made peace with Charlemagne through envoys sent to him, on condition that the Venetians should live under their own laws and right, with the immunity they had retained until that day preserved for them. Egnatius, book 2.

units.la: LEO Armenius, huius nominis Constantinopolis Imperator quintus, ac post Carolum magnum Romanorum Imperatorem, quartus à Nicephoro, dum in oriente Michaëlis supradicti Imperatoris Duce agit, ad imperium aspirans seditione in exercitu excitat, factúsque est à militibus Imperator ann. mun. 4775. à Christo nato 813. hic vbi regiâ ingressus est, Michaëlis filium abscissis genitalibus in exilium misit. victoriam de Bulgaris retulit, Thraciâ recuperauit, quàm plurimos hostes cepit, repressitque eorum audaces conatus, qui iam Adrianopoli potiti, in Constantinopolim arma meditabatur. Diuorum imagines quas sustulerat ipse, cum nollet restituere, noctu per insidias dū sacris operatur, in ipso templo ab imaginum cultoribus capite truncatur, ac multis confoditur vulneribus, anno imperij octauo: vxor in monasterium truditur, filij in exilium pelluntur. Vide Egn. lib.2. ac Cosmographiam Munsteri lib.4. & Blond.
units.tr: LEO the Armenian, the fifth emperor of that name at Constantinople, and, after Charlemagne the Roman emperor, the fourth from Nicephorus, while serving as general in the East under the aforementioned emperor Michael, aspiring to the throne, stirred up a revolt in the army, and was made emperor by the soldiers in the year of the world 4775, from the birth of Christ 813. When he entered the palace, he sent Michael's son into exile after having cut off his genitals. He won a victory over the Bulgarians, recovered Thrace, captured very many enemies, and checked the bold attempts of those who, having already taken Adrianople, were planning to attack Constantinople with arms. Since he refused to restore the images of the saints which he himself had removed, he was attacked by night through an ambush while performing sacred rites in the very temple, and was beheaded by worshippers of images, and pierced with many wounds, in the eighth year of his reign; his wife was thrust into a monastery, and his sons were driven into exile. See Egnatius, book 2; and Münster's Cosmography, book 4; and Blondus.

units.la: MICHAEL Balbus prauissimis moribus imbutus, qúeque Leonē prædictum confoderat, imperat Constantinopoli anno mundi 4783. à Christo nato 821. Hic humili ac sordido loco natus, Thomam virum quidem obscurum, qui tyrannidē inuaserat, vario primùm rerum euentu aggressus, tandem oppressit: cùm prius eò desperationis deductus esset, vt ex arce Constantini ad Peram, oppidulum, ferreā catenā produxisset. Itaque traditum sibi Thomā, qui Adrianopolim se receperat, manibus pedibúsq; truncauit, multisque cruciatibus affectum, tandè iugulauit. Saraceni hoc principe Cretam occupant, totámq; ferè in ditionē redigunt, Græcos duplici vincunt prælio. Obiit Michaël vētris profluuio anno imperij nono. Vetus oraculum innotuit, tum rem Romanam ruitura, cùm & Balbus & auarissimus princeps imperaret. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: MICHAEL the Stammerer, imbued with the most depraved morals, who had stabbed the aforementioned Leo, ruled at Constantinople in the year of the world 4783, from the birth of Christ 821. Born of a humble and squalid station, he first attacked Thomas, a man indeed obscure, who had usurped the tyranny, with varying fortune, and at last overcame him; although previously he had been driven to such despair that he had drawn an iron chain from the citadel of Constantine to Pera, a small town. Accordingly, having seized Thomas, who had withdrawn to Adrianople, he cut off his hands and feet, and after subjecting him to many tortures, at last cut his throat. The Saracens under this prince occupied Crete and reduced almost the whole of it to their dominion, and they defeated the Greeks in a twofold battle. Michael died of a flux of the bowels in the ninth year of his reign. An ancient oracle became known: "The Roman affair will be ruined when both Balbus and a most avaricious prince rule." See above.

units.la: CAROLVS-MAGNVS, Francorum Rex, vicesimus quartus, scito Romani populi, clerique rogatu, Romanorum Imperator dicitur, ob egregia in Christianum nomen, & Romanæ sedem merita: inunctúsque cum Pipino filio à Papa Leone tertio Augustus consecratur, anno mundi 4762. à Christo nato 800. acclamatúmque est ter à populo Romano: Carolo Augusto à Deo coronato, Magno, & pacifico, vita & victoria. Hic Pipini filius fuit (eius qui huius nominis primus Francorum Rex primus item Christianissimus vocatus est) filiúmq; Pipinum alterum suscepit ex Hildegrāde. Carolus & Nicephorus diuiserunt imperium: hic Orietis, ille Occidetis Imperator est dictus: sub regni initia bello defunctus Aquitanico, Longobardorum regnum, capto eorum Rege, Francico nomini subegit. Saxones sæpe rebellantes, tricenali tandem bello vicit: & vera pietate imbuit, Saracenos, Hispaniam ferè omnem vastantes, intra Beticæ angulum cōpulit. Sclauos, Danos, & Boiarios tumultuantes, in ditionem suam redegit. Hunnicum bellum octauo post anno feliciter cōfecit. Moritur anno ætatis 71. regni 46. imperij 13. obiit febre, atque Aquisgrani sepultus est: vocatus est Magnus à magnanimitate, sicut & ante eum Pompeius & Alexander hoc nomine, magni, donati sunt. Parisiense gymnasium & Papiense viris undique doctis accersitis, instituit: templa diuis erexit: iniurias illatas civili animo tulit: in hostes raro acerbè sæuiit. His meritis ad hæc usque tempora à multis ut cœlitum unus colitur. Æmy.li.2.Egn.lib.3.Ab. Vrsper.lib.4.Hic synodos quinque pro statu ecclesiastico celebrauit.
units.tr: CHARLES THE GREAT, king of the Franks, the twenty-fourth, by the decree of the Roman people and at the request of the clergy, is called Emperor of the Romans, on account of his outstanding services to the Christian name and to the Roman See; and anointed together with his son Pipin, he was consecrated Augustus by Pope Leo the Third, in the year of the world 4762, from the birth of Christ 800, and the Roman people acclaimed him three times: "To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-bringing, life and victory!" He was the son of Pipin (he who was the first king of the Franks of that name and who was also called the first most Christian), and he begot a second son, Pipin, by Hildegard. Charles and Nicephorus divided the empire: the one was called emperor of the East, the other of the West. At the beginning of his reign he finished the war in Aquitaine, and, having captured their king, subdued the kingdom of the Lombards to the Frankish name. The Saxons, who often rebelled, he finally conquered in a war lasting thirty years, and imbued them with true piety; the Saracens, laying waste almost all of Spain, he drove within the corner of Baetica. The Slavs, Danes and Boii, when they stirred up tumults, he reduced to his dominion. He successfully concluded the Hunnish war eight years later. He died at the age of 71, in the forty-sixth year of his reign and the thirteenth of his empire, of a fever, and was buried at Aachen. He was called Great from his magnanimity, just as before him Pompey and Alexander were given the title of Great by this name. He founded the Paris and Pavia academies, having summoned learned men from everywhere; he erected temples to the divine; he bore injuries inflicted on him with a civil spirit; he rarely raged bitterly against enemies. On account of these merits he is worshipped down to our own times by many as one of the heavenly ones. See Aimoin, book 2; Egnatius, book 3; Ab. Urspergensis, book 4. He held five synods for the state of the Church.

units.la: HILDEGRANDIS Sueuæ nobilitatis princeps, Caroli-Magni vxor secunda fuit, ex qua Carolum, Pipinum, & Lodoicum sustulit.
units.tr: HILDEGARD, princess of the Swabian nobility, was the second wife of Charlemagne; by her he had Charles, Pepin and Louis. ## LOUIS THE PIOUS

units.la: LUDOVICUS Pius, patri Carolo Magno succedit, imperátque Romæ & Franciæ anno mundi 4776. à Christo nato 814. à pietate, cognominatus est Pius. Dacicum bellum conficit: nec multò post Bernardũ Pipini fratris filium, in Italia res nouas moliente, capite plectit. Coniurarunt in eum filij eius, & optimates, maximè verò prælati, in quos non alia animaduersione usus est, quàm quòd in monasteria eos intrusit. Synodum habuit in qua uanitates uestium, luxúmq; gemmarũ, & auri & argéti nimia pompa ecclesiasticis sunt interdicta. A filiis tribus imperio præter spé deturbatur, & in cœnobiũ truditur, imperiúmque eiurare cogitur, tàquam in Carolum natu minimum propensior esset, sed tumultuáte optimo quoque, eodem anno restituitur. Lotarius filius in Italiam pedè refert: data fide ad patrem redit, reconciliatur: eíq; pater imperij dignitaté, regníque tribuit coronam. Obiit Ludouicus Maguntiæ anno ætatis 64. imperij 26. in Mediomatricibus sepultus est. Vide Gaguin. li. 4. Egna. lib. 3.
units.tr: Louis the Pious succeeded his father Charlemagne and ruled over Rome and France in the year of the world 4776, from the birth of Christ 814. He was surnamed Pious for his piety. He brought the Dacian war to an end, and not long afterwards he had Bernard, the son of his brother Pepin, beheaded, because Bernard was plotting revolution in Italy. His sons conspired against him, and so did the nobles, and especially the prelates; against these last he took no other punishment than shutting them up in monasteries. He held a synod in which vanity in dress and excessive display of jewels, gold and silver were forbidden to churchmen.
