Deposed from the throne by three of his sons, contrary to all expectation, he was shut up in a monastery and compelled to renounce the empire, as though he had been more inclined towards Charles, the youngest. But with the support of all the best men, he was restored in the same year. His son Lothair marched into Italy on foot; having given his pledge, he returned to his father, was reconciled, and his father granted him the dignity of the empire and the crown of the kingdom. Louis died at Mainz in the 64th year of his life and the 26th of his reign, and was buried in Metz. See Gaguin, book 4; Egnatius, book 3.

units.la: IUDITH Comitis Altorf filia, & Ludouici Pij uxor, suscepit ex eo Carolũ Caluum: hanc Ludouicus Pius maritus repudiauit, ac postea recepit: inde concitati prioris uxoris filij, odiũ in patrem aluerunt: eúmque in monasterium intruserunt. Vide Chronica Regum Francicorum.
units.tr: Judith, daughter of the Count of Altorf and wife of Louis the Pious, bore him Charles the Bald. Her husband Louis the Pious repudiated her, and afterwards took her back again. Thereupon the sons of the former wife, stirred up, nursed hatred against their father and shut him up in a monastery. See the Chronicles of the Kings of the Franks.

units.la: THEOPHILVS Michaëlis Balbi filius, post patrem imperat Constantinopoli anno mundi 4792. à Christo nato 830. Hic erga subditos iustum ac æquum se præstitit, diuorū autem imagines execratus est, eorúmque cultores acriter puniuit, patrem imitatus. Cum Saracenis Asiæ provincias vastantibus, bis congressus, bis victus est, castrísque exutus. Amorium, unde illi genus, ab iis obsessum, ac proditione captum, direptū est. inde ob animi mœrorē ab omni cibo ille abstinēs, solámque aquam frigidam potans, in dysenteriam incidit, qua periit post annum imperij decimumquintum. Vide ut supra, in huius Imperatoris patre.
units.tr: Theophilus, son of Michael the Stammerer, succeeded his father as emperor at Constantinople in the year of the world 4792, from the birth of Christ 830. He showed himself just and fair towards his subjects, but he detested the images of the saints and punished their worshippers harshly, imitating his father. When the Saracens were laying waste the provinces of Asia, he fought them twice and was twice defeated and stripped of his camp. Amorium, his family's home, was besieged by them and taken by treachery and plundered. Thereafter, from grief of mind, he abstained from all food and drank only cold water, fell into dysentery, and died in the fifteenth year of his reign. See above, under this emperor's father.

units.la: MICHAEL Theophili filius, successit patri adhuc infans, & sub tutela matris Theodorae, quae pro filio imperiū administrauit Constantinopolitanum anno mundi 4807. à Christo nato 845. Michaël autem adolescentiam ubi attigit, regni negocia tractare coepit, cefsitq; ei mater. Hic auo quàm patri similior, per ignauiam ac prodigalitate rem afflixit: irruetibus subinde multis bellis, à cursu equorū in quem omne studium collocarat, auocari non potuit. Circēfibus itaque ludis dum plus nimio indulget, Basilium Macedonē Barda interfecto consortem imperij ascivit: à quo mox occisus est, cùm imperasset annis tredecim. Vide Blondum lib.2. Deca.2. Baptist. Egna.lib.Ro.principum 2.& Cosmog.Mun.lib.4. IMP. LOTTARIVS P. F. AVG. IMP. LVDOVICVS II AVG.
units.tr: Michael, son of Theophilus, succeeded his father while still an infant, and under the guardianship of his mother Theodora, who administered the empire on behalf of her son at Constantinople, in the year of the world 4807, from the birth of Christ 845. When Michael reached adolescence, he began to manage the affairs of the kingdom, and his mother gave way to him. Being more like his grandfather than his father, he ruined the state through sloth and extravagance; as many wars broke out one after another, he could not be diverted from the horse races on which he had concentrated all his zeal. Indulging too much in the circus games, he took Basil the Macedonian as co-emperor after killing Bardas; soon afterwards he himself was killed by him, after reigning thirteen years. See Blondus, Decade 2, book 2; Baptista Egnatius, book on the Roman princes, 2; and Cosmography, book 4. IMP. LOTHAIR P. F. AUG. IMP. LOUIS II AUG.

units.la: LOTARIVS post patrem Ludouicum Piūm Romæ imperat anno mundi 4802. à Christo nato 840. hic paterna diuisione inter filios minimè contentus, omnia sibi, tanquam natu maximo, & Imperatori à patre declarato, vendicabat. Bellum inter fratres utrinque atrox & cruentum die paschæ, dum uterque alteri insidias parat, committitur ad Fontoniacum in Altissiodorensibus: tot hominum millia utrinque cecidere, ut conuulsæ prope sint imperij vires: victus tamen est Lotarius à Carolo Caluo: qui cùm bellum iterum reparárent, iterum fusi, pacem petiere: quadraginta utrinque dictis arbitris, fœdus ineunt: imperij titulo, Lotario Italia, cum Prouincia, & Lotaringia, ab se sic dicta, cessit: Ludouico Germania, Carolo Francia, quæ Britannicum Oceanum & Mosam terminos haberet. Huic Carolo Francici nominis primo, separatim contigit quod veræ Franciæ regnum nunc dicitur: nam Carolus Magnus, & qui præcesserant, Germanicum quiddam referebant. Lotarius Ludouicum filium in consortem imperij assumpsit: & post aliquot annos imperio se abdicans, monasticam vitam vixit, tædio (ut opinantur) rerum aduersarum. Imperat Lotarius annos 15. Vide Blond. Aemy. lib. 3. Egna. lib. 3.
units.tr: Lothair, after his father Louis the Pious, reigned at Rome in the year of the world 4802, from the birth of Christ 840. Not at all content with his father's division among his brothers, he claimed everything for himself as the eldest son and as emperor declared by his father. War broke out between the brothers, fierce and bloody on both sides, on Easter Day, while each was laying snares for the other, at Fontenoy in the territory of Auxerre. So many thousands of men fell on both sides that the strength of the empire was almost torn apart. Yet Lothair was defeated by Charles the Bald; when they renewed the war, they were again routed and sought peace. With forty arbiters chosen from each side, they made a covenant: Lothair kept the title of emperor, together with Italy, Provence, and Lotharingia, so named after himself; Louis got Germany; Charles got France, which had the British Ocean and the Meuse as its boundaries. To this Charles, the first of that name in France, it fell separately to have what is now called the kingdom of true France; for Charlemagne and his predecessors had been more like a German realm. Lothair took his son Louis as co-emperor, and after some years, abdicating the empire, he lived a monastic life, from weariness (as is thought) of adverse circumstances. Lothair reigned fifteen years. See Blondus; Aemilius, book 3; Egnatius, book 3.

units.la: LVDOVICVS Lotarij filius, post patrem Romæ imperat: inter eum, & Carolum Caluum patruum, minimè conueniebat, propter Austrasiam quæ Lotarij fuerat, quam tamen sibi Caluus vendicabat: sed compositis rebus, cum imperasset annos 21. moritur, superstite filio Ludouico. Vide Egn. lib. 3.
units.tr: Louis, son of Lothair, reigned at Rome after his father. Between him and his uncle Charles the Bald there was no agreement, on account of Austrasia, which had belonged to Lothair, and which Charles nevertheless claimed for himself. But when affairs were settled, he died after reigning twenty-one years, leaving a surviving son, also named Louis. See Egnatius, book 3.

units.la: Two coin medallions are printed here, the left one inscribed MACEDO BASILIVS, the right one inscribed LEO BAS. and PHS.
units.tr: Two coin medallions are printed here, the left one inscribed MACEDO BASILIVS, the right one inscribed LEO BAS. and PHS.

units.la: BASILIVS Macedo, qui Michaëlem occiderat, eiusdem imperium occupauit Constantinopolitanum, anno mundi 4831. à Christo nato 869. Hic in pueritia captiuus inter venales Constantinopolim adductus fuerat: praefuit tamen, & eo rerum succeßu, vt ad eius nepotes imperij maiestas transferiet. Adepto imperio, Michaelis largitiones ita reuocauit, vt dimidium eorum quae quisque acceperat, aerario inferret. Treis liberos imperij haeredes instituit: deinde plurima cum Saracenis gessit bella, victoria plerunque potitus: multos Iudaeos ac Scythas ad Christum perduxit. Anno imperij 17. à ceruo in venatione cornu ictus, mox periit, vir frugi, & quem principem non contemnas. Vide Liut. li. 1. Egna. lib. 2. Cosmog. Mun. lib. 4.
units.tr: BASIL the Macedonian, who had killed Michael, seized the same empire at Constantinople in the year of the world 4831, from the birth of Christ 869. He had been brought to Constantinople as a captive in boyhood, among the slaves for sale, yet he held power, and with such success that the majesty of the empire passed to his descendants. Having obtained the empire, he revoked Michael's grants so that half of what each had received was paid into the treasury. He appointed three sons as heirs to the empire. Then he waged many wars against the Saracens, mostly winning the victory; he brought many Jews and Scythians to Christ. In the 17th year of his reign he was struck by a stag's antler while hunting and soon died, a worthy man and one whom you would not despise as a prince. See Liutprand, book 1; Egnatius, book 2; Cosmography, book 4.

units.la: LEO Basilij filius, huius nominis Imperator sextus, Constantinopoli imperat anno mundi 4848. à Christo nato 886. Bulgaros desciscentes, Turcarum auxilio primò vicit: postea ab his per inanes inducias delusus, magna ipse clade affectus est: inde in Saracenos classe comparata, Niceta ductu insignem adeptus est victoriam. Philosophus fuit, literarum omnium, Astrologiae in primis studiosus, qua etiam filium Constantinum imperaturum praedixit, ac diuinauit: in rep. moderanda, ac vrbe custodienda sollicitum ac folertem se praestitit. Huius prouidentiam ac vigilantiam pro Reipub. salute, describit Liuthprādus, qui à Basilio Imperatore ad Nicephorū Phocam, historiam rerum per Europam conscripsit. Hic Leo vt vigilum siue custodiarum vrbis fidem experiretur, noctu solus è regia mutato habitu se proripuit: à primis custodibus numerata se liberat pecunia, ab aliis verò, pugnis, flagrisque caesus, in carcerem traditur: hos postea muneribus donat, illos autem bonis exutos expellit. Vide vt supra.
units.tr: LEO, son of Basil, the sixth emperor of that name, reigned at Constantinople in the year of the world 4848, from the birth of Christ 886. He first defeated the Bulgarians, who were revolting, with the help of the Turks; afterwards, deceived by them through empty truces, he himself suffered a great defeat. Then, having prepared a fleet against the Saracens, he won a notable victory under the leadership of Nicetas. He was a philosopher, devoted above all to all literature and to astrology, by which he also predicted and foretold that his son Constantine would become emperor. He showed himself watchful and diligent in governing the state and guarding the city. His foresight and vigilance for the safety of the commonwealth are described by Liutprand, who wrote a history of events throughout Europe at the request of Emperor Basil to Nicephorus Phocas. Here Leo, to test the loyalty of the city watchmen or guards, slipped out alone from the palace at night in changed clothing: the first guards, having counted out money, let him go; but others, beating him with fists and whips, threw him into prison; afterwards he rewarded the former with gifts, and expelled the latter, stripped of their property. See above.

units.la: CAROLVS Caluus Ludouici Pij filius, Francorum Rex vigesimus sextus, mortuo Ludouico secundo huius nominis, Imperatore, Lotarij filio, Italiam petit: à Ioanne Pontifice huius nominis octauo, corona imperij donatur, anno mundi 4838. à Christo nato 876. Hic antea cum Britonibus & Normanis varia fortuna dimicauerat: nam Normani Danis finitimi, qui à Carolo magno debellati fuerant, ditionem Caroli Calui infestarunt, & piraticam exercentes, Nannetes vsque peruolarunt molestis incursionibus: contra quos Carolus annis ferè decem pugnauit. tandem fortiter apud Andegauum, quod ceperant, obsessi, pecunia se redimunt. Carolus in Seracenos mouens, facile conatus eorum repressit: inde in Galliam reuersus, breui Italiam repetit: aduersus quem dum Ludouici Imperatoris filij bellum parant, ipse curis confectus, & Mantuæ morbo correptus, veneno à Sedechia, medico Iudaici sanguinis, dato, moritur anno regni sui Francici tricesimo octauo, imperij verò, secundo. Nec tradunt autores quo solicitatore, corruptoréque id sceleris perpetrarit Hebræus ille: neque an sæuitum in eum sit, ut domesticis magis insidiis quàm externis petitus videatur Caluus: qui impotentiæ, superbiæque à suis insimulabatur: & quòd contemptis patriis moribus, cultu in externos ritus degenerasset: ita dum oculis hominum augustiorem se facit, pectoribus inuisus fuit. Paul.Æmyl.de rebus Francorum lib.3.Bap.Egna.Rom.prin.lib.3. R. FRAN. 27. LVDOVICVS FRAN. R. 28. CAROLOMA[?]
units.tr: CHARLES the Bald, son of Louis the Pious, the twenty-sixth King of the Franks, after the death of Louis II, the emperor and son of Lothair, made for Italy. He was crowned emperor by Pope John VIII in the year of the world 4838, from the birth of Christ 876. Previously he had fought with the Britons and the Normans with varied fortune: for the Normans, neighbours of the Danes, who had been subdued by Charlemagne, attacked the dominion of Charles the Bald, and, carrying on piracy, flew with troublesome raids as far as Nantes; against them Charles fought for nearly ten years. At last, besieged bravely at Angers, which they had taken, they ransomed themselves with money. Charles, moving against the Saracens, easily checked their attempts; then returning to Gaul, he soon went back to Italy. While his son-in-law... [sic] the sons of Emperor Louis were preparing war against him, he, worn out by cares and seized by illness at Mantua, was poisoned by Sedechias, a physician of Jewish blood, and died in the thirty-eighth year of his reign as King of the Franks, and the second of his empire. The authors do not say at whose instigation that Hebrew committed this crime, nor whether it was done with such cruelty that Charles seems to have been attacked more by domestic plots than by foreign ones; he was accused by his own people of weakness and pride, and because, having despised the customs of his country, he had degenerated into the worship of foreign rites. Thus, while he made himself more august in the eyes of men, he was hated in their hearts. Paul Aemilius, On the Affairs of the Franks, book 3; Baptista Egnatius, Roman Princes, book 3. FRANKS KING 27. LOUIS FRANKS KING 28. CAROLOMA[?]

units.la: LVDOVICVS Balbus Caroli Calui filius,à Papa Joanne huius nominis octauo,qui in Galliam se contulerat , coronam imperij accipit anno mundi 4840.à Christo nato 878. Hic Papa præter Italiæ multorum principum voluntatem solus titulum imperij Balbo asseruit:nam è custodia fugiens,cui Romani illum incluserant , & in Galliam contendens, ratum Balbo imperium suo assensu fecit:quod tamen valetudinarius princeps biennio vix obtinuit.Hic paruam expeditionem in Cenomanos fecit, ac Gotthofredi Cenomanensium comitis filios præfractos quidem,ac patri,ipsi denique Imperatori minus obsecundantes ad obseruantiam compulit: interminatus nisi ad officium redirent,ultima passuros.Obiit Compendij, quo die Christus passus est:uxorem reliquit grauidam, quæ Simplicem peperit: cui Odo Roberti Andium Ducis filius, in spem ventris, fuit à patre tutor designatus.Æmy.lib.3.Egna.lib.3. Chron. Reg. Franc.
units.tr: LUDOVICUS Balbus, son of Charles the Bald, receives the crown of the empire from Pope John VIII, the eighth of that name, who had withdrawn into Gaul, in the year of the world 4840, from the birth of Christ 878. Here the Pope, against the wishes of many princes of Italy, alone asserted the title of emperor for Balbus: for, when he escaped from custody, in which the Romans had shut him up, and hastened into Gaul, he gave Balbus's rule his assent and made it valid. Yet the prince, being in poor health, barely held it for two years. He undertook a small expedition against the Cenomani, and forced the sons of Gotthofred, Count of the Cenomani, who were headstrong, and less obedient to their father and finally to the Emperor himself, back to their duty, threatening that they would suffer the worst unless they returned to their obligations. He died at Compiègne, on the day Christ suffered; he left behind a pregnant wife, who bore Simplex. Odo, son of Robert, Duke of the Andes, was appointed by the father as guardian of this child, in hope of the unborn child. Aemylius, book 3; Egnatius, book 3; Chronicle of the Kings of the Franks.

units.la: LVDOVICVS Carolomanúsque fratres, Balbi ex pellice filij, Franciæ regnum obtinent anno mundi 4842. à Christo nato 880. Hi duo nothi initio feliciter rem gerunt adversus Normanos & Danos,qui numeroso exercitu,igni ferróque Galliam perquinquennium vastabant. Carolomanus in equo ludibundus dum refugientem domum puellam insequitur, impetu equi intra humile ostium illatus , corporis compagem soluit, Lugdovicus aprum venabulo premens, intorto aliundè telo transfigitur: hic anno regni quarto, ille quinto: Porrò Carolomanus,quòd natu maior esset,Rex præ altero censetur. Consulito Æmyl. lib.3.
units.tr: LUDOVICUS and Carloman, brothers, sons of Balbus by a concubine, obtain the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the world 4842, from the birth of Christ 880. These two bastards at first carried on the war successfully against the Normans and Danes, who for five years had been laying waste Gaul with fire and sword, with a large army. Carloman, playing carelessly on horseback, was chasing a girl who was fleeing into her house; the horse's rush carried him in through a low doorway, and he broke his body's frame. Louis, pressing a boar with a hunting spear, was pierced by a spear thrown from another direction. The former died in the fourth year of his reign, the latter in the fifth. Moreover, Carloman is considered the king before the other, because he was the elder. Consult Aemylius, book 3.

units.la: LVDOVICVS nihili,mortuo patre Carolomano coronam regni Franciæ suscipit, anno mundi 4846. à Christo nato 884.hunc non annumerat Paulus Æmylius in serie regū Franciæ,vel quòd eundem hunc putet cum Carolo Simplice, Balbi posthumo cuius simplicitas hic, sub nomine Ludouici nihili, interpolita sit:(nam etiam hic attentioribus turbata & consusa videtur historia) vel quòd huius Ludouici loco (si quidem alter sit ab illo Simplice) ob ignauiam quasi reiecti, censeatur potius Carolus Crassus, qui Romæ tunc imperabat, Franciæ quoque Rex:nam & is Carolus regnum etiam optimè dicitur administrasse,ab Italia euocatus, vt statim dicetur. Fertur Ludouicus hic pulsus fuisse regno,anno quinto: cuius regni annos quinque in Carolum Crassum, ob eam quam diximus causam,transferimus. Gag.li.s.[?]
units.tr: LUDOVICUS the Worthless, on the death of his father Carloman, takes up the crown of the kingdom of the Franks, in the year of the world 4846, from the birth of Christ 884. Paulus Aemylius does not count him in the series of kings of the Franks, either because he thinks him the same as Charles the Simple, the posthumous son of Balbus, whose simplicity has here been inserted under the name of Louis the Worthless (for this history too seems confused and muddled to the more attentive reader), or because, in place of this Louis (if indeed he is another from that Simplex), Charles the Fat, who then ruled at Rome and was also King of the Franks, is thought rather to be put in his place, as one rejected for his sloth. For that Charles is also said to have governed the kingdom well, having been summoned out of Italy, as will be said at once. It is reported that this Louis was driven from the kingdom in the fifth year; for this reason, which we have mentioned, we assign the five years of his reign to Charles the Fat. Gagnier, book 5.

units.la: CAROLVS, cognomento grossus,siue crassus, Ludouici 2.Germaniæ regis filius,Romæ imperat post Balbū,anno mundi 4842.à Christo nato 880.hic cum subsidio opus esset Italis contra Saracenos,à Papa Ioanne octauo,necessitate compulsus, è Germania accersitus,profligatis Saracenis,imperialem coronam accipit. Accersitus à Francis aduersus Normanos,Franciæ Rex appellatur. Neustrij publicè detrectabant imperiū:pacem cum eis composuit: ídque Neustriæ,quod nunc Normania est, nomine à nouis incolis indito, incolendum eis dedit. Exin qui iuuenis mira indole fuerat, adeo degenerauit ab illa Caroli Magni stirpe, vt quòd rebus suis, publicisque superesse non posset,curator ei daretur,nouo exemplo fratris filius patruo: is est Arnulphus. Aemy.Egna. lib.3.imperat annis 10.
units.tr: CHARLES, surnamed the Fat or Thick, son of Louis, King of Germany, reigns at Rome after Balbus, in the year of the world 4842, from the birth of Christ 880. Here, when the Italians needed help against the Saracens, he was compelled by necessity by Pope John VIII, was summoned from Germany, and, having routed the Saracens, received the imperial crown. Summoned by the Franks against the Normans, he is called King of the Franks. The Neustrians openly refused him obedience; he made peace with them and gave them that part of Neustria, now called Normandy, to inhabit, under a name given it by its new inhabitants. Afterwards he, who had been of remarkable character in his youth, degenerated so far from that stock of Charles the Great that, since he could not manage his own affairs or those of the state, a guardian was given him, in a new example, a brother's son over his uncle: this is Arnulf. Aemylius, Egnatius, book 3. He reigned ten years.

units.la: ODO, Roberti Andium Ducis filius, alienus à Genere Caroli Magni, tutórque Caroli Simplicis, iussus regnat apud Francos post Carolum Crassum, anno mundi 4852. à Christo nato 890. nec obstitit Arnulphus Crasi curator, & Augustus Imperator salutatus, qui regnū occupare satagebat. Is Odo aduersus Normanos pręclarè se gessit. Franci biennio postquã Odonem Regem salutarũt, in Aquitania omnino eum regnare iubent, assumpto Rege, ante tempus, Simplice adolescētulo: id æmulatione factū putarim: multi enim pro vno tutores exorti sunt, atque armis in Odonem actum ac decertatum est: aduersus quem Arnulphus Augustus accersitus est: virtute tamen, opibus, fortunaque superior Odo euasit. Odo in Galliam attulit nobile illud signum innumeris sparsum liliis, quod ad Caroli sexti tempora durauit. numerantur anni regni huius nouem. Vide Aemy.lib.3.& Gag. Chro.lib.5. moriens Odo pupillo Simplici regnum restitui iussit.
units.tr: ODO, son of Robert, Duke of the Andes, a stranger to the family of Charles the Great, and guardian of Charles the Simple, is ordered to reign among the Franks after Charles the Fat, in the year of the world 4852, from the birth of Christ 890. Arnulf, guardian of Charles the Fat, did not stand in the way, nor did the Emperor, who was hailed as Augustus and who was trying to seize the kingdom. This Odo acquitted himself splendidly against the Normans. Two years after the Franks had hailed Odo as king, they ordered that he reign over Aquitaine alone, having taken up a king, Simplex, a young man, before his time: I would suppose this was done out of rivalry, for many guardians arose for one ward, and there was fighting and contending in arms against Odo, against whom Arnulf, the Augustus, was summoned; yet Odo came out superior by valour, resources and fortune. Odo brought into Gaul that famous emblem, scattered with countless lilies, which lasted down to the times of Charles VI. The years of this reign are counted as nine. See Aemylius, book 3, and Gagnier, Chronicle, book 5. Dying, Odo ordered that the kingdom be restored to his ward Simplex.

units.la: CAROLVS Simplex, Balbi filius, post Odoné tunc demum dicitur regnasse apud Francos, nempe anno mundi 4861. à Christo nato 899. huic pupillo coram proceribus regnū iubet restitui Odo animam agens. hoc Rege finitum est bellum Normanicum: Rhollo primus Normaniæ Dux factus est. Tot rerum fluctus in Gallia extitere à Balbo ad Simplicem, vt vix certò sciri possit quis potissimum regnarit. Robertus Odonis frater, regni æmulus, aduersus Simplicē pugnans occiditur. Herbertus, cuius sororem in vxorem duxerat Robertus, Simplicem ad se in speciem rei componendæ accersit, & in carcerem Peronæ coniicit: vbi post annos tres moritur, ac Peronæ sepelitur. Acmyl.lib.3.regnat annis 27. fuitque iuxta nostram supputationem 32. Francorum Rex. IMP. ARNVLPHVS. P.F. AVGVST. NVL. FIL. P.F. AVG. LVDOVICVS AR[?]
units.tr: CHARLES the Simple, son of Balbus, after Odo was then at last said to have reigned among the Franks, namely in the year of the world 4861, from the birth of Christ 899. Odo, at the point of death, ordered that the kingdom be restored to this ward in the presence of the nobles. Under this king the Norman war was ended; Rollo became the first Duke of Normandy. So many waves of affairs arose in Gaul from Balbus to Simplex that it can hardly be known for certain who reigned chiefly. Robert, brother of Odo and rival for the kingdom, fighting against Simplex, is killed. Herbert, whose sister Robert had married, summons Simplex to himself on the pretext of settling affairs, and throws him into prison at Péronne, where after three years he dies and is buried at Péronne. Aemylius, book 3. He reigned twenty-seven years, and by our reckoning was the 32nd King of the Franks. EMPEROR ARNULF, AUGUSTUS, ...

units.la: ARNVLPHVS, Carlomani filius, patruo Carolo crasso, cui curator datus fuerat (nempe nouo ac inusitato modo nepos patruo) succedit in imperio Romano anno mundi 4852. à Christo nato 890. eodem nempe anno quo Odo apud Francos regnat. Hic Normanos strenuè superat:mox in rapinas conuersus, iusta numinum ira plectitur: nam pediculari morbo consectus obiit, anno imperij 12. Vltimus hic è Caroli Magni prosapia imperat Romæ: in eóque imperij maiestas deficit ad Germanos, quæ per centum annos apud Francos steterat:sub quorum principatu Francorum, adeò floruit, vt vetera tempora non desideres. imperat annis duodecim. Vide Baptistam Egn.libro Romanorum principum sexto.
units.tr: ARNULF, son of Carloman, succeeds his uncle Charles the Fat, to whom he had been assigned as guardian (namely, in a new and unusual way, a nephew over his uncle), in the Roman empire, in the year of the world 4852, from the birth of Christ 890, in the very year in which Odo reigns among the Franks. He vigorously overcame the Normans; soon, turning to plunder, he was struck by the just anger of the gods: for, worn down by a lice-borne disease, he died in the twelfth year of his reign. This last of the line of Charles the Great reigns at Rome; and with him the majesty of the empire passed from the Franks to the Germans, having stayed with the Franks for a hundred years; under whose rule the Franks flourished so greatly that you do not miss the old times. He reigned twelve years. See Baptista Egnatius, book 6 of the Roman princes.

units.la: LVDOVICVS à Gallis & Germanis successor Arnulpho patri creatur, anno mundi 4864. à Christo nato 902. imperat annis decem in Germania & Galliis, puta Lotaringiæ.adversus Berengarium bellum mouit, quem primò vicit: deinde Veronæ victus, luminibus priuatur. Imperat annis decem. Hic grauiter prostrauit Hungaros Germaniam vastantes. Sed ab illis postea vicissim victus est, coronam accepisse nusquam legitur. Vide Chron. Imperatorum, & Carionem lib.3. IMP. BERLINGARIVS. I. AVG [?] IMP. CAES. BERLINGARIVS. II [?]
units.tr: LUDOVICUS, created by the Gauls and Germans as successor to his father Arnulf, in the year of the world 4864, from the birth of Christ 902. He reigned ten years in Germany and in Gaul, that is, Lotharingia. He waged war against Berengar, whom he first defeated; then, defeated at Verona, he was deprived of his eyes. He reigned ten years. Here he sorely crushed the Hungarians who were laying waste Germany. But afterwards he was in turn defeated by them; it is nowhere read that he received the crown. See the Chronicle of the Emperors, and Carion, book 3. EMPEROR BERENGAR, I, AUGUSTUS; EMPEROR CAESAR BERENGAR, II.

units.la: BERENGARIVS hoc nomine primus, Foroiulij Princeps,ex genere Longobardorum, Arnulpho successor in imperio ab Italis creatur,eodem anno quo Ludouicus, de quo proximè,à Gallis & Germanis. Itali siquidem assiduis barbarorum incursionibus vexati,ius antiquum,& veterè imperij gloriā amittere nolentes,hunc sibi præfecerūt:fuit ingenio & re bellica potens.Guidonem Spoletinum Ducem interfecit. imperat annos ferè quinque.Videto Chro. Impe. Scribit Ioannes Carion lib.3. hunc Berengarium collectis ingentibus copiis aduersus Hungaros quanquàm infeliciter pugnasset, attamen ex ea expeditione tantâ nominis existimationem consecutū esse, vt postea Cæsarem se voluerit nominari. Chronica Phry. referunt hunc Berengarium ad Arnolphi Imperatoris Romani tépora. Cæterum imperij Romani maiestas in Arnulpho defecit, quæ tanta indole à Carolo magno quæsita fuerat, & ad Germanos translata est. terra certè Itala sub Gallorum principatu adeò floruit, vt vetera Romanorum principum tempora minimè desiderares:sed & anni sexaginta vsque ad Othonem primum Saxonū Regem, quibus nullū non calamitatis genus sensit Rom.imperium,ac terra Itala, effecere vt Gallicum nomen desiderabilius foret. Vide Egn.li.3.
units.tr: BERENGAR, first of this name, Prince of Friuli, of the stock of the Lombards, is created emperor in succession to Arnulf by the Italians, in the same year as Louis, of whom we spoke just before, by the Gauls and Germans. For the Italians, harassed by the constant incursions of barbarians, unwilling to lose their ancient right and the old glory of the empire, set this man over themselves; he was powerful in intellect and in military affairs. He killed Guy, Duke of Spoleto. He reigned for nearly five years. See the Chronicle of Emperors. John Carion, book 3, writes that this Berengar, although he fought unsuccessfully after gathering vast forces against the Hungarians, nevertheless gained from that campaign such esteem for his name that he afterwards wished himself to be called Caesar. The Chronicle of Phry. reports that this Berengar belongs to the times of the Emperor Arnulf of Rome. Otherwise, the majesty of the Roman empire failed in Arnulf, which had been sought by Charles the Great with such great ability, and was transferred to the Germans. Certainly the Italian land flourished so greatly under the rule of the Gauls that you would not at all miss the old times of the Roman princes; but also the sixty years until Otto I, King of the Saxons, during which the Roman empire and the Italian land felt every kind of calamity, made the French name more desirable. See Egnatius, book 3.

units.la: BERENGARIVS secundus priori succedit anno mundi 4868. à Christo nato 906. Hic post tertium aut quartum annum à Rudolpho Burgundo Rege pellitur. Vide vt supra. LEO F. CONSTANTIN ALEXANDER
units.tr: BERENGAR the second succeeds the former, in the year of the world 4868, from the birth of Christ 906. He was driven out by Rudolf, King of Burgundy, after the third or fourth year. See as above. LEO, EMPEROR, CONSTANTINE, ALEXANDER.

units.la: ALEXANDER Leonis supradicti Imperatoris frater, eidē in imperio Constantinopolitano succesfsit, anno mun. 4866. à Christo nato 904. Hic & Basilio patri, & Leoni fratri disimilis, luxu & delitiis perditus, annum & mesem imperauit: turpissimum queque rebus praefecit: erumpete tandē è naribus & pudendis toto die sanguine, ob crapulam ac ludum pilæ intempestiuū, obiit. Vide vt supra, vbi de patre ac fratre huius memini.
units.tr: ALEXANDER, brother of the aforesaid Emperor Leo, succeeds him in the Constantinopolitan empire, in the year of the world 4866, from the birth of Christ 904. He, unlike his father Basil and his brother Leo, lost in luxury and pleasures, ruled for one year and a month; he put the most disgraceful men in charge of affairs, and died when blood burst out of his nostrils and genitals all day long, through overindulgence and an untimely game of ball. See as above, where I mentioned his father and brother.

units.la: CONSTANTINVS Leonis supradicti filius, septennis à patre sub matris tutela relictus est, imperauit Constantinopoli post patruum Alexandrum prædictum anno mundi 4867. à Christo nato 905. Huic Romanus quidā Lecapenus insidias tetendit, vtque eū omnino imperio deturbaret, nullū non lapidē mouit: frustratus tamen spe sua, à propriis filiis captus, ac in monasterium trusus est, qui antea matrē Constantini Zoen, in monasterium truserat. Cùm autē hi Romani Lecapeni filij idē Constantino facere tentarēt, capti ipsimet, & tonsi in monasteriū detrusi sunt. Constantinus itaque qui à Romano vitrico multis annis oppressus fuerat, monarchiam sic recuperat, solúsque prudenter satis administrat, tyrannis quibusdam oppressis, Turcarúmq; principibus aliquot, Christianam amplectentibus pietatem. Hic literas penè extinctas ab interitu vindicauit. Librum filio Romano, qui alter est à Romano Lecapeno, reliquit: in quo totius imperij summam, sociorum fœdera, hostium vires rationes, & consilia aperuit, quem Veneti in bibliotheca vt thesaurum adseruant: nam & multa de Venetorum rebus disserit liber ille. Vide vt supra. Imperauit Constantinus hic, tam solus, quàm cum Romano Lecapeno annos 55.
units.tr: CONSTANTINE, son of the Leo mentioned above, was left by his father at the age of seven under the guardianship of his mother. He reigned at Constantinople after his uncle Alexander, mentioned above, in the year of the world 4867, from the birth of Christ 905. Against him a certain Romanus Lecapenus laid snares, and, in order to drive him utterly from the throne, moved every stone; but, disappointed in his hope, he was seized by his own sons and shut up in a monastery, the same monastery into which he had earlier thrust Constantine's mother Zoë. When these sons of Romanus Lecapenus then tried to do the same to Constantine, they themselves were captured, tonsured and sent into a monastery. Constantine, therefore, who had been oppressed for many years by his stepfather Romanus, thus recovered the monarchy and governed alone with considerable prudence, having put down certain tyrants and several princes of the Turks who embraced the Christian piety. He rescued letters, nearly extinct, from destruction. He left a book for his son Romanus, who is the other Romanus, not Lecapenus; in it he set out the sum of the whole empire, the alliances of its allies, the strength, plans and counsels of its enemies, and the Venetians keep this book in their library as a treasure; for that book also discusses much about the affairs of the Venetians. See above. This Constantine reigned, both alone and together with Romanus Lecapenus, for 55 years.

units.la: CVNRADVS Ludouici, Arnulphi filij, ex fratre nepos,, ultimus ex nobilissima posteritate Caroli Magni, Germaniæ Rex, Cæsar designatur anno mundi 4873. à Christo nato 911. nec tamen à Pontifice coronatur. Hic Hungaros, quos instigarat Berengarius (qui Imperatoris sibi nomen in Italia usurpabat) ut iterum Germaniam depopularentur, superauit, Othonis Saxonũ ducis præsidio: cuius filius Henricus à Cunrado morituro Imperator declaratur. Consulito Chron.
units.tr: CONRAD, son of Louis, nephew through his brother of Arnulf, the last of the most noble posterity of Charlemagne, was named King of Germany and Caesar in the year of the world 4873, from the birth of Christ 911, yet he was not crowned by the Pontiff. He defeated the Hungarians, whom Berengarius (who was usurping the title of Emperor in Italy) had stirred up to lay waste Germany again, with the help of Otto, duke of the Saxons; and on his deathbed Conrad declared Otto's son Henry Emperor. Consult the Chronicle.

units.la: HENRICVS Saxonum Dux, supradicti Othonis filius, in Germanorum imperio succedit, defuncto Cunrado anno mundi 4881. à Christo nato 919. tum imperium à Caroli magni posteris ad Saxones translatum est. Hic Hungaros vicit, Sclauos subegit, Dalmatas tributarios fecit: Boemos imperij legibus subiecit, quadragintamillia Hungarorum apud Meresburgum prostrauit: Brādeburgum cepit. Vandalos subegit ad mare usque (hi Christiana religionem tunc amplexi sunt) toti Germaniæ summam tranquillitatē peperit: hic cognomēto auceps, iam morti proximus successorem imperij instituit Othonem filium suum, cū ipse imperasset annos octodecim. Vide Liuthp. lib. 2. ca. 9, Vuitich. lib. 1.
units.tr: HENRY, duke of the Saxons, son of the aforementioned Otto, succeeded to the German empire on the death of Conrad, in the year of the world 4881, from the birth of Christ 919; then the empire was transferred from the posterity of Charlemagne to the Saxons. He conquered the Hungarians, subdued the Slavs, and made the Dalmatians tributary; he subjected the Bohemians to the laws of the empire; he laid low forty thousand Hungarians at Merseburg; he took Brandenburg. He subdued the Vandals as far as the sea (these had then embraced the Christian religion), and brought the greatest tranquillity to all Germany. He, surnamed the Fowler, when already near death, appointed as successor to the empire his son Otto, after he himself had reigned eighteen years. See Liutprand, book 2, chapter 9, Widukind, book 1.

units.la: BERENGARIVS tertius, in Italiam accersitus anno mundi 4872. à Christo nato 910. una cum filio Adalberto Italiæ regnum administrauit. Sed cum tyrannū verius quam principem ageret, accersitur à Romanis Otho, cuius tunc nomē ac pietas celebris erat, qui Berengarium cum filio Italia expulit. Vide Bapt. Egna. lib.3. & Carionem lib.item tertio.
units.tr: BERENGARIUS the Third, summoned into Italy in the year of the world 4872, from the birth of Christ 910, governed the kingdom of Italy together with his son Adalbert. But since he acted more like a tyrant than a prince, Otto was summoned by the Romans, whose name and piety were then famous, and he drove Berengarius out of Italy together with his son. See Baptista Egnatius, book 3, and Carion, likewise book 3.

units.la: OTHO Henrici supradicti Saxonum Ducis filius, in Italiā accersitus, cum quinquaginta millibus armatorum venit: Berengarium, eiusque filium ad obsequium retrahit: quos, data venia, magna Galliæ Cisalpinæ parte donat. Romam inde prosectus, à populo Imperator & Augustus salutatur, à Pontifice coronatur anno mundi 4923. à Christo nato 961. iamque annos 25. Rex Germaniæ extiterat, succedens Henrico patri. Hic Otho conscripto exercitu Franciam intrauit, cuius Regem Ludouicum à Normanis proditum, & in carcerem coniectum, libertati regnoque restituit. Berengarium cum filio res nouas iterum molientes, facile vicit: captosque alterum Bizantij, alterum in Austriam relegauit. Huic, cum administrasset annos 36. successit eiusdem nominis filius, quem etiam pater Romam vocatum, Imperatorem designarat. Vide Egn.lib.3. Aemy.lib.3. Vuit.lib.2. Luithpr.lib.6.ca.6. LECAPENVS ROMANVS IVNIOR ROMANVS LEO
units.tr: OTTO, son of the aforementioned Henry, duke of the Saxons, was summoned into Italy and came with fifty thousand armed men. He brought Berengarius and his son back to obedience; having granted them pardon, he gave them a large part of Cisalpine Gaul. Setting out from there to Rome, he was hailed as Emperor and Augustus by the people and crowned by the Pontiff in the year of the world 4923, from the birth of Christ 961; he had already been King of Germany for 25 years, having succeeded his father Henry. Otto, having raised an army, then entered France, and restored to liberty and to the kingdom its King Louis, who had been betrayed by the Normans and thrown into prison. When Berengarius and his son again attempted revolutionary plans, he defeated them easily; and, having captured them, he banished one to Byzantium and the other to Austria. After him, when he had governed for 36 years, his son of the same name succeeded, whom his father had already designated Emperor, having summoned him to Rome. See Egnatius, book 3; Aimoin, book 3; Widukind, book 2; Liutprand, book 6, chapter 6. LECAPENUS ROMANUS THE YOUNGER ROMANUS LEO

units.la: ROMANVS Lecapenus obscuro genere natus, insidias Constantino parauit, imperiique Constantinopolitani socius ac particeps ab eodem necessario adscitus est eodem quo regnare coepit Constantinus anno, uti supra videre est: Helenamque Constantini filiam, pulsa matre Zoë uxorem habuit. Nec tamen iusiurandum sanctissimum quod praestiterat Lecapenus nec gener Constantinus obstitit, quo minus imperium & sibi & Christophoro filio idem Lecapenus assereret. Cum autem aduersus Bulgaros, Simeonémque eorum ducem, infeliciter congressus esset, à Stephano & Constantino, filiis suis captus, imperio exuitur, & in vicinam insulam in monasterium ad Philosophandum relegatur. At cum iidem ipsi aduersus Constantinum Leonis filium idem molirentur, in laqueum quem tetenderant incidunt, nam & ipsimet, Lecapeni inquam filij, monasterio mancipantur. Imperauit Romanus Lecapenus annos
units.tr: ROMANUS Lecapenus, born of obscure stock, laid snares for Constantine, and was of necessity taken on by him as partner and sharer in the empire of Constantinople, in the same year in which Constantine began to reign, as can be seen above; and he took as wife Helena, daughter of Constantine, after Zoë, the mother, had been expelled. Yet neither the most sacred oath which Lecapenus had sworn nor his son-in-law Constantine stood in the way of the same Lecapenus claiming the empire for himself and for his son Christopher. When he had engaged unsuccessfully against the Bulgarians and their leader Simeon, he was captured by his sons Stephen and Constantine, deprived of the empire, and banished to a nearby island, into a monastery, to devote himself to philosophy. But when these same sons plotted the same thing against Constantine, son of Leo, they fell into the snare they had set: for they themselves, I mean the sons of Lecapenus, were handed over to a monastery. Romanus Lecapenus reigned for years

units.la: ROMANVS Constantini, Leonis filij, filius iunior, post patrem imperium suscepit Constantinopolitanum, quod tamen alieno rexit arbitrio, nempe Nicephori Phocæ, de quo statim meminerimus, ubi & annorum supputationem inferam, non hic ne bis id faciam. Fuit Romanus hic foris aduersus Saracenos Cretam occupantes, & Turcas Asiam vastantes, Nicephori ductu felix: domi in matrem ac sorores impius, ut regia eiectæ, ob mærorem quòd regio essent exutæ vestitu, quæstum fecerint meretricium: ipse ludis ac crapulæ deditus, anno imperij decimo, veneno potionatur. Vide ut supra. FRAN.32 RODVLPHVS REX[?] FRAN.35 LVDOVICVS REX[?]
units.tr: ROMANUS, younger son of Constantine, son of Leo, after his father took up the Constantinopolitan empire, which however he ruled at the discretion of another, namely Nicephorus Phocas, of whom we shall speak presently, where I shall also give the reckoning of the years, so as not to do it twice here. This Romanus was fortunate abroad against the Saracens who occupied Crete and the Turks who laid waste Asia, under the leadership of Nicephorus; at home he was impious toward his mother and sisters, who, expelled from the palace and stripped of their royal garments, out of grief took up prostitution. He himself, given to games and drunkenness, was poisoned in the tenth year of his reign. See above. FRANCIS 32 KING RODULPH[?] FRANCIS 35 KING LOUIS[?]

units.la: RODVLPHVS post Carolum Simplicem Franciæ trigesimus tertius Rex imperat;anno mundi 4888.à Christo nato 926.Nam dum anceps fertur Carolus Simplex in potestatem Herberti Veromandui, Peronam profectus, præsidio custodibusque circumfusis,adducitur,& velut cogitur ut regni iure cedere se in procerum concilio profiteatur, illúdque dono dare huic Rodulpho Burgundiæ Regi,Richardi filio, post Ludovicum in Italia captum,luminibúsque orbatum. Hic imperij veluti vagi ac in medio positi spem affectans,in Italiam transcendit,Berengarióque victo,rerum illarum magna ex parte triennium potitur. At verò mortuo in custodia Simplice, cùm Italos iam eius pœniteret,in Galliam rediit.Continuo Hugo Arelatensium Rex,in Italiam tanquam vacuam possessionem,spe imperij se contulit:quòd Provinciæ Regibus Italiam deberi diceret,Gallis,Germanísque ac Italis de imperio decertantibus.Regnat in Francia Rudolphus Burgundio,annos duos: alij dicunt 1 2. Ad fanum D. Columbæ apud Senonas sepultus est. Vide Chro.Reg.Franc.
units.tr: RUDOLPH, the thirty-third King of France after Charles the Simple, reigned in the year of the world 4888, from the birth of Christ 926. For while Charles the Simple is said to have been wavering in the power of Herbert of Vermandois, he was brought to Péronne, surrounded by a guard and keepers, and, as if forced to yield the kingdom by right, he declared before a council of the nobles that he gave it to this Rudolph, King of Burgundy, son of Richard, after Louis had been captured in Italy and deprived of his sight. This man, aspiring to the power of an empire that was, as it were, drifting and up for grabs, crossed into Italy, and after defeating Berengarius he held a great part of those affairs for three years. But when Charles died in custody, and the Italians already repented of him, he returned to Gaul. Immediately Hugh, King of the Arelatenses, betook himself to Italy as to an empty possession, in hope of the empire, since he said that Italy was owed to the kings of Provence, while the Gauls, Germans and Italians contended over the empire. Rudolph of Burgundy reigned in France for two years; others say twelve. He was buried at the church of St. Columba near Sens. See the Chronicle of the Kings of France.

units.la: LVDOVICVS, huius nominis quartus,Simplicis filius, ex Anglia,quo se ad avunculum Regem cum Ogenia seu Oginia matre post comprehensum ab Herberto patrem, cotulerat, revocatur:inde huic Transmarino cognomen est: regnatque apud Francos anno mundi 4890. à Christo nato 928. De regno fuit inter ipsum & Rodulphum controversia: Rodulphus moritur anno regni huius nono.Rex adversus Othonem Cæsarem, in Lotaringiam bellum mouet: Gerberga Gisleberti vidua Othonis soror nubit Regi.Hugo Roberti filius, Regi facessit negocium: cuius opera quidam aiunt Regem à Normanis captum,& Laudunum in carcerem ductum, unde eum liberat Otho.Regnat Ludouicus annis 27. Apud Remos sepultus est. Vide ut supra R. FRANC[?] LOTHARIVS R. FRANC[?] LVDOVICVS
units.tr: LOUIS, the fourth of that name, son of Charles the Simple, was recalled from England, whither he had retreated with his mother Ogiva, or Oginia, to his uncle the King, after his father had been seized by Herbert; hence he received the surname Transmarinus. He reigned among the Franks in the year of the world 4890, from the birth of Christ 928. There was a dispute over the kingdom between him and Rudolph; Rudolph died in the ninth year of this reign. The King made war against Otto Caesar in Lorraine: Gerberga, widow of Gislebert and sister of Otto, married the King. Hugh, son of Robert, caused the King trouble; through his efforts some say the King was captured by the Normans and led into prison at Laon, from which Otto freed him. Louis reigned for 27 years. He was buried at Reims. See above, R. FRANC[?] LOTHAIR R. FRANC[?] LOUIS

units.la: LOTARIVS, Ludouici transmarini filius, post patrem apud Francos regnat anno mundi 4917. à Christo nato 955. Hic Imperatorem Othonem huius nominis secundum, bello adortus, pene opprimit: is vicissim ab octobri ad decembrem Regem persecutus, praeter templa, résque sacras nihil non funditus euertit Lutetiam vsque: sed pedem cum suis referre coactus, eruptione ciuium ac praesidij, fortissimos suorum, & nobilissimos amisit. Mox ad colloquium cogressis Rege & Caesare, in possessione Lotaringiae Carolus Regis frater perseuerauit, sed angustioribus finibus descripta quàm ante fuisset. Mortuo Othone secundo, imperij anno decimo, successit Otho tertius. Tunc Francus repetito Lotaringico bello, Viriduum, eiusque oppidi Comitem Gothofredum capit: sed supremis suis diebus Caesari Comitem, Comiti opes restituit. Regnat Lotarius hic annos 31. Obiit, sepultúsque est Remis. Vide Æmy. lib. 3. & chro. Reg. Francicorum.
units.tr: LOTHAIR, son of Louis Transmarinus, after his father reigned among the Franks in the year of the world 4917, from the birth of Christ 955. He attacked the Emperor Otto the Second in war and nearly overwhelmed him; Otto in turn pursued the King from October to December, and, besides temples and sacred things, he overturned nearly everything from the foundations, as far as Lutetia; but, forced to bring his foot back with his men, through a sortie of the citizens and the garrison he lost the bravest and most noble of his men. Soon afterwards the King and the Caesar met for a conference, and Charles, the King's brother, persisted in possession of Lorraine, though it had been marked out with narrower bounds than before. When Otto the Second died, in the tenth year of his empire, Otto the Third succeeded. Then the Frank, renewing the Lorraine war, captured Verdun and its count, Godfrey; but in his last days he restored the count to the Caesar and the count's wealth. This Lothair reigned 31 years. He died and was buried at Reims. See Aimoin, book 3, and the Chronicle of the Frankish Kings.

units.la: LVDOVICVS huius nominis quintus, supradicti Lotarij filius, mortuo patre, apud Francos regnat anno mun. 4948. à Christo nato 986. vltimus hic ex agnatione Caroli magni regnat: nam cum is annum omnino regnasset, veneno periit, Compendiique sepultus est, cui Capetus subrogatur. Ita tertium stemma in solio locatur, haudquaquam Francis poenitendum: nempe Pipini, Martelli, & Capeti. Vide Æmy. lib. 3. huius Capeti agnatio ad haec vsque nostra tempora feliciter perdurat. Caeterum à Faramundo ad vsque Hugonem Capetum anni sunt 568. à Clodoueo Christiano 487. à Pipino 237. Vide vt supra. PHOCAS NICEPHORVS ZIMISCEN[?] JOANNES
units.tr: LUDOVICUS, the fifth of this name and son of the above-mentioned Lothar, after his father's death reigned among the Franks in the year of the world 4948, from the birth of Christ 986. He was the last of Charlemagne's line through the male line to reign; for when he had reigned barely a year, he died of poison and was buried at Compiègne, and Capet was put in his place. Thus a third family was placed on the throne, by no means to be regretted by the Franks: namely, that of Pepin, Martel and Capet. See Aimoin, book 3. The line of this Capet has happily endured down to our own times. Moreover, from Pharamond to Hugh Capet there are 568 years; from Clovis, the first Christian king, 487; from Pepin, 237. See as above. PHOCAS NICEPHORUS ZIMISCES JOHN

units.la: NICEPHORVS Phocas Constantinopoli imperat anno mundi 4922. à Christo nato 960. Cum Saracenis sæpe ac feliciter congressus est, qui Calabriam, Siciliam, Candiam, Cilicia & Cyprum occuparant: in Sicilia res haud ita bene per duces acta est: ipse Ciliciam, & bonam Asiæ partem lætis recepit auspiciis: mox Antiochiam noctu aggressus, pulsis Saracenis imperio eam adiecit. Invisus omnibus fuit, quòd bellorum prætextu novis tributis & exactionibus populum expilaret, numismata adulteraret, ac pondus imminueret: quare odiosus civibus, facile à Joanne Zimisce, noctu dormiens in cubili occiditur: intromittente etiam sicarios, Theophania Nicephori uxore. imperat annos decem. Vide Egnat. Ro. prin. lib. 2. & Cosmograp. Mun. de Græcia lib. 4.
units.tr: NICEPHORUS Phocas ruled at Constantinople in the year of the world 4922, from the birth of Christ 960. He often and successfully engaged the Saracens, who had seized Calabria, Sicily, Crete, Cilicia and Cyprus. In Sicily affairs were not going so well, being conducted through his generals; but he himself received Cilicia and a good part of Asia under happy auspices. Soon, attacking Antioch by night, he drove out the Saracens and added it to the empire. He was hated by everyone, because under the pretext of wars he plundered the people with new taxes and exactions, debased the coinage and reduced its weight. Being therefore odious to his subjects, he was easily killed while sleeping in his bed at night by John Zimisces, with Theophano, the wife of Nicephorus, letting in the assassins. He reigned ten years. See Egnatius, Roman history, book 2, and Münster's Cosmography, book 4, on Greece.

units.la: JOANNES Zimisces occiso, ut dixi, Nicephoro, post eum imperat Constantinopoli, an. mun. 4932. à Christo nato 970. Hic clarus antea militari laude, in Roxolanos feliciter movet, Bulgariamque totam, quam sibi[?] Roxolani vendicabant, imperio subiicit, Sphendoslauo eorum Rege ad deditionem coacto. Basilium & Constantinum fratres, Romani secundi supradicti filios, Cæsares facit, ac imperij consortes creat: Nicephoro deditos è medio tollit: & damnatos exilio ab eodem, reducit. At mox parta de Roxolanis victoria, cum triumphantis specie Constantinopolim ingressus esset, veneno potatur, post annum imperij sextum. Vide ut supra. D.N. OTHO. AVG. P.M.I. VXOR OTHONII[?] THEOPHANIA
units.tr: JOHN Zimisces, after Nicephorus was slain, as I have said, ruled at Constantinople after him, in the year of the world 4932, from the birth of Christ 970. Previously famous for his military glory, he successfully campaigned against the Russians (Roxolani), and brought all of Bulgaria, which the Russians claimed for themselves, under the empire, after forcing Svyatoslav, their king, to surrender. He made Basil and Constantine, the sons of the aforementioned Romanus the Younger, Caesars and created them partners in the empire. He removed from the scene those who had been loyal to Nicephorus, and recalled from exile those whom Nicephorus had condemned. But soon after the victory over the Russians was won, when he had entered Constantinople in the manner of a triumphant conqueror, he was poisoned, in the sixth year of his reign. See as above. D.N. OTHO. AVG. P.M.I. WIFE OF OTHO[?] THEOPHANO

units.la: OTHO iunior, siue Otho huius nominis secundus, superioris Othonis filius, patri Romanorum Imperatori succedit anno mundi 4935. à Christo nato 973. attamen à patre iam ante sex annos fuerat Imperator creatus: cuius etiam opera Saracenos, Græcósque Calabria expulerat. Hic mortuo patre Henricum Bauariæ Ducem nouis rebus studentem, debellauit: atque aduersus Lotarium Francorum Regem, qui sibi Lotaringiam asserebat, Galliam ingressus, fœdis populationibus eam vastauit. At dum reuertitur, in Axonæ fluuii transitu graui incommodo à Fracis[?] afficitur, quibusdam ex suis militibus vorticibus absorptis, pluribus ab insequente hoste interfectis. Dum in Italiam festinat ad famam Græcorum principum, qui Saraceno etiam milite instructi Italiam sibi vendicabant, vincitur: ac scapha conscensa, à piratis captus, in Siciliam ducitur: liberatus, omnem in Beneuentanos iram, quòd signa deseruissent, effundit: ciuitatem capit, spoliat, incendit. Tandem fato concessit, cum imperasset solus post patrem annos decem. Consulito Blond. lib. 3. Deca. 2. Egna lib. 3. Ab. Vrfper.
units.tr: OTHO the younger, or Otho the second of this name, son of the former Otho, succeeded his father as Emperor of the Romans in the year of the world 4935, from the birth of Christ 973; yet he had already been created Emperor by his father six years earlier. By his father's efforts he had also driven the Saracens and Greeks out of Calabria. When his father died, he crushed Henry, Duke of Bavaria, who was plotting revolution. Then he invaded Gaul against Lothar, King of the Franks, who claimed Lorraine for himself, and devastated it with foul ravages. But as he was returning, at the crossing of the river Aisne he suffered heavy losses: some of his soldiers were swallowed up by whirlpools, and many were killed by the pursuing enemy. Hurrying into Italy on news of the Greek princes, who, supported by Saracen soldiers, claimed Italy for themselves, he was defeated; and having boarded a boat he was captured by pirates and taken to Sicily. Freed, he poured out all his anger on the people of Benevento, because they had deserted their standards: he captured the city, plundered it and set it on fire. At last he died by fate, having ruled alone for ten years after his father. Consult Blondus, book 3, decade 2; Egnatius, book 3; Ekkehard of Aura.

units.la: THEOPHANIA uxor huius Othonis secundi filia fuit Nicephori Græcorum Imperatoris, quem regno pulsum, restituit, & confirmauit Otho. Vide Sup. Chro. lib. 12. CONSTANTINVS F[?] BASILIVS ET[?] GYROPILVS[?] ROMANVS AR[?]
units.tr: THEOPHANO, wife of this Otho the second, was the daughter of Nicephorus, Emperor of the Greeks, whom Otho restored after he had been driven from the throne and confirmed in power. See the Supplement to the Chronicle, book 12. CONSTANTINE, F[?] BASIL AND[?] GYROPILUS[?] ROMANUS AR[?]

units.la: BASILIVS & Constantinus fratres, Romani iunioris filij, post Ioanne Zimiscen Constantinopoli imperant anno mundi 4938. à Christo nato 976. nulliquę diuturnius imperarunt, nam annos 53. praefuerunt: ille 50. hic treis etiam solus, post fratrem: & ne fine ciuili bello rem transfigerent Baldæ Scleri ambitio effecit, quem imperium invadentem, victum ad Persas fugarunt: postea Phocam, ægrè ferentem se contemni post rem in Sclerum se duce egregiè navatam, in acie caesum, ac tyrannidem usurpantem superarunt. Inde Bulgari victi sunt praeliis aliquot: horum 15. milibus captis oculos eruit Basilius, uno tantum incolumi, qui ad Samuelem eorum Ducem praeiret: idq; ad compescendam eorum perfidiam, qui Thraciam, Macedoniam & Graeciam flammis & ferro vastarat. Tunc demum Bulgaria tota subditur imperio Constantinopolitano, quae in illū usque die semper rebellarat: moerore ob id confectus Samuel, nō ita diu vixit. Obiit autem septuagenario maior Basilius, cui per treis annos successit Constatinus frater, qui cum eo dignitatis potius quam potentiae particeps fuerat: hic totus deliciis diffluens, gulae, veneri ac ludis operam dedit. Vide Egna.lib.2. Cosmog. Munst. lib.4.
units.tr: BASIL and Constantine, brothers, sons of Romanus the Younger, ruled at Constantinople after John Zimisces, in the year of the world 4938, from the birth of Christ 976. No one ruled for longer, for they held power for 53 years: the one for 50, the other for three more, alone after his brother. Lest they should bring the matter to an end through civil war, the ambition of Bardas Sclerus was the cause: when he attacked the throne, they put him to flight, beaten, to the Persians. Afterwards they overcame Phocas, who was resentful at being despised after he had distinguished himself with great success under Sclerus as commander; he was cut down in battle while attempting to seize the tyranny. Then the Bulgarians were defeated in several battles; Basil had the eyes put out of 15,000 of their captives, leaving only one eye in each man, so that he could lead them to Samuel, their commander. He did this to curb the treachery of those who had ravaged Thrace, Macedonia and Greece with fire and sword. At last all Bulgaria was made subject to the empire of Constantinople, which until that day had always been in rebellion; Samuel, worn down with grief over this, did not live long. Basil died, being more than seventy years old, and was succeeded for three years by his brother Constantine, who had shared with him the dignity rather than the power; he, wholly given over to pleasures, devoted himself to gluttony, lust and games. See Egnatius, book 2, and Münster's Cosmography, book 4.

units.la: ROMANVS Argyropylus Constantini, de quo hic memini, gener, eidem vitrico successit in imperio, anno mundi 4991. à Christo nato 1029. hic sub initia, liberalis fuit: verum cūparum ex sententia illi cesisset in Saracenos expeditio, statim ignaviae ac pecunię corradendae se totum tradidit. Zoae uxoris falacisimae ac sterilis insidiis, & Michaelis Paphlagonis adulteri, dolo intra balneas immersus obiit, anno imperij sexto. Vide ut supra.
units.tr: ROMANUS Argyrus, son-in-law of Constantine, of whom I have just spoken, succeeded his father-in-law on the throne in the year of the world 4991, from the birth of Christ 1029. At first he was generous; but when a campaign against the Saracens, as he wished, had turned out well, he at once gave himself wholly to idleness and the hoarding of money. Through the plots of Zoe, his most deceitful and barren wife, and of Michael the Paphlagonian, her adulterous lover, he was drowned by treachery in his bath and died in the sixth year of his reign. See as above.

units.la: OTHO tertius, secundi Othonis supradicti filius, post patrem imperat anno mundi 4945. à Christo nato 983. ætate puer erat vixdum annum duodecimum egressus, cum more-retur pater: quare Henricus Bauariæ Dux, cognatus eius, ser-vandum eum Romæ curavit, & iterum cœpit imperij dignitatem sibi usurpare. Itali plerique Crescentium declarandū Cæ-sarem censebant, ut ad Italos imperij maiestas rediret: sed fi-deles erga dominū suum Germani, hunc Othonem Cæsarem creant: hic iam natus annos 28. eo fuit ingenio præditus, ut mirabilia mundi vocaretur. hic Brunonem Saxonem cogna-tum suum, Gregorium quintum appellatum, Pontificem creat, qui à populo Romano minis & maledictis ex urbe pellitur. Cre-scentius Numentanus Consulem se Romanum titulo præferens, urbis dominium ante cœperat: Romam itaque ingenti-bus copiis accintus aduolat Otho. Papa Joannes 18. quem Romani designarant, cū Crescentio fugit. Crescentius captus interficitur, prius naso & auribus truncis retrorsum asino impositus. Joannes Papa exoculatur: sed Gregorius pristinæ restituitur: qui statim sanctionem eam tulit, quæ in hunc usque diem durat, in hæc verba: Imperatorum nullus hæreditariam dignitatem vendicato. Principes sex, sacri ordinis tres, profani totidem eum deligunto: hi si discordes fuerint, Bohemiæ Regem coaptanto. Egna. lib 3. Blon.lib.3.decade 2. Imperauit hic Otho tertius, annos 19. vixit 30. missóque per insidias à Crescentij uxore veneno, necatus est, ac Augustæ sepultus.
units.tr: OTHO the third, son of the above-mentioned Otho the second, ruled after his father in the year of the world 4945, from the birth of Christ 983. He was a boy, scarcely past twelve years of age, when his father died; so Henry, Duke of Bavaria, his cousin, took care to keep him safe at Rome, and again began to usurp for himself the dignity of the empire. Most of the Italians thought Crescentius should be declared Caesar, so that the majesty of the empire might return to the Italians; but the Germans, faithful to their lord, created this Otho Caesar. Already twenty-eight years old, he was so gifted that he was called the wonder of the world. He appointed his cousin Bruno, a Saxon, who was called Gregory the Fifth, as Pontiff; but the Roman people drove him out of the city with threats and curses. Crescentius of Nomentum, who had earlier seized control of the city, styling himself Roman consul, then flew to Rome with a great army, Otho girded for war. Pope John the Eighteenth, whom the Romans had appointed, fled with Crescentius. Crescentius was captured and put to death, first having his nose and ears cut off and being paraded backwards on an ass. Pope John had his eyes put out; but Gregory was restored to his former position, and he at once issued that decree which lasts down to this day, in these words: "Let no Emperor claim the dignity as hereditary. Let six princes and three of the sacred order and as many of the secular elect him; if they disagree, let them choose the King of Bohemia." See Egnatius, book 3; Blondus, book 3, decade 2. This Otho the third reigned 19 years and lived 30. He was poisoned by the wife of Crescentius, sent as a snare, and died, and was buried at Augsburg.

units.la: MARIA, Regis Arragonum filia, uxor fuit huius Othonis tertij, intemperans quidem mulier, uti autorū scripta testantur.
units.tr: MARIA, daughter of the King of Aragon, was the wife of this Otho the third, a woman indeed of intemperate habits, as the writings of the authors attest.

units.la: HVGO Capetus Parisiorum Comes, mortuo sine liberis Ludouico huius nominis quinto Francorum Rege, Lotaringię Ducem ac Lotarij Regis fratrem, Franciæ regno inhiantem, repressit, atque ex insidiis cepit: deinde vi & militum fauore, Hugo primùm Nouioduni Rex salutatur, mox Remis consecratur,anno mundi 4949. à Christo nato 987. Hic cùm annum solus regnasset,Robertum filium, liberalioribus literis institutum, Aureliani coronandum curauit. Nam ipse Hugo neque diademate,neque regiis insignibus vnquam, sed tantum vi & armis vsus est. Regnat, tam solus quàm cum filio Roberto, annis nouem. Vide Æmy.lib.3. Chron.Reg. Franc. Sabaudiæ domus apud Allobrogas, hoc Rege in Comitatum primùm erigitur. Gag.lib.5.
units.tr: HUGH Capet, Count of Paris, when Louis the fifth of this name, King of the Franks, died without children, checked Lothar's brother, the Duke of Lorraine, who was coveting the kingdom of France, and took him by ambush. Then, by force and with the favour of the soldiers, Hugh was first hailed as king at Noyon and soon afterwards crowned at Reims, in the year of the world 4949, from the birth of Christ 987. When he had reigned alone for a single year, he arranged for his son Robert, who had been educated in the liberal arts, to be crowned at Orléans. For Hugh himself never used a diadem or royal insignia, but relied only on force and arms. He reigned, both alone and with his son Robert, for nine years. See Aimoin, book 3, Chronicle of the French Kings. Under this King the house of Savoy among the Allobroges was first raised to the rank of county. Gagnier, book 5.

units.la: ROBERTVS, Hugonis Capeti filius, succedit patri, & solus apud Francos regnat anno mundi 4958. à Christo nato 996. Henricus Dux Burgundiæ, quòd liberos nullos suscepisset, Ducatum suum Regi testamento legat: quem confestim Rex Hugonis filio eiusdem nominis Roberti, tradit: eúmque mittit aduersus Landricum Niuernensem Comitem Burgundionibus acceptissimum. Senonum urbs ob Comitis Reginaldi scelus, Regis patrimonio adiicitur. Rex cum Ricardo Normaniæ Duce Valentianas proficiscitur,opem laturus Balduino Flandriæ Comiti, quas is contra Henricum Imperatorem occupauerat. Aduentu Francorum Cęsar soluere obsidionem cogitur: sequitur exinde incredibilis fames & pestis. Pace terris, veniáque à numine reddita,Henricus Cæsar, Robertúsq; Rex, ad Charum fluuium conueniunt, ac pacem firmant. Regnat annis 34. Vide Æmy.lib.3. D.N. HENRICVS CLAVDII HENRICI II VXOR CVNIGVNDA[?]
units.tr: ROBERT, son of Hugh Capet, succeeds his father and reigns alone over the Franks in the year of the world 4958, from the birth of Christ 996. Henry, Duke of Burgundy, having no children, bequeaths his duchy to the King by will; the King at once gives it to Hugh's son, who bore the same name, Robert, and sends him against Landry, Count of Nevers, who was most acceptable to the Burgundians. The city of Sens is added to the King's patrimony because of the crime of Count Reginald. The King sets out for Valenciennes with Richard, Duke of Normandy, intending to bring aid to Baldwin, Count of Flanders, whom he had seized from Henry the Emperor. At the approach of the Franks the Emperor was forced to raise the siege; after this an incredible famine and pestilence followed. When peace had returned to the lands and pardon had been granted by the divinity, the Emperor Henry and King Robert met at the river Chér and confirmed the peace. He reigned for 34 years. See Aimoin, book 3. LORD HENRY, WIFE OF CLAUDIUS HENRY II, CUNIGUNDA [?]

units.la: HENRICVS huius nominis secundus, Bauarus, dictus Claudus Othonis primi vel filius, vel ex filio nepos (nā id ambigitur) designatus est Imperator Romanus, anno à mundo condito 496 4.à Christo nato 1002. Romæ post aliquot annos coronatur. Principio Bohemos & Vandalos bello fatigatos tributarios ac subditos fecit: Metas & Gandauū obsedit: Lotaringiam ac Flandriā debellauit: post hæc accepta Romæ imperiali corona, in Capuam mouit: Saracenos ex Italia expulit. Constantinopolitani Imperatoris Ducem Bubaganum, Saracenis fauentem, bello insecutus est acerrimo. Troiam in Apuliæ finibus, vbi olim Annibalis castra fuere, à Græcis ædificatam obsedit, & per deditionem accepit. Hic Episcopatus Bambergensis fundator, Bambergæ sepultus est. Hungaros debellatos ad fidem Christianam pertraxit, data sorore Hungarorum Regi in matrimonium. Cunradum Francum, hoc nomine secundum, Cæsarem creauit, addito legitimo Electorum suffragio. Hunc cum vxore Cunegunda virginitatem perpetuam obseruasse sunt qui scribant, ac post mortem miraculis claruisse. Primus Electorum principum suffragiis Cæsar, iuxta Gregorij formulam designatur: imperatque annis 22. Vide Blon. lib.3. deca.2. Egna. lib.3.
units.tr: HENRY, second of this name, the Bavarian, called the Lame, designated Roman Emperor, whether son or, as is disputed, grandson by a son of Otto the First, was chosen in the year of the world 4964 (sic: 4964 in the reading) from the birth of Christ 1002. He was crowned at Rome some years later. At the beginning he wore down the Bohemians and Vandals, already worn out by war, and made them tributary and subject. He besieged Metz and Ghent, and subdued Lorraine and Flanders. After this, having received the imperial crown at Rome, he moved against Capua and drove the Saracens out of Italy. He pursued with the fiercest war Buboganus, the Duke of the Constantinopolitan Emperor, who favoured the Saracens. He besieged Troia, built by the Greeks on the borders of Apulia, where the camps of Hannibal once stood, and took it by surrender. He was the founder of the bishopric of Bamberg, and was buried at Bamberg. He brought the defeated Hungarians to the Christian faith, giving his sister in marriage to the King of the Hungarians. He created Conrad the Frank, of this name the second, Emperor, with the lawful votes of the electors added. Those who write say that he and his wife Cunigunda kept perpetual virginity, and that after death they became famous for miracles. Emperor, first designated by the votes of the princely electors, according to the formula of Gregory; he ruled for 22 years. See Blondus, book 3, decade 2; Egnatius, book 3.

units.la: CVNEGVNDA Henrici secundi supradicti Imperatoris vxor fuit: quam castissimam fuisse, quinimo virginitatem perpetuam vnà cum viro obseruasse, memoriæ proditum est. Vide autores quos supra. DN CONRADVS AVGVSTVS GISLAM[?] AVG COR IMP VXO
units.tr: CUNIGUNDA was the wife of the above-mentioned Emperor Henry the Second; it is recorded in memory that she was most chaste, and indeed that she kept perpetual virginity together with her husband. See the authors cited above. LORD CONRAD AUGUSTUS, GISLAM [?] AUG, EMPEROR, WIFE COR

units.la: CONRADVS Francus, huius nominis secundus, successit Henrico proximè supradicto, Imperatorque designatus est, anno mundi 4986. à Christo nato 1024. Hic sub initium imperij, cum videret turbari passim omnia, effecit vt in consortium imperij filius suus eligeretur. Catulos Sueuos, cum Ernesto Sueuiæ Duce, compescuit: ad domandos Hungaros, Hungariam cum exercitu intrauit: res composuit. Burgundi ad eum defecerunt: vnde Burgundia diuisa, altera quæ Campaniam attingit Francis, altera quæ Bisantinos spectat, Imperatori fuit subiecta. Lugdunum, & regnum Arelatense cepit, & subiectum suo imperio administrauit. Mediolanum obsedit, cúmque exitium vrbi minaretur, deterritus oraculo recessit. Inde Romam veniens, à Pontifice coronam accepit: insurgunt Romani, quos reprimit. Ernestus Sueuiæ Dux, nouos iterum motus concitans, à Conrado, in regressu, fugatur, & confoditur: Ducatum donat Hermanno, Ernesti fratri.Imperauit Conradus annos quindecim: dicitur fuisse Othonis ex filia nepos, eius inquam qui Henrico Imperatori successit. Gag. lib.5[?]. sub finem. Æmyl. lib.3. Hic magnis sumptibus extruxit Basilicam Spirensem, in qua cum vxore sua Gisela, seu Gisla sepultus est. Vide Carionis Chron. lib.3.
units.tr: CONRAD the Frank, second of this name, succeeded Henry shortly before mentioned, and was designated Emperor in the year of the world 4986, from the birth of Christ 1024. At the start of his reign, seeing that everything was everywhere in turmoil, he arranged for his son to be chosen as partner in the empire. He held down the Suabian whelps together with Ernest, Duke of Swabia; to subdue the Hungarians he entered Hungary with an army and settled affairs. The Burgundians defected to him, whereby Burgundy was divided: the part reaching to Champagne was made subject to the Franks, the other part, facing Byzantium, was made subject to the Emperor. He took Lyon and the kingdom of Arles, and governed it as subject to his empire. He besieged Milan, and when he threatened the city with destruction, he withdrew, deterred by an oracle. Coming from there to Rome, he received the crown from the Pontiff; the Romans rose up, and he suppressed them. Ernest, Duke of Swabia, stirring up new disturbances, was put to flight by Conrad on his return and was run through; he gave the duchy to Herman, brother of Ernest. Conrad reigned for fifteen years; he is said to have been the grandson of Otto through a daughter, namely of him who succeeded the Emperor Henry. See Gagnier, book 5, near the end; Aimoin, book 3. He built the basilica of Speyer at great expense, in which he was buried with his wife Gisela, or Gisla. See Carion's Chronicle, book 3.

units.la: GISLA, siue Gisela, Regina fuit Burgundica, ex posteritate Caroli, de qua magnæ laudes feruntur, maritum primò hæc habuit Ernestum Sueuiæ Ducem, ex quo duos suscepit filios, Ernestum, qui pulsus est, & Hermannum: postea in matrimonium accepit Conradum. Vide autores quos supra. [?]REX 38 HENRICVS FREX 39[?] PHILIPPVS
units.tr: GISLA, or Gisela, was a Burgundian queen, of the posterity of Charles, and great praises are spoken of her. She first had as husband Ernest, Duke of Swabia, by whom she bore two sons, Ernest, who was driven out, and Herman; afterwards she took Conrad in marriage. See the authors cited above. [?] KING 38, HENRY, KING 39 [?] PHILIP

units.la: HENRICVS huius nominis primus, Roberti Francorum Regis filius, fucccdit patri, regnatque apud Francos anno mundi 4992. à Christo nato 1030. Contendit Henricus hic (minor natu, vt aiunt, sed à patre hæres nuncupatus) cum Roberto fratre, cuius partes Odo Campaniæ, & Balduinus Flandriæ Comites sequuntur: Henrici verò partes Robertus Normaniæ Dux sequitur: priores ab Henrico vincuntur: frater Robertus Ducatu Burgundiæ contentatur. Rodulphus TransIurensis Burgundiæ Rex, regnum Imperatori Conrado dat: Odo Campanus suum iure censet, armisque inuadit: tunc in Comitatum qui ad imperij ditionem, & in Ducatum, qui ad regiam pertineret ditionem, diuiditur Burgundia. Henricus Philippum filium Regem creandum, coronandúmque Remis curat: moriens Balduinum Flandriæ Comitem filiis suis tutorem dat. Vide Aemi.lib.3.Gag.lib.5.Regnat Henricus annos triginta, & sepelitur in æde Diui Dionysij ad Parisios,
units.tr: HENRY, first of this name, son of Robert, King of the Franks, succeeded his father and reigned over the Franks in the year of the world 4992, from the birth of Christ 1030. This Henry (the younger by birth, as they say, but named heir by his father) contended with his brother Robert, whom Odo, Count of Champagne, and Baldwin, Count of Flanders, supported; Robert, Duke of Normandy, supported Henry's side. The former were defeated by Henry; his brother Robert was content with the duchy of Burgundy. Rudolf of Transjura, King of Burgundy, gave his kingdom to the Emperor Conrad; Odo of Champagne claimed it as his own by right and invaded with arms. Then Burgundy was divided into the county, which fell under the imperial dominion, and the duchy, which belonged to the royal dominion. Henry had his son Philip made King and took care that he be crowned at Reims; dying, he gave Baldwin, Count of Flanders, as guardian to his sons. See Aimoin, book 3; Gagnier, book 5. Henry reigned thirty years, and was buried in the church of St Denis near Paris.

units.la: PHILIPPVS Henrici supradicti filius adulescens, succedit patri in regno Franciæ anno mundi 5022. à Christo nato 1060. Balduinus Regis tutor, simulat in Saracenos bellum, quo audaces nobilium animos reprimat. Hoc Rege è Galliis duæ illustres prodiere familiæ, quæ apud exteros duo potentissima regna erexerunt. Gulielmus nothus, Normanorum Dux, Angliam Rege cæso occupat: Gothofredus Bulionius terram sanctam, & Ierusalem postea obtinet 39. obsidionis die, anno mundi 5060. à Christo nato 1098. Obiit Philippus Meleduni, anno regni sui 49. Ad æde Benedicti prope Ligerim sepelitur. Vide Gaguin.lib.6.
units.tr: PHILIP, the young son of the above-mentioned Henry, succeeded his father in the kingdom of France in the year of the world 5022, from the birth of Christ 1060. Baldwin, the King's guardian, feigned war against the Saracens, so that he might restrain the bold spirits of the nobles. In this King's time two illustrious families came forth from Gaul, which set up two very powerful kingdoms among foreigners. William the Bastard, Duke of the Normans, seized England after killing the King; Godfrey of Bouillon afterwards obtained the Holy Land and Jerusalem on the 39th day of the siege, in the year of the world 5060, from the birth of Christ 1098. Philip died at Melun in the 49th year of his reign. He was buried in the church of St Benedict near the Loire. See Gaguin, book 6.

units.la: MELLUSINA, quæ olim apud Mellam & Lusignanum dominabatur (unde forte Mellusinæ nomen accepit) Comitis cuiusdam Pictaviensis soror, aut (ut alij volunt) filia fuit: hæc Raimondo, Comitis cuiusdam filio, seu nepoti, nupsit, ex quo Gotfridum Magni dentis suscepit, atque alios fortissimos milites: idque circiter annum à mundo condito 5040. à Christo nato 1078.regnante apud Francos Philippo huius nominis primo, Roberti, Capeti filij, aut (ut alij censent) Henrici, Roberti filij, filio: non autem regnante Philippo illo secundo, qui Ludovici filius,fuit: ut malè quidem, Aquitaniæ Annales ferunt. Quod autem fingitur fuisse Mellusina semiserpens, id fortasse non absurdū fuerit fortilegio tribuere, cuius peritissima esset, sicuti etiam tunc temporis ars magica erat vulgatissima: vel quòd pro insigni tale etiam monstrum ipsa gestaret. Vide Annales Aquitaniæ.
units.tr: MELUSINE, who once held lordship at Melle and Lusignan (whence perhaps she took the name Melusine), was the sister, or (as others would have it) the daughter, of a certain Count of Poitou. She married Raymond, son or grandson of a certain count, from whom she bore Geoffrey of the Great Tooth and other very brave soldiers; this was about the year of the world 5040, from the birth of Christ 1078, in the reign among the Franks of Philip, first of this name, son of Robert, son of Hugh Capet (or, as others judge, son of Henry, son of Robert), and not in the reign of that second Philip, who was the son of Louis; so the Annals of Aquitaine wrongly report. But as for the fiction that Melusine was half serpent, this perhaps would not be absurd to attribute to sorcery, in which she was most skilled, just as magic art was then very widespread; or because she herself bore such a monster as a distinguishing emblem. See the Annals of Aquitaine.

units.la: GOTFRIDUS Magni dentis, Mellusinæ supradictæ filius, unà cum fratre, Gotfridum Bolionium, sive Bilionensem, in expeditione Ierosolimitana secutus est, ubi strenuum se militem præstitit. Ab hoc Gotfrido Magni dentis originem traxere Cypri insulæ Reges complures, cognominis Lusignani. Videto Annalium Aquitaniæ, partem tertiam: nam in partes quatuor digestus est liber 15.
units.tr: GEOFFREY of the Great Tooth, son of the above-mentioned Melusine, together with his brother, followed Godfrey of Bouillon, or Bouillon, on the Jerusalem expedition, where he showed himself a valiant soldier.
