He is generous towards those whom he has judged worthy of his benefits, for this wise man does not fail to know how each person ought to bestow benefits on anyone at all. Moreover, he excels in an admirable knowledge of almost all things, and especially in the doctrine of theology, and he shows himself in deed such as he certainly wishes to be seen. So great is his uprightness that, just as he surpasses all others in authority and dignity, so he most easily outdoes all others in the integrity of his life and conduct. How inclined his mind is towards the Catholic religion and the whole commonwealth is shown by that most learned oration which he delivered at Blois, in the public assembly of the orders of France.

units.la: HENRIC. BORBON. D. G. REX NAVAR.[?]
units.tr: HENRY BOURBON, BY THE GRACE OF GOD KING OF NAVARRE.
MARGARET, BY THE GRACE OF GOD QUEEN OF NAVARRE.

units.la: HENRICVS Borbonius Rex Nauarrae, patrem amisit cum nondum adolescentiae primos annos attigisset: & patre mortuo (ex vulnere accepto in obsidione Rothomagensi) mater eum accuratè instituendum & formandum curauit. Deinde grandior effectus, cùm Rex Carolus Nonus esset in ciuitate Turonum, adductus est vt rege consentiente, nuptiae fierent inter eum & Margaretam illustrissimam Regis sororem: & spōsione[?] facta, 10. Iunij 1572. cum pararentur nuptiae, Regina Nauarrae huius mater, fatis cessit Lutetiae: unde maximum dolorem tulit filius, qui tamen decimo octauo Augusti, cum apparatu magnificentissimo, in aede diuae Mariae, nupsit clarissimae Margaretae Regis sorori, nunc serenissimae Nauarrae Reginae. Hic post tumultum diei D. Bartholomei, reuocatus à Caluini doctrina, quorundam virorum doctorum admonitionibus religionem, in qua fuerat à matre institutus, adiurasse dicitur & Ecclesiae Romanae sese submisisse, quodquidem satis liquet ex instructionibus nobilissimi Ioannis Durefortij, Domini de Duras, qui missus fuit ad Pontificem, vt eius sanctitati & sedi Apostolicae, eiusdem serenissimi regis voluntatem & obedientiam offerret: quod etiam apparet mandatis ipsius Regis, quibus subditis suis imperauit vt catholicè viuerent, & Ecclesiasticos, in pristinũ eorum gradum quàm primùm restituerent. Nescio an eius dictis paruerint.
units.tr: Henry Bourbon, King of Navarre, lost his father when he had not yet reached the first years of adolescence; and after his father's death (from a wound received at the siege of Rouen) his mother took care to have him carefully instructed and formed. Later, when he had grown older, while King Charles IX was in the city of Tours, it was arranged, with the king's consent, that a marriage should take place between him and Margaret, the most illustrious sister of the king. The betrothal having been made, on 10 June 1572, while the wedding was being prepared, the mother of this man, the Queen of Navarre, died at Paris; this caused the son the greatest grief. Nevertheless, on 18 August, with the most magnificent ceremony, in the church of the divine Mary, he married the most renowned Margaret, sister of the king, now the most serene Queen of Navarre. Afterwards, following the tumult of St Bartholomew's Day, he is said to have been recalled from the doctrine of Calvin by the admonitions of certain learned men, and to have sworn to the religion in which his mother had instructed him and to have submitted himself to the Roman Church. This is quite clear from the instructions of the most noble John Duresort, Lord of Duras, who was sent to the Pope to offer to his holiness and to the Apostolic See the will and obedience of the same most serene king; it also appears from the orders of the king himself, by which he commanded his subjects to live as Catholics and to restore the ecclesiastics to their former rank as soon as possible. I do not know whether they obeyed his commands.

units.la: ILLVSTRISSIMA Margareta Regis Henrici 2. filia, & Regũ Francisci secundi, Caroli noni, & nunc Christianissimi Francorum & Polonorum Regis Henrici tertij soror, Henrico Borbonio Regi Nauarrae illustrissimo nupsit, decimo octauo Augusti, anno salutis 1572. omnibus regiis virtutibus & summa pulchritudine dotata.
units.tr: The most illustrious Margaret, daughter of King Henry II, and sister of the kings Francis II, Charles IX, and now the most Christian King of the French and Poles, Henry III, married the most illustrious Henry Bourbon, King of Navarre, on 18 August in the year of salvation 1572, endowed with all royal virtues and the greatest beauty.

units.la: RODOLPHUS secundus Austrius Maximiliani secundi Imperatoris filius, nunc Imperator Romanorū, paternæ virtutis verè heres creditur, quòd eius vestigia, in moderandis imperij habenis sapientissimè equidem, ex quo pater vitam cum morte mutauit, sit semper sequutus. Unde laudatissimi certè & prudentissimi Imperatoris nomen adepturus est qui Austriam gloriā, tā ingentē, tótque trophęis insignitam, magis ac magis augebit, quique spem dat omnibus imperio subditis, futurū ut ab maiorū suorū præstantissimis virtutibus ne latū quidem unguē discedat, & cū res præclaras & magno Imperatore dignas egerit, longè maiores etiam quotidie expectentur, unde magni Imperatoris famam, omnis ætas sit celebratura. Fuit coronatus Imperator anno salutis 1576.
units.tr: Rudolf II of Austria, son of the Emperor Maximilian II, now Emperor of the Romans, is believed to be a true heir of his father's virtue, because he has always followed his father's footsteps in governing the reins of the empire most wisely, ever since his father exchanged life for death. Hence he will obtain the name of a most praiseworthy and most prudent emperor, who will increase more and more the glory of Austria, so great and so distinguished by so many trophies, and who gives hope to all subjects of the empire that, from the most excellent virtues of his ancestors, he will not depart even the breadth of a fingernail; and that, when he has performed illustrious deeds worthy of a great emperor, far greater ones will be expected every day, so that every age will celebrate the fame of a great emperor. He was crowned emperor in the year of salvation 1576.

units.la: HERCULES Franciscus Valesius, Dux Andegauensis, Henrici secundi filius & tertij nūc Regis nostri Christianissimi frater, virtute clarissimus, iisdem titulis provinciisque potitur, quibus, vivente Carolo nono, eius laudatissimæ memoriæ frater Henricus tertius potiebatur, antequam utriusque regni & Poloniæ & Frāciæ fasces & imperiū suscepisset: quòd Rex charissimi fratris animum cognouerit erga se & Rempublicā valdè propensum: quæ tot annorū spacio, cruentis bellis civilibus, latrociniis, exustionibus, rapinis atque incendiis labefactata, recreari cœpit ex quo Rex prudentissimus, eū suæ maiestatis Locum-tenentem constituit, & universæ tanti Regni militiæ præfecit. Nam post eius è Polonia reditū, cum quidam ab eius imperio defecisset, illustrissimus iste Dux, eos ita repressit, ut alios vicerit, alios ad deditionē coëgerit. Est tam addictus omnium virtutum generi, ut nunquam otiosus videatur, suísque prodesse maximè cupiat. HENRICVS III FR[?] ANC. ET POLON. REX[?] LVDOVICA FRANC[?] REGINA[?]
units.tr: Hercules Francis of Valois, Duke of Anjou, son of Henry II and brother of our now most Christian king Henry III, most renowned for his virtue, holds the same titles and provinces which his brother Henry III, of most praiseworthy memory, held while Charles IX was living, before he had assumed the rods and rule of both kingdoms, Poland and France. This is because the king knew his brother's disposition towards himself and the commonwealth to be very well inclined; the commonwealth, shaken over so many years by bloody civil wars, brigandage, burnings, plunderings and fires, began to be restored since the most prudent king appointed him his lieutenant and placed him in charge of all the army of so great a kingdom. For after his return from Poland, when a certain man had revolted from his rule, this most illustrious duke repressed them in such a way that he conquered some and forced others to surrender. He is so devoted to every kind of virtue that he never seems idle, and he most eagerly desires to be of help to his own people.

units.la: HENRICVS III. Christianissimus Francorum, & Polonorum, Rex regni administrationem suscepit, post mortem fratris Caroli noni, anno salutis 1574. Nam in Polonia certior factus de fratris interitu, in Galliam quàm primum properat: id quod videre licet in libris de ea re impressis. Plures Galliæ primates, obviam ierūt, ut eius maiestatem salutarent, eíque de tam fœlici & pernecessario Gallis adventu, summè gratularētur. Augustæ Taurinorū exceptus fuit valde humaniter à duce Sabaudiæ & illustrissima Margareta, ubi quasdam urbes transalpinas Duci reddidit. Ibidem aliquid propositum de componendis Gallicis tumultibus, sed frustrà, magno Reipublicæ damno. Interea Dux Mompenserius princeps virtute clarus, nonnullas urbes, in regione Pictonum, expugnatione capit. Rex Lugdunum venit, magno Lugdunensium applausu & ovatione, sub finem Augusti, ubi edictum constituit, quoquidem his ignoscit, qui tempore fratris sui Caroli noni arma ceperūt inimica, promittitque, si sibi obediant, securum in privatas eorum domos reditū. Fuit sacratus in urbe Rhemorū, ab illustrissimo Cardinale Guisio, eius loci Archiepiscopo, 13. Februarij. 1575. & 15. die eiusdem mensis nobilissimam Ludovica Lotharenā clarissimi Comitis Vaudemontij filiam, sibi matrimonio iunxit. Cúmque toto hoc anno, omnia belli incendio flagrarent, & miserè populus à militibus vexaretur, huic humanissimus Rex opem tulit, Pacificationis Edicto publicato Lutetiæ 14. Maij 1576. Deum precemur ut tātus Rex diutissimè Galliæ cōservetur, vivatq; annos Nestoreos.
units.tr: Henry III, the most Christian King of the French and the Poles, took up the administration of the kingdom after the death of his brother Charles IX, in the year of salvation 1574. For, having learned in Poland of his brother's death, he hastens to France as soon as possible; this may be seen in the books printed on that matter. Several chief men of France went to meet him, to greet his majesty and to congratulate him most warmly on his so happy and most necessary arrival for the French. At Turin he was received very kindly by the Duke of Savoy and by the most illustrious Margaret, where he handed back some towns beyond the Alps to the Duke. There a proposal was made about settling the French disturbances, but in vain, to the great loss of the commonwealth. Meanwhile Duke Montpensier, a prince distinguished for his valour, took some towns in the region of Poitou by storm. The king came to Lyons, to the great applause and rejoicing of the people of Lyons, towards the end of August, where he issued an edict by which he pardoned those who in the time of his brother Charles IX had taken up arms against the crown, and promised that, if they obeyed him, they would have a safe return to their private homes. He was consecrated in the city of Reims, by the most illustrious Cardinal Guise, Archbishop of that place, on 13 February 1575; and on the 15th day of the same month he joined in marriage to himself the most noble Louise of Lorraine, daughter of the most distinguished Count of Vaudémont. And since, throughout this whole year, everything was ablaze with the fire of war, and the people were miserably harassed by soldiers, the most humane king brought help to them by publishing the Edict of Pacification at Paris on 14 May 1576. Let us pray God that so great a king may be preserved for France for a very long time, and may live the years of Nestor.

units.la: LVDOVICA Lotharena, clarissimi Comitis Vaudemontij filia, Christianissimi Francorum & Polonorum Regis Henrici tertij uxor, tantum præstat cęteris omnibus heroinis formæ admirabili & prope divina elegātia, quantâ animi sublimitate nobilitate, morûque & grauitate & humanitate plusquâ insigni. IO. ANT. BAIFIVS BERN. S. GIRARDVS
units.tr: Louise of Lorraine, daughter of the most distinguished Count of Vaudémont, wife of Henry III, Most Christian King of the French and Poles, surpasses all other heroines in admirable beauty and almost divine elegance, as much as in loftiness of mind, nobility, and in morals, gravity and courtesy, which are more than remarkable. JOHN ANTHONY BAIF, BERNARD GIRARD

units.la: IOANNES Antonius Bayfius à secretis Regij cubiculi, oriundus à stirpe doctorū hominū nobilis Bayfiorū familiæ, ex Andegauensi prouincia, egregius poeta Græcus, Latinus & Gallicus, inter primos fuit qui tetrum illud ignorationis monstrum fugans è Gallia, introduxit veterē illam ac iucundā Græcorum ac Latinorū Poesin, mensuramque carminū cum orthographia metris accōmodata: idque ad cōmunem Musices usum. Et unà cū Petro Ronsardo & Remigio Bellaquæo (qui uno fere tēpore tanquā ex equo Troiano, ut fertur, é schola Io. Aurati prodiere) Callimachum, Pindarū, Horatium, excitauit é mortis caligine. Immensæ suæ doctrinæ & eruditioni indicio sunt eius opera, edita & edenda. Viget adhuc Parisiis scribens perdocta poemata, quæ breui editurus est in lucem.
units.tr: John Antony de Baïf, secretary of the king's bedchamber, sprung from a stock of learned men of the noble family of the Baïfs, from the province of Anjou, an outstanding poet in Greek, Latin and French, was among the first who, putting to flight that foul monster of ignorance, brought out of France that old and pleasant poetry of the Greeks and Latins, and the measure of verses fitted to metres together with orthography, and this for common use in music. And together with Pierre de Ronsard and Remy Belleau (who came forth almost at the same time, as is said, like the men from the Trojan horse, from the school of Jean Dorat), he revived Callimachus, Pindar and Horace from the darkness of death. The works he has published and is yet to publish are evidence of his immense learning and erudition. He is still alive and living at Paris, writing very learned poems, which he is about to bring out into the light shortly.

units.la: BERNARDVS Girardæus Dominus de Haillan. à Secretis Regis, & eiusdem Historiographus, elegāter scripsit Gallico idiomate historiam regum Frācię, ab eorū origine ad Carolum usque eius nominis septimū, antea fere mendosam, ob assentationem Gallicorum scriptorum erga suos reges, & incuriā externorum, aut eorundē male affectum in nostrates animum: seu certe propter æmulationē aliquam, qua detrahebāt nationi Gallicæ. Veritatem (oculū historię) pro scopo habuit, ad quā omnē suam ita retulit industriam, ut (quando de Regibus, ministris, magistratibus & subditis sermone instituit) deprimat ea quæ digna vituperio sunt & reprehensione, & efferat quę laudem in iis comereri iudicauit, Virtuti præmium suum, hoc est laudem, vitio vituperationem deferens. Neque unquà regibus suis & nationi proprię adulatus est, ne mutilatā aliquā parte faceret historiam suam. Ideoque veri & integri Historici nomē adeptus est. Scripsit & alia pleraque Latinè & Gallicè, cùm numerosa tum soluta oratione: quæ omnia digna lectione sunt, & præcipuè is liber qui de Statu & successu rerum Gallicarum inscribitur. FRANC. BELLEFOR. ANDR. THEVET. COSMOG.
units.tr: BERNARDUS Girardus, Lord of Haillan, Secretary to the King and his Historiographer, wrote elegantly in the French language a history of the kings of France, from their origin down to Charles VII, which before was largely faulty, owing to the flattery of French writers toward their own kings, and the carelessness of foreigners, or the ill disposition of these toward our nation; or certainly because of some rivalry by which they belittled the French nation. He took truth, the eye of history, as his aim, and referred all his diligence to it, so that (when he discourses about kings, ministers, magistrates and subjects) he lowers those things that deserve blame and reproach, and extols those things which he judged worthy of praise, rendering to virtue its reward, that is praise, and to vice blame. Nor did he ever flatter his kings or his own nation, lest he make his history maimed in some part. Therefore he obtained the name of a true and upright historian. He also wrote many other works in Latin and French, both in verse and in prose, all of which are worth reading, and especially the book entitled On the State and Success of French Affairs. FRANC. BELLEFOR. ANDR. THEVET. COSMOG.

units.la: FRANCISCVS Belleforestus Comming.ob editionem Carlaidos, Tragicarum enarrationum, Cōcionum militarium, Historiæ uniuersi orbis, Cosmographiæ, Annalium Franciæ,& innumerorum aliorum operum quę edidit,iure dici potest Ornamentum linguæ Gallicæ.Nec minus hunc mirabilem reddit summus in dicendo lepos, quam eius labor assiduus. Scripsit enim (cum vix annum ætatis suæ quadragesimum attigerit) plura volumina quam quiuis alius, & scribit[?] quotidie. Catalogum suorum operum habebis in Bibliotheca Gallica Antonij Verderij.
units.tr: FRANCISCUS Belleforestus, Commingeois, may rightly be called an Ornament of the French tongue, on account of his edition of Carlaida, Tragic Narrations, Military Harangues, the History of the Whole World, Cosmography, the Annals of France, and countless other works which he has published. Nor does his supreme charm in writing make him any less admirable than his constant labour. For he has written (though he has scarcely reached forty years of age) more volumes than anyone else, and he writes still every day. You will have a catalogue of his works in the French Bibliotheca of Antoine Verdier.

units.la: ANDREAS Theuetus, Engolismensis, Cosmographus Regius,terras veteribus & neotericis ignotas perlustrauit, cum nullus antea fuisset ausus optare, ne dicam aggredi nauigationem ultra nostrum Tropicum. Atque hoc iter susceptum ad quatuor mundi partes per spatium 17. annorum persecutus; Cosmographiam construxit,in qua mira refert: quod opus excusum est in folio & in duos diuisum tomos, Parisijs apud Petrum Lhullier, & Gulielmum Chauldiere. PET. PRIMALDAVS ANT. VERDERIVS D. VALLISPRIVATVS[?]
units.tr: ANDREAS Thevet, of Angoulême, Royal Cosmographer, traversed lands unknown to the ancients and moderns alike, when no one before him had dared even to wish, not to say attempt, a voyage beyond our Tropic. Having pursued this journey through the four parts of the world over a span of seventeen years, he constructed a Cosmography, in which he reports marvels; this work was printed in folio and divided into two volumes, at Paris, by Pierre L'Huillier and Guillaume Chaudière. PET. PRIMALDAVS ANT. VERDERIVS D. VALLISPRIVATVS

units.la: PETRVS Primaldayus, Andegauensis, Scutifer, dominus à Primaldaya & Barrea, Academiam Gallicam scripsit in qua per Dialogum non minus doctè quam ornatè de rectâ morum informatione, ac de ratione bene beatèque viuendi in quouis vitæ genere disputat. Atque huius operis beneficio debet in eorum numero constitui qui sua ætate floruerūt in bene dicēdo. Eóque maiore laurea dignus est, quod armis dat operam & literis. Prior huius Academiæ pars tam fœliciter excepta fuit ab omnibus iis qui fauent literis; vt motus fuerit ad editionem alterius partis, quæ simul typis mandata est.
units.tr: PETRUS Primaldaye, of Anjou, Esquire, Lord of Primaldaye and Barrea, wrote the French Academy, in which, through a Dialogue, he discourses no less learnedly than elegantly on the right formation of morals, and on the method of living well and happily in every kind of life. And by the benefit of this work he ought to be counted among those who flourished in his age in good speaking. And he is all the more worthy of the laurel because he devotes himself both to arms and to letters. The first part of this Academy was so favourably received by all who favour letters that he was moved to publish the second part, which was printed at the same time.

units.la: ANTONIVS Verderius, Scutifer, dominus Vallispriuatæ & Luriaci, Regis consiliarius & Ærarij Regij apud Lugdunenses Antigraphæus, oriundus ex Verderiorum familia Foresiensis prouinciæ; orbatus cum esset patre menses tres natus, Mater eius nomine Omnisanēta Terrassa, curauit postquam grandior euasit paulò, vt instituereter in literis: in quas tam amico fuit animo, vt nihil præter virtutem & scientias amplecteretur. Magna fuit suorum expectatio de illo: & nisi rei Familiaris administrationem suscepisset, vxorem ducens annum agens duntaxat xix. dici non potest quantos fructus percepisset. Quamuis ab eo tempore literarum studia commiscuit cum disciplina militari & publicorum munerum administratione: nec parum profuere vigiliæ suæ, ex quibus scripta permulta emanarunt: videlicet, Poemata Gallica, Prosopographia, Variæ lectiones, in Aristophanis Plutum comment. Bartholomæi Tegij responsa, Bibliotheca Gallica, Imagines deorū qui ab antiquis colebantur, partim ex Italico sermone in Gallicū versæ, partim de propria industria adauctæ, & alia pleraq;. Habet etiā præ manibus Senecæ philosophi omnia opera in Gallicā linguā versa, cum annotationibus & scholiis, quæ breui in lucē editurus est.
units.tr: ANTONIUS Verdier, Esquire, Lord of Vaux-Privé and Luriace, Councillor of the King and Antigrapheus of the Royal Treasury at Lyon, descended from the Verdier family of the province of Forez. Left fatherless at the age of three months, his mother, Omnisainte Terrasse, took care, when he grew a little older, that he should be educated in letters; and he was so fond of them that he embraced nothing but virtue and the sciences. Great was his family's expectation of him; and had he not taken up the management of his household affairs, marrying when he was only nineteen, one cannot say how many fruits he would have gathered. Yet from that time he combined his literary studies with military discipline and the administration of public offices; nor did his night vigils profit him little, from which very many writings have issued forth: namely, French Poems, Prosopography, Various Readings, a commentary on Aristophanes' Plutus, the Responses of Bartholomew Taillet, the French Bibliotheca, Images of the gods worshipped by the ancients, partly translated from Italian into French, partly enlarged by his own diligence, and many others. He also has in hand all the works of the philosopher Seneca, turned into the French language, with annotations and scholia, which he is about to publish shortly.

units.la: [Portrait medallions: left "IO. GORREVS D. M.D."; right "LAVR. IOVBERTVS." — printed as legends on the medallions]
units.tr: [Portrait medallions: left "IO. GORREVS D. M.D."; right "LAVR. IOVBERTVS."]

units.la: IOANNES Gorreus Parisiensis, Doctor Medicus, Latine scripsit Definitionum Medicarum libros x x iiii. literis Græcis distinctos, & iuxta Alphabeti ordinem. Ex Græco etiam Hipocratis Iusiurandum, De arte, De antiqua medicina, De medico, Latina ciuitate donauit. Vitam cum morte commutauit non multo postquam Christianiss. Henricus iii. Regni Franciæ suscepit gubernacula. Quantæ doctrinæ erat testantur nonnulli uersus Iacobi Greuini eius discipuli in limine Poematum Theriacōn, & Alexipharmacōn Nicandri Poëtæ Græci ab eodem Greuino è Græco uersibus Gallicis expressorum & eidem Gorreo dicatorum.
units.tr: IOANNES Gorreus, of Paris, Doctor of Medicine, wrote in Latin the books of Medical Definitions, twenty-four in number, distinguished by Greek letters and arranged according to the order of the alphabet. He also translated from Greek into Latin the Oath of Hippocrates, On the Art, On Ancient Medicine, and On the Physician, granting them the citizenship of Latin. He exchanged life for death not long after the most Christian Henry III took up the governance of the kingdom of France. The extent of his learning is attested by some verses of his disciple Jacques Grévin, prefixed to the Poems of the Theriaca and Alexipharmaca of the Greek poet Nicander, which the same Grévin rendered from the Greek into French verse and dedicated to this Gorreus.

units.la: LAVRENTIVS Ioubertus, Valentinus Delphinas, Medicus Regius, post obitum Gulielmi Rondeletij professoris Regij & Cancellarij in schola Monspeliensi, in huius locum suffectus est, tanquam omnium qui tunc ibi degebant dignissimus: quod munus exercet hoc tempore: nec minus celebratur eius experientia in re medica, quam doctæ & exquisitæ illius Lucubrationes quas edidit tam in Latina quam vernacula lingua. Has videre licebit in Bibliotheca Gallica.
units.tr: LAURENTIUS Joubert, of Valence in Dauphiné, Royal Physician, after the death of Guillaume Rondelet, royal professor and chancellor at the school of Montpellier, was appointed in his place, as the most worthy of all who were then living there; he holds this office at present. His experience in medicine is no less celebrated than those learned and exquisite Lucubrations which he has published in both Latin and the vernacular tongue. These may be seen in the French Bibliotheca.

units.la: APPENDIX ALIQUOT IMAGINUM ANTIQUARUM. GULIELMUS ROVILLIUS LECTORI.
units.tr: APPENDIX OF SOME ANCIENT IMAGES. GUILLAUME ROVILLE TO THE READER.

units.la: Hoc nostro qualicunque Iconum Promptuario ferme ad exitum perducto, oblata nobis fuerunt pauca aliquot Illustrium virorum, qui iamdudum emicuerunt, effigies. Quas, quòd pauca admodum essent, nonnullis aliis, prout nobis diligenter inuestigantibus reperire licuit, augere conati sumus. Eas ergo sub finem huiusce de Iconibus Libelli, velut additamentum, Benewolentiæ tuæ offerimus. Quibus in-terea frui poteris: dum proxima editione singulas, ordine suo, ac tempore quo illustres illi viri floruerunt, inseri ac disponi, Deo auxiliante, curabimus.
units.tr: Now that this little storehouse of images of ours is nearly brought to an end, a few portraits of some illustrious men who have long shone forth were offered to us. Since these were very few, we have tried to enlarge them with several others, which we were able to find by careful investigation. We therefore offer them to your goodwill at the end of this little book on images, as an addition. You may enjoy them in the meantime; in the next edition, with God's help, we will take care to insert and arrange each one in its proper order and at the time when these illustrious men flourished.

units.la: HIPPOCRATES domo & genere Doriensis, vrbe Cous, Heraclidæ & Phænaretis filius, natus est primo anno LXXX. Olympiadis, anno scilicet mundi 3505. vt computat Funccius. Vir ingenio summus & dignus qui medicinæ præcepta, sparsa vndique & dissipata, primus in ordinem redigeret, diuinisque suis scriptis illustraret: in quibus nullum est verbum, quod non ex penetralibus naturæ depromptum, & profunda sapientia imbutum esse videatur. Populares suos Græcos tanto est amore prosequutus, vt ad Artaxerxem Persarum regem, quamuis maximis donis ab Hystanide Hellespontiorum præfecto euocatus proficisci noluerit. Mortuus est Larissæ, post Democritum, annos natus centum & quatuor: vel vt alij referunt centum & nouem. Honores eosdem cum Hercule à grata Græcia obtinuit, quod venientem ab Illyriis pestem prædixisset, eíque malo per discipulos suos occurrisset, vt Sabellicus scribit libro decimo, capite octauo. Statua ei posita, capite tecto pileo. Filios reliquit Thessalum & Draconem.
units.tr: Hippocrates, by home and birth a Dorian, of the city of Cos, son of Heraclides and Phaenarete, was born in the first year of the 80th Olympiad, that is, in the year of the world 3505, as Funccius computes. A man of the highest talent and worthy to have reduced the precepts of medicine, scattered and dispersed everywhere, into order for the first time, and to have illuminated them with his divine writings. In these there is not a word that does not seem to have been drawn from the innermost secrets of nature and steeped in profound wisdom. He showed such love for his fellow Greeks that, although summoned by Hystanes, the governor of the Hellespont, with very great gifts, he refused to go to Artaxerxes, king of the Persians. He died at Larissa, after Democritus, at the age of 104, or, as others report, 109. He obtained the same honours as Hercules from grateful Greece, because he had foretold a plague coming from the Illyrians and had met that evil through his disciples, as Sabellicus writes in book 10, chapter 8. A statue was erected to him with his head covered by a cap. He left sons, Thessalus and Draco.

units.la: HERODOTVS Halicarnasseus (vt author est Suidas) claróque apud suos genere ortus, quem Cicero libro secundo de Legibus patrem historiæ appellat, anno mundi 3522. vt supputat Funccius, Græcè scripsit historiam libris nouem, quorum quilibet Musæ nomine inscribitur. Cœpit à Cyro Persarum rege, vt scribit Volater. lib. 15. Anthrop. Fuit omnibus tyrannis infensissimus. Quare cùm patriâ à Lygdamo tyranno videret occupatâ, secessit in Samū: eóque extincto, quò ad suos rediisset, inuidiæ obnoxius factus, sponte Thurii Atheniensium colonia in exilium prosectus est, vbi etiâ mortuus esse dicitur & sepultus. Plinius asserit lib. 12. cap. 14. eũ Thurij historiá scripsisse: & quidē Ionicè eam confecit, laxior Thucydide. Quapropter hunc Liuio, illum Salustio, Quintilianus comparat.
units.tr: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (as the author Suidas says), sprung from a family distinguished among his own people, whom Cicero in the second book of On the Laws calls the father of history, wrote a history in Greek in nine books, each of which is inscribed with the name of a Muse, in the year of the world 3522, as Funccius reckons. He began with Cyrus, king of the Persians, as Volaterranus writes in book 15 of Anthropology. He was most hostile to all tyrants. Therefore, when he saw his homeland occupied by the tyrant Lygdamis, he withdrew to Samos; and when that man had been killed, he returned to his own people, but, having become subject to envy, he went of his own accord into exile with the Athenian colony at Thurii, where he is said to have died and been buried. Pliny asserts in book 12, chapter 14, that he wrote a history of Thurii; and indeed he composed it in the Ionic manner, looser than Thucydides. For this reason Quintilian compares him with Livy and the other with Sallust.

units.la: (Portrait medallion, left, labelled THEOPHRASTVS; portrait medallion, right, labelled ÆSCVLAPIVS. Not transcribed as text: these are woodcut images.)
units.tr: The passage contains only two woodcut portrait medallions, one labelled THEOPHRASTVS on the left and one labelled ÆSCVLAPIVS on the right; there is no printed text to translate.

units.la: <bl>THEOPHRASTVS</bl> Eresius Aristotelis discipulus fuit, magistrū imitatus est, & in Physicis multa scripsit: præsertim vero doctissimos illos commentarios de plātarū historia & causis. Plurima sortitus est nomina: primū enim Tyrtamus appellabatur: deinde Euphrastus est appellatus, & postremò Theophrastus, ob oris & eloquētię suauitatem propemodū diuinam. Hic Peripateticorum doctissimus & eloquentissimus fuit, Aristotelis præceptoris in schola successor, quiquidem dicere solebat, doctum hominē ex omnibus solū neque alienis locis peregrinū esse, neque inopem amicorum. Habuit discipulos ad duo millia. Opera eius à Diogene commemorantur. Floruit anno mundi 3645. Excessit è vita admodum senex. Vide Laertium, Suidam, & Strabonem.
units.tr: <bl>THEOPHRASTUS</bl> of Eresus was a pupil of Aristotle, imitated his master, and wrote many works on natural philosophy, above all those most learned commentaries on the history and causes of plants. He received a great many names: at first he was called Tyrtamus, then he was called Euphrastus, and finally Theophrastus, on account of the almost divine sweetness of his face and eloquence. He was the most learned and eloquent of the Peripatetics, the successor of Aristotle, his teacher, in the school; he used to say that a learned man alone, of all men, is neither a stranger in foreign places nor poor in friends. He had about two thousand disciples. His works are mentioned by Diogenes. He flourished in the year of the world 3645. He departed from life at a very advanced age. See Laertius, Suidas, and Strabo.

units.la: <bl>ÆSCVLAPIVS</bl> Apollinis filius fuit, cui plerique inuētū medicinę referūt acceptū: at potius Apollinem eius patrem, primum esse qui medicinę vsum attulerit dicendum est, vnde meruerit deitatem: idcirco dicit Ouidius libr. 1. Metamorph.
units.tr: <bl>ÆSCULAPIUS</bl> was a son of Apollo, to whom most people refer the discovery of medicine; but it must rather be said that Apollo, his father, was the first to bring in the use of medicine, and for this he deserved to be deified. Hence Ovid says in book 1 of the Metamorphoses:

units.la: Inuentum Medi-ina meum est, opifexque per orbem Dicor, & herbarum subiecta potentia nobis.
units.tr: The invention of medicine is mine, and I am called the maker of help throughout the world, and the power of herbs is subject to me.

units.la: Sed filius qui Romā adductus fuit, anno mundi 3673. vrbis 461. in ea adeo excelluit, vt mortuum Hippolytū fingatur ad vitam reuocasse, & Androgeum Minois filium, ab Athenien-sibus interfectum, vt recitat Propertius lib. 2. Hic fulmine ictus periit, quod medicinę arcana discipulos docere noluissęt: vnde ars medica per quadringentos annos, vsque ad Hippocratis tempora (qui eam erexit) intermortua, magno hominum detrimento, iacuit.
units.tr: But the son, who was brought to Rome in the year of the world 3673, in the year 461 of the city, excelled there to such a degree that he is said to have restored Hippolytus, who was dead, to life, and Androgeos, son of Minos, killed by the Athenians, as Propertius relates in book 2. He perished by a thunderbolt, because he would not teach the secrets of medicine to his disciples; from then on the medical art lay dormant for four hundred years, until the time of Hippocrates (who restored it), to the great detriment of mankind.

units.la: TITVS Liuius nobilis historiæ Romanæ scriptor,patria Patauinus, natus est anno ab vrbe condita D C.XCIIII. anno mundi 3095. Hûc Caius princeps tanquâ verbosum insectatur: Pollio verò tanquam Patauinitatem redolentem. Quintiliano maximè laudatur,eúmque Herodoto comparat, in cocionibus præsertim:suadétque pueris ediscendum,vt Ciceronis imitatorem. De hoc Hieronymus ad Paulinũ sic scribit,Ad T.Liuium lacteo eloquentiæ fonte manãtem,de vltimis Hispaniæ Galliarúmque finibus,quofdã venifle nobiles legimus,& quos ad cõtemplationem fui Roma non traxerat,vnius hominis fama perduxit.Habuit illa ætas inauditû omnibus seculis celebrandúmque miraculum,vt tantâ vrbem ingressi, aliud extra vrbẽ quærerent. Excessit Paduæ,anno quinto imperij Tiberij, ætatis autem 70. mundi, 3983. salutis nostræ, 21.
units.tr: TITUS Livius, the noble writer of Roman history, a native of Padua, was born in the year 694 from the founding of the city, in the year of the world 3095. Gaius the emperor attacks him as verbose; Pollio, however, as smelling of Paduan provincialism. Quintilian praises him highly and compares him with Herodotus, especially in speeches, and advises that boys should learn him by heart as an imitator of Cicero. Jerome writes of him thus to Paulinus: "We read that noble men came to Titus Livius, who flows with the milk-like fount of eloquence, from the farthest limits of Spain and Gaul, and those whom Rome had not drawn to contemplate himself, the fame of one man brought to him. That age had a miracle unheard of and worthy of celebration in all centuries: that men who had entered so great a city sought another outside the city." He died at Padua, in the fifth year of the reign of Tiberius, in the seventieth year of his age, in the year of the world 3983, of our salvation 21.

units.la: DIOSCORIDES Anazarbeus Medicus, magnæ existimationis, Marci Antonij & Cleopatræ familiaris fuit. Scripsit plura ad medicinam maximè spectatia[?]:libros 5. de medica materia & vnum de lethalibus venenis,eorúmque præcautione & curatione:déque notis quæ morsus iétúfue[?] animaliũ venenum relinquentium sequuntur,& eorum curatione.Eiusdem extant à capite vsque ad pedes libri duo Græci,in Bibliotheca Augustę Vindelicorũ, libri duo de medicamentis simplicibus paratu facilibus, secundum morbos & affectus corporis digesti, extant etiá manuscripti Græcè in Bibliotheca Augustana, quos Ioannes Moibanus medicus transtulit,& opus propter ipsius immaturam mortem, nondum absolutum Conradus Gesnerus perfecit. Additæ sunt annotationes &Græcus contextus, Dioscoridis item & Stephani Atheniensis medicorum Alphabetum Empiricum Græcè manuscriptum aliud à paratu facilibus Dioscoridis,extat apud Gasparum Vuolphium medicum. Ferûtur & multa alia Dioscoridis. Floruit circiter annum mundi 3918.
units.tr: DIOSCORIDES of Anazarbus, a physician of great repute, was a friend of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. He wrote several works chiefly concerning medicine: five books on medical materials and one on deadly poisons, their prevention and cure, and on the signs that follow bites or stings of animals that leave poison behind, and their cure. Two Greek books of his are extant, from head to foot, in the Library of Augsburg; two books on simple medicines, easy to prepare, arranged according to diseases and conditions of the body, also exist in manuscript in Greek in the Augsburg Library, which the physician Johannes Moibanus translated; and because of his premature death the work, not yet finished, was completed by Conrad Gesner. Annotations and the Greek text were added. An Empirical Alphabet of Dioscorides and Stephanus of Athens, physicians, a Greek manuscript different from the Dioscorides on easy preparations, is in the possession of the physician Gaspar Wolf. Many other works are also attributed to Dioscorides. He flourished about the year of the world 3918.

units.la: CORNELIVS Celsus vir doctus scripsit de Arte Rhetorica, de re rustica & de medicina. Verum ad nos tantum eius medicina pervenit oratorio modo conscripta. Volaterran. lib. 14. Sub primis Cæsaribus vixit, quo tempore Latini sermonis puritas & elegantia effloruit. Ius ciuile & Philosophiam monumentis illustrauit: rei militaris, & rei rusticæ libros edidit: qui & dignus (ut ait Fabius) vel ipso proposito, ut eum illa omnia tenuisse credamus. Columella scribit eum fuisse non solùm agricolationis, sed etiam universæ naturæ prudentem. Fabius Quintilianus in Rhetoricis quamuis artis æmulus Celsum perstringat, tamen ipsa veritate coactus, eruditum virum appellat libro nono, & sequenti sic tradit, Scripsit non parum multa Cornelius Scepticos secutus, non sine cultu ac nitore. Plinius vero sæpè Celsum inter authores retulit, in indice librorum qui primus inscribitur. Apud Marcellum Empiricum autem, quædam Epistolæ Celso falsò tribuuntur.
units.tr: CORNELIUS Celsus, a learned man, wrote on the art of rhetoric, on agriculture, and on medicine. However, only his medical work has come down to us, written in an oratorical style. Volaterranus, book 14. He lived under the first Caesars, at a time when the purity and elegance of the Latin language flourished. He illustrated civil law and philosophy in his writings; he published books on military affairs and on agriculture, and he was worthy (as Fabius says) of that very undertaking, so that we may believe he had mastered all those things. Columella writes that he was skilled not only in farming but in the whole of nature. Fabius Quintilian in his Rhetoric, although as a rival of the art he disparages Celsus, is nevertheless compelled by the truth itself to call him a learned man, in book 9, and in the following passage he says: "Cornelius wrote not a little, following the Sceptics, and not without polish and elegance." Pliny, however, often counts Celsus among his authorities, in the index of books which comes first. In the work of Marcellus the Empiric, however, certain letters are falsely attributed to Celsus.

units.la: STRABO Amaseus Philosophus, insignis Geographus extitit, qui temporibus Augusti & Tiberij claruit. Scripsit commentarios Geographicos, qui etiam hodie omnium manibus teruntur. Huius Geographicorum libri septemdecim, olim ut putatur, à Guarino Veronensi, ac Gregorio Tifernate Latinitate donati fuere, ac denuò à Conrado Heresbachio recogniti, ac plerisque locis, de integro versi fuere. Epitome etiam eorundem librorum, incerto authore, in Latinum sermone è Græco conversa, Hieronymo Gemusæo interprete. Opus excusum est Basileæ, in officina Curionis 1539. idem Græcè excusum Venetiis apud Aldum 1516. & Latinè ibidem 1511. Basileæ, Græcè & Latinè è regione duabus columnis. Idem rerum Geographicarum libri 17. à Gulielmo Xylandro recogniti & emendati & ab eodem in sermonem Latinum transcripti, adiectis annotatiunculis ibidem editi fuère anno 1571. PHIL. NAT. ALEX. PHILO IUDÆUS L. SENECA.
units.tr: STRABO of Amaseia, a philosopher, was an outstanding geographer, who flourished in the times of Augustus and Tiberius. He wrote geographical commentaries, which even today are handled by everyone. His seventeen books of Geography were, as is thought, once given a Latin form by Guarino of Verona and Gregorio of Tifernum, and again revised by Conrad Heresbach, and in many places translated afresh from the beginning. An epitome of the same books, by an unknown author, was also turned from Greek into Latin, with Jerome Gemusaeus as translator. The work was printed at Basel, in the workshop of Curio, in 1539; the same work was printed in Greek at Venice by Aldus in 1516, and in Latin there in 1511; at Basel, in Greek and Latin on facing columns. The same seventeen books of Geographical matters, revised and corrected by Wilhelm Xylander, and translated by him into Latin, with small added annotations, were published there in 1571. PHIL. NAT. ALEX. PHILO THE JEW, L. SENECA.

units.la: PHILO Iudæus Philosophus fuit clarus, Alexãdriæ natus, disciplinisque omnibus eruditus, & in nostra & Græcorũ philosophia bene versatus: eloquentiæ autem Platonicæ tam diligens æmulator, ut illud vulgò de eo iactaretur, ὁ πλάτων φιλωνίζει ἢ φίλων πλατωνίζει [?], id est, aut Plato Philonissat, aut Philo Platonissat. In diuinis autem legibus, & patriis institutis quantus fuerit, ex his quæ nobis librorum suorum tradidit monumẽtis, indicatur. Temporibus Caij, quanta acciderint Iudæis mala, voluminibus absoluit, quibus & suam legationem, pro Iudæis, apud Imperatorem retulit, quam obiit, sub Pontio Pilato Iudææ præfecto, anno mundi 3993. Christi, 31. triennio ante quàm pro peccatis nostris pateretur. Iosephus huius legationis meminit libro 18. Hunc Porphyrius quoque libro quarto, magnis laudibus est prosecutus.
units.tr: Philo the Jew was a famous philosopher, born at Alexandria, learned in every branch of learning, and well versed in both our philosophy and that of the Greeks. He was so diligent an imitator of Plato's eloquence that the common saying about him went: "Either Plato Philonizes or Philo Platonizes" [ὁ Πλάτων φιλωνίζει ἢ φίλων πλατωνίζει], that is, either Plato plays the Philonist or Philo plays the Platonist. How great he was in the divine laws and the ancestral institutions is shown by the records he left us in his books. In the time of Caius he composed volumes on the many evils that befell the Jews, and in them he also gave an account of his embassy on behalf of the Jews to the Emperor, which he undertook under Pontius Pilate, governor of Judea, in the year of the world 3993, of Christ 31, three years before he suffered for our sins. Josephus mentions this embassy in book 18. Porphyry too praised him highly in book 4.

units.la: SENECA natione Hispanus fuit, patria Cordubẽsis, Academicus Philosophus & Neronis præceptor: à quo diuitiis ingentibus auctus, quum in Pisonianæ cõiurationis suspicionem venisset, eiusdem iussu incisis venis, mortem obiit, anno ab urbe condita 818. Christi 68. mundi 4030. Fuit & alter Seneca tragicus Poëta, cuius fabulæ decem ad nos peruenerunt. Utriusque meminit Sidonius Apollinaris ad felicem,
units.tr: Seneca was a Spaniard by birth, from Corduba, an Academic philosopher and the tutor of Nero. Enriched by immense wealth, he came under suspicion of the conspiracy of Piso, and by Nero's order he died after his veins were opened, in the year from the founding of the city 818, of Christ 68, of the world 4030. There was also another Seneca, the tragic poet, of whose plays ten have come down to us. Sidonius Apollinaris mentions both in his letter to Felix:

units.la: Non quod Corduba præpotens alumnis / Facundum ciet, hic putes legendum, / Quorum unus colit hispidum Platona, / Incassúmque suum mouet Neronem: / Orchetram canit alter Euripidis, / Pictum facibus Aeschylum sequutus, / Aut plaustris solitum sonare Thespim, / Qui post pulpita trita sub cothurno / Ducebant olidæ patrem capella.
units.tr: "It is not that powerful Corduba stirs up an eloquent pupil, you might think this one should be read, / Of whom one cultivated the rough Plato and vainly stirred up his own Nero; / The other sings the orchestra of Euripides, / Following Aeschylus painted with torches, / Or Thespis, used to resound from wagons, / Who after the worn stage under the buskin / Led the father of the foul goats."
PLINY OF JERUSALEM. JOSEPHUS THE JEW.

units.la: PLINIVS secundus Veronensis, temporibus Vespasiani undecimi Romanorū Imperatoris vixit, cuius negotia administrabat, anno mundi 4032. Christi 70. Noctibus vero & succisiuis(ut ipse inquit)temporibus opus de rerum natura conscripsit, unus omnium parcissimus temporis.Periit in motis Vesuvij incendio, dum eius causam indagare & curiosius inuestigare cupit,circiter annum ab Urbe condita 832. Eius vitam diligentius narrat sororis filius Caecilius Plinius, cuius extat liber Epistolarūm,& Panægyricus, Traiano Cæsari dicatus, quo illi gratias agit Cōsul ab eo factus.Quintiliani filiam dote iuvit, & Martialem Poëtam secedentem viatico prosecutus est, ut ipse testatur in epistolis. Volater. lib. 18.
units.tr: Pliny the Younger, a native of Verona, lived in the time of Vespasian, the eleventh Roman emperor, whose affairs he managed, in the year of the world 4032, of Christ 70. But he composed his work on the nature of things by night and in stolen moments of time (as he himself says), being the most sparing of all men with time. He perished in the fire of the eruption of Vesuvius, while he wished to investigate its cause more closely, about the year 832 from the founding of the city. His life is told more fully by his sister's son Caecilius Pliny, whose book of Letters survives, and the Panegyric dedicated to the Emperor Trajan, in which he thanks him as consul, having been made consul by him. He aided Quintilian's daughter with a dowry, and he supplied the poet Martial, when he was retiring, with provisions for the journey, as he himself testifies in his letters. Volaterranus, book 18.

units.la: IOSEPHVS Judæus conscripsit Græcè antiquitatis Judæorum historiā libris viginti, ab exordio mundi usque ad decimum tertium annum Domitiani: bellū verò Judaicum cum Romanis gestum scripsit libris septem: anno ab urbe condita, 845. ut ipse docet in peroratione antiquitatum: Nonio Aspreana & Flavio Clemente consulibus, anno mundi 4057. Christi, 95. quo tempore agmina Hæreseon exorta, Menandro Simonis Magi discipulo, & Cerintho quodam, autoribus. Quin & Ebionei eo ipso tempore exorti sunt: de quibus Irenæus scribit lib. 1. cap. 21. & sequentibus. IVVENALIS SATIR. C. GALENVS.
units.tr: Josephus the Jew wrote the Antiquities of the Jews in Greek in twenty books, from the beginning of the world down to the thirteenth year of Domitian; and he wrote the Jewish War, fought against the Romans, in seven books. This was in the year from the founding of the city 845, as he himself notes in the conclusion of the Antiquities, in the consulship of Nonius Asprenas and Flavius Clemens, in the year of the world 4057, of Christ 95. At that time the hosts of heresies arose, with Menander, a disciple of Simon Magus, and a certain Cerinthus as authors. Indeed the Ebionites too arose at that very time, concerning whom Irenaeus writes in book 1, chapter 21 and following. Juvenal, Satires. Galen.

units.la: IVVENALIS Aquinas, Poëta insignis, discipulus fuit Frontini Grammatici, qui quidem scripsit quinque libros satyrarum, sed non inveniuntur, quod eorum iactura sit facta, exceptis sexdecim satyris, in lucem ubique editis, propter magnam authoris celebritatem, in eo versus genere, in quo, Lucilio caeterisque Poëtis Satyricis, qui ad hoc usque tempus fuerūt, longè acrior fuisse palàm est omnibus. Vixit tempore Martialis, cum quo maxima ei intercessit familiaritas. Obiit in Ægypto 80. annis natus, floruitque circiter annum mundi 4060. & Christi 100. Vide Gesnerum in sua Bibliotheca..
units.tr: Juvenal of Aquinum, an outstanding poet, was a pupil of the grammarian Fronto, who indeed wrote five books of satires, but they are not found, since they have been lost, except for sixteen satires, published everywhere for the great fame of the author, in that kind of verse in which he was plainly far sharper than Lucilius and the other satirical poets who had existed up to this time. He lived in the time of Martial, with whom he had a very close friendship. He died in Egypt at the age of eighty, and flourished about the year of the world 4060, and of Christ 100. See Gesner in his Bibliotheca.

units.la: GALENVS Pergami natus, patre Nicone insigni geometra & architecto divite, cuius praeceptor fuit Pelops, ut ipse testatur libro quarto de Locis affectis capite 7. & in libr. de Atra bile. Vixit Romae temporibus Traiani, Cōmodi & Antonini Pij Imperatorum anno mundi 4100. salutis vero humanae 140. Plurima scripsit in Geometria, Dialectica, Rhetorica, Philosophia, maximè vero in Medicina. Itaque Averroes in S. Collect. illum omnibus medicis anteferre non dubitavit. Vixit annos 70. secundum Suidam: alij 140. annos asserunt, ut testatur Coelius lib. 16. Antiq. lect. cap. 40. In patria tandem fatis cessit.
units.tr: Galen was born at Pergamum, the son of Nico, a distinguished geometer and architect of wealth, whose teacher was Pelops, as he himself testifies in book 4 of On Affected Places, chapter 7, and in the book On Black Bile. He lived at Rome in the times of the emperors Trajan, Commodus and Antoninus Pius, in the year of the world 4100, but of human salvation 140. He wrote a great deal on geometry, dialectic, rhetoric, philosophy, and above all on medicine. So Averroes in his Colliget did not hesitate to prefer him to all physicians. He lived seventy years according to Suidas; others assert one hundred and forty years, as Coelius testifies in book 16 of Antiquae Lectiones, chapter 40. At last he met his fate in his homeland.

units.la: ORIGENES Damascenus vixit tempore Seueri Imperatoris circiter annum mundi 4160. & Christi 210. Erat tanta doctrina cumulatus, vt omnes eum admirarentur tanquā in omni literarum genere consummatissimū, Quod ad Theologiam attinet, quantum in ea valuerit testātur eius scripta, & Commentarij in magnā partem veteris & noui Testameti. Si plura de eo, Lector videre voluerit, consulat Tritemij librū de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, legatque vitā eius quae est in principio eius operum quae Lutetiae edita fuere, anno 1574. Poterit etiam videre Bibliothecam Gesneri.
units.tr: Origen of Damascus lived in the time of the Emperor Severus, about the year of the world 4160, and of Christ 210. He was so filled with learning that all admired him as most accomplished in every kind of literature. As regards theology, how much he achieved in it is attested by his writings and his Commentaries, which cover for the most part the Old and New Testaments. If the reader wishes to see more about him, let him consult Trithemius' book on Ecclesiastical Writers, and read the life of him which is at the beginning of his works, published at Paris in 1574. He may also see Gesner's Bibliotheca.

units.la: TERTVLLIANVS, Afer, Centurionis proconsularis filius Theologus primus Christianorū, qui Latinè scripserunt, multa opuscula conscripsit, maximo eloquentiae splendore, in quibus indicat, animā immortalem quidē esse, sed eam effigiatū corpus esse contendit, neque hanc tantū, sed ipsum etiā Deū corporeū esse dicit, licet non effigiatum, neque tamen hinc hereticus creditur esse factus. Fuit acris & magni ingenij, vt pote qui res diuinas & humanas probè calluerit. Docuit enim, in maxima celebritate Rhetoricam apud Carthaginenses. Huius scripta beatissimus martyr Cyprianus in tanta veneratione habuit, vt nullū, sine eorū lectione diem preteriret. Scripsit de Patientia Dei lib. vnū. Aduersus Praxeā lib. 1. contra Marcionem libros. 5. contra Iudaeos lib. 1. Contra omnes haereses libr. 1. De proscriptionibus haereticorū lib. 1. Aduersus Hermogenē. Cotra Valentinianos. De carne Christi. De resurrectione carnis. De corona militis. Ad martyres. De poenitentia. De velandis virginibus, De habitu muliebri, & alia plurima. Floruit anno mundi 4171. Christi vero 209. sub Seuero Imperatore.
units.tr: Tertullian, an African, son of a proconsular centurion, was the first theologian of the Christians who wrote in Latin. He composed many small works with the greatest brilliance of eloquence. In them he holds that the soul is indeed immortal, but that it is a bodily form, and he contends that not only the soul but God himself is corporeal, though not shaped; yet he is not believed on this account to have become a heretic. He was keen and of great talent, as one who was thoroughly skilled in divine and human things. He taught rhetoric at Carthage with the greatest renown. The blessed martyr Cyprian held his writings in such high regard that he let no day pass without reading them. He wrote one book On the Patience of God; book 1 Against Praxeas; books 5 Against Marcion; book 1 Against the Jews; book 1 Against All Heresies; book 1 On the Prescription of Heretics; Against Hermogenes; Against the Valentinians; On the Flesh of Christ; On the Resurrection of the Flesh; On the Soldier's Crown; To the Martyrs; On Repentance; On the Veiling of Virgins; On Women's Dress, and very many others. He flourished in the year of the world 4171, but of Christ 209, under the Emperor Severus.

units.la: D. AMBROSIVS in Gallia sub Côstantij imperio natus fuit, patre Symmacho, præfecto Galliæ. Infanti in prætoria domo dormienti, apes circaos visæ sunt oberrare: patre, impubes amisit, inde cum matre & sorore Marcellina Romam profectus ibi studiis sese addixit: & tandē causas agere cœpit. Mox à Probo prætorij præfecto, consiliorū & gubernationis socius fuit adscitus. Consulari posteā dignitate insignitus, ad regendā Liguriā missus est à Probo. Mortuo Auxentio Mediolanensi Episcopo, fuit is à populo, Episcopus electus: renuit illud munus: sed Imperator populi electione delectatus, eā confirmat. Elegitur in Episcopū, anno Christi 378. sub Damaso Papa. Plurima scripsit: contra omnes fere hæreses acriter pugnauit. Præfuit Episcopatui, annis 22. obiit anno Christi 400. Arcadij & Honorij tertio, senex admodū. Claruit sub Theodosio Imper. [|] domini 380.
units.tr: Saint Ambrose was born in Gaul under the rule of Constantius, his father Symmachus being prefect of Gaul. While the infant was sleeping in the praetorian house, bees were seen to hover around him. He lost his father while still a boy, and then went with his mother and sister Marcellina to Rome, where he devoted himself to study, and finally began to plead cases. Soon he was taken up by Probus, prefect of the praetorium, as a companion in counsel and governance. Afterwards, honoured with consular rank, he was sent by Probus to govern Liguria. When Auxentius, bishop of Milan, died, he was chosen bishop by the people; he refused that office, but the Emperor, delighted by the choice of the people, confirmed it. He was elected bishop in the year of Christ 378, under Pope Damasus. He wrote a great deal and fought vigorously against almost all heresies. He presided over the bishopric for twenty-two years, and died in the year of Christ 400, in the third year of Arcadius and Honorius, a very old man. He flourished under the Emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

units.la: D. AVGVSTINVS, matre Monica, patre Patricio in citate Thaguftensi natus, Christianus quidē, sed mediocri fortuna. In pueritia à matre de Christo institutus est, sed baptismus dilatus. Apueris ludū frequentauit, præceptore Manlio Theodoro. Manichæorū opinionem diu sectatus est. Romæ docuit Rhetoricā: inde Mediolanū accersitus, sensimà Manichæis defecit, cū Ambrosij cōciones diligēter audiret, & ad religionem Christianā transiit, & suscepit baptismū cum Alipio, & naturali filio Adeodato, natus annos 33. post Maximi tyranni mortem. Domū inde in Africā rediit, & in agris suis vixit. Mox Hipponensis ecclesiæ presbyter à Valerio ordinatus, & tandē etiā eius coëpiscopus. Eo mortuo ad Episcopatū euectus est, quē sanctissimē & factis & cōcionibus & scriptis administrauit. Cōtra hæreticos accerrimē disputauit. Donatistarū secta multū ei negotij exhibuit: cū mulieribus, necognatis quidē, ppter suspicionē, nō habitauit. Vestitu mūdo, mēsa frugali vtebatur, & vino. Tandē præsente Possidonio & aliis piè in Domino obdormiuit, cū vixisset annos 76. anno mūdi 4395. Christ. 434. in ecclesiastica fūctione 40. Huius vitā Possidonius Calamēsis episcopus descripsit.
units.tr: Saint Augustine was born at Thagaste in Africa, of the mother Monica and the father Patricius, a Christian indeed, but of modest means. In boyhood he was instructed about Christ by his mother, but his baptism was postponed. As a boy he attended school under the teacher Manlius Theodorus. For a long time he followed the opinion of the Manichaeans. He taught rhetoric at Rome; then, summoned to Milan, he gradually fell away from the Manichaeans, while he listened diligently to the sermons of Ambrose, and passed over to the Christian religion, and received baptism along with Alypius and his natural son Adeodatus. He was thirty-three years old, after the death of the tyrant Maximus. He then returned home to Africa and lived on his estates. Soon he was ordained presbyter of the church of Hippo by Valerius, and finally became its co-bishop. When he died, he was raised to the episcopate, which he administered most holily, both in deeds, sermons and writings. He disputed most keenly against heretics. The sect of the Donatists gave him much trouble. He did not live with women, not even relatives, because of suspicion. He used clean clothing, a frugal table, and wine. At last, with Possidius and others present, he fell asleep piously in the Lord, having lived seventy-six years, in the year of the world 4395, of Christ 434, and in ecclesiastical office forty years. His life was written by Possidius, bishop of Calama.

units.la: PAULUS Ægineta, mirabili ardore discendi percitus, difficillimas peregrinationes sustinuit, ut medicam artem cognoscere. Libros reliquit in medicina, non sua inventione, sed Galeni imitatione, cuius veluti simia dici potest. A Ioanne filio Serapionis allegatur simpliciter Pauli nomine, & similiter ab aliis Medicis. Scripsit lib. 7. Græcos, collatione vetustorum exemplariū restitutos, & quibusdam in locis auctos, per Hieronymū Gemusceum impressos Basileæ, qui fuerunt versi à Ioane Guinterio Andernaco, & ab Albano Tornio, quos prior commentariis illustravit. Aeginetæ libros Henricus Stephanus, cum aliis præcipuorum medicorum libris excudit. Floruit anno mundi 4398. salutis 439. MAGN. ACCURSIUS DINUS MAGELL.
units.tr: Paulus Aegineta, driven by an amazing zeal for learning, undertook very difficult journeys in order to learn the medical art. He left books on medicine, not of his own invention but in imitation of Galen, of whom he may be called a kind of ape. John son of Serapion cites him simply under the name of Paulus, and other physicians do the same. He wrote seven books in Greek, restored by collating old copies and in some places enlarged; they were printed at Basel by Hieronymus Gemusceus, and were translated by Johannes Guinterius of Andernach and by Albanus Torinus, the former of whom illustrated them with commentaries. Henricus Stephanus printed the books of Aegineta together with other books of the chief physicians. He flourished in the year of the world 4398, of salvation 439.

units.la: ACURSIUS natione Florentinus, juris consultissimus, fuit. Azonis Doctoris discipulum fuisse eü perhibetur, qui cum admirabili ingenio, & multarū rerum cognitione, valeret, Reipublicae moderandae maximè idoneus, universum juris Civilis corpus, primus glosis ornauit & explanauit. Huius autem libros semper imprimendos curauere docti, ubicunque fuit excusum corpus Juris, cum glosis & commentariis: eáque de causa omnium Jurisconsultorum celeberrimus existimatur, utpote qui primus Jus Civile interpretatus fuerit. Floruit is anno salutis 1236. ut ipse in Autetica testatur. Scripsit etiam super instituta.
units.tr: Accursius, a Florentine by birth, was a most learned jurist. He is said to have been a pupil of the teacher Azo, and since he had a remarkable intellect and wide knowledge of many things, he was especially fitted to govern the commonwealth. He was the first to adorn and explain the whole body of the civil law with glosses. The learned have always ensured that his books are printed wherever the body of the law is printed, with the glosses and commentaries. For this reason he is considered the most celebrated of all jurists, inasmuch as he was the first to interpret the civil law. He flourished in the year of salvation 1236, as he himself testifies in the Authentica. He also wrote on the Institutes.

units.la: DINUS Mugelanus Juris utriusque peritissimus, tāta fuit animi solertia, ut omnes suę ætatis Jurisconsultos superasse creditus sit. Fuit acutus & eloquens in dicendo, disputando & decidendo: & idcirco eleganter & copiosè totum jus Civile, multis scriptis, exposuit & clarius legum studiosis reddidit. De mādato Bonifacij Papę viii. primus eleganter, post Archidiaconū, scripsit super 6. Decretalium lib. 1. super Codice lib. 10. super ff. veteri libr. 24. super ff. nouo. libros 12. super ff. Infortiato lib. 14. Consilia multa lib.1. super Titulū de actionibus in Institutis. Super titulū, De regulis Juris, & infinita alia quę nō reperiuntur. Floruit anno salutis 1300. ALBERTUS MAGN. NICOLAUS DE LYRA ANGL.
units.tr: Dinus of Mugello, most skilled in both laws, had such keenness of mind that he is believed to have surpassed all the jurists of his age. He was sharp and eloquent in speaking, disputing and deciding, and therefore he set out the whole civil law elegantly and fully in many writings, and made it clearer to students of the laws. At the command of Pope Boniface VIII, he was the first, after the Archdeacon, to write elegantly on the sixth book of the Decretals; on the Code, book 10; on the Digest, the Old, book 24; on the Digest, the New, books 12; on the Digestum Infortiatum, book 14; many Consilia, book 1; on the title "On actions" in the Institutes; on the title "On the rules of law"; and countless other things which are not found. He flourished in the year of salvation 1300.

units.la: ALBERTUS Magnus, natione Teutonicus, patria Suevus, ex Laugingē oriundus in Academia Parisiensi encyclopediam ac praesertim Theologiae scientiam hausit, quam disseminavit postea in Germania. Fuit & alius eiusdem nominis, propter eruditionem, natione Patauinus. Prior fuit Episcopus Ratisponēsis, qui Episcopi officio, integerrimè aliquot annos functus, tanta dignitate sese tandem spōte exuit, ut animae saluti magi[?] vacarer. Itaque Coloniam reversus ad suos, cucullā induit, & ibi usque ad finem vitae, docendo & scribendo perseveravit. Scripsit multa & penè infinita opuscula, Summam Theologiae lib. 4. super sententias lib. 4. De quatuor coaevis lib.1. De homine:de bono:de vita spirituali:in officiū Missae:de corpore Christi:de muliere forti:de multiplici timore:de laudibus sanctę Mariae:defensorium mendicantium, & multa alia. Obiit sub Rodulpho Imperatore, anno domini 1280. Coloniae sepultus.
units.tr: Albertus Magnus, a German by nation, a Swabian by homeland, born at Lauingen, drew in the Parisian Academy the whole encyclopedia of learning, and especially the science of theology, which he afterwards spread abroad in Germany. There was also another of the same name, on account of his learning, a Paduan by nation. The former was bishop of Regensburg, and having discharged the office of bishop with the utmost integrity for some years, he at last laid down such a dignity of his own accord, so that he might devote himself more freely to the salvation of his soul. So, returning to his own people at Cologne, he put on the cowl, and there he persevered in teaching and writing until the end of his life. He wrote many and almost countless little works: the Summa of Theology, 4 books; on the Sentences, 4 books; On the Four Co-eternals, 1 book; On Man; On the Good; On the Spiritual Life; On the Office of the Mass; On the Body of Christ; On the Strong Woman; On Manifold Fear; On the Praises of Holy Mary; A Defence of the Mendicant Orders; and many others. He died under the Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280, and was buried at Cologne.

units.la: NICOLAUS de Lyra natione Anglus, monachus Franciscanus, in Theologia valde eruditus fuit, multaque scripsit ad Christianam pietatem promovendam, ut ex eius scriptis facile cuiuis Theologiae studioso constare poterit. Hebraicā linguam is perfectè calluit: fuit ingenio prompto, nec minus conversatione, quā scientia venerandus. Eius opera omnibus sacrā scripturā discere cupientibus, necessaria esse, nemo melius novit, quàm qui se in eorū lectione exercitauit. Sūt qui eū ob verborū simplicitatem contemnēdum existimant, sed si res ipsas, non verba isti detractatores spectarint, non dubium est quin ab eis maximè laudetur. Scripsit super sententias lib. 4. In Genesim ad literā lib. 1. In exodum:in Leuiticum:in Numeros:in Deuteronomiū:in Iosuë:in Ruth:in Paralipomenon:in Esdram & Neemiam,in Tobiā:in Iudith:in Ester. Claruit tēporibus Ludovici Imperatoris 4. & Ioānis Papę vicesimi secūdi anno domini 1320. BARTOLVS . I.C. BALDVS . UBALDVS
units.tr: Nicolaus de Lyra, an Englishman by nation, a Franciscan monk, was very learned in theology and wrote much to promote Christian piety, as will readily be evident from his writings to any student of theology. He thoroughly mastered the Hebrew language. He had a ready mind, and no less venerable in his conversation than in his learning. No one knows better than those who have exercised themselves in reading his works that they are necessary to all who wish to learn Holy Scripture. There are those who think he should be despised on account of the simplicity of his words, but if these detractors had looked at the things themselves rather than the words, there is no doubt they would praise him most highly. He wrote on the Sentences, 4 books; On Genesis, literally, 1 book; On Exodus; On Leviticus; On Numbers; On Deuteronomy; On Joshua; On Ruth; On Chronicles; On Ezra and Nehemiah; On Tobit; On Judith; On Esther. He flourished in the time of the Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

units.la: BARTOLVS Sentini in Umbria natus, Iurisconsultus fuit perspicacissimus, qui in omnibus Italiae gymnasiis exactae doctrinae documenta reliquit. In studendo erat valde assiduus, laboris patiens, sobrius. Quare voluptates omnes adeo severe reiecerat, ut ne horula quidem extra naturae necessitate studiis subtraheretur. Eam severitatem etiam retinuit in condamnandis sontibus, cum rerum capitalium iudiciis praesset, ut reum furti nec rite confessum & insontem,pręcipiti sententia supplicio affecerit. Ob id invidiae plebis obnoxius, ut hominum consortium fugeret, in quandam villam se recepit, studiorum gratia, è qua demum egressus, aequales suos doctrinae firmitate, & mira iudicij constantia superauit. Obiit Perusiae, quadragesimo sexto aetatis suae anno. Domini 1355.
units.tr: Bartolus of Sassoferrato in Umbria, was a most penetrating jurist, who left proofs of exact learning in all the schools of Italy. He was very assiduous in study, patient of labour, and sober. Therefore he so strictly rejected all pleasures that not even a single hour was withdrawn from his studies beyond the necessities of nature. He kept the same severity in condemning the guilty, when he presided over capital trials, so that he punished with a hasty sentence a man accused of theft who had not properly confessed and was innocent. Because of this he was exposed to the hatred of the common people, so that, to avoid the company of men, he withdrew to a certain villa for the sake of his studies, from which he at last emerged and surpassed his peers by the firmness of his learning and his remarkable steadfastness of judgement. He died at Perugia in the forty-sixth year of his age, in the year of the Lord 1355.

units.la: BALDVS, honesta Ubaldorū gente Perusiae natus, Bartholum praeceptorem habuit,quem ingenij subtilitate & varietate doctrinae superauit. Huic tamen multa conuoluenti,inuertentique stabilis scientiae constantia deerat. Ioannes Galeacius Vicecomes,cum Ticini Gymnasium conderet,magnis praemiis eum euocauit. Peruenit ad longuam senectutem, & annos natus septuaginta sex,fato functus est, paulo antequam ille princeps,moreretur. Scripsit super Codice lib.9. super ff. veteri libros 24. super ff. nouo,lib.12. super ff. (infortiati lib. 14. super Institutis lib.4. De usu feudorum lib.1. Super Autenti. lib.1. super 2. Decretalium lib.1. Additiones speculi,lib.1. consilia multa,lib.1. & alia complura. Scripsit commentarios, super totum corpus iuris ciuilis. Item practicam Lugduni impressam, & Margaritam seu Repertorium. Baldi lectura accuratissimè edita sunt, cum annotationibus,nouis summariis & Indice, Venetiis apud Iuntas 1572. P · CASTRENSIS · P. FRANC · ZABARELLA
units.tr: Baldus, born at Perugia of the honourable family of the Ubaldi, had Bartolus as his teacher, whom he surpassed in subtlety of intellect and variety of learning. Yet he lacked the steady constancy of established knowledge, which Bartolus had, in working through and turning over many things. Giovanni Galeazzo Visconti, when he was founding the university at Pavia, summoned him with great rewards. He reached a long old age, and having lived seventy-six years, he died shortly before that prince himself died. He wrote on the Code, book 9; on the Digest, the Old, books 24; on the Digest, the New, book 12; on the Digestum Infortiatum, book 14; on the Institutes, book 4; On the Use of Fiefs, book 1; on the Authenticum, book 1; on the 2nd book of the Decretals, book 1; Additions to the Speculum, book 1; many Consilia, book 1; and many others. He wrote commentaries on the whole body of civil law. Also the Practica, printed at Lyon, and the Margarita or Repertorium. The lectures of Baldus have been most carefully published, with annotations, new summaries and an index, at Venice, at the Giunta press, 1572.

units.la: PAULUS de Castro, Jureconsultus celeberrimus, multa conscripsit ad leges pertinentia, stylo non minus elegati quàm utili, quibus, vir admirabilis suæ eruditionis & prudentiæ testimonia omnibus clara exhibuit. Jus docuit, in omnibus ferè claris Italiæ Academiis. Scripsit super Codice lib.9.super ff. veteri lib.24. Consilia elegantissima, singularia, & opus Consiliorum in duo volumina partitum, cum pluribus aliis cōmētationibus composuit: ut posteritati, singulari beneficio, & propensa in studiosos omnes, voluntate, sese profuturum aliquando gloriaretur, quemadmodum ipsis profuit qui eodem seculo vixerunt. Scripsit etiam super ff. novo libros duodecim: super ff. inforciati, libros quatuordecim: super Institutis lib.quatuor. Citatur quoque repetitio eius in i.ff.ver. de indiciis, l. si de vi. Consilia eius ab erroribus vindicata & additionibus, novisque rerū notabilium summis, supra priores editiones feliciter aucta, studio & opera Leonardi à lege, Venetiis impressa sunt 1570. in folio, & anno 1571. Claruit anno reparatæ salutis humanæ 1437.
units.tr: Paulus de Castro, a most celebrated jurist, wrote much pertaining to the laws, in a style no less elegant than useful, by which, a man admirable for his learning and prudence, he presented clear evidence of both to all. He taught law in almost all the famous academies of Italy. He wrote on the Code, book 9; on the Digest, the Old, book 24. He composed most elegant and singular Consilia, and a work of Consilia divided into two volumes, together with several other commentaries; so that he was glad to think he would one day benefit posterity by a singular kindness and his favourable disposition towards all students, just as those who lived in the same century benefited from him. He also wrote on the Digest, the New, twelve books; on the Digestum Infortiatum, fourteen books; on the Institutes, four books. His repetition is also cited in the law "De indiciis" and the law "Si de vi". His Consilia, cleared of errors and augmented with additions and new summaries of notable matters, were happily enlarged beyond the earlier editions by the labour and effort of Leonardus à Lege, and printed at Venice in folio in 1570, and in 1571. He flourished in the year of restored human salvation 1437.

units.la: ZABARELLA natione Patauinus, Roma. ecclesiæ Cardinalis presbyter juris pontificij consultissimus, unde amplissimam dignitatem suam exornavit, ut prelatos decet, erat maximo ingenio & doctrina præditus, cuius specimen frugiferum edidisse eum, ipsius scripta satis testantur. Floruit circiter annum Domini 1443.
units.tr: Zabarella, a Paduan by nation, presbyter of the Roman church and cardinal, a most learned jurist of the pontifical law, by which he adorned his very ample dignity, as befits prelates. He was endowed with the greatest intellect and learning; his fruitful work, which he published, sufficiently attests this in his own writings. He flourished about the year of the Lord 1443.
